j-b-m-hertzog: James Barry Munnik Hertzog was born on 3 April 1866. He studied law at Victoria College in Stellenbosch and then at the University of Amsterdam, receiving his doctorate on 12 November 1892. He practised in Pretoria until 1895, when he was appointed to the Orange Free State High Court. In the Boer War of 1899–1902 he rose to general and became assistant chief commandant of the Free State's commandos. He signed the Treaty of Vereeniging in May 1902, convinced that more bloodshed was futile. In 1907 he joined the Orange River Colony cabinet, where his insistence that Dutch be taught as well as English aroused bitter opposition.

Hertzog was Minister of Justice in the new Union of South Africa until 1912, when antagonism to British authorities and Premier Botha led to a ministerial crisis. He founded the National Party in 1914. In the 1924 election it defeated Jan Smuts's South African Party and formed the Pact Government with the Labour Party. Afrikaans replaced Dutch as the second official language in 1925, and the Statute of Westminster was approved in 1931. White women received the vote in 1930, and in 1936 black voters were removed from the common voters' roll and given separately elected Native Representatives.

The government built what one historian calls the foundations of an Afrikaner welfare state. Its Civilised Labour Policy replaced black workers with whites through job reservation and a colour bar, and these laws helped pave the way for apartheid. In 1934 the National Party and South African Party merged into the United Party. In the 1930s Hertzog favoured distance from Britain and saw Nazi Germany as a normal state. On 4 September 1939 his party caucus voted against his neutrality in the Second World War, and he resigned.

Hertzog then lost the support of Daniel Malan's party and left politics. In October 1941 he issued a statement praising Nazism as in keeping with Afrikaner traditions and saying it needed adapting to South African conditions under a dictator. He died on 21 November 1942, aged 76. Supporters of his invented the Hertzoggie, a jam-filled tartlet that is still eaten in South Africa.
j-g-strijdom: Johannes Gerhardus Strijdom was born on 14 July 1893 on the family farm of Klipfontein near Willowmore in the Cape Colony. His father, Petrus Strijdom, was a farmer and businessman in the Baviaanskloof. He trained as a lawyer at Victoria College and the University of Pretoria and served in the German South West Africa campaign in the First World War, reaching the rank of corporal. He settled at Nylstroom in the Transvaal and became a leader of the local Afrikaners. In 1929 he was elected to the House of Assembly for Waterberg, representing the National Party under J. B. M. Hertzog, and led the party in the Transvaal.

When Hertzog's party merged with Jan Smuts's South African Party in 1932 to form the United Party, Strijdom joined the breakaway Purified National Party under D. F. Malan, and he was the only member of parliament from the Transvaal to support Malan. After the National Party's victory in 1948 he became Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation.

Strijdom was elected leader of the National Party, and so prime minister, on 30 November 1954, after Malan resigned and against Malan's wishes, for Malan had preferred the more moderate Nicolaas Havenga. Party members trusted him to move towards a republic. He began to sever ties with the British monarchy, deepened Afrikaner ascendancy and strengthened apartheid, including through the Group Areas Development Act. He was an open proponent of baasskap, white domination, and believed in perpetuating white minority rule by removing Cape Coloured voters from the common roll.

The long Treason Trial of 156 activists, Nelson Mandela among them, took place during his term. His government broke off diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union, and the National Party increased its seats in the general election of 1958. His health was weak in his last year, with long absences.

Strijdom died in Cape Town on 24 August 1958 and was succeeded by Hendrik Verwoerd. He is buried in the Heroes' Acre in Pretoria. The republic he favoured was established in 1961. Monuments to him once stood in several places: a bust in central Pretoria collapsed in 2001, injuring two people, and his house at Modimolle, formerly Nylstroom, is now a museum. The Hillbrow Tower in Johannesburg bore his name until 1995, and a street in Pretoria named after him was renamed in 2012.
j-r-ackerley: Joe Randolph Ackerley was born on 4 November 1896, the son of Roger Ackerley, a successful fruit merchant known as the Banana King of London, and the actress Janetta Aylward; his parents married only in 1919. He was educated at Rossall School in Fleetwood, Lancashire, and his father gave him a generous allowance without insisting that he join the business.

Commissioned as a second lieutenant in the East Surrey Regiment in September 1914, he was wounded at the Battle of the Somme on 1 July 1916. His elder brother Peter, who served under him, was killed on 7 August 1918, a loss that haunted Ackerley all his life. Wounded again near Arras in May 1917, he was taken prisoner and interned in neutral Switzerland, where he began his play The Prisoners of War.

After the war Ackerley studied at Magdalene College, Cambridge, and graduated in English in 1921. E. M. Forster, whom he turned to for guidance, arranged his post with the Maharaja of Chhatarpur. His play was finally produced in 1925, opening at The Three Hundred Club on 5 July before transferring to the Playhouse Theatre.

In 1928 he joined the BBC's Talks Department, which arranged radio lectures by prominent scholars and public figures. As literary editor of The Listener he discovered and promoted younger writers, among them W. H. Auden, Christopher Isherwood, Philip Larkin and Stephen Spender. He was openly homosexual at a time when homosexual activity was forbidden by law, and he explored his sexuality in his writings.

From 1943 Ackerley lived in a small flat at Putney overlooking the Thames, where he produced almost all his significant work. In 1946 he acquired an Alsatian named Queenie, his companion for the next 15 years and the subject of My Dog Tulip and, as Evie, of his only novel, We Think the World of You, which won the W. H. Smith Literary Award in 1962. He called Queenie's death on 30 October 1961 the saddest day of his life.

His father's death in October 1929 revealed a second family of three daughters, whose story Ackerley told with his own in My Father and Myself, published after his death. His sister Nancy found him dead in bed on 4 June 1967; his biographer Peter Parker gives the cause as coronary thrombosis. Nancy later endowed the J. R. Ackerley Prize for Autobiography, first awarded in 1982.
j-r-jayewardene: Junius Richard Jayewardene was born on 17 September 1906 in Colombo, the eldest of twelve children of the lawyer Eugene Wilfred Jayewardene, in a family with a strong association with the legal profession. He was educated at Royal College, Colombo, where he played cricket and captained the rugby team, and at Ceylon Law College, and passed his advocates' examinations in 1931.

He converted from Anglicanism to Buddhism and in 1943 gave up full-time practice to become an activist in the Ceylon National Congress. In 1943 he was elected to the State Council, and in 1944 he moved a motion that Sinhala alone should replace English as the official language. He was a founder member of the United National Party in 1946 and became finance minister in the island's first cabinet in 1947.

After the UNP's defeat in 1956 he lost his seat, and he pushed the party to endorse the Sinhala Only Act, which the island's minorities bitterly opposed. He succeeded Dudley Senanayake as party leader in 1973. The UNP won the election of 21 July 1977 with five-sixths of the seats, and he was sworn in as prime minister on 23 July. A constitutional amendment made the presidency an executive post, and he became the first executive president on 4 February 1978. A new constitution of 31 August 1978 granted the president sweeping powers, almost dictatorial according to some critics. He opened the state-controlled economy to market forces and moved the legislative capital to Sri Jayawardanapura Kotte.

He passed the Prevention of Terrorism Act in 1979 against Tamil militant groups. After the ambush of Four Four Bravo, the Black July riots of 1983 transformed the militancy into a civil war that lasted from 1983 to 2009. In 1987 he and the Indian prime minister Rajiv Gandhi concluded the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord, which provided for devolution to Tamil-dominated regions and an Indian peacekeeping force in the north. The LTTE rejected it, Sinhala nationalists were outraged, and an attempt was made on his life. A revolt by the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna was put down by 1989, when he retired from politics.

Jayewardene died of colon cancer on 1 November 1996, aged 90, in Colombo. His economic policies are often credited with transforming a stagnant economy, while his response to the Black July riots has been heavily criticised and accused of heightening ethnic tensions. He is respected in Japan for his call for peace and reconciliation with Japan at the San Francisco Peace Conference in 1951, and a statue of him stands at the Kamakura Temple in Kanagawa Prefecture. The J. R. Jayewardene Centre, established by an act of Parliament in 1988, holds his library and papers.
ja-vi-elsker-dette-landet: Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson wrote the words between 1859 and 1868, and his cousin Rikard Nordraak wrote the melody during the winter of 1863 to 1864. The song was first performed in public on 17 May 1864, in connection with the 50th anniversary of the constitution. Bjørnson wrote in a modified version of the Danish used in Norway at the time, and the text sung today keeps his words with modernised spelling and punctuation. Usually only the first and the last two verses are sung, the first by far the most often. In each verse the last two lines are sung twice, with one or two words repeated a further time.

Until the mid-1860s the songs Sønner av Norge and Norges Skaal were commonly regarded as national anthems, Sønner av Norge being the better known. Ja, vi elsker dette landet gradually came to be recognised as an anthem from the mid-1860s, and until the early 20th century both were used, with Sønner av Norge preferred in official situations. Norway had no official anthem until 11 December 2019.

The original version contained a verse that hailed the king, who had succeeded his father in July 1859. It described the king as a strong and open border guard whose best weapon was the brethren pact, a military treaty by which Norway, Sweden and Denmark were to help one another if any was attacked. When German troops invaded South Jutland in February 1864, none of the partners came to Denmark's rescue, and the failure shattered hopes of a united Scandinavia. Bjørnson went from monarchist to republican, and the tribute to the sovereign was struck from the song.

In 1905 the Norwegian Storting declared the union with Sweden dissolved on 7 June, which brought the two nations to the brink of war in the autumn. Swedish Social Democrats, whose leaders Hjalmar Branting and Zeth Höglund spoke for a peaceful settlement, sang the song to support the Norwegian right to leave the union. During the Second World War it was used both by the Norwegian resistance and by Nazi collaborators, mainly for propaganda, and the German occupiers eventually forbade any use of it.
Norway also has an unofficial royal anthem, Kongesangen, based on God Save the King, and the psalm Gud signe vårt dyre fedreland, by Elias Blix, which is often called the national psalm.
jaan-anvelt: Jaan Anvelt was born on 18 April 1884 into a peasant family in Oorgu, in Võisiku Parish (now Viljandi Parish), in Kreis Fellin of the Governorate of Livonia. He trained as a schoolteacher, first in Dorpat (now Tartu) and then in St. Petersburg, where he joined the Bolshevik faction of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party. He worked as a schoolteacher from 1905 to 1907 while taking part in revolutionary activity, and from 1907 to 1912 he studied jurisprudence part-time at St. Petersburg University. As a writer he used several pseudonyms, among them Eessaare Aadu, Jaan Holm and Kaarel Maatamees.

On 5 November 1917 by the Gregorian calendar (23 October by the Julian calendar then still used in Russia), Anvelt led his revolutionaries in taking political power in Tallinn. He became one of the leaders of the Communist Party of Estonia and the first premier of the Soviet Executive Committee of Estonia. After the defeat of the revolutionaries in the Baltic he went underground and remained active, emerging as one of the leaders of the attempted coup of 1924 in Estonia.

In the USSR, Anvelt served from 1926 to 1929 as political commissar of the Zhukovsky Air Force Engineering Academy. From 1929 to 1935 he held senior positions in the main administration of the civilian air fleet, and from 1935 to 1937 he was a member and executive secretary of a department of the Comintern.

Anvelt was arrested in 1937, during Joseph Stalin's Great Purge. Under interrogation in the custody of the NKVD he was beaten by the interrogator Aleksandr Langfang, and he died of his injuries on 11 December 1937; afterwards he was denounced as an enemy of the people. He was rehabilitated in 1956, during the thaw under Nikita Khrushchev. Langfang was arrested in 1957 and in 1958 sentenced to 15 years in prison for torture and falsifying evidence; he served the whole sentence and was released in 1973.

Anvelt was married to the Social Democratic politician Alma Ostra from 1909 to 1910, and in 1912 he married a Russian woman, J. Vassiljeva, in St. Petersburg. With his third wife, Alise Stein-Anvelt, he had a daughter, Kima, and a son, Jaan. His grandson Andres Anvelt became Estonian Interior Minister for the Social Democratic Party in 2016.
jaan-poska: Jaan Poska was born on 24 January 1866 at Laiusevälja, near Jõgeva, the fifth of 12 children of an Eastern Orthodox parish schoolmaster. He received his secondary education at the church's school in Riga and entered medical school at the University of Tartu, but soon moved to law and graduated in 1890. He was the first native Estonian speaker admitted to the bar in Tallinn, where he worked as a barrister.

As mayor of Tallinn from 1913 to 1917 Poska supported reforms in healthcare and the founding of two schools. In April 1917 he was put at the head of the Autonomous Governorate of Estonia. On 28 November 1917 the Maapäev refused to recognise the new Bolshevik rule and proclaimed itself the supreme legal authority of Estonia, and the Republic of Estonia declared independence on 24 February 1918, only to be occupied by the German Empire until the end of the First World War in November 1918.

Poska was appointed Minister of Foreign Affairs on 24 February 1918. He worked in Western Europe to win diplomatic recognition for Estonia and took part in the Paris Peace Conference. He then led the peace talks with Soviet Russia that ended the Estonian War of Independence, and the Treaty of Tartu was signed on 2 February 1920. He also helped to write the first Estonian constitution.

Poska died unexpectedly in Tallinn on 7 March 1920, aged 54, only weeks after the treaty was signed. He was the first Estonian ever to be given a state funeral, and over 20,000 people attended it. His daughter Vera Poska-Grünthal became a leading Estonian feminist and lawyer and married the politician and lawyer Timotheus Grünthal.
jabal-al-druze: Jabal al-Druze, Arabic for Mountain of the Druze, is also known as Jabal al-Arab or Jabal Hauran. It is an elevated volcanic region in Hauran, in the Suwayda Governorate of southern Syria. Its volcanic field, the southernmost in Syria, lies on the Haurun-Druze Plateau near the border with Jordan and forms the northern part of the large Harrat al-Sham field, which extends to Saudi Arabia. It consists of 118 basaltic volcanoes active from the lower Pleistocene to the Holocene, and its highest feature rises to 1,800 metres. In Jabal al-Druze the Arabic word tell, mound or hill, refers to a volcanic cone: Tell Qeni, at 1,803 metres, is the highest peak.

Safaitic inscriptions were first found in this area. In the past the name Jabal al-Druze was used for a different area, in Mount Lebanon. From 1921 to 1936 the Jabal Druze State was an autonomous area within the French Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon, and it had 42 of the roughly 180 towns of the Hauran.

Most of the inhabitants of the region are Druze, and there are also significant Christian communities. Suwayda Governorate takes in almost all of Jabal al-Druze and is the only governorate in Syria with a Druze majority. In the 1980s Druze made up 87.6 per cent of its population, Christians, mostly Greek Orthodox, 11 per cent and Sunni Muslims 2 per cent. In 2010 the governorate had about 375,000 inhabitants, 90 per cent of them Druze, 7 per cent Christians and 3 per cent Sunni Muslims. The proportion of Christians has declined because of low birth rates and high emigration.
jabal-amil: Jabal Amil, historically known as Jabal Amila, takes its name from the Amila, an Arab tribe once affiliated with the Ghassanid client kings of the Byzantine Empire, which moved into the region and neighbouring Galilee after the Muslim conquests of the 7th century. Its boundaries were never fixed: the region was not generally recognised as a distinct political entity, and its identity came from its largely Twelver Shia inhabitants, who called themselves Amilis.

In the definition generally accepted by its Shia community it covers roughly 3,000 square kilometres, from the Awali River north of Sidon to the Wadi al-Qarn in Upper Galilee, and from the Mediterranean to the valleys of Wadi al-Taym, the Beqaa and the Hula. The Litani River cuts it into northern and southern parts, the southern also being known as Bilad Bishara. Other scholars draw its limits more narrowly or more widely.

The 10th-century geographer al-Muqaddasi described Jabal Amila as a mountainous district with many fine villages and springs, rain-fed fields of grapes, olives and other fruit, and some of the best honey in Syria; with Jabal Jarash it was the largest source of revenue for Tiberias, capital of Jund al-Urdunn. In 1300 al-Dimashqi placed it in the Safad Province and described its Twelver Shia population.

Local tradition credits Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, a companion of Muhammad, with bringing Shi'ism to the area, but scholars largely dismiss the account, and Shia Islam seems to have developed there between the mid-8th and the 10th centuries. Early Amili scholars studied at Hillah in Iraq; only in the 14th century did the region gain scholarly institutions of its own, and in the 15th and 16th centuries it became the leading centre of Shia learning before many scholars migrated, chiefly to Safavid Iran.

Five fortified sites of the region, the castles of Beaufort, Toron, Dubieh, Maron and Chamaa, were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in July 2026 as the Mount Amel Castles and then classified as endangered. The traditional definition of Jabal Amil also takes in villages now in Israel whose Twelver Shia inhabitants were displaced in the 1948 Palestine war.
jabala-ibn-al-ayham: In the Islamic literature Jabala appears as the last Ghassanid king, or phylarch, and the commander of the Christian Arab contingent of the Byzantine Empire during the Muslim conquest of Syria in the 630s. He is named at the siege of Dumat al-Jandal in northern Arabia around 630, leading the Ghassanid and Tanukhid tribes against the Muslims, and at the Battle of the Yarmuk in southern Syria in 636. The Abbasid-era authors Ibn Ishaq, al-Waqidi and al-Baladhuri say that at Yarmuk he led 12,000 men of the Ghassanids, Lakhm, Judham and groups of the Quda'a such as the Balqayn and Bali.

The stories of his conversion exist in several versions. Generally he comes to Medina with his followers, sets out on the Hajj with Caliph Umar, quarrels with a lowly pilgrim whose nose he breaks, and, refusing the equal treatment Islam demanded, threatens to leave the faith and escapes by night to the territory of Emperor Heraclius.

His flight is placed around 639, through Raqqa with 30,000 Christian Arab tribesmen, including Tanukhids and Iyad, and their families. Near the Baghras crossing into Cilicia they were attacked by Maysara ibn Masruq, sent by Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah. Some sources speak of a massacre, but the attacking force was much smaller and several of the refugees later served Byzantium. The survivors settled in the Charsianon region, where the geographer al-Istakhri knew their descendants in the 10th century. The historian Walter Kaegi sees such flights as a reason the Muslims went on to conquer Raqqa and Upper Mesopotamia. Emperor Nikephoros I is said to have descended from Jabala.

Historians are divided on whether Jabala was a historical figure, since no contemporary sources survive. The historian Shahid sees him as possible evidence that the Byzantines revived the Ghassanid phylarchate after the Sasanian invasion of 614. Julia Bray reads him as an archetype of the passing of the age of jahiliyya, Christianity and kingship, and Greg Fisher calls him a semi-mythical figure used to test the purity of the new faith.
jabalpur: Jabalpur lies on the banks of the Narmada River and is the administrative headquarters of the Jabalpur district and division. Its name is traditionally derived from a sage named Jabali who meditated on the river's banks, though another theory takes it from the Arabic jabal, meaning boulders. The city is known for the Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat, a gorge of marble cut by the Narmada below the Dhuandhar Falls. In 1828 the British officer William Henry Sleeman found a dinosaur fossil near Bara Simla Hill, the first such find in Asia.

Ashokan relics from about 300 BCE at Rupnath, north of the city, indicate Mauryan presence. Later the region came under the Satavahana dynasty and then became a vassal state of the Gupta Empire. The Kalachuri dynasty conquered it in 875. Under the Gond kings of Garha-Mandla the city was an important centre of power: Madan Shah built a watchtower and small fort at Madan Mahal, and Rani Durgavati built more than 85 ponds. A Maratha invasion in 1742 made the kingdom a tributary, and the Maratha rulers of Sagar annexed it in 1781. The Bhonsle kings of Nagpur held the Narmada valley until 1818, when the East India Company seized it after the Battle of Sitabuldi.

The British made Jabalpur the headquarters of the Narmada territories, set up a cantonment and made it the capital of the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories, which joined the Central Provinces in 1861. The Congress session at nearby Tripuri in 1939 re-elected Subhas Chandra Bose as president against Mahatma Gandhi's candidate, and he resigned in April of that year. After independence in 1947 the Central Provinces and Berar became Madhya Pradesh.

Jabalpur is the seat of the Madhya Pradesh High Court and the zonal headquarters of the West Central Railway. Its municipal population was 1,081,677 at the 2011 census, and Hindi is the predominant language. Its cantonment is one of the largest in India, and ordnance factories, including the Gun Carriage Factory begun in 1904, make it a centre of defence industry. It is generally accepted that snooker originated here, devised in 1875 by Colonel Neville Chamberlain. The Hanumantal Bada Jain Mandir, a seventeenth-century temple with 22 shrines, is the largest independent Jain temple in India. The name Jubbulpore was replaced by Jabalpur in 2006.
jabesh-gilead: Jabesh-Gilead, sometimes shortened to Jabesh, means Jabesh of Gilead, the town of that name in the region of Gilead as distinct from other places called Jabesh. In Hebrew Jabesh means dry, a name perhaps given for the well-draining soil of the site, while Gilead is read as heap of stones of testimony or, in another theory, rocky region. The town appears in the Book of Judges, the books of Samuel and the Book of Chronicles.

In the episode of the Levite's concubine, after eleven tribes of Israel had nearly destroyed the Tribe of Benjamin, they sought wives for the 600 surviving Benjaminite men, having sworn not to give their own daughters. Jabesh, the one city that had not joined the fight, was put under the herem: its people were killed except for 400 virgins, who were given to the men at the Rock of Rimmon (Judges 21:8–15).

In 1 Samuel 11 Nahash of Ammon offered the besieged townspeople death by the sword or the loss of their right eyes. Granted seven days, they sent messengers through Israel, and Saul raised an army and defeated Nahash at Bezek; the Israelites then gathered at Gilgal to renew his kingship. When the Philistines displayed the bodies of Saul and his three sons on the wall of Beit She'an, the men of Jabesh took them down by night, burned them and buried the bones under the tamarisk tree at Jabesh. David sent messengers to bless them, and later moved the bones of Saul and Jonathan to the tomb of Saul's father at Zela.

In 2 Kings the father of Shallum of Israel is named Jabesh, which may instead mean that Shallum came from the town. Josephus, writing around 93–94 CE, called Jabesh Gilead a metropolis of the Transjordan, and in the early 4th century Eusebius placed Iabeis Galaad on the mountains six miles from Pella on the road to Gerasa.

The town lay in what is now northwest Jordan, but its exact site is debated. Most scholars identify it with Tell el-Maqlub, though Tell Abu al-Kharaz is often suggested. Both sites were inhabited in the Iron Age and lie along Wadi al-Yabis, a stream thought to keep the ancient name.
jabiyah: Jabiyah lay between the Hawran plain and the Golan Heights, west of the town of Nawa. Its name may be related to the Arabic word for a reservoir or to a Syriac word meaning the Chosen. It is first mentioned around 520, in a Syriac letter that Bishop Simeon of Beth Arsham wrote from the camp of the Ghassanid king Jabalah IV ibn al-Harith; foreign envoys and other dignitaries met the Ghassanid kings there.

A Syriac letter of 569 mentions a monastery of St. Sergius at Jabiyah, and in 587 two rival Monophysite groups, led by the Syriac Patriarch Peter and the Coptic Pope Damian of Alexandria, met there in a vain attempt to settle their disputes. The town apparently escaped harm in the Lakhmid-led raids and the Persian invasion of Syria.

After the nearby Battle of Yarmouk, Jabiyah became the main Muslim military camp in Syria. At Umar's meeting of 638 the companions of Muhammad settled the distribution of spoils, the military administration of Syria and soldiers' wages, and in his speech known as khuṭbat al-Jābiya the caliph decreed the dīwān. During the plague of Imwas sick soldiers recuperated there, and a large mosque with a minbar put the town on a par with provincial capitals. From 639/40 to 660 it was the capital of all Islamic Syria under Mu'awiya I.

The summit of 684 was presided over by Ibn Bahdal of the Banu Kalb and agreed that Marwan I would be followed by Khalid ibn Yazid and then Amr ibn Sa'id al-Ashdaq; the Qaysi tribes stayed away. Abd al-Malik spent spring months at Jabiyah and there named al-Walid I and Sulayman as his successors. Its role declined when Sulayman moved the main camp to Dabiq, and further after the rise of the Abbasid Caliphate in 750.

In the words of the historian Irfan Shahid, Jabiyah has entirely vanished. Its name survives in Tell al-Jabiyah, a nearby hill with two peaks, the higher reaching 2,322 feet above sea level, which a 19th-century Western archaeologist called the most conspicuous point of the surrounding country, and in the Bab al-Jabiyah gate of old Damascus.
jablonec-nad-nisou: Jablonec nad Nisou lies about 7 km south-east of Liberec and 83 km north-east of Prague, at the confluence of the Lusatian Neisse and the Bílá Nisa in the eastern tip of the Zittau Basin, ringed by the Jizera Mountains. The Czech name means little apple tree, because the village was founded where an apple tree grew. German-speaking settlers of the 16th century turned it into Gablonz, and in 1904 the suffix nad Nisou, or an der Neisse, was made official in both languages.

The first written mention is in a Latin document of 1356, which treats the village as founded in the 14th century. Troops of rebelling Lusatians burned it in August 1469 during their war with King George of Poděbrady, and it was resettled in the 1530s and 1540s by mostly German-speaking colonists. In the first half of the 17th century it belonged to Albrecht von Wallenstein, who sold it to the Desfours family, and it was burned again in 1643 during the Thirty Years' War.

Glass production began to flourish in the second half of the 17th century. The first bijou was made in the 18th century, and the exporter J. F. Schwann spread the village's name through Europe. Emperor Francis II made it a market town on 21 April 1808, and Emperor Franz Joseph I made it a town on 28 March 1866. After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 to 1871 damaged competitors, its traders took over foreign markets. By the turn of the 20th century Bohemian garnet jewellery sold in Chicago came from Gablonz. The crash of 1929 hit the glass and jewellery trade, and foreign competition and changing fashion added to the crisis of the 1930s.

After the Munich Agreement the town was annexed to Nazi Germany in October 1938 and administered as part of Reichsgau Sudetenland until 1945. Between 1945 and 1949 most of the Germans were expelled under the Beneš decrees. Some of them founded a new settlement in Bavaria and named it Neugablonz, new Jablonec. It is now a district of Kaufbeuren.

Jablonec nad Nisou is a city of about 46,000 inhabitants, the second largest in the Liberec Region, and it forms a conurbation with Liberec. Its historic centre is protected as an urban monument zone. The New Town Hall, built in the functionalist style in 1930 to 1933, is a national cultural monument. The Church of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross of 1900 to 1902 is counted among the most important Art Nouveau churches in Europe. The Museum of Glass and Costume Jewellery, founded in 1904, presents the local tradition of costume jewellery and beads.
jablunkov-pass: The Jablunkov Pass lies at 553 metres (1,814 ft) above sea level in the municipality of Mosty u Jablunkova in the Czech Republic. It separates the Moravian-Silesian Beskids from the Jablunkov Intermontane, or in a broader sense the Moravian-Silesian Beskids from the Silesian Beskids, and it is one of the most important transport routes of the Western Carpathians.

Archaeological research suggests that the route was important long before the Middle Ages, when it connected Upper Hungary with Cieszyn Silesia. Travelling caravans were often attacked by bandits, so fortifications were built on the site of present-day Mosty u Jablunkova, probably in the 13th century, as archaeologists presume. As the trade route grew in importance, new fortifications were built in 1529 for fear of a Turkish attack.

The pass played an important role during the Thirty Years' War. After the war its defences were renovated, and Duchess Elizabeth Lucretia had new and larger works built nearby, which became a station with a permanent garrison. The fortifications were last renovated in 1808; they then fell into decay, and local people took their parts as building material.

In October 1938 Poland captured the whole Trans-Olza area, the pass included. On the night of 25–26 August 1939 a group of armed German Abwehr agents of the Brandenburg Regiment attacked the railway station at Mosty in the Jabłonków Incident, which has been called the first commando operation of World War II.

The E75 road from Žilina to Český Těšín and the Košice–Bohumín Railway both run through the pass. The remains of the old fortifications at Mosty u Jablunkova are a popular tourist spot, visited for what survives of the defences that once guarded the route.
jaca: Jaca stands on the Aragón River near the Pyrenees and the border with France, at a height of 820 metres. It lies at the crossing of two great early medieval routes, one from Toulouse to Santiago de Compostela and one from Pau to Zaragoza. The County and Kingdom of Aragon developed out of the city, and it was the capital of the district of Jacetania.

The origins of the city are obscure, but its name apparently derives from the Iacetani, whom Strabo lists among the small tribes of the Ebro basin. Jaca minted coins from the second half of the 2nd century BCE, showing a horseman with a spear and the Iberian inscription iaka. The Roman consul Cato the Elder began the conquest of the city in 195 BCE and finished it in the spring of 194 BCE. Huesca fell to the Muslims in 720, and the region of Jacetania then served as a buffer zone for the Carolingian Empire; by 799 Aureolo had stabilised an independent county.

Ramiro I of Aragon, who reigned from 1035 to 1063, gave it the title of city and capital of the Kingdom of Aragon, and in 1063 it was the site of the Synod of Jaca. As the Aragonese conquered land to the south from Muslim rule, the capital was moved to Huesca in 1096, though Jaca remained a market city for its region. It was home to Aragon's oldest Jewish community until the expulsion of 1492. In 1592 Philip II ordered the pentagonal citadel, designed by the Italian engineer Tibúrcio Spannocchi, to defend the Pyrenees against a possible French invasion. A mutiny there on 12 and 13 December 1930, whose leaders demanded the abolition of the monarchy, was suppressed with some difficulty.

Jaca has medieval walls and towers around the 11th-century Romanesque cathedral, and the citadel of the late 16th century. The Diocesan Museum of Jaca keeps Romanesque and Gothic frescoes from the district. From the early 1970s the town changed from a small garrison town into the gateway to winter resorts such as Astún and Candanchú.
jachymov: Jáchymov, in German Sankt Joachimsthal or Joachimsthal, lies in the Ore Mountains in the Karlovy Vary District, about 15 kilometres north of Karlovy Vary on the border with Germany. The town stands in a valley at 733 metres, and its territory includes Klínovec, the highest mountain of the range at 1,244 metres. It was founded in a valley called in German simply Thal and was named after Saint Joachim, so that the name means Saint Joachim's Valley.

The village of Joachimsthal was founded by Steffan Schlick in 1516. The silver caused the population to grow rapidly and made the Counts of Schlick one of the richest families in Bohemia. From 1520 they minted silver coins, the Joachimsthalers, called Thaler in German and tolar in Czech, from which, through the Dutch daalder, the word dollar derives. In 1528 Ferdinand I seized the right of mining. Georgius Agricola based his metallurgical studies on observations made here in the late 1520s. In 1534, with about 20,000 people, Jáchymov was the second most populous town in the Kingdom of Bohemia, behind Prague.

The Church of Saint Joachim, built in 1534 to 1540, was the first Lutheran church in the Kingdom of Bohemia; after the Counter-Reformation took effect in 1621 many Lutheran citizens migrated to nearby Saxon territory. The war and the lack of pumps to drain deep mines left the town unable to compete with cheap Spanish silver from the American colonies. Later Martin Heinrich Klaproth found that pitchblende could colour glass yellow, and discovered a new element in 1781, naming it uranium. The Austrian government sent 100 kilograms of waste from the uranium pigment factory to Marie Skłodowska-Curie and Pierre Curie, who found radium in it. Until the First World War this was the foremost source of radium in the world.

Jáchymov was annexed by Nazi Germany after the Munich Agreement in 1938, and most of its German population was expelled in 1945 and 1946. After the Second World War uranium mining began on a large scale, and almost all the uranium was exported to the Soviet Union. Prison camps held prisoners of war, forcibly recruited citizens, political prisoners and opponents of the communist regime. At the peak in 1955 over 46,000 people worked there, 20 per cent of them involuntarily. Mining ceased in 1964.

Jáchymov has about 2,200 inhabitants. The first radon spa in the world was founded there in 1906. The town is part of the Ore Mountain Mining Region, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its historic centre is protected as an urban monument zone. The Royal Mint, built in 1533 to 1536, houses a museum of mining.
jacmel: Jacmel is a commune on the south coast of Haiti, the capital of the department of Sud-Est, 24 miles (39 kilometres) southwest of Port-au-Prince across the Tiburon Peninsula. Its name comes from the Taíno name Yaquimel. The area was Taíno territory, part of the Xaragua chiefdom ruled by the cacique Bohechio, before the French renamed it Jacmel.

The Compagnie de Saint-Domingue founded the town in 1698 as the capital of the southeastern part of the French colony of Saint-Domingue. It was developed to boost sugar production and trade but soon became a centre of the coffee trade. A fire in 1896 destroyed most of its buildings. The city was rebuilt, often with prefabricated cast-iron pillars and balconies shipped from France, and the mansions of wealthy coffee merchants from this period survive with little change. In 1925 Jacmel was the first town in the Caribbean to have electricity.

During the Haitian Revolution, in 1791 and 1792, Romaine-la-Prophétesse led thirteen thousand rebels in besieging, occupying and later burning Jacmel, and in attacking the plantations around it and freeing their slaves. In the War of the South, which began in June 1799, Toussaint Louverture fought André Rigaud for the city. By November the rebels had been pushed back to this strategic port, defended by Alexandre Pétion, and Jacmel fell to Toussaint's troops in February 1800. Pétion and other leaders went into exile in France.

In 1806 Francisco de Miranda raised the first flag of Gran Colombia from the corvette Leander, anchored in the Bay of Jacmel, on 12 March, a day still kept as Venezuelan Flag Day. The flag was the model for those of Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador. In 1870 the Puerto Rican independence leader Ramón Emeterio Betances spent a short time in Jacmel gathering support for an uprising in the Dominican Republic, which the Haitian president Nissage Saget backed.

Jacmel is known for its well-preserved gingerbread houses of the early 19th century, which are said to have influenced the houses of New Orleans. It is also known for its papier-mâché masks and handicrafts, a month-long carnival and a film school, the Ciné Institute. It was heavily damaged in the Haiti earthquake of 12 January 2010. The town has been tentatively accepted as a World Heritage Site, and its main square is named for Toussaint Louverture.
jacob-baradaeus: Jacob was born in the city of Constantia, near modern Viranşehir, the son of Theophilus bar Manu, a priest. At the age of two he was left in the care of Eustathius, abbot of the Monastery of Fsilta, where he studied Greek, Syriac and religious texts, and when his mother later tried to bring him home he refused. After his parents died he gave his inheritance to the poor and freed the slaves he had inherited. Ordained deacon and priest at the monastery, he became known as a miracle-worker.

His church grew out of the division that followed the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and the persecution of its opponents under Emperor Justin I from 518 left them with few leaders. Empress Theodora, herself a non-Chalcedonian, invited Jacob to Constantinople, where he lived for 15 years in the Monastery of Sykai. When Ephraim, Patriarch of Antioch, persecuted the non-Chalcedonians, Theodora and Al-Harith ibn Jabalah, King of the Ghassanids, urged Pope Theodosius I of Alexandria to consecrate bishops, and Theodosius made Jacob bishop of Edessa.

Jacob then ordained clergy across Mesopotamia, Anatolia, Syria, Palestine and Egypt. The Roman government tried to imprison him, and he travelled in disguise, which earned him the name Burde'ana, man in ragged clothes, the source of Baradaeus. He ordained Sergius of Tella as Patriarch of Antioch in 544 and Paul in 550, and consecrated Ahudemmeh as Metropolitan of the East in 559. After the Second Council of Constantinople of 553 failed to win over the Syrian non-Chalcedonians, he began to form the separate church that became the Syriac Orthodox Church.

His later years were troubled by disputes. In 571 he approved an edict of union with the Chalcedonians, then withdrew his approval when many of his own side protested. When Pope Peter IV of Alexandria deposed Paul as patriarch in 576, Jacob first denounced him and then accepted the deposition to reconcile the Syrian and Egyptian non-Chalcedonians, a compromise that set off violence between his supporters and Paul's in Syria.

Jacob left Syria for Alexandria with several bishops, fell ill on the way at the Monastery of St. Romanus in Maiuma, and died there on 30 July 578. According to Cyriacus, Bishop of Mardin, his remains stayed there until they were moved to the Monastery of Fsilta in 622. He is venerated as a saint in the Oriental Orthodox Churches, with a feast day on 31 July.
jacob-cats: Jacob Cats was born on 10 November 1577 in Brouwershaven. He lost his mother early, and he and his three brothers were adopted by his aunt Anna Breyde and her husband Doen Leenaerts. He went to school in Breda, studied law, and settled in The Hague as a lawyer, where his defence of a person accused of witchcraft brought him many clients. A tertian fever, a form of malaria, then resisted every cure for about two years. He returned to Zeeland to die but was cured by the powder of a travelling doctor, later said to be a quack. On 26 April 1605 he married Elisabeth van Valckenburg and lived at Grijpskerke in Zeeland, devoted to farming and poetry.

The end of the twelve-year truce with Spain in 1621 brought the breaking of the dykes, which drove him from his farm. He became pensionary of Middelburg and two years later of Dordrecht. In 1648 he was made keeper of the great seal, and he resigned his offices in 1651. As Grand Pensionary he proved a rather colourless statesman: during his tenure Andries Bicker and his cousin Cornelis de Graeff of Amsterdam took over the leadership of the republican-leaning regents. In 1657 he was sent to England on a mission to Oliver Cromwell, which proved unsuccessful.

Cats retired to his villa Sorghvliet, meaning Fly From Worry, with a formal garden that appeared in seventeenth-century collections of engravings of European gardens. He wrote his autobiography, Eighty-two Years of My Life, and his poems. His moralistic emblem books, notably Sinne en Minnebeelden, with plates by Adrian van der Venne, brought fame in his lifetime. He was a contemporary of Hooft and Vondel, but his Orangist and Calvinist opinions separated him from the liberal Amsterdam poets.

He died on 12 September 1660 and was buried by torchlight in the Kloosterkerk in The Hague. For nearly two centuries his work was enormously popular, and he is still called Father Cats. His diffuse style and old-fashioned diction later made him better known than read, though some of his coined phrases remain everyday Dutch.
jacob-kettler: Jacob Kettler was born on 28 October 1610 in Kuldīga (Goldingen), the son of Wilhelm Kettler and Duchess Sophie of Prussia, a daughter of Albert Frederick, Duke of Prussia. He was a godson of King James I of England. While his father was exiled from the duchy, Jacob lived at the courts of Stettin and Berlin, studied at Rostock and at the University of Leipzig, and sympathised with the ideas of mercantilism. In 1634 he made a grand tour of Europe, visiting Paris, London and Amsterdam, where he studied shipbuilding. He became co-ruler of the duchy in 1638 and sole duke in 1642.

Under Kettler the duchy traded with the Netherlands, Portugal, England and France. He began large-scale reforms of the economy, improved agriculture, opened many manufactures and started a shipbuilding industry, and he founded the Fleet of Courland and Semigallia, a navy and merchant fleet. The duchy became de facto independent of the Polish crown, since all contracts with foreign powers were signed as between independent states, and after 1646 the duke controlled its customs administration.

In 1651 he sent a fleet to build Fort Jacob on the Gambia River, on an island later known as Kunta Kinteh Island. In 1654 he took Tobago with forces carried on the ship Das Wappen der Herzogin von Kurland, which had 45 cannons and carried 25 officers, 124 Courlander soldiers and eighty families of Latvian colonists, and the colony was named Neu Kurland. In 1651 he also offered Pope Innocent X 40 warships and 24,000 soldiers and sailors to conquer land in Australia, in return for the commercial profits. The plan was dropped in 1655 with the pope's death.

During the Second Northern War the Swedes took the duke prisoner and held him and his family in Riga and later at Ivangorod from 1658 to 1660. His colonies were attacked and lost and his fleet was destroyed. After the war he rebuilt the fleet and retook Tobago from the Dutch, and for the rest of his reign he tried, only partly successfully, to regain the earlier level of wealth. He died at Mitau (Jelgava) on 1 January 1682. He is remembered as a fair ruler who gave opportunities to Latvian peasants and knew the Latvian language.
jacob-roggeveen: Jacob Roggeveen was born in Middelburg, the capital of the province of Zeeland, on 1 February 1659. His father, Arend Roggeveen, was a mathematician learned in astronomy, geography and the theory of navigation, who studied the supposed southern continent Terra Australis and obtained a patent for an exploring voyage that he never made. Jacob became a notary of Middelburg and took a doctorate in law at the University of Harderwijk on 12 August 1690.

In 1706 he joined the Dutch East Indies Company and worked from 1707 to 1714 as a councillor of justice at Batavia. He married twice and was widowed twice, and returned to Middelburg alone in 1714. There he became involved in religious controversy by publishing a leaflet of the liberal preacher Pontiaan van Hattem, The Fall of the World's Idol. The city council confiscated and burned the first part in 1718, and Roggeveen moved to Flushing and then to Arnemuiden, where he published two further parts.

On 1 August 1721 Roggeveen, aged 62, set out at the head of an expedition paid for by the Dutch West India Company, rival of the East Indies Company. His brother Jan helped plan it. The aims were to find Terra Australis and to open a western trade route to the Spice Islands. He had three ships, the Arend, the Thienhoven and the Afrikaansche Galey, with 223 men. He sailed to the Falkland Islands, which he renamed Belgia Australis, passed through the Strait of Le Maire and went beyond 60 degrees south before entering the Pacific. He landed near Valdivia in Chile and spent from 24 February to 17 March 1722 at the Juan Fernandez Islands.

On Easter Sunday, 5 April 1722, the ships reached Easter Island, where he reported seeing between 2,000 and 3,000 inhabitants. He then charted six islands in the Tuamotu Archipelago, two in the Society Islands and four in Samoa, and was the first European to find Bora Bora, Maupiti and Samoa. He lost the Afrikaansche Galey at Takapoto atoll. At Makatea he fired on a crowded beach after a violent encounter, and the islanders ambushed a shore party and killed ten of his crew.

The two remaining ships passed New Guinea and reached Batavia in 1722. There the East Indies Company arrested Roggeveen for violating its monopoly and confiscated the ships. After a long lawsuit in the Netherlands the company was forced to compensate him for his losses and to pay his crew. After his return he published a fourth part of his religious work. He died on 31 January 1729.
jacob-van-artevelde: Jacob van Artevelde was born in Ghent into a wealthy commercial family. He married twice and amassed a fortune in the weaving industry. He is also known as the Wise Man and the Brewer of Ghent. He rose to prominence in the early stages of the Hundred Years' War. Fearing that hostilities between France and England would damage the prosperity of Ghent, he entered political life and set up an alliance with Bruges and Ypres, later called the Four Members, to show neutrality.

He gained control of the insurrection against Louis I, Count of Flanders, who had abandoned his father's anti-French policies. Louis was forced to flee to France, and van Artevelde served as captain general of Ghent from then until his death. Flemish relations with England had traditionally been good because of the wool and textile trade. The neutrality was eventually broken, and the towns took the side of the English in 1340. In that year van Artevelde persuaded the federation to recognise King Edward III of England as sovereign of France and overlord of Flanders. Flemish trade and industry flourished under his semi-dictatorial rule.

In 1345 rumours that he planned to recognise Edward III's son, the Black Prince, as count of Flanders, suspicion of embezzlement and an excommunication by the Pope caused a popular uprising in Ghent, and an angry mob killed van Artevelde on 17 or 24 July. His son Philip van Artevelde later took up the Flemish cause and died at the Battle of Roosebeke in 1382.
jacobin-club: The club began in 1789 as the Club Breton, a group of Breton deputies at the Estates General at Versailles, and deputies from other regions soon joined. Early members included the comte de Mirabeau, the Abbé Sieyès, Antoine Barnave and Robespierre. It was re-founded in November 1789 and rented the refectory of the Dominican monastery of the Jacobins in the Rue Saint-Honoré, next to the Assembly. In January 1790 it took the name Société des amis de la Constitution, though its opponents had already dubbed it the Jacobins.

Once in Paris the club admitted citizens besides deputies. There were one hundred and fifty-two affiliated clubs by August 1790 and, at the peak, at least 7,000 chapters with a membership estimated at half a million or more. Women were not members but could follow debates from the balconies, and the high subscription confined membership to well-off men.

The club supported the monarchy until the eve of the Republic on 20 September 1792. In late 1791 a group around Brissot, later called Girondins, urged war with Prussia and Austria, which Robespierre opposed in the club; the war was decided in April 1792, and the two groups then polarised. On 2 June 1793 a crowd of armed men besieged the Convention, which expelled 22 leading Girondins. Robespierre and the Mountain then dominated the government until July 1794. In October 1793 twenty-one Girondins were sentenced to death, and between September 1793 and July 1794 there were 17,000 death sentences across France.

On 28 July 1794 the Convention had Robespierre and 21 associates guillotined. The club's membership fell to about 600, and gangs of the jeunesse dorée attacked it. On 12 November 1794 the National Convention decreed its permanent closure by a nearly unanimous vote, and within a year 93 percent of the Jacobin clubs had closed. An attempt to revive it in July 1799, the Club du Manège, was suppressed after about a month.

In power the Jacobins completed the abolition of feudalism, decided in principle on 4 August 1789 but held back by a clause requiring compensation. They set up the Cult of Reason and the Cult of the Supreme Being in place of Catholicism. They consolidated republicanism in France, while their unjudicial methods discredited the Revolution in many eyes. The term Jacobin was later applied to radicals of similar views.
jacobite-rising-of-1715: The Glorious Revolution of 1688 replaced the Catholic James II and VII with his Protestant daughter Mary II and her husband William III, and the Act of Settlement 1701 excluded Catholics, among them James Francis Edward Stuart, from the throne. When Anne died in August 1714 the crown passed smoothly to George I, and the pro-Hanoverian Whigs took control of government. They turned on the Tories: Robert Harley was imprisoned in the Tower of London, and Lord Bolingbroke fled to France and became James's Secretary of State.

French support had been crucial to the exiled Stuarts, but France had accepted the Protestant succession in the peace that ended the War of the Spanish Succession. On 14 March 1715 James appealed to Pope Clement XI for help, and on 23 August, believing that Marlborough would join him, he wrote to the Duke of Berwick that it was now more than ever now or never.

The Earl of Mar acted without a commission from James. On 6 September at Braemar he raised the standard of James the 8th and 3rd before 600 supporters. The Jacobites took Inverness, Gordon Castle, Aberdeen and Dundee but not Fort William. By October Mar's force of nearly 20,000 held all Scotland north of the Firth of Forth except Stirling Castle, but his hesitation gave the Duke of Argyll time to gather reinforcements.

In England the government arrested the leaders of a planned western rising on the night of 2 October. A rising in Northumberland under James Radclyffe, 3rd Earl of Derwentwater, went ahead on 6 October, joined a force of Scottish Borderer Jacobites led by William Gordon, 6th Viscount Kenmure, and the men of Mackintosh of Borlum, and surrendered after the Battle of Preston on 12–14 November. Under the Barrier Treaty the Dutch sent 6,000 troops to defend the Protestant succession.

James landed at Peterhead on 22 December, but by the time he reached Perth on 9 January 1716 his army numbered fewer than 5,000. Mar burned villages between Perth and Stirling to deny Argyll supplies and led the Jacobites out of Perth on 30 January; on 4 February James wrote a farewell letter to Scotland and sailed from Montrose the next day.

Many prisoners were tried for treason and sentenced to death. The Indemnity Act of July 1717 pardoned all who had taken part, except the whole of Clan Gregor, Rob Roy MacGregor among them. James tried again in 1719 and was defeated at the Battle of Glenshiel.
jacobite-rising-of-1745: The Glorious Revolution of 1688 replaced the Catholic James II and VII with his Protestant daughter Mary and her husband William. James Francis Edward Stuart was the closest natural heir, but the Act of Settlement 1701 excluded Catholics, and in 1714 the throne passed to George I of Hanover. Jacobite risings in 1715 and 1719 failed, and by 1737 James was living tranquilly in Rome. By the late 1730s French statesmen saw the exiled Stuarts as a means of weakening Britain, and the Highlands as a place to start. A French invasion planned for February 1744 was wrecked by storms, and Louis XV cancelled it and declared war on Britain.

Charles Edward Stuart launched the rising on 19 August 1745 at Glenfinnan in the Highlands, captured Edinburgh and won the Battle of Prestonpans in September. The Jacobite army entered England on 8 November, and Carlisle capitulated on 15 November. At Manchester it received its first notable English recruits, who formed the Manchester Regiment. When it reached Derby on 4 December there was no sign of English reinforcements or a French landing, and on 5 December the council voted overwhelmingly to retreat. Charles had admitted that he had not heard from the English Jacobites since leaving France, and his relationship with the Scots was irretrievably damaged.

The Jacobites won a narrow victory at Falkirk Muir on 17 January 1746 but abandoned the siege of Stirling Castle and retreated to Inverness. At the Battle of Culloden on 16 April, fewer than 5,000 Jacobites faced a better trained government force of 7,000 to 9,000 under the Duke of Cumberland. The government guns were far superior, and when Charles ordered a charge, boggy ground drove his centre to the right, where the regiments became entangled. The battle lasted less than an hour.

Government forces spent weeks searching for rebels, confiscating cattle and burning meeting houses. Of 3,500 Jacobites indicted for treason, 120 were executed, 650 died awaiting trial, 900 were pardoned and the rest were transported to the colonies. Lords Kilmarnock, Balmerino and Lovat were beheaded, and the remaining prisoners were released under the General Pardon Act 1746. Charles escaped to France and died in Rome in 1788. The rising was the last of a series that began in 1689 and ended Jacobitism as a major factor in British politics.
jacobitism: Jacobite ideology originated with James VI and I, who in 1603 became the first monarch to rule England, Scotland and Ireland together. Its basis was divine right, which emphasised the crown's descent by hereditary right. His concept of personal rule, and his wish for political and religious union, were widely unpopular in all three kingdoms, above all in England. His son Charles I continued the policy, and his Personal Rule from 1629 led to a crisis that ended in the First English Civil War in 1642. In November 1688 the Glorious Revolution replaced James II with his daughter Mary II and her husband William III. Jacobites held that, since kings held office through divine right, the whole post-1688 regime was illegitimate.

Jacobitism drew on a political theology shared by mostly non-juring Tories in the Church of England and members of the Scottish Episcopal Church. It held that kings ruled by divine right and were accountable to God, not to Parliament, that the crown descended by dynastic right that could not be annulled, and that subjects owed passive obedience. Frank McLynn noted that the movement contained sincere men who aimed solely to restore the Stuarts but also gave legitimacy to political dissent of all kinds.

Support differed in the three kingdoms. Irish Catholic backing rested on James's religion and his supposed willingness to support Irish autonomy, while most Irish Protestants opposed his policies. In England Jacobitism was often associated with the Tories, but the Church of England's supremacy and the doctrine of non-resistance held most back. In Scotland about 20,000 men fought for the Jacobites in 1715, against 11,000 in the government army. Many Jacobites were Protestant Lowlanders, not the Catholic Highlanders of legend, and many Highland clansmen were raised through feudal obligation to their landlords.

Besides the Williamite War in Ireland of 1689 to 1691 and the Scottish rising of 1689, there were serious revolts in 1715, 1719 and 1745, and French invasion attempts in 1708 and 1744. The defeat of the 1745 Rising ended Jacobitism as a serious political movement. The Heritable Jurisdictions Act then removed the feudal controls of Highland chiefs, and the Act of Proscription outlawed Highland dress unless worn in military service, though its impact is debated and it was repealed in 1782.

Later the movement became a romantic symbol of the past. A brief neo-Jacobite revival began in the late 1880s with the Order of the White Rose, founded in 1886, and largely ended with the First World War. Jacobitism also inspired the Irish Aisling poems, among them Mo Ghile Mear by Seán Clárach Mac Domhnaill, and the Scottish Gaelic poetry of Iain Lom and Alasdair Mac Mhaighstir Alasdair.
jacobo-arbenz: Juan Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán was born on 14 September 1913 in Quetzaltenango, the son of a Swiss German pharmacist who had emigrated in 1901 and a Guatemalan schoolteacher. His father's morphine addiction ruined the family business, and since the family could not afford a university, Árbenz took a scholarship at the Polytechnic School as a military cadet in 1932. He graduated in 1935 and was the school's first sergeant, an honour given to only six cadets from 1924 to 1944. As a junior officer he had to lead squads escorting chain gangs of prisoners under the dictator Jorge Ubico, an experience that traumatised him and shaped his views.

Ubico fell in 1944 after protests that included students, workers and junior officers, and a successor junta under Federico Ponce Vaides took over. Árbenz, who had been living in El Salvador, was one of the leaders of the plot within the army, and insisted that civilians take part. After the October revolution he served as Minister of National Defense from 1944 to 1950 under President Juan José Arévalo and helped put down a military coup in 1949. He resigned on 20 February 1950 to run for the presidency, and he easily defeated Miguel Ydígoras Fuentes, taking office on 15 March 1951.

The centrepiece of his programme was the agrarian reform law, passed by the National Assembly on 17 June 1952, which transferred uncultivated land from large estates to poor labourers, with compensation. When he took office, 2% of the population owned 70% of the land. About 500,000 people benefited, most of them indigenous. The United Fruit Company, the country's largest landowner and employer, lobbied the United States government against him, and Washington also feared communist influence. President Eisenhower authorised the CIA's Operation PBSuccess in August 1953, led by Carlos Castillo Armas with about 150 mercenaries, and the coup of 1954 ousted Árbenz.

Árbenz and his family spent 73 days in the Mexican embassy before leaving the country, then lived in Paris, Prague, Moscow, Uruguay from May 1957 and Cuba from July 1960. His daughter Arabella died by suicide in Bogotá in 1965, and he settled in Mexico, where he died on 27 January 1971. In October 2011 Guatemala's president Álvaro Colom apologised for the government's role in his overthrow. Historians dispute his legacy, which they say the CIA's media campaign shaped. Greg Grandin wrote that the land reform decree represented a fundamental shift in the power relations governing Guatemala, though the United States-backed military governments that followed reversed much of the reforms of Árbenz and Arévalo.
jacopo-peri: Jacopo Peri was born in either Rome or Florence to a middle-class family. He himself claimed to be from Rome. The reigning Fernando de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, held pro-Roman sentiments, and it may have been a disadvantage to be known as a Florentine, which may have led Peri to misstate his birthplace. He was employed to sing at the Servite monastery of Santissima Annunziata in Florence, and probably received an education at its school. Because the Medici court attended mass there each week, the monastery was a route by which musical students developed their careers and found patrons. Peri studied with Cristofano Malvezzi and worked in several Florentine churches as an organist and singer.

Around September 1588 Peri began work at the Medici court, first as a tenor and keyboard player and later as a composer. His earliest works were incidental music for plays, intermedi and madrigals. In the 1590s he became associated with Jacopo Corsi, the leading patron of music in Florence. They believed contemporary art inferior to that of classical Greece and Rome and set out to recreate Greek tragedy as they understood it. Their work added to that of the Florentine Camerata of the previous decade, which produced the first experiments in monody, solo song over a continuo bass that eventually developed into recitative and aria.

Peri and Corsi brought in the poet Ottavio Rinuccini to write a text. The result, Dafne, is seen as the first work in a new form, opera. Rinuccini and Peri next collaborated on Euridice, first performed on 6 October 1600 at the Palazzo Pitti for the wedding of Marie de' Medici and Henry IV. Unlike Dafne it survives, though it is hardly ever staged. It used recitatives between the arias and choruses to move the action along. Peri wrote further operas, among them La Flora with Marco da Gagliano, and pieces for court entertainments.

Few of Peri's pieces are still performed. By the time of his death on 12 August 1633 his operatic style was considered old-fashioned beside the work of younger reformers such as Claudio Monteverdi. His influence on those composers, however, was considerable. He was sometimes known by the byname Il Zazzerino, the blond one.
jacquard-machine: Figured designs were traditionally made on a drawloom, where a second operator, the draw boy, rather than the weaver, selected the heddles whose warp ends were to be pulled up. The work was slow and labour-intensive, and the complexity of the pattern was limited by practical factors. The first prototype of a Jacquard-type loom was made in the second half of the 15th century by an Italian weaver from Calabria, known as Jean le Calabrais, who was invited to Lyon by Louis XI. In 1725 Basile Bouchon applied the principle of a perforated band of paper, a continuous roll punched by hand in sections, each representing one row of the pattern.

Joseph Marie Jacquard saw that a mechanism could be developed for sophisticated patterns. He possibly combined the mechanical elements of other inventors, but certainly innovated. His machine was generally similar to Vaucanson's arrangement, but used Jean-Baptiste Falcon's individual pasteboard cards and square prism, which he is credited with perforating on all four sides in place of Vaucanson's perforated barrel. It had eight rows of needles and uprights where Vaucanson had a double row, increasing its figuring capacity.

The cards are fastened into a continuous chain that passes over a square box. At each quarter rotation a new card is presented, representing one pick of the weft shuttle. For each hole a control rod passes through and is unmoved, while where there is no hole a rod is pushed in and displaces its hook. A beam then lifts the hooks left in place, and the cords attached to them raise the heddles and open the shed. One advantage claimed was that the figuring shed could be drawn on every shot, rather than once for every four, giving a fabric with greater definition of outline.

The term Jacquard loom is somewhat inaccurate, since the Jacquard head adapts to many dobby looms. Jacquard machines are more costly to maintain than dobby or cam shedding, need highly skilled operators and run more slowly, and changing the chain of cards takes time. In 1855 a Frenchman adapted the mechanism to work by electromagnets, but trials were unsuccessful. Bonas Textile Machinery NV launched the first successful electronic Jacquard at ITMA Milan in 1983.

A silk prayer book of 58 pages, woven in Lyon and issued in 1886 and 1887, needed an estimated 106,000 to 500,000 punched cards. The idea of changing a pattern by changing cards was a conceptual precursor of programming. Charles Babbage knew of Jacquard machines and planned to use cards to store programs in his Analytical Engine, and Herman Hollerith used punched cards for the 1890 United States census. Punched cards stayed in computing until the mid-1980s.
jacqueline-countess-of-hainaut: Jacqueline was born on 15 July 1401 in Le Quesnoy, the only legitimate child of William II, Duke of Bavaria, and Margaret, a daughter of Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy. Betrothed to John, Duke of Touraine, a son of King Charles VI of France, she married him in The Hague on 6 August 1415. When his elder brother died that December she became Dauphine. John died, probably poisoned, on 4 April 1417, and her father died of a dog bite infection on 31 May, leaving her a widow at sixteen with her inheritance to defend.

In Hainaut, where female succession was customary, she was recognised as countess on 13 June 1417, but in Holland and Zeeland her rights were contested. The old aristocracy backed her; the towns backed her uncle John III, who gave up his bishopric of Liège in expectation of succeeding. She married John IV, Duke of Brabant, on 10 March 1418, an unfortunate match, as the papal dispensation was revoked and his finances were poor. Her Hooks fought her uncle's Cods.

In 1421 she fled to England, where Henry V received her, and in 1423 she married Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, in secret, after a divorce valid only in England. Her only recorded pregnancy ended in a stillbirth. When John III died in January 1425, Humphrey intervened with limited force, which harmed the English-Burgundian alliance, and Pope Martin V ruled the marriage illegitimate.

By the Reconciliation of Delft on 3 July 1428 she kept her titles but Philip the Good administered her lands and became her heir. Her marriage to Humphrey was annulled that year. At Easter 1433 she signed a treaty giving Philip all her lands and titles, keeping the income of estates mostly in Zeeland. In spring 1434 she married Frank van Borssele, whom Philip made Count of Oostervant. She died of tuberculosis at Teylingen Castle on 8 October 1436, childless, and Philip inherited Hainaut and Holland. Legend holds that she had secretly married Frank in 1432, but there is no evidence of it.
jacques-callot: Callot was born and died in Nancy, the capital of the Duchy of Lorraine, then an independent state on the north-eastern border of France. He came from an important family; his father was master of ceremonies at the ducal court, and he often described himself as noble in the inscriptions to his prints. At fifteen he was apprenticed to a goldsmith but soon travelled to Rome, where he learned engraving from the expatriate Frenchman Philippe Thomassin. He probably then studied etching with Antonio Tempesta in Florence, where he lived from 1612 to 1621. More than 2,000 preparatory drawings survive, but no paintings by him are known.

In Florence Callot became an independent master and often worked for the Medici court. After the death of Cosimo II de' Medici in 1621 he returned to Nancy, where he lived for the rest of his life, visiting Paris and the Netherlands later in the decade. The courts of Lorraine, France and Spain commissioned work from him, as did publishers, mostly in Paris. His prints were distributed widely through Europe, and Rembrandt was a keen collector. He made more than 1,400 etchings of soldiers, clowns, drunkards, Romani, beggars and court life, as well as religious and military subjects, and most were small, at most about 15 centimetres on their longest dimension.

Callot developed the échoppe, an etching needle with a slanting oval end that let etchers make a swelling line like an engraver's. He also seems to have introduced an etching ground of lute-makers' varnish in place of a wax-based one, so that lines could be etched more deeply and the risk of foul-biting was reduced, allowing detailed work that had been the monopoly of engravers. He used multiple stoppings-out more extensively than earlier etchers, achieving subtle effects of distance and light and shade. Abraham Bosse spread his innovations with the first published manual of etching.

His best known prints are two series on the Miseries and Misfortunes of War: 18 prints published in 1633 and the earlier, incomplete Les Petites Misères. They show soldiers pillaging and burning through towns, country and convents, before being arrested and executed by their superiors, lynched by peasants or surviving as crippled beggars. In 1633 Lorraine was invaded by the French during the Thirty Years' War. The series is still ranked with Francisco Goya's Disasters of War, which it influenced, among the most powerful artistic statements of the inhumanity of war.
jacques-cartier: Jacques Cartier was born on 31 December 1491 in Saint-Malo, the port on the north-east coast of Brittany. A respected mariner, he improved his social standing in 1520 by marrying Mary Catherine des Granches, a member of a leading aristocratic family. In 1534 Jean Le Veneur, bishop of Saint-Malo, introduced him to King Francis I, citing voyages to Newfoundland and Brazil as proof of his ability to lead ships to new lands.

Cartier sailed on 20 April 1534 under a royal commission, hoping to find a western passage to the East Indies. He explored the coasts of Newfoundland, the Gaspé and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and on 24 July planted a 10-metre cross in Gaspé Bay to claim the land for France. There he kidnapped the two sons of the St. Lawrence Iroquoian chief Donnacona, who agreed on condition that they return with European goods.

On a second voyage in 1535 he sailed up the St. Lawrence with three ships and 110 men to Stadacona, and on 2 October reached Hochelaga, now Montreal, where over a thousand people greeted the French. The rapids blocked his way; convinced that the river was the Northwest Passage, he named them the Lachine Rapids after the French word for China. The fleet wintered frozen at the mouth of the St. Charles River, and scurvy killed about 50 Iroquoians. A remedy from the tree annedda, learned from Domagaya, saved 85 of the French. Cartier then took Donnacona to France to tell of the Kingdom of Saguenay, said to hold gold and rubies.

In 1541 Jean-François de La Rocque de Roberval was named lieutenant general of the colonisation project, with Cartier as chief navigator. Cartier sailed ahead with five ships and settled at Cap-Rouge, founding the fortified Charlesbourg-Royal. The minerals he took to be diamonds and gold proved to be quartz and iron pyrites. Iroquoians reportedly killed about 35 settlers during the winter, and he returned to France in 1542; the settlement was abandoned in 1543.

Cartier spent his last years in Saint-Malo and on his nearby estate, and died on 1 September 1557 at the age of 65 during an epidemic, possibly of typhus, and was buried in Saint-Malo Cathedral. He was the first European to describe and map the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the St. Lawrence River, and the first to document the name Canada, which comes from the Iroquoian word kanata, meaning village. Eastern parts of the continent had been visited before him by the Norse and by Basque, Galician and Breton fishermen, and no permanent European settlement followed before 1605.
jacques-francois-menou: Menou was born at Boussay in Indre-et-Loire into an aristocratic family and had reached the rank of maréchal de camp in the French Royal Army by 1789, when the Second Estate of the bailiwick of Touraine elected him to the Estates General. A liberal nobleman, he supported the reforms of the National Constituent Assembly, served on its diplomatic committee, became its secretary in December and was its president from 27 March to 12 April 1790.

After the Assembly closed in September 1791 he served in Paris and then with the Army of the West, fighting in the Vendée through 1793. On 1 Prairial III (20 May 1795), commanding one of the sections of Paris, he forced the rebellious Faubourg Saint-Antoine to capitulate. As general in chief of the Army of the Interior he was then denounced as a traitor, tried and acquitted in 1795.

In 1798 he commanded one of the five divisions of the Armée d'Orient in Napoleon's campaign in Egypt. As Kléber's successor after his assassination on 14 June 1800, he was less popular than his predecessor and lacked the support of the other officers. His wife was Zubaidah bint Muhammad El Bawwab, the daughter of a rich Egyptian, and their son Jacques Mourad Soliman was born at Rosetta on 28 July 1800. Allowed to evacuate the remaining French troops, Menou handed over the Rosetta Stone, whose discovery Captain Pierre-François Bouchard had reported to him.

Menou then became a member of the Tribunat on 17 May 1802 and soon afterwards administrator of the 27th Military Division in Piedmont. He was made a member of the Legion of Honor on 11 December 1803 and a grand officer on 14 June 1804, and was created comte de l'Empire in 1808. Appointed governor of Venice, he became a knight of the Order of the Iron Crown on 23 December 1807. He died in office at the Villa Corniani near Mestre on 13 August 1810, and his name is inscribed on the south side of the Arc de Triomphe.
jacques-lauriston: Jacques Alexandre Bernard Law, later marquis de Lauriston, was born on 1 February 1768 at Pondicherry in French India, where his father, Jean Law de Lauriston, was Governor-General. His father was a nephew of the financier John Law, who had inherited Lauriston Castle in Scotland in 1729, and his mother came from the Carvallho family of Portuguese traders. He was commissioned around 1786 and served in the artillery and on the general staff in the early campaigns of the Revolution, becoming brigadier of artillery in 1795.

Lauriston resigned in 1796 and was recalled in 1800 as aide-de-camp to Napoleon, a friend from his cadet years. He directed the artillery school at La Fère, served as special envoy to Denmark and in 1802 carried the ratification of the Peace of Amiens to England. A general of division by 1805, he was made governor-general of Venice in 1807, took part in the Erfurt negotiations of 1808 and commanded the division that besieged and won Pamplona in Spain.

At the Battle of Wagram on 6 July 1809 Napoleon ordered him to form a grand battery against a surprise Austrian attack on the left flank. Lauriston gathered 112 guns, 60 from the Imperial Guard, 24 from General Karl Philipp von Wrede's Bavarian division and 38 from the Army of Italy, and brought them within grapeshot range. Their fire halted the Austrian III Armeekorps of General Johann Kollowrat and gave Napoleon time to organise his counterattack. In 1812 he was noted for his firmness in covering the retreat from Moscow, and he commanded the V Corps at Lützen and Bautzen.

Held prisoner until the fall of the empire, Lauriston then joined King Louis XVIII and stayed loyal to him during the Hundred Days. He was rewarded with a seat in the Chamber of Peers and a command in the Royal Guard, was created a marquis in 1817 and took command at Brest and in the Finistère. As a marshal he commanded a corps during the Spanish expedition of 1823. He died of a stroke in Paris in June 1828, and his name is inscribed on the Arc de Triomphe.
jacques-louis-randon: Jacques Louis César Alexandre Randon was born on 25 March 1795 at Grenoble in Dauphiné into a Protestant family; later in life, under the influence of his second wife, he converted to Catholicism. He was a nephew of General Jean-Gabriel, Count Marchand, and the revolutionary Antoine-Joseph Barnave was a first cousin of his mother.

He enlisted in the French Army at sixteen, joined his uncle Marchand in Warsaw and was promoted to sergeant on 11 April 1812. He took part in the Russian campaign, the taking of Moscow and the retreat, and then fought in Napoleon's campaigns in Germany and France, at the battles of Lützen, Bautzen and Leipzig among others.

Randon was Minister of War from January to October 1851 and was then appointed Governor-General of Algeria, holding the post from 11 December 1851 to 31 August 1858. At first he did not favour the coup of December 1851, but he came to support the Second French Empire. In 1852 he was made a count, by reversion of the title of his uncle Marchand, and in 1856 he became a Marshal of France at the same time as Canrobert and Bosquet. He served again as Minister of War from 1859 to 1867.

Because of his age he received no command in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870. He was nevertheless held partly responsible for the French defeat, accused of neglecting preparations during his second ministry and of dissuading Napoleon III from acting on Austria's side at the time of the Battle of Sadova in 1866. Modern research has shown the second charge to be unfounded: Randon had in fact urged immediate action against Prussia.

Randon died in Geneva on 16 January 1871, leaving one surviving daughter.
