Mariachi is thought to have originated in the town of Cocula, and the music became most developed around Guadalajara.

Jalisco has 125 municipalities, and its capital and largest city is Guadalajara. The 2020 census counted 8,348,151 people, over half of them in the Guadalajara metropolitan area. The Huichols and the Nahuas are its two significant indigenous populations. Tequila is made from the blue agave of a small region of the state, and José Antonio Cuervo received the first official permission to make and sell it in 1758. San Juan de los Lagos, where an image of the Virgin Mary made in the 16th century is venerated, is one of the most visited pilgrimage sites in Mexico.
jallianwala-bagh-massacre: During the First World War British India supplied millions of soldiers and labourers and large quantities of food, money and ammunition. The war's costs, inflation, heavy taxation and the 1918 flu pandemic increased suffering, and nationalist feeling revived as moderate and extremist groups of the Indian National Congress ended their differences. The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1917 were judged insufficient, and Mahatma Gandhi emerged as a leader of growing civil disobedience. In April 1919, especially in Punjab, rail, telegraph and communications were disrupted, and Lieutenant-Governor Michael O'Dwyer is said to have believed that a coordinated revolt was planned for May.

On Sunday 13 April 1919 Dyer banned all meetings. At 09:00 he proclaimed a pass system, a curfew from 20:00 and a ban on gatherings of four or more, read in English, Urdu, Hindi and Punjabi, though many paid no heed or learned of it later. Many villagers gathered in the Bagh to celebrate the Baisakhi festival and to protest peacefully against the arrest and deportation of Satyapal and Saifuddin Kitchlew. Dyer was told of the meeting at 12:40.

He surrounded the crowd with Gurkha and Sikh troops of the British Indian Army. The garden could be left only on one side, since buildings enclosed the other three, and Dyer blocked that exit and ordered his troops to fire. They continued even as people tried to flee, until their ammunition ran low. Estimates of the dead range from 379 to 1,500 or more, and over 1,200 others were injured, 192 of them seriously. Many people jumped into a well to escape the bullets and drowned. Dyer reported that he had faced a revolutionary army, and O'Dwyer obtained martial law. At least 115 people were killed by security forces in the following days, by one historian's count.

The Hunter Commission was set up on 14 October 1919 to inquire into the disturbances. Winston Churchill, then Secretary of State for War, called the massacre unutterably monstrous, and on 8 July 1920 the House of Commons voted 247 to 37 against Dyer. Many moderate Indians abandoned their loyalty to the British, and the anger fed the non-cooperation movement of 1920-22. Sikh clergy at the Golden Temple gave Dyer a saropa, which shocked Sikhs and contributed to the founding of the Shiromani Gurudwara Prabandhak Committee in 1920. In 1940 Udham Singh, who had been wounded at the Bagh, shot O'Dwyer in London.

A memorial designed by Benjamin Polk was inaugurated on 13 April 1961. Bullet marks remain on the walls, and the well is a protected monument. The British Army was retrained in less violent crowd control, with the principle of minimal force.
jalon: The Jalón, known in Latin as the Salo, is one of the principal tributaries of the Ebro. It is 224 kilometres long and drains a basin of 9,338 square kilometres. Its flow at Calatayud averages 20.8 cubic metres per second but is highly irregular because of the Mediterranean pattern of rainfall. E. Bascuas derives the name from the old European hydronymy and from an old root *sal-, meaning flowing water or stream.

The river rises in a spring at the foot of the Sierra Ministra, in Esteras de Medinaceli in the province of Soria, and runs through Arcos de Jalón to Monreal de Ariza in the province of Zaragoza. The Nágima joins at Monreal de Ariza and the Henar at Cetina, before the river enters a limestone gorge at Alhama de Aragón. It then crosses Paleozoic country in the Cordillera Ibérica near Bubierca and is joined by the Piedra and the Manubles at Ateca.

At Calatayud the valley widens and the Jiloca, Perejiles and Ribota join the river. It then winds through the Sierra de Algairén and the Sierra de la Virgen and, once out of the mountains, enters the Ebro valley, where the Aranda, Grío and Alpartir join it. It meets the Ebro at Torres de Berrellén, a suburb of the city of Zaragoza. The valley forms the main route of communication between the Castilian Plateau and the Ebro.

Much of the river's course has been declared a Special Zone for Bird Protection, and its birds include falcons, eagles, vultures, owls, wrens and herons. Poplar, willow and ash grow along it. Carp, trout and eels were economically important in the past and are returning as pollution is combated. In 2007 the Spanish Ministry of the Environment and the governments of Aragon, Castile and León and Castile-La Mancha adopted a river management plan, the Plan Hidrológico del río Jalón.
jalore: Jalore, also called Jalor and known as the Granite City, is in the western Indian state of Rajasthan and is the administrative headquarters of Jalore District. It lies south of the Sukri River, a tributary of the Luni, and the Jawai River passes through it. The town is about 140 km south of Jodhpur and 489 km from the state capital, Jaipur. The hill on which its fort stands was known as Suvarngiri or Songir, the Golden Mount.

In ancient times the town was called Jabalipura, after the Hindu saint Jabali. It was flourishing in the 8th century, and according to some historical sources one branch of the Pratihara empire ruled there in the 8th and 9th centuries. The writer Uddyotana-suri composed the Kuvalaya-mala at Jabalipura in 779 CE, in the reign of the Gurjara-Pratihara king Vatsaraja. After the Paramara king Vakpati Munja invaded the region in the late 10th century, he divided the conquered lands among his princes, and Jalore was given to Dharnivarah Paramara. The town was ruled by the Paramaras in the 10th century.

Kirtipala, the youngest son of Alhana, the Chahamana ruler of Nadol, captured Jalore from the Paramaras and founded the Jalore line of Chauhans. His son Samarasimha succeeded him, followed by Udayasimha, who expanded the kingdom by recapturing Nadol and Mandor from the Turks and, during his reign, was a tributary of the Delhi Sultanate. Samantasimha and then his son Kanhadadeva followed. In 1311 Alauddin Khalji, the Sultan of Delhi, attacked and captured Jalore, and Kanhadadeva and his son Viramadeva died defending it.

Later the Turkic rulers of Palanpur State in Gujarat briefly ruled Jalor in the 16th century, and it became part of the Mughal Empire. It was restored to Marwar in 1704 and remained part of that kingdom until shortly after Indian independence in 1947.

Jalore was the hometown of Jaiwanta Bai, mother of Maharana Pratap, who was the daughter of Akhey Raj Songara. The Rathore rulers of Ratlam used the Jalore fort to keep their treasure. The town has 12 Hindu monasteries and 13 mosques. It is known as the cradle of the Marwari horse, an indigenous breed.
jaluit-atoll: Jaluit Atoll, in Marshallese Jālwōj or Jālooj, is a large coral atoll of 91 islands in the Pacific Ocean and a legislative district of the Ralik Chain of the Republic of the Marshall Islands. Its land area totals 11.34 square kilometres and it encloses a lagoon of 690 square kilometres. Most of the land is on the largest islet, also called Jaluit. The atoll lies about 220 kilometres southwest of Majuro and is a designated conservation area and Ramsar Wetland.

The British merchant vessel Rolla sighted Jaluit in 1803. The German Empire annexed it with the other Marshall Islands as a protectorate in 1885. From 1888 to 1906 the Jaluit Company administered the islands for Germany's colonial government, under imperial commissars, and from 1906 until October 1914 the governors of German New Guinea held the jurisdiction.

After World War I the atoll became part of Japan's South Seas Mandate and the seat of Japanese administration over the Marshall Islands. During World War II the garrison numbered 1,584 men of the Imperial Japanese Navy and 727 of the Army, and B-24 Liberator bombers of the USAAF 7th Air Force bombed it at least five times in November and December 1943. It then came under the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands until the independence of the Marshall Islands in 1986.
Some Bikini people, displaced by nuclear tests from 1945, moved to Jaluit about a decade later to produce copra; typhoons in 1957 and 1958 struck their homes and sank their supply ship.

The population of the atoll was 1,409 in 2021. The islet of Jabor has the largest settlement, about 1,200 people. Imiej, a 45-minute boat ride away, was the headquarters of the Japanese navy garrison and a major seaplane base, and the ruins of its power station, barracks, antiaircraft guns and a Shinto shrine remain. Jaluit High School is a boarding school serving the atoll and the southern atolls.
jama-masjid-bijapur: Ali Adil Shah I of the Bijapur Sultanate began the mosque in 1576, paying for it with money looted at the Battle of Talikota, in which an alliance of the Deccan Sultanates had defeated the Vijayanagara Empire. Most of the building was standing by 1686, but it never reached completion. It nonetheless became the principal mosque of Bijapur, taking the place of an older and smaller congregational mosque built by Ibrahim Adil Shah I. Later rulers added to it: the murals around the central mihrab were probably made under Muhammad Adil Shah, and Aurangzeb altered the flooring of the prayer hall.

The rectangular complex covers 5,040 square metres within perimeter walls and is entered by its eastern gate. A square courtyard 50 metres on each side holds fountains and an ablution reservoir. The prayer hall on the west, 70 by 36 metres, has a facade of seven arches, only the central one decorated, and a hemispherical dome with a crescent-moon finial and a balustrade at its base. Inside, piers divide it into five bays parallel to the qibla wall, and its floor is marked into 2250 rectangles like prayer mats, a later addition by Aurangzeb.

The design is plain, and ArchNet explains this by the Shiism of Ali Adil Shah, as followers of that branch often preferred little decoration in places of worship. The mihrab breaks the austerity with gilded murals in blue, black and gold dominated by Quranic writing; Muhammad Adil Shah, unlike Ali, was a Sunni. Corner buttresses on the eastern facade show that two minarets were planned, and the gallery parapets lack their merlons.

The mosque is the largest in Bijapur, holding 4,000 worshippers, and is counted among the finest works of Adil Shahi architecture. Bianca Alfieri traces elements of earlier Bahmanid building in it, and Richard Eaton sees it as showing Iranian influence more than local traditions. Michell and Zebrowski rank its mihrab among the finest in the Islamic world, comparing it to that of the Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba. In 2014 UNESCO placed it on its tentative list as part of the Monuments and Forts of the Deccan Sultanate.
jama-masjid-jaunpur: The Sharqi dynasty of Jaunpur was founded by the eunuch Malik Sarwar, who took Jaunpur in 1394 and declared himself an independent sultan in 1398, after Timur's sack of Delhi. Its rulers made Jaunpur a centre of Islamic culture known as the Shiraz of India. Ibrahim Shah laid the foundation of the mosque in 1438, and building above ground began in 1440. Why it was built is unknown: one story says it spared a hermit a barefoot walk to a distant mosque, another that it gave work during a famine. It rose in stages and was finished by the last Sharqi ruler, Hussain Shah.

Wars between Hussain Shah and the Lodi sultans Bahlul Lodi and Sikandar Lodi ended in the fall of Jaunpur to Delhi. Most sources say Sikandar Lodi then damaged the East Gate of the mosque, though the historian Ram Nath argues that a devout Muslim ruler would not have harmed mosques.

The mosque follows the model of the nearby Atala Mosque: a courtyard with four large gateways, the western one holding the pishtaq, or portal, which hides the dome behind it. Unlike the Atala Mosque it stands on a base nearly 20 feet high reached by steps, as many Delhi mosques do, and some arches beside the portal are thought to derive from Bengal. Cloisters surround the courtyard; A. A. Führer held that they were once two storeys high. It is built of brick, some taken from Hindu temples, and one reused stone bears a 6th-century Sanskrit inscription of the Maukhari dynasty praising its first four rulers. The Sharqi royal family is buried near the mosque without monumental tombs.

William Hodges sketched its entrance in 1783 for his Select Views in India, and in 1919 the mosque came under the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act 1904. The scholar Karamat Ali Jaunpuri later restored the five daily prayers there, after the building had been used for gatherings such as weddings. Abha Narain Lambah sees it as the fulfilment of the Tughlaq style, while Ram Nath judges it a series of failed experiments whose value lies in its stonework.
jamaica: Jamaica covers 10,991 square kilometres and is the third-largest island in the Greater Antilles and the Caribbean, after Cuba and Hispaniola. It lies about 145 km south of Cuba and 191 km west of Hispaniola. Mountains dominate the interior, among them the Blue Mountains in the east, where Blue Mountain Peak rises to 2,256 metres, and a narrow coastal plain surrounds them. The island lies within the main development region for Atlantic tropical cyclones and sometimes suffers heavy storm damage. When the Spanish arrived in 1494 the country was deeply forested, and European settlers later cleared much of it for timber and cultivation.

There is no archaeological evidence of human presence until about 500 CE. A group known as the Redware people, after their pottery, arrived around 600 CE, followed by the Taíno around 800 CE, who most likely came from South America. The Taíno lived by farming and fishing, and at their height are thought to have numbered some 60,000 people in around 200 villages headed by caciques. Christopher Columbus claimed the island for Spain after landing in 1494 on his second voyage. The first Spanish settlement, Sevilla, was founded in 1509 by Juan de Esquivel and abandoned around 1524; the capital moved to Spanish Town, then St. Jago de la Vega, around 1534.

The Taíno died in large numbers from introduced diseases and from enslavement by the Spanish, who then imported enslaved Africans. Many escaped and formed autonomous communities in the remote interior, mixing with the remaining Taíno; these became the Jamaican Maroons, who kept their freedom for generations under leaders such as Juan de Serras. By the early 17th century an estimated 2,500 to 3,000 people lived on the island.

England conquered Jamaica from Spain in 1655. Under British rule it became a leading sugar exporter, with a plantation economy that depended on importing enslaved Africans. The British emancipated all slaves in 1838, and many freedmen chose subsistence farms over plantation work. From the 1840s the British brought Chinese and Indian indentured labourers. Independence from the United Kingdom came on 6 August 1962.

Jamaica is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy and a Commonwealth realm, with a bicameral Parliament, and its constitution dates from 1962. The capital and largest city is Kingston. Most Jamaicans are of African or partly African descent, with minorities of European, Indian, Chinese and Lebanese origin. The Maroon communities of Accompong and elsewhere continue to keep their own traditions. The island is the birthplace of the Rastafari religion and of reggae, ska, dub and dancehall music, and its national motto is Out of Many One People.
jamaica-labour-party: The Jamaica Labour Party was founded on 8 July 1943 by Alexander Bustamante, formerly a member of the People's National Party (PNP), as the political wing of the Bustamante Industrial Trade Union. It won the 1944 general election with 22 of the 32 seats and the 1949 election with a reduced majority: the PNP received more votes, 203,048 to 199,538, but the JLP took 17 seats to its 13. The party lost power in 1955, when Norman Manley became chief minister, and remained in opposition after 1959.

After Jamaica voted by 54 per cent in the 1961 referendum to leave the West Indies Federation, Manley called elections in April 1962 to secure a mandate for independence. The JLP won 26 of the 45 seats, and Bustamante replaced Manley as premier before independence on 6 August 1962.

Bustamante suffered a stroke in 1964 and largely withdrew from politics, though he kept the title of party leader until 1974. Donald Sangster, acting prime minister, led the party to victory in the election of 21 February 1967 but died of a brain haemorrhage about six weeks later. Hugh Shearer succeeded him and lost power to Michael Manley's PNP in 1972. Under Edward Seaga, leader from 1974, the JLP won 51 of the 60 seats in 1980, and in 1983 all sixty, when the PNP boycotted the election.

Defeats followed in 1989, 1993, 1997 and 2002. Bruce Golding succeeded Seaga in 2005 and won the 2007 election by 32 seats to 28, ending 18 years of PNP rule. Andrew Holness took over in 2011, lost an early election, then won by one seat in 2016, by 49 seats to 14 in 2020 and with 35 of the 63 seats in 2025.

Despite its name the JLP is a conservative party, believing in a market-driven economy and individual personal responsibility, although it historically embraced Fabianism and in 1967 The Guardian described it as left of centre, only slightly to the right of the PNP. Since the 1990s it has stated its intention for Jamaica to become a republic. Its electoral symbols are a bell, the victory sign and the colour green, and it is a member of the Caribbean Democrat Union.
jamaican-maroons: The word maroon comes through French from the Spanish cimarrón, wild or untamed. When the English invaded in 1655, escaped slaves joined free Black people and mulattoes in mixed groups in the interior. Juan de Bolas led one at Lluidas Vale and Juan de Serras the Karmahaly Maroons at the western end of Cockpit Country. De Bolas sided with the English in 1659 and was granted land by the first maroon treaty in 1663, while the Karmahaly group withdrew into the Blue Mountains, where Sir Henry Morgan failed to subdue them.

Between 1673 and 1690 uprisings led largely by Akan captives known as Coromantee added to their numbers. On 31 July 1690 some 500 slaves rose on the Sutton estate in Clarendon, and more than 200 stayed free, forming an Akan-style polity in the western Cockpit Country under Cudjoe. In the east the Windward Maroons gathered around Nanny Town under Queen Nanny, an Ashanti woman, and Quao.

In the war of the 1730s the British destroyed Nanny Town in 1734, but its people dispersed and Cudjoe's forces held the west. Under the treaty made with Governor Edward Trelawny, Cudjoe's Maroons received 1500 acres between Trelawny Town and Accompong and a measure of autonomy, in return for military help and the return of runaways for a bounty. White superintendents later took control of the towns. The Maroons grew from 664 in 1739 to 1,288 in 1796, and in 1760 Davy the Maroon killed Tacky, the Fante leader of a major slave uprising in Saint Mary Parish.

In the war of 1795 Governor Balcarres demanded the unconditional surrender of Trelawny Town and, against General George Walpole's promise, deported the defeated Maroons. Maroons helped suppress the Samuel Sharpe revolt of 1831–32 and, in 1865, the Morant Bay Rebellion, committing atrocities before capturing Paul Bogle. As many as one-third of the Sierra Leone Maroons returned to Jamaica in the 1840s and settled at Flagstaff, near the old Trelawny Town.

The four official Maroon towns, Accompong Town, Moore Town, Charles Town and Scott's Hall, still hold lands granted in the treaties of 1739–1740. Their councils are called Asofo, from the Akan asafo, and Accompong marks the treaty each 6 January. Queen Nanny is the only woman among Jamaica's National Heroes, and the Maroon heritage of Moore Town, above all its music, is on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
jamal-al-din-al-afghani: His name al-Afghani claims an Afghan origin, and by his own account he was born in Asadabad near Kabul. Nikki Keddie and several other scholars hold that he was raised in a Shia family in Asadabad near Hamadan in Iran, and that he claimed Afghan birth to win influence among Sunni Muslims or to escape the Shah. His rivals Shaykh Yusuf al-Nabhani and Shaykh Abu al-Huda al-Sayyadi called him Mutaʾafghin, meaning the one who claims to be Afghan. He was educated at home, then in Qazvin, Tehran and the Twelver shrine cities of Ottoman Iraq.

In 1856–57 he travelled to British India and spent some years studying religions. In 1866 he is recorded in Afghanistan, where he advised Mohammad Afzal Khan and urged a turn to Russia; Sher Ali Khan expelled him in 1868. In Istanbul he joined the Council of Education and spoke at the opening of Istanbul University, but conservative clerics found his views too radical and he was expelled in 1871. In Egypt he met the young Muhammad Abduh, preached political reform, and sought the removal of Isma'il Pasha. He was exiled to India in August 1879.

In 1884 he and Abduh published the Arabic newspaper al-Urwah al-Wuthqa in Paris, calling for a return to the principles of Islam and for unity among Muslims. After Russia and Munich he returned to Iran in 1889, took sanctuary in the Shah Abdol-Azim Shrine, and was expelled in 1891. His agitation is thought to be one source of the Tobacco Protest of 1891. Sultan Abdul Hamid II then invited him to Istanbul.

He joined a critique of Western imperialism to an appeal for Muslim unity, urging the adoption of Western science and institutions, and held that Islam was compatible with reason. He wanted Hindus and Muslims to cooperate against British rule in India. In 1881 he published Refutation of the Materialists, which included an early Islamic argument against Darwin; in later work he accepted evolution for animals but rejected it for humans, because humans have souls.

In Istanbul in 1895 he met his former disciple Mirza Reza Kermani, and the two planned the assassination of Naser al-Din Shah. Kermani shot the Shah on 1 May 1896 and was hanged in August 1897. Iran failed to obtain al-Afghani's extradition. He died of cancer of the jaw in Istanbul on 9 March 1897. In 1944 his remains were taken to Afghanistan and laid in a mausoleum at Kabul University.
jameh-mosque-of-isfahan: The mosque results from continual construction, reconstruction and renovation on one site from about 771 CE to the end of the 20th century. The first mosque was built around 771 in the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur. It was relatively small, about 52 by 90 metres, made of mud-brick with stucco decoration in the Syro-Mesopotamian style. Excavations in the 1970s showed it stood over earlier structures from the Sasanian or early Islamic period, part of the ancient town of Yahūdiyya.

In 840, under al-Mu'tasim, a larger mosque of about 88 by 128 metres replaced it, with a different qibla orientation. It had a large central courtyard surrounded by an arcade and a hypostyle hall of baked brick pillars, six bays deep on the qibla side. Under the Buyid dynasty another arcade of polylobed brick piers was added around the courtyard, decorated with patterned brickwork, together with two minarets at the entrance, the first recorded instance of the double minaret arrangement that later became common in Iran.

The Seljuks made the next great changes. Isfahan became their first capital after its conquest in 1050. In 1086, under the patronage of the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, columns in front of the mihrab gave way to a large domed space, the largest masonry dome in the Islamic world at the time, with eight ribs and a new type of squinch. In 1088 his rival Taj al-Mulk had another dome built on the north side, whose interlacing ribs form pentagons and five-pointed stars. It is considered a masterpiece of medieval Iranian architecture.

By the early 12th century, probably after a fire in 1121, a large iwan replaced the columned space between the dome and the courtyard, and three more monumental iwans were built, giving the mosque the four-iwan form that became prevalent in Iran and elsewhere. Around 200 smaller cross-ribbed vaults, each with a different design, renovated the old hypostyle halls.

Nearly every later period saw work on the mosque. Under the Ilkhanid sultan Uljaytu a winter hall was added with a stucco mihrab dated to 1310, signed by the calligrapher Haydar. The Muzaffarids added a madrasa, and the tilework of the southern iwan was first added under the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan in 1475. Most Safavid rulers worked on the mosque, and its present minarets, either side of the southern iwan, were erected in the 17th century.

The mosque today combines styles and periods that cannot always be easily dated, and its perimeter is enmeshed with the surrounding bazaar and old city, so that it presents few clear exterior façades. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012, and the Grand Bazaar of Isfahan lies towards its south-western wing.
james-augustus-grant: Grant was born at Nairn in the Scottish Highlands, where his father was the parish minister, and was educated at Nairn Academy, Aberdeen Grammar School and Marischal College, Aberdeen. He joined the Indian army in 1846, saw active service in the Sikh War of 1848–49 and served throughout the Indian Mutiny of 1857, when he was wounded in the operations for the relief of Lucknow. He returned to England in 1858.

The expedition with John Hanning Speke left Zanzibar in October 1860 and reached Gondokoro in February 1863. Speke led it, but Grant carried out several investigations on his own and made botanical collections. On the western side of Lake Victoria, in December 1861, his right leg became inflamed; abscesses formed for three months, local healers tried their cures, and only by the fifth month had the disease run its course. In April 1862 men sent by Muteesa I of Buganda carried him north on a wicker stretcher.

In July 1862 Grant was still unable to march twenty miles a day, so he and Speke parted, and he was not with Speke when Speke reached the outflow of the White Nile from Lake Victoria. Grant later insisted that only his health had kept him away. His account may be the first recorded description of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection, known as Buruli ulcer.

In 1864 Grant published A Walk across Africa as a supplement to Speke's narrative, dealing with the daily life and customs of the peoples they met and the economic value of the lands they crossed. He received the Patron's Medal of the Royal Geographical Society in 1864 and the Companionship of the Bath in 1866. He served in the intelligence department of the Abyssinian expedition of 1868, was made a Companion of the Order of the Star of India, and retired as a lieutenant-colonel.

He married Margaret Thompson Laurie of Edinburgh in 1865 and settled at Nairn, where he died in 1892; he was buried in the crypt of St Paul's Cathedral. His Botany of the Speke and Grant Expedition appeared in the Transactions of the Linnean Society, and Grant's gazelle is named after him.
james-bond: Ian Fleming began writing the first Bond novel, Casino Royale, on 17 February 1952 at his Goldeneye estate in Oracabessa, Jamaica, where he wrote all his Bond books during the months of January and February each year. Jonathan Cape, who did not like the manuscript as much as Fleming's friend William Plomer did, published it in 1953 on the recommendation of Fleming's older brother Peter, an established travel writer. Between 1953 and 1966 twelve novels and two short-story collections appeared, the last two books posthumously.

Bond is an officer of the Secret Intelligence Service, commonly known as MI6, and a Royal Naval Reserve Commander, known by his code number 007. Fleming said he was a compound of all the secret agents and commando types met during the war, among them his brother Peter. For the first five novels Bond carried a Beretta, until the gun expert Geoffrey Boothroyd wrote to Fleming that it was a lady's gun and suggested a Walther PPK; Fleming then named the armourer of MI6 Major Boothroyd. The films added gadgets from Q Branch, which became one of the motifs of the series.

After Fleming's death in 1964 other authors wrote authorised Bond novels, among them Kingsley Amis, John Gardner and Sebastian Faulks. The character has also been adapted for television, radio, comic strips and video games. CBS aired a live one-hour adaptation of Casino Royale on 21 October 1954, in which Barry Nelson played an American Bond.

Eon Productions, owned by Harry Saltzman and Albert R. Broccoli, released Dr. No in 1962 with Sean Connery as 007. The role passed to George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and, from Casino Royale in 2006, Daniel Craig, whose fifth and final film, No Time to Die, appeared in 2021. After Dr. No other studios rushed out imitations, 22 secret agent films in 1966 alone, and Bond was parodied in Carry On Spying (1964) and later the Austin Powers series. The Harry Palmer films, beginning with The Ipcress File (1965), were seen as an anti-Bond. Critics have accused the series of sexism and imperial nostalgia.
james-brooke: James Brooke was born on 29 April 1803 at Bandel, near Calcutta. His father, Thomas Brooke, was an English judge in the Court of Appeal at Bareilly. He was sent to England at twelve for a brief schooling at Norwich School, from which he ran away, and returned to India in 1819 as an ensign in the Bengal Army of the East India Company. He fought in Assam in the First Anglo-Burmese War until he was seriously wounded in 1825. Back in Madras in 1830 he arrived too late to rejoin his unit and resigned his commission. In 1835 he inherited 30,000 pounds, which he used to buy the schooner Royalist.

Brooke sailed for Borneo in 1838 and arrived at Kuching in August to find an uprising against the Sultan of Brunei. He helped the sultan's uncle Pengiran Muda Hashim crush it, and Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II offered him the governorship of Sarawak in 1841 in return. Brooke suppressed piracy in the region. Some Malay nobles in Brunei, unhappy with these measures, arranged the murder of Muda Hashim and his followers, and Brooke, helped by a unit of Britain's China Squadron, took over Brunei and restored the sultan. He was granted the title of Rajah of Sarawak on 24 September 1841, though the official declaration was made on 18 August 1842.

He reformed the administration and codified laws, and pacified the Dayaks, many of whom served in his forces. Britain took possession of the island of Labuan on 24 December 1846, and in 1848 he became its governor and commander-in-chief. On a visit to England in 1847 he received the Freedom of the City of London, became consul-general in Borneo and was made a Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath. In 1851 he was accused of excessive force against native peoples under the guise of anti-piracy, and a commission of inquiry at Singapore in 1854 dismissed the charges. In 1857 he put down an uprising led by Liu Shan Bang.

Brooke died unmarried. He had acknowledged a son to his family in 1858, and in 1861 he named his nephew John Brooke Johnson Brooke as his successor. After a quarrel he deposed John and named John's brother Charles Anthoni Johnson Brooke instead. He died on 11 June 1868 at Burrator in Devon, after three strokes in his last ten years, and was buried at St Leonard's Church at Sheepstor. The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace praised his hospitality at Sarawak. Brooke's Point on Palawan in the Philippines is named after him, as are several species, among them Rajah Brooke's birdwing.
james-bruce: James Bruce of Kinnaird was born on 14 December 1730 at Kinnaird, Stirlingshire, and was educated at Harrow School and Edinburgh University. He began to study for the bar but entered the wine trade through his marriage to a merchant's daughter, who died in October 1754, within nine months of the marriage. Examining oriental manuscripts at the Escorial led him to the study of Arabic and Geʽez. In 1763 he reached Algiers as British consul, and from August 1765 he explored Roman ruins in Barbary, then travelled to Crete, Syria, Palmyra and Baalbek, making careful drawings and acquiring enough medicine to pass in the East as a physician.

In June 1768 Bruce arrived at Alexandria, resolved to discover the source of the Nile. He gained the support of the Mamluk ruler Ali Bey at Cairo, reached Massawa on 19 September 1769 and Gondar, then the capital of Ethiopia, on 14 February 1770. He was well received by Emperor Tekle Haymanot II and Ras Mikael Sehul, and received court appointments, including command of the Koccob Horse, the emperor's household cavalry. Setting out again in October 1770, he reached Gish Abay, the source of the Lesser Abay, on 14 November 1770. He admitted that the White Nile was the longer stream but argued that the Blue Nile was the Nile of the ancients.

The Jesuit Pedro Páez had reached the source of the Blue Nile in 1618, and Jerónimo Lobo had visited it in 1629. Bruce disputed Páez's visit and suggested that Athanasius Kircher had fabricated the passage, though later research showed that Lobo's description was correct in its details. Leaving Gondar in December 1771, Bruce went by Sennar to Nubia, the first European to trace the Blue Nile to its confluence with the White Nile. At Sennar his house was attacked by thieves, whom he suspected of acting with the knowledge of the king. He reached Aswan on 29 November 1772, Cairo in January 1773 and France in March.

Bruce came to London in June 1774 and was interviewed by James Boswell; offended by the incredulity with which his story was received, he retired to Kinnaird. His Travels to Discover the Source of the Nile, in five quarto volumes, appeared in 1790 and sold well but was assailed by other travellers as unworthy of credence; the substantial accuracy of his Ethiopian travels has since been demonstrated. He brought back Ethiopian manuscripts, including three copies of the Book of Enoch, a text lost in Europe since the Middle Ages, whose arrival marks the beginning of modern studies of it. He died on 27 April 1794 of injuries from a fall down stairs at Kinnaird House the day before.
james-bruce-8th-earl-of-elgin: James Bruce was born in London on 20 July 1811, the son of the 7th Earl of Elgin and his second wife, Elizabeth Oswald. Bruce was educated at Eton College and Christ Church, Oxford, graduating with a first in Classics in 1832, and became a friend of William Ewart Gladstone there. He was elected a Member of Parliament for Southampton in 1841, but the election was declared void, and in November 1841 he succeeded his father as Earl of Elgin.

Elgin was Governor of Jamaica from 1842. In 1847 he became Governor General of the Province of Canada, where the first real attempts at responsible government began. In 1849 the Baldwin-Lafontaine government passed the Rebellion Losses Bill, compensating French Canadians for losses in the rebellions of 1837. Elgin gave royal assent, and an English-speaking mob burned the Parliament Buildings in Montreal and assaulted him. Rather than call in the military he withdrew his family to their country residence and let the civil authorities restore order. In 1854 he negotiated the Reciprocity Treaty with the United States and gave assent to the law abolishing the seigneurial system in Quebec, then resigned.

In 1857 he was appointed High Commissioner and Plenipotentiary in China and the Far East. He signed the Treaty of Tientsin on 26 June 1858 and in August 1858 the Treaty of Amity and Commerce with Japan. After Chinese troops attacked British positions in 1859 he returned in 1860 to demand an apology, the execution of the treaty and an indemnity. On 18 October 1860 he ordered the Old Summer Palace destroyed in retaliation for the torture and execution of almost twenty European and Indian prisoners, and on 24 October he signed the Convention of Peking, which ceded part of Kowloon Peninsula to Britain.

In 1862 Elgin became viceroy and governor-general of India, the first viceroy appointed directly by the Crown. While travelling to Sialkot in 1863 he suffered a heart attack as he crossed a rope and wood bridge over the Chadly river, and he died on 20 November 1863. He was buried at St. John in the Wilderness in Dharamshala. Places named for him in Ontario include Elgin County, Bruce County and the towns of Kincardine, Port Elgin and Bruce Mines, and the Bruce Peninsula.
james-busby: Busby was born in Edinburgh, the son of the English engineer John Busby and Sarah Kennedy, and emigrated with his parents to Sydney in 1824. Under a policy that encouraged free settlers with capital, he received a grant of 2,000 acres in the Coal River area of the Hunter Valley and began growing grapes, while running the farm and teaching viticulture at the Male Orphans School near Liverpool.

After losing that post in 1827 and serving as head tax collector until 1829, he returned to England in 1831 to petition the Colonial Office and toured the vineyards of Spain and France, bringing back the first collection of vine stock to Australia. A report on the state of New Zealand won him the post of British Resident in March 1832.

Busby married Agnes Dow in the Hunter Region on 1 November 1832 and reached the Bay of Islands on HMS Imogene on 5 May 1833. His duties, set by Governor Richard Bourke of New South Wales, were to protect British commerce and mediate between European settlers and Māori, but he was given no means to enforce his authority. The Treaty House built for him at Waitangi still stands, and wine was made there from his vines before those in Australia bore fruit.

The flag was proposed after an unregistered New Zealand ship was seized in Australia, and the Declaration of Independence answered the plan of Baron Charles de Thierry to claim French sovereignty. Tribal fighting in 1836 and 1837 led Busby to call his position untenable, and Bourke sent William Hobson to assess it. With Hobson he co-wrote the Treaty of Waitangi, first signed on 5 and 6 February 1840.

Busby declined a post in the colonial government and turned to farming, but debt and long litigation over his land titles followed; in 1868 he settled for scrip worth £36,800, which he sold for £23,000 after spending nearly £14,000 on legal fees. He sat on the Auckland Provincial Council from 1853 and edited the Aucklander from 1861 to 1863. He died at Anerley in England on 15 July 1871 and was buried at West Norwood Cemetery. Viscount Bledisloe bought the derelict Waitangi property in the 1930s and gave it to the New Zealand Government.
james-butler-1st-duke-of-ormonde: James Butler was born on 19 October 1610 at Clerkenwell in London, the eldest son of Thomas Butler, Viscount Thurles, and his English Catholic wife Elizabeth Pointz. His father died in a shipwreck off Anglesey in 1619, and in 1623 King James I made the boy a ward of Richard Preston, Earl of Desmond, and placed him with George Abbot, Archbishop of Canterbury, to be brought up a Protestant. Unlike almost all his Butler relatives he remained one. At Christmas 1629 he married his cousin Lady Elizabeth Preston, Desmond's heiress, ending a long quarrel between the families.

Having succeeded his grandfather as 12th Earl of Ormond, he became the chief supporter of Thomas Wentworth, later Earl of Strafford, and in 1640 was made commander-in-chief of the forces in Ireland. After the rebellion of 1641 he cleared the country around Dublin, lifted the siege of Drogheda and won the Battle of Kilrush, and he was created Marquess of Ormond on 30 August 1642. In 1643 he agreed a ceasefire with the Catholic Confederation and sent troops to fight for Charles I in England, and he was sworn in as Lord Lieutenant on 21 January 1644.

The Confederates rejected his First Ormond Peace of 28 March 1646, and in 1647 he handed Dublin to the Parliamentarians. Returning in 1648, he made peace with the Confederates on 17 January 1649 and commanded their armies with the Royalists, but he was routed at the Battle of Rathmines in August 1649 and could not stop the Cromwellian conquest. Ousted from command late in 1650, he spent the following years in exile with Charles II, his Irish lands confiscated.

After the Restoration he was created Duke of Ormond on 30 March 1661 and became Lord Lieutenant again, passing the Act of Explanation in 1665. Removed in 1669, he was elected Chancellor of the University of Oxford, escaped an attempt by Thomas Blood to carry him off and hang him in December 1670, and served once more as Lord Lieutenant from 1677, his last act being to proclaim James II in Dublin. He died at Kingston Lacy in Dorset on 21 July 1688 and was buried in Westminster Abbey; his grandson James succeeded as 2nd Duke.
james-clerk-maxwell: James Clerk Maxwell was born on 13 June 1831 at 14 India Street, Edinburgh, the son of John Clerk Maxwell of Middlebie, an advocate, and Frances Cay. His mother took charge of his early education, and at eight he could recite long passages of John Milton and the whole of the 119th psalm. She died of abdominal cancer in December 1839. On 12 February 1842 his father took him to Robert Davidson's demonstration of electric propulsion and magnetic force. He studied at the University of Edinburgh from 1847 and discovered photoelasticity there. In October 1850 he went to Cambridge and graduated in 1854 from Trinity.

In 1856 Maxwell became head of the department of natural philosophy at Marischal College in Aberdeen. He studied the rings of Saturn and correctly proposed that they were made of numerous small particles, for which he won the Adams Prize in 1859. At King's College London, from 1860 to 1865, he did what was probably the most productive work of his career: he won the Rumford Medal in 1860 for his work on colour, was elected to the Royal Society in 1861. Around 1862 he calculated that an electromagnetic field travels at about the speed of light, and his paper A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field of 1865 showed that electric and magnetic fields travel through space as waves.

He also worked on the kinetic theory of gases, first deriving the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. In 1871 he came back to Cambridge as the first Cavendish Professor of Physics and oversaw the construction of the Cavendish Laboratory.

In April 1879 Maxwell began to have difficulty swallowing, the first symptom of his fatal illness. He died in Cambridge of abdominal cancer on 5 November 1879, aged 48, the same age and of the same type of cancer as his mother. Albert Einstein described his work on the centenary of Maxwell's birth as the most profound and fruitful that physics had experienced since the time of Newton, and when told in 1922 that he stood on Newton's shoulders he replied that he stood on those of Maxwell.
james-cook: James Cook was born on 7 November 1728 in the village of Marton in the North Riding of Yorkshire, the second of eight children of a Scottish farm labourer. His father's employer paid for him to attend a school run by a charitable foundation, and after five years of schooling he began working for his father, by then a farm manager. On 17 June 1755 he enlisted in the Royal Navy at Wapping. In the Seven Years' War he took part in the capture of the Fortress of Louisbourg in 1758 and surveyed the entrance to the St. Lawrence River, then spent five seasons charting the coast of Newfoundland. This work brought him to the attention of the Admiralty and the Royal Society.

Cook's first voyage, in HMS Endeavour from 1768 to 1771, was sponsored jointly by the Royal Navy and the Royal Society. Its stated purpose was to observe the 1769 transit of Venus from Tahiti, and secret orders told him to search for the supposed southern continent, Terra Australis, and to claim lands for Britain. In October 1769 he landed at Poverty Bay in New Zealand and, with the aid of the Tahitian priest Tupaia, was the first European to communicate with the Māori, though early encounters turned violent and several Māori were shot dead. On 19 April 1770 the crew sighted Point Hicks, the first European encounter with Australia's eastern coast.

On the second voyage, from 1772 to 1775, his crews became on 17 January 1773 the first recorded Europeans to cross the Antarctic Circle, though Cook never sighted Antarctica. He concluded that no polar landmass reached beyond about 50°S. The third voyage, from 1776, sought a North-West Passage; Cook visited Kerguelen Island and Hawaii and explored the coast of North America to the Bering Strait. He is credited with early work on preventing scurvy, and the Royal Society awarded him the Copley Medal.

Cook returned to Hawaii in late November 1778 and landed at Kealakekua Bay on Hawaiʻi Island, where King Kalaniʻōpuʻu received him with respect. Many Hawaiians appear to have thought him an embodiment of the god Lono. After the ships left, a gale broke Resolution's foremast and they returned for repairs. Relations had worsened, and on 13 February 1779 Hawaiians stole one of his cutters. Cook was killed the next day. His voyages greatly expanded European knowledge of the Pacific. Historians debate his responsibility for violent encounters with Indigenous peoples, for the spread of infectious diseases and for claiming lands without consent.
james-ensor: James Sidney Edouard Ensor was born on 13 April 1860. His father, James Frederic Ensor, was born in Brussels to English parents, and his mother, Maria Catherina Haegheman, was Belgian. He spent his childhood in a souvenir shop run by his parents and was fascinated by the carnival masks sold there, which became a source of inspiration. He left school at fifteen to train with two local painters, and from 1877 to 1880 he attended the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts in Brussels. He first exhibited in 1881. From 1880 until 1917 he had his studio in the attic of his parents' house, and he travelled very little.

His early works, such as Russian Music of 1881 and The Drunkards of 1883, show realistic scenes in a sombre style. His palette then brightened and his subjects became increasingly bizarre. Paintings such as The Scandalized Masks of 1883 and Skeletons Fighting over a Hanged Man of 1891 show figures in grotesque masks, and he dressed skeletons up in his studio. The years from 1888 to 1892 were a turning point, when he turned to religious themes, often the torments of Christ. Although he was an atheist, he identified with Christ as a victim of mockery.

In Christ's Entry into Brussels in 1889 a vast carnival mob in grotesque masks advances toward the viewer, with Belgian politicians and members of Ensor's family among them and Christ on his donkey nearly lost in the throng. Les XX rejected it, and it was not publicly shown until 1929. Ensor also made 133 etchings and drypoints, 86 of them between 1886 and 1891. Late 19th-century critics often rejected his work as scandalous.

Recognition came slowly. In 1895 the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium acquired his painting The Lamp Boy, and he had his first solo exhibition in Brussels. He was named a baron by King Albert in 1929 and received the Légion d'honneur in 1933. His output fell after the first decade of the 20th century, and historians have generally seen his last forty or fifty years as a period of decline. He turned increasingly to music and played the harmonium for visitors. He died in Ostend on 19 November 1949, aged 89.

He influenced expressionist and surrealist artists such as Paul Klee, Emil Nolde, George Grosz and Alfred Kubin. His work is in the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Musée d'Orsay, among others.
james-fitzjames-1st-duke-of-berwick: FitzJames was born at Moulins in France on 21 August 1670, before his father's accession, and was brought up in France as a Catholic. His mother was Arabella Churchill, sister of John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough. He was educated at the Stuarts' expense at the College of Juilly, the Collège du Plessis and the Jesuit College of La Flèche, served the Duke of Lorraine at the Siege of Buda in 1686 and fought at the Battle of Mohács. In 1687 his father created him Duke of Berwick, and he became Governor of Portsmouth and a Knight of the Garter. After the Glorious Revolution he went into exile with James II in December 1688.

In Ireland he fought at the Siege of Derry, the Battle of Cavan and the Battle of the Boyne, where he led a charge and was unhorsed. He was at Aughrim on 22 June 1691, with Patrick Sarsfield's corps, and the Treaty of Limerick of 3 October sent the Irish troops, the Wild Geese, to the Continent.

Berwick then served in Louis XIV's army under the Duke of Luxembourg, at Steenkerque and Landen, where his uncle Charles Churchill took him prisoner and he was ransomed for 30,000 florins. His support for his father led Parliament to attaint him in 1695, forfeiting his English peerages. In the War of the Spanish Succession he commanded in Spain, and after his expedition against Nice in 1706 he became a French subject and Marshal of France.

On 25 April 1707 he won the Battle of Almanza, where an Englishman leading a Franco-Spanish army defeated the Frenchman Ruvigny leading an Anglo-Portuguese-Dutch one. The victory ended Allied hopes of putting the Habsburg candidate on the Spanish throne. Philip V made him Duke of Liria and Jérica, and Louis XIV made him Duke of Fitz-James in 1710. In 1708 he kept his army intact while Lille fell. The storming of Barcelona on 11 September 1714 was the last great event of the war, and he was named a Knight of the Golden Fleece.

Berwick was military governor of Guienne, where he befriended Montesquieu, and in December 1718 he led an army into Spain against Philip V in the War of the Quadruple Alliance. In 1733 he led the Army of the Rhine in the War of the Polish Succession and took Kehl. He was decapitated by a cannonball at the Siege of Philippsburg on 12 June 1734. He married twice, first Honora, widow of Patrick Sarsfield, and then Anne Bulkeley, and his descendants were the French Dukes of Fitz-James and the Spanish Dukes of Liria and later of Alba.
james-francis-edward-stuart: James Francis Edward Stuart was born on 10 June 1688 at St. James's Palace, the only surviving son of James II of England and his second wife, Mary of Modena, and was created Prince of Wales in July 1688. His birth was unexpected, coming five years after his mother's tenth pregnancy, and it revived disputes over religion. Rumours spread among Anglicans that the child was an impostor smuggled into the birth chamber in a warming pan, and James II published the testimony of over seventy witnesses in October 1688.

On 9 December Mary of Modena, disguised as a laundress, escaped to France with the infant. He grew up at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye, which Louis XIV had given to the exiled king, and received a military education. When James II was dying in 1701 he urged his son never to give up his Catholic faith.

On his father's death in September 1701 Louis XIV proclaimed him rightful king, and Spain, the Papal States and Modena also recognised him; he was attainted for treason in London on 2 March 1702. A French attempt to land him at the Firth of Forth on 23 March 1708 was intercepted by the fleet of Admiral Sir George Byng. He served as a volunteer in the French army in the War of the Spanish Succession and was noted for his valour at Oudenarde.

In 1714 Robert Harley and Lord Bolingbroke hinted that his conversion to Protestantism would ease his accession, but he refused, writing that he had chosen his own course. After the Hanoverian accession he reached Scotland on 22 December 1715, set up court at Scone Palace in January 1716 and sailed back to France from Montrose on 5 February, leaving his allies ill-disposed towards him. A further expedition from Spain in 1719 ended at the Battle of Glen Shiel.

James settled in papal territory and from 1718 lived in Rome, in the Palazzo Muti offered by Pope Clement XI, where he held a Jacobite court and received English visitors on the Grand Tour. On 3 September 1719 he married Maria Clementina Sobieska, a granddaughter of King John III Sobieski of Poland; their sons were Charles Edward Stuart and Henry Benedict Stuart, later a cardinal. The 1745 rising was led by Charles, and the two quarrelled bitterly.

James died on 1 January 1766 at the Palazzo Muti and was buried in the crypt of St. Peter's Basilica. The pope then declined to recognise Charles, and over the following decade Rome accepted the Hanoverian dynasty as rulers of Britain and Ireland.
james-frazer: Frazer was born on 1 January 1854 in Glasgow, the son of Katherine Brown and Daniel F. Frazer, a chemist. He studied at the University of Glasgow and at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he graduated with honours in classics and remained a Classics Fellow all his life. He went on to study law at the Middle Temple but never practised. He was knighted in 1914. In 1896 he married Elizabeth Grove, known as Lilly, a writer who became his manager and publicist and arranged translations of his work into French.

Frazer's interest in social anthropology was aroused by E. B. Tylor's Primitive Culture of 1871 and encouraged by his friend, the biblical scholar William Robertson Smith. Except for visits to Italy and Greece he did not travel widely; his data came from ancient histories and from questionnaires mailed to missionaries and imperial officials around the world. He was the first scholar to describe in detail the relations between myths and rituals.

The Golden Bough appeared in two volumes in 1890, in three in 1900, and in a third edition of twelve volumes finished in 1915, with a thirteenth added in 1936. Lilly Frazer compiled an abridgement in 1922. In the third edition Frazer proposed that cultures pass from magic to religion to science. He saw magic and science as alike in their stress on experiment, and religion as belief in personal supernatural forces that are to be appeased. He also wrote a six-volume commentary on Pausanias's description of Greece, which scholars still value.

The Golden Bough reached beyond academia. Sigmund Freud cited Frazer's Totemism and Exogamy in Totem and Taboo, and the cycle of life, death and rebirth that Frazer saw behind many peoples' myths captivated artists and poets; the most notable product was T. S. Eliot's poem The Waste Land of 1922. Frazer's vision of the annual sacrifice of a Year-King has not been borne out by field studies.

Late-20th-century scholars criticised the work. Edmund Leach objected to its comparisons between widely separated cultures, and the historian Timothy Larsen argued that Frazer applied Christian terms such as baptism to non-Christian cultures. More recently the book has been criticised for assuming that European peasants, Aboriginal Australians and Africans represented earlier stages of cultural evolution. Frazer and his wife died in Cambridge within a few hours of each other on 7 May 1941.
james-hannington: James Hannington was born on 3 September 1847 at Hurstpierpoint in Sussex, into the family that ran the Hanningtons department stores. He was an indifferent pupil at the Temple School in Brighton, left at fifteen to work in his father's Brighton counting house, and rose to the rank of major in the 1st Sussex Artillery Volunteer Corps. The family, who had been Congregationalists, joined the Church of England in 1867.

At twenty-one Hannington entered St Mary Hall, Oxford, to prepare for a clerical career. He was made a deacon on 1 March 1874 by Frederick Temple, Bishop of Exeter, served a curacy at Martinhoe with Trentishoe in Devon, and from 1875 was curate-in-charge at St George's, Hurstpierpoint. Moved by news of the murder of two missionaries by Lake Victoria, he offered himself to the Church Missionary Society and in 1882 sailed for Zanzibar at the head of a party of six missionaries, but fever and dysentery forced him home in 1883.

On 24 June 1884 Edward White Benson, Archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated him bishop for the See of Eastern Equatorial Africa, and in January 1885 he left again for Africa. From Freretown near Mombasa he set out to open a shorter and healthier highland road to Buganda, unaware of how sensitive Busoga was for the Buganda state. German moves at the coast and an oracle saying that Buganda's conqueror would come from the east deepened the suspicion of Kabaka Mwanga II, who forbade him to cross Busoga; Hannington refused to turn back.

He reached a spot near Lake Victoria on 21 October and was imprisoned by Basoga chiefs on Mwanga's orders. After eight days his porters were killed, and on 29 October 1885 he was speared at Kyando village; his reported last words were "Go, tell Mwanga I have purchased the road to Uganda with my blood." Widespread persecution of Christians followed, and Hannington and his companions are counted among the first Martyrs of Uganda. His remains were reburied at Namirembe on 31 December 1892, and the Church of England and the Episcopal Church honour him on 29 October.
james-hargreaves: James Hargreaves was born at Stanhill, Oswaldtwistle, in Lancashire, and was described as a stout, broad-set man of about five foot ten. He was illiterate and worked as a hand loom weaver for most of his life. Baptismal records show he had thirteen children, of whom the author Baines in 1835 knew six or seven. He was one of three men credited with the mechanisation of spinning: Richard Arkwright patented the water frame in 1769, and Samuel Crompton combined the jenny and the frame into the spinning mule in 1779.

The spinning jenny was invented in 1764 or 1765. The idea is said to have come when a one-thread spinning wheel was overturned on the floor and Hargreaves saw both the wheel and the spindle still revolving. He realised that if several spindles were placed upright side by side, several threads might be spun at once. The jenny could produce only cotton weft threads and not yarn of enough quality for the warp, which Arkwright's spinning frame later supplied.

Hargreaves built a jenny for himself and sold several to neighbours. Other hand spinners welcomed it at first, until the price of yarn fell. Opposition to the machine led him to leave for Nottingham, where the cotton hosiery industry gained from the increased supply of yarn. There he made jennies for a man named Shipley. His patent of 12 June 1770 provided the basis for legal action, later withdrawn, against Lancashire manufacturers who had begun using the machine. With a partner, Thomas James, he ran a small mill at Hockley and lived in the next house.

Hargreaves carried on the business until he died on 22 April 1778, when his wife received a payment of £400. Samuel Crompton stated that he had learned to spin in 1769 on a jenny that Hargreaves had built.

A distorted account of his life has persisted since Richard Guest wrote in the Edinburgh Review in 1828. Parish burial records show that Hargreaves did not die in the workhouse, as was claimed. In the 1780s a legal battle annulled Arkwright's most important patents, with Thomas Highs claiming to be the true inventor of both the spinning frame and the jenny, but the question of authorship was not settled. Records show that neither Hargreaves's wife nor any of his daughters was called Jenny, contrary to a myth repeated in school textbooks; jenny was Lancashire slang for an engine in the eighteenth century.
james-henry-craig: Craig came of a Scottish family; his father was a judge of the civil and military courts in Gibraltar. In 1763, at the age of 15, he was enrolled as an ensign in the 30th (Cambridgeshire) Regiment of Foot. With the backing of Colonel Robert Boyd, lieutenant governor of Gibraltar, he became an aide-de-camp, which later allowed him to command a company of the 47th (Lancashire) Regiment of Foot in the American colonies.

In the American War of Independence he was badly wounded at the Battle of Bunker Hill but stayed with his regiment, took part in the defence of Quebec in 1776, and was wounded twice in 1777 in the actions at Fort Ticonderoga, Hubbardton and Freeman's Farm. On the recommendation of Major-General John Burgoyne he was made a major in the 82nd Regiment of Foot, with which he served from 1778 to 1781 in Nova Scotia, at Penobscot and in North Carolina, usually leading light infantry.

Promoted lieutenant-colonel in 1781, he became Lieutenant Governor of Guernsey in 1793 and adjutant general to the Duke of York in the Netherlands in 1794. After French revolutionary armies overran the Netherlands he led the British force sent to secure the Cape, which he governed until 1797, receiving the Order of the Bath. He then fought in India, was promoted lieutenant-general in January 1801, and in 1805, despite poor health, led the Anglo-Russian invasion of Naples, abandoned after the Austrian defeat at the Battle of Ulm.

From 1807 to 1811 he was both Governor-General of British North America and lieutenant-governor of Lower Canada. He considered creating English counties and replacing the legislative assembly with an appointed government to strengthen English speakers in a mainly French province, and encouraged immigration from Britain and the United States in the hope of making the French a minority. In 1809 he employed a former army officer of the United States, John Henry, to learn whether the Federalist New England states wished to secede; Henry later sold the correspondence to President James Madison for $50,000. Craig died on 12 January 1812.
james-i-of-aragon: James was born at Montpellier on 2 February 1208, the only son of Peter II of Aragon and Marie of Montpellier. His father tried to placate the crusaders of the Albigensian Crusade by arranging a marriage between the two-year-old James and Amicie, daughter of Simon IV de Montfort, and in 1211 entrusted the boy to Montfort's care. Peter was killed at the Battle of Muret on 12 September 1213, and Pope Innocent III insisted that Montfort give James up.

James was raised at Monzón by Guillem de Montredó, head of the Knights Templar in Aragon and Provence. In 1217 the Templars and some loyal nobles brought him to Zaragoza. In 1221 he married Eleanor, daughter of Alfonso VIII of Castile, and rebellions by nobles filled the next six years until the Peace of Alcalá of 31 March 1227.

After a scheme to inherit Navarre came to nothing, James turned south and east. On 5 September 1229 a fleet of 155 ships carrying 1,500 horsemen and 15,000 soldiers sailed for Majorca, which fell on 31 December 1229; Menorca followed in 1232 and Ibiza in 1235. Valencia capitulated on 28 September 1238. By the Treaty of Almizra of 26 March 1244 James and Alfonso X of Castile fixed the border of the new Kingdom of Valencia.

In May 1258 the Treaty of Corbeil ended his conflict with Louis IX of France: France renounced claims of sovereignty over Catalonia, and James gave up his rights in Provence. Catalonia's ties with Languedoc faded as a result. In 1269 he assembled a fleet for a crusade, but a storm drove him to Aigues-Mortes and he abandoned the voyage.

James compiled the Llibre del Consolat de Mar, which governed maritime trade, and sponsored the University of Montpellier. In 1263 he presided over the Barcelona Disputation between the rabbi Nahmanides and the convert Pablo Christiani. He wrote or dictated the Llibre dels fets, the first autobiography by a Christian king and an early work of Catalan prose. At the urging of his confessor Ramon de Penyafort he brought the Inquisition into his realm in 1233.

In his will he divided his lands between his sons by Yolanda of Hungary: Peter received the mainland kingdoms and James the Kingdom of Majorca, a division that led to conflict between the brothers. James died at Valencia on 27 July 1276.
james-ii-of-aragon: James II, called the Just, was born at Valencia, the second son of Peter III of Aragon and Constance II of Sicily. He succeeded his father in Sicily and, on the death of his elder brother Alfonso III in 1291, in Aragon and the rest of the Spanish territories, including Majorca. He was also Count of Barcelona and King of Valencia. His full title for the last three decades of his reign was James, by the grace of God, king of Aragon, Valencia, Sardinia and Corsica, and count of Barcelona.

In Sicily James was crowned at Palermo and was excommunicated by Pope Honorius IV in response. By a peace treaty with King Charles II of Naples he agreed to give up Sicily, but the Sicilians installed his younger brother Frederick on the throne, and Frederick reigned there until his death in 1337. Pope Boniface VIII then asked James, with Charles II, to remove Frederick, and enticed him by investing him with the title to Sardinia and Corsica and appointing him papal gonfalonier. James could not disguise his apathy and returned to Aragon. By the Treaty of Anagni in 1295 he returned the Balearic Islands to his uncle James II of Majorca, who recognised his suzerainty by the Treaty of Argilers in 1298.

Back in Aragon, James sought access to the Muslim south, from which Castile restricted his kingdom. With his admiral Bernat de Sarrià he allied with the enemies of the young Ferdinand IV of Castile, wanting Murcia for access to Granada; his allies entered it from all directions in 1296, and he held Murcia until 1304. In 1313 he granted administrative and political autonomy to the Aran Valley, described in a Latin manuscript called the Querimonia. He was nominally king of Sardinia and Corsica from 1297 but acquired Sardinia only by conquest in 1324. In 1321 he ordered the arrest and torture of French lepers seeking shelter in his realm.

James composed one surviving piece of Occitan poetry, a religious dansa to the Virgin Mary titled Mayre de Deu, probably during his time in Sicily. Arnau de Vilanova wrote a verse-by-verse Latin commentary on it in 1305. It compares the Church to a ship in a storm, poorly guided by its pilot, the Pope, and its final verses ask Mary to protect the king from sin. It seems to have been written when James was in conflict with the papacy, perhaps to show his piety and fidelity to the Church.

James married four times: Isabella of Castile, a marriage never consummated and annulled; Blanche of Anjou, daughter of Charles II of Naples, with whom he had several children, among them his successor Alfonso IV; Marie of Lusignan; and Elisenda de Montcada.
james-ii-of-cyprus: James was born in Nicosia to John II of Cyprus and Marietta de Patras, and he was a favourite of his father. In 1456 he was appointed Archbishop of Nicosia. After he murdered Iacopo Urri, the royal chamberlain, on 1 April 1457, he lost the archbishopric and fled to Rhodes on a ship of the Catalan Juan Tafures. His father pardoned him and restored the see to him.

When John II died in 1458, his daughter Charlotte became queen. In 1460, backed by the Mamluk sultan of Egypt Sayf al-Din Inal, James challenged her right to the throne and blockaded her and her husband, Louis of Savoy, in the castle of Kyrenia for three years. Charlotte fled to Rome in 1463, and with the fall of Kyrenia in 1464 she and Louis lost their throne in fact. James was crowned in her place.

In gratitude he made his friend and supporter Juan Tafures Master of his Household and titular Count of Tripoli. Seeking political support, he married the 14-year-old Venetian Catherine Cornaro by proxy in Venice on 30 July 1468. She sailed to Cyprus in 1472, and they married in person at Famagusta in October or November of that year.

James died in Famagusta on 10 July 1473, a few months after the wedding, amid suspicion that agents of Venice, possibly Catherine's uncles, had poisoned him. Under his will the pregnant Catherine became regent. Their son, James III, died in suspicious circumstances in 1474 before his first birthday, and Catherine reigned as queen with the island in the hands of Venetian merchants.

Before his marriage James had three children by a mistress: Eugene, Janus and Charlotte of Lusignan. The younger Charlotte was imprisoned by Queen Charlotte's opponents and died in captivity in 1480, shortly before her twelfth birthday. Another mistress, Eschive de Nores, married his cousin Philippe, titular Prince of Galilee.
james-ii-of-england: James was born on 14 October 1633 at St James's Palace, the second surviving son of Charles I and Henrietta Maria of France, and was designated Duke of York at birth. At the age of three he was appointed Lord High Admiral, an honorary post that became a substantive office after the Restoration. He was present at the Battle of Edgehill in October 1642 and spent most of the next four years in the Royalist capital of Oxford.

After the Restoration of 1660 he was created Duke of Albany in Scotland and was confirmed as Lord High Admiral. In October 1660 Charles II made him Governor of the Royal Adventurers into Africa, the company later reformed as the Royal African Company, which over its lifetime carried more enslaved Africans across the Atlantic than any other single institution.

The Exclusion Crisis of 1679–81, when the Whigs tried to bar him from the succession, failed because the memory of the Commonwealth made the public reluctant to undermine hereditary succession. Charles II died on 6 February 1685, and James succeeded with widespread support, many believing that a Catholic monarchy would be temporary. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 23 April 1685.

He enlarged the standing army and used his dispensing power to let Roman Catholics command regiments without taking the oath required by the Test Act. When Parliament objected he prorogued it in November 1685, and it never met again in his reign. In April 1688 he re-issued the Declaration of Indulgence and ordered the clergy to read it. Seven bishops who petitioned against it were tried for seditious libel and acquitted on 30 June, and the birth of his son James Francis Edward on 10 June raised the prospect of a Catholic dynasty.

Leading English figures invited William of Orange, James's nephew and son-in-law, who landed at Brixham on 5 November 1688. James's army deserted and he went into exile in France on 23 December. In February 1689 a Convention Parliament held that he had vacated the throne and installed William and Mary. James landed in Ireland in March 1689 with French help, but William defeated him at the Battle of the Boyne on 1 July 1690 (Old Style), and James fled to France, never to return. He lived at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, under Louis XIV's protection, until his death on 16 September 1701.

His son was recognised as James III and VIII by his supporters, later called Jacobites, and led a rising in 1715. Historians have disagreed on James: Macaulay cast him as a cruel absolutist, while some 20th-century writers praised his advocacy of religious tolerance, and more recent scholarship takes a middle course.
james-ii-of-majorca: James II of Majorca was born on 31 May 1243, the second son of James I of Aragon and his wife Violant, daughter of Andrew II of Hungary. He inherited from his father three of the Balearic Islands, Majorca, Ibiza and Formentera, together with the counties of Roussillon and Cerdanya, the lordship of Montpellier, the barony of Aumelas and the viscounty of Carladès. He also received tribute from Menorca, which stayed under Muslim control throughout his life. He was King of Majorca and Lord of Montpellier from 1276 until his death.

James ruled as a vassal of his brother Peter III of Aragon, a status he tried to escape. France and Aragon contested Sicily, and James, holding borderlands that could not be defended, made an agreement with King Philip III of France, the widower of his sister Isabella. This strained relations with Aragon. Peter seized Perpignan, and although James escaped, Peter sent two of his sons to Barcelona. James then sided with the French. By the Treaty of Perpignan in 1279 he became a vassal of the Crown of Aragon. His nephew Alfonso III of Aragon annexed the Balearic Islands, but the Treaty of Anagni returned them in 1295.

After that James worked to make the kingdom viable. He reformed urban planning, set agricultural policy, created a new monetary system, promoted textile industries and increased the crown's power over the nobility and the Church. In 1302 he began creating his own consulates along the North African coast. The suppression of the Knights Templar let him seize their tithes on the islands.

James ordered the construction of the palace at Perpignan, the Palace of Almudaina, the Cathedral of Santa Maria at Palma de Mallorca, known as La Seu, and Bellver Castle. In 1275 he married Esclaramunda of Foix, daughter of Roger IV of Foix, in a marriage he arranged himself. They had six children, among them Sancho, who succeeded as king, and Ferdinand, father of James III. Another son, James, became a Franciscan friar. He died on 29 May 1311.
james-ii-of-scotland: James was born at Holyrood Palace on 16 October 1430, the younger twin son of James I and Joan Beaufort. His brother Alexander died within months, leaving him the only surviving son. The Auchinleck chronicle called his birthmark, which covered one side of his face, the fyre mark in his face. He was crowned at Holyrood Abbey on 26 March 1437, aged six. The regency was marked by disorder, famine and plague. On 24 November 1440 the regents Crichton and Avandale invited the young William, 6th Earl of Douglas, to Edinburgh Castle, where he was beheaded in the event known as the Black Dinner.

The Douglas family dominated Scottish politics in the 1440s under William, 8th Earl of Douglas, who in 1443 used the twelve-year-old king's banner to take a Crichton tower. James began his personal rule in 1449, and married Mary of Guelders at Holyrood Abbey on 3 July 1449. In September 1449 he attacked the Livingston family, and the comptroller Robert Livingston was executed. In 1451 John, Earl of Ross, attacked royal castles, and Douglas, allied with Ross and the Earl of Crawford, refused to support the king.

On 22 February 1452 the king and Douglas dined at Stirling. James asked him to dissolve the alliance, Douglas refused, and James stabbed him twice before his attendants joined in. The killing of a man under royal protection damaged James's standing.

The new earl, James, 9th Earl of Douglas, burned Stirling in March 1452. A parliament cleared the king of the murder. In August 1455 parliament disinherited the Douglases for treason, and James distributed their lands, creating new earldoms after 1457. He attacked English Berwick in 1455, exploiting the Wars of the Roses, and renounced the truce with England in May 1456.

James was killed at Roxburgh on 3 August 1460 when a bombard near him exploded, probably during a salute for the queen's arrival at the siege. The historian John Major blamed him for being over-curious in the matter of engines of war. The castle fell on 8 August, and James III was crowned at Kelso Abbey on 10 August. James II was buried at Holyrood Abbey. His widow Mary of Guelders became the leading figure in Scottish politics and was formally appointed regent in 1461. James has been described as a largely successful king who strengthened the Scottish monarchy.
james-ii-of-urgell: James was born at Balaguer to Peter II of Urgell and Margaret Palaiologue of Montferrat. He belonged to a younger branch of the House of Barcelona and was its last legitimate male member. Besides the county of Urgell, which he inherited from his father in 1408, he was Viscount of Àger and lord of Antillón, Alcolea de Cinca and Fraga. In Valencia on 29 June 1407 he married Isabella, a daughter of Peter IV of Aragon, and in 1408 he was made lieutenant of the Kingdom of Aragon.

When Martin the Younger, heir to the Aragonese crown, died in 1409, King Martin appointed James governor-general, which James took as a sign that he was to be the heir. On the king's death in 1410 he became one of six candidates for the throne. Succession through the male line, as laid down in the will of James I of Aragon, would have given him the crown, but the Compromise of Caspe chose Ferdinand of Antequera instead, and James became the centre of opposition to the House of Trastámara.

Urged on by his mother and by Antón de Luna, he refused to recognise Ferdinand and took up arms. Defeated at Castelflorite and Montearagón, he withdrew to the castle of Balaguer, which royal troops besieged, and surrendered on 31 October 1413. He was held at Teruel and then at Xàtiva, where he died on 1 June 1433. His daughters married into leading houses: Isabella married Peter, Duke of Coimbra, in 1428, and Joanna married John I, Count of Foix, and later John Ramon III, Count of Cardona.
james-iii-of-majorca: James was born in Catania, Sicily, on 5 April 1315, the son of Ferdinand of Majorca and Isabella of Sabran. His maternal grandmother, Margaret of Villehardouin, had fought to reclaim the Principality of Achaea from the Angevins of Naples. Isabella died shortly after his birth, and James was declared Prince of Achaea, with his father as guardian. Ferdinand invaded the Morea and was killed at the Battle of Manolada in 1316. From 1331 the feudal lords of Achaea gradually acknowledged James's rights, and by 1333 the recognition was complete, although the Angevin heirs of Philip I of Taranto continued to press their claim.

James inherited the Kingdom of Majorca on the death of his uncle Sancho in 1324, and his uncle Philip acted as regent until 1329. To keep good relations with the Crown of Aragon he married Constance, daughter of Alfonso IV of Aragon. Kings of Majorca traditionally swore fealty to the kings of Aragon, but James held that no king could exercise authority over another. He supported the University of Montpellier, in his lands on the mainland, and its legal scholars upheld his royal prerogatives.

On 9 May 1337 he issued the Leges palatinae, an intricate legal code for his court, the first of its kind. He also commissioned a finely made illuminated manuscript in an Italian style, which he kept after losing his throne, took to the Roman curia and eventually sold to Philip VI of France.

In 1342 James declined to swear fealty to his cousin Peter IV of Aragon. The scholars of Montpellier and the Aragonese troubadour Thomàs Périz de Fozes, who wrote a poem in his defence, supported him. The dispute led to a brief conflict in which Peter expelled James from Majorca and annexed the Balearic Islands to the Crown of Aragon again. James was called the Rash, or the Unfortunate. He died on 25 October 1349 at the Battle of Llucmajor while trying to recapture the island. His son James IV of Majorca, by Constance, married Joanna I of Naples, and his daughter Isabella married John II of Montferrat.
james-iii-of-scotland: James was the first surviving son of King James II and Mary of Guelders, daughter of Arnold, Duke of Guelders. The exact date and place of his birth are debated. He became king when his father was killed at the siege of Roxburgh Castle on 3 August 1460, and he was crowned at Kelso Abbey a week later. His minority lasted almost a decade.
