He oversaw a systematic effort to establish useful plants, including grapes, potatoes, apples and citrus, and in 1659 established a vineyard to make red wine against scurvy. His daily diary became a basis for exploring the region's resources, and shows that some of his knowledge came from the indigenous peoples.

Van Riebeeck left the Cape in 1662. His wife Maria died in Malacca on 2 November 1664, and he died in Batavia on 18 January 1677. Many Afrikaners came to regard him as the founding father of their nation, and until 1994 his image appeared on stamps and banknotes. His landing was marked on 6 April as Van Riebeeck's Day until the holiday was cancelled after the 1994 election. Statues of him and his wife stand in Adderley Street, Cape Town.
jan-van-ruusbroec: John of Ruusbroec took his name from his native hamlet, modern Ruisbroek near Brussels. His mother was devout, and nothing is known of his father. At eleven he left home without warning to study under his uncle Jan Hinckaert, a canon regular of St. Gudule's in Brussels, who lived with a fellow canon, Frank van Coudenberg. He was ordained in 1318, and his mother, who had followed him to Brussels and entered a beguinage, died shortly before.

From 1318 to 1343 he was a parish priest at St. Gudule's, living with his uncle and Van Coudenberg in great austerity. When Heilwige Bloemardinne spread the ideas of the Brethren of the Free Spirit in popular pamphlets, he answered with pamphlets of his own in Middle Dutch. None survive.

In 1343 Ruusbroec, Hinckaert and Van Coudenberg left for the hermitage of Groenendaal in the Sonian Forest, given to them by John III, Duke of Brabant. The reasons were a wish for a more retired life and possibly the persecution that followed his attack on Bloemardinne. The hermitage became a community of canons regular on 13 March 1349, with Ruusbroec as prior. His fame spread to Holland, Germany and France, and about 1378 he was visited by Geert Groote, founder of the Devotio Moderna. He died at Groenendaal on 2 December 1381, aged 82.

Ruusbroec wrote twelve books, seven epistles, two hymns and a prayer, all in Middle Dutch, the language of ordinary people, to reach a wider audience than Latin allowed. He was beatified on 9 December 1908 by Pope Pius X. His best-known work, The Spiritual Espousals, written around 1340, survives in 36 Dutch manuscripts as well as Latin and Middle High German translations. Its three books treat the active, the interior and the contemplative life. He held that the soul finds God in its own depths and keeps its identity at the summit, and that people are one with God in love, not in essence. Groote felt uneasy about some phrases, and Jean Gerson and Bossuet later found traces of pantheism.
jan-willem-janssens: Janssens was born in Nijmegen on 12 October 1762 and became a cadet in the Dutch army at the age of nine. He was promoted steadily, and by 1793, at the start of the French Revolutionary Wars, was a colonel; he was wounded in that campaign. After the Dutch surrender of 1795 opened the way to the Batavian Republic, a satellite of the French First Republic, he served until 1802 mostly as an administrator in the new Batavian Army.

When the Treaty of Amiens returned the Cape Colony to the Dutch in 1802, Janssens was made its governor. He found few trained troops and little to strengthen its defences, and was promoted lieutenant-general while there. In the War of the Third Coalition a British force under Lieutenant-General Sir David Baird invaded, and Janssens, expecting defeat, met it on 8 January 1806 at the Battle of Blaauwberg near Cape Town. His force was routed, the colony was surrendered on 18 January, and he was shipped back to The Hague, arriving on 8 June 1806.

Louis Bonaparte, king of the new Kingdom of Holland, made him Secretary-General of the Department of War. After France annexed the Netherlands in 1810 he was appointed on 11 November to succeed Herman Willem Daendels as governor-general of the East Indies, reaching Batavia on 15 May 1811. A British fleet under Sir Samuel Auchmuty arrived on 30 July; Janssens defended the fortress of Meester Cornelis, then retreated to Buitenzorg before he surrendered. He was held in Britain until 12 November 1812.

In mid-March 1814 Janssens gathered 3,600 French soldiers from various garrisons and marched through Allied-held country to join Napoleon at Reims. His division fought under Marshal Michel Ney at the Battle of Arcis-sur-Aube, and on 21 March he was wounded in the struggle for the village of Grand-Torcy. He left the French Army on 9 April 1814 and served the new Kingdom of the Netherlands as provisional commissary-general of war, but resigned when he was refused the governorship of the East Indies again, and retired from active duty on 22 May 1815. He died in The Hague on 23 May 1838, aged 75, holding among other honours the Grand Cross of the Military William Order.
jan-zizka: Žižka was born in the village of Trocnov in the Kingdom of Bohemia, into the lower gentry, which owned little estate. His birth date is unknown. A document of 3 April 1378 names a Johannes dictus Zizka de Trocnov as a witness to a marriage contract, and from it historians assume a birth around 1360, though the historian Tomek and others thought that man might have been the general's father. According to the Polish chronicler Jan Długosz, he served as a mercenary on the Polish-Lithuanian side at the Battle of Grunwald on 15 July 1410. A later report says he served Sophia of Bavaria, wife of Wenceslas IV, as chamberlain; his activity in the years 1411 to 1419 is not entirely certain.

Žižka first appears prominently on 30 July 1419, when he joined a Hussite procession led by the priest Jan Želivský in Prague. The crowd stormed the New Town hall and threw councillors from the windows, the First Defenestration of Prague, which is regarded as the start of the Hussite revolution. Žižka then left Prague, defeated partisans of King Sigismund at Sudoměř on 25 March 1420, the first pitched battle of the Hussite wars, and went to Tábor, where he became one of four captains of the people. Pope Martin V proclaimed a crusade on 17 March 1420.

Žižka helped develop the wagon fort. Carts were joined wheel to wheel in a square or circle, with a ditch in front, each crewed by 16 to 22 soldiers, including crossbowmen, handgunners and men with pikes or flails. Artillery provoked the enemy knights into attacking, and shooters aimed first at the horses. He was the first European commander to manoeuvre with medium-calibre cannon mounted on carts.

At Kutná Hora at the end of 1421 he was trapped but broke out to Kolín, and on 6 January 1422 defeated Sigismund's army at Nebovidy. Německý Brod was stormed on 10 January, and its defenders were put to the sword contrary to his orders.

In 1423 dissent among the Hussites led to civil war. As leader of the Taborites, Žižka defeated the men of Prague and the Utraquist nobles at Hořice on 20 April 1423, and the Utraquists under Bořek at Strachov on 4 August. He died on 11 October 1424. A monument to him stands on Vítkov Hill in Prague, and he is regarded as a Czech national hero.
jana-gana-mana: The song's lyrics first appeared in five stanzas in the Bengali magazine Tattwabodhini Patrika, the official publication of the Brahmo Samaj, of which Tagore was then editor, under the title Bharat Bhagya Bidhata. Tagore composed the melody himself in the raga Alhaiya Bilaval, possibly with some help from his musician grand-nephew Dinendranath Tagore.

It was first sung in public on the second day of the Indian National Congress session in Calcutta on 27 December 1911, by Tagore's niece in her school assembly. It was followed in January 1912 at the annual event of the Adi Brahmo Samaj, but remained largely unknown except to readers of the Brahmo journal. On 28 February 1919 Tagore sang it at the Besant Theosophical College in Madanapalle, where Margaret Cousins, the vice-principal, preserved it in Western notation from notes he provided, and where he made his own English translation, The Morning Song of India.

The poem is composed in Sadhu Bhasha, a heavily Sanskritised literary register of Bengali. Its five verses make up a hymn; only the first was adopted as the national anthem. A formal rendition takes about 52 seconds, and a shortened version of the first and last lines takes about 20 seconds.

Its first stanza names the provinces that were under direct British rule, among them Punjab, Sindh, Gujarat, Maratha, Dravida, Utkala and Bengal, but none of the princely states. Defenders hold that Tagore named only border regions in order to include all of India.

Subhas Chandra Bose chose the song as a national anthem while in Germany, and on 11 September 1942 the Hamburg Radio Symphony Orchestra played it as India's anthem at the founding meeting of the German-Indian Society. The Constituent Assembly closed its midnight session on 14 August 1947 with a unanimous performance, and adopted the first stanza as the National Anthem on 24 January 1950.

A dispute arose from reports in the British Indian press that a song of welcome to the Emperor had been sung at the 1911 Congress. Many historians hold the reports mistaken, because a different Hindi song, Badshah Humara, praised George V at the same session, and the nationalist press and the official Congress report distinguished the two. Tagore wrote in 1937 and 1939 that the Lord of Destiny of the song could never be George V or any other George. He had renounced a knighthood in 1919 in protest over the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
janaka: Janaka was the title adopted by the kings of Videha, who ruled from their capital, Mithila, and were descended from King Nimi and his son Mithi, the first king of Videha to bear the title. According to the Vishnu Purana, Nimi founded a city called Jayantpur, later Janakpur, and was cursed to death by the sage Vashishta. As he had no successor, the sages churned his lifeless body, which produced a prince called Mithi, from manthan, churning. He was also called Videha, "the son of the bodiless", and Janaka, because he was born without a father.

The best known Janaka in the Ramayana is Sīradhvaja, son of Hrasvaroman and Kaikasi, who defeated and killed Sudhanvan, king of Samkasya, and gave that kingdom to his brother Kushadhvaja. With his queen Sunayana he found Sita while ploughing as part of a yagna and adopted her; Sunayana later bore Urmila.

Janaka held the svayamvara of Sita, which Rama won, and Urmila married Rama's younger brother Lakshmana. Janaka accompanied Bharata to Chitrakoot when Bharata went to persuade Rama, Sita and Lakshmana to return to Ayodhya. After Rama's return from exile and crowning as king of Kosala, Janaka became an important figure at his court, and Rama took his advice on many occasions. According to legend he was a devotee of Shiva and set up Shivalingas at the four corners of Janakpur.

Late Vedic literature, the Shatapatha Brahmana and the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, mentions a King Janaka, dated to about the 8th or 7th century BCE, as a philosopher-king of Videha whose court was an intellectual centre for Brahmin sages such as Yajnavalkya, Uddalaka Aruni and Gargi Vachaknavi. Janakas are revered as examples of non-attachment, and conversations between a Janaka and sages are recorded in the Ashtavakra Gita and the Parashar Gita. In the Mahabharata he debates the ascetic Sulabha.

In Buddhism Mahājanaka, a king of Mithila, is a previous birth of the Bodhisatta and the hero of Jātaka No. 539, which exemplifies perseverance. After shipwreck, a swim of seven days and the winning of the throne, he renounces it and declares that although Mithila burns, nothing of his is burned. The story appears in temple murals in Burma and Thailand.
janamejaya: The name Janamejaya means man-impelling or victorious from birth. According to the Mahabharata he was the son of King Parikshit and Queen Madravati, the grandson of Abhimanyu and the great-grandson of Arjuna, and he came to the Kuru throne at Hastinapura on his father's death. The epic gives him three brothers, Srutasena, Ugrasena and Bhimasena.

The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa calls him a great conqueror whose family priest, Tura Kāvaṣeya, consecrated him king and officiated at his horse sacrifice. It also records that at one of his sacrifices he employed the Bhūtavīras as priests instead of the Kaśyapas, though he later took back the Asitamr̥ga family of Kaśyapas. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa says he and his brothers performed a horse sacrifice under Indrota Daivāpa Śaunaka to cleanse themselves of sin, and both texts place his capital at Āsandīvat.

His date is uncertain. H. C. Raychaudhuri placed his father in the ninth century BCE, while Michael Witzel links the dynasty with the Black and Red Ware of the Punjab and northern India. Raychaudhuri also noted two pairs of Parikshits and Janamejayas in the genealogies and suspected a bardic duplication of one king. Four copper-plate grants said to date from his reign, found in the 20th century, were shown by historians to be fakes.

The Mahabharata tells that Parikshit died of snakebite through a sage's curse fulfilled by the Naga king Takshaka, and that Janamejaya set out to destroy all serpents in a great Sarpa Satra. A learned sage named Astika, still a boy, intervened, and the king freed the captive Takshaka and ended his enmity with the Nagas. Local tradition places the sacrifice at Parham in Mainpuri district, where a tank called Parikshit kund is said to have been built by him.

According to the Vayu Purana and the Matsya Purana he quarrelled with Vaishampayana, and he may have abdicated afterwards in favour of his son Shatanika. The Devi Bhagavata Purana was also narrated to him, by Vyasa.
janani-luwum: Janani Jakaliya Luwum was born to Acholi parents in the village of Mucwini in the Kitgum District. He attended Gulu High School and Boroboro Teacher Training College and then taught at a primary school. He converted to Christianity in 1948 and in 1949 went to Buwalasi Theological College.

In 1950 Luwum was attached to St. Philip's Church in Gulu. He was ordained a deacon in 1953 and a priest the following year, and served in the Upper Nile Diocese and later in the Diocese of Mbale. In 1969 he was consecrated Bishop of the Diocese of Northern Uganda at Gulu. Five years later he became archbishop of the Metropolitan Province, the second African to hold the office, and he became a leading critic of the excesses of the regime that had taken power in 1971.

In 1977 he delivered a note of protest to Idi Amin against arbitrary killings and unexplained disappearances, and soon afterwards he and other leading churchmen were accused of treason. On 16 February 1977 he was arrested with the cabinet ministers Erinayo Wilson Oryema and Charles Oboth Ofumbi. At a rally in Kampala that day, other suspects read out confessions implicating them, and Luwum was accused of being an agent of the exiled former president Milton Obote and of planning a coup.

The next day Radio Uganda announced that the three had been killed when their car collided with another vehicle as they tried to overpower the driver. Luwum's body was riddled with bullets when it was released to his family. Henry Kyemba, Amin's minister of health, later wrote in A State of Blood that the archbishop had been shot through the mouth and in the chest. Witnesses later testified that the men were taken to an army barracks, beaten and shot. Amin denied reports that he had fired himself; according to Vice President Mustafa Adrisi and a human rights commission, Isaac Maliyamungu carried out the killing.

Luwum was survived by his widow, Mary Lawinyo Luwum, and nine children, and was buried at Mucwini. The Anglican Communion recognises him as a martyr, several Anglican churches honour him on 3 June or 17 February, and since 2015 Uganda has kept 16 February as Archbishop Janani Luwum Day.
janata-party: The Janata Party, whose name means People's Party, was formed from Indian parties opposed to the Emergency that Prime Minister Indira Gandhi imposed between 1975 and 1977. They included the Indian National Congress (Organisation), the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, the Bharatiya Lok Dal, the Socialist Party and defectors from Gandhi's Congress. The Allahabad High Court had found Gandhi guilty of corrupt electoral practices on 12 June 1975, and on 25 June President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed accepted her recommendation to declare the Emergency. Elections were postponed, rallies and strikes banned, the press censored, and thousands of opposition figures were arrested, among them Jayaprakash Narayan, Morarji Desai, Atal Bihari Vajpayee and L. K. Advani.

When elections were called for 1977 and political prisoners released, Narayan insisted that the opposition form a united front. The Janata Party was officially launched on 23 January 1977, and Chandra Shekhar became its first president. Its constituents' ideologies were diverse and often conflicting, but they united behind Narayan's appeal.

In the election campaign Gandhi defended the Emergency as essential to national security, while Janata leaders accused her of ruling as a dictator. The party defeated the Congress (R) in the 1977 general election, and Raj Narain defeated Gandhi in Rae Bareli. Jayaprakash Narayan and Jivatram Kripalani chose Morarji Desai as parliamentary leader, and he became the first non-Congress prime minister of independent India. His government ended the Emergency and censorship, amended the Constitution to make a future emergency harder to declare, and set up inquiries into Emergency-era abuses. Fresh state elections left Janata in power in seven states. Atal Bihari Vajpayee, as Minister of External Affairs, changed foreign policy, and in 1979 visited Beijing.

The party's veteran socialists, trade unionists and pro-business members, and former Jana Sangh members tied to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, were soon divided. When most Janata leaders demanded that Vajpayee and Advani choose between the government and the RSS, the former Jana Sangh members stayed in the RSS and resigned. In July 1979 Desai was forced to resign and Charan Singh replaced him.

Indira Gandhi's new Congress (I) won the 1980 general election, and the Janata Party won only 31 seats, losing 172. The Hindu nationalists regrouped in the Bharatiya Janata Party, and Raj Narain's Janata Party (Secular) became part of the Lokdal, which later merged into the Janata Dal. Many parties still bear the name Janata, among them the Bharatiya Janata Party, the Janata Dal (United) and the Rashtriya Janata Dal. Its end of 30 years of uninterrupted Congress rule helped strengthen India's multi-party democracy.
janatha-vimukthi-peramuna: The party was founded to lead a communist revolution at a time when Sri Lanka already had four other leftist parties, among them the Lanka Sama Samaja Party and the Communist Party of Sri Lanka. Rohana Wijeweera's father, a Communist Party activist, had been paralysed after an assault by UNP members during an election campaign. The party then arranged a scholarship for the son at the Patrice Lumumba Friendship University in Moscow, where he read Marx, Engels and Lenin; after the Sino-Soviet split he joined the pro-Chinese Ceylon Communist Party (Maoist).

In March 1971 an accidental explosion led police to fifty-eight bombs in a hut at Nelundeniya, and Wijeweera was arrested. The other leaders began the uprising at 11:00 p.m. on 5 April. The young and poorly armed insurgents held parts of the southern and central provinces, but within two weeks the government had regained almost all of them, and the army and police were widely seen to have used excessive force. Wijeweera received a twenty-year sentence.

President J. R. Jayewardene released him in 1977, and in the 1982 presidential election he won 4.16% of the vote. After the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord the party rose again in 1987, enforcing general strikes by violence and killing probably thousands of people. Government forces captured and killed Wijeweera and his deputy in Colombo in November 1989, amid credible accusations of brutality and extrajudicial methods; official and unofficial reports put the death toll of the insurgency above 60,000.

Rebuilt under Somawansa Amarasinghe, the party joined the United People's Freedom Alliance government in 2004 and later left it. From 2019 it contested elections within the National People's Power coalition, which won 159 seats in the parliamentary elections of 2024.

The party's first ideology drew on Maoist stress on the rural peasantry, Guevarist views of armed insurrection and Trotskyist criticism of Stalinism. In 1983 it adopted Jathika Chintanaya, a national ideology that moved it towards Sinhalese Buddhist nationalism and opposition to Tamil demands. Amarasinghe later abandoned that line for a pragmatic socialism while the party remained officially Marxist-Leninist. In the early 1970s North Korea gave it training, and Sri Lanka expelled 18 North Koreans and cut diplomatic ties.
jane-austen: Jane Austen was born on 16 December 1775 in Steventon, Hampshire. Her father, George Austen, was the rector of the Anglican parishes of Steventon and Deane. He came from an old and wealthy family of wool merchants, but his own branch fell into poverty as each generation's eldest sons received the inheritances, and he was orphaned as a child. At sixteen he entered St John's College, Oxford, where he most likely met Cassandra Leigh, who came from the prominent Leigh family.

In 1809 her brother Edward offered his mother and sisters the use of a large cottage in Chawton, and Jane, Cassandra and their mother moved there on 7 July 1809. Life was quieter there than at any time since the family's move to Bath in 1800.

Austen wrote major novels before the age of 22 but was not published until she was 35. Like many women authors of her time she published anonymously. The ideal roles for a woman were then wife and mother, and a woman who wished to be a full-time writer was felt to be degrading her femininity. Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814) and Emma (1815) were moderate successes but did not bring her public fame in her lifetime.

Sir Walter Scott wrote an anonymous review of Emma in 1815, praising her realism. She died on 18 July 1817. Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published after her death, and her brother Henry Austen's Biographical Note, dated December 1817, first identified her as the author of the novels. She left unfinished the novel Sanditon.

Austen's six novels implicitly interpret and criticise the English landed gentry at the end of the 18th century. Her plots often explore the dependence of women on marriage for social standing and economic security. Her works critique the sentimental novels of the second half of the 18th century and are part of the transition to 19th-century literary realism. Critics have praised her social commentary, wit and irony.

In 1832 Richard Bentley bought the remaining copyrights to her novels and in October 1833 released the first collected edition, in his Standard Novels series. Her novels have been continuously in print since. Her nephew published A Memoir of Jane Austen in 1869.
jang-bahadur-rana: Jung Bahadur Rana was born Bir Narsingh Kunwar on 18 June 1817 at Balkot in southern Nepal, the son of Bal Narsingh Kunwar, a bodyguard of King Rana Bahadur Shah, and Ganesh Kumari, sister of Mathabar Singh Thapa. When Bhimsen Thapa was dismissed in 1837 the family lost its positions and property, and Jung Bahadur worked in Varanasi and as a mahout before settling in Kathmandu in 1839. King Rajendra promoted him to captain in 1840, and as a Kaji he learned the state's finances. He won favour with the youngest queen, then the real ruler, and after Mathabar Singh Thapa was assassinated he was promoted general.

On 14 September 1846 Jung Bahadur and his brothers killed about 40 members of the court, among them Prime Minister Fateh Jung Shah, in the palace armoury, the Kot. The massacre left King Rajendra and Prince Surendra powerless and marked the beginning of Rana autocracy. The queen appointed him prime minister and commander-in-chief on 15 September. When she conspired to have him killed at the garden of Bhandarkhal, he learned of it from his spies, arrived with armed troops and left 23 dead, and the queen went to Benaras.

In May 1847 he had Rajendra dethroned and Surendra crowned. Rajendra gathered troops at Bettiah, but government forces defeated him in July 1847 at the Battle of Alau and took him to Kathmandu. By 1850 Jung Bahadur had beaten his main rivals.

Wanting a direct relationship with the British government, he left Kathmandu for Calcutta on 15 January and reached Southampton on 15 May 1850. He met Queen Victoria on 19 June and visited Parliament, and he later saw the president of France. Neither government agreed to direct relations, but he came away convinced that close cooperation with the British was the best way to keep Nepal independent. On his return he set up a body to draft a legal code. The Muluki Ain was enacted on 6 January 1854. It did not address caste inequality, and it laid the foundation of modern law in Nepal.

Jung Bahadur remained prime minister until 1877, suppressing conspiracies and local revolts. Later prime ministers of his family added his name to their own, and the Rana rule is historically known as iron-fisted. Historians differ: some blame him for starting a dark period of oppressive dictatorship, while others blame his nephews, the Shumsher Ranas. His supporters point to his removal of factional fighting at court, innovations in the bureaucracy and judiciary and efforts to modernise Nepal.
jang-bogo: Jang Bogo was the son of a boatman, and his childhood name, Kungbok, meant a good archer; he excelled in martial arts and swam well from his youth. Being of lowly origins, he could not become a general in Silla, so he went to Tang China with his companion Jeong Yeon. Their skill with horses and spears won them military office, and both were named Junior Generals of Wuning District, in what is now Jiangsu province.

The sources for his life are few: the Chinese New Book of Tang, the Japanese Shoku Nihon Kōki, the journal of the Japanese monk Ennin and a brief biography in the Samguk sagi, compiled three centuries after his death.

By the ninth century thousands of Silla subjects lived in Tang, mostly as merchants in coastal Shandong and Jiangsu, and they were a favoured target of bandits who sold their captives into slavery. Back in Silla around 825, with a private fleet based on Wando, Jang petitioned King Heungdeok of Silla to found a permanent maritime garrison. According to the Samguk sagi, the king gave him 10,000 men to build and hold it. The force was nominally the king's but in practice his own, and he became the arbiter of commerce and navigation on the Yellow Sea; Ennin relied on his ships to reach China and return.
When Kim Ujing sought help to take the throne from the usurper who had killed his father, Jang sent 5,000 men under Jeong Yeon. Ujing's success as King Sinmu won Jang the post of prime minister.

Jang then sought to marry his daughter to King Munseong of Silla, son of Sinmu, and aristocrats at court, resenting a commoner of obscure provincial origins, plotted his death. Whether the king or the aristocracy was behind it is unclear. The Samguk sagi and the Samguk yusa relate that Yŏm Chang, an emissary from the court who pretended to have fled the capital, stabbed him with a hidden knife as they shared wine at his garrison headquarters. The garrison was disbanded in 851, and his burial place is unknown. He was later worshipped as a god, especially on the island of Jangdo, and a South Korean navy anti-piracy unit formed in 2009 takes its name from Cheonghaejin.
jang-yeong-sil: His precise date of birth is unknown; it is recorded only in the genealogy of the Chang family and in the Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty. According to these records his father, Chang Seong-hwi, belonged to the eighth generation of the family and was the third of five brothers who had served as ministers in Goryeo; the father was of Yuan dynasty descent. His mother was a government-registered courtesan, which made him a government-owned nobi, one of the lowest classes of Joseon society.

He first developed his skill in metal working in Gyeongsang Province, where he had spent his early life as a man-slave in government employ. His reputation brought him to the royal court in Hanseong, present-day Seoul, where selected commoners displayed their talents before the king, and Sejong made him a court technician.

His first celestial globe, built after two months of study from incomplete Arabian and Chinese instructions, was of mediocre accuracy. In 1433 he made an armillary sphere, the honcheonui, turned by a waterwheel so that it showed the positions of the sun, moon and stars by day and night. These instruments, with sundials and water clocks, stood around the Gyeonghoeru Pavilion in Gyeongbok Palace, and in 1442 the court astronomers compiled the Chiljeongsan, a calendar of the courses of the sun, moon and five visible planets.

After early attempts failed, he travelled to China to study water clocks. His Jagyeokru announced the hour with a bell, gong and drum: floating arrows released iron balls that struck a cymbal and worked levers moving 12 wooden figures. With Ichun, Kimjo and others he made the bronze bowl sundial Angbu-ilgu, engraved with the animals of the Chinese zodiac for those who could not read, and in 1441 the Supyo, a calibrated stone column for measuring water. He is often credited with the rain gauge, but no written record links him to it; Crown Prince Yi Hyang, later King Munjong, is recorded as first proposing the idea.

Sejong also sent him back to Gyeongsang Province to survey its metals for better weapons. His rise from humble origins made some officials jealous. When the sedan chair, or gama, that he had built for Sejong broke during a journey in 1442, he was held responsible; against the king's wishes he was jailed, flogged 80 times and expelled from the palace. Nothing more is recorded of his life. Some have speculated that he died from the flogging or went to China.
jangsu-of-goguryeo: Jangsu was born in 394 as the eldest son of Gwanggaeto the Great and was the twentieth monarch of Goguryeo, the northernmost of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. He became crown prince in 409 and succeeded his father, at the age of 18, when Gwanggaeto died. He inherited an empire that had grown suddenly through his father's conquests, and he devoted his early reign to stabilising it. He built a large tomb for Gwanggaeto and a tombstone about six metres tall engraved with the king's accomplishments, now known as the Gwanggaeto Stele.

In 427 Jangsu moved the capital from Gungnae Fortress, at present-day Ji'an, to Pyongyang, a region better suited to grow into a large city. He handled a divided China by playing the northern and southern states against each other. He opened a formal relationship with Northern Wei in 435, imprisoned the emperor of Northern Yan in 438 and later executed him, and defeated the southern Liu Song troops who then attacked, making peace the next year with a gift of 800 horses. In 479 he made friends with the Rouran Khaganate to keep Northern Wei in check.

He turned his ambitions south. Baekje and Silla made marriage alliances from 433, and their alliance lasted more than a century. In 475 Jangsu invaded Baekje by land and sea, helped, according to the account, by a Buddhist monk named Dorim whom he had sent to corrupt the court of its king Gaero. Gaero was killed, the capital was burned, and Baekje moved to Ungjin, present-day Gongju. Goguryeo gained control of the Han River valley. Jangsu also invaded Silla in 468 and again in 489.

Jangsu died in 491 at the age of 97, and his posthumous name means Long Life. At his death Goguryeo stretched from Inner Mongolia to the present-day province of North Chungcheong. He is credited with changing the state's official name to the shortened Goryeo, the source of the English name Korea.
jani-beg: After his father Öz Beg died in 1341, Jani Beg's older brother and rival Tini Beg was in the east, possibly preparing an attack. As soon as Tini Beg entered the central lands he was killed by Jani Beg's followers, and a younger brother, Khiḍr Beg, was also killed on Jani Beg's orders. The kurultai elected Jani Beg khan in 1342 with the support of his mother Taydula Khatun. He kept his father's policy of centralisation and integrated the old territories of Orda Khan back into the Golden Horde, though the Blue Horde never submitted, especially after a major revolt in 1342.

Like his father he supported the house of Moscow and its heads, Simeon and Ivan II, and Russian chroniclers called him the good tsar. He interfered in Moscow's relations with Suzdal, backed anti-Muscovite elements in Ryazan and contributed to Tver's fragmentation. In 1342 he briefly taxed the Russian Church, restoring its exemption in September 1347 and confirming it in 1351. When the throne of Vladimir was contested after Simeon's death in 1353, he sided with Ivan II, keeping the balance among the principalities.

In September 1343 a Venetian noble, Andreolo Civran, killed a Mongol official in Tanais, and Jani Beg expelled all the Latins from the Italian colonies. He demanded that Civran be judged by a Mongol court; the Genoese and Venetians formed a temporary alliance and imposed a trade embargo, and Jani Beg sent more troops to the Genoese colony of Kaffa in Crimea. The siege there lasted three years, with high losses on both sides, while boats carried supplies through the harbour.

According to an Italian source, Gabriel de Mussis of Piacenza, writing in 1348, plague broke out among Jani Beg's troops and they catapulted infected corpses into Kaffa. This story is disputed, and it is thought more likely that rats with infected fleas passed from his camp to the city. Genoese sailors then sailed from Kaffa to Genoa, Messina and Constantinople. In the winter of 1356–1357 he attacked Azerbaijan, took Tabriz and installed his own governor, with the support of the Shirvanshah; coins were minted in the city. The governor soon declared independence, and the region was annexed by the Jalayirids.

Jani Beg fell ill and died in 1357 on his way back to Sarai. Persian sources blame Berdi Beg or the beys, while the later Nikon Chronicle says the beys strangled him; the cause is unknown for lack of direct sources. Berdi Beg reigned after him and eliminated his brothers. His quarrel with the Latins harmed the Horde's trade and caused a silver shortage and a decline in minting. He appears as Jambech, lord of Sarra, in the Catalan Atlas of 1375.
janiculum: The Janiculum, Gianicolo in Italian, is a hill in western Rome, the second tallest in the present city after Monte Mario. It is not counted among the proverbial Seven Hills of Rome because it lies west of the Tiber and outside the boundaries of the ancient city. It is one of the best places for a view of central Rome with its domes and bell towers.

The Janiculum was a centre for the cult of the god Janus, and its position overlooking the city made it a good place for augurs to observe the auspices. In Roman mythology Janiculum was an ancient town founded by Janus, and in Book VIII of Virgil's Aeneid King Evander shows Aeneas the ruins of Saturnia and Janiculum. According to Livy, the hill was brought into Rome under King Ancus Marcius to keep an enemy from occupying it, fortified with a wall and joined to the city by a bridge across the Tiber. In the war between Rome and Clusium in 508 BCE the forces of Lars Porsena are said to have occupied it and laid siege to Rome.

In the third century CE a complex of water mills was built on the hill to grind grain for the city's bread. Excavations in the 1990s under the American Academy in Rome showed that they sat astride the aqueduct Aqua Traiana, with undershot wheels. The emperor Aurelian, who reigned from 270 to 275, extended the Aurelian Walls up the hill to include them. In 537 the Goths besieging Rome cut their water supply by cutting the aqueduct. The mills were later restored and may have worked until at least the time of Pope Gregory IV, who held office from 827 to 844.

In 1849 the Janiculum was the scene of a battle between the forces of Garibaldi, defending the revolutionary Roman Republic, and French forces fighting to restore the temporal power of the Pope over Rome.

The crest is dominated by the equestrian Monument to Garibaldi, designed by Emilio Gallori and dated 1895, near the Villa Doria Pamphili, where Garibaldi organised his defence in late April 1849. Other monuments honour the fallen of the wars of Italian independence, and a guide of 2011 listed 84 busts on the hill. Also on the hill are the church of San Pietro in Montorio, with Donato Bramante's Tempietto, built at the supposed site of Peter's death, the Baroque Fontana dell'Acqua Paola and the American and Spanish Academies in Rome. A cannon has been fired daily at noon from the hill as a time signal, a tradition that goes back to December 1847.
janid-dynasty: The dynasty traced its descent to Jochi, the eldest son of Genghis Khan, through Tuqa-Timur, one of Jochi's sons, and this lineage was the basis of its claim to rule. Its Tuqay-Timurid branch had ruled the Astrakhan Khanate until the Russians drove them out in 1555. Prince Yar Muhammed of that house had a son, Jani Muhammed Beg, who gave the dynasty the name Janid; the name Ashtarkhanid comes from Astrakhan itself.

When the Shaybanid khan Abdullah Khan II, who had ruled Bukhara since 1583, died in 1598, his only son Abd al-Mumin was soon killed by rebels. Abdullah's first cousin Pir Muhammad II was chosen khan, but the choice was contested by Tauekel Khan of the Kazakhs, Kasim Sultan and Baqi Muhammad, the son of Jani Muhammed Beg and of Abdullah's sister. Baqi Muhammad prevailed, Pir Muhammad II was killed in battle, and with him the Shaybanid line ended.

Baqi Muhammad Khan, who reigned until 1605, was followed by Vali Muhammad Khan, Imam Quli Khan, whose reign lasted from 1611 to 1642, Nadr Muhammad Khan, Abd al-Aziz Khan, Subhan Quli Khan, Ubaidullah Khan and Abu al-Fayz Khan. After Bukhara was conquered by Persia in 1740, Abu al-Fayz kept the throne, but real power lay with the ataliq Muhammad Rahim, who had the khan killed in 1747. The khans who followed were puppets of their ataliqs, until the ataliq Shah Murad deposed Khan Abu'l Ghazi, proclaimed himself Emir of Bukhara and founded the Manghud dynasty.

Under the Janids Bukhara was governed as an Islamic state that patronised religious institutions, kept traditional forms of government and relied on the prestige of Chinggisid descent. The khans sponsored mosques and madrasas in Bukhara and Samarkand, including major additions to the Registan ensemble, which became lasting symbols of Central Asian Islamic culture.
janio-quadros: Jânio Quadros was born in Campo Grande, now in Mato Grosso do Sul, on 25 January 1917. He paid for his studies at the University of São Paulo by teaching geography and Portuguese, and graduated in law in 1939. He entered politics in 1945 and was elected to the São Paulo city council in 1947. In 1953 he defeated a well-funded candidate and became mayor, gaining a reputation for honesty and balancing the city's budget in under a year. In 1955 he resigned to run for governor, defeating his longtime rival Adhemar de Barros by 1 per cent. He took a broom as his campaign symbol, pledging to sweep away corruption.

Quadros was nominated for the 1960 election by several opposition parties and won with 48 per cent of the vote, a margin of 15.6 per cent over Marshal Henrique Lott. It was the first peaceful transfer of power to an elected member of the opposition since Brazil became a republic in 1889. He took office on 31 January 1961. An anti-inflation programme in March cut public spending, won the approval of the IMF and allowed him to renegotiate debts, with 1.64 billion dollars in new loans. He tried to bypass the bureaucracy by decree, which alienated many in Congress.

He pursued an independent foreign policy, seeking closer relations with Africa and balance between the United States and the Eastern Bloc. His award of the Order of the Southern Cross to Che Guevara was controversial, and his foreign policy contributed to the decline of his support in Congress.

On 25 August 1961 Quadros unexpectedly resigned, citing foreign and terrible occult forces in a cryptic letter. It is commonly believed he expected to be called back, but Congress accepted the resignation. The vice president, João Goulart, took the oath on 7 September, with his powers limited by a constitutional amendment, and the crisis helped set the stage for the military coup of 1964. The military did not allow Quadros to take part in politics, but he returned in the 1980s and served again as mayor of São Paulo from 1985 to 1988. He died in São Paulo on 16 February 1992.
janis-balodis: Jānis Balodis was born on 20 February 1881, the son of the historian and teacher Voldemārs Balodis. He joined the Imperial Russian Army in 1898, served in Kaunas and studied at the Vilnius War School from 1900 to 1902. In the Russo-Japanese War, from November 1904 to July 1905, he was seriously wounded in the arm. He served in Vilnius until 1914, was lightly wounded in East Prussia early in the First World War, and on 20 February 1915, while recovering in hospital, was captured by the German Army; he spent the rest of the war in a prisoner-of-war camp in Silesia.

Balodis returned to Latvia in November 1918 and joined the first armed units of the new republic on 18 December. He retreated from Riga with the army and government on 3 January 1919, and after the death of Oskars Kalpaks on 6 March he was made colonel and took charge of the few Latvian soldiers in Courland. He commanded the Southern Group in an uneasy alliance with German troops and then the 1st Courland division against the Red Army in Latgale. Appointed commander-in-chief on 16 October 1919, during the attack of the West Russian Volunteer Army, he was promoted to general on 23 January 1920.

After the post of commander-in-chief was abolished in February 1921, Balodis left the army and joined the Latvian Farmers Union, the largest party of the time, led by Kārlis Ulmanis, entering the Saeima in 1925. As minister of war from 7 December 1931 he helped organise the coup of 15 May 1934 and co-signed the proclamation of martial law. He became vice president on 12 March 1936 and deputy prime minister on 11 February 1938, though his real role was limited to military matters. On 5 April 1940 he was relieved of all his posts without a clear official explanation.

Arrested with his wife on 31 July 1940, Balodis was held under house arrest in Syzran and from 1941 in Kuibishev. Only in 1952 was he tried and sentenced to 25 years in a jail in Vladimir. Released in 1956, he lived in a small flat in Riga and died on 8 August 1965. The KGB removed the tombstone with a sword and the words General Balodis that his widow set up.
janis-cakste: Jānis Kristaps Čakste was born on 14 September 1859 in the Lielsesava parish of Dobele county in the Courland Governorate, the son of a wealthy peasant farmer. He attended St Anne's Primary School and then the Academia Petrina in Jelgava, where he took part in student evenings advocating Young Latvian ideals. After graduating in 1882 he entered the law faculty of Moscow University and in 1883 founded the Latvian Student Society, later the fraternity Austrums, which was active in the Moscow Latvian community alongside Krišjānis Valdemārs and Fricis Brīvzemnieks. He graduated in 1886 and returned to Jelgava.

Čakste worked in the legal department of the Courland Governorate and from 1888 as a lawyer in Jelgava. In 1889 he became editor of the newspaper Tēvija, one of the most widely read Latvian-language papers in Courland, and in 1895 he was a chief organiser of the fourth All-Latvian Song Festival, partly financed from his own pocket. In the Russian Revolution of 1905 he worked on a project for Latvian national autonomy within the Russian Empire.

In 1906 he was elected to the First State Duma and joined the liberal Constitutional Democratic Party. When Emperor Nicholas II dissolved the Duma, Čakste was among the 166 members who signed the Vyborg Manifesto calling for non-violent resistance, and he served three months in prison. After the German invasion of Courland in 1915 he moved to Tartu and helped lead the committee for Latvian refugees. In 1919 he led the Latvian delegation to the Paris Peace Conference.

On 17 November 1918 the Latvian People's Council elected Čakste its chairman in his absence. He was at his country home and did not arrive in time for the declaration of independence the next day, which the vice-chairman, Gustavs Zemgals, proclaimed. On 1 May 1920 he was elected Speaker of the Constitutional Assembly, again acting as provisional head of state, defeating the poet Rainis.

At the first session of the first Saeima on 7 November 1922 he was elected the first President of Latvia, unopposed, with 92 votes for and 6 against. The office was largely ceremonial, though he followed foreign affairs closely. During his tenure he promulgated 402 laws, returned three to the Saeima and pardoned 549 people. He won re-election in 1925 with 60 votes. He died in Riga on 14 March 1927, before his second term ended, and was buried in the Forest Cemetery. He remains the only Latvian president to die in office.
janissaries: The Janissary Corps was formed in the 14th century, either under Murad I or under his father Orhan. The Ottoman government took a tax of one-fifth on all slaves taken in war, and from this pool of men the sultans built a personal army loyal only to themselves. From the 1380s to 1648 the corps was filled through the devşirme, a levy of boys, predominantly Balkan Christians, who were enslaved, circumcised by force and converted to Islam. The levy was abolished in 1648. Jews were never subject to it.

A boy was first sent to a Turkish family in the provinces to learn Turkish and the customs of Ottoman society, and was then trained in the acemi oğlan, or cadet, school in the capital, where the brightest were selected for the palace institution of the Enderun. Janissaries lived in strict discipline in nearly monastic conditions and were forbidden to marry until retirement, typically in their forties. The devşirme was deeply resented among Christians in the Balkans, and in Serbian, Greek and Bulgarian memory it became one of the most enduring symbols of Ottoman rule.

Janissaries were kapıkulları, door servants of the sultan, neither freedmen nor ordinary slaves. They wore distinctive uniforms, lived in barracks, marched to the music of the mehter band and received regular salaries and pensions. The corps was divided into orta, or battalions, led by a commander called the ağa. Under Suleiman I there were 165 orta, rising to 196, in three sub-corps: the cemaat, the bölük and the sekban. A semi-autonomous corps was based in Algiers.

In the classical period the Janissaries were only about a tenth of the Ottoman army, the provincial cavalry being the main force. They numbered about 1,000 in the 14th century and about 6,000 in 1475, and from the 1530s the corps expanded, to about 40,000 men by 1609. They began adopting firearms in the early to mid 1400s and in 1605 became one of the first European armies to use rotating lines of volley fire. They took part in the capture of Constantinople in 1453.

In the late 16th century a sultan gave in to pressure and allowed Janissaries' sons to join, a practice forbidden for 200 years, and by the 17th century civilians bought their way in for the status it gave. Janissaries came to own land and businesses, mutinied, dictated policy and changed sultans by palace coups, and they resisted modernisation of the army. Mahmud II abolished the corps in 1826 in the Auspicious Incident, in which 6,000 or more were executed. Janissary music influenced Mozart and Beethoven, and the mehter band was organised again in 1952 under the Istanbul Military Museum.
janos-kadar: János Kádár was born out of wedlock on 26 May 1912 in Fiume, now Rijeka, to the servant Borbála Csermanek and the soldier János Krezinger. His mother found work in Budapest, and he met his father only once, in 1960. His first meeting with Marxist literature came in 1928, when he won a junior chess competition and received Friedrich Engels's Anti-Dühring as the prize. He was the first to be dismissed when the Great Depression struck Hungary, and by his own account he joined the Communist Party in 1931.

Kádár became First Secretary of the illegal party before the war. In 1936 he feigned its dissolution and renamed it the Peace Party to throw the police off its trail; the plan failed, and the Moscow-based Hungarian Communists under Mátyás Rákosi condemned it. After the war he sat on the Politburo, and from 1948 to 1950 he was Interior Minister. In 1951 he was imprisoned by the government of Rákosi and released in 1954 by the reformist Prime Minister Imre Nagy.

On 25 October 1956, two days after the Hungarian Revolution began, Kádár replaced Ernő Gerő as General Secretary and joined Nagy's government. A week later he broke with Nagy over the decision to withdraw from the Warsaw Pact. The Soviet leadership decided in early November to crush the revolution by force, and after the intervention Kádár was selected to lead the country. He ordered Nagy to be executed.

Kádár judged that breaking away from the Communist bloc was impossible. From the early 1960s he lifted the harshest of Rákosi's controls on speech and movement, eased limits on cultural life and tolerated samizdat publications to a greater extent than other bloc leaders did. An amnesty in 1963 released most remaining prisoners. He allowed collective-farm members large private plots, raised trade with Western Europe and favoured consumer goods, in what became known as Goulash Communism. He called himself a toiler for compromise.

On 22 May 1988 he resigned as General Secretary, under pressure, amid economic difficulties and ill health; Károly Grósz succeeded him. He lost his remaining posts in May 1989 and died on 6 July 1989. His legacy remains disputed in Hungary: supporters stress peace, job security and social protection, while critics hold that the country remained a dictatorship and a Soviet satellite.
jantar-mantar: A Jantar Mantar is an assembly of stone-built astronomical instruments designed to be used with the naked eye; each of these mixed instruments, Mishra Yantra, gathers up to 19 different kinds. Among them were the Samrat Yantra, Jai Prakash Yantra, Disha Yantra, Rama Yantra, Chakra Yantra, Rashiwalya Yantra, Dingash Yantra and Utaansh Yantra. Their main purpose was to compile astronomical tables and to predict the times and movements of the Sun, Moon and planets. Sawai Jai Singh II, who ordered them built, had a keen interest in mathematics, architecture and astronomy.

The largest instrument is the Samrat Yantra at Jaipur, an equinoctial sundial and the world's largest stone sundial. It consists of a gigantic triangular gnomon whose hypotenuse lies parallel to the Earth's axis, with a quadrant of a circle on either side parallel to the plane of the equator. A skilled observer can use it with an accuracy of about 20 seconds to find the time of day and the declination of the Sun and other heavenly bodies.

The observatory at Mathura and the fort that protected it were destroyed before 1857, and it no longer exists; the others stand at Jaipur, Delhi, Ujjain and Varanasi. The name Jantar Mantar is at least 200 years old, appearing in an account of 1803, though the archives of the Kingdom of Amber of 1735 and 1737–1738 use Jantra instead. Jantar is a spoken form of jantra, from yantra, instrument, and Mantar comes from mantrana, to consult or calculate.
januarius: Little is known of Januarius' life, and no contemporary sources are preserved. What is told derives mostly from later Christian sources, among them the Acta Bononensia, not earlier than the 6th century, and the Acta Vaticana of the 9th century, and from folk tradition. The earliest historical reference is a letter of 432 by Uranius, bishop of Nola, on the death of Paulinus of Nola in 431. It says that the ghosts of Januarius and Martin of Tours appeared to Paulinus three days before he died, and calls Januarius a bishop and martyr, an illustrious member of the Neapolitan church.

According to the hagiographies, he was born at Benevento to a rich patrician family descended from the Samnite Caudini tribe, and became bishop as a young man. During Diocletian's persecution of Christians he hid fellow believers, but he was arrested while visiting Sossius in jail. He and his companions were condemned to be thrown to wild bears in the amphitheatre at Pozzuoli, but fear of public disturbance changed the sentence, and they were beheaded at the Solfatara crater. Other legends say the beasts refused to eat him or that he came out of a furnace unharmed.

His feast, San Gennaro, falls on 19 September in the General Roman Calendar and on 21 April in the Eastern Church. Naples has more than fifty official patron saints, but Januarius is the principal one, and he was invoked in 1631 to stop an eruption of Mount Vesuvius. His relics were moved several times: to Benevento in the early ninth century, to the Abbey of Montevergine, and in 1497 back to Naples, where Cardinal Oliviero Carafa commissioned the Succorpo crypt beneath the cathedral, finished in 1506. In the United States the Feast of San Gennaro is a highlight of New York's Little Italy.

A chronicle of Naples written in 1382 describes his cult in detail but does not mention the relic or the miracle. The first certain date for the liquefaction of the blood is 1389. Reports then declared that it melted once, then twice, then three times a year, and thousands gather in Naples Cathedral on 19 September, 16 December and the Saturday before the first Sunday of May. The blood is kept in two sealed ampoules, and the Church has never made an official statement on the phenomenon, nor does it allow the ampoules to be opened. Several natural explanations have been proposed, among them a thixotropic gel, and they remain debated.
january-uprising: Despite the Russian Empire's defeat in the Crimean War, Alexander II warned the Poles in 1856 to forget any dreams. Two currents emerged in the Kingdom of Poland. The Whites, liberal-conservative and mostly landowners, centred on Andrzej Zamoyski, hoped for an orderly return to the constitutional status before 1830. The Reds, a democratic movement of peasants, workers and some clergy, wanted the peasantry freed unconditionally. In February 1861 the Russian army attacked a demonstration in Warsaw, killing five, and on 8 April Russian fire killed 200 and wounded 500.

Aleksander Wielopolski, head of civil administration, brought forward to January 1863 the conscription of young Polish activists into the Imperial Russian Army for 20 years of service, hoping to derail the national movement. It sparked the uprising he had meant to avoid, and many young men fled to the forests.

The uprising began on 22 January 1863, organised by the clandestine Central National Committee and then by the Polish National Government. About 10,000 men rallied at first, mostly city workers and minor clerks, with younger sons of the poorer szlachta and lower priests. The insurgents fought as lightly armed guerrilla bands that avoided large battles. On 1 February 1863 the uprising spread to the former Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and by spring it reached the Kiev Governorate. France, Britain and Austria did not intervene militarily.

Disagreement between Whites and Reds weakened coordination, and the peasantry could be mobilised only where Polish units dominated. Romuald Traugutt took command on 17 October 1863. On 27 December 1863 he decreed that peasants would be granted the land they worked, but the policy came too late, since Russia had already begun offering peasants parcels of land. Alexander II abolished serfdom in Poland in 1864.

According to official Russian information, 396 people were executed and 18,672 exiled to Siberia, and over 60,000 people were imprisoned and exiled from Poland to distant regions of Russia. Whole villages and towns were burned. The authorities confiscated 1,660 estates in Poland and 1,794 in Lithuania, ended the remaining autonomy of the Kingdom of Poland, and restricted the official use of Polish. Mikhail Muravyov, called the Hangman, supervised hangings, and Count Fyodor Berg pursued Russification.

The uprising failed militarily but became a symbol of continuing resistance. In the 1860s and after, two movements grew out of it, the Polish Socialist Party under Józef Piłsudski and the National Democracy movement under Roman Dmowski. Many turned to organic work and self-improvement.
janus-of-cyprus: Janus was born in Genoa, where his father, James I of Cyprus, was held captive. His mother, Helvis of Brunswick-Grubenhagen, named him after the god Janus, the founder of Genoa according to mythological tradition. When his father was elected king, he agreed with the Genoese on 2 February 1383 to be released, and they were given new commercial privileges, but they demanded that Janus stay in their city as a hostage. According to the Cypriot historian Leontios Makhairas, James ordered a special tax requiring Cypriots to buy salt, to raise the money to release his son, who was freed in October 1392, aged 18.

After the death of his father on 9 September 1398 Janus inherited the throne and was crowned in Saint Sophia Cathedral in Nicosia on 11 November 1398. In 1402 he conspired with a priest and with Peter Makhairas to retake Famagusta from the Genoese, but the plan was betrayed and 28 conspirators were executed. He then besieged Famagusta for three years without success, because the city could be supplied from the sea, and the siege ended in 1406. Epidemics and locusts struck the island from 1408, and a new epidemic in 1419-1420 probably caused the death of his second wife, Charlotte de Bourbon, on 15 January 1422.

Christian pirates raided from Cyprus, and Janus could not stop them, which gave the Mamluk sultan Barsbay reason to retaliate. After smaller attacks, a large army of over 3,000 men, with 180 ships, landed near Avdimou in summer 1426. Janus asked Europe for help in vain. In the battle that followed, on 7 July 1426, he was captured, and the Mamluks went on to pillage Larnaca again and the capital, Nicosia, taking much loot and many captives.

Janus was held in Cairo for ten months, during which his brother Hugh of Lusignan, Archbishop of Nicosia, governed Cyprus. He was taken before the sultan in chains on a donkey and forced to kneel nine times. Europeans raised the ransom, and Cyprus also had to pay the sultan an annual tax, which continued to be paid even after the end of Frankish rule in Cyprus. During his captivity serfs revolted under a man named Alexis, who was declared king at Lefkoniko, and the rebellion was put down after ten months. Janus arrived in Paphos from Cairo on 12 May 1427. He died on 29 June 1432 and left nine children.
janusz-iii-of-masovia: Janusz was born around 27 September 1502, a son of Konrad III the Red and his third wife Anna, daughter of Mikolaj Radziwiłł the Old, Voivod of Vilnius and the first Grand Chancellor of Lithuania. When his father died on 28 October 1503, Janusz and his brother Stanisław inherited the duchies of Czersk, Warsaw, Liw, Zakroczym and Nur under the regency of their mother. Their inheritance, apart from Czersk, was threatened by the Kingdom of Poland until 14 March 1504, when King Alexander, fearing the protests of the local nobility, granted them the whole patrimony as a fief.

Because of constant unrest among the nobility, the brothers took the government in 1518, though Anna Radziwiłł kept the real power until her death in 1522. That year they attended the wedding of King Sigismund I the Old and Bona Sforza in Kraków. As Polish vassals they sent auxiliary troops to the king in the Polish-Teutonic War of 1519–1520. Janusz took no part in government until Stanisław died on 8 August 1524; ruling alone, he forbade Lutheranism in his lands in 1525 on pain of confiscation and death. Like his brother he became known for drink and women, and his way of life probably hastened his death in the night of 9 to 10 March 1526.

Janusz was buried at St. John's Archcathedral in Warsaw, and with him the male line of the Masovian Piasts descended from Siemowit III died out. King Sigismund I looked into the accusations of murder and found no foul play. Tuberculosis, an inherited disease of the Masovian princes, has been named as a possible cause, while the contemporary historian Marcin Bielski suggested alcohol poisoning. Some Masovian nobles argued that the duchy should pass to female relatives such as Anna or Sophia of Masovia, but the king held to the agreements that made him heir. Masovia kept some autonomy until 1576. Janusz appears in Jan Matejko's painting Prussian Homage.
japan: Japan is an island country in East Asia, made up of 14,125 islands that stretch over 3,000 kilometres along the Pacific coast of Asia. The five main islands, from north to south, are Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and Okinawa. About 75% of the terrain is mountainous and heavily forested, so the population is concentrated on the coastal plains. Japan lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire and is prone to earthquakes, tsunami and volcanic eruptions; the 1923 Tokyo earthquake killed over 140,000 people, and the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake triggered a large tsunami.

The first known habitation dates to the Upper Paleolithic. The Jōmon period began around 14,500 BCE, and the Yayoi people later entered the archipelago from the Korean Peninsula, bringing wet-rice farming and metallurgy. According to legend, Emperor Jimmu founded a kingdom in central Japan in 660 BCE. Japan first appears in written history in the Chinese Book of Han, completed in 111 CE. Buddhism was introduced from Baekje in 552, and in 645 the Taika Reforms aimed at greater centralisation of power in the imperial court, on the model of China.

From the 12th century actual power was held by military aristocrats known as shōgun and feudal lords called daimyō. After the Kamakura and Ashikaga shogunates and a century of warring states, the Tokugawa shogunate unified the country in 1600 and implemented an isolationist foreign policy. An American fleet forced Japan to open trade in 1853, which led to the end of the shogunate and the restoration of imperial power in 1868. Japan annexed Taiwan in 1895 and Korea in 1910, invaded China in 1937 and entered World War II as an Axis power in 1941. It surrendered in 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and was under Allied occupation until 1952.

Japan has a population of nearly 123 million, and Tokyo is the capital and largest city. It is a constitutional monarchy in which the emperor's role is ceremonial, and its legislature is the bicameral National Diet. The Constitution of Japan was adopted in 1947. Minority groups include the indigenous Ainu and Ryukyuan people.
japan-korea-treaty-of-1905: The treaty followed earlier agreements that had narrowed Korea's independence. The Japan–Korea Protocol of 23 February 1904 let Japan occupy strategically important places, and the First Japan–Korea Agreement of August 1904 required Korea to accept financial and diplomatic advisers sent by Japan. After the victory over Russia, a Japanese cabinet meeting on 27 October 1905 agreed eight provisions for a second treaty giving Japan absolute authority over Korea's foreign affairs.

Itō Hirobumi arrived in Seoul on 9 November 1905. Gojong first refused to meet him, citing illness, and gave way on 15 November when Itō ordered Japanese troops to encircle the palace. He refused to order his foreign minister to negotiate, arguing that such matters needed the approval of the Korean Privy Council.

On 17 November the Korean ministers refused to sign at the Japanese legation and again at an Imperial Conference at Gyeongungung palace. That evening Itō and Field Marshal Hasegawa Yoshimichi came with military police and questioned each minister, with the implied threat of bodily harm. Han Kyu-seol and Min Yeong-gi objected openly, and with the approval of five of the eight present Itō declared the agreement valid. The Foreign Minister's seal was affixed about 1:30 in the morning of 18 November.

The treaty had five articles. It forbade the Korean government to sign any treaty of an international nature without Japanese supervision. Under Article 3 a Resident-General was to be sent to Seoul to handle diplomatic affairs, with the right to visit the Korean emperor privately. It was to remain in force until Korea became wealthy and strong, a clause proposed by Yi Wan-yong.

Korea closed its legations abroad, among them those in Beijing and Washington, D.C., and foreign legations in Seoul began to withdraw, France being the last. The Residency-General was established in February 1906 with Itō as first Resident-General. Gojong sought help from other countries: a telegram to Homer Hulbert in the United States and a secret letter smuggled to China by the reporter Douglas Story brought no result. In 1907 he sent three emissaries to the Second Hague Peace Conference, who were barred from the conference; he was then forced to abdicate, and the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1907 of 24 July transferred authority over Korea's internal affairs to the Resident-General.

Min Yeong-hwan and Cho Byeong-se killed themselves in protest, and local yangbans and commoners formed righteous armies. In Korea the five ministers who approved the treaty are widely called the Five Eulsa Traitors. The 1965 Treaty on Basic Relations confirmed the treaty as already null and void, but its legality in 1905 remains disputed. Korean scholars argue that it was never valid, being negotiated under threat of force without Gojong's approval, while several Japanese studies conclude that he consented, evidence Korean academics question.
japanese-tea-ceremony: The first documented evidence of tea in Japan dates to the 9th century. An entry in the Nihon Kōki describes the Buddhist monk Eichū bringing tea back from Tang China, and in 815 he personally served sencha to Emperor Saga on an excursion at Karasaki. By imperial order in 816, tea plantations began to be cultivated in the Kinki region, though interest in tea then faded. Buddhists used tea to prevent drowsiness during long meditations.

In the 1500s Sen no Rikyū revolutionized tea culture. He redefined the rules of the tea house, tea garden, utensils and procedures, introduced a much smaller chashitsu and rustic, distorted ceramic tea bowls, and based the ceremony on the aesthetic of wabi. His great-grandchildren founded the Omotesenke, Urasenke and Mushakōjisenke schools, and the practice spread from daimyo and samurai to the general public. Zen Buddhism and Shinto also shaped it: washing the hands and mouth before the ceremony follows the Shinto purification ritual of misogi.

The ceremony is known as sadō or chadō, the way of tea, or chanoyu, and centres on the presentation of powdered green tea, matcha, a procedure called temae. Koicha, thick tea, uses about three times as much tea to the same water as usucha, thin tea, which is whipped with a bamboo whisk. A relatively simple gathering, a chakai, includes confections, thin tea and perhaps a light meal. A formal chaji usually includes a full kaiseki meal, then confections, thick tea and thin tea, and may last up to four hours.

The year is divided into the sunken hearth season, traditionally November to April, and the brazier season, May to October. Rooms are ideally tatami-floored, with a hanging scroll in the tokonoma alcove chosen for the season and occasion, and a simple flower arrangement, chabana, which Sen no Rikyū developed. Most ceremonies are conducted in kimono, whose sleeves and obi shape many of the movements.

Schools teach many styles of temae. Obon temae, a simple procedure for thin tea on a tray, is usually the first learned. Ryūrei, with host and guests seated on chairs, originated in the Urasenke school, initially for non-Japanese guests, who, it was thought, would be more comfortable that way. Ten artisans hold the title Senke Jusshoku for supplying utensils to the three main schools.

The English term Teaism was coined by Okakura Kakuzō to describe the worldview of the way of tea, not only its presentation. A separate tradition, senchadō, uses leaf tea and was introduced from China in the 17th century by Ingen, founder of the Ōbaku school of Zen, and popularized in the 18th century by the Ōbaku monk Baisao, who sold tea in Kyoto.
japji-sahib: The Japji Sahib is held to be the first composition of Guru Nanak, and it is mostly his writing, given its form by Guru Angad. Sikhs regard it as the comprehensive essence of Sikhism, of which the whole Guru Granth Sahib is an expansion. Besides reciting or chanting, jap is also understood to mean to understand, as in a line of Gurbani where it refers to understanding wisdom.

The work opens with the Mool Mantra, followed by 38 stanzas, or paudis, in different poetic metres, and ends with a final Salok by Guru Angad. Its themes are what true worship is and what the nature of God is. The first stanza holds that bathing at holy sites, silence or material gain cannot cleanse a person whose thoughts are unclean, and that purity comes from abiding in love of the divine. The second says that suffering and happiness, rebirth through karma and release from it all come by God's command.

Later stanzas say that good karma and God's grace are the gate to mukti, liberation, praise listening to the word and faith, and describe God as formless and beyond description. Hymns 21 to 27 say that all from the Vedas to the Puranas, Brahma, Shiva, the Buddha and Krishna speak of God, yet no words can describe Him fully; Hymn 31 calls God the primal one, the pure light, without beginning or end.

The scholar Christopher Shackle describes it as designed for individual meditative recitation and as the first item of daily prayer for the devout. It is the first text of the Nitnem, is chanted at morning and evening prayers in gurdwaras, and is recited at the Khalsa initiation and at cremations. It is distinct from the Jaap Sahib of Guru Gobind Singh, which opens the Dasam Granth. Many printed editions appeared in the second half of the 19th century in Lahore, Amritsar, Karachi, Sialkot and Rawalpindi, and Max Arthur Macauliffe published a tentative English translation in 1897.
jarasandha: In the Hindu texts Jarasandha is a powerful king of Magadha and a prominent enemy of Krishna. In the Jain Harivamsa Purana he is the ninth pratinarayana. His name is explained as jara and sandha, meaning joining: the one who is joined by Jara.

The story of his birth tells that King Brihadratha, who had married the twin daughters of the king of Kashi but had no son, received a fruit from the sage Chandakaushika and divided it between his wives. Each bore half a human body, which the king ordered thrown into the forest. A rakshasi named Jara joined the two halves into a living child and brought him to the king, who named him Jarasandha in her honour.

Jarasandha married his two daughters to Kamsa, the ruler of Mathura. When Krishna killed Kamsa, as a divine prophecy had announced, Jarasandha vowed revenge. According to the legend he attacked Mathura seventeen times and was defeated by Krishna and Balarama each time. Krishna then had the divine architect Vishvakarma build the city of Dvaraka by the sea and moved the people of Mathura there. In the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, Jarasandha fought Karna and was defeated, and he gave Karna the land of Malini to please him.

When Yudhishthira wished to perform a sacrifice, Jarasandha stood in his way as a powerful warrior. Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna, disguised as brahmins, went to Magadha, and Krishna challenged him to a duel in which he could choose his opponent. He chose Bhima, and they wrestled for fourteen days. When Bhima tore him in two, the halves rejoined. Krishna split a blade of grass and threw the pieces in opposite directions, and Bhima, understanding, tore Jarasandha apart again and threw the halves far apart. The text places this at Girivraja, which many scholars identify with modern Rajgir. His son Sahadeva became a vassal of the Pandavas and was killed by Karna in the Kurukshetra War.
jarl: The Old Norse word jarl, Old Swedish iarl and Old Danish jærl has been connected with similar Germanic words, among them Old English eorl, from which modern English earl comes, Old Saxon erl, meaning man or nobleman, and Old High German erl- in personal names. In Norway the word is known from the late ninth-century poem Háleygjatal. The poem Rígsþula tells how the god Ríg fathered Thrall, Karl and Jarl, ancestors of thralls, peasants and the warrior nobility. Some scholars date the poem to the twelfth century or later, so it may not be a good source for the tenth.

According to the saga of Harald Fairhair, the king set a jarl in every district to administer the laws and collect fines and land dues. The saga says the jarls' power exceeded that of earlier kings. The most powerful Norwegian jarls were those of Lade, who ruled over Trøndelag and Hålogaland.

In later medieval Norway there was usually no more than one jarl in the mainland at a time, and sometimes none. The title served to appoint a de facto ruler when the king was a minor or seriously ill, as with Håkon Galen in 1204 and Skule Bårdsson in 1217, or to appease a pretender without making him king, as with Eirik, brother of King Sverre. The ruler of Orkney also held it.

In Sweden jarls were local rulers or viceroys over provinces, and the sveajarls of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, such as Birger Brosa, Ulf Fase and Birger Jarl, were often the true rulers of the kingdom. In Denmark the jarl was the king's deputy, as Ulf Jarl was to Canute the Great. Gissur Þorvaldsson was the only jarl of Iceland. When Canute became king of England in 1016 he divided it into earldoms on the pattern of Scandinavia.

The title gave way to that of duke. Canute Lavard, the last jarl of Southern Jutland, became the first Danish duke, of Schleswig, and died in 1131. In Norway Skule Bårdsson was made duke in 1237, the first use of that title there, which meant that jarl was no longer the highest rank below the king. The last jarl in mainland Norway was appointed in 1295. In Sweden the first duke was Birger Jarl's son Magnus, later known as Ladulås, in the thirteenth century.
jaroslav-hasek: Jaroslav Hašek was born on 30 April 1883. His father Josef, a mathematics teacher, died early, and poverty forced his mother to move the family more than fifteen times. In 1897, as a student, he took part in anti-German riots in Prague, was arrested and was forced to leave his grammar school. He trained as a druggist and then graduated from the Czech-Slavonic Business Academy. In 1903, with Ladislav Hájek, he wrote a parody of lyrical poetry, his first humorous work. He was dismissed from the Slavia Bank on 28 May 1903 for absence, and then lived by journalism and writing, in a bohemian way.

In 1907 Hašek edited the anarchist magazine Komuna and was briefly imprisoned. In 1909 he had sixty-four short stories published, and he became editor of Svět zvířat, a magazine on animals, until he was dismissed in October 1910, reportedly after writing articles about non-existent animals. In 1911 he founded with friends the Party of Moderate Progress Within the Bounds of the Law, a parody of political life. He also co-wrote cabaret performances with František Langer, Emil Artur Longen and Egon Erwin Kisch.

He was called up in February 1915 into the Austro-Hungarian 91st Infantry Regiment and was captured by the Russians on 24 September 1915. He joined the Czechoslovak Legion in 1916 and fought at the Battle of Zborov. In 1918 he left the Legion for Moscow and the Red Army, and served in Samara, Ufa and Siberia, where he published several magazines. He returned to Prague in December 1920.

Back in Czechoslovakia, where the Soviets had sent him to organise the communist movement, he was prevented by circumstances and returned to a bohemian life in the pubs of Prague. On 25 August 1921 he moved to Lipnice nad Sázavou, seriously ill, and began The Fateful Adventures of the Good Soldier Švejk During the World War. When he could no longer write, he dictated chapters from his bedroom. He died of heart disease on 3 January 1923, and the novel was left unfinished. It satirises the ineptitude of authority figures and is the most translated novel in Czech literature, in about 60 languages. Josef Lada, with whom Hašek lived at the outbreak of the First World War, later illustrated it.
jarrow: Jarrow lies on the south bank of the River Tyne in South Tyneside, about 5 km from the east coast and 10 km north of Sunderland. It was historically part of County Durham. Its name comes from the Gyrwe, an Anglian tribe whose name means fen dwellers. Jarrow was an ancient parish of seven townships and was incorporated as a municipal borough in 1875; the borough was abolished in 1974 and absorbed into South Tyneside.

The Monastery of St Paul at Jarrow, with Wearmouth part of the twin foundation Monkwearmouth–Jarrow Abbey, was the home of the Venerable Bede, whose works include the Ecclesiastical History of the English People. The two houses became a centre of learning, with the largest library north of the Alps, largely through the travels of their founder Benedict Biscop. In 692 Ceolfrid commissioned three copies of the Bible, among them the Codex Amiatinus, the world's oldest complete Latin Bible, which Ceolfrid was taking to Pope Gregory II when he died on the way. It was later at Monte Amiata in Tuscany and since 1786 has been in the Laurentian Library in Florence.
Vikings, who had plundered Lindisfarne in 793, attacked Jarrow in 794, and in 875 Halfdan Ragnarsson's force sacked the monasteries at Tynemouth and Jarrow. Henry VIII later dissolved the monastery.

Jarrow stayed a small town until heavy industry arrived. Charles Mark Palmer set up a shipyard there in 1852, and about 1,000 ships were built at Palmer's, which also made the first iron screw collier, John Bowes, and the first modern cargo ship. At times the yard employed up to 80 per cent of the town's working population. It closed in 1933 after National Shipbuilders Securities bought it to cut capacity, though the yard was relatively efficient and modern.

The Depression left Jarrow, in the words of Life, cursed. In 1936 the town was the starting point of the Jarrow March to London against unemployment; its MP Ellen Wilkinson wrote of these events in The Town That Was Murdered (1939). Historians doubt how effective such marches were, though some evidence suggests they stirred interest in regenerating distressed areas. The Second World War revived shipbuilding, and the last shipyard closed in 1980.

Jarrow's built-up area had 29,470 inhabitants at the 2021 census. The church of St Paul stands on the monastery site, incorporating its ruins, and beside it is Jarrow Hall, a museum of Bede's life and times.
