jarrow-march: Jarrow, on the River Tyne in County Durham, grew from a coal-mining village into a shipbuilding town after Palmer's shipyard opened in 1851. Its population rose from around 3,800 in 1850 to 35,000 by 1891, and more than 1,000 ships were launched there. After the First World War, mismanagement and changed world trade brought decline. The last ship, HMS Duchess, was launched on 19 July 1932, a receiver was appointed in June 1933, and the yard closed in 1934.

National Shipbuilders Security Ltd, a company created by the government to buy and dismantle failing yards, barred closed yards from shipbuilding for at least 40 years. A plan by the American entrepreneur T. Vosper Salt to build a modern steelworks on the site was frustrated by the British Iron and Steel Federation, an employers' organisation with its own plans for the industry.

In July 1936 David Riley, chairman of Jarrow Borough Council, proposed a march on London. The mayor Billy Thompson, the town's MP Ellen Wilkinson and the local Labour, Conservative and Liberal parties, churches and businesses all supported it. It was to be a local affair without political connotations, unlike the communist-led hunger marches of the National Unemployed Workers' Movement, and limited to 200 fit men. A fund with a target of £800 raised nearly double that.

The marchers left on 5 October. The Labour Party's conference in Edinburgh was critical of the march, and the Unemployment Assistance Board reduced the marchers' benefits. Along the route, Conservative towns such as Harrogate often gave as much help as Labour ones. In London a meeting in Hyde Park on 1 November drew a crowd the police put at 3,000 and the journalist Ritchie Calder at 50,000. The petition reached the House of Commons but was not debated.

The marchers went home believing they had failed. By 1939 about 100 men worked in a small furniture factory and up to 500 more in metal-based industries on the Palmer's site, but large-scale employment returned only with the Second World War. Cornelius Whalen, the last survivor of those who walked the full distance, called it a waste of time.

The historians Malcolm Pearce and Geoffrey Stewart argue that the march helped to shape later perceptions of the 1930s and so prepared the way for social reform after the war. The town holds several memorials, and re-enactments marked the 50th and 75th anniversaries. The post-war Labour leadership, cold towards the march in 1936, later adopted it as a metaphor for working-class fortitude.
jasenovac-concentration-camp: The Independent State of Croatia (NDH) was founded on 10 April 1941 after the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia. It was essentially an Italo-German quasi-protectorate, but its daily administration lay almost wholly with Croatians under the Ustaše. Among the first decrees of its leader Ante Pavelić were laws restricting Jews and seizing their property, and a ban on the Cyrillic script used in the rites of the Serbian Orthodox Church. The first mass killing of Serbs, 196 people at Gudovac, took place on 30 April.

The camp was set in marshland at the confluence of the Sava and Una rivers near the village of Jasenovac, in the German occupation zone. It was a complex of five subcamps over 210 square kilometres on both banks of the rivers, with its largest camp at a brickworks about 100 kilometres south-east of Zagreb.

Jasenovac was established in August 1941, when the earlier camp at Jadovno was closed. The complex was built between August 1941 and February 1942, and it was run by Department III of the Ustaše Supervisory Service. Most inmates were Serbs, many brought after refusing to convert to Catholicism or taken from the Kozara region in 1942; others were Romani, Jews and political opponents. Unlike German camps it had no gas chambers. Prisoners were mostly killed with knives, hammers and axes, or shot, and some were cremated in the brickworks kilns.

Near the end of the war the Ustaše dug up and burned corpses to destroy evidence. On 19 April 1945 Maks Luburić ordered the camp destroyed. On 22 April about 600 prisoners revolted and only 92 escaped. The Ustaše burned the buildings, and when the Partisans entered in May they found ruins and skeletal remains.

Estimates of the dead are disputed, partly because the Ustaše destroyed records and many victims were never registered. Most modern sources give about 100,000. The Jasenovac Memorial Area keeps a list of 83,145 named victims, among them 47,627 Serbs, 16,173 Romani and 13,116 Jews. The memorial site was established in 1960, with the Flower Memorial designed by Bogdan Bogdanović as its central symbol, and a museum was added in 1968.
jasna-gora-monastery: Jasna Góra, in Polish Luminous Mountain, in Latin Clarus Mons, is a shrine dedicated to the Virgin Mary in Częstochowa and one of Poland's places of pilgrimage. It was founded in 1382 by Pauline monks who came from Hungary at the invitation of Vladislaus II of Opole, and the new monastery was entrusted with the icon of the Mother of God with the Christ Child, known as the Black Madonna of Częstochowa or Our Lady of Częstochowa, to which miraculous powers are attributed. It was originally a single-nave church, enlarged around 1463 into a three-nave Gothic hall church. The site is one of Poland's official national Historic Monuments.

On 14 April 1430 Jasna Góra was sacked by the Hussites. In the winter of 1655 the Swedish army unsuccessfully besieged the monastery during the Second Northern War, or the Deluge. The event stimulated Polish resistance, and on 1 April 1656, in the cathedral of Lwów, King Jan Kazimierz solemnly vowed to consecrate the country to the protection of the Mother of God and proclaimed her Patron and Queen of the lands of his kingdom. The Swedes besieged the monastery again without success in 1702, 1705 and 1709, and Russians besieged it in 1770-1772 during the Bar Confederation.

Reconstruction in the Baroque style took place between 1690 and 1693, and between 1693 and 1696 the walls of the nave and chancel were raised, turning the church from a hall into a basilica. In 1717 the icon was crowned by decision of Pope Clement XI. From 1760 to 1772 Jacob Frank, the founder of the Frankist sect, who considered himself a messiah, was imprisoned in the monastery. In 1909 thieves stole jewels, pearls and other valuables worth millions of rubles, though the icon was not damaged. Pope Pius X offered to replace the stolen crown, and a new coronation in 1910 drew crowds of up to 60,000. A monk, Damazy Macoch, confessed to the theft in 1910.

Every year since the Middle Ages thousands of Poles have walked to Jasna Góra in pilgrim groups. In 2011 it was estimated that 3.2 million pilgrims from 80 countries came to the shrine, about 830,000 of them in 228 organised pilgrimages, and the average group travelled about 350 kilometres in 11 days. Visitors are expected to be silent in the monastery, and pilgrims pass in front of the icon on their knees. Among its exhibits is the medal of the 1983 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Lech Wałęsa.
jason-of-pherae: Jason succeeded Lycophron I of Pherae, possibly his father, as tyrant of Pherae; Lycophron's aggressive rule had built a power base but also left instability in the city. The geographer Pausanias records that Jason knew the teachings of the Sophist Gorgias, and Isocrates claims to have been in contact with him, though none of their letters survives. Aristotle, in the Rhetoric, quotes Jason as saying that he had to do some few unjust things in order to do many just ones.

Jason enters history suddenly, in Xenophon's account of Theban hegemony in the 370s. Xenophon quotes him boasting of six thousand mercenaries from other states, picked men who could endure toils as hard as his own, unlike citizen armies with their old men and boys. Polydamas of Pharsalus suggested that Jason did not rely on intimidation alone but offered the local aristocracies and cities a united Thessaly under a recognised tagus, with a common army to protect them from rivalry and foreign intervention.

Abroad he combined military and naval power with diplomacy. He cultivated the Molossian kingdom of Alcetas I in Epirus and the Macedonian court of Amyntas III, entered the Second Athenian League and supported the Athenian admiral Timotheus at his trial. After intervening in central Greece he destroyed the fortifications of Heraclea in Trachis, so that no rival could use the city to block his movements. After the Battle of Leuctra he warned Thebes not to destroy Sparta, and later writers credit him with the half-cuirass worn by officers.

Jason was killed in 370 BCE by a group of unidentified young men. Xenophon suggests they feared he meant to take control of the Oracle of Delphi after the Pythian Games, and reports that when the people of Delphi asked the oracle what to do, it answered that Apollo could take care of his own shrine. Diodorus Siculus says the killers sought fame or acted on the orders of his brother Polydorus. Alexander, possibly his son, later inherited the title of tagus and ruled harshly until the Thebans defeated him. Historians see in Jason a ruler whose early death left unrealised a regional empire like that of Dionysius I in Sicily.
jasper-tudor: Jasper Tudor was born at the bishop of Ely's manor at Hatfield, Hertfordshire, in 1431, the second son of Sir Owen Tudor and Catherine of Valois, widow of Henry V, and so half-brother to Henry VI. After his mother died in 1437 Owen Tudor was arrested and sent to Newgate prison, and Jasper and his brother Edmund were put in the care of Katherine de la Pole, abbess of Barking, until March 1442. Henry VI then brought them to court and had them educated. Jasper was created Earl of Pembroke on 23 November 1452. His parents' marriage was not recognised, but he was made a Knight of the Garter.

Jasper's only major battle before Bosworth was Mortimer's Cross in February 1461, where he lost to the future Edward IV and his father Owen was captured and beheaded. Attainted when Edward took the throne, he held Denbigh Castle for the Lancastrians and lost Pembroke Castle to William Herbert in 1468. He regained the earldom briefly when Henry VI was restored, and fled again after Edward IV's return in 1471. Storms forced him and his nephew Henry Tudor to land in Brittany, where Duke Francis II sheltered them at the Château de Suscinio for eleven years.

An invasion from Brittany in October 1483 failed. In 1484 the Duke's treasurer Pierre Landais agreed to hand the Tudors to Richard III, but John Morton warned them and they escaped into France, to the court of Charles VIII. Jasper had brought up his nephew Henry Tudor, whose father Edmund had died before his birth.

After Henry's accession in 1485 Jasper's attainders were annulled and he was created Duke of Bedford. He helped Henry VII put down the Stafford and Lovell Rebellion in 1486 and Lambert Simnel's rising, ending at the Battle of Stoke Field, in 1487.

He married Katherine Woodville, widow of the Duke of Buckingham, on 7 November 1485; they had no children. After 1485 he described himself as "high and mighty Prince Jasper, brother and uncle of Kings, Duke of Bedford and Earl of Pembroke", and in 1488 he took possession of Cardiff Castle. He paid for the rebuilding of the north-west tower of Llandaff Cathedral, called the Jasper Tower. He died at Thornbury Castle on 21 December 1495 and was buried at Keynsham Abbey in Somerset.
jassa-singh-ahluwalia: Jassa Singh was born on 3 May 1718 into a Kalal Sikh family in the village of Ahlu near Lahore. Known at first as Jassa Singh Kalal, he took the name Ahluwalia from his ancestral village. A story of descent from the Bhatti Rajputs of Jaisalmer was created much later, in the time of Kharak Singh, and the British administrator Lepel Griffin dismissed it as fictitious.

He rose within the Dal Khalsa, the Sikh forces that Nawab Kapur Singh had organised in 1733 into the veteran Budha Dal and the younger Taruna Dal. At a meeting of the Sarbat Khalsa in 1748, Kapur Singh named him his successor, and his followers gave him the title Sultan-ul-Qaum, King of the Nation.

In early 1758 he and Sodhi Vadhbhag Singh helped Adina Beg defeat the Afghans at Mahilpur, and with the Marathas under Raghunathrao they drove the Afghans from Lahore. When the governor of Lahore, Khawajah Abed Khan, attacked Charat Singh at Gujranwala in September 1761, Jassa Singh led the Dal Khalsa to his aid, and in November the Sikhs took the city and its fort. Abed Khan was killed, and the Sikhs declared Jassa Singh Padshah. The Sikhs suffered one of their worst defeats in the Vadda Ghalughara of 1762, when Ahmad Shah Durrani attacked a convoy near Malerkotla.

In the following years he took Sirhind in January 1764, where the province was divided among seven misls and the Phulkian states, raided the upper Ganga Doab, and led 40,000 Sikhs to help Jawahar Singh of Bharatpur against Najib ad-Dawlah. He collected tribute from hill states such as Kangra, Bilaspur and Nalagarh. A long rivalry with Jassa Singh Ramgarhia led to open fighting in 1775.

In March 1783 the Dal Khalsa under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and Baghel Singh entered the Red Fort in Delhi, where the Sikhs placed him on the throne. Jassa Singh Ramgarhia challenged this, and Ahluwalia renounced the honour to avoid a fight. He died in Amritsar on 23 October 1783.

The historian Hari Ram Gupta stressed that he conquered Lahore, issued his own coin and sat on the Mughal throne while remaining a humble disciple of Guru Gobind Singh. A government college in Kapurthala, founded in 1856 by Raja Randhir Singh, bears his name, and the Government of India issued a stamp in his honour on 4 April 1985.
jassic-people: The Jász are an Iranian ethnic group of Eastern Iranic descent who have lived in Hungary since the 13th century. They originated as a nomadic Alanic people of the Pontic steppe. In English they are sometimes called Jassic, and their own names for themselves include Iasi and Jassy. They came to the Kingdom of Hungary together with the Cumans when their lands to the east, in what later became Moldavia, were invaded by the Mongol Empire in the middle of the 13th century. King Béla IV was willing to admit them in the hope that they would help resist the Mongol and Tatar invasion.

Soon after their arrival relations between the Hungarian nobility and the Cuman and Jász tribes worsened sharply, and the tribes left the country. They returned after the invasion ended and settled in the central Pannonian Plain, near the rivers Zagyva and Tarna. Their main occupation was at first animal husbandry. Over the next two centuries they were assimilated into the Hungarian population, but they kept a distinct Jász identity. The Hungarian rulers gave them special privileges, and they were largely self-governing in the area called Jászság, where Jászberény became the regional centre.

In the 16th and 17th centuries their lands were under Ottoman administration. After the lands were recaptured by the Habsburg monarchy, Emperor Leopold I sold the area to the Knights of the Teutonic Order, ending the privileged position of Jászberény. The Jász collected half a million Rhenish gold florins by 1745 to buy their freedom, and in the Act of Redemption Empress Maria Theresa restored their land and hereditary privileges. Their regional autonomy lasted until 1876, when the area became part of Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok County.

The Jász spoke Jassic, a dialect of Ossetian, an East Iranian language, which was replaced by Hungarian; it had reportedly died out by the 16th century. The only literary record of it was found in the 1950s in the Hungarian National Széchényi Library, and the language has been reconstructed with the help of Ossetian parallels. Their name survives in more than a dozen settlements of the Great Hungarian Plain, among them Jászberény and Jászárokszállás. The name is unrelated to that of the Sarmatian Iazyges, a confusion that goes back to medieval scholars. In 1995 the 250th anniversary of the Act of Redemption was marked at Jászberény.
jaswant-singh-of-marwar: Jaswant Singh was born on 26 December 1626 at Burhanpur, the youngest son of Maharaja Gaj Singh of Marwar. He succeeded on 6 May 1638 by special decree of Emperor Shah Jahan and was installed at Mehrangarh in Jodhpur on 25 May 1638. His father's favourite concubine, Anara Begum, who regarded him as her own son and was at odds with the heir apparent Amar Singh Rathore, had a part in his accession; Amar Singh was later given Nagore in compensation. He held in jagir the parganas of Jodhpur, Siwana, Merta, Sojat, Phalodi and Pokharan, and Shah Jahan granted him the personal title of Maharaja on 6 January 1654.

Shah Jahan sent him to stop the advance of the rebel princes Aurangzeb and Murad. The armies met at Dharmatpur, fifteen miles from Ujjain, on 15 April 1658. His advisers proposed a night raid on Aurangzeb's artillery and gunpowder, since the Rajput army was almost wholly light cavalry; he is quoted as answering that it was inconsistent with the manliness of the Rajputs to employ stratagems or make a night attack. He was defeated and lost 6,000 men, among them Ratan Singh Rathore of Ratlam and Mokand Das Hada of Kota.

Posted to the Deccan, he made Pune his headquarters. In 1664 he besieged Kondana without success, and he left for Delhi after Jai Singh was sent to the Deccan. He returned in 1667 with Prince Muazzam, the new viceroy, and acted as an intermediary between Shivaji and Aurangzeb. In 1670 he was posted at Burhanpur.

His son Prithviraj Singh died at Delhi on 8 May 1667; the khyats, the chronicles of Marwar, say that Aurangzeb had given him a poisoned robe. Jaswant Singh died at Jamrud, near Peshawar, on a date usually converted as 28 December 1678, though another scholar makes it 28 November 1678. Two of his wives were pregnant at his death and both bore sons, which led to a war over the installation of Ajit Singh Rathore as ruler of Marwar. He was also a man of letters, the author of the Siddhant-Bodh, the Anand Vilas and the Bhasha-Bhushan.
jataka-tales: The word jātaka means of the birth. According to the traditional account in the Pali Jātakanidāna, a prologue to the stories, Gautama vowed in front of a past Buddha, Dipankara, to become a Buddha himself, and then spent many lifetimes on the path. The stories from those lives are recorded as jātakas. The genre rests on the idea that the Buddha could recall all his past lives and used the memories to illustrate his teachings.

The tales may be very old. Depictions in early Indian art go back as far as the second century BCE, and many narratives survive in almost identical form in the canons of different schools, which suggests that they date from before the schisms between those schools. Sarah Shaw dates the verse portions of the Pali Jātaka to the fifth century BCE and says later parts were added up to the third century CE.

In these stories the future Buddha may appear as a king, an outcaste, a deva or an animal, and whatever his form he shows a virtue that the tale teaches. Many follow a threefold plan: a narrative in the present, a story from a past life, and a link in which the characters of the past are identified with those of the present. The tales illustrate the perfections of a bodhisattva, such as generosity, and teach moral lessons within the framework of karma and rebirth.

The largest known collection is the Jātakatthavaṇṇanā of the Theravada school, part of the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Pali Canon, which holds 547 jātakas in verse and prose and was collected around 500 CE. Other sources include the Cariyāpiṭaka, which includes 35 jātakas, and Āryaśūra's Sanskrit Jātakamālā.

Jātakas were among the first texts translated into Chinese, and Kāng Sēnghuì, working at Nanking around 247, was one of their first translators. The earliest known illustrations are on the railings of the Bharhut stupa and at Sanchi, from the late second to the first century BCE, and they later appear at Ajanta and at Bagan, where the Ananda Temple depicts 554 tales. The Chinese pilgrim Yijing said that jātaka plays were performed throughout the five countries of India in the 7th century.

The Vessantara Jataka is still recited and performed in Theravada countries. E. B. Cowell and others translated the Pali collection into English in six volumes between 1895 and 1907. A jātaka was also adapted by the 10th-century Shia scholar Ibn Bābūya as Balawhar wa-Būdāsf, which became the Christian story of Barlaam and Joasaph.
jats: The Jats, also spelt Jaats and Jatts, were originally nomadic pastoralists in the lower Indus River Valley of Sindh and Makran, and they gradually became farmers. Many moved north into the Punjab and then into Delhi, north-eastern Rajasthan and the western Gangetic Plain at the turn of the second millennium CE. The word Jat comes from the Prakrit Jaṭṭa, itself from Jarta or Jartika, the name of an ancient non-Vedic Bahlika tribe. The first mention of Jats is in an inscription from Gilgit-Baltistan dated to the 6th or 7th century. From the Mughal era in Punjab, Jat was used more as a socioeconomic status than an ethnic label, and the Jats were often associated with the peasantry.

Before they settled in the Punjab and other northern regions, the pastoralist Jats had little exposure to the mainstream religions, according to the historians Catherine Asher and Cynthia Talbot, and they adopted the dominant religion of the people among whom they lived. Several clans have traditions of converting to Islam in the first half of the second millennium CE under the influence of Sufi saints, and by the 16th century many Punjabi clans west of the Ravi River were Muslim. Jats moved onto the Gangetic Plain in two large migrations, in the 17th and 18th centuries, as an umbrella group of peasant-warriors rather than a caste in the usual Hindu sense.

Significant conversions of Jats to Sikhism occurred as early as the time of Guru Angad, but the first large-scale conversions are commonly held to have begun under Guru Arjan, who founded towns such as Tarn Taran Sahib, Kartarpur and Hargobindpur. The Jats formed the vanguard of Sikh resistance against the Mughal Empire from the 18th century onwards. At the partition of India many Muslim Jats migrated to Pakistan, while some stayed in India as Muley Jats. By the 20th century landowning Jats had become an influential group in Punjab, western Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi.

Jat marriage is traditionally structured around clan (gotra) exogamy and village exogamy, while Jats marry within their own community. The Khap system, councils of clan elders and notables, was historically the prevailing form of organisation, and it continues today as an extrajudicial body without legal recognition. Scholars disagree on the varna status of the Jats in Hinduism: the historian Irfan Habib cites a Shudra status in the 11th century that had become Vaishya by the 17th. The Arya Samaj, popular among them, advanced a claim to Kshatriya status.
jauja: Jauja lies in the fertile Mantaro Valley of the central highlands of Peru, at an altitude of about 3,400 metres and 45 kilometres northwest of Huancayo, the capital of the Junín Region. The Mantaro River flows near the town into a large alluvial plain, and the valley is bounded by Cordillera ranges and fed by three tributaries, the Masma, the Paca and the Yanamarca. The Laguna de Paca lies a few kilometres to the north. The Quechua name is Sausa or Shawsha, and the Spanish formerly wrote it Xauxa, with the x pronounced sh.

Before the Inca, the area belonged to the Xauxa-Wanka confederation. The Xauxa were warriors who accepted Inca rule and sent soldiers on campaigns towards Quito. The Inca made Hatun Xauxa the administrative centre of the province, joined to the rest of the empire by the main section of the Qhapaq Ñam, the royal road between Cusco and Quito. In the Inca civil war the Xauxa supported Waskar, and the town became the military headquarters of his army against Atawallpa until the general Challco Chima took it. Francisco Pizarro later had Challco Chima burned alive there, on suspicion of secret communication with Quiz Quiz.

After the Spanish took Cusco in 1533, Pizarro established Xauxa as Peru's first capital in April 1534, under the name Santa Fe de Hatun Xauxa. He and his men found great stores of Inca food, clothing and wealth there. In 1535 the capital was moved to Lima, nearer the port of Callao, and Lima overshadowed Jauja. In colonial times Jauja came to depend on Tarma, and later Huancayo surpassed it as a commercial centre. Its dry climate was later found helpful for tuberculosis patients, and the sanatorium Domingo Olavegoya drew patients from many parts of the world until antibiotics reduced its role.

Jauja is the capital of Jauja Province, with a population of 15,432 in 2015. Its main activity is the retail trade of agricultural products from the Mantaro Valley, and it holds a Wednesday and a Sunday market. Partial ruins of the Inca and Xauxa settlement stand on a hill about three kilometres southeast of the town. The Jauja cathedral dates from 1564. The name Jauja entered Spanish in the expression país de Jauja, a land of plenty, which is said to have grown from the wealth the Spanish found there at the conquest.
java: Java is one of the Greater Sunda Islands, lying between Sumatra to the west and Bali to the east, with the Java Sea to the north and the Indian Ocean to the south. It is almost entirely of volcanic origin, and a chain of volcanic mountains forms the east–west spine of the island and splits the interior into relatively isolated regions suited to wet-rice cultivation. Indonesian coffee was first grown there from 1699. Fossils of Homo erectus, known as Java Man and dated to 1.3 million years ago, were found on the banks of the Bengawan Solo River.

Wet-field rice cultivation required cooperation between villages, and out of these alliances small kingdoms developed. The period from the 5th to the 15th century is called the Hindu-Buddhist or Classic period. The Taruma kingdom of western Java existed from the 5th to the 7th centuries, and the first state to leave a substantial record was the Mataram kingdom, founded in central Java at the beginning of the 8th century. Its rulers patronised both Hindu and Buddhist institutions. From the second half of the 8th century they called themselves members of the Sailendra dynasty, and Borobudur was built in the late 8th century and Prambanan in the mid-9th.

Islam became the dominant religion through the 16th century, first in the north-coast port cities such as Surabaya, Gresik, Demak and Cirebon, through contact with foreign Muslim traders. Demak was the first Muslim kingdom to achieve a degree of hegemony and defeated the remnants of the Majapahit kingdom. At the turn of the 17th century the inland kingdom of Mataram became dominant in central and eastern Java, and under Sultan Agung, who reigned from 1613 to 1646, it subjugated the coastal principalities of Surabaya and Cirebon.

Contact with European powers began in 1522 with a treaty between the Sunda kingdom and the Portuguese in Malacca. A Dutch expedition under Cornelis de Houtman made the first Dutch contact in 1596. By the end of the 18th century the Dutch East India Company had extended its influence over the interior sultanates, intervening in wars between rival Mataram claimants. In the 1750s Sultan Mangkubumi tried to restore Mataram's control, but the Dutch divided the kingdom into the Surakarta and Yogyakarta principalities. Indonesian nationalism took hold in the early 20th century, and independence was recognised in 1949.

Java is part of Indonesia and the world's most populous island, home to about 56 percent of the country's people. Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia, lies on its north-western coast. The main languages are Javanese, Sundanese, Madurese and Betawi. Five of Indonesia's World Heritage Sites are on the island, among them Borobudur and Prambanan.
java-sea: The Java Sea lies on the Sunda Shelf, between Borneo to the north, Java to the south, Sumatra to the west and Sulawesi to the east. The Karimata Strait on its north-western side links it to the South China Sea. It is generally considered part of the western Pacific Ocean, though it is occasionally counted as part of the Indian Ocean. The sea covers the southern section of the Sunda Shelf, with a surface area of about 320,000 square kilometres. It measures about 1,600 kilometres from east to west and 380 kilometres from north to south, and its mean depth is only 46 metres.

The sea formed as sea levels rose at the end of the last ice age. Its almost uniformly flat bottom, and drainage channels that can be traced to the mouths of island rivers, show that the Sunda Shelf was once a stable, dry land of low relief. A few granite hills that resisted erosion were left standing above it and are now the islands.

From February to March 1942 the Battle of the Java Sea was fought here, one of the costliest naval battles of the World War II. The naval forces of the Netherlands, Britain, Australia and the United States were nearly destroyed in trying to defend Java from Japanese attack.

The seafloor of the southern part is geologically similar to northern Java, where oil fields occur and extend under the sea, and the exploration of petroleum and natural gas here has become the basis of Indonesia's national export programme. Fishing is an important activity, and more than 3,000 species of marine life are found in the area. Karimunjawa is one of several national parks, and the Thousand Islands lie north of Jakarta, forming the city's only regency.
java-war: The Treaty of Giyanti of 1755 divided the Mataram Sultanate into the princely states of Yogyakarta and Surakarta, and the Mangkunegaran was formed in 1757. The weakness of the Dutch in the late 18th century left the princely states with de facto sovereignty. Prince Diponegoro, born in 1785, was the eldest son of Sultan Hamengkubuwono III of Yogyakarta, and through his mother he claimed descent from the Wali Sanga, the early apostles of Islam in Java. By 1824 several of his allies had been expelled from court, and in early 1825 the Dutch annexed territory from the Sultanate as a lease without consulting him.

On 17 June 1825 the Dutch Resident Smissaert ordered a road to be repaired that passed Diponegoro's estate at Tegalreja. Fights broke out between the road workers and his men, and on 20 July a detachment was sent to arrest him. He withdrew to Selarong Cave and declared his rebellion on 21 July 1825.

Hendrik Merkus de Kock commanded about 12,500 Dutch Indies troops, half of them native recruits whose loyalty the Dutch doubted, and later received 3,154 European soldiers and over 10,000 auxiliaries. Diponegoro's followers included seventy members of the royal family, and he divided his forces under sixteen commanders of noble birth. The princely courts were split. Rebel forces besieged Yogyakarta until a Dutch relief force arrived, and the war became a guerrilla struggle in which disease, hostile villagers and manpower shortages hampered the Dutch. By April 1827 some 1,600 of de Kock's men had been killed.

From 1827 the Dutch built a system of field fortifications, the Benteng-stelsel, of which 133 of 258 forts were built in 1828 and 1829. Kyai Maja, Diponegoro's spiritual adviser, surrendered in November 1828, and Sentot Prawirodirdjo surrendered in October 1829. Diponegoro was left with about fifty men. On 28 March 1830, during negotiations at Magelang, de Kock announced his arrest.

Diponegoro was exiled to Manado, moved to Makassar in 1833 and died on 8 January 1855. At least 200,000 Javanese were killed, with some 15,000 dead on the Dutch side and about 20,000 among the rebels. One third of Java's population of 6 million was directly affected and about a quarter of its arable land was damaged. The war was the last significant armed resistance to Dutch rule until the Indonesian National Revolution, and the princely states lost much of their remaining power. Diponegoro wrote the Babad Diponegoro in exile, and he was declared a National Hero of Indonesia in 1973.
javad-khan: Javad was the son of Shahverdi Khan and his wife Sharafjahan Khanum. In 1778, when his elder half-brother Muhammad Khan seized the throne of Ganja and began killing his relatives, Javad fled to Ibrahim Khalil Khan of Karabakh. He came to power in 1786, after his brother Rahim Khan was deposed through Georgian and Karabakh intervention, and was the sixth and last khan of Ganja.

His first years were dominated by pressure from King Heraclius II of Georgia, who demanded Ganja for himself. A joint Georgian and Russian march on the town in 1787 ended when the Russian battalions were recalled at the start of the Russian-Turkish war, and in early 1789 Georgian troops under Prince Vakhtang defeated Javad. The death of Fath Ali Khan of Quba in March 1789 let him recover his position. He was the first to acknowledge Agha Muhammad Khan Qajar as shah, joined him at Ganja in 1795 and guided his army to Tiflis, which the shah's forces plundered for nine days.

When the Russian expedition of 1796 under Valerian Zubov arrived, Javad handed over the keys of Ganja and admitted a Russian garrison, but the troops were withdrawn after Catherine died. In 1797 Agha Muhammad imprisoned him at Shusha for failing to resist the Russians; the shah was assassinated there on 17 June 1797, and Javad escaped. After the death of George XII of Georgia in 1800 he raided Georgian lands and claimed Kazakh and Shamshadil.

Pavel Tsitsianov marched on Ganja in November 1803 and claimed it as a former Georgian possession; Javad's reply cited the town's Safavid past and declared himself ready for battle. Bombardment began on 15 December, and on 14 January 1804, after Armenians in the town opened a gate, Russian troops under Major Lisanevich took the fortress. Javad was killed by Lisanevich, and his son Hossein Qoli died hours later. Between 1,500 and 3,000 inhabitants were killed, and the fall of Ganja set off the Russo-Persian War of 1804–1813.

Russian sources called him stubborn, and the historian Abbasgulu Bakikhanov described him as skilful and ruthless. In Azerbaijan he is regarded as a hero, with streets in Baku and Ganja named after him. His descendants in the Russian Empire took the surname Ziyadkhanov.
javanshir: Juansher was the second of the four sons of Varaz Grigor, prince of Albania from 628 to 637, whom he succeeded. His family, the Mihranids, were of Parthian origin but claimed descent from the Sasanian kings; their ancestor Mihran was said to have received Gardman from Khosrow II, and around 600 a Mihranid prince conquered all of Albania and took the title Arranshah. The name Juansher comes from the Persian for young lion. He probably spoke Middle Persian and Armenian and knew Albanian, some Greek and perhaps a little Arabic.

Juansher led the Albanian contingent in the army of Rostam Farrokhzad against the Arab invasion of Iran. He was badly wounded at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah and escaped by swimming the Euphrates, and later commanded 3,000 men guarding Yazdegerd III's withdrawal from Ctesiphon. In 644/45, losing faith in the Sasanians, he returned home and rebelled. The Sasanians retook the lowlands and the capital, Partaw, but his guerrilla war, backed by leading men of Iberia, forced them to grant him wide autonomy.

After the fall of the Sasanian Empire in 651 his father acknowledged the caliph but had Juansher offer his services to the Byzantine emperor Constans II, who made him protopatrikios and sent him a piece of the True Cross. This allegiance took effect during the caliphate's civil war of 656–661, when Constans anointed him king of all the eastern peoples in 661. Juansher made peace with the North Caucasian Huns after their raid of 665 and married their king's daughter.

He then submitted to the Umayyad caliph Mu'awiya I and, by report, advised him on how to kill Constans II, who was assassinated on 15 July 669. Juansher was rewarded with Siwnik and a third of the tribute the caliphate drew from Albania. He was murdered at Partaw during the Feast of the Cross by a traitor named Varaznoy; the historian James Howard-Johnston thinks he had lost the caliph's trust. His nephew Varaz-Tiridates I succeeded him.

Although a Christian, Juansher kept the Zoroastrian New Year feast of Nawasard and enjoyed the performances of the gusank, minstrels. A chapter of Movses Kaghankatvatsi's History of the Caucasian Albanians contains a poem to him by Davtak Kertogh, counted the first long secular poem in Armenian literature.
javier-de-burgos: Francisco Javier de Burgos y del Olmo was born into a noble but poor family and was meant for a career in the Roman Catholic Church. He soon abandoned his studies in Granada and went to Madrid to study law. When the French invaded under Napoleon I at the start of the Peninsular War, he became one of the afrancesados, the supporters of King Joseph I, and took up administrative duties in Andalusia. His collaboration made him an enemy of the House of Bourbon, and in 1812 he left for Paris.

In France he studied the classics and began translating Horace into Castilian. Andrés Bello judged him a poor translator but an excellent commentator; the revised version Burgos published in 1844 remained a reference, valued for its use of the sapphic stanza with free verse. He returned to Madrid in 1819 and in 1822 became editor of El Imparcial, a paper of moderate liberals and afrancesados. He also wrote the many volumes of the Biografía universal, and on 7 January 1830 he took up seat R of the Real Academia Española.

Burgos entered the administration of Ferdinand VII as undersecretary of State in the ministry of Francisco Cea Bermúdez. Under the regency of Maria Christina he was the driving force behind the territorial division of 1833, approved in November and December of that year, which replaced the old administrative system with a provincial one and reflected his belief in centralised government. The design conflicted openly with the self-government of the Basque districts and above all of Navarre, still a kingdom of its own.

Under Isabella II he was a senator of the Moderado liberals, a royal counsellor, and minister in the first government of Ramón María Narváez y Campos, Duke of Valencia, an office taken over under Narváez's successor Francisco Javier Istúriz. He also wrote occasional poems, on the death of María Isabel de Braganza and the wedding of Ferdinand VII and Maria Christina, and the Oda a la Razón. He died in Madrid.
javier-perez-de-cuellar: Javier Pérez de Cuéllar was born on 19 January 1920 in Lima, to a rentier family of Spanish descent whose ancestors had migrated from Spain in the sixteenth century. His father died when he was four. He attended the Colegio San Agustín, learned French from a governess and took a law degree at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru in 1943. He joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 1940 as an intern and the diplomatic service in 1944, serving first at Peru's embassy in France, where he married Yvette Roberts-Darricau in 1947.

He was a member of the Peruvian delegation to the first session of the United Nations General Assembly in London in 1946, and later served as ambassador to Switzerland, the Soviet Union and Poland, and Venezuela.

In 1971 he became Peru's permanent representative to the United Nations. He sat on the Security Council in 1973 and 1974, presiding when the Cypriot coup took place in July 1974, and from 1975 to 1977 he was the Secretary-General's Special Representative in Cyprus. In 1979 he became under-secretary-general for Special Political Affairs and in 1981 the Secretary-General's personal representative on Afghanistan. In December 1981 he was selected to succeed Kurt Waldheim as Secretary-General, and he was re-elected unanimously in October 1986.

As Secretary-General he mediated between the United Kingdom and Argentina after the Falklands War, supported the Contadora group in Central America and in 1983 initiated the World Commission on Environment and Development. He worked on Namibian independence, Western Sahara, Cyprus, the Iran–Iraq War and the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan, and in March 1986 formally accused Iraq of using chemical weapons against Iran. His second term ended on 31 December 1991, after Boutros Boutros-Ghali was agreed as successor in November.

Pérez de Cuéllar ran unsuccessfully against Alberto Fujimori for the presidency of Peru in 1995 and was prime minister and foreign minister from November 2000 to July 2001. He then served as ambassador to France until 2004. In 1997 he published a memoir of his United Nations years, Pilgrimage for Peace. He received the Prince of Asturias Award for International Cooperation in 1987 and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1991. He died at his home in Lima on 4 March 2020, two months after his hundredth birthday, the first secretary-general of the United Nations to become a centenarian.
jawaharlal-nehru: Jawaharlal Nehru was born on 14 November 1889 in Allahabad to Swarup Rani and Motilal Nehru, a wealthy, self-made barrister who served as president of the Indian National Congress in 1919 and 1928. Both parents were Kashmiri Pandits. Nehru grew up in the mansion Anand Bhavan and was educated at home by governesses and tutors. He became an ardent nationalist in his youth, stirred by the Second Boer War and the Russo-Japanese War.

He was educated at Harrow School and Trinity College, Cambridge, from which he graduated in 1910 with an honours degree in natural science, and trained in the law at the Inner Temple. After returning to India in August 1912 he enrolled at the Allahabad High Court, but had little interest in the law, and nationalist politics gradually replaced his practice.

Nehru met Mahatma Gandhi in 1916. During the non-cooperation movement of 1920 he directed political activity in the United Provinces, and on 6 December 1921 he was imprisoned for the first of eight periods of detention between 1921 and 1945, lasting over nine years in all. He pressed the Congress to break all ties with the British Empire, and as its president at the Lahore session on 29 December 1929 he introduced a successful resolution calling for complete independence.

The Congress swept the 1937 provincial elections under his leadership. After the Quit India Resolution of 8 August 1942, senior Congress leaders were imprisoned, and in their absence the Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah grew in power.

Nehru became interim prime minister in September 1946. On 15 August 1947 he gave the speech Tryst with Destiny and was sworn in as prime minister of the Dominion of India, and on 26 January 1950 he became first prime minister of the Republic. He held office for 16 years and 286 days, and the Congress won the elections of 1951, 1957 and 1962 under him.

In 1961 the Indian Army invaded Portuguese-controlled Goa, which he formally annexed. From 1959 his Forward Policy set up military outposts in disputed territory on the Sino-Indian border, and China attacked some of them, beginning the Sino-Indian War of 1962, which India lost. He died in office in 1964.

Bhikhu Parekh regards Nehru as the founder of the modern Indian state, for the national philosophy of modernisation he formulated, with goals including national unity, parliamentary democracy, industrialisation, socialism, the scientific temper and non-alignment. He advocated a mixed economy, with a government-controlled public sector coexisting with private industry, and directed investment into steel, iron, coal and power. In December 1953 he appointed the States Reorganisation Commission to prepare states on linguistic lines. In foreign affairs he led the establishment of the Non-Aligned Movement. His books include An Autobiography (1936) and The Discovery of India (1946).
jawor: Jawor lies in the Lower Silesian Voivodeship in south-western Poland, on the river Raging Nysa (Nysa Szalona), and is the seat of Jawor County. Its name comes from the Polish word for the sycamore maple; it was first written down as Jawr in 1133 and as Jawor in 1203. The German name Jauer comes from the Slavic name and became official after 1763.

Jawor was the main stronghold of the Trzebowianie tribe and became part of the emerging Polish state in the 10th century. It received town rights between 1242 and 1275. After the fragmentation of Poland it belonged to the Duchy of Silesia and from 1248 to the Duchy of Legnica, and from 1274 it was the capital of the Duchy of Jawor, the south-westernmost duchy of medieval Poland. It was joined to the Duchy of Świdnica in 1346 and remained part of it until 1392, always under the Piast dynasty.

Stone walls were built by the end of the 13th century. In 1329 Duke Henry I of Jawor granted the town staple right, and guilds of furriers, tailors, clothiers and merchants were founded in the 14th century. Jawor became one of the main centres of weaving in Lower Silesia.

After Poland lost the town it was ruled by Bohemia and later by Austria. In the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) it was repeatedly invaded and occupied by the Austrians, Saxony and the Swedes, and in 1648 the Austrians plundered and burned it and expelled its inhabitants. Under the Peace of Westphalia the Church of Peace was built, although Protestants continued to be discriminated against by the Austrian administration. The town passed to Prussia in 1763 and became part of Germany in 1871. Most of its population was evacuated in early 1945, the Soviets took it in February, and it passed to Poland in April, after which the remaining Germans were expelled and Polish settlers became the majority.

Jawor keeps a medieval street plan with Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque buildings, including the Piast castle, the medieval town walls, the Town Hall and the churches of St. Martin and St. Barbara. The Church of Peace is a Historic Monument of Poland and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Local industries include electrical machinery, chemicals, paper and food, and there are granite and basalt quarries nearby.
jaxa-of-kopenick: Twelfth-century sources name several men called Jaxa with similar careers: the son-in-law of the magnate Piotr Włostowic, the founder of the Holy Sepulchre monastery at Miechów, and the prince of the Sprevane on the Spree. Gerard Labuda, following Jan Długosz, held them to be different people, but the view with most supporters today is that they were one man. Some scholars think his mother was Przybysława, sister of the Stodoran prince Przybysław Henryk.

In 1145 Jaxa married Agapia, also called Beatrice, daughter of Piotr Włostowic. Her dowry of estates in Silesia, Greater Poland and Lesser Poland, centred on Miechów, made him one of the most powerful lords in Poland. Their only son died in 1158 as a hostage at the court of the Bohemian king Vladislav II.

How he came to rule the Sprevane, in his own right or as a vassal of Duke Bolesław IV the Curly, is unknown. The chief source for his war over Brenna is the Tractatus de captione urbis Brandenburg of Henry of Antwerp, who says Jaxa came with a large Polish army, seized the city and took captives to Poland. After Brenna capitulated on 11 June 1157 he ruled from Köpenick, whose island castle was rebuilt in the mid-12th century. The capture is generally regarded as the beginning of the Margraviate of Brandenburg.

His bracteates, with legends read as Jaksa knez of Copnic, are virtually the only case of a West Slavic ruler naming his title in the vernacular rather than Latin. In 1162 he made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem and gained leave from Patriarch Amalric of Nesle to found a house of the Canons Regular of the Holy Sepulchre at Miechów. In 1167 he joined the rebellion against Bolesław the Curly in support of Casimir the Just.

After his son's death Jaxa founded or endowed many churches, among them the Norbertine houses of Zwierzyniec and Krzyżanowice and the Church of St. Michael in Wrocław, completed by his widow. He most likely died in the 1170s, in 1176 according to the Chronicle of the Kraków Chapter. His principality on the Spree probably lasted until around 1200, when Margrave Conrad II of Lusatia conquered it. A monument to him stands on the Schildhorn peninsula in the Havel.
jayachamarajendra-wodeyar: He was born at Mysore Palace on 18 July 1919, the only son and last child of Yuvaraja Kanteerava Narasimharaja Wadiyar and Yuvarani Kempu Cheluvajamanni. He was schooled at the Royal School, Mysore, and taught Sanskrit and Kannada by Motaganahalli Ramasesha Sastri. He graduated from Maharaja's College, Mysore, in 1938 with five awards and gold medals, married Satya Prema Kumari on 15 May of that year and toured Europe in 1939. His hopes of becoming a concert pianist ended when the deaths of his father and of his uncle, Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV, brought him to the throne.

He ascended the throne on 8 September 1940. He was the first ruler to accede to the new Indian Union, signing an instrument of accession on the eve of independence in 1947, and the kingdom was merged into the Republic of India on 26 January 1950. He kept a privy purse and the title of maharaja until the 26th Amendment to the Constitution ended all such compensation in 1971.

After the Kannada-majority parts of the Madras and Hyderabad States were joined to Mysore, he became the first governor of the reorganised state on 1 November 1956, and was governor of Madras from 4 May 1964 to 28 June 1966. His Kannada teacher Kuvempu said that he became a great king by renouncing a throne.

He wrote on Indian philosophy, including Dattatreya: The Way and The Goal and The Gita and Indian Culture, and sponsored Kannada translations of Sanskrit classics, among them 35 parts of the Rigveda. A Licentiate of the Guildhall School of Music, he became the first president of the Philharmonia Concert Society in 1948, founded the Medtner Society in London and paid for recordings of Nikolai Medtner's works; Medtner dedicated his third piano concerto to him. His subsidy to Walter Legge helped secure the Philharmonia Orchestra.

He learnt the veena and composed 94 Carnatic works under the name Shri Vidya, and is credited with creating the raga Jayasamvardini. He died at his Bangalore Palace on 23 September 1974 and was succeeded as head of the royal family by his son Srikantadatta Narasimharaja Wadiyar.
jayadeva: Little is known of Jayadeva's life. He was born into a Brahmin family, though the date and place of his birth are uncertain; the Gita Govinda gives the village of Kindubilva, which scholars have identified with Kenduli Sasan near Puri in Odisha, Jaydev Kenduli in Birbhum district in West Bengal, or Kenduli near Jhanjharpur in Bihar. Several sixteenth-century texts say that he came from Utkala, another name for Odisha. His parents are named as Bhojadeva and Ramadevi. According to tradition he married a dancer named Padmavati at Puri, though early commentators and modern scholars do not support this.

Inscriptions at the Lingaraja temple and at the Madhukeswara and Simhachala temples show that Jayadeva was a member of the teaching faculty of a school at Kurmapataka, identified near Konark in Odisha, where he may also have studied. He probably left his village for Kurmapataka after his childhood education and gained experience in composing poetry, music and dancing. He is described as a mendicant known for his poetic genius in eastern India.

Jayadeva is known above all for the Gita Govinda, a poem on the love of Krishna and the gopi Radha, in a rite of spring, which presents Radha as greater than Krishna and is an important text in the Bhakti movement. The earliest commentary was written in Odisha around 1190. In the Jagannatha temple at Puri it is sung every night during the Badasinghara ritual, set to Odissi ragas and talas, and tradition holds that this has continued since the poet's time. The Odisha State Museum holds two hundred and ten manuscripts of it.

A few poems of Jayadeva in archaic Odia have been published, and he is widely considered one of the earliest musicians of Odissi music. He is the earliest dated author of hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib, which includes two of his.
jayanegara: Jayanegara's formal regnal name was Sri Maharaja Wiralandagopala Sri Sundarapandya Dewa Adhiswara, and from 1295 he was Prince of Kediri. His father, Dyah Wijaya, who took the throne as King Kertarajasa Jayawardhana in about 1293/1294, had married all four daughters of Kertanegara to secure his claim to the Singhasari legacy, and also Indreswari, or Dara Petak, a princess of the Malayu Kingdom brought from Sumatra by Kertanegara's Pamalayu expedition.

His name comes from the Sanskrit-derived Old Javanese words jaya, glorious, and nagara, city or nation, and so means glorious nation. To reconcile the differing accounts of his mother, some historians suggest that Jayanegara was Dara Petak's son by birth but was adopted and raised by the childless Queen Tribhuwaneswari.

Former companions in arms of his father rose against him, among them Gajah Biru in 1314. During the Kuti rebellion of 1319 the king barely escaped from the capital with the help of Gajah Mada and the palace guard and hid in the village of Badander. Gajah Mada returned to the capital, found that Kuti had the support of neither the people nor the nobles, and led the forces that crushed the revolt.

Tradition remembers the king as strikingly handsome but immoral, desiring the wives and daughters of his subordinates. He kept his half-sisters, Princess Tya and Princess Wiyat, in a fortified palace, unmarried past a suitable age, perhaps to prevent their suitors from contesting his throne. His Malayu mother also made him seem foreign rather than truly Javanese. He sent embassies to China from 1325 to 1328.

Gajah Mada killed Tanca at once, before any investigation. George Coedes wrote that the king was assassinated by a noble whose wife he had seduced, and some historians identify that noble with Tanca; another theory suspects Gajah Mada, a trusted adviser of Princess Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi. Jayanegara died childless. Gayatri Rajapatni had become a bhikkhuni, so her daughter Tribhuwana became regent, and Tribhuwana's son Hayam Wuruk became king in 1350. The Bajang Ratu gate at Trowulan has traditionally been linked to Jayanegara's memorial compound.
jayapala: Jayapala, or Jayapaladeva, son of Hutpal or Āśtapāla, ruled the Hindu Shahi kingdom from 964. The Barikot inscription gives his full title as Parama Bhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Sri Jayapaladeva. His lands stretched from Lamghan in the west to Kashmir in the east and from Sirhind to Multan. Kabul fell in 977 to the new Ghaznavid dynasty under Sabuktigin, and the Shahis at Udabhandapura tried repeatedly to win it back.

In 986–987 Jayapala marched on Ghazni and met Sabuktigin at Ghuzak. After days of inconclusive fighting a thunderstorm turned the battle against the Shahis, and Jayapala agreed to pay one million Shahi dirhams and fifty war elephants and to cede frontier forts. Back in his own lands he broke the treaty and imprisoned the Ghaznavid commanders sent to take the forts. Sabuktigin plundered Lamghan in reply.

In 991 the Shahis, with troops from other rajas, were routed near Kindi despite their greater numbers, and the land up to Peshawar was lost for a time. In the east Jayapala's son Anandapala, governor of Punjab, defeated Bharat, raja of Lahore, who was reinstated as a feudatory; around 998–999 the Shahis annexed Lahore after Bharat's son Chandrak had deposed his father.

Mahmud of Ghazni took the Ghaznavid throne in 998. On 27 September 1001 he attacked Jayapala at Peshawar before Shahi reinforcements could arrive, and Jayapala and fifteen of his relatives were taken prisoner. About 100,000 men and women were enslaved, and the royal necklaces alone were valued at over six million Shahi dirhams. Within months the whole Shahi territory west of the Indus had submitted to Mahmud.

Later accounts say that Jayapala, feeling himself disgraced, entered a funeral pyre. His son Anandapala ruled until 1010 and was followed by Trilocanapala, who reigned until 1021, and Shahi rule ended in 1026 with the death of Bhimapala. The wars between the Hindu Shahis and the rulers of Ghazni stretched over fifteen years before the Ghaznavids established their rule over the region, Kabul included.
jayapura: Jayapura lies on the northern coast of New Guinea, on Yos Sudarso Bay, and covers 835.48 km2. The land varies from valleys to hills, plateaus and mountains up to 700 metres, and about 30% of the area is inhabited, the rest being rough terrain, swamp and protected forest. It borders Papua New Guinea to the east, and has a tropical rainforest climate with heavy rain throughout the year. The name is Sanskrit for city of victory and was given by Suharto as part of the removal of Sukarno's name from the city. Some people have proposed local names such as Port Numbay, after the Numbay river, whose name means clear water.

Before Dutch colonial government the place was known as Numbay. Trade there was active, centred on the island of Metui Debi, and was carried on by barter for spices, cassava, salted fish and bird-of-paradise plumes. The society of Numbay, or Tabi in general, was led by an ondoafi, the chief of the tribe. By 1849 the region was a tributary of the Tidore Sultanate. On 28 September 1909 a Dutch naval detachment under Captain F.J.P. Sachse came ashore at Humboldt Bay to explore northern New Guinea and look for a natural border between the Dutch and German spheres. Their camp, Kloofkamp, gives its name to an old district of the city.

The Dutch flag was raised on 7 March 1910 and the settlement named Hollandia. Across the bay was a German camp, Germania-Huk. The Dutch made Hollandia the capital of Netherlands New Guinea in 1945. Japanese forces occupied the north of the territory in 1942, and Allied forces drove them out after landings near Hollandia from 21 April 1944. Naval Base Hollandia then served as General Douglas MacArthur's headquarters until the conquest of the Philippines in March 1945, with more than twenty U.S. bases and half a million U.S. personnel passing through the area.

After the territory passed to the United Nations Temporary Executive Authority on 1 October 1962, the city had the dual name Hollandia and Kota Baru. Indonesia took control on 1 May 1963, and the city was briefly called Sukarnopura before it received its present name at the end of 1968. In 1949 the Roman Catholic Church had established the Apostolic Prefecture of Hollandia, which since 1973 has been the Diocese of Jayapura.

Jayapura is the capital and largest city of the province of Papua. It was estimated to have 410,852 inhabitants in mid 2024, which makes it the second most populous city on the island of New Guinea after Port Moresby. As the provincial capital it has drawn migrants from other regions of Indonesia, and its football club Persipura has won the national league four times.
jayasimha-siddharaja: Jayasimha was the son of the Chaulukya king Karna and his Kadamba queen Mayanalladevi. The 14th-century author Merutunga has him seated on the throne at the age of three, on 7 January 1094, which would place his birth in 1091, but the story is absent from earlier writers and does not seem accurate. His courtier Hemachandra relates that Karna's nephew Devaprasada burned himself on Karna's funeral pyre. The historian A. K. Majumdar thinks this hides an unpleasant truth: that Devaprasada tried to usurp the throne from the young king and was killed by Mayanalladevi and her minister Santu, after which she ruled as regent.

Literary sources and inscriptions agree that he defeated Khangara, also called Navaghana, king of Saurashtra; his Dahod inscription boasts that he imprisoned that king. He appointed Sajjana governor at Girnar, which an inscription of 1120 corroborates, but he could not take all of Khangara's lands.

Inscriptions disagree on whether the Paramara king he defeated was Naravarman or his successor Yashovarman. Majumdar holds that the war began under the first and ended under the second, and dates the capture of the Paramara capital Dhara to 1135-1136; the title Avantinatha, Lord of Avanti, first appears in an inscription of 1137. The Shakambhari Chahamana king Arnoraja, whom several sources say he subdued and to whom he gave his daughter Kanchana in marriage, helped him in this war, as did Asharaja of Naddula. Chaulukya chronicles claim that he then subdued the Chandela king Madanavarman, while a Chandela inscription claims the reverse, which suggests an inconclusive war.

He was a Shaivite who tolerated other faiths. Jains held important posts under him, and the Muslim historian Muhammad Aufi records that he inquired in person at Khambhat after a mosque was destroyed and eighty Muslims killed, and paid for its rebuilding. He renovated or rebuilt the Rudra Mahalaya Temple at Siddhapura, completed in 1142. The Sahastralinga lake was a renovation of one built by his ancestor Durlabha, ringed by 1008 small shrines each holding a linga. The grammar he commissioned from Hemachandra, the Siddha Hema Shabdanushasana, carries his name in its title.

Jayasimha had no son. According to Hemachandra he learned by divination that his grand-nephew Kumarapala would succeed him; later Jain chronicles say that he hated Kumarapala and persecuted him. It is not known how long he held Malwa. Bohra and Satpanth traditions claim that he was converted to Islam, but there is no evidence that he ever gave up Shaivism.
jayavarman-ii: Few firm facts survive about Jayavarman II. No inscriptions written by him have been found, and later Khmer kings remembered him as a warrior and the most powerful king of that time. Before he came to power the local overlords of Cambodia were in constant warfare, and much of the area fell within the orbit of the Shailendra dynasty of Srivijaya. According to one account he spent his childhood in captivity or exile in Java and was installed as its vassal around 800. The Baksei Chamkrong inscription of 947 makes him a descendant of Rudravarman and of the semi-mythical Kaundinya and Soma.

Jayavarman II is widely regarded as the king who set the foundation of the Angkor period, beginning with the consecration ritual of 802 on Mount Mahendraparvata, now Phnom Kulen. The Sdok Kak Thom inscription, dated to 1052, two centuries after his death, says the Brahmin Hiranyadama and the chief priest Sivakaivalya performed a rite that released the kingdom from subjection to Java and consecrated him as a chakravartin, lord of the universe. It also records the creation of the cult of the devaraja.

Records suggest that he and his followers moved over some years from southeast Cambodia to the northwest, subduing principalities on the way. He founded Hariharalaya near present-day Roluos. No temple is associated with him, but some historians suggest he built Ak Yum, a ruined brick stepped pyramid.

Jayavarman II died in 850 and received the posthumous name Parameshwara, supreme ruler. His son Jayavarman III followed him, and he was honoured in the Preah Ko temple at Roluos, inaugurated in 880. Scholars disagree about what Java means in the inscription: Coedès and Briggs took it for the island, Charles Higham doubts that, Michael Vickery reads it as the Chams, and Takashi Suzuki places it on the Malay Peninsula. Historians also debate whether his rule was a turning point or part of a long process. Pol Pot saw Angkorian achievements as proof of the greatness of the Khmer people, and the flag of Democratic Kampuchea, adopted on 5 January 1976, bore a three-towered temple representing Angkor Wat.
jayavarman-vii: Jayavarman VII, whose name means victory armour and who is known posthumously as Mahaparamasaugata, was the son of King Dharanindravarman II and Queen Sri Jayarajacudamani. He was the first Khmer king devoted to Buddhism; only one other had been a Buddhist. Suryavarman II, builder of Angkor Wat, died in 1150 and Dharanindravarman II ruled until 1160. Yashovarman II followed, but was overthrown by Tribhuvanadityavarman, assumed to be a usurper. In 1177, according to the usual account, the Cham king Jaya Indravarman IV sailed a fleet up the Mekong, across Lake Tonlé Sap and up the Siem Reap River, sacked the capital Yasodharapura and had Tribhuvanadityavarman put to death. Michael Vickery questions this date and the event, doubting the Chinese sources for the period.

The Chams occupied Cambodia for four years. In his mid-50s Jayavarman led a Khmer army that drove them out, a naval battle shown on the walls of the Bayon and Banteay Chmar. He found the capital in disorder, ended the disputes between factions and was crowned in 1181. Early in his reign he probably repelled another Cham attack and put down a rebellion by the vassal kingdom of Malyang. Helped by the refugee prince Sri Vidyanandana, he sacked and conquered Champa in 1190 and 1191, which remained a dependency for thirty years. He extended Khmer control up the Mekong Valley to Vientiane and south down the Kra Isthmus.

His building programme included 102 hospitals, 121 rest houses at intervals of 15 km along raised highways, and reservoirs. He then built Ta Prohm for his mother, dedicated in 1186, and Preah Khan for his father, and finally the Bayon, set in the new city of Angkor Thom, with the smaller Neak Pean. An inscription says he suffered the pain of his subjects more than his own. The works required the labour of thousands, and his reign saw the state centralised and people gathered into ever larger centres. He set up Buddha images in 23 towns of his empire.

Jayavarman died around 1218. Although he had many sons, only Indravarman II succeeded him, and then Jayavarman VIII, a Shivaite, defaced or removed his Buddhist works: most of the Buddha images in the niches around the city wall were taken out, and the Buddha statue of the Bayon and others in Angkor Thom were converted into linga. Historians generally consider him the most powerful of the Khmer monarchs, and a bust of him is a masterpiece of the National Museum.
je-khenpo: The Je Khenpo, whom orientalists once called the Dharma Raja, leads the Dratshang Lhentshog, the Commission for the Monastic Affairs, which oversees the Central Monastic Body, and arbitrates on matters of doctrine with the help of five Lopen Rinpoches, or learned masters. He also carries out many liturgical and religious duties across the country and is formally the leader of the southern branch of the Drukpa Kagyu sect, part of the Kagyu tradition of Tibetan Buddhism. Apart from the King of Bhutan, only he may wear a saffron kabney.

Under the dual system of government set up by Ngawang Namgyal in the 17th century, the powers of government were ideally divided between the religious branch under the Je Khenpo and the administrative branch under the Druk Desi. The office was filled by election on merit and usually went to the most respected monk of the monastic commission. Unlike reincarnation lineages such as those of the Dalai Lama, the Zhabdrung Rinpoche or the Panchen Lama, it was therefore never held by a child but always by a seasoned monk.

Historically the office was a powerful one. The Je Khenpo and the Druk Desi worked together to weaken the office of the Zhabdrung by finding multiple incarnations of various aspects of him, since both wished to keep the power the dual system had given them. After the monarchy was established in 1907 the influence of the Je Khenpo declined, though he is typically seen as the closest and most powerful adviser to the King of Bhutan.

In 2008 the office was codified in the Constitution of Bhutan. Under Article 3 Section 4 the king appoints the Je Khenpo as spiritual leader of Bhutan on the recommendation of the Five Lopons, and the Je Khenpo in turn appoints the Five Lopons on the recommendation of the monastic commission. The 67th Je Khenpo, Ngawang Thinley Lhundup, known as a strict disciplinarian, died at 84 on 10 June 2005. The Je Khenpo and the Central Monastic Body winter at Punakha Dzong and spend the summer at Tashichho Dzong.
jean-andoche-junot: Junot was born on 25 September 1771 in Bussy-le-Grand, Burgundy, the fifth son of a bourgeois family. He studied law in Dijon and was a law clerk in Chaumont when the Revolution began. He enlisted in 1791 as a grenadier of the Volunteers of Côte-d'Or and received the first of many wounds at La Glisuelle in 1792, earning the nickname la Tempête, the Tempest. At the Siege of Toulon in late 1793 he met Napoleon Bonaparte by volunteering to write a letter for him, and became his aide-de-camp. He followed Bonaparte to Italy, where at Lonato he killed six enemy soldiers in hand-to-hand fighting, and to Egypt, where he was promoted brigade general on 9 January 1799.

Junot married Laure Martin de Permond in 1800, was made a general of division in 1801, served as Military Governor of Paris in 1803 and 1804 and fought at Austerlitz on 2 December 1805. On 29 July 1807 Napoleon appointed him to command the Gironde Observation Corps for the invasion of Portugal. He left on 17 October with about 26,500 soldiers, crossed into Portugal on 19 November and entered Lisbon without a fight on 30 November, three days after the royal family's departure. Napoleon gave him the title Duke of Abrantes but not the rank of Marshal he expected. From late December 1807 he disbanded the Portuguese Army, with about 9,000 soldiers joining the Portuguese Legion, and proclaimed the House of Braganza dethroned.

Revolts spread in 1808, the Spanish troops withdrew and a British force landed on 1 August. After a French defeat at Roliça, Junot was beaten at Vimeiro on 21 August, and the Convention of Cintra let him return to France with the army's weapons, baggage and loot. It caused widespread outrage in Britain. He then fought at the Second Siege of Zaragoza and, in 1810, under Marshal Masséna.

In 1811 Junot was shot in the face, and complications of the wound were blamed for his later mental decline. In Russia in 1812 he was blamed for letting the Russian army retreat after Smolensk, which led to his removal from command, although he commanded the VIII Corps competently at Borodino. Made Governor of the Illyrian Provinces in May 1813, he deteriorated rapidly and was relieved and sent to his father's house in Burgundy. He died of an infection in Montbard on 29 July 1813 after injuring himself. He is buried in Montbard cemetery, where a monument was erected in 1898, and his title passed to his sons.
jean-baptiste-bagaza: Bagaza was born in Rutovu, Bururi Province, in Belgian-ruled Ruanda-Urundi on 29 August 1946, into the Hima, part of the wider Tutsi ethnic group. After Catholic schools in Bujumbura he enlisted in the army of the newly independent Kingdom of Burundi. He was sent to Belgium in 1966, studied at the Royal Military Academy in Brussels until 1971 and earned a sociology degree. Back in Burundi in 1972, he was involved in President Michel Micombero's killings of ethnic Hutu that year, though the extent or nature of his involvement remains unclear. In November 1972 he became lieutenant colonel and chief of the general staff.

Bagaza overthrew Micombero in a military coup on 1 November 1976, and a 30-member military junta, the Supreme Revolutionary Council, declared him president on 10 November, when he was thirty. He attacked corruption, reformed taxation and administration, and made modest reforms to improve conditions for the Hutu. The feudal system of land tenure, the Ubugererwa, was abolished in 1977, as was the ikori poll tax, and this earned him goodwill among the Hutu. Officially he banned all mention of ethnicity, but the political scientist René Lemarchand and the researcher Nigel Watt argued that this disguised the continued dominance of the Tutsi elite. From 1976 to 1979 the Council consisted only of Tutsi officers.

His programme of economic modernisation included two new hydroelectric dams, road building, drinking water and a port on Lake Tanganyika. A constitution of 1981 consolidated a one-party state under UPRONA, and in the election of 1984 he was re-elected with 99.6 per cent of the vote. From 1977-78 he conducted an anti-clerical campaign against the Catholic Church, which grew into a military operation after the 1984 election: foreign missionaries were expelled, Catholic media and church services banned, Church schools nationalised, Church figures arrested and tortured, and 87 churches closed, among them Gitega Cathedral.

In September 1987 Major Pierre Buyoya led a coup while Bagaza was abroad in Quebec. Bagaza went into exile in Uganda and later Libya. He returned to Burundi in 1994 and founded the Party for National Recovery, PARENA, which opposed power-sharing with Hutu factions. He was placed under house arrest in January 1997 for gathering weapons for a plot against Buyoya. He stepped down as head of PARENA in March 2014. He died in Brussels on 4 May 2016, aged 69, and was buried in Bujumbura on 17 May. His infrastructure and development projects remained well remembered in Burundi.
jean-baptiste-colbert: Jean-Baptiste Colbert was born on 29 August 1619 in Reims, where his father and grandfather were merchants. Before the age of 20 he held a post in the war office, attributed to the marriage of an uncle to the sister of the Secretary of War, Michel Le Tellier, and he became Le Tellier's personal secretary. In 1649 he became a councillor of state. In 1652 he was asked to manage the affairs of Cardinal Mazarin while the cardinal was in exile, and Mazarin recommended him to Louis XIV.

After Mazarin died in 1661, Colbert won the King's favour, and he took over finances after the arrest of Nicolas Fouquet for embezzlement. He became Superintendent of Buildings in 1664, Controller-General of Finances in 1665 and Secretary of State of the Navy in 1669, and held power in every department except war. He repudiated some public loans, reduced the interest on others, and lightened direct taxation by raising indirect taxes, though he could not reduce the number of the privileged.

He fostered manufacturing by founding the royal mirror-glass works in 1665 and the royal tapestry works at Gobelins, and by inviting in foreign workmen. He had the quality of goods fixed by law and issued more than 150 edicts regulating the guilds. Pierre Paul Riquet built the Canal du Midi under his patronage. The trading companies he privileged, among them the French East India Company, all proved unsuccessful. In 1682 he commissioned the project that became the Code Noir of 1685, which sanctioned a brutal system of repression to enforce slavery in the French colonies.

Colbert held that the country was enriched by commerce. Critics have condemned parts of his scheme: by maintaining the corporation system he left each industry in the hands of privileged bourgeois and closed advancement to the lower classes, and France still grew impoverished by the King's spending on wars.

He founded the Academy of Inscriptions and Medals in 1663, the Academy of Sciences in 1666, the Paris Observatory in 1667 and the Academy of Architecture in 1671. In 1665 he brought Gian Lorenzo Bernini to Paris to design the east facade of the Louvre, a design finally rejected. He gave pensions to writers such as Molière, Corneille and Racine. He died on 6 September 1683; a large stone was found in his urinary tract. His son, the Marquis de Seignelay, succeeded him as Navy Secretary.
jean-baptiste-du-casse: Du Casse is usually said to have been born at Saubusse, near Dax, the son of a Bayonne ham merchant, but local records point to a Huguenot family in Pau: his father Jacques Ducasse was the son of Gaillard Ducasse, a minister of the Reformed Church of France. He is thought to have forged his baptismal record to hide that background, and he admitted it to the naval minister Pontchartrain in 1691. He renounced his Calvinist faith in 1685, after the Edict of Fontainebleau.

In 1686 at Dieppe he married Marthe Baudry, of a family tied to banking and colonial trade. Their daughter Marthe married Louis de La Rochefoucauld, Marquis de Roye, with a dowry of 1,200,000 livres. Spellings of surnames were not yet fixed, and records also give his name as Ducasse, Ducas and Du Casse.

Du Casse sailed in the Atlantic slave trade with the Compagnie du Sénégal between Africa and the Caribbean, and with its profits bought a ship in Saint-Domingue and turned privateer. After he offered half of his loot to the Crown, Louis XIV made him a lieutenant in the French Navy. He failed to take Elmina from the Dutch in 1687, and as governor of Saint-Domingue he won the respect of the island's buccaneers and attacked Jamaica in 1692, when his forces plundered Port Royal just after its earthquake.

Denied his promised share of the loot of Cartagena, taken under Bernard Desjean, Baron de Pointis, he went to France and obtained 1.4 million francs for himself and his men. On 19 August 1702 off Santa Marta he escaped a larger English squadron under Vice-admiral John Benbow, whose captains failed to support him. Two years later he fought at the Battle of Málaga, brought the Spanish treasure fleet home in 1708 with very few losses, for which Philip V gave him the Order of the Golden Fleece, and commanded the French fleet at the siege of Barcelona in 1714.

Du Casse ended his career as lieutenant général des armées navales and commander of the Royal and Military Order of Saint Louis. He died at Bourbon-l'Archambault on 25 June 1715. His grandson Jean-Baptiste de La Rochefoucauld de Roye became a naval officer and led the Duc d'Anville Expedition, and his grand-nephew Robert wrote his biography in 1876.
jean-baptiste-jourdan: Jean-Baptiste Jourdan was born in Limoges on 29 April 1762, the only surviving child of Roch Jourdan, a surgeon. He was orphaned young and raised by an uncle, a parish priest who ran a boarding school in Beaurecueil. After about a year as a clerk for another uncle, a cloth merchant in Lyon, he enlisted in the Royal army in 1778. He served in the American War of Independence, at the Siege of Savannah in October 1779 and in the West Indies, where illness troubled him for the rest of his career. Demobilised in 1784, he returned to Limoges and worked for a cloth merchant.

Jourdan welcomed the Revolution and in 1792 commanded a battalion of volunteers at Jemappes. He became a general of division in 1793 and took command of the Army of the North on 22 September. He defeated Prince Josias of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld at Wattignies and broke the siege of Maubeuge, though Lazare Carnot claimed the credit. Leading the Army of Sambre-et-Meuse he took Charleroi on 25 June 1794 and won the Battle of Fleurus the next day, after which the Austrian Army evacuated Belgium.

In 1796 Archduke Charles defeated him at Amberg and Würzburg; the chief cause was thought to be the plan imposed by the government, but he was made the scapegoat. As a member of the Council of Five Hundred he framed the conscription law of 1798, the Jourdan Law. Napoleon made him a Marshal of the Empire in 1804. He became military adviser to Joseph Bonaparte, followed him into Spain, and on 21 June 1813 was defeated at the Battle of Vitoria, where the British captured his marshal's baton. The defeat led to the permanent loss of Spain.

After Waterloo Jourdan submitted to the Bourbons and refused to sit on the court that sentenced Marshal Michel Ney to death.
