Edward Lipiński has proposed that they were an Amorite tribe, linking them with the Yabusi'um named in a cuneiform letter from the archive of Mari. The Amarna letters name a king of Jerusalem, Abdi-Heba, whose name invokes the Hurrian goddess Ḫepat, which suggests Hurrian influence or a Hurrian warrior elite in the city.

In the biblical account the Jebusites lived in the hill country beside Jerusalem. Joshua 10 tells of Adonizedek leading a confederation of Jebusites and neighbouring cities against Joshua, who defeated and killed him. Joshua 15:63 and Judges 1:21 say the Jebusites remained in the city, where the Judahites could not dislodge them. According to 2 Samuel, they still held Jerusalem in the time of King David and boasted that even the blind and lame could defend it.

David took the city by a surprise attack led by Joab, which in the Masoretic Text goes through the water tunnels; the version in 1 Chronicles does not mention them. According to some biblical chronologies the conquest fell in 1003 BCE. A majority of scholars hold that the Book of Joshua has little historical value for the early settlement of the Hebrew tribes. 1 Kings 9:20-21 says Solomon made the surviving Jebusites serfs. The Jebusite Araunah, called Ornan in Chronicles, sold David the threshing floor on which he built an altar.

Niels Peter Lemche has argued that no evidence for Jebus or the Jebusites exists outside the Old Testament, and that every non-biblical source calls the city Jerusalem. He suggests that Jebus may be a different place or a pseudo-ethnic name. What became of the Jebusites is unknown. The 'Jebusite hypothesis' holds that they remained in Jerusalem and formed an important faction in the Kingdom of Judah, with the priest Zadok among them.

Rabbinic tradition has its own stories, including a covenant between Abraham and the Jebusites cast in bronze. In modern times Yasser Arafat and Faisal Husseini, among others, have claimed that Palestinian Arabs descend from the Jebusites. Eric H. Cline holds that historians and archaeologists generally find no significant connection between them.
jeddah: Jeddah lies on the Red Sea coastal plain, called Tihamah, in the lower Hijaz mountains. Mecca, the holiest city in Islam, is 65 kilometres to the east, and Medina, the second holiest, is 360 kilometres to the north. The climate is arid, and unlike other Saudi cities Jeddah keeps warm temperatures in winter, while summers often pass 40 °C. Traces of early activity are attested by Thamudic inscriptions found in Wadi Briman and Wadi Boweb, and the oldest mashrabiya, a type of carved wooden screen, found in Jeddah dates to the pre-Islamic era. One account of the name derives it from the Arabic word jaddah, meaning grandmother, and a folk belief places the tomb of Eve, the grandmother of humanity, in the city.

Jeddah first achieved prominence around 647 CE, when the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, made it the port of Mecca in place of the Al Shoaib port, southwest of Mecca. In 969 the Fatimids, who had taken Egypt from the Abbasid governors of the Ikhshidid dynasty, extended their empire to the Hijaz and Jeddah, and developed trade networks in the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean through the Red Sea, with diplomatic ties reaching the Song dynasty of China. In 1517 the Ottomans, under Selim I, conquered the Mamluk Sultanate, and in 1802 forces from Nejd took Mecca and Jeddah from them. Sultan Mahmud II ordered his Egyptian viceroy, Muhammad Ali Pasha, to retake the city, and he did so in the Battle of Jeddah in 1813.

During the First World War Sharif Hussein bin Ali declared a revolt against the Ottoman Empire, seeking a unified Arab state from Aleppo to Aden. Ibn Saud, whose clan came from the central Nejd, later conquered Medina and Jeddah by agreement with the people of Jeddah after the Second Battle of Jeddah. He deposed Ali bin Hussein, who fled to Baghdad and eventually settled in Amman, where his descendants joined the Hashemite royal house of Jordan.

Jeddah is the second-largest city in Saudi Arabia after Riyadh and its main commercial centre, and the principal gateway to Mecca. It has long been a port: in the 19th century it exported mother-of-pearl, tortoise shells, frankincense and spices. The old city, Al-Balad, with its multistorey merchant houses, was granted UNESCO World Heritage status in 2014, and it holds the Bayt Naseef museum. The speech of the region is called the Hejazi dialect. The 2022 census counted 3,712,917 people.
jefferson-davis: Jefferson Davis was the youngest of ten children of Jane and Samuel Emory Davis. He was born on 3 June 1808 at Davisburg, a village his father had established that later became Fairview, Kentucky, and was named after President Thomas Jefferson. The family soon moved to Wilkinson County, Mississippi, where Samuel grew cotton. After Samuel died in 1824, Davis's eldest brother, Joseph Emory Davis, who was 23 years older, became a surrogate father and secured his appointment to the United States Military Academy at West Point, from which he graduated 23rd in a class of 33.

After six years as an army lieutenant, Davis left the service in 1835 and married Sarah Knox Taylor, daughter of the future president Zachary Taylor, who died of malaria three months later. He became a cotton planter, building Brierfield Plantation on his brother's land and eventually owning as many as 113 slaves. He married Varina Howell in 1845, sat in the House of Representatives in 1845–1846 and fought in the Mexican–American War as colonel of the First Mississippi Regiment, whose percussion rifles gave it the name Mississippi Rifles.

As a senator from 1847 he argued that slave owners had an equal right to settle the western territories with their slaves. President Franklin Pierce made him secretary of war in March 1853, and he oversaw the Pacific Railroad Surveys, promoted the Gadsden Purchase and won four new regiments for the army. He returned to the Senate in 1857 and resigned in 1861 when Mississippi seceded. On 9 February 1861 a convention at Montgomery, Alabama, unanimously elected him provisional president of the Confederacy, chosen for his political prominence, his military reputation and his moderate approach to secession.

Davis was captured and on 22 May 1865 imprisoned at Fort Monroe, Virginia, where he was at first shackled and denied contact with his family; the fetters came off after five days, and he was released without trial after two years. He later lived at Beauvoir, Mississippi, writing The Rise and Fall of the Confederate Government (1881). He died in New Orleans on 6 December 1889, aged 81, and more than 200,000 mourners were estimated to have attended his funeral. Journalist Edward A. Pollard, who popularised the Lost Cause, blamed Davis for the defeat, and many historians followed him.
jehoahaz-of-israel: Jehoahaz, whose Hebrew name means Yahweh has held, was the eleventh king of Israel and the son of Jehu. He reigned for seventeen years. William F. Albright dated his reign to 815-801 BCE, while E. R. Thiele offered the dates 814-798 BCE. The account in 2 Kings states that he did evil in the sight of Yahweh and that his people followed the religious practices of the house of Jeroboam, which included the worship of a cultic pole of Asherah in Samaria.

According to 2 Kings, the kings of the Arameans, Hazael and Ben-hadad, prevailed over him. Jehoahaz besought the Lord for a deliverer to relieve Israel from Aramean oppression, and the Lord provided a saviour for Israel, who is not named. The Arameans were defeated, but this left Jehoahaz with an army reduced to 50 horsemen, 10 chariots and 10,000 foot soldiers.

The identity of the deliverer is disputed. The verse 2 Kings 13:25 suggests that Jehoahaz's son Joash, who recaptured a number of Israelite cities in three successful battles, could have been the deliverer, and the Geneva Study Bible maintains this view. The Jerusalem Bible and the Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges argue instead that Jeroboam II, the son of Joash, was the deliverer, citing 2 Kings 14:27, which says that the Lord saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash.

The Pulpit Commentary agrees that this was probably the case. Adad-nirari III, king of Assyria from 812 to 783 BCE, also made campaigns into the west between 804 and 797 BCE and on one of them captured and sacked Damascus, removing the worst enemy of Israel's prosperity, so that he too could be considered the deliverer.
jehoahaz-of-judah: Jehoahaz, also called Shallum, was the fourth son of King Josiah and the seventeenth king of Judah. His mother was Hamautal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, and he was born in 633/632 BCE. In the spring or early summer of 609 BCE Pharaoh Necho II began his first campaign against Babylon, in aid of the Assyrians. He moved his forces along the coastal route towards Syria and prepared to cross the hills that close the Jezreel Valley on the south, where he found his way blocked at Megiddo by the Judean army under Josiah. After a fierce battle Josiah was killed, probably in the month of Tammuz.

Although he was two years younger than his brother Eliakim, Jehoahaz was chosen to succeed his father at the age of 23. This suggests the young man's popularity and probably also that his policy was in line with his father's. According to 2 Kings he reigned for three months and that he disregarded the reforms of Josiah. William F. Albright and E. R. Thiele both dated his reign to 609 BCE.

After the failed siege of Harran, Necho left a sizeable force behind and returned to Egypt. On his march back he found that the Judeans had chosen Jehoahaz as king. Necho brought him to Riblah and imprisoned him, deposed him, and made his older brother Eliakim king, changing his name to Jehoiakim. Necho took Jehoahaz to Egypt as a prisoner, where he ended his days. The prophet Jeremiah said of him that he should be wept for bitterly, since he would never return nor see his native land again.
jehoash-of-israel: Jehoash was the twelfth king of the northern Kingdom of Israel, with its capital at Samaria, and the son of Jehoahaz. He reigned for sixteen years. William F. Albright dated his reign to 801-786 BCE, while Edwin R. Thiele offered the dates 798-782 BCE. When he ascended the throne Israel was suffering from the attacks of Aram-Damascus, whose king Hazael was conquering land controlled by Samaria. According to 2 Kings he was sinful and did evil in the eyes of Yahweh by tolerating the worship of the golden calves, yet outwardly at least he worshipped Yahweh.

According to 2 Kings 13:14, Jehoash visited the prophet Elisha, who was sick with the illness that would lead to his death, held him in honour and wept at his bedside. When Jehoash failed to obey Elisha's instructions completely, Elisha predicted that he would defeat Aram-Damascus only three times rather than five or six. In three successive victories Jehoash overcame the Syrians and retook towns Hazael had captured.

Later he defeated king Amaziah of Judah, whom he had warned with a parable of a thistle and a cedar in Lebanon. The author of Chronicles believes that Amaziah's ruin followed from his worship of idols taken from the Edomites. Jehoash utterly defeated Amaziah at Beth-shemesh, advanced on Jerusalem, broke down a portion of its wall, carried away the treasures of the Temple and the palace, took Amaziah prisoner and took hostages to assure good conduct. A conspiracy that took Amaziah's life followed. Soon after the battle Jehoash died and was buried in Samaria.

The excavation at Tell al-Rimah yielded a stele of Adad-nirari III which mentions Jehoash the Samarian and contains the first cuneiform mention of Samaria by that name. A postulated image of Jehoash has been reconstructed from plaster remains recovered at Kuntillet Ajrud, the ruins of a temple built by the northern kingdom when Jehoash gained control over the kingdom of Judah in the reign of Amaziah.
jehoiada: Jehoiada's name means Yahweh knows. In the Hebrew Bible he was a priest in the kingdom of Judah under Ahaziah, Athaliah and Joash, and he became Ahaziah's brother-in-law by marrying Princess Jehosheba; both she and Ahaziah were children of King Jehoram of Judah. When Ahaziah died a year after taking the throne, his mother Athaliah seized it and ordered the execution of the royal family, and Jehosheba and Jehoiada rescued her one-year-old grandson Joash.

The account in 2 Chronicles stresses Jehoiada's resolve in staging the coup, words that do not occur in the parallel passage of 2 Kings, and records that Athaliah called it treason. Under his guidance the worship of Baal was renounced and the altar and temple of Baal were destroyed. He also made a national covenant between himself, all the people and the king, that they should be the Lord's people.

According to Chronicles Jehoiada lived for 130 years, which would have made him an unlikely age of around 100 at the time of the coup, and he was buried with honour among the kings in the city of David. His son, Zechariah ben Jehoiada, was later killed by King Joash.

Whether he was high priest is uncertain. His name does not appear in the list of the Zadokite line in 1 Chronicles, and Josephus, though he calls him high priest in the Jewish Antiquities, leaves him out of his list of high priests. The medieval chronicle Seder Olam Zutta of 804 makes him a high priest, while 2 Chronicles calls him the chief, which may mean the high priest or one of the leaders of the 24 orders of priests.
jehoiakim: Jehoiakim was the second son of King Josiah and Zebidah, the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah. His birth name was Eliakim. When Josiah was killed at Megiddo, the people proclaimed his younger brother Jehoahaz, also called Shallum, as king. Rabbinic literature explains that Jehoiakim, though the elder, was passed over as unworthy to succeed his father.

Pharaoh Necho II returned from the battle at Harran three months after Josiah's death and deposed Jehoahaz, taking him to Egypt, where he died. Necho placed Eliakim on the throne in 609 BCE and changed his name to Jehoiakim.

Jehoiakim at first ruled as a vassal of Egypt and paid a heavy tribute. To raise the money he taxed the land and took silver and gold from the people of the land according to their assessments. After the Egyptians were defeated by the Babylonians at Carchemish in 605 BCE, Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem, and Jehoiakim changed allegiance to spare the city. He paid tribute from the treasury, gave up some temple artefacts and handed over members of the royal family and nobility as hostages. The Book of Daniel counts Daniel among them.

He remained a Babylonian vassal for three years, until the failure of a Babylonian invasion of Egypt in 601 BCE weakened Babylon's hold on the region. Jehoiakim then switched his allegiance back to Egypt. The prophet Jeremiah criticised the king's policies and urged repentance and strict observance of the law. Another prophet, Uriah ben Shemaiah, proclaimed a similar message, and Jehoiakim ordered his execution.

In late 598 BCE Nebuchadnezzar invaded Judah and laid siege to Jerusalem. Jehoiakim died before the siege ended. The Book of Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound him in fetters to take him to Babylon, while Jeremiah foretold that he would be buried with the burial of a donkey, dragged and cast out beyond the gates of Jerusalem. Josephus writes that Nebuchadnezzar killed him and ordered his body thrown before the walls without burial.

His son Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, reigned three months before Nebuchadnezzar deposed him and installed Jehoiakim's younger brother Zedekiah. Jehoiachin, his household and much of Judah's population were exiled to Babylon. The Babylonian Chronicles record that Jerusalem fell on 2 Adar, which is 16 March, in 597 BCE. Rabbinic literature portrays Jehoiakim as a godless tyrant guilty of atrocious crimes.
jehoram-of-israel: Jehoram, also Joram, was the ninth king of the northern Kingdom of Israel, son of King Ahab and Jezebel and brother of Ahaziah and Athaliah. According to 2 Kings 3:1 he began his reign in the 18th year of Jehoshaphat of Judah and ruled 12 years. In the fifth year of Jehoram of Israel a different Jehoram became king of Judah; the two were brothers-in-law, since Jehoram of Judah married Athaliah. Unlike his predecessors, Jehoram did not worship Baal: 2 Kings 3:2 says he removed the pillar of Baal, probably a special pillar Ahab had erected near his palace at Jezreel. The writer still says he followed in the ways of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who led the Israelites to sin.

With Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram attacked Moab, ruled by Mesha. In the war between Aram-Damascus and Israel, the prophet Elisha befriended him and revealed the enemy's plans. When Ben-hadad of Aram-Damascus besieged Samaria, the capital, the city was reduced almost to starvation and cannibalism, and Jehoram sought to behead Elisha. Elisha foretold a period of plenty, the siege was soon lifted, the food supplies were replenished and the old relation between king and prophet was restored.

When Hazael, king of the Arameans, violently revolted in Damascus, as Elisha had predicted in 2 Kings 8:12, Jehoram allied with his nephew Ahaziah, king of Judah, and the two set out to take Ramoth-Gilead from Aram-Damascus. The battle failed, and Jehoram was wounded and withdrew to Jezreel to recover. His defeat there was likely a disaster. While he recovered, his general Jehu incited a revolt, shot him in the back with an arrow and had his body thrown into the field of Naboth, as punishment for his parents' sin of illegally stealing Naboth's land. Jehoram and his other family members died, the Omride dynasty ended and Jehu claimed the throne of Israel.

The Tel Dan Stele, of the 9th century BCE and found in 1993 and 1994, claims that its author slew both Ahaziah of Judah and Jehoram of Israel. Most scholars identify the author as Hazael, whose reign is dated c. 842 to 806 BCE. On the Mesha Stele, dated to about 840 BCE, Mesha of Moab claims a victory against Israel after forty years of oppression by Omri and his son; some scholars understand 'son' to mean a later descendant of Omri, such as Ahaziah or Jehoram.
jehoshaphat: According to the Hebrew Bible, Jehoshaphat was the fourth king of the Kingdom of Judah, succeeding his father Asa; his mother was Azubah. Chronicles gives chapters 17 to 21 to his reign, and the First Book of Kings treats him more briefly. He ascended the throne at the age of thirty-five and reigned twenty-five years. He is said to have walked in the ways of David, spent his first years fortifying his kingdom against Israel and suppressed worship at the high places. In his third year he sent priests and Levites through the land to teach the Law.

His later reforms appear to have included judges in the cities of Judah and a form of court of appeal in Jerusalem. The Chronicler praises his reign for peace and prosperity, though modern commentary treats the figure of a vast army of 1,160,000 men and the rich tribute from the Philistines and Arabs as not historical.

He allied himself with the northern kingdom: his son Jehoram married Athaliah, a daughter of King Ahab of Israel. He nearly lost his life accompanying Ahab to the siege of Ramoth-Gilead, and the prophet Jehu, son of Hanani, rebuked him for the alliance. He joined Jehoram of Israel in a war against the Moabites, who were under tribute to Israel; the Moabites were subdued, but when King Mesha offered his own son as a sacrifice on the walls of Kir of Moab, the allies withdrew in horror.

Chronicles also tells of a confederacy of Moabites and neighbouring peoples that marched against Jehoshaphat and camped at Ein Gedi. After the king prayed in the court of the Temple, the Levite Jahaziel announced that the host would be overthrown; the invaders quarrelled and killed one another. Jehoshaphat died soon after, at sixty, and his son Jehoram succeeded him. The medieval commentator Rashi held that he died two years later and gave up his throne earlier. William F. Albright estimated his reign at 873-849 BCE. He appears in the genealogy of Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew.
jehu: Jehu was the tenth king of the northern Kingdom of Israel since Jeroboam I, the son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi, and possibly a great-grandson of Omri, although the biblical text does not support the last claim. The main source for his reign is 2 Kings, which gives it as 28 years; scholars date it slightly differently, by about a year. Jehu was a military commander at the time of the Battle of Ramoth-Gilead against the Arameans, in which King Jehoram of Israel was wounded and withdrew to Jezreel, attended by his nephew Ahaziah, king of Judah.

According to Kings, the prophet Elisha sent one of his students to anoint Jehu as the agent of divine judgment against the house of Ahab. Jehu at first dismissed the young man as a madman, but his companions blew trumpets and proclaimed him king. At Jezreel he shot Jehoram with an arrow, and Ahaziah died at Megiddo of his wounds. Queen Jezebel was thrown from a palace window at his command. At his order the chief men of Samaria killed the 70 royal princes, and he killed 42 relatives of Ahaziah at Beth-eked. He then trapped and killed the worshippers and priests of Baal.

Little else is known of his reign apart from his tolerance of the golden calves at Dan and Bethel, which was criticised, and the pressure of Hazael, king of the Arameans, who defeated his armies beyond the Jordan River. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III depicts Jehu kissing the ground before the Assyrian king and records his tribute of much silver, dated about 841 BCE; it is the earliest preserved depiction of an Israelite. It calls him the son of Omri, which may reflect the Assyrian name for Israel as the House of Omri. The Book of Hosea says God would punish the house of Jehu for the massacre at Jezreel.
jeju-island: Jeju Island lies in the Korea Strait, 82.8 km south of the nearest point on the Korean Peninsula. It covers 1,833.2 km2, which is 1.83% of the area of South Korea, and has an oval shape about 73 km from east to west, with a gentle slope around Hallasan in the centre. The coastline is 258 km long. The island consists chiefly of basalt and lava, and Hallasan, a volcano 1,947 metres high, is the highest mountain in South Korea.

The island formed from volcanic eruptions about two million years ago, in the Pleistocene epoch. A magma chamber formed under the sea floor about 1.2 million years ago and began to erupt, and activity stopped for about 100 thousand years before it restarted along the coast about 300 thousand years ago. Hallasan took shape about 100 thousand years ago, and lateral eruptions about 25 thousand years ago left some 360 oreum, small extinct parasitic cones such as Geomunoreum and Yongnuni Oreum.

The Jeju people are indigenous to the island, which has been populated by modern humans since the early Neolithic period. Its many historical names include Juho, Tammora, Seomna, Tangna and Tamna, and later Samdado, the Island of Three Abundances. Before the Japanese annexation of 1910 Europeans usually called it Quelpart, a name from French attested in Dutch by 1648, which may come from a Dutch ship, the quelpaert de Brack, said to have first sighted the island around 1642. The first European explorers to sight it, the Portuguese, called it Ilha de Ladrones, the Island of Thieves. Under Japanese occupation it was known as Saishū, and Cheju remained the usual spelling until 7 July 2000.

Jeju forms the majority of Jeju Province together with its outlying islands. It has a humid subtropical climate with four seasons, cool winters and hot, very wet summers, and the south around Seogwipo is warmer in winter than Jeju City because Hallasan blocks the continental winds. About 12% of the island is gotjawal, forest on rough lava that stayed uncultivated until the 21st century and is the main source of groundwater for the island's half million people.

The Jeju language is considered critically endangered by UNESCO, and the island is one of the regions of Korea where shamanism is most intact. It contains the natural World Heritage Site named Jeju Volcanic Island and Lava Tubes, and tourism is a large part of its economy.
jelgava: Jelgava lies on a fertile plain only 3.5 metres above mean sea level on the right bank of the Lielupe, about 41 kilometres south-west of Riga. At high water the plain and sometimes the town are flooded. It is the largest town of the Semigallia region and a railway centre at the junction of over six lines. Until 1917 the city was officially called Mitau; Jelgava is believed to derive from a Livonian word meaning town on the river, while the origin of Mitau is unclear.

Settlement began between the rivers Lielupe and Driksa in the 10th century. The crusading Livonian Order, under Grand Master Konrad von Mandern, built a castle on the natural island fortification of Pilssala in 1265–1266, and used it to subdue the surrounding Livonians and Semigallians by 1290. Lithuanians plundered the town in 1345. After the fall of the Livonian Order in the Livonian War it became a town of the Duchy of Courland, received city rights in 1573 and became capital of the united duchies of Courland and Semigallia in 1578.

The duchy was a vassal of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, and Swedish invasions subjected Mitau to several sieges, though it grew as a centre of trade and industry. In 1710 Duke Friedrich Wilhelm married Anna Ioannovna, later Empress of Russia, who ruled as duchess from 1711 to 1730. Ernst Johann von Biron expanded the city's cultural life, building the ducal palace and opening its first public library, and the last duke, Peter von Biron, founded the Academia Petrina in 1775. Russia annexed the city in 1795, in the Third Partition of Poland, and the future Louis XVIII lived in the palace in 1798–1801 and 1804–1807. Rail arrived in 1868, and by 1914 Mitau had over 45,000 inhabitants.

In 1919 Mitau was a battleground between Bolshevik Red Guards, German paramilitaries and Latvian forces, and after the Latvian victory in November it was renamed Jelgava. The Soviet Union occupied it in 1940. German police and Latvian auxiliaries murdered its Jewish inhabitants in mass shootings during the German occupation of 1941–1944, and the main synagogue was burned. Fighting in 1944 destroyed almost 90% of the city, including the Kurland Provincial Museum and Athenaeum. It was rebuilt in Soviet style as part of the Latvian SSR.

Jelgava had 54,694 inhabitants on 1 January 2022 and is home to the Latvia University of Life Sciences and Technologies, which occupies the palace. Designed by Bartolomeo Rastrelli and built between 1738 and 1772, the palace holds the sarcophagi of almost all the Courland dukes. Other landmarks include the baroque St Anne's Church, the tower of the destroyed St. Trinity Church and the Academia Petrina.
jelling: Jelling lies in Vejle municipality in the Region of Southern Denmark, about 10 km north-west of Vejle and 105 metres above sea level. It grew up as a railway town, on the line from Vejle to Holstebro. Until the municipal reform of 1 January 2007 it was the capital of Jelling municipality, and it was the only town in the former Vejle County to house the headquarters of a bank, Jelling Sparekasse, whose slogan said that if King Gorm were alive today, it would probably be the country's national bank. One source claims that Jelling was the capital of an ancient kingdom of Denmark known as Jellund.

Jelling is an old and important town in the history of Denmark. In the Viking Age it was the royal seat of the first monarchs of the Kingdom of Denmark, among them Gorm the Old, Þyra and Harald Bluetooth. Gorm ruled from Jelling from about 936 to about 958 and made the oldest of the Jelling stones.

The site has a large stone ship, two great burial mounds, the Jelling stones and Jelling Church. Beneath the two mounds lies the stone ship, from around the end of the 9th century. The North Mound, built in 958 or 959 CE and possibly for Gorm, held an empty burial chamber. The South Mound, built around 970, contains no burial. Between them stand the two rune stones. Near the stones Harald Bluetooth built a wooden church in 965 and beneath it re-interred, in 965 and 966, the remains of his father.

Jelling has 4,038 inhabitants. The monuments have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 1994. The town centre was rebuilt around the monument area: the main road, Gormsgade, was closed and a bypass built, at an estimated cost of 250 million DKK, a new culture house and square were added, and some houses of historical value were moved to the museum Den Gamle By in Aarhus. The Jelling Music Festival is held every year.
jemdet-nasr-period: Clay tablets with an archaic form of Sumerian cuneiform began to appear on the antiquities market in the early 1900s. A collection of 36 tablets was bought by the German excavators of Shuruppak in 1903, and although they believed the tablets came from Tell Jemdet Nasr, they probably came from nearby Tell Uqair. In 1925 the Assyriologist Stephen Herbert Langdon was shown similar tablets and painted pottery that local people said came from Jemdet Nasr. He started excavations there in 1926 and uncovered a large mudbrick building with 150 to 180 proto-cuneiform tablets.

The period was officially defined at a conference in Baghdad in 1930, which also defined the Uruk and Ubaid periods. Some material once thought unique to it also occurs in the Uruk and Early Dynastic periods, but it is still generally recognised as distinct. The culture grew out of the Uruk period and continues into Early Dynastic I.

The period is generally dated from 3100 to 2900 BCE on the basis of radiocarbon dating; older literature used 3200 to 3000 BCE. It was contemporary with the early Ninevite V period of Upper Mesopotamia and the Proto-Elamite period of Iran, which share with it an emerging bureaucracy and hierarchy. Its distribution is limited to south-central Iraq, and it has been found at Abu Salabikh, Shuruppak, Khafajah, Nippur, Tell Uqair, Ur and Uruk.

Its hallmark is painted monochrome and polychrome pottery, with geometric designs and figures of trees, birds, fish, goats, scorpions and snakes. This pottery is only a small share of the whole assemblage and often appears in contexts linked with high-status people or activities. At Jemdet Nasr it was found only in the large central building, thought to have administered many economic activities.

The period is a formative stage in the development of cuneiform. By then the script had moved from pictographs to simpler, more abstract signs and had acquired its wedge-shaped appearance. The language is thought to have been Sumerian, though this cannot be established with certainty. The tablets deal only with administration, such as rationing food and listing objects and animals; hymns and king lists, common later, are absent. Two counting systems were used, a sexagesimal one for animals and humans and a bisexagesimal one for goods such as grain, cheese and fresh fish.

Central buildings, tablets and cylinder seals suggest a highly organised society with a central administration regulating crafts, agriculture and rationing. The economy rested on agriculture, sheep-and-goat herding and small-scale trade, and few precious stones or exotic goods have been found. A sealing from Jemdet Nasr lists cities that can be identified, including Ur, Uruk and Larsa.
jena: Jena lies in a hilly landscape in the east of Thuringia, in the wide valley of the Saale river. The city centre stands at about 160 metres, and the hills on both sides of the valley rise to about 400 metres. Until the High Middle Ages the Saale was the border between Germanic regions in the west and Slavic regions in the east. Jena was a river crossing, but its relevance in the Middle Ages was local.

The first unequivocal mention of Jena is in a document of 1182, and its first local rulers were the Lords of Lobdeburg. The Protestant Reformation reached it in 1523, when Martin Luther visited to reorganise church affairs, and the townsmen attacked the Carmelite and Dominican convents, which were abolished in 1525 and 1548. The city remained a small town until the 19th century.

Around 1790 the university became the largest and most prominent among the German states. It made Jena the centre of idealist philosophy, with professors such as Johann Gottlieb Fichte, Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, Friedrich Schiller and Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, and gave rise to Jena Romanticism, the first phase of German Romanticism, with a group led by Caroline Schlegel and poets such as Novalis, August and Friedrich Schlegel and Ludwig Tieck. Goethe and Schiller met at the university in 1794 and formed a long friendship.

On 14 October 1806 Napoleon defeated the Prussian army near the district of Vierzehnheiligen in the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt. Resistance to the French occupation was strong, especially among the students, many of whom fought in the Lützow Free Corps in 1813, and the Urburschenschaft fraternity was founded in the city two years later. Industrialisation then changed the social structure: the former academic town became a working-class city, and its population rose from 8,000 around 1870 to 71,000 at the beginning of the Second World War. The optical and glass industry, around companies such as Carl Zeiss and Schott, grew steadily, and Jena was a world centre of the optical industry for most of the 20th century.

Jena is the second largest city in Thuringia, with about 110,000 inhabitants. The Friedrich Schiller University, founded in 1558, remains the heart of its education and research. Its main church, St Michael's, built between 1422 and 1557, is one of the biggest Gothic monuments in Thuringia, and the botanic garden, established in 1794, is one of the oldest in Germany.
jeolla-province: Jeolla was bounded by Chungcheong Province to the north and Gyeongsang Province to the east, with the East China Sea to the south and the Yellow Sea to the west. The Sobaek Mountains form its eastern edge, and it is drained by the Yeongsan, Seomjin and Mangyeong rivers. Its provincial capital was Jeonju, and the whole inland region was called Honam, south of the lake, a name still in common use.

In the Samhan era the area belonged to the Mahan confederacy, with the Tamna kingdom on Jeju; fifteen of the 45 Korean tribes had their bases here. Baekje took over Mahan by the 5th century. After Silla conquered Baekje with the help of Tang China in 660, the region was organised as the districts of Wansan, later renamed Jeonju, and Namwon in the north and Mujin, renamed Mu in 757, in the south.

Goryeo reorganised the country several times. In 983 Jeonju became Jeonju-mok and Muju was split into Naju and Seungju; in 995 these became Gangnam-do and Haeyang-do. In 1018, in the ninth year of Hyeonjong of Goryeo, the two were joined as Jeollaju, named after Jeonju and Naju. It was the first time the region was united in one division, and it stayed so for nearly eight centuries. Joseon kept it among the Eight Provinces set up in 1413, and the name was shortened to Jeolla-do.

The Donghak Peasant Revolution of 1894-1895 began in Jeolla, fed by belief in a coming local messiah, protests at Seoul's high taxes on rice and the growing number of Japanese traders. On 26 May 1895 Gojong of Korea replaced the provinces with 23 districts, and on 4 August 1896 Royal Order 36 restored the provinces and divided Jeolla into north and south.

The old province corresponds to the South Korean provinces of North Jeolla and South Jeolla, the city of Gwangju and Jeju Province. Its largest city is Gwangju; Jeonju remains the capital of North Jeolla. The name Jeolla-do reached its thousandth year in 2018.
jeong-do-jeon: Chŏng Tojŏn, also known by his art name Sambong, was born on 6 October 1342 in Yeongju, in Goryeo, into the Bonghwa Chŏng clan. His family had emerged from commoner status about four generations earlier and had slowly risen through government service, and his father was the first of them to reach a high post. According to the Veritable Records his maternal grandmother was a slave, though the credibility of that account is questioned. He studied under Yi Che-hyŏn alongside other leading thinkers such as Chŏng Mong-ju. He first met Yi Sŏnggye in 1383, when he visited him at his quarters in Hamgyong province.

After Yi Sŏnggye, later King Taejo, founded Joseon in July 1392, he appointed Chŏng Tojŏn to the highest civilian and military office at once. Chŏng decided policy from military affairs and diplomacy to education. He laid down Joseon's political system and tax laws, replaced Buddhism with Confucianism as the national religion, moved the capital from Kaesong to Hanyang, present-day Seoul, and wrote a code of laws that became in effect Joseon's constitution. He chose the names of the palaces, the eight provinces and the districts of the capital, worked to free many slaves and reformed land policy.

He saw Joseon as a kingdom led by ministers, with a largely symbolic king, and held that government, including the king, existed for the sake of the people. He argued that Goryeo's rulers had given up their right to rule. He also urged that private armies, including the princes', be abolished and sent to the central government. Yi Pangwŏn, Taejo's fifth son, was displeased, and none of the princes complied. Chŏng persuaded Taejo to name his young eighth son Yi Pangsŏk crown prince instead of Yi Pangwŏn, who had done most to bring his father to power.

In 1398, after the sudden death of Queen Sindeok, Yi Pangwŏn raided the palace in the coup known as the First Strife of the Princes. He killed Chŏng Tojŏn and his supporters and the queen's two sons, including the crown prince. The Veritable Records show Chŏng begging for his life, while the Sambong chip portrays him leaving a death poem and accepting death with dignity. Neither account is held fully credible. Taejo abdicated, and Yi Pangwŏn later became King Taejong.

For about three centuries Chŏng was regarded as a treacherous villain, and the philosopher Song Si-yŏl always called him insidious. In the 18th century King Chŏngjo republished the Sambong chip, and Chŏng was rehabilitated in 1865 in recognition of his role in designing Gyeongbokgung. His treatise Bulssi Japbyeon attacked Buddhism as corrupt in practice and nihilistic in doctrine, as a student of Zhu Xi's thought.
jeong-mong-ju: Chŏng Mongju was born on 13 January 1337 in Yeongcheon, Gyeongsang Province, to a family of the Yeonil Jeong clan, the eldest of five siblings. At 23 he took three civil service literary examinations and received the highest marks possible in each. In 1367 he became an instructor of Neo-Confucianism at the Gukjagam, then called Songgyungwan, and held a government post at the same time. King U had great confidence in his knowledge and judgment, and he took part in national projects.

In 1372 Chŏng Mongju was sent as an envoy to the Ming dynasty. Because raids by the Waegu, Japanese pirates, on the Korean Peninsula were severe, he was sent in 1377 to Kyūshū, where his negotiations led to promises of Japanese aid against the pirates. The tandai of Kyūshū, Imagawa Sadayo, made several repressions against the Waegu, probably as a result. In 1384 he travelled to the Ming capital, and his negotiations led to peace with the Ming in 1385. He also founded an institute devoted to Confucian theory.

He had been a moderate supporter of Yi Sŏng-gye and backed his takeover of the court after the Wihwado Retreat of 1388. But he came to realise that Yi and his more radical supporters, such as Chŏng To-jŏn and Cho Chun, planned to found a new dynasty. A staunch Neo-Confucian and Goryeo loyalist, he called it an immoral act.

On 9 April 1392 Yi Sŏng-gye was seriously injured in a riding accident, and Chŏng planned to use the chance to destroy his faction. On 26 April he went to Yi's residence to learn how badly he was hurt. At a banquet he and Yi Pang-wŏn, Yi's fifth son and later Taejong of Joseon, exchanged poems. Yi Pang-wŏn's Hayeoga urged him to give up his loyalty, and Chŏng replied with the Dansimga, which ends: how can this red heart ever fade away? On the way home he was assassinated on the Sonjuk Bridge in Gaeseong by five of Yi Pang-wŏn's subordinates. Yi Sŏng-gye is said to have lamented the death and rebuked his son.

The Goryeo dynasty symbolically ended with his death, which was followed by the Joseon period. Joseon monarchs venerated him, and Yi Pang-wŏn inscribed the words Defender of Goryeo on his tombstone. In 1517 he was canonized into Sungkyunkwan, the National Neo-Confucian Academy. His grave is at Yongin in Gyeonggi Province, beside his wife's.
jeong-yak-yong: He came from the Naju Chŏng clan, a family of the Southerners faction, which had been excluded from office since 1694. He was born in Mahyeon-ri, east of Seoul, in the year Crown Prince Sado was executed by his father the king. Shocked by the execution, his father Chŏng Chaewŏn withdrew from official life, named the boy Kwinong (back to farming) and gave him an intense education at home.

In 1776 he married Hong Hwabo and moved to Seoul. At 15 he was introduced to the writings of Yi Ik by Yi Kahwan and his brother-in-law Yi Seung-hun, and resolved to devote his life to similar studies. He passed the literary licentiate examination in 1783.

King Jeongjo was impressed by his answers to a set of royal questions in 1784, and in 1789 he took top place in the higher civil service examination and entered the Office of Royal Decrees. His family was closely tied to the first Korean Catholics: Yi Seung-hun had been baptised in Beijing in 1784, and his older brother Chŏng Yakchong led the first Catholic community. Rivals of the Old Doctrine faction used these ties against him.

After he designed a pontoon bridge in 1792, the king asked him to plan the walls of the Hwaseong Fortress, for which he drew on European, Chinese and Japanese techniques. In 1794 he served as secret envoy to Gyeonggi province, investigating corruption, and he later held posts at the Geumjeong post station and as county magistrate at Koksan.

When Jeongjo died in 1800, Queen Jeongsun launched a purge of Catholics; Chŏng Yakchong and Yi Seung-hun were executed in the spring of 1801. After the Silk Letter Incident, in which his relative Hwang Sayŏng asked the bishop of Beijing for Western warships, he arrived at Gangjin on 28 December 1801. He lived first in a tavern room, then near the temple of the monk Hyejang, and from 1808 in a thatched house on a hill called Tasan, where he taught students and built a library of over a thousand books.

Allowed home in 1818, he was kept out of office by factional politics and lived quietly near the Han River until his death in 1836, on his sixtieth wedding anniversary. His proposals included a village land system in which land was farmed in common and its produce shared by the labour given.
jeongjo-of-joseon: Jeongjo, whose personal name was Yi San, was the second son of Crown Prince Sado and Lady Hyegyŏng. His elder brother, Crown Prince Uiso, died in infancy. In 1762 Yeongjo had Sado executed by confinement in a rice chest, after long conflicts and Sado's years of mental illness. On 21 February 1764 Yi San became the adoptive son of Crown Prince Hyojang and Princess Consort Hyosun by Yeongjo's order, because Yeongjo feared that the heir would be opposed as Sado's son.

The Noron faction protested that Yi San was the son of a prisoner or of a madman and so unfit to succeed. Between 1762 and 1777 some of its members tried to depose him in favour of his half-brothers. Hong Guk-yeong strongly supported his accession, and Kim Jong-su, though a Noron, also helped him. In 1775 Yi San was made regent, but received no military power.

Jeongjo was crowned in the Gyeonghuigung palace on 10 March 1776. His first statement to his officials was that he was the son of Sado, whom the former king had executed. He made his mother a Dowager Queen and spent much of his reign trying to clear his father's name. In 1776 Hong Sang-beom, Hong Kye-neung and other Noron members tried to stage a military coup and assassinate him; he had them executed, along with Prince Eunjeon, Hong In-han and Jeong Hu-gyeom.

He continued Yeongjo's Tangpyeong policy of balancing political factions, favoured members of the Soron and Namin parties over the Noron as a check on them, and relied on Silhak scholars such as Chŏng Yagyong and Pak Chiwŏn. He founded the Kyujanggak Royal Library to improve scholarship and recruit able officers, and opened government posts to men previously barred by social status. From 1782 he chose officers for the Changyongyeong guard, created in 1785, by competitive examination. He ordered the building of Hwaseong Fortress, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In 1791 he issued the Shinhae Tonggong law, which let anyone sell goods at the market and ended the monopoly of the capital's merchant groups.

In his last years Jeongjo arranged the marriage of his second son and successor, Sunjo, to the daughter of Kim Jo-sun of the Andong Kim clan. He died suddenly in 1800, at the age of 47, in uncertain circumstances, and speculation about the cause continues. He is buried with Queen Hyoui at the royal tomb of Geonneung. His appointment of Hong Guk-yeong let state affairs be swayed by close retainers, and the Andong Kim marriage tilted power to one side and became the background of the era of sedo politics. In 1899 he was honoured as Emperor Seon.
jeonju: Jeonju lies in a basin surrounded by mountains, with Moryongsan to the north and Namgosan to the south, and the Jeonjucheon River flows through the centre of the city. Wanju County almost entirely surrounds it, so the city is both urban and rural. Its name is glossed as "Perfect region". Jeonju is divided into two wards, Deokjin District and Wansan District.

The kingdom of Baekje lay in south-western Korea and included the area of Jeonju, which is believed to have been founded as a market town within Baekje around 57 BCE. Silla conquered Baekje in 660, and in 685 Jeonju became one of the nine provincial capitals of the Silla kingdom. From 889 peasant revolts caused by over-taxation spread across the kingdom, and in Jeonju they gave a base to one of the most powerful rebel leaders, Gyeon Hwon. He renamed the city Wansan and made it the capital of Later Baekje. From there he campaigned against Silla, destroying its capital Geumseong and assassinating King Gyeongae in 927. Wang Geon of Goryeo then invaded Later Baekje in 934, and Jeonju surrendered to him in 935.

Under Goryeo, Jeonju was again a provincial capital and enjoyed relative stability and economic growth. In 1182 peasant rebels took the city with the help of government troops stationed there, who resented being made to do heavy labour alongside slaves, but the rebellion was suppressed forty days after it began. The Joseon dynasty, founded in 1392, regarded Jeonju as its ancestral home. It became the capital of a reorganised Jeolla province, and in 1413 it was one of four cities given copies of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty to keep. The Donghak Peasant Revolution occupied the town in 1894.

Japan occupied Korea from 1910 to 1945 and renamed Jeonju Zenshū. The Japanese authorities destroyed the old city walls, leaving only the gate Pungnammun. Jeonju received metropolitan status in 1935 and its modern boundaries and government in 1963. It was not on the front line in the Korean War, but suffered bombardment and the loss of many male residents who fought.

Jeonju is the capital and largest city of Jeonbuk province in South Korea, known for its cuisine, historic buildings and festivals. Jeonju bibimbap is a well-known local dish, and UNESCO named the city a Creative City for Gastronomy in 2012. Jeonju Hanok Village holds over 800 traditional hanok buildings. Gyeonggijeon enshrines the portrait of Lee Seonggye, the first king of Joseon, and the Jeongdong Catholic Church, built from 1908 to 1914, stands on the site of the Korean Catholic martyrs of 1791 and 1801.
jepara: Jepara lies on the north coast of Java, northeast of Semarang and not far from Mount Muria, and is the main town of Jepara Regency in the province of Central Java. It has a tropical monsoon climate, with heavy rainfall from November to April and little from May to October. As a pesisir, or coastal, area it received traders from many lands over the centuries, and some of its people have European, Chinese, Arab, Malay or Bugis ancestry. The population is almost entirely Javanese and overwhelmingly Muslim, though the villages of Plajan and Tempur have a comparatively mixed religious population.

In the 16th century Jepara was an important port. Early in 1513 its king, Yunnus, also called Pati Unus, led an attack on Portuguese Malacca with a force said to number one hundred ships and 5000 men from Jepara and Palembang, but he was defeated; between 1518 and 1521 he ruled over Demak. The rule of Ratu Kalinyamat in the later 16th century was the most influential in the town's history. Jepara attacked Malacca again in 1551, this time with Johor, and was defeated, and in 1574 it besieged Malacca for three months. In the 17th century the Dutch had a fort there.

Jepara had a population of 85,970 in mid 2024, and the regency as a whole had 1,283,687 people; the metropolitan area of Greater Jepara had 227,062 inhabitants at the 1990 Census. The town is known for its carving of Javanese teak and as the birthplace of the national heroine Kartini, a pioneer of women's rights in Indonesia.
jerash: Archaeologists have found ruins of Neolithic settlements at Jerash and evidence of Bronze Age settlement in the region. The Greek city of Gerasa, also called Antioch on the Golden River, is traditionally linked to Alexander the Great and his general Perdiccas, who allegedly settled aged Macedonian soldiers there in 331 BCE. Its former name, Antioch on the Chrysorrhoas, points instead to a Seleucid founding, and still others credit Ptolemy II of Egypt. In the early 80s BCE the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus conquered it.

The Roman conquest of 63 BCE ended this rule, and Pompey attached the city to the Decapolis, a league of Hellenistic cities that enjoyed considerable autonomy under Roman protection. In the second half of the 1st century CE Gerasa grew prosperous, and in 106 it was absorbed into the Roman province of Arabia. Hadrian visited in 129–130, and the Arch of Hadrian was built to mark the occasion. The first cathedral was built in the 4th century, the first of at least 14 churches built between the 4th and 7th centuries, many with fine mosaic floors.

The Persian Sassanids invaded in 614, and in 636 the Byzantine army lost the Battle of the Yarmuk, after which the region passed to the Rashidun Caliphate. The city did well under the Umayyad Caliphate, with a mint that struck coins naming Jerash, until the earthquake of 749 destroyed much of it. A fortress built by a garrison sent by Zahir ad-Din Toghtekin, atabeg of Damascus, was captured and burned by Baldwin II, King of Jerusalem, in 1121–1122. In 1596 an Ottoman census recorded 12 Muslim households, and in 1838 the site was described as a ruin.

Jerash is regarded as one of the largest and best preserved sites of Greek and Roman architecture outside Italy. Its monuments include an oval forum about 300 feet long with an Ionic colonnade, sanctuaries of Artemis and Zeus, two theatres, the colonnaded cardo, two tetrapyla, two baths, a nymphaeum and an almost complete circuit of walls. Wealthy citizens paid for most of these buildings. Excavation has gradually revealed the ancient city since 1925, and the western side with its monuments has been preserved, while the modern city lies east of the river.
jeremiah: According to the biblical narrative, Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, a priest from the village of Anathoth in the land of Benjamin. He was called to prophecy in about 626 BCE, the thirteenth year of Josiah, king of Judah, and he remained a prophet until after the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of Solomon's Temple in 587 BCE, a span covering the reigns of five kings of Judah. He is said to have resisted the call, protesting that he was only a child and did not know how to speak. He was to proclaim that invaders from the north would destroy Jerusalem because the nation had forsaken God.

In his early years Jeremiah was chiefly a preaching prophet, condemning idolatry, the greed of priests and false prophets. His message prompted plots against him: the men of Anathoth, his priestly kin, plotted to kill him, and a temple official, Pashur, had him beaten and put in the stocks. Under King Zedekiah he made a yoke to show that the nation would be subject to the king of Babylon. The prophet Hananiah broke the yoke, and Jeremiah answered that he had made instead a yoke of iron.

After he prophesied that Jerusalem would be handed to the Babylonian army, the king's officials persuaded Zedekiah that he should be put to death. They cast him into a cistern, where he sank into the mud, and Ebed-Melech, an Ethiopian, pulled him out. He stayed imprisoned until Jerusalem fell. The Babylonians then released him, and he went to Mizpah with Gedaliah, whom they had made governor. When Gedaliah was assassinated, Johanan fled to Egypt, taking Jeremiah and his scribe Baruch against his counsel. The prophet probably spent the rest of his life there, and there is no authentic record of his death.

Jewish tradition holds that Jeremiah, with the help of Baruch, wrote the Book of Jeremiah, the Books of Kings and the Book of Lamentations. The consensus among scholars is that there was a historical prophet of the name and that parts of the book were probably written by him or by Baruch. Views range from the belief that its narratives and poems are contemporary with his life to the view that the original prophet's work cannot now be recovered. Rainer Albertz proposed that early collections of oracles were followed by several redactions between about 550 and 520 BCE.

Jeremiah is an essential figure in both Judaism and Christianity. His words are read in synagogues as part of the haftara and quoted about forty times in the New Testament. Islam regards him as a prophet, and the word jeremiad, a mournful complaint, derives from his name.
jeremie: Jérémie, in Haitian Creole Jeremi, is a commune and the capital city of the Grand'Anse department in Haiti. It is relatively isolated from the rest of the country, and the Grande-Anse River flows near the city. At the census of 2015 it had a population of about 134,317. About 40 nautical miles, or 74 kilometres, to the west lies Navassa Island, which is claimed by both Haiti and the United States. The city has an airport, Jérémie Airport, whose area is known as Numero Deux, and its districts include Beaudrouin, Campagne, Carrefour Sanon, La Forêt and Rampe des Lions.

General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, a Creole, was born here in 1762, the son of a French nobleman and his African slave. His father took him to France at the age of 18, and he became known for fighting under Napoleon in Italy and Egypt and as the father of the writer Alexandre Dumas. In 1954 Hurricane Hazel hit Jérémie and destroyed much of the city and many neighbouring inland villages. In 1964, during the event known as the Jérémie Vespers, the Haitian army and the Tonton Macoutes massacred 27 people in the city.

In the early 2000s archaeologists uncovered an ancient synagogue of Crypto-Jews in the city, the only one found on the island, and Jérémie has historically been inhabited by many mixed-race families of Jewish descent. After the earthquake of 2010 a food aid convoy that had been delivered to Jérémie Airport met a hijacking attempt by 20 men on 30 January 2010, and medical supplies were also flown in through the airport for injured refugees arriving after the quake. In October 2016 Hurricane Matthew almost completely destroyed the city.

Jérémie is called the city of the poets because of the many writers, poets and historians born there. Among them are the poets Emile Roumer, who lived from 1903 to 1988, and Etzer Vilaire, from 1872 to 1951. Joseph Serge Miot, Archbishop of Port-au-Prince, who was killed in the earthquake of 2010, was also born in the city. So was Modeste Testas, an Ethiopian woman who was formerly enslaved and who lived from 1765 to 1870; a statue of her in Bordeaux commemorates the transatlantic slave trade. Elisabeth Dieudonné Vincent, who lived from 1798 to 1883, was a free colored businesswoman.
jeremy-bentham: Jeremy Bentham was born in Houndsditch, London, in February 1748, the son of the attorney Jeremiah Bentham, in a wealthy Tory family. He was reportedly a child prodigy: found as a toddler reading a multi-volume history of England at his father's desk, he began Latin at three and at seven played Handel sonatas on the violin at dinner parties. His one surviving sibling, Samuel Bentham, became a close companion. In 1786 and 1787 he visited Samuel in Krichev, in the Russian Empire, where Samuel had conceived a circular building from which a few managers could oversee a large workforce. Bentham developed the idea as a prison design, the Panopticon, and acknowledged that the basic idea was his brother's.

Bentham took as the fundamental axiom of his philosophy that right and wrong are measured by the happiness of the largest number of people, a principle he said he had borrowed from Joseph Priestley. His ambition was a Pannomion, a complete utilitarian code of law, and he coined the verb to codify; his efforts were unsuccessful in his lifetime, though they laid a foundation for David Dudley Field II's codification work in the United States. In A Fragment on Government (1776), published anonymously, he criticised William Blackstone's defence of judge-made law, legal fictions and the social contract. He argued that the ability to suffer, not to reason, should decide who has rights, and he is regarded as an early voice for animal rights.

He favoured the separation of church and state, equal rights for women including the vote and divorce, and the abolition of slavery, capital punishment and physical punishment. He opposed empire, writing Emancipate Your Colonies! in 1793. In 1823 he co-founded The Westminster Review with James Mill, a journal for the Philosophical Radicals, among them John Bowring and Edwin Chadwick.

Bentham died on 6 June 1832 at his home in Queen Square Place, Westminster, aged 84, having written until a month earlier. His instructions, attached to his will of 30 May 1832, directed Thomas Southwood Smith to dissect his body and preserve it as an auto-icon, which is now on display at University College London. Although he is called the spiritual founder of the college, he only bought a single £100 share. He left manuscripts of an estimated 30 million words, now largely held by UCL and the British Library.
jerez-de-la-frontera: Jerez de la Frontera lies in southwestern Iberia on the Campiña de Jerez, an inland lowland plain crossed by the Guadalete River, midway between the Atlantic Ocean, the Guadalquivir and the western reaches of the Subbaetic System. The municipality covers 1,188.14 square kilometres and includes Los Alcornocales Natural Park. Its inland position gives mild winters and hot, long summers.

Human presence in the area goes back at least to the Copper or Neolithic Age. The first major protohistoric settlement, around the third millennium BCE, is attributed to the Tartessians, and the Roman city of Asta Regia stood about 8 kilometres to the north. The Vandals and Visigoths ruled the area until the Umayyad conquest of Hispania in the early 8th century. In the 11th century it briefly became the seat of an independent taifa, and it was annexed to Seville in 1053. Under the Almohads it grew into the largest urban centre between Seville and the Strait of Gibraltar.

The Crown of Castile conquered Jerez in the 13th century. After the conquest of Granada in 1492 and the discovery of the Americas it became one of the most prosperous cities of Andalusia through trade. English, Flemish, Portuguese and above all Genoese merchants settled there, drawn by winemaking. In January 1892 a peasant uprising was violently repressed.

Jerez is the most populated municipality in the province of Cádiz, with 214,844 people. Winegrowing has long been its main economic driver, and its grapes are made into sherry; through most of the 19th century the wine was produced overwhelmingly for export. It is home to the Spanish Military Stud farm. The Alcázar, a Moorish fortress, dates to the 11th century, and the Old City Hall was built in 1575. Motorcycle Grand Prix racing has been held at the Circuito de Jerez since 1987.
jericho: Jericho lies in the Jordan Valley, with the Jordan River to the east and Jerusalem to the west, in an oasis in Wadi Qelt 258 metres below sea level. The nearby spring of Ein es-Sultan irrigates some 10 square kilometres through channels. The Bible calls it the city of palm trees. Its Arabic name, Arīḥā, means fragrant and, like its Hebrew name, is generally thought to derive from a Canaanite word rēḥ.

The earliest excavated settlement lies at Tell es-Sultan, a couple of kilometres from the present town, where archaeologists have found the remains of more than 20 successive settlements, the first from about 9000 BCE. Jericho is the type site for the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and B periods. In the Early Bronze Age it became a fortified town, reaching its largest extent around 2600 BCE. In the Middle Bronze Age it had extensive walls with rectangular towers and a large cemetery whose rich offerings may reflect the emergence of local kings. It was destroyed in the Late Bronze Age and settled again from the 11th century BCE until the Babylonian conquest of Judah.

In the second half of the 2nd century BCE Jericho became part of the kingdom of Judea under the Hasmoneans. Around 135 or 134 BCE the local commander Ptolemy son of Abubus assassinated the Hasmonean leader Simon Thassi, his father-in-law, at the nearby fortress of Duq. Josephus calls its district the most fruitful country of Judea, rich in date palms and balsam. By the Byzantine period the built-up area had moved about 1,600 metres east to the site of the modern town, and monasteries and churches were built.

An earthquake destroyed Jericho in 659. The Crusaders ran large-scale sugar production there until Saladin's forces evicted them in 1187. It became part of the Ottoman Empire in 1517, came under British rule after the First World War, under Jordan after the 1948 Arab–Israeli War, and was occupied by Israel in 1967. In 1994 it became the first city handed to Palestinian Authority control.

Jericho is a city in the West Bank and capital of the Jericho Governorate, with 20,907 people in 2017. In 2023 Tell es-Sultan was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List. Other sites include the Umayyad palace at Khirbet al-Mafjar, known as Hisham's Palace, the Crusader sugar works at Tawahin es-Sukkar and Qasr al-Yahud on the Jordan, traditionally identified as the place of the baptism of Jesus.
jeroboam-i: According to the Hebrew Bible, Jeroboam was the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zereda, and of Zeruah, a widow. King Solomon made the young man a superintendent over his tribesmen in the building of the fortress Millo in Jerusalem and other public works. There he became familiar with the widespread discontent that the extravagance of Solomon's reign had caused.

Encouraged by the prophet Ahijah, he began to plot to become king. The plots were discovered, and he fled to Egypt, where he stayed under the protection of Pharaoh Shishak until Solomon died. He had at least two sons, Abijah and Nadab.

Hearing of Solomon's death, Jeroboam returned and joined a delegation that asked the new king Rehoboam to reduce taxes. Rehoboam refused, and ten of the tribes withdrew their allegiance to the house of David and proclaimed Jeroboam king, forming the northern kingdom of Israel. Only Judah and Benjamin stayed loyal to Rehoboam. According to 1 Kings he reigned for 22 years. Edwin Thiele dates the reign from 931 to 910 BCE and William F. Albright from 922 to 901 BCE.

Jeroboam rebuilt and fortified Shechem as his capital. Fearing that pilgrimages to the temple in Jerusalem might draw his people back to their old allegiance, he built two state temples with golden calves, at Bethel and at Dan. An unnamed prophet condemns this in 1 Kings 13, and the biblical writers often describe the king as doing evil in the sight of the Lord. He also moved the festival of Sukkot to the eighth month instead of the seventh.

The Bible reports constant war between Jeroboam and the house of Judah, with a long boundary dispute that lasted most of his reign. Chronicles says that Abijah, Rehoboam's son, defeated him in the mountains of Ephraim, with forces of 400,000 against 800,000, and that 500,000 of Jeroboam's men were killed. He is said to have lost Bethel, Jeshanah and Ephron, and he died soon after Abijah.

Later Jewish tradition made him a prototype of the evildoer. Some modern scholars have asked in recent years whether Jeroboam I existed and whether he may be a retrojection of the later Jeroboam II, though there is no consensus on the question.
jeroboam-ii: Jeroboam II, also called Jeroboam son of Jehoash, succeeded Jehoash as the thirteenth king of the ancient Kingdom of Israel and was the fourth king of the House of Jehu. He ruled for about four decades from Samaria and was the longest-reigning king of the northern kingdom; scholars date his reign differently, William F. Albright giving 786 to 746 BCE. His reign was contemporary with those of Amaziah and Uzziah of Judah. He is described as a military commander who fought Syria, and he extended Israel to its former limits, from the entering of Hamath to the sea of the plain.

Archaeological evidence confirms the biblical account of his reign as the most prosperous the northern kingdom had known. In 1910 G. A. Reisner found 63 inscribed potsherds at the royal palace at Samaria, later dated to his reign, which give information about the script, language, religion and administration of the period. A Hebrew seal found at Megiddo in 1904 reads Belonging to Shema, servant of Jeroboam. By the late 8th century BCE the territory of Israel was the most densely settled in the Levant, with about 350,000 people, and its prosperity rested on trade in olive oil, wine and possibly horses with Egypt and especially Assyria.

His reign was the period of the prophets Hosea, Joel, Amos and Jonah, who condemned the materialism and selfishness of the Israelite elite. According to Amos, the king's triumphs bred boastful overconfidence, the oppression of the poor by the mighty and luxury in palaces. The Book of Kings condemns him for doing evil in the eyes of the Lord, meaning both the oppression of the poor and his support of the cult centres at Dan and Bethel. The archaeologist Israel Finkelstein has argued that many stories of Solomon's rule over a large, prosperous kingdom were inspired by memories of the reign of Jeroboam II.

The Book of Amos mentions a major earthquake in the days of Jeroboam son of Jehoash. It is dated to about 760 BCE, and Yigael Yadin and Finkelstein dated the destruction level at Tel Hazor to it, as David Ussishkin did the destruction at Lachish. His name occurs in the Old Testament only in 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Hosea and Amos; elsewhere Jeroboam I is meant.
jerome: Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus was born at Stridon and was of Illyrian ancestry. He went to Rome with his friend Bonosus of Sardica to study rhetoric and philosophy, learned Latin under the philologist Aelius Donatus, and was baptized there. He described the guilt that followed the escapades of his student days, and how he visited the tombs of the martyrs in the catacombs on Sundays. Drawn to ascetic penance, he went for a time to the desert of Chalcis, south-east of Antioch, known as the Syrian Thebaid for its many hermits. There he began to learn Hebrew under a converted Jew.

As a protégé of Pope Damasus I, Jerome revised the Vetus Latina Gospels in Rome against Greek manuscripts. He gathered around him well-born women, among them the widows Marcella and Paula and Paula's daughters Blaesilla and Eustochium, who turned towards the monastic life. His unsparing criticism of the Roman clergy brought hostility, and after Damasus died on 10 December 384 he was forced to leave Rome after an inquiry into allegations of an improper relationship with Paula. Paula's money later paid for his stay in a monastery at Bethlehem, next to the Church of the Nativity, where he completed his translation of the Bible. He died on 30 September 420.

Jerome began in 382 by correcting the Vetus Latina New Testament. By 390 he was translating the Hebrew Bible from Hebrew, and he finished by 405. Earlier Latin versions of the Old Testament rested on the Septuagint, and his choice of a Hebrew text went against the advice of most Christians, among them Augustine, who thought the Septuagint inspired. The result became known as the Vulgate, and in 1546 the Council of Trent declared it authoritative. From 405 to 420 he wrote commentaries on Scripture.

His other writings include the Chronicon, a translation and continuation of the chronicle of Eusebius, and On Illustrious Men, a biobibliography of Christian writers written in 392 and 393. His letters give a vivid picture of the age. After Augustine, he is the most voluminous writer of ancient Latin Christianity, and the Catholic Church counts him among the four Great Latin Church Fathers and as patron saint of translators, librarians and encyclopedists. Artists often show him with a lion.
jerome-bonaparte: Jérôme Bonaparte was born Girolamo Buonaparte at Ajaccio, Corsica, on 15 November 1784, the eighth and last surviving child of Carlo Buonaparte and Letizia Ramolino. He studied at the Catholic College of Juilly and at the Irish College in Paris, and joined the French Navy in January 1800. Given a frigate in the West Indies, he fled to the United States under the name Mr. Albert after accidentally firing on a British ship. In Baltimore he married Elizabeth Patterson on 24 December 1803. Napoleon, who wanted to marry his siblings into royal houses, had the marriage annulled by imperial decree on 11 March 1805, and Jérôme submitted.

In return Jérôme was made an admiral, a general and an imperial prince, and in 1807 King of Westphalia, a realm formed from several states of north-western Germany in the Confederation of the Rhine, with its capital at Kassel. Napoleon had arranged his marriage to Princess Catharina of Württemberg, daughter of King Frederick I. The kingdom received the first constitution and parliament on German soil, and Jérôme brought the Empire style from Paris and had Leo von Klenze design a court theatre beside the summer residence, renamed Napoleonshöhe. His spending emptied the treasury, and Napoleon refused to support him financially.

In 1812 he commanded a corps of the Grande Armée marching towards Minsk. Reprimanded for travelling in state, he returned to Westphalia with his court after the Battle of Mir, and historians hold that tens of thousands of lives were probably lost in the invasion of Russia as a result. In 1813 the main allied force took Kassel, the kingdom was dissolved and Jérôme fled to France. At Waterloo his division was drawn into a prolonged assault on Hougoumont. Frederick I forced him and Catharina to leave Württemberg in 1814, and in July 1816 he gave Jérôme the title Prince of Montfort.

After his nephew Louis Napoleon became president of the Second Republic in 1848, Jérôme was made Governor of Les Invalides, Marshal of France in 1850 and President of the Senate in 1852. He was for a time heir presumptive to the imperial throne. He died on 24 June 1860 at Villegenis (now Massy) and is buried in Les Invalides. Historians such as Owen Connelly stress his financial, military and administrative successes, while others, including Helen Jean Burn, stress his failures; most agree he was the least successful of Napoleon's brothers. His grandson Charles Joseph Bonaparte served as United States Secretary of the Navy and Attorney General.
jeronimo-de-aguilar: Aguilar was a Franciscan friar born in Écija, Spain, and was sent to Panama as a missionary. He settled at the colony of Santa María la Antigua del Darién, founded there in 1510. Because of disputes between the colony's leaders, in 1511 he sailed for Santo Domingo on the caravel Santa María de la Barca, carrying legal documents for a case against the rival faction and a large sum of gold for the proceedings. The ship, with sixteen men and two women aboard, struck a sandbar off Yucatán, and currents carried the survivors in the ship's boat to the coast of what is now the Mexican state of Quintana Roo.

Aguilar and 11 or 12 others were captured by the local Maya. Valdivia and four others were sacrificed, others died of disease, and the women died overworked as slaves. Aguilar and the sailor Gonzalo Guerrero escaped, only to be enslaved by another chief, Xamanzana, an enemy of the first, among whose people they learned the language. Aguilar kept his religious vows and refused the women the chief offered him, while Guerrero became a war chief for Nachan Kaan, Lord of Chektumal, and married a Maya woman.

When Hernán Cortés reached Yucatán in 1519 and heard of bearded men among a neighbouring people, he sent word to them, and Aguilar joined the expedition. He proved his loyalty by naming the correct day of the week, which he had kept through his captivity with his breviary. Speaking Maya and Spanish, he worked with La Malinche, who spoke Maya and Nahuatl, as Cortés's interpreter during the conquest of the Aztec Empire, until she learned Spanish and could translate directly.

After the conquest Aguilar became a vecino, or resident, of Mexico City, and in 1526 Alonso de Estrada awarded him two encomiendas for his services. He died in 1531 without heirs, and the encomiendas reverted to the Crown. His house in Mexico City later became the site of the first printing press to operate in the New World.
jeronimos-monastery: The Jerónimos Monastery, near the Tagus in the parish of Belém, replaced a church of Santa Maria de Belém, where monks of the Order of Christ assisted seafarers. Manuel I ordered the new building at the cortes of Montemor o Velho in 1495 as a final resting place for the House of Aviz, and in 1496 he petitioned the Holy See for permission to build the monastery. Vasco da Gama and his men spent the night in prayer at the old church before leaving for India in 1497.

Construction began on 6 January 1501 and took a century. It was funded by the Vintena da Pimenta, a 5 percent tax on commerce from Africa and the Orient, equal to 70 kilograms of gold a year. Manuel I chose Hieronymite monks to pray for his soul and to give spiritual help to navigators leaving from Restelo, which they did until 1833.

The monastery is among the most prominent examples of the Manueline style, a richly ornate architecture carved in limestone with maritime themes and objects found on naval expeditions. Diogo de Boitaca drew the plans, and the Spaniard Juan de Castillo took charge around 1517, moving gradually towards the Spanish Plateresque. Building halted when Manuel I died in 1521. Diogo de Torralva resumed work in 1550 and added the main chapel and choir, and Jérôme de Rouen continued from 1571.

The church is a hall church with a single-span ribbed vault over a nave 19 metres wide and a transept vault without piers, which seems to float in the air. Six slender octagonal columns, 25 metres high, are carved with Renaissance decoration. The south portal, designed by Castillo, is 32 metres high, while Nicolau Chanterene built the western portal in 1517. The cloister, 55 by 55 metres, carries Manueline motifs with nautical elements and symbols of Portugal's growing world power.

Work stopped in 1580 with the union of Spain and Portugal, when the building of the Escorial drained funds. In 1604 Philip of Spain made it a royal funerary monument. The monastery withstood the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 with little damage, but on 28 December 1833 it was secularized and transferred to the Real Casa Pia de Lisboa. Restoration began after 1860.

The church holds the tombs of kings Manuel I and John III, and of the explorer Vasco da Gama and the poet Luís de Camões, whose remains were moved to carved tombs in 1880. The monastery and the nearby Tower of Belém were classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983, and the Treaty of Lisbon was signed there on 13 December 2007. Its west wing houses the Maritime Museum, inaugurated in 1963.
jerriais: Jèrriais is the traditional language of the Jersey people, a Romance language and the form of Norman spoken on the island. Its closest relatives are the other Norman languages, such as Guernésiais in Guernsey, and the other langues d'oïl. It is more accurately described as Norse adapted to the langue d'oïl than as a mixture of Old Norse and French: when Norse-speaking Normans conquered Normandy they began speaking the language of their new subjects, and kept some Norse vocabulary, such as mielle for sand dune and mauve for seagull. The language of Sark, Sercquiais, descends from the Jèrriais brought by Jersey colonists who settled the island in the 16th century.

A feature that distinguishes Jèrriais from its neighbours is the voiced dental fricative, written th, which typically occurs between vowels. Vowel length matters, and long vowels are usually written with a circumflex accent. Verb tenses show regular doubling of consonants, written with an apostrophe, as in pâl'la, "she will speak". It is distinct from Jersey Legal French, the language used for contracts, laws and official documents.

Until the 19th century Jèrriais was the everyday language of the majority of the population, and at the beginning of the Second World War up to half the population could still communicate in it. Louis Lucien Bonaparte visited the island and interested himself in the language, and Victor Hugo, in exile in Jersey, knew some Jèrriais writers. During the German occupation islanders used it among themselves as a language that neither the Germans nor their French interpreters could understand. English use then increased sharply after the Liberation, and the last monolingual adult speakers probably died in the 1950s.

Jersey fishing companies took the language to the cod fisheries of the Gaspé peninsula in Quebec, where it was the common language of business, and some speakers remained there in the 1960s. Efforts to preserve it include a Jèrriais section at the Jersey Eisteddfod since 1912, the Assembliée d'Jèrriais, founded in 1951, and Le Don Balleine, a trust set up under the will of Arthur E. Balleine. Dictionaries include the Glossaire du Patois Jersiais of 1924 and a Dictionnaire Jersiais–Français of 1966. On 13 February 2019 the States of Jersey adopted Jèrriais as an official language.
jerusalem-of-gold: The melody is largely based on the Basque lullaby Pello Joxepe, which Paco Ibáñez sang during a visit to Israel in 1962 to a group that included Shemer and Nehama Hendel. Shemer later acknowledged hearing Hendel perform it and drawing on its melody, and she regretted the likeness; Ibáñez said he was pleased the tune had contributed and did not regard it as plagiarism.
