The surviving volume measures 24.6 by 17.0 centimetres on very thin white paper. The lines are askew, the ink varies in thickness, and a few characters, such as 日 and 一, are printed in reverse. A woodblock edition made at Chwiamsa in 1378 survives complete in two volumes.

The metal-printed volume became known in 1901, when the French scholar Maurice Courant listed it in the appendix of his Bibliographie coréenne. The French diplomat Victor Collin de Plancy had collected it in Seoul, and in 1911 Henri Véver bought it for 180 francs and later left it to the National Library of France in his will. It drew wide attention when shown in Paris in 1972, and Cheongju University confirmed the site of Heungdeok Temple by excavation in 1985. UNESCO inscribed it on the Memory of the World Register on 4 September 2001. Ownership remains disputed: the French library holds that it is a shared heritage of humanity, while Korean organisations argue that it belongs in Korea.
jilin: In ancient times the Jilin area was inhabited by the Xianbei, Sushen, Mohe, Jurchens and Wùjí, and the kingdoms of Buyeo and Goguryeo ruled parts of it. The region then fell successively under the Xiongnu, the Xianbei state, Goguryeo, Balhae, the Khitan Liao dynasty, the Jurchen Jin dynasty and the Mongol Yuan dynasty. Under the Qing, much of the area was controlled by the General of Jilin, whose territory extended to much of what is now Russia's Primorsky Krai.

After Primorsky Krai was ceded to Russia in 1860, the government began to open the area to Han Chinese migrants, most of them from Shandong, and by the early 20th century the Han had become the dominant ethnic group of the region. In 1932 the area was incorporated into Manchukuo, a puppet state set up by Japan, with Changchun, then called Xinjing, as its capital. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the Red Army captured Jilin in Operation August Storm, and the region, with the rest of north-eastern China, passed to the Communists. Manchuria was the staging ground from which they conquered the rest of China in the Chinese Civil War.

In 1949 the province was smaller, taking in only the environs of Changchun and Jilin City, with its capital at Jilin City, while Changchun was an independent municipality. It was expanded to its present borders in the 1950s. During the Cultural Revolution it was enlarged again to include part of Inner Mongolia, giving it a border with Mongolia, but this was later reversed. The name comes from the Manchu phrase girin ula, meaning along the river, written in Chinese as jilin wula and shortened to Jilin.

Jilin is one of the three provinces of Northeast China, bordering North Korea and Russia to the east and south and Heilongjiang, Liaoning and Inner Mongolia. Its capital and largest city is Changchun, 113 kilometres west of Jilin City. The Changbai Mountains in the south-east hold its highest peak, Paektu Mountain at 2,744 metres, and the Yalu and Tumen rivers form parts of the border with North Korea. Agriculture centres on rice, wheat, maize and sorghum, and the province is known for ginseng and deer antlers used in Chinese medicine.
jilin-city: Jilin City lies in central Jilin Province, in a hilly area on the Songhua River, which surrounds much of the city and gives it the nickname River City. Four mountains stand round it: North Mountain (Beishan) to the west, Long Tan Mountain to the east, Zhuque Mountain to the north and Turtle Mountain to the south. With the river they form a bagua in the Taiji pattern. Beishan is the best known of them and is home to several Buddhist temples. The climate is humid continental, with long, cold winters. The Songhua is the only river in the region that does not freeze in winter, and water vapour rising from it crystallises on willow branches as rime ice in January and February.

Jilin City is one of the oldest cities in Northeast China. Under the Yongle Emperor, the Ming sought to extend control throughout Manchuria, and river fleets built here sailed several times to make local chieftains swear allegiance. After the Manchu-led Qing dynasty was established, the territory of today's Primorsky Krai was placed under Jilin's administration. As the Russian Empire advanced east towards the Pacific coast, the Qing government ordered a naval shipbuilding factory set up here in 1661.

Jilin was officially established as a fort city in 1673, when the Deputy Lieutenant-General Anzhuhu was ordered to build a castle. In 1676 the Military Governor of Ninguta was transferred to Jilin because of its more convenient location and growing military importance, and the city then developed rapidly. Its nickname comes from a line of a poem written by the Kangxi Emperor on his visit in 1682. Jilin remained important in the 18th and 19th centuries as one of the few cities beyond the Willow Palisade, with Qiqihar, Ninguta and Mukden.

When Manchukuo made Xinjing, now Changchun, its capital, Jilin's importance fell. By 1940 Jilin had 173,624 people and Xinjing 544,202. Soviet forces captured Jilin during the August Storm operation. It was the provincial capital of Jilin Province from the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 until Changchun took that role in 1956.

Jilin City is a prefecture-level city and the only major city in China that shares its name with its province. It co-hosted the Asian Winter Games in 2007, and winter sports such as skiing and skating are popular. Among its sights is Wulajie Old City, a walled Qing town downstream on the Songhua. It was a collecting point for local products sent to the imperial court, and the Kangxi Emperor went there in 1682 to fish for sturgeon. A Meteorite Museum there displays the largest stony meteorite of a documented meteorite fall.
jim-crow-laws: The Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery was ratified on 18 December 1865. During Reconstruction, between 1865 and 1877, federal laws protected the civil rights of freedmen in the South. In the 1870s Democrats gradually regained power in Southern legislatures while paramilitary groups such as the Ku Klux Klan, the White League and the Red Shirts drove out Republican officeholders and lynched Black voters to suppress the Black vote.

The term Jim Crow probably derives from Jump Jim Crow, a minstrel dance performed in blackface by the white actor Thomas D. Rice, first staged in 1828. By the end of the nineteenth century the name meant the social separation of the races.

The laws were passed by white-dominated state legislatures to remove the gains that African Americans had made during Reconstruction. Beginning in the 1870s they mandated segregation in public facilities across the South, and companion laws excluded most African Americans from the vote. The Civil Rights Act of 1875 guaranteed equal treatment in public accommodations but had little effect, and an 1883 Supreme Court decision found it unconstitutional in some respects.

In Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 the Supreme Court upheld the doctrine of separate but equal facilities. In practice the facilities for African Americans were consistently inferior and underfunded, and sometimes did not exist. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909, campaigned against the laws and the doctrine.

In Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka in 1954 the Supreme Court unanimously held public school segregation unconstitutional and overturned Plessy. In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, and the Montgomery bus boycott that followed lasted more than a year. Mass demonstrations organised by the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, headed by Martin Luther King Jr., drew national attention on television.

Congress overcame Southern filibusters to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which overturned most remaining Jim Crow laws. Laws against interracial marriage were struck down in Loving v. Virginia in 1967. Historians count the laws among the causes of the Great Migration, in which African Americans left the rural South for cities in the Northeast, Midwest and West.
jimena-diaz: Jimena, whose name is also spelled Ximena, was born before July 1046. She was the daughter of Diego Fernández, Count of Oviedo, himself the son of Count Fernando Flaínez, and of his wife Cristina, and she was a sister of Fernando Díaz, Count of Asturias. She married Rodrigo Díaz between July 1074 and 12 May 1076.

It is unclear whether she lived with her husband in the Taifa of Zaragoza during his first exile, from 1080 to 1086, when he led the army of its rulers, or whether she went to Asturias in those years. A legal action from Tol dated 1083 suggests that she kept a presence there even while the two were apart. At the start of his second exile, in 1089, she was imprisoned with her children Cristina, Diego and María by order of Alfonso VI. Nothing more is known of her until the end of 1094.

Rodrigo Díaz conquered Valencia on 17 June 1094 and secured it by his victory at the Battle of Cuarte on 21 October, after which Jimena rejoined him and stayed with him until his death. The principality he had founded was an independent state, and she succeeded him as its ruler. Their son Diego had been killed in 1097, fighting under Alfonso VI. A deed of gift that she made to the Cathedral of Valencia in 1101 survives with her signature. When the king judged the city impossible to defend, he escorted her back to Castile.

In 1103 she signed a document at the Monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña selling a monastery she owned to two canons of Burgos. This does not show that she spent her old age in the abbey, as the monastery maintained until the 18th century in the hagiographic texts known as the Legend of Cardeña; it is more likely that she lived her last years in or near Burgos. She died between 29 August 1113 and 1116, probably in 1116.

Through her daughters her descendants entered several ruling houses. Cristina married Ramiro Sánchez of Monzón and was the mother of King García Ramírez of Navarre, and María married first a prince of Aragon and then Ramon Berenguer III, Count of Barcelona. Jimena and her husband were buried at San Pedro de Cardeña. After the tombs were ransacked during the Napoleonic Wars the remains were reburied in Burgos, and they now lie in Burgos Cathedral.
jimenez-dynasty: The family was also called the Jimena, the Sancha, the Banu Sancho, the Abarca or the Banu Abarca. Its first known member, García Jiménez of Pamplona, is obscure: the Códice de Roda calls him king of another part of the kingdom of Pamplona, probably the frontier areas of Álava and the western Pyrenees beyond the direct rule of the Íñiguez kings. It was long believed that the family came from Gascony. His younger son Sancho Garcés used foreign help to displace the Íñiguez ruler Fortún Garcés.

Muslim sources called the family the Banu Sanjo after Sancho, while the chronicler Ibn al-Kardabūs named Sancho III ibn Abarca, after a nickname of Sancho I. Sancho I repelled several attacks from the Emir of Córdoba, crushed the neighbouring Banu Qasi, extended Pamplona to the upper Ebro valley and took in the County of Aragon.

After Sancho I's death in 925 his brother Jimeno Garcés held power, and then Sancho's young son García Sánchez I ruled under the guidance of his mother, Toda Aznárez, who built alliances among the Christian states and in 934 pledged allegiance to her nephew Abd-ar-Rahman III. Three generations of defeat and subjection by the Caliphate followed, until Sancho the Great, who ruled from 1000 to 1035, freed the kingdom and also ruled Aragon, Castile, Ribagorza and eventually León.

His lands were divided among his sons. Ferdinand I killed the King of León and Galicia in 1037 and inherited his realms, and his son Alfonso VI conquered Toledo. In 1076 Sancho IV of Navarre was assassinated by his siblings, and his kingdom was shared between Castile and Aragon. Alfonso the Battler briefly reunited the family's lands through his marriage to Urraca, Queen of Castile and León, but the marriage failed. Aragon passed through the heiress Petronilla to the ruler of Barcelona, and Navarre through Blanca, sister of Sancho VII.

In the 15th century the Borgias of Italy claimed descent from Pedro de Atarés, lord of Borja, a grandson of Sancho Ramírez, Count of Ribagorza, which would have made them male-line descendants of the dynasty. The pedigree was a fabrication.
jimmy-carter: James Earl Carter Jr. was born on 1 October 1924 in Plains, Georgia, at the Wise Sanitarium, where his mother worked as a registered nurse. He was the eldest child of Bessie Lillian Gordy and James Earl Carter Sr., a local businessman who ran a general store. The family settled in nearby Archery, a community populated almost entirely by impoverished Black families. His father was staunchly pro-segregation, yet allowed his son to befriend the children of the Black farmhands.

Carter graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 1946 and joined the submarine service. In 1952 he began an association with the Navy's nuclear submarine program, led by Captain Hyman G. Rickover, who he later said had the most influence on his life after his parents. He then returned to Plains and expanded the family peanut-growing business.

Carter won a seat in the Georgia State Senate in 1962, after a repeat election because early counting was shown to be the result of fraudulent voting. He served from 1963 to 1967. Sworn in as the 76th governor of Georgia on 12 January 1971, he declared in his inaugural speech that the time for racial discrimination was over, which caused many segregationists who had supported him to feel betrayed. He merged about 300 state agencies into 22.

He announced his presidential campaign on 12 December 1974. Little known outside his home state, he was derided with the question Jimmy Who?. With the Watergate scandal fresh in voters' minds, his position as an outsider helped him, and he narrowly defeated the Republican incumbent Gerald Ford.

Inaugurated on 20 January 1977, Carter issued an unconditional amnesty for Vietnam War draft evaders. His administration negotiated the Camp David Accords, the Panama Canal Treaties and the second Strategic Arms Limitation Talks agreement, established diplomatic relations with China, and created the Departments of Energy and Education. His term was marked by inflation and recession, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran hostage crisis. He lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan in a landslide.

After the presidency Carter established the Carter Center to promote human rights, and he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002. He travelled widely to conduct peace negotiations, monitor elections and combat neglected tropical diseases, and he was a key figure in Habitat for Humanity. He died at his home in Plains on 29 December 2024, aged 100, and was buried next to his wife Rosalynn. Historians have generally rated his presidency below average, while his post-presidency, the longest in U.S. history, is viewed more favourably.
jimo: Jimo lies in the southwest of the Shandong Peninsula, bordered by the Yellow Sea on the east and by Mount Lao on the south. It has a moderate monsoon climate. The settlement was established under the Eastern Zhou dynasty, when it was the second largest in Shandong.

Its siege is remembered for the ruse that ended it. Tian Dan, a general of the State of Qi, had lost 70 cities to the Yan, and Jimo was the last but one city left. He gathered more than 1,000 oxen, tied daggers to their ears and straw to their tails and dressed them in coloured cloth so that they looked like dragons. At night the tails were set alight and the oxen driven into the enemy camp; the panicking soldiers were destroyed, and Qi regained all the lost cities.

On 6 March 1898 the city, then written Tsimo, became part of the German Kiautschou Bay Leased Territory. During the First World War the Germans kept a small outpost there, which Japanese cavalry took on 13 September 1914 during the Siege of Tsingtao. The Japanese built an airfield at Tsimo, from which Nieuport aircraft tried without success to bomb the German airfield. After the war the territory passed to Japan and was returned to China in 1922. In the Chinese civil war, 90,000 peasants from Jimo fought on the communist side, and women of the district supplied the People's Liberation Army with 5,000 pairs of shoes.

Formerly Jimo City, Jimo is now a district of Qingdao. Qingdao University, Qingdao Agricultural University and a campus of Shandong University stand there, and Aoshan Bay and Tianheng Island are its chief places for visitors. Three expressways and the Jiaoji, Lanyan and Qingrong railways cross the district.
jin-midi: The Prince of Xiutu was one of the major princes under the Xiongnu Junchen Chanyu, and with the Prince of Hunye he defended the Xiongnu's south-western border with the Han in what is now central and western Gansu. In 121 BCE the Han general Huo Qubing dealt the Xiongnu a heavy defeat there, killing the Princes of Zhelan and Luhu and 8,900 soldiers and seizing the golden statues the Prince of Xiutu used to worship heaven. Fearing execution by Yizhixie Chanyu, the two princes planned to defect. After the Prince of Xiutu was killed, his son Midi, Midi's mother and his brother Lun were taken as imperial servants.

Once the emperor favoured him, the court resented the rise of a barbarian boy, as the Hanshu reports, but Emperor Wu of Han only treated him more generously. When Midi's mother died, the emperor had her portrait hung in the Sweet Spring Palace under the title The Princess of Xiutu. Two of Midi's sons became the emperor's attendants; when Midi saw one of them, grown, flirting with the ladies in waiting, he killed him and reported it, and the emperor, though saddened, was further impressed.

Ma Heluo had been anxious since Emperor Wu slaughtered the clan of his friend Jiang Chong, whose false charge of treason had driven Crown Prince Liu Ju to rebel in 91 BCE. When Ma plotted with his brothers against the emperor, Midi held him until other guards arrived.

As Emperor Wu lay dying in 87 BCE, Huo Guang, younger brother of Huo Qubing, first declined the regency, saying Midi was more capable. Midi answered that as a Xiongnu he would be thought of lightly by officials and by the Xiongnu alike. Emperor Wu's will made the three regents marquesses for suppressing Ma's plot, but Midi declined because Emperor Zhao of Han was so young. When he fell seriously ill in late 86 BCE, Huo Guang had the emperor create him Marquess of Du on his deathbed, and he died the next day. He was buried beside the mausoleum of Huo Qubing, near Emperor Wu's tomb, and his family served the throne for seven generations, until the end of the Western Han.
jin-shuren: Jin Shuren was born in Yongjing, in Hezhou in Gansu. After graduating from the Gansu provincial academy he served as principal of the provincial normal school and then entered the imperial civil service, where he came to the notice of Yang Zengxin, then district magistrate of Hezhou. When Yang became Governor of Xinjiang in 1908, Jin followed him as a county magistrate, and after the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911 he rose under Yang's absolute rule. In 1927 he was made Provincial Commissioner for Civil Affairs in Ürümqi.

When Yang was assassinated in July 1928, Jin took his place and asked the Kuomintang government in Nanking to recognise him. It did so with new titles, Provincial Chairman and Commander-in-Chief. Jin enlarged the secret police, doubled the pay of the army and police and bought new weapons. He kept the old administration but, like Yang, appointed relatives and men from his own province, replacing officials from Yunnan with Han Chinese from Gansu and above all from Hezhou; one brother, Jin Shuhsin, became commissioner for military affairs. He also introduced internal passports, which tightened control of travel and raised revenue.

His rule was marked by corruption and repression. He confiscated local lands for redistribution but gave them to his own associates, and in 1932 his officials obstructed the French Yellow Expedition. By signing an arms treaty with the Soviet Union without approval he angered the Kuomintang, which ordered the Hui general Ma Zhongying, whose troops became the 36th Division of the National Revolutionary Army, to overthrow him.

Revolts spread against his government, and in April 1933, after the First Battle of Urumqi, his White Russian troops under Colonel Pavel Pappengut turned against him and ended his rule. Sheng Shicai succeeded him. In October 1933 the Kuomintang arrested Jin; he was tried in March 1935 and sentenced to three and a half years in prison, but was pardoned on 10 October 1935 and released the next day. He died in 1941.
jin-song-wars: The two powers began as allies. After Wanyan Aguda united the Jurchen tribes and in 1115 named himself emperor of the Jin, the Song emperor Huizong sought his help against the Khitan-led Liao dynasty, hoping to recover the Sixteen Prefectures lost in 938. The Jin took the Liao capitals quickly, while Song attacks on Yanjing failed twice in 1122. By the treaty of 1123 the Song received only seven prefectures and agreed to pay the Jin 300,000 bolts of silk and 200,000 taels of silver a year.

The alliance soon broke down. Zhang Jue, a former Liao governor, turned his city over to the Song, though the treaty forbade harbouring defectors, and in 1124 Song officials asked for nine more prefectures. In November 1125 the Jin emperor Taizong ordered the attack.

Two Jin armies invaded. Kaifeng was first besieged on 31 January 1126, and after 33 days the new emperor Qinzong bought a withdrawal by ceding three prefectures; when he went back on the agreement the Jin returned and broke into the city on 9 January 1127. The Jin then tried to rule the north through puppet states, Da Chu in 1127 and Da Qi from 1130 to 1137. Gaozong, enthroned on 12 June 1127, was pursued as far as the sea in 1130, but the Song navy on the Yangtze and an insurgency in the north checked the invaders.

The peace of 1142 was broken twice. The Jin emperor Wanyan Liang invaded in 1161, was defeated at the Battle of Caishi in November and was assassinated by his own officers in December. Under the Song chancellor Han Tuozhou war was declared on 14 June 1206; the offensive failed, and the treaty of 2 November 1208 raised the tribute. Pressed by the Mongols, the Jin attacked the Song again from 1217 until a peace in 1224 ended the tribute. In 1233 the Song allied with the Mongols, and in 1234 their troops took Caizhou, where the Jin emperor Aizong killed himself.

Some two to three million Jurchens came to rule about 30 million Han Chinese in the north. Over half a million people fled south in 1126–1127. Lin'an, declared the capital in 1138, grew into a major commercial centre. The wars also spurred gunpowder weapons: the fire lance is first reported at the siege of De'an in 1132, and the iron-cased bombs the Jin used at Qizhou in 1221 are the first known hard-casing bombs. After the Jin fell the Mongols turned on the Song, which collapsed in 1279.
jind-kaur: Jind Kaur was born in Chachar, Gujranwala, the daughter of Manna Singh, overseer of the royal kennels, in an Aulakh Jat family; her elder brother was Jawahar Singh Aulakh. Her father praised her beauty and virtues to Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who married her in 1835 by sending his arrow and sword to her village. On 6 September 1838 she gave birth to her only child, Duleep Singh. After Ranjit Singh's death she and her son lived in relative obscurity at Jammu.

On 16 September 1843, after the assassination of Maharaja Sher Singh and his vizier, the army proclaimed the five-year-old Duleep Singh sovereign. Jind Kaur defended her son's rights before the regimental committees, took control of the government with the army's approval and cast off her veil. She reconstituted the Supreme Council of the Khalsa, held court in public and reviewed the troops. She raised the army's pay, fined Gulab Singh, Raja of Jammu, 68 lakh rupees, and made her brother Jawahar Singh vizier. After Jawahar had Pashaura Singh, a rival claimant, strangled in 1845, he was stabbed to death in front of her for his part in it.

After the First Anglo-Sikh War, which began in December 1845, the Treaty of Lahore left her as regent, but in December 1846 she was replaced by a Council of Regency under a British Resident. In August 1847 the Resident, Henry Lawrence, imprisoned her in Lahore Fort and then at Sheikhupura, separating her from her son, and in 1848 Sir Frederick Currie called her the rallying point of rebellion and exiled her to Chunar Fort.

On 18 April 1849 she escaped from Chunar disguised as a maid and travelled 800 km to Kathmandu, where the Prime Minister of Nepal, Jung Bahadur Rana, gave her refuge and a residence, Charburja Durbar. In 1860 the British Resident reported her much changed and blind, and she was allowed to meet her son in Calcutta on 16 January 1861 and went with him to England. She died in her sleep at Abingdon House, Kensington, on 1 August 1863. As cremation was then illegal in Britain, her body was taken to India in 1864 and cremated there, against her wish to be cremated in Lahore.
jindeok-of-silla: Her personal name was Kim Seung-man. Her father, Kim Gukban, was the youngest brother of King Jinpyeong, and her mother was Lady Wolmyeong of the Park clan; through her father she was a granddaughter of Crown Prince Dongryun, son of King Jinheung. She succeeded her cousin Queen Seondeok as the 28th ruler of Silla, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, and was the last monarch drawn from the Seonggol, the highest class of Silla's caste system. The Samguk sagi describes her as beautiful and tall, standing 7 chi.

Foreign policy was the chief concern of her seven-year reign, as Silla competed with Baekje for favour at the Tang court. With the help of General Kim Yushin she strengthened Silla's defences and greatly improved relations with Tang China, efforts that laid the foundation for the later unification of Silla, Baekje and Goguryeo. She also expanded the Pumju tax-collecting system. She wrote a poem in praise of the Tang emperor Gaozong, the Chidangtaepyeongsong.

Her era names show the shift towards China. She used Inpyeong from January to July 647, the year of her crowning, then Taehwa from July 647 to June 650, and afterwards the Tang era name Yeonghwi. Taehwa was the last era name Silla used independently.

A tomb on a hill in Gyeongju is attributed to her, but some historians doubt it, since the Samguk sagi places her burial at Saryangbu, in the opposite direction. A statue of her lower body was found at the Zhao Mausoleum, the tomb of Emperor Taizong of Tang in Xi'an. When King Jeonggang was dying in 887 and named his sister Jinseong as his heir, he justified the choice of a woman by pointing to the successful reigns of Seondeok and Jindeok.
jing-ke: Jing Ke was a youxia, a wandering knight, from the minor state of Wei, educated and skilled with the sword. When Qin annexed Wei in 239 BCE he fled to Yan, where the youxia Tian Guang introduced him to Crown Prince Dan. Qin had destroyed the state of Han in 230 BCE and Zhao in 228 BCE, and Yan was next. Dan, who had been a hostage in Qin, resolved as a last resort to send an assassin, either to kidnap King Zheng and force him to give up his conquests or to kill him, in the hope that Qin would fall into disorder. His story is told in the Biographies of Assassins in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian.

Jing Ke was to pose as an envoy offering the map of Dukang, Yan's fertile border district. The Qin general Fan Yuqi, who had fled to Yan with a price of 1,000 gold pieces on his head, agreed to kill himself so that his head could be offered as a further gift. Dan gave Jing Ke a poisoned dagger and the young killer Qin Wuyang as his companion. At the Yi River the prince and his guests saw them off in white, and Jing Ke is said to have sung that a hero who sets out never returns.

At Xianyang, Qin Wuyang froze in fear, and Jing Ke went up to the king alone. As the map was unrolled he seized the dagger and grabbed the king's sleeve, but King Zheng tore free and fled around a pillar, unable at first to draw his long sword. The physician Xia Wuju threw his medicine bag at the assassin, and the king, drawing the sword from behind his back, wounded Jing Ke in the thigh. Jing Ke threw the dagger and missed, and was stabbed eight more times before the guards killed him and Qin Wuyang.

Qin sent the general Wang Jian against Yan, and in 226 BCE Prince Dan's army was defeated at Ji. King Xi of Yan put his son to death to appease Qin, but Yan was destroyed nonetheless. The attempt has been retold in films such as The Emperor and the Assassin of 1999 and Hero of 2002, and in Mo Yan's play Our Jing Ke.
jingdezhen: Jingdezhen lies in the north-east of Jiangxi province, on the Poyang Lake Plain, bordering Anhui. It looks an unpromising place for potteries, a remote town in hilly country, but it stands close to the best deposits of petuntse, or pottery stone, in China and is surrounded by forests, mostly of pine, that fed the kilns. The Chang River carried fragile wares down to Poyang Lake and on to the Yangtze, from where they could reach the coast for export.

Kaolin, which the local kilns first used together with petuntse to make hard-paste porcelain, takes its name from the French Jesuit d'Entrecolles's rendering of the local term gaolingtu, from Gaoling, a village in Fuliang County that supplied most of the kaolin in the early and mid-Qing dynasty.

The area belonged to the state of Chu, then to the Qin and Han empires. The town was renamed Fuliang in 742 CE and Jingdezhen in 1004. In the Ming and Qing dynasties it counted as one of China's four great towns for commerce and industry, with Foshan, Hankou and Zhuxian. From the Ming period official kilns there were controlled by the emperor and made imperial porcelain in large quantity for the court and for imperial gifts; the imperial kilns stood in the centre of the town at Zhushan (Pearl Hill), with many other kilns four kilometres away at Hutian.

Its best-known wares were successively Qingbai ware in the Song and Yuan dynasties, blue and white porcelain from the 1330s, and famille rose and other famille colours under the Qing. It made a great variety of pottery for the Chinese market and for export. In 1855, during the Taiping Rebellion, Taiping forces destroyed all 9,000 kilns, which were rebuilt after the war in 1866. During the Cultural Revolution the town produced many porcelain Mao badges and statues of a seated Mao Zedong.

Jingdezhen is a prefecture-level city that kept the word zhen, town, in its name after it was upgraded in 1949, to honour its history. It was named one of China's historical and cultural cities in 1982. In 2004 it marked 1,000 years as an imperial kiln centre and as Jingdezhen. It still makes tablewares in great quantity and costlier decorative pieces, and its Ceramic Institute teaches the craft. A blue and white jar of the Yuan dynasty sold in London in 2005 for $27.7 million.
jingkang-incident: In 1120, under the Alliance Conducted at Sea, the Jin and Song agreed to destroy the Liao dynasty and divide its lands. The Jin sacked the Liao capital of Shangjing, while the Song army under Tong Guan failed to break the Liao defences, exposing its weakness. The Jin then sold the Sixteen Prefectures to the Song. Relations broke down after the Jin general Zhang Jue defected to the Song in 1123, and in the autumn of 1125 Emperor Taizong of Jin ordered a full-scale attack.

The Jin northern army under Wanyan Zongwang met little resistance and in February 1126 crossed the Yellow River and besieged Bianjing. Emperor Huizong abdicated in favour of his son Qinzong and fled. The siege ended when the Song paid a ransom and gave up Taiyuan, after Zhao Gou had been held hostage in the Jin camp.

Qinzong then dispersed many troops and generals, believing the Jin would not return, and sent a secret letter inviting two Jin envoys to join an alliance against their ruler. The envoys handed it to Taizong, who sent a larger army. Both Jin armies, under Wanyan Zongwang and Wanyan Zonghan, reached Bianjing by the middle of December 1126, and relief forces could not enter the city. Qinzong also trusted an official who claimed he could summon divine soldiers. Bianjing fell on 9 January 1127.

The Jin demanded wine, silk, gold, books, printing blocks, maps and craftsmen, plundered the palace and the imperial library, and on 20 March demoted the two emperors to commoners. Many palace women killed themselves to escape captivity, and others were killed for resisting rape. Over 14,000 people, including much of the imperial family, were marched north, and many died on the way. Women prisoners were enslaved, sold or made concubines of Jin princes.

Qinzong spent the rest of his life in captivity. Zhao Gou escaped south and refounded the dynasty with its capital at Lin'an, but the Southern Song never recovered the lost territories, which were regained only under the Ming dynasty about 200 years later. The loss of treasures, art and scrolls was without precedent. Some researchers hold that the event led later rulers to stress women's chastity, and the poem Man Jiang Hong, long attributed to Yue Fei but written in the Ming period, recalls the Humiliation of Jingkang.
jingle-bells: It is not known where or when James Lord Pierpont first composed the song that became Jingle Bells. A plaque at 19 High Street in Medford Square, Massachusetts, claims that Pierpont wrote it there in 1850, at what was then the Simpson Tavern. The researcher Kyna Hamill proposes instead that he composed it in Boston, before moving to Savannah in the autumn of 1857.

By the time of its release Pierpont was organist and music director of the Unitarian church in Savannah, Georgia, where his brother Rev. John Pierpont Jr. was minister. In August 1857 he married Eliza Jane Purse, daughter of the mayor of Savannah, and he never returned north. The song belonged to the then-popular genre of sleighing songs, and Hamill argues that its lyrics closely resemble lines from many others and that Pierpont's need for money led him to release it as a financial enterprise. It was possibly intended as a drinking song and had no original connection with Christmas.

The song was republished in 1859 by Oliver Ditson and Company of Boston as Jingle Bells; or, The One Horse Open Sleigh. The music historian James Fuld notes that jingle in the title is apparently an imperative verb, though jingle bells is commonly read as a kind of bell. In pre-automobile New England horses' harnesses carried bells to avoid collisions at blind intersections, since a sleigh in snow makes almost no noise, and the rhythm of the tune seems to imitate a trotting horse.

The first two stanzas and the chorus of the 1857 lyrics differed slightly from the modern words, and it is unknown who changed them. The 1857 version also had a substantially different chorus. The simpler modern refrain has an unknown origin but dates back at least to 1898.

The song became associated with winter and Christmas in the 1860s and 1870s. The banjoist Will Lyle recorded it on an Edison cylinder on 30 October 1889, believed to be the first Christmas record, though no copy survives. The earliest surviving vocal recording, by the Edison Male Quartette, dates from 1898. In 1943 Bing Crosby and the Andrews Sisters sold over a million copies of their recording. On 16 December 1965 the Gemini 6 astronauts Tom Stafford and Wally Schirra broadcast it from space as a prank, with a smuggled harmonica and sleigh bells. The tune is also used for the French song Vive le vent and for several German songs, none with related lyrics.
jingzhou: Jingzhou is a prefecture-level city in southern Hubei province, on the banks of the Yangtze River. It covers 14,067 square kilometres on the Jianghan Plain, in the middle reaches of the river, and is crossed by a dense network of waterways and lakes. Wuhan, the provincial capital, lies downstream to the east, and Yichang, the Three Gorges and Chongqing lie to the west. The central urban area grew out of Shashi City and Jingzhou Town, which was also known as Jiangling. The city is named after the ancient province of the same name, one of the nine provinces of ancient China, which took its name from the nearby Jing Mountains.

The area has been inhabited for roughly 5,000 to 6,000 years, and the Daxi culture lived in present-day Jingzhou. Situated in the middle Yangtze, it has been a strategic military location since ancient times. The State of Chu was founded here, and Ying, an ancient city within the borders of present-day Jingzhou, became its capital in 689 BCE and remained so for over 400 years, through the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods of the Zhou dynasty.

In the Han dynasty and the Three Kingdoms era the area was known as Nanjun. Guan Yu lost the city to Eastern Wu in the Three Kingdoms period, which gave rise to the modern phrase dàyì shī Jīngzhōu, carelessness lost Jingzhou. Under the Tang dynasty it was the southern capital, Nandu. Jiangling was later the capital of the Southern Qi and Liang dynasties. In July 1949 the People's Liberation Army took the area, and in 1994 Jiangling County and Shashi City were merged into the city of Jingsha, which was renamed Jingzhou in 1996.

Numerous sites survive from the Chu period, including the ruins of five Chu cities, 73 sites with Chu culture and more than 800 ancient tombs, among them those of 18 Chu kings. Sites from the Three Kingdoms period include the Wulin Battlefield, where the Battle of Red Cliffs took place, and the Huarong Path. The city walls are 9 metres high and 10 metres thick, with a perimeter of 10.17 kilometres. The Jingzhou Museum displays a well-preserved male corpse about 2,000 years old, together with silk and lacquerware of the Warring States period.
jinheung-of-silla: Jinheung was the 24th monarch of Silla, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His father was Galmunwang Ipjong, a son of King Jijeung, and his mother was Queen Jiso, a daughter of King Beopheung, so that Beopheung, whom he succeeded, was both his uncle and his grandfather. He came to the throne as a child, and his mother ruled as regent until he came of age; the change of era name in 551 marks the start of his own rule.

In 541 Kim Isabu was made head of military affairs, and he played a large part in Jinheung's conquests. In 551 Jinheung allied with Baekje against Goguryeo, and the two kingdoms took the Han river estuary and agreed to share it equally.

In 553, under a secret agreement with Goguryeo, Silla troops turned on the exhausted Baekje army, although Jinheung had married a daughter of King Seong of Baekje as a lesser consort. When Seong attacked in 554, he was caught in an ambush led by a Silla general and killed. Jinheung then sent Kim Isabu to conquer Daegaya, set up monuments and provinces in the new lands, and in 576 established the Hwarang, young warriors who studied arts and music as well as fighting.

Access to the Han valley gave Silla direct contact with China, from which it acquired Buddhist relics. Jinheung was a devout Buddhist who saw himself as a Chakravarti, the ideal universal ruler; temples such as Hwangnyongsa in Gyeongju were founded and monks were given roles at court. He also ordered the compilation of a history of Silla, the Guksa, which is lost but appears to have been a source for the later Samguk sagi.

Jinheung died in 576 after a reign of conquest and advancement. As Crown Prince Dongryun had died in 572, he was succeeded by his second son, Prince Saryun, who became King Jinji. His achievements laid the basis for the later unification of Korea, and he is remembered today by the Korean people as one of the most important rulers of Silla.
jinseong-of-silla: Jinseong, personal name Kim Man, was the only daughter of King Gyeongmun and Queen Munui and the younger sister of the kings Heongang and Jeonggang. Both brothers died without issue. When Jeonggang was dying in 887 he named her his heir, saying she was smart by nature and tall like a man, and justified the choice of a woman by pointing to the successful reigns of Queen Seondeok and Queen Jindeok.

A serious drought in 888 forced local governments to grant tax relief, and by 889 the state's storehouses were empty. The commissioners she sent out to collect taxes provoked banditry in the far regions, and prefectural officials and local true-bone nobles were drawn into revolt. She put down the rebellions that threatened the Silla heartland, but the kingdom began to lose its remote provinces. In the north-west Yang Gil rose, later surpassed by another leader, and rebels there and in the south-west founded kingdoms that revived Goguryeo and Baekje as Later Goguryeo and Later Baekje.

In 895 she named Kim Yo, the illegitimate son of Heongang, crown prince. In 896 bandits who had overrun the south-west raided as far as the outskirts of the capital, and in June 897 she abdicated in his favour. She died in December 897 and was buried north of Sajasa temple in Gyeongju.

The Samguk sagi, written by Confucian scholars hostile to female rule, accuses her of bringing attractive men into the palace and of an affair with the high commander Kim Wi-hong, whom the Samguk yusa says she married. The historian Richard McBride argues that Korean scholarship has blamed Silla's fall on her though the decline began before her reign. Her contemporary Ch'oe Ch'i-wŏn called her a good-hearted ruler without greed; she welcomed his ten-point memorial on reform, but the true-bone nobles who monopolised government blocked it. She ordered the Samdaemok, the first compilation of hyangga poems.
jinsha-site: Jinsha lies in Qingyang, Chengdu, on the Chengdu Plains, and the Modi River divides it into a northern and a southern part. Unlike Sanxingdui it had no city walls or moats. It was found by accident on 8 February 2001, when builders of a housing project about 5 kilometres from the centre of Chengdu uncovered a drain holding bronze, jade, stone and ivory objects; the Chengdu Municipal Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology began excavating the next day. The name also covers smaller digs made since 1995 in Huangzhongcun, over an area of 3 square kilometres.

Its pottery, plain jars and pointed-bottom saucers of the Shi'erqiao culture, dates the settlement to the late Shang and Western Zhou periods. Locus Mei Yuan was a place of religious and social events, with pits of Asian elephant tusks; one pit held tusks up to 150 centimetres long laid in 8 layers. Lan Yuan and Tiyu Gongyuan were residential quarters, the latter for wealthier people, that later became burial grounds. About 50 buildings of wattle and daub, 200 pottery kilns and 300 burial pits have been found, and the burials show no clear social hierarchy.

Among the finds are the gold sun bird, a disc of 94.2% gold with a 12-point sun and four flying birds, the smiling gold mask, 3.7 centimetres high, and 12 kneeling stone figures with bound hands, which probably represent shamans, ritual performers or sacrifices. The settlement ended abruptly; experts have proposed political upheaval, floods or earthquakes as the cause, and sediment studies support the last two.

The Jinsha Museum, built over the site in 2007 as a shelter across 6 hectares, displays the finds and has the gold sun bird as its logo. The site is on the UNESCO World Cultural Heritage Tentative List and is a Major Site Protected at the National Level.
jinshi: Although an examination system for officials first appeared under the Han dynasty, the jinshi degree itself was created under Emperor Yang of Sui. At first it was awarded in six categories, which were later consolidated into a single degree. The final examination was usually held in the palace in the imperial capital, and holders are sometimes called Imperial Scholars in English.

Under the Tang dynasty only around one to two percent of the one to two thousand candidates each year obtained the title, yet by the second half of the dynasty most senior officials were jinshi. The Song dynasty awarded more degrees, held the examinations every three years, and drew most of its senior officials from jinshi holders.

The examinations became irregular under the Yuan dynasty and were resumed by the Ming dynasty, which conferred an average of around 89 degrees a year. After the reign of Emperor Yingzong of Ming only jinshi holders could enter the Hanlin Academy. Under the Qing dynasty around 102 degrees were awarded a year.

The graduates were ranked in three classes. The first class, Jinshi Jidi, usually held only the top three: the zhuangyuan, who came top in the whole country, the bangyan in second place and the tanhua in third. The second class were called Jinshi Chushen and the third Tong Jinshi Chushen.

Korea used a related title. Under the Goryeo Dynasty anyone who passed the civil service examination was called jinsa. Under the Joseon dynasty the title went to Confucian students who passed the poetry and rhapsody section of the Saengwonjinsa-gwa; unlike the Chinese degree, it was a lower-level title that qualified its holders only for minor posts and for admission to the Sŏnggyun'gwan. In China the word zhuangyuan survives for a top scorer in the gaokao or for anyone very good at a skill.
jinshin-war: The name refers to jinshin, the ninth year of the sexagenary cycle. After the defeat of Baekje and its Yamato allies by Silla and Tang China at the Battle of Baekgang, Emperor Tenji moved his capital to the Ōmi Ōtsu Palace and tried to build a centralised state on the Tang model; he is credited with the Ōmi Code. His empress, Yamato hime, had no children, and his son Prince Ōtomo, though able, was the child of a mother of low birth, while the higher-born Prince Ōama was known for his martial prowess.

Tenji first designated Ōama but later favoured Ōtomo, who became the first Daijō-daijin in 671. Asked by the dying emperor whether he wanted the throne, Ōama, suspecting a trap, said he would become a Buddhist monk, and withdrew to Yoshino with Uno no Sarara, the future Empress Jitō.

Ōama secretly gathered weapons and soldiers, and on learning that the Ōmi court plotted to kill him he left Yoshino. Local clans dissatisfied with Tenji's reforms joined him as he passed through Uda, Iga and Suzuka, his sons escaped from Ōmi to join him, and his eldest son Prince Takechi distinguished himself. He seized strategic checkpoints such as the Fuwa Barrier to cut off reinforcements from the east, and marked his troops' clothing in red to tell them from the enemy.

The war lasted about a month. Ōtomo no Fukei took the old capital of Asuka for Ōama, while Murakuni no Oyori led the advance on Ōmi, losing a battle on the River Yasukawa but winning at Seta. The outnumbered court forces were defeated west of the Seta Bridge, and Ōtomo fled to Mount Nagara, where he strangled himself.

Ōtomo's supporters were arrested and punished as criminals, and many ancient clans were destroyed or fell into obscurity. Ōama burned the Ōmi capital, returned to Asuka, built the Asuka-Kiyomihara Palace and married Uno no Sarara. As Emperor Tenmu he was the first monarch of Japan contemporaneously documented as using the title Tennō; his predecessors received it only from later generations. The war was one of the largest conflicts in classical Japanese history.
jinul: Jinul, whose birth name was Jeong, left his family at the age of 15 and in 1173 was ordained by the Seon Master Jonghwi of the Sagulsan School, one of the nine mountain schools of Seon, receiving the name Jinul. According to his biographer he never had a permanent teacher, and the scholar Buswell observes that he made up for this lack of instruction by drawing on the Buddhist scriptures and testing their path through his own meditation.

In 1182 Jinul passed the royal examination for monks but turned down the higher administrative post it qualified him for and joined the Seon community at Bojesa in Pyongyang. When that community showed no interest in his reforms, he moved to Cheongwonsa at Changpyeong and then to Bomunsa on Hagasan. In these years of travel and study he is said to have read the entire Tripiṭaka and to have had a series of awakenings.

He sought to found a samadhi and prajñā society (Jeonghyesa), a community of disciplined, pure-minded practitioners deep in the mountains, and achieved it with the founding of Songgwangsa on Jogyesan. King Huijong honoured him by ordering Mount Songgwangsan renamed Jogyesan, and on his death in 1210 the king gave him a posthumous title. He is credited with founding the Jogye Order by working to unify the disparate sects of Korean Buddhism.

By 1209 Jinul had completed his principal work, the Excerpts from the Dharma Collection and Special Practice Record with Personal Notes, an extensive study of the schools of Chan Buddhism in China with commentaries on the writings of the Chinese monk Guifeng Zongmi. The concept of Essence-Function, central to Korean Buddhism, takes a particular form in his writings.

Jinul held that nirvana is a sublime essence present in all beings, the very nature of the Buddha, which has always been within them. Right faith, he wrote, stresses that everyone is originally a Buddha and has no need to search elsewhere. He also taught that the true nature of all people does not change and that their minds are numinous and aware even when they seem deluded.
jiroft: Jiroft is the capital of both Jiroft County and its Central District in Kerman province, 230 km south of the city of Kerman and 1,375 km south of Tehran along Road 91. It was once also called Sabzevaran, and because its land is so fertile it is known as Hend-e-Koochak, the little India. The city lies in the alluvial plain of the Halil River, on the southern outskirts of the Jebal Barez mountain chain, in a tectonically active basin at the northern end of the Bandar Abbas-Jiroft fault zone.

Two intermittent streams, the larger the Melenti River, join the Halil there. Its mean elevation is about 650 metres, and its hot desert climate makes it one of the hottest places in Iran in summer, with moderate winters.

A Jiroft culture has been postulated as an early Bronze Age archaeological culture of the third millennium BCE, in the territory of present-day Sistan and Kerman provinces. The hypothesis rests on a collection of artifacts that were confiscated in Iran and are accepted by many to come from the Jiroft area. The proposed type site is Konar Sandal, near Jiroft, and other sites associated with the culture include Shahr-e Sukhteh, Tepe Bampur, Espiedej, Shahdad, Tal-i-Iblis and Tepe Yahya. According to some, the early Bronze Age civilization found in Jiroft County is the oldest human civilization, and its script may antedate the cuneiform of Mesopotamia.

Since February 2003 archaeologists have recovered artifacts from the necropolis named Mahtoutabad, where one grave held animal bones, food offerings, ceramics and stone and copper items, pointing to a framework of about 2400 to 2200 BCE.

At two nearby mounds, Konar Sandal South and North, work from 2006 to 2009 revealed three successive settlements of the fourth millennium BCE in the south mound. Excavation resumed in 2014 and revealed artworks of complexity and beauty and artifacts showing that the society had several writing systems. The north mound held a cult building and the south mound a fortified citadel, and the two may have formed one urban settlement stretching many miles across the plateau; artifacts have been dated to between 2500 and 2200 BCE.

The census of 2016 counted 130,429 people in the city, up from 95,031 in 2006. Its local language is Jirofti, a dialect of Garmsiri, an Iranian language. The Jiroft Dam on the Halil River, 40 km north-east of the city and operating since 1992, irrigates 14,200 hectares downstream and generates electricity. Jiroft is served by Jiroft Airport.
jiuquan: Jiuquan occupies the westernmost part of Gansu, bordering Zhangye to the east, Qinghai to the south, Xinjiang to the west, and Inner Mongolia and Mongolia to the north. Its territory measures about 680 km from east to west and 550 km from north to south, and its built-up area lies mostly in Suzhou District, about 1,500 metres above sea level. The climate is a cold desert one, with long cold winters, hot and somewhat dry summers, and clear skies throughout the year. The legend behind its name tells that the young Han general Huo Qubing, after a victory over the Xiongnu, poured a vat of precious alcohol into a local creek to share its taste with his troops.

The place was founded in 111 BCE as Fulu, an outpost in the Hexi Corridor near the Yumen Pass on the overland Silk Road. It was a Han prefecture and under the Eastern Han an active military garrison. Under the Sui it became the seat of Su Prefecture and so took the name Suzhou; under the Tang the prefecture was renamed Jiuquan Commandery, and Jiuquan County was established in 624. In 763 the Tibetan Empire occupied it, after which it was controlled by the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom, and in 1028 it was seized by Xixia.

In the Yuan dynasty Suzhou Lu was established under Gansu Province, and the city sometimes served as the provincial capital. It was a great centre of the rhubarb trade as well as a guardian of Silk Road traffic.

Under the Ming the Portuguese Jesuit missionary Bento de Góis was robbed at Suzhou and died there in 1607, during the journey that finally established that Cathay and China were one country. Meng Qiaofang took the city from Ding Guodong in 1649. The Hui under Ma Wenlu held it during the Dungan Revolt, and it was completely destroyed by the time the Qing general Zuo Zongtang recovered it in 1873, but it was swiftly rebuilt.

Jiuquan is a prefecture-level city of Gansu, served by China National Highway 312 and the Lanzhou-Xinjiang railway, and it is known within China as the first site of rhubarb cultivation. The Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, built in 1958, lies more than 100 km away, in the neighbouring Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. China's first crewed spaceflight, Shenzhou 5, was launched from it on 15 October 2003 with the astronaut Yang Liwei.
jixia-academy: The academy stood outside the western gate of Linzi, a gate named for the harvest god Ji or Hou Ji. Passages in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian are usually read as crediting King Xuan of Qi with its foundation, around 318 BCE, but the writer Xu Gan credited it to King Xuan's grandfather, Duke Huan of Tian Qi, and Sima Qian's text is consistent with King Xuan having restored rather than founded it.

It has been described as the first recorded case of a state acting as patron of scholarship from the conviction that this was a proper task of the state. Others argue that the project, and the Huanglao political theories it fostered, served to bolster the legitimacy of the Tian clan after it had displaced the Jiang dynasty of Qi.

Scholars came from great distances, drawn by mansions, stipends and honours. The chief scholar held the rank of Grand Prefect, other leaders were called Master and treated as high ministers of state, and they were exempt from corvée labour. Discourses on Salt and Iron, of 81 BCE, speaks of more than a thousand scholars disputing there, and says Mencius, Chunyu Kun and others neglected the offices they were given in favour of speeches on affairs of state.

Those associated with it include the Taoist philosophers Shen Dao and Peng Meng and possibly Zhuangzi, Zou Yan of the School of Naturalists, Yin Wen, a forerunner of the School of Names, the Mohist Song Xing, and the Confucian philosophers Mencius and Xun Zi. It was the first centre of the Huanglao school and was involved in compiling Neiye, the Inward Training chapter of the Guanzi, the oldest received writing on the cultivation of qi.

The academy thrived until the reign of King Min and was scattered in 284 BCE, when Yan sacked Linzi. Sima Qian credited its example with inspiring the academies of the Four Lords: Lord Mengchang in Qi, Lord Pingyuan in Zhao, Lord Chunshen in Chu and Lord Xinling in Wei. In Qin the chancellor Lü Buwei supported thousands of scholars between 250 and 238 BCE.

In February 2022 archaeologists announced the discovery of its ruins in Zibo, Shandong, after five years of excavation. They found four rows of building foundations on a site of nearly 40,000 square metres, shaped roughly like a right-angled trapezoid.
jizya: Jizya, from an Arabic word probably derived from the Middle Persian gazītak, a tax on the lower classes of Sasanian Persia, was levied on non-Muslim subjects of a state governed by Islamic law. The Muslim Arab conquerors largely kept the taxation systems of the Sasanian and Byzantine empires, and its origins are complex because the system arising from the conquests was not uniform but resulted from a variety of agreements. William Montgomery Watt traced it to a pre-Islamic practice in which a powerful Arabian tribe protected weaker neighbours for tribute, refunded if protection failed.

Jews and Christians in parts of Arabia began paying tribute called jizya during Muhammad's lifetime, at first as a share of produce and fixed goods rather than a poll tax. In the first century of expansion jizya and kharaj were each used for individual taxes, land taxes and collective tribute.

The Quran and the hadiths mention jizya without a limiting rate. Classical jurists understood it as payment for the protection the ruler gave, for exemption from military service and for permission to practise another faith with some communal autonomy. Most required it only of adult, free, sane, able-bodied men, and exempted women, children, the old, the sick, monks, slaves and non-Muslim foreigners staying temporarily; dhimmis who served in the army did not pay, and in some accounts the poor paid nothing. The rate was not fixed. Under Harun al-Rashid the jurist Abu Yusuf set amounts of 48 dirhams for the richest, 24 for those of moderate wealth and 12 for craftsmen and labourers, and payment could be made in kind.

The Bayt al-Mal, the public treasury, collected it, and in later times its revenues were commonly allocated to scholars. Jurists differed on its purpose: some saw a payment for protection, others an incentive to convert, and by the end of the 8th century some regarded it as a mark of inferior status.

In the Indian subcontinent Islamic rulers imposed jizya from the 11th century, and the Delhi Sultanate expanded it. After the Norman conquest of Sicily a poll tax on the Muslim minority, locally called gisia, continued the jizya of the earlier Muslim rulers of southern Italy.

In the Ottoman Empire jizya from Christian and Jewish communities was among the main sources of tax income; in Lebanon and Egypt it was paid by the community collectively as maqtu. In Persia the Zoroastrian minority paid it until 1884, when pressure from the Persian Zoroastrian Amelioration Fund led the Qajar government to remove it. It was eliminated in Algeria and Tunisia in the 19th century, with French colonisation, and continued in Morocco until the first decade of the 20th century. No Muslim state imposes it now.
joab: Joab was the son of Zeruiah, a sister of King David, according to 1 Chronicles 2:15-16. Josephus gives his father's name as Suri. His name is theophoric, formed from the name of Yahweh and the Hebrew word for father, and means Yahweh is the Father. He had two brothers, Abishai and Asahel. Asahel was killed in combat by Abner, and Joab later took revenge by murdering Abner against David's wishes, shortly after David and Abner had secured peace between the House of David and the House of Saul.

The Hebrew Bible states that Joab killed Abner to avenge the blood of his brother Asahel. Josephus tells it differently: Joab had forgiven Abner, who had slain Asahel honourably in combat, but killed him as a threat to his own rank after Abner had switched to David's side and given David control over the tribe of Benjamin.

After Joab led the assault on the fortress of Mount Zion, David made him captain of his army. He led the army against Aram, Ammon, Moab and Edom, and the Hebrew Bible says he colluded with David in the murder of Uriah. During the rebellion of David's son Absalom, which forced David to flee with only his most trusted men, Joab commanded David's forces. David ordered that none of his men should harm Absalom, but when Absalom was reported caught alive in a tree, Joab and his men killed him.

Hearing of David's grief, Joab confronted the king, who followed his advice to make a public appearance to encourage his troops. David later replaced him as commander with his nephew Amasa, but Joab treacherously killed Amasa and regained his position.

Late in David's reign Joab and other commanders began questioning the king's judgment. As David neared the end of his reign, Joab gave his allegiance to David's eldest living son, Adonijah, rather than to Solomon, who became king. On the brink of death David told Solomon to have Joab killed, citing his past betrayals and the blood he was guilty of. Joab fled to the Tent of the Tabernacle, where Adonijah had earlier found refuge, and told Benaiah that he would die there. Benaiah killed him on Solomon's orders, replaced him as commander and Joab was buried in the wilderness.
The ATS Bible Dictionary describes Joab as a valiant warrior and an able general whose influence on public affairs was often exerted for good, but as a man imperious, revengeful and unscrupulous.
joachim-ernest-prince-of-anhalt: Joachim Ernest was born in Dessau on 21 October 1536, the second son of John V, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, and of Margaret, daughter of Joachim I Nestor, Elector of Brandenburg. He was a member of the House of Ascania. Educated under his father's supervision, he was admitted to the University of Wittenberg on 1 February 1549, at the age of thirteen, and studied there with the theologian Georg Helt among others.

On his father's death in 1550 he inherited Anhalt-Zerbst together with his brothers Karl I and Bernhard VII. The deaths of his uncles brought the brothers Anhalt-Plötzkau in 1553 and Anhalt-Dessau in 1561, and in 1562 his cousin Wolfgang gave up Anhalt-Köthen in his favour. When Bernhard VII died in 1570, Joachim Ernest became sole ruler of all the Anhalt lands, united for the first time since their first partition in 1252, and he made Dessau the seat of his government.

He governed as a Renaissance prince who supported the arts. He sent his sons with their tutors on educational journeys across Europe and had Tobias Hübner, the son of his chancellor, describe the knights' games held at the Dessau court. In 1572 he issued the Regional Legal Code of Anhalt, and in 1582 he founded the Francisceum High School in Zerbst. He was a committed supporter of the Reformation and of the Huguenots.

He married twice: in 1560 Agnes of Barby-Mühlingen, with whom he had six children, and in 1571 Eleonore, daughter of Christoph, Duke of Württemberg, with whom he had ten. He died in Dessau on 6 December 1586. Since succession in Anhalt did not follow primogeniture, his seven sons shared the government of the territories until 1603, when the five surviving sons divided the lands among themselves.
joachim-ernst-duke-of-anhalt: Joachim Ernst Wilhelm Karl Albrecht Leopold Friedrich Moritz Erdmann was born on 11 January 1901 in Dessau, then the capital of the duchy. He was the fourth child and eldest surviving son of Prince Eduard of Anhalt and Princess Louise Charlotte of Saxe-Altenburg, and a grandson of Duke Friedrich I of Anhalt. He was the only German monarch born in the 20th century.

He succeeded his father on 13 September 1918, with his uncle Prince Aribert of Anhalt as regent because of his age. Aribert abdicated in his name on 12 November 1918, so that Joachim Ernst was the last ruler of a constituent state of the German Empire to come to the throne before the German monarchies were abolished. The abdication ended the rule of the House of Ascania in central Germany, which had lasted since the 11th century. The family kept Ballenstedt Castle in the Harz Mountains as private property, and all his children were born there.

Joachim Ernst joined the Nazi Party in 1939 but later became a critic of Nazi rule; arrested in the winter of 1944, he spent three months in the Dachau concentration camp. He welcomed the fall of the regime and stayed in the Soviet occupation zone, believing his record as an anti-Nazi would protect him. On 31 August 1945 the NKVD arrested him in a general round-up of landed gentry and seized his estate of 20,000 hectares. He died on 18 February 1947 in NKVD special camp Nr. 2, the former Buchenwald concentration camp, near Weimar.

His first marriage, to Elisabeth Strickrodt, a daughter of an opera singer, in 1927 ended in divorce in 1929 without children. In 1929 he married Editha Marwitz von Stephani, with whom he had five children. After his death the headship of the ducal house was disputed between his elder son, Prince Friedrich, and his brother, Prince Eugen.
joachim-ii-hector: Joachim II was born in Cölln on 13 January 1505, the eldest son of Joachim I Nestor, Elector of Brandenburg, and Elizabeth of Denmark, Norway and Sweden. He took the cognomen Hector from the Trojan prince for his prowess. He was educated at the imperial court. His father made him sign an inheritance contract promising to remain Roman Catholic, partly to help Joachim Nestor's younger brother Albert, Archbishop-Elector of Mainz, who had borrowed heavily from the Fugger bank to pay the Holy See for his offices. Repayment depended on selling indulgences to Catholic believers in Brandenburg, and had Joachim refused, he would likely have been passed over in the line of inheritance.

Joachim's first wife, Magdalena of Saxony, died in 1534, and in 1535 he married Hedwig, daughter of King Sigismund I the Old of Poland, promising not to make her change her religion. After the deaths of his father in 1535 and of Sigismund in 1548 he turned gradually to the Reformation. On 1 November 1539 he received Communion under both kinds in St. Nicholas' Church in Spandau. He promulgated a conservative church order that was Lutheran in doctrine but kept the episcopate, much of the Mass in Latin, religious plays and feast days, avoiding open confrontation with his ally, Emperor Charles V.

In early 1539, at the Fürstentag in Frankfurt, Philipp Melanchthon revealed that the anti-Jewish pogroms of 1510 in Brandenburg had rested on a feigned host desecration. Josel von Rosheim pleaded with Joachim, who allowed the Jews to settle in Brandenburg again on 25 June 1539. Joachim spent great sums on hunting and on animal fights and kept eleven alchemists at court over ten years, so that by 1540 he was over 600,000 thalers in debt, which he tried to pay off by confiscating church property and raising taxes. In 1542 he led an army for Ferdinand of Habsburg at the Siege of Buda, but retreated, and was defeated again at the Siege of Pest.

In 1569 Joachim paid his brother-in-law, King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland, for a deed of enfeoffment making himself and his heirs successors to Ducal Prussia if the Prussian Hohenzollern line died out. He died on 3 January 1571 in Köpenick Palace, which he had built in 1558, and was succeeded by his son John George.
joachim-murat: Joachim Murat was born on 25 March 1767 at La Bastide-Fortunière in Guyenne, in the present-day department of Lot, the youngest of six surviving children. His father, Pierre Murat-Jordy, was an affluent yeoman, innkeeper and postmaster who also served as steward for the Talleyrand family. His parents intended him for the church, and he studied at the College of Saint-Michel at Cahors and then at the Lazarist seminary in Toulouse. In February 1787 he left the seminary, either expelled or, as others say, having run away with a girl, and enlisted in a cavalry regiment, the Chasseurs des Ardennes.

An ardent Republican, Murat served in the revolutionary army and, at the royalist rising of 13 Vendémiaire in October 1795, brought the cannons of the Camp des Sablons to the centre of Paris, which let General Napoleon Bonaparte save the National Convention. He went with Bonaparte to northern Italy in 1796, commanded the cavalry in Egypt, where he led the charge that broke the Ottoman line at Abukir on 25 July 1799, and played a pivotal role in the coup of 18 Brumaire. He married Caroline Bonaparte in a civil ceremony on 20 January 1800.
Napoleon made him a Marshal of the Empire on 18 May 1804 and Admiral of the Empire in 1805. He fought at Ulm, Austerlitz, Jena and Eylau, where he led a massed cavalry charge against the Russians.

Murat was Grand Duke of Berg and Duke of Cleves from 15 March 1806 and King of Naples from 1 August 1808. In the Russian campaign of 1812 he was the best cavalry commander of the Grande Armée at Smolensk and Borodino, though he showed little concern for the horses, which starved and tired on the long marches. After the Battle of Leipzig he reached a secret agreement with the Allies to save his throne.

When Napoleon returned from exile, Murat changed sides again, and on 15 March 1815 Naples declared war on Austria. His army of about 45,000 invaded the Papal States and Tuscany, but he was defeated at Occhiobello and decisively at Tolentino on 2 and 3 May, and returned to Naples on 18 May. After Waterloo he fled to Corsica and tried to invade Calabria with about 200 men. He was captured, sentenced to death and shot at Pizzo Calabro on 13 October 1815. Murat and Caroline had four children.
joachim-vadian: Vadian was born in St. Gallen into a family of wealthy and influential linen merchants. After school in his home town he moved to Vienna at the end of 1501 and studied in the university's faculty of arts, in particular under Conrad Celtis and Matthias Qualle. There he took the Latin name Joachimus Vadianus, as many humanists did in admiration of the classical authors. He escaped the bubonic plague of 1506/07 by moving to Villach, where he taught and studied music, and on a study trip through northern Italy he met the Irish scholar Mauritius Hibernicus at Padua.

Vadian completed his Master of Arts in 1509. From 1512 he held the chair of poetry at the University of Vienna, known for his Latin poems; after a visit to Buda in 1513, Emperor Maximilian I named him poeta laureatus, and in 1516 he became a dean of the university. He then studied medicine and the sciences, geography and history above all, under Georg Tannstetter, and graduated as a doctor of medicine in 1517. In 1518, back in Switzerland, he climbed Pilatus near Lucerne, the first documented ascent of the mountain.

In St. Gallen he became city physician and in 1519 married Martha Grebel, sister of the future Anabaptist leader Conrad Grebel. He joined the city council in 1521 in succession to his father, Leonhard. A friend of Huldrych Zwingli, he took up the reformed teaching from 1522, though he had no theological schooling, and as mayor from 1526 he kept St. Gallen Protestant even after the victory of the Catholic cantons in the Second War of Kappel.

His works include a history of literature, De poetica et carminis ratione (1518), a chronicle of the abbots of the abbey of St. Gallen (1529), the Epitome trium terrae partium of 1534, a world atlas that was one of the first to include America, and a treatise of 1535 on the eucharist as a symbol. He died in St. Gallen in 1551 and left his large library to the city, where it became the nucleus of the cantonal library, the Vadiana.
joan-countess-of-toulouse: Joan was the daughter of Raymond VII, Count of Toulouse, by his first wife, Sancha of Aragon. In 1225, at the age of five, she was betrothed to Hugh, eldest son and heir of Hugh X of Lusignan and of Isabella, Countess of Angoulême and dowager queen of England, but the engagement was soon broken.

The Treaty of Paris, signed on 12 April 1229, required her marriage to Alphonse, Count of Poitiers, and a papal dispensation for their kinship in the fourth degree is dated 26 June of that year. She was then brought up at the French royal court. The date of the marriage itself is uncertain; both 1234 and 1241 have been suggested, the earlier being thought more likely.

Joan accompanied her husband on the Seventh Crusade in 1249. Her father died that year, and she succeeded him as ruler of Toulouse, with Alphonse as co-ruler. While they were away, her mother-in-law installed a governor for them. The couple took control of their lands in October 1250 and made their formal entry as countess and count of Toulouse in May 1251, after which they confirmed the governor and left again; they seldom visited the county. She went with Alphonse on the Eighth Crusade in 1270.

Joan died on 25 August 1271, four days after Alphonse. In her will of 23 June 1270 she named as her universal heiress Philippa de Lomagne, her closest relative, a great-granddaughter of Constance of Toulouse, half-sister of Raymond VII. The Parlement invalidated the will in 1274. One bequest in Alphonse's will was allowed: the lands of the Comtat Venaissin passed to the Holy See, which held them as papal territory until 1791.
joan-i-of-navarre: Joan was born on 14 January 1273 at Bar-sur-Seine in Champagne, the daughter of King Henry I of Navarre and Blanche of Artois. When her father died the following year she became Countess of Champagne and Queen of Navarre, and her mother Blanche acted as guardian and regent in Navarre. Foreign and Navarrese powers sought to exploit the heiress's minority and the supposed weakness of a female regent, so Blanche took Joan to the court of Philip III of France in 1274. By the Treaty of Orléans in 1275 Joan was betrothed to one of Philip's sons, and she grew up with the future Philip IV. It is uncertain whether she ever lived in Navarre as a child.

Joan married the future Philip IV on 16 August 1284, at the age of 11, and became queen consort of France a year later. Their three surviving sons all ruled as kings of France, and their daughter Isabella became queen consort of England. Philip is reported to have loved and respected her deeply, and in 1294 he named her regent of France in case his son succeeded him as a minor. She never visited Navarre, which French governors ruled in her name; they were unpopular, but loyalty to her was not questioned. She came no closer than Carcassonne in 1300.

In Champagne, a richer and more strategic county, she was an active ruler who visited regularly. In 1297 she raised and led an army against Count Henry III of Bar when he invaded Champagne, and she captured him and had him imprisoned while Philip took no part. She also brought a case against Bishop Guichard of Troyes, whom she accused of stealing funds from Champagne and from her mother by fraud. In 1305 she founded the College of Navarre in Paris.

Joan died in 1305, most likely from complications of childbirth. In 1308 Bishop Guichard of Troyes was arrested and accused of killing her by witchcraft, and he was released in 1313. She was buried at the Cordeliers Convent in Paris. Her eldest son became Louis I of Navarre in 1305 and king of France in 1314 as Louis X, and Philip V and Charles IV also ruled both kingdoms. Through her marriage Navarre and Champagne passed under the French crown.
joan-ii-of-navarre: Joan was born on 28 January 1312, the only surviving child of Louis I of Navarre and Margaret of Burgundy. Her paternity was in doubt because in 1314 her mother was arrested with her sisters-in-law on charges of adultery with two knights, the brothers Philip and Walter of Aunay. The brothers were executed and Margaret died in prison at Château Gaillard. Joan's father became Louis X of France later that year, and on his deathbed in 1316 he declared Joan his legitimate daughter.

After the death of Louis's posthumous son John, Philip the Tall was crowned Philip V in January 1317, and the Estates-General declared that a woman could not inherit the French crown. Her uncle Odo IV of Burgundy fought for her claim to Champagne and Brie, but Charles of Valois defeated her supporters. In March 1318 she was promised in marriage to her cousin Philip of Évreux, and the marriage took place on 18 June 1318.

Philip V was succeeded in 1322 by Charles IV, whom most Navarrese lords refused to acknowledge. After Charles died on 1 February 1328 and his daughter Blanche was born, the direct male Capetian line was extinct. Philip of Valois was crowned in France on 29 May, and the general assembly of Navarre asked Joan to take control of the kingdom as her inheritance. In July Philip VI acknowledged her right to Navarre, and she and her husband gave up Champagne and Brie in exchange for the counties of Longueville, Mortain and Angoulême.

Joan and Philip were crowned at Pamplona on 5 March 1329. Of eighty-five surviving decrees of their joint rule, forty-one were issued in both names, thirty-eight by Philip alone and six by Joan alone. They punished those responsible for anti-Jewish riots, repaired fortresses and supported irrigation near Tudela. They lived mostly in their French domains, leaving French governors in charge. A border dispute over the Monastery of Fitero led to war with Castille in 1335, ended by a treaty on 28 February 1336.

Philip died in September 1343. In 1346, during the Hundred Years War, Joan made a truce with the Earl of Lancaster that let Edward III's troops cross her county of Angoulême in return for protection of her lands. She died of the Black Death on 6 October 1349 and was buried at the Basilica of St Denis, her heart in Paris beside her husband's.
The couple had nine children. Their son Charles succeeded as count of Évreux and king of Navarre, and their daughter Blanche became the second wife of Philip VI of France.
joan-of-arc: Joan was born c. 1412 in Domrémy, a small village in the Meuse valley. Her date of birth is unknown. Her parents were Jacques d'Arc and Isabelle Romée, and her father was a peasant farmer with about 20 hectares of land, who also collected taxes and headed the local watch. Joan was not taught to read and write and dictated her letters.

She grew up during the Hundred Years' War, in a France divided between Armagnacs and Burgundians since the Duke of Burgundy had the Duke of Orléans assassinated in 1407. Domrémy's people were loyal to the Armagnac cause. After a raid in 1425 in which cattle were stolen, Joan had her first vision. She later testified that she saw Saint Michael, and later Saint Margaret and Saint Catherine, and that she swore a vow of virginity to these voices.

Joan met Charles VII at Chinon in late February or early March 1429, when she was seventeen and he was twenty-six. Theologians at Poitiers declared her a good Catholic, and women directed by Yolande of Aragon verified her virginity. Charles commissioned plate armor for her, and she designed her own banner.

She reached Orléans on 29 April 1429. At first a figurehead for morale with no formal command, she gained the support of the Armagnac troops and sometimes advised their commanders. On 4 May her arrival rallied soldiers retreating from the bastille of Saint-Loup, and they took it. After the victory at Patay, Charles was crowned at Reims with Joan at his side. The sieges of Paris in September and La Charité in November failed, and her role in these defeats reduced the court's faith in her.
