Burgundian troops captured Joan on 23 May 1430, and she was handed to the English in November. Her trial for heresy opened at Rouen on 9 January 1431 under Bishop Pierre Cauchon. She was accused of wearing men's clothes, of acting on demonic visions and of refusing to submit to the church. The trial was politically motivated: her claims, if unchallenged, would undermine the English claim to the French throne. She was burned at the stake on 30 May 1431.

A court reinvestigated the trial in 1456 and overturned the verdict, declaring it tainted by deceit and procedural errors. Joan became a national symbol of France after the French Revolution. She was canonized in 1920 and, two years later, declared one of the patron saints of France.
joan-of-england-queen-of-sicily: Joan was born in October 1165 at the Château d'Angers in Anjou, the seventh child of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine. As an infant she travelled with her mother's household through France and England, and much of her childhood was spent at Fontevraud Abbey alongside her younger brother John. Her education prepared her for a dynastic marriage. In 1174, after the Revolt of 1173–1174, her father removed her from Fontevraud and sent her to Salisbury and later Winchester, where her mother was under house arrest.

In 1176 William II of Sicily sent ambassadors to ask for her hand, seeking an alliance with Henry II, who was then one of Europe's pre-eminent figures. Henry raised money for the journey and dowry by taxing his English subjects. Joan sailed from Southampton in late August and reached Palermo in late January. On 13 February 1177 she married William and was crowned Queen of Sicily in Palermo Cathedral. She had no surviving heir, though a rumoured son Bohemond, born in 1181 or 1182, is said to have died in infancy if he existed. William did not annul the marriage and named his aunt Constance as heir.

After William died in November 1189, his cousin Tancred seized Sicily, took the lands William had given Joan and put her under house arrest at Zisa in Palermo, in retaliation for her backing of Constance. Richard I arrived in Italy in 1190 on his way to the Holy Land and demanded her return and her dowry. He seized a monastery and the castle of La Bagnara and subdued Messina, and Tancred finally agreed. In 1191 Joan sailed with Richard's bride, Berengaria of Navarre, and the fleet was scattered by a storm. Richard rescued them near Cyprus and sent them on to Acre. He proposed marrying her to Saladin's brother Al-Adil, but high-ranking priests opposed the plan.

In October 1196 Joan married Raymond VI, Count of Toulouse, at Rouen, as his fourth wife. She was the mother of Raymond VII, born in July 1197, and of a daughter, Joan, born in 1198. The Chronicle of Guillaume de Puylaurens says she took arms against the lords of Saint-Felix and besieged their castle at Les Cassés, then hurried to her brother Richard, only to find he had died. She was admitted to Fontevrault Abbey and veiled a nun on her deathbed, and died in childbirth in 1199, aged thirty-three. Her son lived long enough to be baptised Richard. She was buried at Rouen and later re-interred at Fontevrault.
joan-of-penthievre: Sometimes called Joan the Lame, she was the only child of Guy of Penthièvre, brother of John III, Duke of Brittany, and Joan of Avaugour. Her claim rested on the right of representation: whether a child, of either sex, could take the place of a deceased parent, so that she inherited the rights of her father as the second brother of the late duke. Her rival was her half-uncle John, Count of Montfort, a son of the second marriage of Arthur II, Duke of Brittany, to Yolande of Dreux, whom John III had tried to bar from the succession.

A marriage with John of Eltham, Earl of Cornwall, brother of King Edward III of England, was discussed in December 1335 but apparently came to nothing. In 1337 she was betrothed to Charles of Blois in Paris, and the couple were living together by 1338 or 1339.

When John III died in 1341, Joan and Charles took over the rule of the duchy, and Charles was allowed to do homage to King Philip VI of France by the arrêt of Conflans on 7 September 1341. Most of the local nobility and administration appeared to support them, but John of Montfort kept his claim, and after his death in 1345 his widow, Joanna of Flanders, defended the rights of their son John IV. Charles was taken prisoner by the English in 1347, with Thomas Dagworth as his official captor, and was released for a ransom of about half a million écus before resuming the war.

The First Treaty of Guérande of 1365 gave Joan a substantial pension, paid until 1372, the ducal title for life and her family lands of Penthièvre and Avaugour free of homage, while women were now formally barred from inheriting the duchy. When King Charles V of France tried to annex Brittany in 1379, her supporters and those of the Montfort line together invited John IV back from exile in England. On 2 May 1381 she ratified the Second Treaty of Guérande, which renewed the first.

Joan died on 10 September 1384 and was buried in the church of the Friars Minor of Guingamp. Her descendants, among them her son John I, Count of Penthièvre, never regained the duchy, though they kept up their conflicts with the House of Montfort and at times held high office in Brittany under the kings of France.
joanna-duchess-of-brabant: Joanna was born on 24 June 1322, the daughter of John III, Duke of Brabant, and Marie d'Évreux. In 1334 she married William II, Count of Hainaut, who later died in battle; their only son, William, died young, and with him the plan of uniting their territories. Her second husband was Wenceslaus of Luxemburg, with whom she ruled Brabant from 1355.

The Joyous Entry (Blijde Inkomst) of January 1356, seen as the foundation of the rule of law in Brabant, was meant to give Joanna and her consort a peaceful entry into their capital and to settle the inheritance on her natural heirs, her sisters, whom the burghers of Brabant preferred to the House of Luxembourg. It soon became a dead letter. Later in 1356 Louis II of Flanders, husband of Joanna's younger sister Margaret, who considered himself duke by right of his wife, invaded and overran the duchy.

Joanna and Wenceslaus signed the Treaty of Ath, ceding Mechelen and Antwerp to Louis, and by August 1356 had called on Emperor Charles IV for armed support. At Maastricht the emperor, the parties and representatives of the towns agreed to cancel certain terms of the Joyous Entry to satisfy the Luxembourg dynasty. The duchy's position worsened again when Wenceslaus was defeated and captured at the Battle of Baesweiler in 1371.

Joanna died on 1 December 1406. By agreement the duchy passed to Antoine, the second son of her niece Margaret III, Countess of Flanders. Her tomb in the Carmelite church in Brussels was erected in the late 1450s and paid for in 1459 by Philip the Good, her sister's great-grandson. It was destroyed in the French Revolutionary Wars; the historian Lorne Campbell reconstructed its appearance from drawings and descriptions and concluded that it was an afterthought, an inexpensive piece of propaganda for Philip's dynastic rights.
joanna-i-of-naples: Joanna was the eldest surviving daughter of Charles, Duke of Calabria, only surviving son of King Robert of Naples, and Marie of Valois, sister of Philip VI of France. Her father died in 1328, and three years later Robert named Joanna his heir and ordered his vassals to swear fealty to her. He arranged her marriage to Andrew, younger son of his nephew King Charles I of Hungary, who also hoped to secure the inheritance for Andrew. On his deathbed in 1343, however, Robert named Joanna sole heir and set up a regency council to govern until her twenty-first birthday.

After Robert died on 20 January 1343, Andrew was knighted and the marriage consummated, but the couple rarely met except at ceremonies. Petrarch described them as two lambs entrusted to a multitude of wolves. Andrew's mother, Elizabeth of Poland, came to Naples in the summer of 1343 to press for his coronation, which Joanna delayed. Joanna's sister Maria was betrothed to Charles of Durazzo in March 1343, and he then abducted her and had her secretly married, to the outrage of the dowager queen Catherine of Valois.

Andrew was murdered in 1345, and the Hungarians openly accused Joanna when she announced she would marry Louis of Taranto. She married him on 22 August 1347 without the papal dispensation their close kinship required. King Louis I of Hungary invaded to avenge his brother, and a further Hungarian offensive reached the walls of Naples in 1350. Louis of Taranto took control of the government and was recognised by Pope Clement VI as co-ruler on 23 March 1352. After his death Joanna married James IV of Majorca in 1363 and later Otto of Brunswick-Grubenhagen on 25 March 1376, but none of her children survived her.

During the Western Schism Joanna supported the Avignon papacy, and Pope Urban VI declared her a heretic and usurper on 11 May 1380. She had arranged the marriage of her niece Margaret of Durazzo to Charles of Durazzo to settle the succession, but Charles captured and imprisoned her. She was moved to the castle of Muro Lucano and killed on 27 July 1382. Charles claimed she died of natural causes; two early sources say she was strangled or smothered, and no eyewitness account survives. Excommunicated, she could not be buried in consecrated ground, and her body was thrown into a well at Santa Chiara in Naples.

The kingdom was left to decades of wars of succession. Giovanni Boccaccio wrote her biography in his De mulieribus claris, defending her right to rule, and Alexandre Dumas the elder made her the subject of a romance.
joanna-ii-of-naples: Joanna was born at Zara, present-day Zadar, the daughter of Charles III of Naples and Margaret of Durazzo. In the autumn of 1401 Joanna married her first husband, William, Duke of Austria, in Vienna. They had no children, and William died in 1406. Joanna then took a lover, Pandolfello Piscopo, called Alopo, whom she appointed Grand Chamberlain, the first of several powerful favourites.

In 1414 Joanna succeeded her brother Ladislaus. In early 1415 she was engaged to John, a son of King Ferdinand I of Aragon, but the betrothal was annulled, and on 10 August 1415 she married James II, Count of La Marche, to gain French support. When he did not receive the promised title of Prince of Taranto, he had Alopo killed, forced Joanna to name him King of Naples and imprisoned her in her apartments, from which the nobles released her. A riot in 1416 forced him to send back his French administrators and renounce his title, and he later left Naples for France. Meanwhile Joanna had begun her relationship with Sergianni Caracciolo, who later gained overwhelming power over the court.

She was crowned Queen of Sicily and Naples on 28 October 1419, but her relationship with Pope Martin V worsened, and he called in Louis III of Anjou, who invaded Campania in 1420. Joanna turned to King Alfonso V of Aragon, promising him the hereditary title to Naples, and he entered Naples in July 1421. After Alfonso had Caracciolo arrested in May 1423 and besieged the Castel Capuano, Joanna declared the adoption null and void and named Louis her heir. Alfonso returned to Spain. In August 1432 Caracciolo, who had become ruler in all but name, was stabbed in his room in the Castel Capuano, after Joanna had plotted his assassination.

The last years of the reign were relatively peaceful. Louis took up residence in Calabria but died in 1434, and Joanna designated his younger brother René of Anjou as heir. She died in Naples on 2 February 1435 and was buried in the Church of the Santissima Annunziata. With her death the senior line of the Capetian House of Anjou became extinct, and she was succeeded by René. Her reputation for scandalous relationships gave rise in popular tradition to lurid tales, among them a legend of a trapdoor in the Castel Nuovo through which used lovers were thrown to sea monsters, later a crocodile, though the legend is likely fictional.
joanna-la-beltraneja: Joanna was born on 28 February 1462 at the Royal Alcazar of Madrid, the daughter of Henry IV of Castile and Joan of Portugal, whom he had married in 1455. On 9 May 1462 she was proclaimed heir to the throne and created Princess of Asturias. In 1464 a faction of nobles led by Juan Pacheco, Alfonso Carrillo de Acuña and Pedro Girón, angered by the royal favourite Beltrán de la Cueva's appointment as master of the Order of Santiago, circulated rumours that Joanna was his child. Her opponents began to call her la Beltraneja, a mocking reference to her supposed illegitimacy, and later also argued that her parents had lacked the papal dispensation needed for their marriage.

Civil war broke out in 1465, when the rebels deposed Henry in effigy and crowned his half-brother Alfonso. After Alfonso died in 1468, Henry and his half-sister Isabella agreed the Treaty of the Bulls of Guisando in September 1468, naming Isabella heir instead of Joanna. The Mendoza family rallied to Joanna's cause. Isabella married Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469 without Henry's consent, and in October 1470 Joanna was again proclaimed legitimate heir and betrothed to Charles, Duke of Berry, who in the end withdrew. She was then promised to her uncle, King Afonso V of Portugal.

When Henry died in 1474, some nobles recognised Joanna as queen and others preferred Isabella, beginning the four-year War of the Castilian Succession. On 10 May 1475 Afonso invaded Castile, and he married Joanna at Plasencia 15 days later. At the Battle of Toro on 1 March 1476 the outcome was indecisive, but Ferdinand sent word of a great victory to the cities of Castile, and the prestige of Joanna and Afonso dissolved. The Portuguese returned to their kingdom.

In 1478 Pope Sixtus IV annulled the marriage of Joanna and Afonso on grounds of consanguinity, and she renounced the title of queen of Castile. In the Treaty of Alcáçovas of 1479 she was offered a choice between a convent and marriage to Isabella's one-year-old son John; she chose the Convent of Santa Clara in Coimbra. Ferdinand and Isabella lobbied the Holy See to ensure that she kept her vows. In 1522 she relinquished her title and offered the crown to John III of Portugal. She signed her letters La Reina until she died, and was known in Portugal as the Excellent Lady. She died in Lisbon on 12 April 1530.
joanot-martorell: Joanot Martorell was born in Valencia around 1410. According to the historian Jaume Chiner his family came originally from Gandía. His grandfather Guillem Martorell was a royal adviser, and his father Francesc, who married Damiata Abelló, was butler to King Martin the Humane. His sister Isabel married the poet Ausiàs March. His first appointment to knighthood dates from 1433.

He was a combative knight with a hectic life of journeys and knightly adventures, though most of his disputes, including challenges to the death, did not go beyond verbal duels. He spent many years in England, where he translated the poem Guy of Warwick in 1438, and in Portugal and Naples. Fourteen of his battle letters survive.

One quarrel with his cousin Joan de Monpalau, who had promised to marry a sister of Martorell and then refused, lasted from 1437 to 1445. In 1454 he travelled to Naples to help Alfonso the Magnanimous.

On 2 January 1460 Martorell began to write Tirant lo Blanch, which he dedicated to Prince Ferdinand of Portugal, whom he had met in that country. The novel tells the war exploits of the knight Tirant and his romance with Carmesina. It was first published at Valencia in 1490 and later at Barcelona, and four copies of the first two editions survive. In the first half of the 16th century it was translated into Spanish and Italian, and later into French. Ariosto, Shakespeare and Cervantes knew it.

Some evidence suggests that the 1490 text does not exactly match the manuscript Martorell gave to his friend Martí Joan de Galba as a pledge for a loan of a hundred reales; Galba died before he could recover the money. Martorell also left unfinished Guillem de Varoic, which he incorporated into the first chapters of Tirant.

After the sale of his estates Martorell fell into financial ruin, and Galba often lent him money. He died in Valencia, leaving no descendants, at the beginning of 1465. His novel is often regarded as one of the peaks of Catalan literature and as one of the first works of alternate history. In Don Quixote, in the scene where books of chivalry are burned, Cervantes has a character say of Tirant lo Blanch: 'I swear to you, my friend, this is the best book of its kind in the world.'
joao-figueiredo: João Baptista de Oliveira Figueiredo was born in Rio de Janeiro on 15 January 1918, the third of six children of General Euclides Figueiredo. His father was exiled for trying to topple the Estado Novo regime of Getúlio Vargas in 1938, and two of his brothers also became generals. After studying at military schools in Porto Alegre and Realengo he was promoted to captain in 1944 and major in 1952. He was military attaché in Paraguay from 1955 to 1957 and became a general in the late 1960s. He headed the military staff of President Emílio Garrastazu Médici from 1969 to 1974 and then led the National Intelligence Service until 1978, when President Ernesto Geisel picked him as his successor.

The legislature, dominated by the pro-military National Renewal Alliance Party, elected Figueiredo easily against the nominal opposition candidate, General Monteiro. He continued the gradual abertura, or opening, begun in 1974. On 28 August 1979 he signed an amnesty law covering those convicted of political or related crimes between 1961 and 1978. The two-party system set up in 1966 could no longer be kept up, and the government dissolved ARENA and allowed new parties. In the general election of 1982 the pro-government Democratic Social Party won 43.22 per cent of the vote and the opposition Brazilian Democratic Movement Party 42.96 per cent, and the opposition won the governorships of São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais.

Politics was overshadowed by economic crisis, with high international interest rates, the oil shock of 1979, soaring inflation and a foreign debt so large that Brazil sought help from the International Monetary Fund in 1982. In 1983 the Diretas Já movement demanded direct presidential elections, but Congress rejected the amendment. The opposition candidate Tancredo Neves succeeded him after an indirect election.

After the presidency Figueiredo did not return to politics and lived away from public attention in Rio de Janeiro. He died on 24 December 1999, aged 81, of kidney and heart failure, and President Fernando Henrique Cardoso declared three days of mourning. According to CIA documents he supported the continuation of summary executions of political dissidents. His presidency also saw several terrorist attacks attributed to hardline right-wing and military factions.
joao-goulart: João Belchior Marques Goulart, nicknamed Jango, was born on 1 March 1919 at Yguariaçá Farm in São Borja, Rio Grande do Sul. Most sources give 1918, because his father had a second birth certificate made adding a year so that he could attend law school. His father was a rancher who had been a National Guard colonel. Goulart graduated in law in 1939 but never fully practised; a knee paralysed by illness left him with a disability, and after his father's death in 1943 he inherited land that made him one of the region's most influential ranchers.

Encouraged by the former president Getúlio Vargas, a friend of his father, Goulart joined the Brazilian Labour Party (PTB) and later led it nationally. In 1953 Vargas appointed him minister of labor in a time of strikes. After Vargas's suicide he turned the PTB into a party of reformist character. He was vice-president under Kubitschek and, as president of the Senate, helped keep stability by negotiating with the trade unions, though conservatives accused him of promoting strikes.

As president, Goulart called for unity, democracy and reform. His first cabinet, led by the prime minister Tancredo Neves, was named on 8 September. A plebiscite in 1963 overwhelmingly rejected the parliamentary system and restored full presidential powers. His Basic Reforms plan proposed education reform using Paulo Freire's method, tax measures on multinational profits, votes for illiterates and low-ranking military officers, and the redistribution of unproductive properties over 600 hectares. Eletrobrás was created in 1962. Accused of communism, he denied it, and in 1967 even his accuser Carlos Lacerda acknowledged he was not a man from the Communist Party.

On 31 March 1964 General Olímpio Mourão Filho moved troops from Juiz de Fora towards Rio de Janeiro. Goulart went to Brasília, found no political support, and flew to Porto Alegre; Senate president Auro de Moura Andrade declared the presidency vacant, and Pascoal Ranieri Mazzilli was sworn in on 2 April. Goulart sought asylum in Uruguay on 4 April, farmed cattle, joined the Frente Ampla in 1966 and later lived in Argentina. He died on 6 December 1976 in Mercedes, Corrientes, apparently of a heart attack, though without an autopsy the cause is unconfirmed. About 30,000 people attended his funeral.
joaquim-nabuco: Joaquim Aurélio Barreto Nabuco de Araújo was born on 19 August 1849, the son of José Tomás Nabuco, a major political figure of the Empire of Brazil, a lifetime senator, counsellor of state and wealthy landowner. His father moved from conservatism to liberalism in the 1860s, helped establish the Liberal Party in 1868 and supported the reforms that led to abolition. Between 1873 and 1878 the younger Nabuco spent most of his time travelling and living abroad.

On a voyage to Europe in 1873 Nabuco began a relationship with the financier and philanthropist Eufrásia Teixeira Leite, one of the richest people in the world at the time, which lasted until her last letter to him in 1887. He later married Evelina Torres Soares Ribeiro, and he was a friend of the writer Machado de Assis. After the monarchy was overthrown he withdrew from public life for a time.

As Brazil's first ambassador to the United States, Nabuco worked in Washington with Elihu Root, who shared his idea of Pan-Americanism, and he presided over the third Pan-American Conference, held in Rio de Janeiro in 1906. He died on 17 January 1910. At the dedication of the newly completed Pan-American Building in Washington soon afterwards, the Secretary of State mourned him as dean of the American diplomatic corps and a commanding figure in the international movement of which the building was part.

Nabuco was also a historian, jurist, journalist, orator and poet. O Abolicionismo is counted perhaps the most important work against slavery in the Portuguese language, and Minha formação portrays the slave-holding society of 19th-century Brazil through the paradox of a man raised among slaveholders who chose to fight slavery. He confessed to a nostalgia for the slaves, whose generosity he contrasted with the selfishness of their masters, and wrote that slavery would long remain the national characteristic of Brazil.

Historians have asked whether he feared that the enslaved population would Africanize Brazil; he is quoted as saying that free labour and slave labour cannot coexist, and neither can slavery and immigration. Both of his best-known books have been translated into English, as Abolitionism and My Formative Years.
joaquin-balaguer: Joaquín Balaguer was born on 1 September 1906 in Navarrete, later Villa Bisonó, in Santiago Province. He was the only son in a family of several daughters and wrote verses that were published in local magazines when he was very young. He earned a law degree at the University of Santo Domingo and briefly studied at the Sorbonne.

His political career began in 1930 with an appointment as Attorney in the Court of Properties, before Rafael Trujillo took control of the government. Under Trujillo he served as secretary of education from 1949 to 1955 and as secretary of foreign relations. In 1957 Trujillo had his brother Héctor re-elected president and chose Balaguer as vice president.

In 1960 pressure from the Organization of American States persuaded Trujillo that it was inappropriate to have a relative as president, and Balaguer succeeded Héctor. After Trujillo's assassination in May 1961, real power lay with his son Ramfis. A Council of State led by Balaguer was formed in January 1962, but riots followed, and he resigned on 16 January and went into exile in New York and Puerto Rico.

After the Dominican Civil War of 1965, in which United States troops intervened, Balaguer returned with American backing and founded the Reformist Party. In 1966 he easily defeated Juan Bosch. His twelve years in office saw schools, hospitals, dams and roads built and steady economic growth, and he won re-election in 1970 and 1974. His rule had an authoritarian character: opponents were jailed and sometimes killed. According to Luisa de Peña Díaz, director of the Memorial Museum of Dominican Resistance, 11,000 people were tortured, imprisoned, disappeared or killed between 1966 and 1978.

In 1978 he lost to Antonio Guzmán of the Dominican Revolutionary Party, and he lost again in 1982. He won the presidency in 1986, at 80 and almost blind, and his third presidency was more tolerant of opposition parties and human rights. His narrow victories over Bosch in 1990 and over José Francisco Peña Gómez in 1994 were met with charges of fraud, and in 1994 an investigation found that about 200,000 people had been removed from the voting rolls. He agreed to hold new elections in 1996, in which he did not run. He died of heart failure on 14 July 2002, aged 95.
joaquin-prieto: Joaquín Prieto Vial was born on 20 August 1786, one of five sons of a Creole officer in Concepción, and was of Spanish descent. After school he joined the cavalry garrison of his home town. In 1810 he joined the Chilean fight for independence against his father's will. He married Manuela Warnes García de Zúñiga, whom he had met in Buenos Aires, in 1812. In the dispute between Bernardo O'Higgins and José Miguel Carrera he took O'Higgins's side, and O'Higgins made him quartermaster general of the southern army. After the defeat at Rancagua, in which he took no part, he fled to Mendoza to help build the Liberation Army of the Andes, and after Chacabuco in 1817 he was appointed commanding general of Santiago.

His military record in the south earned him the respect of conservative and centralist circles. In 1823 he was elected to the House of Deputies and appointed to the State Council, where he advocated a strong central government against regionalist federalists. In 1828 he was elected vice-president of Chile and was promoted to general and commander of the army in the south.

In the presidential election of 1829 neither he nor the liberal-federalist Joaquín Vicuña won an absolute majority. The liberal majority in Congress named Francisco Ramón Vicuña vice-president, which the conservatives held to be unconstitutional, and a civil war began. Prieto marched on Santiago and on 14 December 1829 defeated the liberal army under Francisco de la Lastra at the Battle of Ochagavía. After the defeat of Ramón Freire at the Battle of Lircay in 1830 an agreement was reached.

After the transitional president José Tomás Ovalle died, Prieto replaced the provisional president Fernando Errázuriz Aldunate on 10 April 1831 and took office as elected president on 18 September 1831, for a five-year term. He relied on Diego Portales to restore law and order, and ordered Manuel Bulnes to seize the bandits led by the Pincheira brothers. A new constitution passed on 25 May 1833 and, with a few amendments, remained valid until 1925; it gave the president much authority and allowed one re-election.

Prieto expanded government power and laid the foundation of a public administration. The Instituto Nacional and other schools were founded, and ministries for justice and public education were created in 1837. Chile fought Peru between 1836 and 1839; the army under Manuel Blanco Encalada suffered heavy losses and signed the Treaty of Paucarpata, after which Bulnes took command and won the Battle of Yungay. Bulnes succeeded him in 1841. Prieto served as senator until 1852 and died in Santiago on 22 November 1854.
joash-of-judah: Jehoash, also called Joash, was the eighth king of Judah. After the massacre of the royal family ordered by his grandmother Athaliah he was the sole surviving son of Ahaziah. His mother was Zibiah of Beersheba. According to the Hebrew Bible, his paternal aunt Jehosheba, who was married to the high priest Jehoiada, saved him from Athaliah, and he was hidden in the Temple for seven years. Jehoiada then had him crowned and anointed in a coup against Athaliah, who was killed.

Jehoash was seven years old when he became king and is said to have reigned for forty years. William F. Albright dated his reign to 837–800 BCE and E. R. Thiele to 835–796 BCE. After his coronation the covenant was renewed between God, the king and the nation, the cult of Baal was suppressed, and the priest of Baal, Mattan, was killed. According to 2 Kings, Jehoash directed that money paid by worshippers at the Temple should fund its repair; by the 23rd year of his reign the priests had failed to carry out the work, and he made his own arrangements, funded by popular contributions.

Archaeological finds suggest that Jerusalem expanded around this time, with a large dam wall at the Pool of Siloam built about 800–795 BCE. Jehoash was a pious king while under Jehoiada's guidance, but afterwards he listened to the princes of Judah and turned to idols.

According to 2 Chronicles, Jehoiada's son Zechariah rebuked them, and Jehoash had him stoned, an act the author of Chronicles criticises strongly. When King Hazael of Syria marched on Jerusalem, Jehoash, according to 2 Kings, gave him all the gold of the royal and sacred treasuries to call off the attack; 2 Chronicles says the Syrian army killed the leaders of the people and left the king severely wounded.

Jehoash was assassinated by his own servants at Beth Millo, an act portrayed as revenge for the blood of Zechariah. He was buried in the City of David but not in the sepulchres of the kings, and his son Amaziah succeeded him. The Gospel of Matthew omits him from the genealogy of Jesus. An unprovenanced inscription published in 2001, the Jehoash Inscription, appears to record repairs to the Temple; Israeli archaeological authorities declared it a forgery, though some experts maintain it is not.
jobst-of-moravia: Jobst was the eldest legitimate son of Margrave John Henry, the younger brother of Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV. He was presumably born in the Moravian residence of Brno. His cousins therefore included Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia and Wenceslaus's half-brother Sigismund. Designated heir on his father's death in 1375, Jobst ruled the Margraviate of Moravia. He often quarrelled with his younger brother Prokop and with the Bishops of Olomouc.

In 1388 Jobst received the Duchy of Luxembourg, given in pawn by his cousin Wenceslaus, who was King of the Romans and the son of the late Charles IV. The same year he became Prince-elector of Brandenburg, which Sigismund pawned to him while Sigismund concentrated on ruling the Kingdom of Hungary. In 1394 Jobst joined the League of Lords, a rebellion of Bohemian nobles led by Boček II of Poděbrady against Wenceslaus. He had the king arrested at Prague Castle, and Wenceslaus was later taken into custody by the Austrian Starhemberg dynasty at Wildberg.

Peace was made at the urging of Wenceslaus's brothers Sigismund and John of Görlitz, but once released the king had Jobst expelled from Prague. Sigismund and Jobst signed a mutual inheritance treaty in 1401, though they later fell out again. Jobst's titles also included Margrave of Lusatia and Brandenburg, Vicarius of Italy and Vicarius of the Holy Roman Empire.

After the death of the King of the Romans Rupert III in 1410, Sigismund was elected by three of the seven prince-electors on 10 September. Jobst was elected by four electors on 1 October, in opposition to his cousin. The deciding vote came from Wenceslaus, voting as King of Bohemia. Although Jobst had the greater support among the electors, he died on 18 January 1411, possibly having been poisoned.

His death cleared the way for Sigismund's election as King of the Romans and his later coronation as Holy Roman Emperor in 1433. Jobst had married twice: in 1372 Elisabeth of Opole, daughter of Duke Władysław Opolczyk, and in 1374 Agnes of Opole, daughter of Duke Bolesław (Bolko) II of Opole. A fictionalised Jobst appears in the video games Kingdom Come: Deliverance and its sequel.
jodensavanne: The settlement stood in what is now Para District, about 50 km south of Paramaribo, on a raised area of ground beside the Suriname River. It was laid out with one main road and four side streets and took its name from the savanna fields around it. The English, who controlled Suriname in 1639, allowed Sephardi Jews from the Netherlands, Portugal and Italy to settle in the colony, first at the old capital Torarica. A further group came in 1664 after their expulsion from Brazil and then French Guiana, led by David Cohen Nassy.

The English tried to keep the newcomers by guaranteeing them privileges, among them their own court and freedom of religion, and the Dutch, who later gained control of Suriname, preserved and extended these rights, adding in 1691 a land grant of 100 acres for a synagogue and burial ground. The community's wealth rested on sugar-cane plantations worked by African slaves; according to some accounts, newly settled families received four or five slaves as part of their grant. A school taught Spanish and Portuguese besides Jewish subjects.

The settlement lived with repeated violence. Carib (Kalina) people attacked the European settlements there late in 1678, when enslaved people also revolted; in 1690 another revolt killed the planter Immanuel Machado, whose former slaves fled to a Maroon community, and French sailors raided the town in 1712. The colonists built defences around it. The centenary of the brick synagogue in October 1785 drew more than 1,500 people, many of them from Paramaribo, although by then only about twenty Jewish families still lived there.

Mounting loans, the collapse of a major Amsterdam sugar importer in 1773, the spread of sugar beet in Europe from 1784, exhausted soils, the Maroon Wars and the growth of Paramaribo as the colony's only trading port drew the planters away. Around 1790 the free population numbered about twenty-two. In 1942 an internment camp named after the settlement was built nearby for 146 political prisoners from the Dutch East Indies, among them the Indonesian nationalist Ernest Douwes Dekker.

The ruins of the synagogue remain at the site with three cemeteries, whose headstones are inscribed mainly in Hebrew and Portuguese; the Cassipora Cemetery holds about two hundred tombstones. In September 2023 Jodensavanne and the Cassipora Creek Cemetery were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
jodhpur: Jodhpur lies in the Thar Desert near the geographic centre of Rajasthan, about 250 kilometres from the border with Pakistan. Its name combines that of its founder, Rao Jodha, with the Sanskrit suffix pur, meaning city or settlement. The old city circles Mehrangarh Fort and is bounded by a wall with several gates. It is also called the Blue City for the dominant colour of the buildings in the old town. Average rainfall is around 362 millimetres but varies greatly: the famine year of 1899 brought only 24 millimetres and the flood year of 1917 as much as 1,178.

Marwar formed part of the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire. A Rathore chieftain named Chunda received Mandore as a dowry from the Pratiharas and ruled there while the Tughlaq dynasty declined. Rao Jodha, a Rajput chief of the Rathore clan from Mandore, founded Jodhpur in 1459 after conquering the surrounding territory from the Delhi Sultanate. Mandore at first served as the capital but Jodhpur soon took over. The city stood on the road linking Delhi to Gujarat, which brought it a trade in opium, copper, silk, sandalwood and dates.

After Rao Chandrasen Rathore died in 1581, Akbar annexed the kingdom, and Marwar became a Mughal vassal with internal autonomy. Aurangzeb briefly took over the state around 1679 after the death of Maharaja Jaswant Singh, and Durgadas Rathore restored Jaswant's son Ajit Singh in 1707. Strife at court then invited the intervention of the Marathas. Under the British Raj Jodhpur was the largest state of Rajputana by area, and its Marwari merchants came to dominate trade across India. On 11 August 1947 Maharaja Hanwant Singh, the last ruler, signed the Instrument of Accession to India, having at first not wished to join. On 30 March 1949 the state became part of Rajasthan.

Jodhpur is the second-largest city of Rajasthan after Jaipur and the administrative headquarters of Jodhpur district and division, with about 1.6 million people. Its main sights are Mehrangarh Fort, Umaid Bhawan Palace, Jaswant Thada and the Ghanta Ghar clock tower, with Mandore Garden nearby. Local foods include Mirchi Bada and Mawa Kachori. It is a base for the Indian Army and the Indian Air Force, and a centre of the handicraft industry.
jodo-shinshu: Shinran (1173–1263) lived from the late Heian into the early Kamakura period. He came of the Hino family, a cadet branch of the Fujiwara, entered monastic life in 1181 at the age of nine under the Tendai prelate Jien, and spent two decades as a hall-monk on Mount Hiei. He never said he was creating a separate school, and many early followers saw Hōnen as their founding figure. Lay congregations spread across the Kantō plain, and the school grew chiefly among the rural lower classes.

The Hongan-ji's 8th head priest, Rennyo (1415–1499), united many factions through preaching tours and his widely read letters, the Ofumi, and built a new Hongan-ji at Yamashina in Kyoto. In the 16th century conflict with the warlord Oda Nobunaga ended in the Siege of Ishiyama Hongan-ji (1576–1580), after which Osaka Castle replaced the temple complex. Under the Tokugawa, Shin temples took part in the compulsory danka system, under which every Japanese had to belong to a temple, introduced to prevent the spread of Christianity.

Shinran taught that enlightenment cannot be reached through one's own power, jiriki, whether by moral cultivation, meditation or ritual, but only through the other-power, tariki, of the Vow of Amida Buddha. In Shin belief the nembutsu, the recitation Namo Amida Butsu, is therefore not a meritorious practice but an expression of gratitude for a rebirth in the Pure Land already granted. Its doctrine rests on Shinran's Kyōgyōshinshō and centres on shinjin, true entrusting. Shinran also held that those most burdened by evil are the primary objects of the Vow.

Followers recite the nembutsu at temples, at home shrines called butsudan and in daily life, holding prayer beads with their hands joined in gassho. The most important service of the year is the Hōonkō, held on the anniversary of Shinran's death. Shin clergy keep no Buddhist clerical precepts and may eat meat, drink alcohol and have families; until the Meiji period it was the only Buddhist sect in which clerical marriage was openly permitted.

Japanese emigrants carried the school abroad in the 19th century, to Hawaii, the United States, Canada, Mexico and South America. Its first organised mission in the United States began when Shuya Sonoda and Kakuryō Nishijima arrived in San Francisco in 1899, and from it grew the Jōdo Shinshū Buddhist Mission of North America.
johan-de-witt: Johan de Witt was born on 24 September 1625 into an old patrician family of Dordrecht, a leading city of Holland. His father Jacob de Witt was an influential regent, and his mother Anna van den Corput was a niece of the cartographer Johannes Corputius. His uncle Andries de Witt had been Grand Pensionary of Holland from 1619 to 1621. Johan and his brother Cornelis attended the Latin school in Dordrecht, and Johan then studied at Leiden, where he excelled at mathematics and law, taking his doctorate at Angers in 1645. In 1655 he married Wendela Bicker, whose family belonged to the Amsterdam oligarchy; they had four children.

De Witt became pensionary of Dordrecht in December 1650, the year the stadtholder William II died, and the States of Holland elected him Grand Pensionary in July 1653. With his later uncle, the Amsterdam burgomaster Cornelis de Graeff, he controlled the political system of the Republic. As leader of the States party he pursued the commercial interests of the merchants, opposed the House of Orange and favoured peace. He brought the First Anglo-Dutch War to an end with the Treaty of Westminster in May 1654, and in 1658/59 sent a fleet to the Baltic to keep the Øresund open to Dutch ships.

In the Second Anglo-Dutch War he built larger warships and briefly took command of the fleet himself after the defeat at Lowestoft; Michiel de Ruyter then took over. In 1667 the Dutch burned English ships at Chatham, and the Peace of Breda followed. The same year De Witt issued the Perpetual Edict, abolishing the stadtholdership. The Triple Alliance with England and Sweden was concluded on 23 January 1668, but Charles II then revealed its secret clause to Louis XIV, who made the secret Treaty of Dover with England against the Dutch.

In 1672, the Rampjaar, England and France attacked the Republic. De Witt was badly wounded by an assassin on 21 June and resigned as Grand Pensionary on 4 August. His brother Cornelis was arrested on a charge of treason and, though tortured, did not confess and was sentenced to exile. When Johan came to the jail, both were attacked by members of The Hague's civic militia, shot and left to the mob near the Gevangenpoort. Contemporary accounts report cannibalism, though the extent is uncertain. William of Orange then purged the city councils.

De Witt was also a mathematician. His Elementa Curvarum Linearum, composed in 1646 and printed in 1661 in Frans van Schooten's Latin edition of Descartes, has been called the first textbook in analytic geometry. His work on life annuities is described as one of the first applications of probability in economics.
johan-ferrier: Johan Henri Eliza Ferrier was born on 12 May 1910 in Paramaribo, the capital of Suriname, and trained as a teacher. At sixteen he taught in the Saramacca District and founded his first Scout group, which still exists as the Johan Ferrier group; he co-founded the Boy Scouts van Suriname and was its first Chief Scout. In 1946, while Suriname was a Dutch colony, he was a founding member of the National Party and sat on the National Council until 1948. He then went to Amsterdam to study education theory and received his doctorate in 1950.

Back in Suriname, by then an autonomous country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands, he continued a career in education, serving as head of education, and was prime minister and interior minister from 1955 to 1958. He was governor from 1968 until 1975, the country's last governor-general before independence. On 25 November 1975 Suriname became independent, and Ferrier was sworn in as its first president. Dési Bouterse's coup of 1980 prompted him to resign within six months. Prime Minister Henk Chin A Sen succeeded him and on 3 September 1980 made him Grand Cordon of the Honorary Order of the Yellow Star.

Ferrier then went with relatives to the Netherlands and lived in Oegstgeest, where he told stories about the spider Anansi on Dutch children's television; a picture book, Het Grote Anansi Boek, appeared in 1986. His memoirs, Last Governor, First President, were published in 2005. His daughter Kathleen Ferrier sat in the Dutch House of Representatives. He was named the twentieth century's most important politician in Suriname in 1999. He died of heart failure at home in Oegstgeest on 4 January 2010, aged 99, and was buried there on 11 January. Queen Beatrix paid tribute, and the Johan Ferrier Fund, supporting Surinamese educational and cultural projects, was launched on 12 May 2010.
johan-gustaf-renat: Johan Gustaf Renat was the son of Dutch Jewish immigrants to Sweden who converted to Christianity and took Swedish citizenship in 1681, the year before he was born. During the Great Northern War he served in the army of Charles XII as a warrant officer of the artillery, a styckjunkare, until he was taken prisoner after the Battle of Poltava in 1709.

In 1711 Renat was sent to Tobolsk, then the capital of Russian Siberia, where many Swedish officers were held as prisoners of war. He entered Russian military service on condition that he would not fight against Sweden, and helped to produce maps of Siberia for the Russian government. In 1716 he and other Swedish prisoners joined Ivan Buchholz's expedition to explore the gold deposits around Lake Yamysh on the Irtysh River. A Dzungar force ambushed the expedition, and Renat spent the following years as an Oirat slave.

In Dzungaria he helped the khans Tsewang Rabtan and Galdan Tseren to organise their campaigns against Qing rule in Central Asia, forming an artillery regiment and helping the Dzungars to cast cannon. There he met Brigitta Scherzenfeldt from Scania, another Swedish captive. Twice widowed, she had married a German prisoner in Russian service whom Dzungar raiders killed when they seized his convoy in 1716, and she later married Renat.

In 1733 Renat and his wife were allowed to leave. They reached Stockholm the following year with four Dzungar women servants, who were baptised on arrival, and settled in a house in Gamla stan. In 1739 Renat was promoted to captain in the Swedish army, and the same year he married the industrialist Elisabet Fritz.

Renat brought two detailed maps of Central Asia back to Sweden, but they lay in obscurity for many years. In 1878 August Strindberg, then an assistant librarian at the Swedish Royal Library, found copies of them and sponsored their republication in Russia, where they appeared at St. Petersburg in 1881 as the Carte de la Dzoungarie. Strindberg's interest in the maps lasted for many years. A decade later the originals were found in the library of Uppsala University, which still holds them.
johan-laidoner: Johan Laidoner was born on 12 February 1884 at Raba estate in Vardja, Viiratsi Parish, the first of four sons of a farmhand, Jaak Laidoner, and his wife Mari. His parents were poor and he could not continue his studies after finishing at Viljandi Town School in 1900, so he volunteered for the Imperial Russian Army in 1901. He graduated top of his class from the Infantry Officer School in Vilna in April 1905 and later from the Imperial Nicholas Military Academy in Saint Petersburg. On 30 October 1911 he married Maria Skarbek-Kruszewska, a descendant of Polish nobility. In the First World War he served on staffs in the Caucasus.

On 5 January 1918 Laidoner was appointed commander of the newly formed 1st Estonian Division. After German forces landed on the mainland he resigned and left for Russia. Following the German capitulation, the Red Army invaded Estonia on 28 November 1918, and on 23 December the provisional government appointed him commander-in-chief. On 1 January 1919 the Estonian Army had just over 13,000 men; he launched a counter-offensive on 3 January and within eleven days the 1st Division advanced 200 kilometres. On 24 February 1919 he reported that Soviet forces had been driven from Estonia. He retired from active service in March 1920.

From 1920 to 1929 he sat in the Riigikogu. He was again appointed commander-in-chief when martial law was declared during the communist coup attempt of 1 December 1924. In 1925 the League of Nations commissioned him to head a mission to Iraq, and his committee's report helped to demarcate the border between Turkey and Iraq. On 12 March 1934 Konstantin Päts declared martial law and reappointed him commander-in-chief. With Päts and Kaarel Eenpalu, Laidoner established an authoritarian rule, disbanding political parties and limiting free speech, the so-called Era of Silence. He was promoted general on 24 February 1939.

After the Soviet Union occupied Estonia on 17 June 1940, Laidoner was removed from command on 22 June. On 19 July he and his wife were deported to Penza, and in June 1941 the NKVD imprisoned them. He was sentenced to 25 years on 16 April 1952, and he died in Vladimir Central Prison on 13 March 1953. His remains have not been found. His reputation in Estonia has remained controversial: hailed as a national hero for his leadership in the War of Independence, he has been criticised for his support of Päts, the coup of 1934 and the surrender to the Soviet Union in 1940.
johan-rudolf-thorbecke: Johan Rudolph Thorbecke was born in Zwolle on 14 January 1798 into a Lutheran merchant family of German origin whose fortunes were poor. His father's tobacco factory went bankrupt in 1803 after the anti-British policies of the French occupiers. He attended a Latin school, studied at the Athenaeum Illustre of Amsterdam and then at Leiden, and received his doctorate on 19 June 1820. A state scholarship then took him to the leading German universities, where he lectured at Giessen and Göttingen and was introduced to Romanticism and the German historical school. In 1824 he published a treatise on the nature of history.

Back in the Netherlands he became professor of political history at Ghent in 1825 and, after the Belgian Revolution of 1830, professor of diplomacy and modern history at Leiden. He grew critical of the autocratic government of William I, and his Aanteekening op de grondwet of 1839 criticised the existing constitution and called for its revision. In Over het hedendaags staatsburgerschap (1844) he argued that universal suffrage would eventually be unavoidable.

Elected to the House of Representatives in 1844, Thorbecke joined eight others in the Voorstel der Negenmannen, which proposed ministerial responsibility and direct elections; it was defeated 34 to 21 in 1845. In March 1848, amid the revolutions across Europe, William II appointed a commission to draft a constitutional revision, and it elected Thorbecke chair. The constitution, largely his work, was proclaimed on 3 November 1848. It established civil rights, ministerial responsibility and direct election of the House of Representatives, so making the Netherlands a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system.

His first ministry took office on 13 November 1849, with Thorbecke as interior minister. It passed the Elections Act and the Provinces Act in 1850 and the Municipalities Act in 1851, which set up municipal self-government. It fell in April 1853 after he stayed passive on the restoration of the Catholic episcopal hierarchy and the King sided with the anti-papal April Movement. His second ministry (1862–1866) introduced the Secondary Education Act of 1863, creating the Hogere Burgerschool. He began a third in 1871 and died at The Hague on 4 June 1872.

Thousands attended his funeral. Hated by some, since he made few concessions, he is regarded as a towering figure in Dutch parliamentary history and as the most important Dutch statesman of the nineteenth century. Statues stand in Amsterdam on Thorbeckeplein, in Zwolle and in The Hague.
johan-van-oldenbarnevelt: Van Oldenbarnevelt was born in Amersfoort on 14 September 1547. He studied law at Leuven, Bourges, Heidelberg and Padua, travelled in France and Italy and settled in The Hague. He supported William the Silent's revolt against Philip II of Spain and served as a volunteer for the relief of Haarlem in 1573 and Leiden in 1574. In 1576 he became pensionary of Rotterdam, which gave him membership of the States of Holland, and he promoted the Union of Utrecht of 1579. He opposed the centralising policy of the Earl of Leicester and favoured Maurice of Nassau, a son of William.

On 16 March 1586 he succeeded Paulus Buys as Land's Advocate of Holland, an office he held for 32 years. In a republic with no central executive he made himself the political personification of Holland, which bore more than half the cost of the union, and became its virtual prime minister. His statesmanship after Leicester's departure kept the United Provinces from collapsing. He initiated and brokered the merger of half a dozen trading companies into the Dutch East India Company in 1602, and its joint-stock model later spread worldwide. As leader of Holland's delegation in the States-General he led the negotiations that produced the Twelve Years' Truce of 1609, which Maurice opposed.

In 1610 the Arminians, thereafter Remonstrants, petitioned for a national synod; Van Oldenbarnevelt, who upheld religious toleration, approved, and the States of Holland supported them against the Contra-Remonstrants. When riots broke out, Maurice declared for the Contra-Remonstrants in 1617. On 4 August 1617 the Scherpe Resolutie required Holland's officials and soldiers to swear obedience to the States of Holland, and the States-General saw this as a declaration of sovereign independence. Maurice disbanded the local troops, the waardgelders, in 1618 without a battle.

On 29 August 1618 the States-General arrested Van Oldenbarnevelt, Hugo Grotius and others. He appeared more than 60 times before examiners, without access to papers, and was tried from 20 February 1619 before a special court of twenty-four, only half of them Hollanders. Pardons sought by Louise de Coligny and the French ambassador failed. On 13 May 1619, aged seventy-one, he was beheaded in the Binnenhof in The Hague, saying, "Men, do not believe I am a traitor." In 1623 a conspiracy against Maurice involving both his sons was discovered; Groeneveld was executed and Stoutenburg escaped into Spanish service. A Jacobean play by John Fletcher and Philip Massinger on his fall was staged within three months of his death.
johann-adolf-i-duke-of-saxe-weissenfels: Johann Adolf was born in Halle on 2 November 1649, the first son of Augustus, Duke of Saxe-Weissenfels, and his first wife, Anna Maria of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. On 25 October 1671 he married Johanna Magdalena of Saxe-Altenburg at Altenburg. They had eleven children, several of whom died in infancy.

His father died on 4 June 1680, and the family lost the Archbishopric of Magdeburg, which Brandenburg secularised. Johann Adolf first turned to the unfinished Schloss Neu-Augustusburg, where building resumed on 18 August 1680; the chapel was consecrated on 1 November 1682 and the castle was finally paved in 1694. A large theatre staged opera in German from 1685, and beside the castle he laid out what became the most important formal garden in central Germany of his time. Weissenfels grew into an economic as well as an administrative centre.

Following his father's example, he kept Johann Philipp Krieger as court Kapellmeister and joined the Fruitbearing Society. He noticed the musical talent of the young Georg Friedrich Händel, son of his court surgeon, and urged the father to let the boy train in music.

His inheritance had been reduced: his father left Barby to a younger son, Heinrich, and the old duke's debts forced Johann Adolf in 1687 to sell Burg bei Magdeburg. When Elector Johann Georg III of Saxony refused to recognise the collateral lines of his cousins, Johann Adolf secured his rule over Querfurt and his seat in the Upper Saxon council through the Contract of Torgau of 12 May 1681 and two later agreements signed in Dresden.

After his wife's death in 1686 he married Christiane Wilhelmine of Bünau at Querfurt on 3 February 1692, a morganatic marriage made by contract; at his request she was created an Imperial Countess in 1697. They had no children. He died at Weissenfels on 24 May 1697, and his three surviving sons, Johann Georg, Christian and Johann Adolf II, ruled the duchy in turn.
johann-adolf-ii-duke-of-saxe-weissenfels: Johann Adolf was born in Weissenfels on 19 August 1685, the third surviving son of Johann Adolf I, Duke of Saxe-Weissenfels, and his first wife, Johanna Magdalena of Saxe-Altenburg. As a younger son he made his career as a commander in the Saxon Army. He inherited the duchy in 1736, when his older brother Christian died without children.

In October 1733, in the War of the Polish Succession, Johann Adolf led Saxon troops into Poland. The Saxon army stayed mainly in southern Poland for the next three years, until Elector Frederick August II of Saxony was crowned King of Poland after the defeat of the rival candidate, Stanisław Leszczyński.

During the Second Silesian War, Saxony and Austria agreed to act together against Prussia, Saxon troops planning to cut off the Prussians in northern Silesia while Austrian troops advanced from the south. In June 1745 they were defeated at the Battle of Hohenfriedberg.

Johann Adolf planned a new offensive in September but abandoned it two weeks later, and he was replaced as commander-in-chief by Count Frederick August Rutowski, an illegitimate half-brother of the King-Elector. After the Battle of Kesselsdorf the Elector removed Rutowski and reinstated Johann Adolf, who took up the command again on 1 December 1745 and was also made head of the Saxon government while the Elector and the minister Heinrich of Brühl were absent.

Johann Adolf retreated with the Saxon troops to Bohemia and died of a heart attack on 14 May 1746, at the age of sixty-one. He had married Johannette Antoinette Juliane of Saxe-Eisenach in 1721 and Fredericka of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg in 1734, and of his six children only a daughter, Fredericka Adolfine, survived infancy; she died in 1751, still a child. He was the last of the line, and his lands returned to the Electorate of Saxony, from which they had been separated in 1657 under the will of John George I, Elector of Saxony.
johann-bernhard-fischer-von-erlach: Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach was born in Graz and baptised on 20 July 1656. He trained as a sculptor in the workshop of his father, Johann Baptist Fischer, who worked on the decoration of the Landhaus and Eggenberg Palace in Graz. The Princes of Eggenberg, his father's patrons, arranged for the son to travel to Italy. In 1671, aged sixteen, he moved to Rome and joined the workshop of Johann Paul Schor and of Gian Lorenzo Bernini, and by 1685 he had followed Schor to Naples, where he served the Spanish viceroy. Back in Austria in 1687 he secured the position of court architect, which he kept under three emperors.

Commissions were plentiful, as the nobility sought to repair damage done to their country residences in the Ottoman campaign of 1683. In 1690 he built two temporary triumphal arches in Vienna for Joseph I's coronation, and he later taught Joseph architecture; in 1696 he was raised to the nobility as von Erlach. His emblematic design of the 1690s was the Winter Palace of Prince Eugene of Savoy, begun in 1695. For the Archbishop of Salzburg he built the Holy Trinity Church (1694 to 1702), the Kollegienkirche (1696 to 1707) and Schloss Klessheim (1700 to 1709), whose domes and towers changed the outline of Salzburg.

After Joseph I died in 1711 Fischer was rarely given new commissions, since the designs of his rival Johann Lucas von Hildebrandt were more popular with Charles VI, and he took on administrative tasks. The Clam-Gallas Palace in Prague was begun in 1713, and the Karlskirche in Vienna in 1715; it was completed by his son Joseph Emanuel. Fischer died on 5 April 1723.

In the Karlskirche Fischer sought to harmonise the main elements of the most significant churches in the history of Western architecture: the Temple of Solomon in Jerusalem, Hagia Sophia, the Pantheon, Saint Peter's Basilica, the Dome des Invalides and Saint Paul's Cathedral. His journeys to Prussia, the Netherlands, England in 1704 and Venice in 1707 fed his study of Mansart's country residences and Palladian villas. A visit to Dalmatia gave Western Europe one of its first professional views of Diocletian's Palace. In 1721 he published a groundbreaking book of reconstructions of the buildings of antiquity, one of the first and most popular comparative studies of world architecture.
johann-caspar-lavater: Johann Kaspar Lavater, also spelled Caspar, was born in Zürich on 15 November 1741 and educated at the Gymnasium there, where J. J. Bodmer and J. J. Breitinger were among his teachers. At barely twenty-one he distinguished himself by denouncing, together with his friend the painter Henry Fuseli, an unjust magistrate, who was compelled to make restitution of his ill-gotten gains.

In 1769 he took holy orders in Zürich's Zwinglian Church and served until his death as deacon or pastor in churches of his native city. His oratory and evident conviction gave him wide personal influence. He was consulted extensively as a casuist and welcomed with enthusiasm on journeys through Germany, and his writings on mysticism were popular. In the same year he sent Moses Mendelssohn a translation of Charles Bonnet's Palingénésie philosophique and demanded that he either refute it publicly or convert. Mendelssohn refused both, and many prominent intellectuals, among them Lichtenberg and Herder, took his side.

Lavater became best known for his Physiognomische Fragmente zur Beförderung der Menschenkenntnis und Menschenliebe, published between 1775 and 1778. He introduced the idea that physiognomy related to the specific character traits of individuals rather than to general types. Its fame, which reached France and England as well as Germany, rested largely on the handsome style of publication and the accompanying illustrations. He drew chiefly on the writings of Giambattista della Porta and on Sir Thomas Browne's Religio Medici.

The work is credited with catalysing a golden age of silhouettes: Lavater held that the most accurate readings came from a traced profile outline, filled with black or cut from paper. As a poet he published Christliche Lieder (1776–1780) and two epics in the manner of Klopstock, Jesus Messias (1780) and Joseph von Arimathia (1794). From 1774 he was intimately acquainted with Goethe, who later quarrelled with him and accused him of superstition and hypocrisy. In 1788 William Blake annotated Lavater's Aphorisms on Man, which held 632 aphorisms.

In his later years Lavater's influence waned, and he drew considerable ridicule for his vanity. When the French took Zürich in 1799 he was shot by an infuriated grenadier while trying to appease the invaders. He died in Zürich on 2 January 1801, more than a year later. Ernst Gombrich characterised his influence as a physiognomic fallacy. The Swiss artist Warja Honegger-Lavater was his direct descendant.
johann-dientzenhofer: Johann Dientzenhofer was born on 25 May 1663 on the family farm at St. Margarethen near Rosenheim in Bavaria, the youngest of the eight children of Georg and Barbara Thanner Dientzenhofer. His brothers Georg, Wolfgang, Christoph and Leonhard Dientzenhofer were also builders, and his son Justus Heinrich Dientzenhofer and his nephew Kilian Ignaz Dientzenhofer later became architects too.

After school in Flintsbach he followed his older brothers to Prague, where the building trades offered many opportunities. His sister Anna had married Wolfgang Leuthner, presumably a relative of the Prague architect Abraham Leuthner, and in Leuthner's construction company Johann learned the trade of bricklaying. He married in Prague in 1685.

In 1692 his brother Leonhard moved to Bamberg, became court architect to the Schönborns there in 1695 and invited Johann to join him. Johann worked as a foreman on the Michaelsberg and passed the master mason's examination in 1699. That autumn Lothar Franz von Schönborn sent him to Rome to improve his skills, and on his return in September 1700 Prince-Abbot Adalbert I von Schleifras appointed him court architect at Fulda.

In 1707 he completed the design of the church at Banz Abbey, begun by his late brother Leonhard, and took over Leonhard's post as court architect at Bamberg, moving there with his family in 1708. From 1715 to 1718 he oversaw the building of a hospital at Kronach with its church of St. Anne, and from 1720 to 1723 he was building inspector for the residence of Prince-Bishop Johann Philipp Franz von Schönborn at Würzburg. He died at Bamberg.

Schloss Weißenstein at Pommersfelden, designed from 1711 for Lothar Franz von Schönborn, Prince-Bishop of Bamberg and Archbishop of Mainz, is counted his most significant work and an important step in German late Baroque palace architecture; he designed its grand staircase with Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt. He also built the Fulda Stadtschloss (1707–1712), and in Bamberg the Böttingerhaus, the Palais Rotenhan and the Bibra Palais, as well as the facade of the Neumünster church in Würzburg (1711–1716).
johann-friedrich-bottger: Johann Friedrich Böttger was baptised at Schleiz on 5 February 1682, the third child of a mint master. The family moved to Magdeburg that year, and his father died soon after. In 1685 his mother married the widowed town major and engineer Johann Friedrich Tiemann, who was largely responsible for the boy's versatile training.

Around 1700, as an 18-year-old apprentice chemist with the pharmacist Zorn in Berlin, he shut himself away to seek the Goldmachertinktur, a substance said to cure any disease and turn base metals into gold. Soon he was regarded as an adept in alchemy. King Frederick I of Prussia ordered him taken into protective custody; Böttger escaped but was detained and taken back to Dresden, where Augustus II the Strong, who was always short of money, demanded that he make gold. He was imprisoned in a dungeon.

In 1704, impatient with the lack of progress, Augustus ordered Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus to oversee the young goldmaker. By September 1707 Böttger, fearing for his life, began to cooperate. Under Tschirnhaus and with miners and metal workers from Freiberg, experiments with clays continued. Progress came in 1708, when kaolin from Schneeberg and alabaster as a flux proved suitable; later, china stone and quartz, at 20 per cent, were added. Blended and heated to at least 1300 degrees Celsius, they gave the desired result.

Tschirnhaus died suddenly on 11 October 1708 and the work halted. On 28 March 1709 Böttger informed the king of the invention of porcelain, shortly after Melchior Steinbrück, tutor of Tschirnhaus's family, had arrived in Dresden to administer his estate and had obtained the formula. Böttger became head of the first porcelain manufactory in Europe, at Meissen, established in 1710. He also developed a dark red stoneware, Böttger ware, first sold in 1710, in imitation of Chinese Yixing teapots.

Böttger died in Dresden on 13 March 1719. In that year the arcanist Samuel Stölzel escaped from Meissen to Vienna and betrayed the secret of porcelain, claiming that Tschirnhaus, not Böttger, had made the discovery. The secretary general of the manufactory, Caspar Bussius, reported the same in 1719, and Peter Mohrenthal wrote in 1731 that Tschirnhaus had first found the secret and Böttger worked out the details. Böttger is normally credited with discovering hard-paste porcelain in 1708, though it has also been claimed that English manufacturers or Tschirnhaus produced porcelain first. His story is the subject of Gustav Meyrink's Goldmachergeschichten and features in Bruce Chatwin's novel Utz.
johann-friedrich-struensee: Johann Friedrich Struensee was born at Halle an der Saale and baptized on 7 August 1737, the third of six children of Adam Struensee, a Pietist theologian who later became general superintendent of Schleswig and Holstein. He entered the University of Halle at fifteen and graduated as a doctor of medicine on 12 December 1757. There he met Enlightenment ideas and became a supporter of atheism and of the writings of Claude Adrien Helvétius and other French materialists. In 1758 he moved with his parents to Altona, where he worked as a public doctor and published Enlightenment treatises in his journal Zum Nutzen und Vergnügen.

In Altona Struensee met aristocrats sent away from the court in Copenhagen, among them Count Schack Carl Rantzau, who recommended him as physician to King Christian VII on a tour of western Germany, the Netherlands, England and France. He was appointed in April 1768. During the eight-month tour he won the king's confidence, and in January 1769 he became the king's personal physician. By spring 1770 he was also the lover of Queen Caroline Matilda.

Struensee was named royal adviser on 5 May 1770, and as the king sank into mental torpor his authority became paramount. On 10 December 1770 he abolished the council of state, making the cabinet, with himself at its centre, the supreme authority. His reforms included the abolition of torture, of the corvée, of press censorship and of noble privileges, and a ban on the slave trade in the Danish colonies. Critics objected that he did not speak Danish and conducted business in German. The end of censorship brought a flood of pamphlets against him.

A conspiracy headed by Rantzau, in the name of Queen Dowager Juliana Maria, ended in a palace coup in the early morning of 17 January 1772, when Struensee, his associate Enevold Brandt and the queen were arrested. Struensee was charged with usurping royal authority in breach of the Royal Law. He was condemned to lose his right hand and then be beheaded and quartered, and the sentence was carried out on 28 April 1772, with Brandt executed first. In 1775 the king wrote in German on a drawing that he would have liked to have saved them both.
johann-froben: Froben was born in Hammelburg in Franconia and first appears in 1486 in the Nuremberg workshop of the printer Anton Koberger. He moved to Basel in the 1480s, studied at its university and there came to know the printer Johann Amerbach. He set up as a printer in the city about 1491, when he published the first manageable Bible in octavo format, and soon gained a reputation across Europe for accuracy and taste. In 1500 he married Gertrude Lachner, daughter of the bookseller Wolfgang Lachner, who became his partner.

He employed Sebastian Brant as editor for Gratian's Decretum of 1493 and the Decretales of Pope Gregory IX of 1494. From 1496 to 1512 he joined Amerbach and Johannes Petri in a printing alliance known as the Three Hannsen for large projects such as the collected works of Augustine of Hippo, and in 1507 he bought Amerbach's printing house, the Haus zum Sessel.

In 1513 he published Erasmus's Adagia, and from 1514 Erasmus, who lived in his house when in Basel, had his own works printed there and supervised Froben's editions of Jerome, Cyprian, Tertullian, Hilary of Poitiers and Ambrose. Martin Luther used Froben's edition of Erasmus's Novum Testamentum of 1516 for his translation. Froben and later his son published more than 200 works by Erasmus, distributed to Venice, London, Frankfurt and Paris. Besides Holbein, he employed Urs Graf, who designed his device, and Albrecht Dürer, with block cutters such as Hans Lützelburger. He was known for his Greek type and was among the first printers with a Hebrew typeface.

Froben died in Basel in October 1527. His son Hieronymus Froben carried on the business, working with Johann Herwagen and later Nikolaus Episcopius. A memorial plaque in Hebrew, Greek and Latin stands in St Peter's Church in Basel. In a letter written that year Erasmus said that his grief for his friend was greater than for his own brother. According to his employee Beatus Rhenanus, Froben published only works of importance.
johann-geiler-von-kaysersberg: Geiler was born at Schaffhausen on 16 March 1445, but from 1448 he grew up at Kaysersberg in Upper Alsace. His father was killed in a hunting accident when the boy was three, and his grandfather, who lived in Kaysersberg, brought him up and sent him to school at Ammerschwihr, where his mother lived.

In 1460, aged fifteen, he entered the newly opened University of Freiburg, became Master of Arts and lectured on Aristotle, the Sententiae of Peter Lombard and the commentaries of Alexander of Hales; for a short time he was dean of the philosophical faculty. Drawn to theology by the writings of Jean Gerson, he moved to the University of Basel in May 1471 and took his doctorate in 1475. There he formed a lasting friendship with Sebastian Brant and preached his first sermons in the cathedral.

After a time preaching in Würzburg Cathedral, Geiler was urged by Peter Schott, a senator of Strasbourg, to settle in that city. Strasbourg's preachers had been supplied by the mendicant orders, which brought frequent changes and friction with the cathedral clergy, so the chapter, Bishop Albert of Palatinate-Mosbach and the city set up a permanent post for a secular priest in 1478. In 1481 a pulpit was built for him in the nave, as the chapel of Saint Lawrence had proved too small. He preached every Sunday and feast day, daily during fasts, and often in the city's monasteries. Emperor Maximilian once called him to Füssen for advice.

Suffering from a kidney complaint and then dropsy, Geiler died in Strasbourg on Lætare Sunday 1510 and was buried at the foot of his pulpit before a large crowd. He wrote his sermons out beforehand in Latin, but others took them down in German as he spoke and published them, sometimes without his consent; the scholar E. Martin counted only thirty-five writings as genuine. His sermons on Brant's Ship of Fools of 1494 were the most popular.

Geiler and his friend Jakob Wimpfeling sought reform through the restoration of Christian morals within the Church's doctrine, not in the spirit of Martin Luther, yet his moral reforms laid the groundwork for the Protestant Reformation in Strasbourg. His writings are a source for the speech, customs and beliefs of ordinary people at the beginning of the sixteenth century.
johann-gottfried-herder: Johann Gottfried Herder was born on 25 August 1744 in Mohrungen, now Morąg in Poland, in the Kingdom of Prussia, the son of a teacher. He grew up in a poor household and educated himself from his father's Bible and songbook. In 1762, at seventeen, he enrolled at the University of Königsberg, where he studied under Immanuel Kant and became a protégé of the philosopher Johann Georg Hamann, who disputed the claims of pure secular reason.

In 1764 Herder went to Riga as a Lutheran pastor and teacher, and there he wrote his first major works, which were literary criticism. In September 1770 he met the young Goethe at Strasbourg, whom his criticism inspired to develop his own style, which can be seen as the beginning of the Sturm und Drang movement. In 1771 he became head pastor and court preacher at Bückeburg. By the mid-1770s Goethe, by then a well-known author, used his influence at the court of Weimar to secure Herder the post of General Superintendent, and Herder moved there in 1776, where his outlook shifted towards classicism.

Late in his career he endorsed the French Revolution, which earned him the enmity of many colleagues, and he and Goethe experienced a personal split. He was ennobled in 1802, and he died in Weimar in 1803, aged 59.

Herder was one of the first to argue that language shapes the patterns by which each linguistic community thinks and feels. In his Treatise on the Origin of Language of 1772 he defined language as the natural organ of the understanding. His most ambitious work, the four-volume Ideas for a Philosophy of the History of Mankind, was published between 1784 and 1791 and is regarded as an origin of the modern school of historical thought.

Germans had no nation-state until the nineteenth century, and Herder was among the first German intellectuals to base a national consciousness mainly on language and literature. He taught that every nation carries its own standard of perfection, and that the true spirit of a people lies in its folk songs, poetry and dances. He collected folk songs, published in 1773 as Voices of the Peoples in Their Songs, which Achim von Arnim and Clemens von Brentano later drew on for The Boy's Magic Horn. He refused a rigid racial theory, writing that there is only one species of man throughout the whole earth.
johann-gottlieb-fichte: Fichte was born on 19 May 1762 in Rammenau and baptized a Lutheran, into a pious family that had lived in the region for generations. He was the son of a ribbon weaver, Christian Fichte, who married Maria Dorothea Schurich somewhat above his class. Fichte attended the foundation school at Pforta from October 1774. Miltitz's widow supported him until 1784, which let him study theology at Jena and Leipzig, but when she withdrew her help he had to leave without a degree and worked as a tutor for several families, and in Zürich met his future wife, Johanna Maria Rahn.

In the summer of 1790 Fichte began to study the works of Kant. After a disappointing interview with Kant at Königsberg on 4 July 1791 he wrote, in five weeks, the Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation. The first edition appeared without his name or preface and was believed to be a new work by Kant, until Kant cleared up the confusion and praised the author, and Fichte's reputation soared. He married Johanna on 22 October 1793. He was invited to the University of Jena and began lecturing in May 1794, expounding his system of transcendental idealism with success.

In 1798 he was accused of atheism over an essay in which he argued that the living moral order is itself God. He was dismissed in 1799 and, since every German state but Prussia had joined the outcry, went to Berlin, where he joined the circle of Friedrich and August Wilhelm Schlegel, Schleiermacher and Schelling. In 1807 and 1808 he delivered the Addresses to the German Nation, which attempted to define the German nation. In the new University of Berlin, founded in 1810, he was unanimously elected rector, but resigned in 1812 after friction. He died of typhus on 29 January 1814, aged 51.

Fichte rejected Kant's things in themselves, the supra-sensible reality beyond perception, as an invitation to skepticism. He argued instead that consciousness is not grounded in anything outside itself and that the phenomenal world arises from consciousness, the activity of the I, and moral awareness. In Foundations of Natural Right (1797) he argued that self-consciousness is a social phenomenon: an individual becomes aware of itself as free only when other rational subjects summon it, and mutual recognition is a condition for the individual I. He is also the originator of thesis, antithesis and synthesis, an idea often attributed to Hegel in error.
johann-heinrich-pestalozzi: Pestalozzi was born on 12 January 1746 in Zürich, the second of three children. His father, a surgeon and oculist, died when Pestalozzi was five, and the family was supported with the help of their maid, Barbara Schmid. On holidays he visited his grandfather, a clergyman in Höngg, where he learned of the poverty of country peasants.

He was educated to become a clergyman, but the failure of his first sermon and the influence of Rousseau led him towards law and politics. At 19 he joined the Helvetic Society, founded by his former teacher Johann Jakob Bodmer. He exposed cases of official corruption and was held under arrest for three days; this made him many political enemies and ended his hopes of a legal career.
