He then became a farmer, married Anna Schulthess in 1769 and built a house called Neuhof on heavily mortgaged land that proved unsuitable for farming.

He published the four volumes of Leonard and Gertrude between 1781 and 1787, drawing on his knowledge of peasant life. In it a mother, Gertrude, teaches her children to live morally, and a schoolteacher, a clergyman and a politician follow her example.

When serfdom was abolished in Switzerland in 1798 he decided to become an educator. After the French army invaded Stans in 1798, the Swiss government recruited him on 5 December to run a new orphanage there; the first orphans arrived on 14 January 1799, in a dreadful condition of body and mind. He then taught at Burgdorf from 1800 and opened the Educational Institute for the Children of the Middle Classes in its castle in October 1800.

The institute at Yverdon opened in July 1805 and attracted visitors and pupils from all over Europe, with governments sending educators to study there. Disunion grew among his colleagues, and a state commission in 1810 praised his ideas but not the institute's practices, ending hopes that Yverdon would become a state institution.

Pestalozzi returned to Neuhof and published his Swansong, which provoked bitter replies from Fellenberg and Niederer. He fell ill on 15 February 1827 and died in Brugg two days later. His methods were child-centred and based on individual differences, sense perception and the pupil's self-activity, and he held that human nature is essentially good. Friedrich Fröbel, the creator of the kindergarten, was his student, and Charles and Elizabeth Mayo founded the formal education of infant teachers in Britain after Charles lived with him at Yverdon from 1819 to 1822.
johann-i-joseph-prince-of-liechtenstein: Johann Baptist Josef Adam Johann Nepomuk Aloys Franz de Paula was born on 26 June 1760, the fourth son of Franz Joseph I, Prince of Liechtenstein, and Countess Leopoldine von Sternberg. His two eldest brothers died young. The next eldest, Aloys I, Prince of Liechtenstein, died childless in 1805, which brought Johann to the throne. At the age of 21 he entered the army as a lieutenant in a cuirassier regiment, and in 1785 he joined the Freemason lodge in Vienna.

During the Austro-Turkish War of 1788-1791 Johann was promoted rapidly to colonel and gained a name as a cavalry officer. He received the Knight's Cross of the Military Order of Maria Theresa in 1790. In the French Revolutionary Wars he took part in a cavalry action at Avesnes-le-Sec on 12 September 1793, in which Republican troops lost 2,000 killed and wounded and the Allies only 69 men.

He fought at the Battle of Fleurus after promotion to General-Major in June 1794, and in the War of the Second Coalition he commanded the Austrian Reserve at the Battle of Trebbia and a cavalry division at the Battle of Hohenlinden on 3 December 1800.

At the Battle of Austerlitz he led the 4,600 cavalry of the 5th Column but could not save the Austrian-Russian army from defeat. He then negotiated the Peace of Pressburg with Napoleon. In the War of the Fifth Coalition he commanded the I Reserve Korps under Archduke Charles at Eckmühl, Aspern-Essling and Wagram. When the archduke resigned he took command of the main army until the end of 1809, and Emperor Francis II promoted him Feldmarschall in September. He negotiated and signed the Peace of Schönbrunn, which, like Pressburg, was hard on Austria. He was afterwards accused of little diplomatic skill and resigned from the army in 1810.

Johann ruled as Prince of Liechtenstein from 1805 to 1806 and again from 1814 until 1836, and was regent from 1806 until 1814. In 1806 Napoleon incorporated Liechtenstein in the Confederation of the Rhine and made it a sovereign state. The Congress of Vienna approved its sovereignty, and in 1815 it became a member of the German Confederation.

Johann made forward-looking reforms but governed in an absolutist manner. In 1818 he granted a limited constitution. He expanded agriculture and forestry, reorganised his administration, and laid out Biedermeier gardens and parks on the English model. He married Landgravine Josefa of Fürstenberg-Weitra in 1792, and they had fourteen children. He died in Vienna on 20 April 1836 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Aloys II.
johann-ii-prince-of-liechtenstein: Johann Maria Franz Placidus was the elder son of Aloys II, Prince of Liechtenstein, and Countess Franziska Kinsky of Wchinitz and Tettau. He came to the throne on 12 November 1858, shortly after his eighteenth birthday. His mother acted for him from 10 February 1859 to November 1860, but she was appointed by her son to fulfil his duties because he wished to finish his education, not as a regent for a minor. His reign lasted 70 years and 91 days, and no regent for an underage sovereign was ever employed.

In 1862 Johann issued Liechtenstein's first constitution, which was heavily influenced by Vorarlberg. Liechtenstein left the German Confederation in 1866, and soon afterwards its army was abolished as an unnecessary expense. In 1867 Alexander II of Russia offered him Russian Alaska for purchase, but he refused because he believed the territory was useless.

After the First World War, under significant popular demand, he granted a new constitution, ratified on 5 October 1921. It gave considerable political rights to ordinary Liechtensteiners and made the principality a constitutional monarchy; it has survived with revisions, most notably in 2003. Liechtenstein stayed neutral in the war, which broke its alliance with Austria-Hungary and led to a customs union with Switzerland. Johann cooled relations with Austria-Hungary and its successor states and forged closer ties with Switzerland, and in 1924 the Swiss franc became the official currency.

Johann added much to the Liechtenstein Princely Collections and was a prominent patron of the arts and sciences, though he was considered unsociable and took no part in Austrian politics or the Austrian military. He never married and had no children. From 1884 he rebuilt Liechtenstein Castle near Vienna, which had fallen into ruins, and between 1905 and 1920 Schloss Vaduz was renovated and expanded. Like his ancestors he never lived in the principality but on the family's Austrian and Moravian estates, chiefly at Lednice and Valtice. His eyesight failed in his later years, and he underwent cataract surgery on 12 November 1928. He died on 11 February 1929 and was succeeded by his younger brother Franz I.
johann-ludwig-burckhardt: Burckhardt was born on 24 November 1784 in Lausanne, into a wealthy Basel family of silk merchants. After studying at the universities of Leipzig and Göttingen he travelled to England in the summer of 1806, hoping for a post in the civil service. Unsuccessful, he took employment with the African Association, which wanted the course of the Niger River explained. The expedition called for an overland journey from Cairo to Timbuktu, and to prepare for it he attended Cambridge University, studied Arabic, science and medicine, and began to adopt Arabian costume.

In 1809 he left England for Aleppo to perfect his Arabic and his knowledge of Muslim customs. In Syria he took the alias Sheikh Ibrahim Ibn Abdallah, investigated local languages and archaeological sites, and became the first European discoverer of Hittite or Luwian hieroglyphs. He was robbed more than once by men he had paid for protection. After more than two years he tested his disguise on three journeys through Syria, Palestine and Transjordan, then left Aleppo in early 1812 and headed south.

On 22 August 1812, on the road towards Cairo, he was led through a narrow valley and became the first modern European to see the Nabataean city of Petra. Fearing exposure as a treasure-seeking unbeliever, he could not stay long or take detailed notes. He reached Cairo on 4 September 1812. In March 1813, travelling in Nubia, he found the sand-choked Great Temple of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel but could not clear its entrance. He told Giovanni Belzoni, who returned in 1817 and excavated it.

Burckhardt entered Jeddah on 18 July 1814 and was permitted to travel to Mecca, where he spent several months performing the rituals of the Hajj, which was unheard of for a European. His detailed observations later served Richard Burton. He spent his last two years in Cairo editing his journals and preparing for the caravan across the Sahara. He died there of dysentery on 15 October 1817, never having made his journey to the Niger, and was buried as a Muslim under a tombstone bearing his assumed name.

He bequeathed 800 volumes of oriental manuscripts to the library of Cambridge University. The African Association published his works after his death, among them Travels in Nubia (1819), Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (1822) and Travels in Arabia (1829).
johann-ludwig-krapf: Krapf was born on 11 January 1810 into a Lutheran farming family in southwest Germany and showed a gift for languages from his school days, learning Latin, Greek, French and Italian. He entered the Basel Mission Seminary at 17 but left it, doubting his vocation, and studied theology at the University of Tübingen, graduating in 1834. While an assistant village pastor he met the Basel missionary Peter Fjellstedt, who encouraged him to return to mission work.

Seconded by the Basel Mission to the Church Missionary Society, he worked in Ethiopia from 1837 to 1842, learning Ge'ez and Amharic. He travelled from Tadjura to Shewa, where he presented himself to its ruler, Sahle Selassie, and later turned to the Oromo, then called the Galla, learning their language and translating parts of the New Testament into it. In 1842 he received a doctorate from Tübingen for his research into Ethiopian languages, and in the same year all Western missionaries were expelled from Ethiopia.

After marrying in Alexandria, he went to the East African coast, then mostly part of the Zanzibar sultanate, and Sultan Sayyid Said allowed him to open a station at Mombasa. Soon after arriving his wife and young daughter died of malaria, and he moved to the higher ground of Rabai, where he founded New Rabai and wrote the first dictionary and grammar of Swahili. Joined in 1846 by Johannes Rebmann, he explored the interior; their reports of the snowcapped Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya were ridiculed by experts in Europe. He visited Ukambani, homeland of the Kamba people, in 1849 and 1850.

Failing health forced him back to Germany in 1853. He brought old Swahili manuscripts with him, including copies of the Book of the Battle of Tambuka, the earliest Swahili manuscript, and continued his linguistic and advisory work for the missions in Korntal. He died on 26 November 1881. The Anglican Church of Kenya counts him as its founding father, and his house at New Rabai is now part of the Rabai Museum of the National Museums of Kenya.
johann-lukas-von-hildebrandt: Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt was born on 14 November 1668 in Genoa, the son of an Italian mother and a German father. As a young man he moved to Rome, where he studied architecture under Carlo Fontana and military engineering under Colonel Carlo Cerutti. In 1695 and 1696 he took part as a volunteer engineer in three of Prince Eugene of Savoy's campaigns in Piedmont. In 1696 he settled in Vienna, where he became Prince Eugene's favourite architect and also worked for noble families such as the Dauns, Harrachs, Schönborns and Starhembergs.

Hildebrandt became a court engineer at the Hofburg in 1700 and head of the court's building department in 1711. He was promoted to court architect in 1723, when he also became inspector-general of the imperial buildings. Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach and his son Joseph Emanuel dominated state and court architecture, so he built his reputation working for prominent Viennese families. From 1713 to 1716 he was employed by the Kinsky family, building their residence, the Palais Kinsky in Vienna. He was also involved in projects begun by other architects, such as Würzburg, Göttweig Abbey, Pommersfelden and the Palais Schwarzenberg.

Unlike the monumental works of his rivals, Hildebrandt's designs were more personal and had more decorative elements, which spread their popularity to the middle class. He united Italian and French elements and shaped the development of the baroque style in south Germany and Austria. His two best-known works are the Lower Belvedere (1714–1716) and the Upper Belvedere (1721–1722), both commissioned by Prince Eugene. He built many city palaces in Vienna, among them the Daun-Kinsky in 1716, and religious buildings, including St Peter's Church and the Maria Treu Piarist church in Vienna and the Teutonic Church in Linz. Outside Austria he built the Savoy Castle at Ráckeve in Hungary. He died in Vienna on 16 November 1745, and his principles spread throughout central and southeast Europe.
johann-matthias-von-der-schulenburg: Schulenburg was born at Emden near Magdeburg, a son of Gustavus Adolphus, Baron von der Schulenburg, and came from a Brandenburg-Prussian family; his sister was Melusine von der Schulenburg, Duchess of Kendal. In 1687 and 1688 he fought with the Imperial troops against the Turks in Hungary, and on his return he rose through the ranks of the army of the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg. In 1699 he became colonel of a German regiment in the service of Victor Amadeus II of Savoy, and he was badly wounded in 1701.

In 1702 he joined the Saxon army and fought in the Great Northern War against Charles XII of Sweden, suffering defeats at the Battle of Klissow and the Battle of Fraustadt before the Swedish invasion of Saxony in 1706. Returning to western Europe in 1707, he served under Prince Eugene of Savoy in the War of the Spanish Succession at the Battle of Oudenaarde, the Siege of Tournai and the Battle of Malplaquet.

That service brought him to the attention of Venice, which engaged him against the Ottoman Turks. For his defence of Corfu in 1716 the Serenissima honoured him with a statue and a pension of 5,000 ducats a year, and a Vivaldi oratorio, Juditha triumphans, was commissioned to celebrate the victory.

From 1718 Schulenburg lived in retirement in the Palazzo Loredan on the Grand Canal and became a major collector and patron. He began in earnest in 1724, at the age of sixty-three, buying eighty-eight paintings and a bas-relief by Pierre Puget from the dealer Santi Rota, who had them from the collection of Ferdinando Carlo Gonzaga, the last ruler of Mantua. He paid Gian Antonio Guardi a monthly salary in 1730–36, employed Giambattista Pittoni from 1733 to 1738 and used Giovanni Battista Piazzetta as painter and buying agent; Canaletto painted a view of Corfu, the site of his victories.

His collection was mostly Italian paintings of the 16th and 17th centuries, with some Flemish and Dutch works. He had no children and left it whole to his nephew Count Adolf Friedrich von der Schulenburg-Beetzendorf, on condition that it be kept together in the Palais Schulenburg in Berlin, but the will was not honoured and the collection was dispersed after his death. Frederick II of Prussia was among the buyers, and 150 pieces were auctioned in London in April 1775.
johann-michael-fischer: Fischer was born on 18 February 1692 in Burglengenfeld in the Upper Palatinate. He trained in Bohemia, and his buildings combine Bohemian elements with the Baroque traditions of Bavaria. His first commission was the Benedictine monastery of St. Mauritius at Niederalteich, built in 1724–1726.

In all Fischer designed 32 churches and 23 monasteries in southern Germany, often working with the leading Bavarian artists of his time, among them the brothers Cosmas Damian Asam and Egid Quirin Asam, Johann Michael Feuchtmayer, Matthäus Günther, Ignaz Günther, Johann Baptist Straub and Johann Baptist Zimmermann. In Bavaria his works include the papal basilica of St. Margaretha at Osterhofen Abbey (1727–1740), the church of St. Maria at Dießen am Ammersee, completed in 1739, the Franciscan church of St. Anna im Lehel in Munich, consecrated in 1737, and the pilgrimage church of Maria Schnee at Aufhausen (1736–1751).

The Benedictine church of the Holy Trinity at Ottobeuren occupied him from 1737 until his death, and Zwiefalten Abbey (1741–1747) is regarded as a model of integrated Baroque design. His late works include the Anastasia Chapel at Benediktbeuern (1750–1758) and the abbey church of St. Marinus and St. Anianus at Rott am Inn, begun in 1759. The monastery church of St. Martin at Wiblingen Abbey was built by Johann Georg Specht to his designs.

Fischer died in Munich on 6 May 1766, aged 74, and is buried in the Munich Frauenkirche. Several buildings once credited to him, such as the pilgrimage church of St. Anne at Haigerloch and the parish church of St. Nikolaus at Murnau, are now disputed, though his influence on them is clear.
johann-reinhold-patkul: Patkul was born in prison at Stockholm, where his father was held on suspicion of treason, and entered the Swedish Army young, rising to captain. In 1689 he led a deputation of Livonian gentry to Stockholm to protest against the rigour of Charles XI's land recovery in the province. The king was impressed by his eloquence but ignored the complaint. A second petition, in sharper language, led to a prosecution; Patkul fled to Switzerland, was condemned in absentia to lose his right hand and his head, and had his estates confiscated.

After four years of wandering and a vain plea for pardon from Charles XII, he entered the service of Augustus II the Strong in 1698, intending to wrest Livonia from Sweden. At Dresden he pressed plans for a partition of Sweden, first with Saxony, Denmark and Brandenburg, and when Brandenburg failed him he reluctantly brought in Russia. The tsar was to take Ingria and Estonia and Augustus Livonia. At a secret conference at Preobrazhenskoye, Patkul persuaded Peter the Great to join the league on 18 November 1699. He worked closely with the Danish Privy Councillor Knud Thott for a Danish intervention.

In 1702 he moved to Russian service and in Vienna recruited the Scottish general George Benedict Ogilvie for Peter. His missions had mixed results: in 1703 he failed to end the Paliy uprising in talks with Semen Paliy at Bila Tserkva, but on 19 August 1704 he concluded the alliance of Narva between Russia and the Polish republic. He could not bring Prussia into the league.

When he arranged with the imperial commissioner Stratmann to hire out a Russian auxiliary contingent to the Habsburgs, Saxon ministers arrested him on 19 December 1705 and held him at Sonnenstein, ignoring Peter's protests. Charles XII refused an appeal for mercy from his sister Ulrica, saying a traitor could not be pardoned. Patkul was broken on the wheel at Kazimierz Biskupi in Poland, and the accounts agree that he begged to be beheaded, which took several strikes. The chaplain Hagen, who was with him in his last two days, published a narrative of his death in 1707.
johann-sebastian-bach: Johann Sebastian Bach was born in Eisenach on 21 March 1685 (Old Style; 31 March in the new), the eighth and youngest child of Johann Ambrosius Bach, a violinist and director of the town musicians, and Maria Elisabeth, née Lämmerhirt. The Bach family spanned four generations of musicians across Thuringia. Little is known of his early years, and his musical education is largely conjecture: he probably had early instruction from his father and sang with the local schoolboy choir. He studied theology, Latin and Greek at the Latin school, with poor attendance, perhaps because of a string of family deaths: his mother in May 1694 and his father in February 1695.

In 1703 Bach returned to Thuringia and worked as a musician for Protestant churches in Arnstadt and Mühlhausen. He also paid extended visits to the court at Weimar, where he expanded his organ repertory, and to the reformed court at Köthen, where he was mostly engaged with chamber music. By 1723 he was Thomaskantor in Leipzig, responsible for music in four Lutheran city churches and for the St. Thomas School. He decided to compose annual cycles of church cantatas, and wrote for the university's student ensemble, the Collegium Musicum.

Bach began publishing his organ and other keyboard music in 1726. His relations with his employer in Leipzig were difficult, as they had been in some earlier posts. They eased somewhat when Augustus III of Poland granted him the title of court composer of the Elector of Saxony in 1736. In his last decades he reworked and extended many earlier compositions. He died on 28 July 1750, aged 65, of complications following eye surgery. Four of his twenty children, Wilhelm Friedemann, Carl Philipp Emanuel, Johann Christoph Friedrich and Johann Christian, became composers.

Bach's music covers every genre of his time except opera: more than 200 sacred and secular cantatas, oratorios, Passions, motets and Latin church music, a large body of organ and keyboard music, and collections of orchestral and chamber music. He never left modern Germany apart from two brief trips to Bohemia, yet he knew European music widely. He sought to unite Italian and French traditions, particularly the Italian sonata and the French suite, in a mixed style. From about 1712 the music of Antonio Vivaldi was his most important influence.
johann-tserclaes-count-of-tilly: Johann Tserclaes was born in February 1559 at Castle Tilly in Walloon Brabant, then in the Spanish Netherlands, to a devoutly Catholic Brabantine family. After a Jesuit education in Cologne he joined the Spanish Army at fifteen and served under Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma, in the Eighty Years' War, taking part in the Siege of Antwerp in 1585. He then fought as a mercenary against the Turks in Hungary and Transylvania in the Long Turkish War and became a field marshal within five years. In 1610 Maximilian I, Duke of Bavaria, made him commander of the forces of the Catholic League.

Tilly had trained his soldiers in the Spanish tercio system, with musketeers supported by deep ranks of pikemen. On 8 November 1620 his force of 25,000 men, together with imperial troops, defeated Christian of Anhalt and Count Thurn at White Mountain, near Prague. In 1622 he lost at Mingolsheim, then won at Wimpfen and at Höchst, for which he was made a count, and took Heidelberg after an eleven-week siege. At Stadtlohn he destroyed most of the army of Christian the Younger of Brunswick. At Lutter, on 26–27 August 1626, he defeated the Danes of Christian IV, and Denmark sued for peace.

In 1631 Tilly besieged Magdeburg, which had promised to support Sweden. The city was stormed on 20 May under Gottfried Heinrich Graf zu Pappenheim, and about 20,000 of its 25,000 inhabitants died in the massacre and fire. Many historians think it unlikely that Tilly ordered the city burned, and he had offered terms days earlier. At Breitenfeld on 17 September 1631 he was outmanoeuvred by Gustavus Adolphus and crushingly defeated.

Tilly beat the Swedes at Bamberg on 9 March 1632. On 15 April, trying to stop them crossing the Lech near Rain, he was struck in the right thigh by an arquebus bullet, and he died of a bone infection at Ingolstadt on 30 April, aged 73. He is buried at Altötting in Upper Bavaria. With Albrecht von Wallenstein he was one of the two chief commanders of the Empire's forces in the first half of the war, and the military historian Gaston Bodart counted him among the most notable commanders of modern times.
johann-weikhard-von-valvasor: Valvasor was baptised in Ljubljana Cathedral on 28 May 1641; neither the day nor the place of his birth is known. His family was aristocratic and came originally from Bergamo, and it had been brought to the Duchy of Carniola in the 16th century by Johann Baptist Valvasor. He was the twelfth child of Bartholomäus and Anna Maria Freiin von Rauber. His father died when he was ten and his mother when he was 16, while he was attending the Jesuit school in Ljubljana.

He graduated in 1659 and chose not to go to a university, travelling instead to meet learned men. The journey lasted fourteen years and took him as far as northern Africa. During it he joined the army in the Austro-Turkish War and became closely acquainted with conditions on the Croatian Military Frontier.

Shortly after marrying Anna Rosina Grafenweger in 1672, Valvasor acquired Bogenšperk Castle near Litija, where he arranged a writing, drawing and printing workshop. Among his early works were topographies of Carniola and Carinthia, printed from 1679, and the Theatrum mortis humanae of 1682. In 1687 his extensive treatise on the hydrology of intermittent Lake Cerknica won him a fellowship of the Royal Society, at the proposal of Edmond Halley. He is known as a pioneer in the study of karst phenomena.

His most important work, The Glory of the Duchy of Carniola, appeared in 1689 in 15 books and four volumes, with 3,532 pages, 528 illustrations and 24 appendices. It gives a vivid description of Carniola at the time and records the first written document on vampires, the legend of Jure Grando in Istria. Until the late 19th century it was the main source for older Slovenian history, which makes him a precursor of modern Slovenian historiography.

Valvasor spent a fortune on publishing his books. Towards the end of his life his debts forced him to sell Bogenšperk, his library and his collection of prints. In 1690 Aleksandar Ignacije Mikulić, the Bishop of Zagreb, bought the library and some 7,300 graphics. In 1692 he lost most of his remaining wealth through unprofitable investments in travel, graphics and printbooks. Three months after the death of his first wife in 1687 he married Baroness Anna Maximilla Zetschker of Vrhovo. He died at Krško in 1693, aged 52. A translation of the Glory into Slovene appeared between 2009 and 2012.
johann-wilhelm-ludwig-gleim: Gleim was born on 2 April 1719 at Ermsleben in the Principality of Halberstadt, then part of Prussia. His father, a tax collector, and his mother died early. He attended school in Wernigerode and from 1738 studied law at the University of Halle, where he formed a circle of young poets with his friends Johann Uz and Johann Nikolaus Götz.

He worked as a tutor in Berlin and in 1743 became secretary to the Hohenzollern prince Frederick William of Brandenburg-Schwedt, whom he accompanied in the Second Silesian War, meeting Ewald Christian von Kleist, whose devoted friend he became. After the prince was killed at the siege of Prague, he served Prince Leopold of Anhalt-Dessau but soon left, unable to bear the roughness of the Old Dessauer. In 1747 he became secretary of the Halberstadt Cathedral chapter, and from 1756 also a canon at Walbeck monastery.

Influenced by the lecturers Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten and Georg Friedrich Meier at Halle, Gleim cultivated the Anacreontic tradition of short, easy lyrics. He wrote many imitations of Anacreon, Horace and the minnesingers, a didactic poem inspired by his reading in the Quran, Halladat oder das rote Buch (1774), and collections of fables and romances. C.P.E. Bach, Beethoven, Joseph Haydn, Reichardt, Schubart and Spohr set some of the Anacreontic poems.

His Preussische Kriegslieder von einem Grenadier (1758), inspired by Frederick the Great's campaigns in the Seven Years' War, are often marked by genuine feeling and vigorous expression and were the first of a long series of political songs in German literature. Written to a Chevy Chase tune and first set by Christian Gottfried Krause, they drew wide attention in a collection edited by Lessing in 1758. Later generations judged his other writings commonplace, though only recently has his work been reassessed. His contributions include establishing German as a literary language and promoting young talents such as Heinse, Johann Heinrich Voss, Seume and Jean Paul.

Gleim was known throughout literary Germany as Father Gleim for his kind-hearted but undiscriminating patronage of poets. At his house near Halberstadt Cathedral he created a Temple of Friendship, where poets and intellectuals met and two rooms held more than 120 portraits of friends by the time of his death, by artists such as Anton Graff and members of the Tischbein family. He died in Halberstadt on 18 February 1803, completely blind, and was buried in his garden on the Holtemme. In 1862 his library of 12,000 books and his letters and manuscripts formed the core of the Gleimhaus, one of the oldest literary museums in Germany. The Gleim Prize for Literature has been awarded since 1995 for non-fiction on the 18th century.
johann-wolfgang-von-goethe: Goethe's grandfather, Friedrich Georg Goethe, moved to Frankfurt from Thuringia in 1687 and changed the spelling of the family name from Göthe. He worked first as a tailor and then opened a tavern. Goethe's father, Johann Caspar Goethe, had studied law in Leipzig and held the title of Imperial Councillor, but took no part in the official affairs of Frankfurt, then a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire. He married Catharina Elisabeth Textor on 20 August 1748. Of their children only Johann Wolfgang and his sister Cornelia survived. The father had the boy taught by private tutors in Latin, Greek, French, Italian and English, as well as dancing, riding and fencing.

His tragedy Götz von Berlichingen (1773) first brought him recognition, and The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774) brought him enormous fame; it is arguably the world's first best-seller. Goethe settled in Weimar in 1775 and was ennobled by Karl August, Duke of Saxe-Weimar, in 1782. He sat on the Duke's privy council from 1776 to 1785, oversaw the reopening of silver mines at Ilmenau and carried out reforms at the University of Jena. After a tour of Italy in 1788 he published his first major scientific work, the Metamorphosis of Plants.

In 1791 he became managing director of the Weimar theatre. From 1794 he was friends with Friedrich Schiller, whose plays he premiered until Schiller's death in 1805. The first part of Faust appeared in 1808. His conversations and shared projects in the 1790s with Schiller, Herder, Fichte and others are collectively termed Weimar Classicism.

Goethe also studied natural science, writing on morphology and colour theory, and he told Johann Peter Eckermann he took more pride in his science of colours than in his poetry. By his death he had gathered 17,800 rock samples. He died in Weimar in 1832 of apparent heart failure. His last words are usually abridged to Mehr Licht!, 'more light', although the earliest account, by Karl Wilhelm Müller, gives a longer request to open a second shutter. Composers including Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert and Liszt set his poems to music, and the mineral goethite is named after him.
johannes-brahms: Johannes Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833. His father, Johann Jakob Brahms, a double bass and horn player from Heide in Holstein, gave him his first musical training, and from 1840 he studied piano with Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel. The family lived in poor apartments in the Gängeviertel and struggled economically. By 1845 he had written a piano sonata in G minor, though his parents disapproved of his composing and thought a performer's career offered better prospects.

In 1850 Brahms met the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi and accompanied him in recitals; this introduced him to the csardas, the foundation of the two sets of Hungarian Dances of 1869 and 1880. In 1853 he visited Joseph Joachim at Hanover, a lifelong friendship, and met Franz Liszt at Weimar. In autumn 1862 he first visited Vienna, and he based himself there increasingly and made it his home. In 1863 he became conductor of the Wiener Singakademie, programming Heinrich Schütz and J. S. Bach, and left in 1864 because the post took too much time from composing.

His First Symphony appeared in 1876, having been begun in the early 1860s; Hans von Bülow called it Beethoven's Tenth. The Second Symphony (1877), the Violin Concerto (1878) and the Academic Festival and Tragic Overtures (1880) followed. His admiration for Richard Mühlfeld, clarinettist of the Meiningen orchestra, revived his interest in composing after 1890 and led him to write the Clarinet Trio and Clarinet Quintet in 1891 and two Clarinet Sonatas in 1894.

His major works include four symphonies, two piano concertos and A German Requiem, which sets texts he chose from the Luther Bible and was composed over three periods of his life, with most of it written after his mother's death in 1865. He also wrote chamber music and hundreds of folk-song arrangements and Lieder. Cast as conservative absolute music against the New German School of Liszt and Wagner, his music was praised by Eduard Hanslick, and Hans von Bülow named him the heir of Bach and Beethoven, which Richard Wagner mocked. He died on 3 April 1897; the last notes he wrote were in the final chorale prelude of his Op. 122.
johannes-brand: Johannes Henricus Brand was born in Cape Town on 6 December 1823, the son of Sir Christoffel Joseph Brand, speaker of the Cape legislative assembly, and Catharina Fredrica Küchler. He was educated at the South African College, took the degree of D.C.L. at Leiden in the Netherlands in 1845 and was called to the English bar at the Inner Temple in 1849. In 1851 he married Johanna Sibella Zastron, daughter of the Registrar of Deeds in Cape Town; they had eight sons and three daughters.

Back in Cape Town, Brand practised as an advocate in the Supreme Court of the Cape of Good Hope until 1863, and in 1858 he was appointed professor of law at the South African College. As a young member of the Cape Parliament he supported John Molteno's Responsible Government movement, which sought greater independence from Britain, but he found its principles too moderate and moved to the Orange Free State, whose republican ideals he shared.

Elected president in 1863, Brand took office on 2 February 1864 and was re-elected for five-year terms in 1869, 1874, 1879 and 1884. After trying in vain to persuade Moshoeshoe, the Basuto chief, to keep his people within the Free State boundary, he went to war against them in 1865. The first war ended with the Treaty of Thaba Bosigo, signed on 3 April 1866, and a second with the Treaty of Aliwal North on 12 February 1869. In 1871 he opposed the British annexation of Kimberley, without success.

The same year a large party asked him to become president of the South African Republic as well, uniting the two Boer republics. Because the plan was hostile to Britain he declined, keeping to his policy of neutrality towards it, and in 1882 he was made a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George. He was deeply religious and popular with the burghers, and his saying alles zal recht komen als elkeen zijn plicht doet (all will be well if everyone does his duty) passed into Afrikaans. He died in office on 14 July 1888. A statue paid for by public subscription stands in Bloemfontein, whose main street in the city centre was named President Brand Street.
johannes-brenz: Brenz was born on 24 June 1499 in the then imperial city of Weil der Stadt, west of Stuttgart. He studied at Heidelberg, where he lectured on philology, philosophy and the Gospel of Matthew until the lectures were forbidden for their popularity and novel exegesis. He had already been won over by Luther's Ninety-five Theses and by meeting him at the Heidelberg disputation in April 1518. Threatened with a trial for heresy in 1522, he escaped through a call to the pastorate of Schwäbisch Hall.

At Hall, with his ally Johann Isenmann, he abolished the feast of Corpus Christi, turned the monastery of the Discalced Friars into a school and introduced communion in both kinds. In the German Peasants' War he condemned the peasants' abuse of evangelical liberty but pleaded for mercy for the defeated.

His Syngramma Suevicum of 21 October 1525, against Œcolampadius, defended the real presence of Christ's body and blood in the sacrament, and he went on to attend the Colloquy of Marburg in 1529 and the diet at Augsburg the following year, where he backed Melanchthon but refused any association with the followers of Zwingli. He also helped reform the University of Tübingen in 1537.

After the defeat of the Schmalkaldic League, which Hall had joined in 1538, Brenz opposed the emperor's Augsburg Interim, which he called interitus, ruin. When the imperial chancellor Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle demanded his surrender, he fled on his forty-ninth birthday, 24 June 1548, and Duke Ulrich of Württemberg hid him at Hohenwittlingen and later at Hornberg under false names. In March 1552 he went to the Council of Trent to defend the confessio Wirtembergica.

Made provost of the cathedral of Stuttgart on 24 September 1554, he was Duke Christoph's chief adviser in reorganising the church and schools of Württemberg, through the great church order of 1553 to 1559. His Catechismus of 1551 served many generations. He opposed Calvinist church discipline and taught the omnipresence of Christ's body. Paralysed in 1569, he died in Stuttgart on 11 September 1570 and was buried beneath the cathedral pulpit; the Jesuits later demolished his grave.
johannes-bugenhagen: Bugenhagen was born in Wollin, in the Duchy of Pomerania, on 24 June 1485, one of three children of the town councillor Gerhard Bugenhagen. He studied the arts at the University of Greifswald from 1502 to 1504, then moved to Treptow an der Rega and became rector of its school. Although he had not studied theology, he was ordained a priest in 1509. In 1517 Abbot Johann Boldewan called him to lecture on the Bible at Belbuck Abbey, where the two formed the core of a humanist circle, and Duke Bogislav X ordered him to write the history of Pomerania in Latin.

He first met Luther's theology in the Prelude on the Babylonian Captivity of the Church in 1520 and at first disliked it, but on studying it further became a supporter of the Reformation and moved to Wittenberg in 1521.

In Wittenberg he was elected parish pastor on 25 October 1523, making him Luther's pastor and confessor. He belonged to Luther's team translating the Bible into German and opened the debate on Ulrich Zwingli's reforms. His Latin Interpretations of the Psalms, printed in March 1524 by Adam Petri of Basel, went through four further Latin editions within half a year. On 17 March 1533 he became a doctor of theology together with Johannes Aepinus and Kaspar Cruciger, the first three Protestant doctors of theology, and in September 1535 he was appointed professor of theology at Wittenberg.

He took an active lead in writing church orders for Hamburg (1528/29), Braunschweig (1528), Lübeck (1530 to 1532), the Duchy of Pomerania (1534/5), East Frisia (1534/5), Denmark-Norway (1537), where he also crowned Christian III, Schleswig-Holstein (1542), Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel (1543) and Hildesheim (1544). This earned him the epithet Second Apostle of the North. He drew up rules for worship, schooling and church social work, and persuaded people to follow them. In 1539 he became superintendent of the Lutheran Church in Saxony and refounded the University of Greifswald as a Protestant university on the model of Wittenberg.

After Luther's death in 1546 Bugenhagen took care of his widow and children. He died in Wittenberg on 20 April 1558 and was buried in St. Mary's Church, which holds a memorial painting by Lucas Cranach the Younger. He was valued for his organising ability and for a Middle Low German translation of Luther's Bible in 1534, and he is commemorated as a pastor on 20 April in the calendar of saints of the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod. His family coat of arms shows a harp, for his love of music.
johannes-ciconia: Ciconia was the son of a priest of the same name and a woman of high social standing. Because at least three other men around Liège bore the name, his life was long confused with others', until David Fallows sorted the records in 1975; the Johannes Ciconia who worked in Avignon in 1350 was probably his father, and the young man recorded in Liège in 1385 is taken to be the composer. Papal records suggest he served Cardinal d'Alençon as a clericus capelle, and he may have been in Rome between the early 1390s and 1401.

From 1401 until his death he was a chaplain at Padua Cathedral and held a benefice at the church of San Biagio, probably serving the archpriest Francesco Zabarella, for whom he wrote the motet Doctorum principum. He may have reached Padua earlier: his lament Con lagrime bagnandome, if written for the death of Francesco il Vecchio of Carrara, as scholars have assumed, would place him there by 1393. Some scholars also suggest a stay in Pavia, where he could have met the Visconti court and the ars subtilior.

His works range from northern Italian madrigals such as Una panthera and pieces in the French ars nova to the intricate ars subtilior of Sus un' fontayne, and his setting of O rosa bella points toward the melodic patterns of the Renaissance. Many of his motets and Mass movements survive in the Bologna manuscript Q15, while the Squarcialupi Codex has nothing by him.

Ciconia also wrote two treatises, Nova musica and De proportionibus. Following Marchetto of Padua, he presented himself as a reviver of ancient theory, argued for accepting the third and sixth as consonances, linked musical intervals to the syllables of words, and discussed imitation between voices, an idea that shapes his late settings of poems by the humanist Leonardo Giustiniani. Two complete editions exist, by Suzanne Clercx in 1956 and by Margaret Bent and Anne Hallmark in 1985; the second treated many of the daring intervals of the first as transcription errors, making him seem less of an innovator.
johannes-gutenberg: Johannes Gensfleisch zur Laden zum Gutenberg was born in Mainz, a wealthy city on the Rhine. His exact year of birth is unknown; a later document shows that he had come of age by 1420, and the year 1400 is commonly assigned to him for convenience. His father, Friele Gensfleisch zur Laden, was a patrician and merchant, and his mother, Else Wyrich, was the daughter of a shopkeeper and not of patrician lineage, so scholars assume he could never succeed his father at the mint. After conflict between patricians and guild craftsmen the family probably withdrew to Eltville in 1411 and again in 1413. A letter of March 1434 shows him living in Strasbourg, where he appears as a goldsmith.

In Strasbourg in 1440 Gutenberg is said to have perfected the secret of printing, but the record does not show what he was working on. In 1448 he was back in Mainz, borrowing from his brother-in-law. By 1450 a press was in operation, and he persuaded the moneylender Johann Fust to lend 800 guilders; Peter Schöffer, who became Fust's son-in-law, joined the enterprise. Work on the Bible began in 1452 with a second loan of 800 guilders, while the press also printed more lucrative texts such as Latin grammars and thousands of indulgences.

In 1455 he completed the 42-line Bible, of which about 180 copies were printed, three quarters on paper and the rest on vellum. Fust sued him in 1456 at the archbishop's court, claiming he had misused the funds, and the court gave Fust control of the Bible workshop. The Fust and Schöffer shop brought out the Mainz Psalter of August 1457, the first book with its printer's name and date.

Gutenberg seems to have kept or restarted a printing shop, and probably supplied the type for a Bible printed in Bamberg around 1459. On 18 January 1465 Archbishop Adolph von Nassau gave him the title of Hofmann, gentleman of the court, with a stipend and a court outfit. He died in 1468 and was probably buried in the Franciscan church at Mainz; the grave is lost. How he made his type remains unclear, and scholars still debate whether he used punches and matrices. After the sack of Mainz in 1462 printers went into exile, and Venice became the capital of printing, where Aldus Manutius published major Greek and Latin texts.
johannes-kabin: Käbin was born in 1905 in Kalvi, Virumaa, and his family moved to Saint Petersburg when he was a small child; his father died soon after. In 1916 he moved with his mother and older sister to the village of Sussanino in Petrograd Province, where the family bought a small farm of 0.27 hectares. He was thus what was called a Yestonian, an ethnic Estonian raised in Russia.

In 1926 he entered the Leningrad School of Soviet and Party Construction, and a year later he became chairman of the Susanin Village Council of the Gatchina district. He completed his studies at the Institute of Red Professors in 1938 and then worked as a teacher in Moscow.

After the Second World War he returned to Estonia, where he became deputy head of the Propaganda and Agitation Department of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Estonia, and in 1948 secretary of the Central Committee for propaganda and agitation. He was elected First Secretary at the 8th Plenum in 1950. Beginning as a hardline Stalinist, he grew more moderate and pragmatic, trying to balance Moscow's demands with the needs of the Estonian people, and he held the post for more than 25 years, partly because the Kremlin approved of his policies.

Many Estonians saw him as attentive to the countryside: he often visited farms and talked directly with farmers, workers and local communities. He received many Soviet honours, among them Hero of Socialist Labour in 1975 and six Orders of Lenin between 1950 and 1975. From 1978 to 1983 he was head of state as chairman of the Supreme Soviet.

After Estonia restored its independence he remained in the country. He died in Tallinn in 1999 at the age of 94 and was buried in the Metsakalmistu cemetery of the city. His autobiography, Through Years and Distances, was published in 2020.
johannes-kepler: Johannes Kepler was born on 27 December 1571 in the Free Imperial City of Weil der Stadt. His parents were Lutheran, but he is presumed to have been baptised a Catholic, since Protestant baptisms were not permitted there. His grandfather had been Lord Mayor, but the family fortune was in decline. His father, a mercenary, left when Johannes was five, and his mother, Katharina Guldenmann, was a healer and herbalist. Born prematurely, Kepler said he had been a weak and sickly child, yet he impressed travellers at his grandfather's inn with his mathematical ability.

Kepler taught mathematics at a seminary school in Graz from 1594 to 1600. In 1600 he went to Prague, where Tycho Brahe secured him a place on the project of the Rudolphine Tables. Two days after Tycho's death on 24 October 1601, Kepler was appointed his successor as imperial mathematician to Emperor Rudolf II, and he regarded the next eleven years as the most productive of his life. His main duty was to give astrological advice to the emperor, although he took a dim view of attempts to predict specific events.

In 1612 he moved to Linz as District Mathematician and teacher, keeping his court post. The Rudolphine Tables were completed in 1623 but, because of the emperor's publishing requirements and negotiations with Tycho's heir, printing at Ulm was finished only in September 1627. He then presented them to the emperor in Prague. He died on 15 November 1630.

His first major work, Mysterium Cosmographicum of 1596, nested the five Platonic solids between the spheres of the six known planets. In Astronomia nova of 1609 he replaced the notion of a planetary orb, a spherical shell carrying the planet, with that of an orbit resulting from physical causes, and he set out the first two laws of planetary motion by analysing the orbit of Mars from Tycho's observations. The Epitome Astronomiae Copernicanae contained all three laws. Harmonice Mundi of 1619 explained the proportions of the natural world in terms of music.

In Astronomiae Pars Optica of 1604 he described the inverse-square law of light's intensity, and he is generally considered the first to recognise that the eye's lens projects an inverted image on the retina. He supported Galileo Galilei's discovery of the moons of Jupiter. His laws were not at once accepted: Galileo and René Descartes ignored the Astronomia nova.
johannes-ockeghem: Ockeghem is believed to have been born in Saint-Ghislain in the County of Hainaut, in what is now Belgium; documents of 1607 give "Jan Hocquegam" as a native of the town, which suggests that he was a native speaker of Picard. His birth date is unknown. Details of his early life are lacking, but like many composers of the time he probably began as a chorister. The first documented record of him is from June 1443, when he was employed as a "left-hand choir singer", one who sang composed music, at the Onze-Lieve-Vrouwe cathedral in Antwerp. He probably sang there under Johannes Pullois.

Ockeghem probably studied with Gilles Binchois, and in any case was closely associated with him at the Burgundian court. Between 1446 and 1448 he served, with the composer Jean Cousin, at the court of Charles I, Duke of Bourbon, at Moulins. Around 1452 he moved to Paris, where he served the French court as maestro di cappella, and he was also treasurer of the collegiate church of St Martin at Tours. He served both Charles VII and Louis XI, and held posts at Notre Dame de Paris and St Benoît.

In 1470 he travelled to Spain on a diplomatic mission for the king, which aimed to keep Spain out of an alliance with England and Burgundy and to arrange a marriage between Isabella I of Castile and Charles, Duke of Guyenne.

He probably died at Tours, where he left a will, on 6 February 1497. Many laments were written on his death, among them poems by Erasmus and Jean Molinet, and Josquin des Prez's setting of Nymphes des bois.

Ockeghem's reliably attributed output is small for the length of his career: some 14 masses, an isolated Credo, five motets, a motet-chanson lamenting the death of Binchois in 1460, and 21 chansons. Thirteen of the masses are preserved in the Chigi codex, from around 1500. His Missa pro defunctis is the earliest surviving polyphonic Requiem. He used a cantus firmus in about half of his masses, and three of them, Ma maistresse, Fors seulement and Mi-mi, are based on chansons of his own.

The Missa prolationum consists entirely of mensuration canons, and the Missa cuiusvis toni is designed to be sung in any of the modes. His wide-ranging and rhythmically active bass lines were distinctive among Netherlandish composers. He influenced Josquin des Prez and was known throughout Europe for his expressive music and technical skill.
johannes-sturm: Sturm was born on 1 October 1507 at Schleiden. In 1521 or 1522 he began his studies at the school of St. Jerome in Liège and went on to the University of Leuven, where he had a share in a printing press that issued several Greek works. In 1529 he moved to Paris, where besides selling books he lectured on Cicero and Demosthenes. The writings of Martin Bucer won him to the Protestant Reformation, and in 1534 he took part in an attempt to reconcile the Protestant and Roman Catholic parties.

At the urging of Bucer and the statesman Jacob Sturm von Sturmeck, who was no relation, he went to teach in Strassburg in 1537. Besides running his school, the Schola Argentoratensis, he undertook diplomatic missions for the city, the Protestant estates and the king of France: he attended the conferences of Hagenau and Worms in 1540 and Regensburg in 1541, helped to negotiate peace between England and France in 1545, and sought the help of François I in 1546. His call for German aid to the Huguenots made Lutherans suspicious of him.

After 1555 the stricter Lutheran line in Strassburg drew him into controversies. He defended Girolamo Zanchi against Johann Marbach, offered to resign in 1570, and won his dispute with Marbach in 1575, but the Formula of Concord of 1577 reopened the conflict with the theologian Johannes Pappus, and in 1581 Sturm was relieved of his position.

He retired to Northeim and died in Strassburg on 3 March 1589. His school and teaching were a humanist model across Europe for a century. Its Latin syllabus centred on Cicero, Virgil's Eclogues and Terence, and its Greek on Demosthenes, reflecting his stress on eloquence and rhetoric. He advised on schools such as the gymnasium at Lauingen, and his influence shows in the school regulations of Württemberg, Brunswick and Saxony.

His system of graded classes, textbooks and school management shaped secondary education in Germany, England and France. Roger Ascham recommended his collection of Cicero's letters in The Scholemaster, and a student dormitory in Strasbourg, the Foyer Jean-Sturm, bears his name.
johannes-trithemius: Johannes Trithemius was born Johann Heidenberg, and his byname refers to his native town of Trittenheim on the Moselle, then part of the Electorate of Trier. His father died while he was an infant. His stepfather, whom his mother married seven years later, was hostile to education, so the boy learned in secret and with difficulty, acquiring Greek, Latin and Hebrew. At seventeen he left home to look for good teachers and studied at the University of Heidelberg. In 1482 a snowstorm drove him to take refuge in the Benedictine abbey of Sponheim near Bad Kreuznach, and he decided to stay.

Elected abbot at the age of 21, Trithemius set out to turn a neglected and undisciplined house into a centre of learning. During his time the library grew from around fifty items to more than two thousand. Differences with his convent, and a reputation as a magician that did not help him, led to his resignation in 1506. He accepted an offer from Lorenz von Bibra, Bishop of Würzburg, to become abbot of St James's Abbey, the Schottenkloster in Würzburg, where he remained until his death.

He wrote chronicles of Sponheim and a two-volume history of Hirsau Abbey. His Latin was admired, but critics even in his lifetime pointed out that he had invented sources, such as a Scythian historian called Hunibald, and a chronicler of Fulda called Meginfrid. Among his pupils were Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa and Paracelsus.

His best-known work, the Steganographia, was written around 1499 and printed at Frankfurt in 1606. It appears to be about using spirits to communicate over long distances, but after the decryption key to the first two volumes was published in 1606 they were seen to concern cryptography and steganography. The work was placed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum in 1609 and removed in 1900. His Polygraphia was written in 1508 and published in 1518.

Trithemius also had a reputation as a necromancer. In 1507 he became the first author to mention the historical Johann Faust of Knittlingen, in a letter that criticised Faust's vanity, and later tellings tied the Faust legend to stories of him conjuring the shade of Mary of Burgundy for Maximilian I. He was buried in the church of St James's Abbey, with a tombstone by Tilman Riemenschneider, which was later moved to the Neumünster church.
johannes-van-den-bosch: Van den Bosch was born on 2 February 1780 in Herwijnen in the Dutch Republic, the son of the physician Johannes van den Bosch Sr. and Adriana Poningh. He joined the army of the Batavian Republic in 1797 and a year later, at his own request, was sent to Batavia as a lieutenant. As an adjutant to successive governors-general he took part in the change from trade colonialism to territorial expansion, until a conflict with Herman Willem Daendels in 1808 ended in his honourable discharge as a colonel.

Captured by the British on his way home, he remained a prisoner until 1812. In the Netherlands he joined the provisional government restoring the authority of the Prince of Orange and, recommissioned as a colonel, took Utrecht and Naarden in the prince's name. In 1818 he helped found the Society of Humanitarianism under Prince Frederick, which held labour to be the only means of fighting poverty and set up the free colonies of Frederiksoord, Willemsoord and Wilhelminaoord in Drenthe for the urban poor.

In 1827 he went to the West Indies as commissioner-general, arriving on Curaçao in December and staying eight months. He promoted trade and banking and introduced a regulation applying the Constitution of the Netherlands to the colony, which he used to try to improve the conditions of slaves. Under the cultivation system he brought in as governor-general, Javanese farmers had to give a fifth of their land to export crops such as coffee, sugar and indigo.

Back in the Netherlands, he became Minister of Colonies on 30 May 1834 and demanded ever higher financial returns from the colonies, often at the expense of farmers and slaves. The House of Representatives criticised the opaqueness of his loans policy with the Netherlands Trading Society in 1839, and he stepped down on 1 January 1840. He was made a baron in 1835 and a count in 1839, and was also named Minister of State. He sat in the House of Representatives for South Holland from 1842 until he died at his estate in The Hague on 28 January 1844.
johannes-vermeer: Vermeer was baptized in the Reformed Church on 31 October 1632. His mother, Digna Baltens, came from Antwerp. His father, Reijnier Janszoon, was a silk weaver from Antwerp who moved to Delft, began dealing in paintings and joined the Guild of Saint Luke as an art dealer in 1631. In 1641 he bought a larger inn on the market square. When Reijnier died in October 1652, Vermeer took over the family art business. In April 1653 he married Catharina Bolnes, a Catholic. Her mother, Maria Thins, was at first opposed, and it was probably she who insisted that he convert to Catholicism. The couple lived in her house on the Oude Langendijk for the rest of his life, and Catharina gave birth to 15 children.

It is unclear where Vermeer trained. Some have proposed Carel Fabritius, but there is no hard evidence, and others suggest Abraham Bloemaert. He became a member of the Guild of Saint Luke on 29 December 1653 and was elected its head in 1662, then again in 1663, 1670 and 1671, which shows that his colleagues regarded him as an established craftsman. He worked slowly, probably producing about three paintings a year, and he also dealt in art. His patrons for much of his career were Pieter van Ruijven and his wife Maria de Knuijt, who bought much of his output. That kept him afloat but limited the spread of his fame.

Vermeer used the expensive pigment ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli, more lavishly and earlier than any other artist of the century, often as an underpaint beneath earth colours. He worked in domestic interiors, usually lit from the left, and the same rooms, furniture and women appear in many of his pictures. In 1672, the Rampjaar, French troops under Louis XIV and forces from Münster and Cologne invaded the Dutch Republic. The art market collapsed, and a painting sold that year was Vermeer's last sale.

Vermeer died on 15 December 1675, aged 43, after a short illness, and was buried the same day in the Old Church. His widow told her creditors that the burden of his debts and unsold stock had brought on his death. She had children to raise and asked the High Court for relief from debt, and the microscopist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was named trustee of the estate.

Vermeer was little known outside Delft. After his death he fell into obscurity, was barely mentioned in Arnold Houbraken's survey of 1718 and was omitted from later surveys for nearly two centuries. In the 19th century Gustav Friedrich Waagen and Théophile Thoré-Bürger rediscovered him. Thoré-Bürger called him the Sphinx of Delft, because so little was known of his life, and attributed 66 works to him, of which 34 are universally accepted today.
johannesburg: Johannesburg lies on the Highveld, the eastern plateau of South Africa, at an elevation of 1,753 metres. The former central business district sits on the southern side of the Witwatersrand ridge, which marks the watershed between the Limpopo and Vaal rivers. The climate is subtropical highland, with hot summers and afternoon thundershowers from October to April and dry, sunny winters with cold nights. The city is mineral-rich, and the Witwatersrand has long been at the centre of the international gold trade.

San hunter-gatherers who used stone tools lived in the area up to ten centuries ago. By the mid-18th century the wider region was largely settled by Sotho–Tswana communities, whose stone-walled towns and villages left ruins across the former Transvaal. The main Witwatersrand gold reef was discovered in June 1884 on the farm Vogelstruisfontein, which set off the Witwatersrand Gold Rush and the founding of Johannesburg in 1886. The origin of the name is disputed, and records of the choice were lost. Within ten years the city had 100,000 people.

Like many late 19th-century mining towns it was rough and disorganised. White miners came from all continents, African men were recruited to do unskilled mine work, and the Zulu men known as the AmaWasha dominated laundry work. As the value of controlling the land rose, tensions grew between the Boer-dominated Transvaal government in Pretoria and the British, which led to the Jameson Raid, ending in fiasco at Doornkop in January 1896. In the Second Boer War (1899–1902) British forces under Field Marshal Frederick Sleigh Roberts occupied the city on 30 May 1900.

In 1917 it became the headquarters of the Anglo-American Corporation, founded by Ernest Oppenheimer. In the 1950s and early 1960s the apartheid government built the massive agglomeration of townships known as Soweto, which was designated a blacks-only city until 1994 and became the centre of the 1976 Soweto Uprising. After apartheid ended, the old city and the surrounding townships and settlements were unified administratively in the City of Johannesburg Metropolitan Municipality.

Johannesburg is the capital of the province of Gauteng, the largest city in South Africa and its economic capital. It is the seat of the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, and home to the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the largest on the continent. It has two major public universities, the University of the Witwatersrand and the University of Johannesburg. Its spatial inheritance from apartheid is still visible in the layout of its suburbs and townships.
john-a-macdonald: John Alexander Macdonald was born in Ramshorn parish in Glasgow, the third of five children of Hugh Macdonald, an unsuccessful merchant, and Helen Shaw. After his father's business ventures left the family in debt, they emigrated in 1820 to Kingston in Upper Canada, where they had relatives. His father's shops there failed, and his parents decided that John should become a lawyer. He began to earn his own living at the age of 15, and later said he had had no boyhood.

Macdonald served as a private in the militia during the Rebellions of 1837 and soon became prominent as a barrister in Kingston. He was elected an alderman in 1843 and in 1844 was elected to the legislature of the Province of Canada. He was never an orator; he became an expert on election law and parliamentary procedure. In 1857 he became premier, and in 1864, when no party could govern for long, he agreed to a proposal from his rival George Brown that the parties unite in a Great Coalition. Brown wanted representation by population, while Macdonald's priority was a federation that the other colonies could join.

After Confederation on 1 July 1867 Macdonald became the first prime minister. In his first term he established the North-West Mounted Police and expanded Canada by adding the North-Western Territory, Rupert's Land, British Columbia and Prince Edward Island. He resigned in 1873 over a scandal in which his party took bribes from businessmen seeking the contract for the Canadian Pacific Railway. Returned to office in 1878, he introduced the protective tariff of the National Policy in the budget of February 1879 and completed the railway. In 1879 he commissioned the Davin Report, which provided the basis for the Canadian Indian residential school system. He approved the execution of the Métis leader Louis Riel for treason in 1885, which alienated many francophones from his party.

Macdonald suffered a stroke in May 1891 that left him partly paralysed and unable to speak, and he died on 6 June 1891. Thousands filed past his open casket in the Senate Chamber, and a funeral train took his body to Kingston, with crowds greeting it at each stop. He was buried in Cataraqui Cemetery. He was criticised for his role in the Chinese head tax and for federal policies toward Indigenous peoples, including the residential schools, while he remains respected for his part in Confederation.
john-adams: John Adams was born on 30 October 1735 on the family farm in Braintree, Massachusetts, the son of John Adams Sr., a farmer, cordwainer, deacon and militia lieutenant, and Susanna Boylston Adams. He entered Harvard College at sixteen and graduated in 1755. His father expected him to become a minister, but he taught school briefly, chose the law and was admitted to the bar in 1759. He joined the colonial cause after hearing James Otis Jr.'s 1761 challenge to the writs of assistance, and he rose to prominence in opposing the Stamp Act, writing the Braintree Instructions of 1765.

After British soldiers killed five civilians in the Boston Massacre of 5 March 1770, Adams defended them when no other attorney would, holding that everyone has the right to counsel and a fair trial. A delegate to the First Continental Congress in 1774, he seconded the Lee Resolution on 7 June 1776 and, as one of the Committee of Five, helped Jefferson with the Declaration of Independence. As a diplomat he worked on the Model Treaty with France, secured a Dutch loan, helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris and in 1785 became the first American ambassador to Great Britain. He was the primary author of the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780 and served as vice president from 1789 to 1797.

As president he kept the country out of the war between Britain and France. French seizures of American ships led to the undeclared Quasi-War, during which Congress created the Navy Department. In June 1798 he signed the Alien and Sedition Acts at the urging of his wife and cabinet, though he had not promoted them. He appointed John Marshall Chief Justice and signed the law establishing the Library of Congress.

Defeated by Jefferson in 1800, Adams retired to Peacefield in Quincy. After years of silence the two men resumed their friendship through a continuing correspondence. He lived to see his son John Quincy Adams become president in 1825 and died at Peacefield on 4 July 1826. His pamphlet Thoughts on Government of 1776 was long influential. He was accused of monarchist sympathies, which he denied, and he never owned a slave. Benjamin Franklin said of him that he was always an honest man, often a wise one, but sometimes absolutely out of his senses.
john-albert-ii-duke-of-mecklenburg: John Albert was born at Waren on 5 May 1590, the son of Duke John VII and Sophia of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorp. He became duke on 16 April 1608, jointly with his brother Adolf Frederick I in the Mecklenburg-Schwerin part of the country, but from 1608 to 1611 he was ruler in name only: power lay with the regent, their great-uncle Duke Charles I. After Charles's death the emperor declared Adolf Frederick of age, and he ruled alone until John Albert also came of age.

From 1611 to 1621 the two brothers ruled the whole Duchy of Mecklenburg together. In the division of 1621 John Albert received Mecklenburg-Güstrow, which he ruled alone from then on. In 1623 both brothers joined a defensive alliance of the Lower Saxon Estates, and in the Thirty Years' War they tried to appear neutral while secretly supporting the Danish troops of King Christian IV.

After the Imperial victory at the Battle of Lutter, Tilly treated them as enemies. On 19 January 1628 Emperor Ferdinand II issued a decree at Brandýs Castle declaring that the brothers had forfeited their fief and that Mecklenburg would be granted to Wallenstein. At Wallenstein's request they left the duchy in May 1628. In May 1631, when Swedish troops drove Wallenstein out, they returned.

John Albert died at Güstrow on 23 April 1636 and was buried in the Minster there. He married three times. His first wife, Margaret Elizabeth, daughter of Duke Christopher of Mecklenburg, whom he married on 9 October 1608, bore him four children, among them Elisabeth Sophie, later wife of Duke Augustus II of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. His second marriage, in 1618 to Elizabeth of Hesse-Kassel, a daughter of Landgrave Maurice, was childless. In 1626 he married Eleonore Marie of Anhalt-Bernburg, daughter of Prince Christian I; their children included Gustav Adolph, born in 1633.
john-amos-comenius: Comenius was born on 28 March 1592 in the Margraviate of Moravia. His exact birthplace is uncertain: Uherský Brod, Nivnice and Komňa are all possibilities. He was the youngest child and only son of Martin Komenský and Anna Chmelová, who belonged to the Bohemian Brethren. His parents and two of his sisters died in 1604. Poverty delayed his formal schooling until his later teens. He studied at the Herborn Academy and the University of Heidelberg, and in 1616 was ordained in the ministry of the Brethren.

In 1620 Comenius became pastor and rector at Fulnek. Religious wars cost him his property and writings in 1621, and in 1627 he led the Brethren into exile when the Habsburg Counter-Reformation persecuted Protestants in Bohemia. He settled at Leszno in Poland, where he headed the gymnasium. His Janua linguarum reserata, or The Gate of Languages Unlocked, brought him wide fame. In 1638 the Swedish government asked him to draw up a scheme for its schools, and in 1641 he joined a commission of the English Long Parliament on educational reform, which the English Civil War interrupted.

He later worked in Sweden, Elbląg, England and, from 1650, Sárospatak in Hungary, where he taught until 1654. During the Deluge in 1655 he declared for the Protestant Swedish side, and in 1656 Polish Catholic partisans burned his house, manuscripts and printing press, destroying the manuscript of Pansophia. He took refuge in Amsterdam, where he died in 1670 and was buried in Naarden.

Comenius wrote more than forty educational titles. They rested on shared ideas: learning foreign languages through the mother tongue, gaining ideas through objects rather than words, beginning with what is familiar to the child, making learning a pleasure and making instruction universal. His Didactica Magna outlined a system of schools from kindergarten to university. The Orbis Pictus of 1658 was among the most widely circulated school books for the next century and the first successful use of illustrations in teaching youth.

He also led the seventeenth-century pansophic movement, which sought to organise all human knowledge. As a bishop of the Unity of the Brethren he wrote the Labyrinth of the World and Paradise of the Heart. His influence was little recognised for much of the eighteenth century, but it has been acknowledged since the middle of the nineteenth. Czechs idealised him as a symbol of their nation during the National Revival, and 28 March is Teachers' Day in the Czech Republic.
john-axouch: John Axouch's family is unknown, and it is not known why the Norman forces of Bohemond of Taranto took him at Nicaea; some have speculated that he belonged to an important family. The historian John Kinnamos called him, anachronistically, a Persian. Because the boy was the same age as the emperor's son, Alexios I Komnenos made him John's companion, and the two became close friends. On his accession John II gave Axouch the court title of sebastos, and every member of the imperial family was required to make obeisance to him.

When a plot by the emperor's sister Anna and her husband Nikephoros Bryennios failed, John II offered Axouch her confiscated property. He refused, knowing the gift would turn the imperial family and the aristocracy against him, and asked for clemency for Anna. His part in calming the family left the emperor free to pursue an aggressive foreign policy. Axouch was wounded in the leg fighting the Pechenegs at Beroia in 1122 and again during the campaigns of 1137–1138 in Cilicia, Antioch and northern Syria.

When John II died after a hunting accident in Cilicia, Axouch reached Constantinople before the news, seized the treasuries and regalia, and confined the two princes named Isaac, Manuel's elder brother and uncle, in the Pantokrator Monastery. He is recorded as having urged the dying emperor to prefer the elder Isaac.

Manuel kept him in office, and Axouch introduced an oath of allegiance into the coronation ceremony that lasted until the end of the Empire. After he praised John II over Manuel at the emperor's table in 1145–1146 he lost the privilege of bearing the imperial seal; some historians think it had made him mesazon, the unofficial head of the civil administration. At Corfu he first led the land forces and, after the death of the megas doux Stephanos Kontostephanos in 1149, the whole expedition.

Axouch is believed to have died shortly after Corfu, possibly in 1150 or early in 1151 at the latest. He had a lively interest in theology and put questions to Nicholas of Methone. Michael Italikos called him the Tower of the Empire of the Romans, and Niketas Choniates wrote that the nobility and liberality of his mind overshadowed his humble origins. His son Alexios married Maria Komnene and became protostrator, and his daughter Eudokia married Stephen Komnenos.
john-balliol: Little is known of Balliol's early life. He was born between 1248 and 1250 at an unknown place; Galloway, Picardy and Barnard Castle in County Durham are possibilities. His father, John, 5th Baron Balliol, founded Balliol College, Oxford. His mother Dervorguilla of Galloway was a granddaughter of David, Earl of Huntingdon, brother of William the Lion. From her he inherited lands in Galloway; from his father, large estates in England and France. Around 9 February 1281 he married Isabella de Warenne, daughter of the 6th Earl of Surrey.

After the death of Margaret, Maid of Norway, in 1290, Balliol competed for the crown in the Great Cause. He was a great-great-great-grandson of David I through his mother, one generation further than his main rival Robert Bruce, 5th Lord of Annandale, but senior in genealogical primogeniture. Edward I of England administered the court, which decided for Balliol on 17 November 1292, and he was inaugurated at Scone on 30 November 1292.

Edward I, who had coerced recognition as Lord Paramount of Scotland, steadily undermined him, demanding homage, legal authority over the Scottish king in disputes brought by his subjects, and military support against France. He treated Scotland as a vassal state and repeatedly humiliated the new king. A council of twelve appointed at Stirling in July 1295 took over affairs, according to some English accounts, though Amanda Beam argues it was formed to help defend the realm. On 23 October 1295 Balliol concluded a treaty of mutual assistance with Philip IV of France, later known as the Auld Alliance.

Edward invaded in retaliation, beginning the Wars of Scottish Independence. The English took Dunbar Castle on 27 April 1296, and Balliol abdicated at Stracathro on 10 July 1296. He was held in the Tower of London until 1299, when he was allowed to go to France, and by about 1301 he lived on his family's estates at Hélicourt in Picardy. He died there in late 1314.

His nickname Toom Tabard usually means empty coat, an ineffective king. Scotland had no monarch until Robert the Bruce in 1306. His son Edward Balliol later revived the claim to the throne with English support and had some temporary successes.
john-batman: Batman was born on 21 January 1801 in Parramatta, the son of William and Mary Batman. His father had been sentenced to fourteen years' transportation for receiving stolen saltpetre and reached Sydney aboard the Ganges on 2 June 1797; he later ran a timber-yard at Parramatta and became a devout Wesleyan. Aboriginal people came into Parramatta for charity and education, and the young Batman knew many of them. In 1816 he was apprenticed as a blacksmith in Sydney.

In December 1821 Batman and his younger brother Henry went to Van Diemen's Land to settle as graziers near Ben Lomond in the north-east, where he acquired a property called Kingston. In early 1826 he captured the bushranger Matthew Brady, who was later hanged at Hobart, and was rewarded with a further grant of land. During the Black War he led roving parties, with Aboriginal men hired in Sydney, that hunted Tasmanian Aboriginal people, and in 1830 he took part in the Black Line.

In September 1829 he led a night attack on a family group of 60 to 70 men, women and children in the Ben Lomond district. By his own report 15 were killed, and he shot two wounded men he had captured when they could not walk. A captured woman, Luggenemenener, was gaoled and separated from her two-year-old son Rolepana, whom Batman kept. Governor George Arthur observed that Batman "had much slaughter to account for", and his neighbour, the artist John Glover, called him a murderer of blacks.

After the New South Wales authorities refused him land at Western Port, Batman sailed for the mainland in 1835 in the schooner Rebecca as a leading member of the Port Phillip Association. In June 1835, on the banks of the Merri Creek, he negotiated with Kulin elders for a yearly rent of blankets, axes, knives, mirrors, flour and other goods. It is unlikely that the Kulin understood this as a transfer of land, and Governor Bourke held the treaty invalid because the land was claimed by the Crown.

Batman settled with his wife, the former convict Elizabeth Callaghan, and their seven daughters at what became Batman's Hill. Syphilis, diagnosed in 1833, crippled and disfigured him, and he died on 6 May 1839. In the 21st century his killings in Tasmania have been the focus of criticism: in 2016 Batman Park in Northcote was renamed Gumbri Park, and in 2018 the electoral Division of Batman became the Division of Cooper.
john-boyd-dunlop: John Boyd Dunlop was born on 5 February 1840 on a farm at Dreghorn, North Ayrshire. He studied to be a veterinary surgeon at the Dick Vet, University of Edinburgh, and in 1867 moved to Downpatrick in Ireland. He married Margaret Stevenson in 1871 and they had a daughter and a son. He founded the Downe Veterinary Clinic in Downpatrick with his brother James Dunlop before moving to a practice in May Street, Belfast, which by the mid 1880s was one of the largest in Ireland. Sir Arthur Du Cros later described him as diffident and gentle-mannered but confident in his abilities.

Familiar with making rubber devices, Dunlop developed the first practical pneumatic, or inflatable, tyre for his son's tricycle. In the yard of his Belfast home he fitted a tube of inflated sheet rubber to a wooden disc 96 centimetres across and rolled it beside a metal wheel from the tricycle; the metal wheel stopped, and the pneumatic one kept rolling until it hit a gatepost.

He then fitted both rear wheels, moved on to larger tyres for a bicycle and tested it at Cherryvale sports ground in south Belfast. A patent was granted on 7 December 1888. Unknown to him, another Scot, Robert William Thomson of Stonehaven, had patented a pneumatic tyre in 1847, so his own patent was later found invalid.

In 1889 the cyclist Willie Hume won all four cycling events at the Queen's College Sports in Belfast on pneumatic tyres, defeating sons of Harvey Du Cros, president of the Irish Cyclists' Association.
