Du Cros joined him in a company that bought his rights for a small cash sum and a small shareholding. Commercial production of cycle tyres began in Belfast in late 1890, and Dunlop retired from his veterinary practice in 1892. He withdrew from the business in the mid 1890s, and the company bearing his name was Du Cros's creation. Car tyres were not made until 1900.

Dunlop took no further interest in the tyre or rubber business after he left it and did not make a great fortune from his invention. He died at his home in Ballsbridge, Dublin, in 1921 and is buried in Deans Grange Cemetery. The pneumatic tyre revolutionised the bicycle industry, which had boomed after the introduction of J. K. Starley's safety bicycle in 1885, and it arrived at a crucial time in the development of road transport. The Dunlop name survives on many products, and the Ulster Historical Circle has commemorated him with a blue plaque.
john-browns-body: The tune is that of the folk hymn Say, Brothers, Will You Meet Us, which can be traced in print to camp meeting song collections of 1806–1808 in South Carolina, Virginia and Massachusetts. Its Glory, glory, hallelujah chorus grew out of the oral tradition sometime between 1808 and the 1850s. Sung by African-American and white worshippers along the Methodist and Baptist circuits of the South, it passed into hymn books and became well known in the North by the mid-1800s. William Steffe claimed to have written it in the mid-1850s for a Philadelphia fire company, but the tune and the text were decades older than he was.

In 1890 George Kimball told how the 2nd Infantry Battalion of the Massachusetts militia, the Tiger Battalion, worked out the words together. A jovial Scot in its ranks named John Brown shared his name with the abolitionist executed after Harper's Ferry, and the soldiers' jokes that John Brown was dead and his body mouldering in the grave were put to the hymn's tune. Lines such as His soul's marching on were sung with the chorus always added. Some of the battalion's leaders found the words coarse and irreverent, but the verses were prepared for print with the publisher C. S. Hall, and broadsides followed in July 1861, the month newspapers reported troops singing it in the streets of Boston.

The roughness of the early verses inspired many literary versions, among them William Weston Patton's of October 1861, Edna Dean Proctor's The President's Proclamation of 1863 and, above all, Julia Ward Howe's Battle Hymn of the Republic, written in November 1861. On 1 May 1865 in Charleston, South Carolina, 3,000 Black children singing the song led a parade of 10,000 people honouring 257 Union dead reburied from a Confederate prison camp, considered the first observance of Decoration Day.

The tune later carried the labour anthem Solidarity Forever, the paratroopers' song Blood on the Risers, football chants, the German children's song Alle Kinder lernen lesen and the Assam Regiment's Badluram Ka Badan, and British socialists sang the old words at Labour Party rallies in 1945.
john-c-fremont: John Charles Frémont was born on 21 January 1813, the son of Charles Frémon, a French-Canadian immigrant who taught French and dancing, and Anne Beverley Whiting, who had left her wealthy and much older husband for him. The couple settled in Savannah, Georgia, and were never married. Frémont attended the College of Charleston for two years until he was expelled for irregular attendance. His exploration work with Joseph Nicollet brought him into contact with Senator Thomas Hart Benton of Missouri, an advocate of Manifest Destiny. In 1841 he eloped with Benton's daughter Jessie, and Benton became his patron.

Frémont led five western expeditions from 1842 and became known as the Pathfinder. His strength lay in scientific documentation, reports co-written with Jessie, and maps. On the first expedition, in the summer of 1842, he explored the Wind River Range with Kit Carson as guide. The second, from 1843 to 1844, followed the Oregon Trail to the Columbia River. The third, in 1845, was an armed survey of 60 men that was secretly to become a military force if war broke out with Mexico.

In California in 1846 he joined American settlers rebelling against Mexican authority and took part in attacks on local Native Americans, among them the Sutter Buttes massacre. Commodore Stockton made him military governor in January 1847, but Kearny held orders giving him that authority, and Frémont was court-martialled, convicted of mutiny and insubordination, and resigned from the Army.

He led a fourth expedition in 1848 and 1849 and a fifth in 1853 and 1854, both seeking a railroad route along the 38th parallel. Gold was found on his Mariposa ranch, and in 1850 he became one of California's first two senators. In 1856 he was the first presidential candidate of the new Republican Party and lost to James Buchanan. In 1861 President Abraham Lincoln made him a major general in command of the Department of the West, but Lincoln relieved him for insubordination after he issued an unauthorised emancipation edict in Missouri. The Radical Democratic Party nominated him in 1864, and he withdrew in September.

Frémont lost much of his wealth in the Pacific Railroad venture of 1866 and in the Panic of 1873. He served as Governor of the Arizona Territory from 1878 to 1881 and died destitute in New York City on 13 July 1890. His reputation is polarised. Some regard him as a military hero, others as a failure who defeated his own best interests, and his attacks on Native Americans, which killed men, women and children, have been described as part of the California genocide. The Royal Geographical Society awarded him its Patron's Medal in 1850.
john-cabot: Cabot was born in Italy, the son of Giulio Caboto; Gaeta and Castiglione Chiavarese have both been proposed as his birthplace. He became a citizen of the Republic of Venice in 1476, and by 1484 he was married to Mattea, with sons Ludovico, Sebastian and Sancto. He fell into debt and left Venice as an insolvent debtor by 5 November 1488. In Valencia his harbour proposals were rejected, and in Seville a bridge contract ended when the project was abandoned on 24 December 1494. He probably reached England in mid-1495.

On 5 March 1496 Henry VII gave Cabot and his three sons letters patent to sail to unknown lands. The patent required expeditions to leave from Bristol, with the king taking one fifth of the profit. A first attempt, probably in the summer of 1496, was abandoned because of a confused crew, short supplies and bad weather.

In 1497 Cabot sailed in the Matthew, a small ship of about 50 tons with a crew of 18 to 20. A Bristol chronicle gives her departure as 2 May and return as 6 August, with the land found on 24 June. The sources disagree on details. Cabot is said to have landed once, raised the Venetian and papal banners, and met no one. Newfoundland, Cape Breton Island, Labrador and Maine have all been proposed for the landfall. The king rewarded him with £10 and then a pension of £20 a year.

In 1498 Cabot left Bristol with a fleet reported as five ships, some carrying goods for trade. A storm forced one into Ireland, and the Spanish envoy said the others went on. It is not known whether he died at sea, died after returning, or stayed in the Americas. The historian Alwyn Ruddock argued that he returned in 1500, and researchers of the Cabot Project at the University of Bristol have sought evidence for this. Cabot Tower in Bristol and another in St John's, Newfoundland, both begun in 1897, commemorate his voyage.
john-calvin: John Calvin was born Jehan Cauvin on 10 July 1509 at Noyon, in Picardy, where his father Gérard was the cathedral notary and intended his sons for the priesthood. He was educated in Paris, trained as a humanist lawyer and published a commentary on Seneca's De Clementia in 1532. He broke from the Roman Catholic Church around 1530. After violence against Protestants in France he fled to Basel, where in March 1536 he published the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion.

William Farel recruited him for the Reformation in Geneva, but the city council resisted their proposals and both men were expelled. At Martin Bucer's invitation Calvin became minister of a French refugee church in Strasbourg. Invited back to Geneva in 1541, he saw the council pass the Ecclesiastical Ordinances on 20 November 1541, which defined four orders of ministry and created the Consistory, a court of elders and ministers with no civil jurisdiction. Opposition came from wealthy, interrelated families he called libertines, led by Ami Perrin from about 1546.

Michael Servetus, a Spanish physician whose book rejected the Trinity, arrived in Geneva on 13 August 1553 and was burned at the stake for heresy by the city council after Calvin denounced him. Sebastian Castellio broke with Calvin over the treatment of heretics. In January 1555 the council confirmed that the Consistory should regain its powers, and Calvin's authority was practically uncontested in his last years. The final edition of the Institutes appeared in 1559, in four books and eighty chapters. His theology included predestination and God's absolute sovereignty in salvation, and his critics such as Jérôme-Hermès Bolsec attacked the first.

Calvin preached his last sermon on 6 February 1564 and died on 27 May 1564, aged 54. He was buried in an unmarked grave in the Cimetière des Rois. Geneva sheltered English exiles from 1555, among them John Knox, who carried his ideas to Scotland and England. His reforms reached the Netherlands and the Palatinate, where the Heidelberg Catechism was written in 1563.
john-casimir-of-the-palatinate-simmern: John Casimir was born in Simmern on 7 March 1543, the third son of Frederick III, Elector Palatine, and Marie of Brandenburg-Kulmbach, of the Simmern line of the House of Wittelsbach. In 1564 he offered himself as a husband to Elizabeth I of England and sent her his portrait through the Scottish courtier Sir James Melville, but she showed no interest.

In 1570 he married in Heidelberg the Lutheran Elisabeth of Saxony, a daughter of Augustus, Elector of Saxony, hoping the match would link Calvinism to Saxony. The marriage was unhappy. He accused her of adultery and placed her under house arrest, and she died in prison on 2 April 1590. Of her six children three were stillborn; only Dorothea, who married John George I, Prince of Anhalt-Dessau, lived to adulthood.

From March 1571 he lived at Kaiserslautern. When Frederick III died in 1576, his will ordered that the Palatinate remain Calvinist, but the elder brother Louis VI, raised secretly as a Lutheran by his mother, ignored it. John Casimir received a smaller share that became the Count Palatine of Lautern, and welcomed theologians such as Zacharias Ursinus who left the University of Heidelberg, building the Collegium Casimirianum at Neustadt for them in 1578.

He was in regular contact with Robert Dudley, 1st Earl of Leicester, and Sir Philip Sidney, sent by Elizabeth I to help form a Protestant league. His French campaign at the head of four thousand troops brought him the title of duc d’Étampes from Henry III of France for a few months in 1576–1577, though he never visited the duchy.

In February 1579 he came to England to seek the queen's money for his campaigns on behalf of the United Provinces. Leicester took him to Oxford, he was entertained for three weeks at court and hunted deer in Hyde Park, and he left with gold plate from the queen, hawks and hounds from Leicester and a gold chain from the Earl of Pembroke. From 1583 he governed as regent for his nephew Elector Frederick IV until his death on 16 January 1592.
john-chilembwe: Little is certain of John Chilembwe's birth. An American pamphlet of 1914 placed it at Sangano in Chiradzulu District, and the missionary Joseph Booth said his father was a Yao and his mother a Mang'anja slave captured in warfare. He attended a Church of Scotland mission from around 1890, and in 1892 became a house servant of Booth, a radical Baptist who preached the equality of all worshippers. In 1897 the two travelled to the United States, where Chilembwe studied at the Virginia Theological Seminary and College in Lynchburg, met ideas of Black self-determination and was ordained a Baptist minister in 1899.

Back in Nyasaland with backing from the National Baptist Convention, Chilembwe preached self-respect and self-help in the manner of Booker T. Washington, and by 1912 the schools of his mission had 1,000 pupils and 800 adult students. By 1912 or 1913 he had become openly critical of African land rights in the Shire Highlands, where European estates held almost half of the best arable land, and of the labour tenancy called thangata. On the neighbouring Magomero estate of A. L. Bruce Estates, the manager William Jervis Livingstone burned the churches Chilembwe built on estate land.

Debts, asthma, the death of a daughter and failing eyesight may have deepened his anger. The First World War, in which some 19,000 Nyasaland Africans served in the King's African Rifles and up to 200,000 were forced to work as porters, moved him to act. A letter of protest to the Nyasaland Times was stopped by the censor, and the governor planned to deport him.

On the night of 23 January 1915 about 200 men, mostly from his congregations, attacked the Bruce estates; Livingstone was beheaded and two other European employees were killed, and Chilembwe had ordered that women be spared. The rising found no wider support, and he was tracked down and killed on 3 February. Many of his followers were executed after summary trials, and a commission of inquiry found the conditions on the Bruce estates illegal and oppressive. John Chilembwe Day is observed on 15 January, his portrait has appeared on kwacha notes, and a statue of him was unveiled in Trafalgar Square in London in September 2022.
john-churchill-1st-duke-of-marlborough: John Churchill was the second but eldest surviving son of Sir Winston Churchill of Glanvilles Wootton, Dorset, a Royalist who was heavily fined after the Wars of the Three Kingdoms. After the Restoration his father was knighted and held a post at Whitehall, and John attended St Paul's School. He served as a page at the court of James, Duke of York, and is recorded with Sir Thomas Allin in the Mediterranean in 1670. He was present at the Battle of Solebay on 28 May 1672. In the winter of 1677–78 he married Sarah Jennings, who served in the household of James's second wife, Mary of Modena; they had five children who survived infancy.

Churchill led the infantry under the Earl of Feversham at Sedgemoor on 6 July 1685, which effectively ended the Monmouth Rebellion, but he became a key figure in the conspiracy that deposed James II in the Glorious Revolution. William III made him Earl of Marlborough on 9 April 1689. Rumours of Jacobite treachery led to his dismissal and to five weeks in the Tower of London in 1692, until letters accusing him were shown to be forgeries.

On 4 May 1702 England declared war on France, and Marlborough was given supreme command of the Anglo-Dutch army, although he had never commanded a field army and the Dutch States General limited his powers in twelve articles. He led the allied army against Louis XIV from 1701 to 1711, and won at Blenheim in 1704, Ramillies in 1706, Oudenarde in 1708 and Malplaquet in 1709, the bloodiest battle of the war. His attention to logistics earned him the nickname Corporal John.

After Malplaquet the strategy of forcing peace by a great battle lost its force, and Louis XIV would not agree to remove his grandson Philip V from Spain. Sarah's quarrel with Queen Anne, and political pressure from Harley and St John, led to charges of corruption and Marlborough's removal, after which he went into self-imposed exile. He returned to favour under George I in 1714, but a stroke in May 1716 ended his career; he died on 16 June 1722.

Historians have often described him as one of the finest commanders. He held a fractious coalition together, and his campaigns helped to establish Britain as a front-rank power. Some historians fault him for not pressing his private doubts about the war aim of replacing Philip V in Spain.
john-cicero: John was born on 2 August 1455, the eldest son of Albert III Achilles of Brandenburg and his first wife, Margaret of Baden. His father then ruled as Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach, so John was born and spent his childhood at the Hohenzollern residence of Ansbach in Franconia. In 1466 his uncle, Elector Frederick II of Brandenburg, called him to Brandenburg as presumed heir, and he joined Frederick in the War of the Succession of Stettin against the Pomeranian dukes.

When Frederick resigned in 1470 and was succeeded by John's father, Albert Achilles appointed John regent of the Brandenburg lands in 1473. He then had to deal with the inheritance conflict that followed the death in 1476 of the Piast duke Henry XI of Głogów, husband of his half-sister Barbara. On 25 August 1476 in Berlin he married Margaret of Wettin, a daughter of Landgrave William III of Thuringia.

John succeeded his father as elector in 1486, while the Franconian possessions of the dynasty passed to his younger brothers Frederick I and Siegmund. He was the fourth elector of the House of Hohenzollern. He decreed that the Stadtschloss in Berlin, built at the wish of Frederick II, should be the permanent residence of the electors. The beer excise he introduced in 1488 led to several disturbances, mainly in the towns of the Altmark region.

In 1490 he bought the former Lusatian territory around Zossen, a purchase acknowledged by King Vladislaus II of Bohemia, and he kept up the Hohenzollern claims to the Pomeranian lands held by the House of Griffins. Among his children were his successor Joachim I Nestor, Anna, who married King Frederick I of Denmark, and Albert of Mainz, later cardinal and archbishop of Magdeburg and of Mainz.

John died of pleural effusion at Arneburg Castle on 9 January 1499 and was succeeded by Joachim I. He was the first Hohenzollern elector to be buried in Brandenburg, first at Lehnin Abbey; his grandson Joachim II later had him moved to Berlin Cathedral. The name Cicero, after the Roman orator, was given to him after his death, and how far he deserved it for eloquence or an interest in the arts is debated.
john-compton: Compton was born on 29 April 1925 at Canouan in St. Vincent and the Grenadines and was taken to Saint Lucia in September 1939. He studied law and economics at the University College of Wales from 1948 to 1949 and at the London School of Economics from 1949 to 1951, and was called to the Bar on 7 August 1951. In 1954 he won the Micoud/Dennery seat on the Executive Council as an independent, then joined the Saint Lucia Labour Party, taking part in a sugar workers' strike in 1957 and becoming deputy leader under George Charles.

Objecting to the party's new ministers, Compton left it after the 1961 election and formed the National Labour Movement, which merged in 1964 with the People's Progressive Party into the United Workers Party. The new party won that year's election and he became Chief Minister. At the conference of 1966 that prepared associated statehood he sharply criticised the British government, and when Saint Lucia became an Associated State on 1 March 1967 he was its first and only Premier.

Defeated a few months after independence, he led the opposition until the Labour government collapsed in October 1982, then governed again, also as finance minister, until he retired in 1996 in favour of his chosen successor Vaughan Lewis. His policies were conservative, pro-Western and anti-communist, and he worked for regional integration. Re-elected party leader at 80 in March 2005, he dismissed concerns about his age and led the party to victory against the polls on 11 December 2006.

On 1 May 2007 Compton suffered a series of strokes in New York City, and Stephenson King took over as acting prime minister. After pneumonia and a further stroke he died at the Tapion Hospital in Saint Lucia on 7 September 2007. His state funeral was held at the Minor Basilica of the Immaculate Conception in Castries, chosen for the size of the crowds although he was an Anglican, and his ashes were scattered in the Troumasse River. The John Compton Dam was renamed in his honour.
john-curtin: John Curtin was born on 8 January 1885 at Creswick, Victoria, the eldest of four children of parents born in County Cork. His father had been a policeman, and the family moved to Melbourne when he left the force. Curtin left school at 13 and held a series of short jobs, among them office boy for the magazine The Rambler under Norman Lindsay, before taking permanent work as a clerk in 1903.

He joined the Labor Party and the Marxist Victorian Socialist Party young, holding anti-imperialist and anti-militarist views. From 1911 he was state secretary of the Timberworkers' Union, and he was a militant opponent of overseas conscription in the First World War. He was briefly jailed in December 1916 for refusing a compulsory medical examination. In 1917 he moved to Perth to edit the Westralian Worker.

After losing three earlier contests, Curtin won the seat of Fremantle in 1928. He lost it in 1931 and won it back in 1934. In 1935 he became Labor leader, beating Frank Forde by one vote, with left-wing and union support on the condition that he give up alcohol, which he did. In October 1941 two independents joined Labor in defeating Arthur Fadden's budget, and Curtin was sworn in as prime minister on 7 October. He remains the only prime minister from Western Australia.

On 8 December 1941 Japan bombed Pearl Harbor, and Curtin told Australians that they were at war with Japan. After the fall of Singapore on 15 February 1942 he called it the opening of the Battle for Australia. He cabled Roosevelt and Churchill that Australia would gladly accept United States commanders in the Pacific, placed Australian forces under General Douglas MacArthur, and worked closely with him. He also settled the question of overseas conscription that had split Labor in 1916. His government extended pensions, maternity allowances and welfare entitlements, and created the Universities Commission in 1943.

At the 1943 election Labor won about two thirds of the seats in the House of Representatives. Curtin developed heart disease in 1944, had a heart attack in November and returned to work only in January 1945. He died at The Lodge on 5 July 1945, aged 60, as Australian troops began the Battle of Balikpapan. His successor Ben Chifley carried out many of his post-war reconstruction plans. Curtin is commemorated by a federal seat, a Canberra suburb, Curtin University in Perth and a bronze statue at Fremantle Town Hall.
john-de-britto: João de Brito was born on 1 March 1647 in Lisbon into a powerful aristocratic Portuguese family. His father, Salvador de Britto Pereira, died while serving as Viceroy of the Portuguese colony of Brazil. He joined the Jesuits in 1662 and studied at the University of Coimbra. Before reaching the mission field he spent seven months in Goa completing his theological studies at St Paul's College in Old Goa.

He travelled to the Madurai Mission in 1673 and preached in the Maravar country, taking the Tamil name Arul Anandar. The mission was an attempt to build an Indian Catholic Church relatively free of European cultural domination, following the method of Roberto de Nobili. Britto learned the local languages, went about in yellow cotton and lived as a Tamil sannyasi, eating only legumes, fruits and herbs and taking no wine, and he tried to teach the faith in concepts that made sense to his hearers.

The ruler of the Maravar country imprisoned him in 1684. Expelled, he returned to Lisbon in 1687 and worked as a procurator of the missions. King Pedro II wanted him to stay in Portugal, but in 1690 he went back to the Maravar country with 24 new missionaries. Indian Catholics often call him the Portuguese St. Francis Xavier, and he is also known as the John the Baptist of India.

The convert whose marriage led to his death was Thadiyathevan, a Maravar prince who, as a Christian, had to keep only one wife. One of the women he sent away was a niece of Raghunatha Kilavan Sethupathi, the King of Ramnad, who then launched a general persecution of Christians. Britto and his catechists were seized and taken to Ramnad, and from there to Orur, some 30 miles north along the coast, where he was executed on 4 February 1693.

Pope Pius IX beatified him on 21 August 1853, and Pope Pius XII canonised him on 22 June 1947; his feast day is 4 February. At Orur a shrine built in Portuguese style stands beside the red sand dune believed to have been stained by his blood, and pilgrims from Tamil Nadu and Kerala, Hindus and Muslims as well as Christians, gather there for its festival. Churches and Jesuit schools bear his name in India, Portugal, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Mauritius and Brazil.
john-doukas-megas-doux: John Doukas was born around 1064, the second son of the domestikos ton scholon Andronikos Doukas and Maria of Bulgaria, a granddaughter of Ivan Vladislav, the last ruler of the First Bulgarian Empire; his sister Irene Doukaina married Alexios Komnenos. In 1074 the rebel Norman mercenary Roussel de Bailleul demanded John and his elder brother Michael as hostages from their grandfather, the Caesar John Doukas, in return for their wounded father. Michael escaped, but John stayed with Roussel until the Turks of Artuk captured the rebel later that year.

Raised by his grandfather after his father's death in 1077, John learned in 1081 of Alexios's rebellion against Nikephoros III Botaneiates, told the Caesar, and went with him to join Alexios at Schiza, where Alexios was proclaimed emperor.

From 1085, after Alexios recovered Dyrrhachium from the Italo-Normans, John was military governor (doux) of the province until 1092. He repelled Serbian incursions from Duklja and inner Serbia, and Anna Komnene says that he captured the Dukljan king Constantine Bodin before restoring him as a Byzantine client. Archbishop Theophylact of Ohrid later wrote of his governorship with nostalgia.

Made megas doux in 1092, the first known holder of the title, he moved against Lesbos. After a three-month siege of Mytilene, Tzachas offered the island in exchange for safe passage to Smyrna; as the Turks sailed, Constantine Dalassenos attacked them and captured or sank most of their fleet. With Manuel Boutoumites, John then suppressed the revolts of Karykes in Crete and Rhapsomates in Cyprus.

In 1097 Alexios made him commander-in-chief in Anatolia. Taking with him the captured wife of Sultan Kilij Arslan I and the daughter of Tzachas, he received the surrender of Smyrna, but after its new governor Kaspax was murdered, the fleet's sailors massacred the inhabitants. He went on to take Ephesus, with 2,000 captives, then Sardeis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, and surprised and defeated the surviving Turks at Polybotos.

The Alexiad does not mention John Doukas after his campaign of 1097. Monastic documents show that at some point he retired to a monastery and took the monastic name Antony. The date of his death is not known: a typikon of 1110–1116 names him as alive, while another, of 1136, speaks of him as dead.
john-duke-of-berry: John was born at the castle of Vincennes on 30 November 1340, the third son of King John II of France and Bonne of Luxembourg. His brothers were King Charles V, Duke Louis I of Anjou and Duke Philip the Bold of Burgundy. His father made him Count of Poitou in 1356 and in 1358 named him king's lieutenant of Auvergne, Languedoc, Périgord and Poitou while the king was a captive of the English. When Poitiers was ceded to England in 1360, he was granted the newly raised duchies of Berry and Auvergne. Under the Treaty of Brétigny, signed that May, he became a hostage of the English Crown and remained in England until 1369.

On the death of Charles V in 1380 John and his brothers, with the Duke of Bourbon, acted as regents for the young Charles VI. In 1380 he was also made Lieutenant General in Languedoc, where he faced the Harelle, a peasants' revolt against heavy taxation for the war with the English. After Louis I of Anjou died in 1384, John and the Duke of Burgundy were the dominant figures in the kingdom. The king ended the regency in 1388, governing through his father's former ministers and stripping John of his offices in Languedoc. John and Philip regained power in 1392, when the king had his first attack of insanity.

In the 1390s the dukes of Berry and Burgundy competed for royal favour against the Duke of Orléans, and in April 1401 they made the king return the lieutenancy of Languedoc, Berry, Auvergne and Poitou to John. After Philip's death in 1404 he was the last surviving son of John II and tried to mediate between his nephews Louis I, Duke of Orléans and John the Fearless of Burgundy. After the murder of Orléans in 1407 he generally took the Armagnac side and formed the League of Gien in 1410, though he remained moderate. His urging largely kept Charles VI and his sons from the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, for he remembered his father's capture at Poitiers.

John died in Paris on 15 June 1416, deeply in debt, since spending on his art collection had severely taxed his estates. He commissioned the Très Riches Heures, the Belles Heures and parts of the Turin-Milan Hours, and employed the Limbourg brothers, Jacquemart de Hesdin and André Beauneveu. The Holy Thorn Reliquary and the Royal Gold Cup, both now in the British Museum, were made for him, and Guillaume de Machaut entered his service. His motto was Le temps venra, "the time will come". The scholar Emmanuel Legeard argues that his castles, the Sainte-Chapelle at Bourges Cathedral and his manuscripts expressed a claim to royal standing by a man pushed from power.
john-duke-of-brunswick-luneburg: John belonged to the House of Welf. His father, Otto the Child, had received the Welf allodial possessions in Saxony from Emperor Frederick II and become the first Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg. After Otto's death in 1252 John ruled the duchy jointly with his elder brother, Albert the Tall. In 1265 he married Liutgard, a daughter of Count Gerhard I of Holstein-Itzehoe, with whom he had five children.

Because the brothers could not agree who should govern, they decided in 1267 to divide their possessions, and in 1269 John received the right to choose his part. He chose the northern Lüneburg estates with the city of Hanover, while Albert received Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel with further lands around Calenberg and Göttingen. John thus founded the Old Line of Lüneburg, although under imperial law the duchy remained undivided and all the Welf princes kept the title Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg.

In a fierce feud with Count Gunzelin III of Schwerin, John acquired the settlement of Uelzen, whose residents he granted town privileges in 1270. He tried in vain to gain control of the Lüneburg Saltworks and in the end gave the citizens of Lüneburg a monopoly of the salt trade in his principality, carried mainly along the Old Salt Route to Lübeck and the Baltic Sea.

John died on 13 December 1277 and was buried in the cloister of St. Michael's Church at his residence in Lüneburg. His son and heir, Otto II the Strict, was still a minor and remained under the tutelage of his uncles, Duke Albert the Tall and Bishop Conrad of Verden, until 1282. Of his daughters, Matilde married Henry I, Prince of Mecklenburg-Güstrow, and Elisabeth married John II, Count of Oldenburg; an illegitimate son, Henry of Brunswick, became a canon in Walsrode.
john-eliot-missionary: Eliot was born in Widford, Hertfordshire, grew up at Nazeing and studied at Jesus College, Cambridge. He became assistant to Thomas Hooker at a school in Little Baddow, Essex, and after Hooker fled to the Netherlands he sailed for Boston as chaplain on the ship Lyon, arriving on 3 November 1631. He became teaching elder of the First Church in Roxbury, where he served for sixty years. In 1637–1638 he took part in the trials of Anne Hutchinson during the Antinomian Controversy, and in 1645 he founded the Roxbury Latin School.

With Thomas Weld, Thomas Mayhew and Richard Mather he is credited with editing the Bay Psalm Book of 1640. To learn Massachusett he relied on Cockenoe, a young man captured in the Pequot War of 1637, who spoke the language and English. His first sermon to the Massachusett under the sachem Cutshamekin at Dorchester Mills failed; his second, in the wigwam of Waban at Nonantum, now Newton, began on 28 October 1646.

His Bible was printed by Samuel Green and Marmaduke Johnson, with the help of Indigenous people including the Nipmuc James Printer (Wowaus). He published The Indian Grammar Begun in 1666, and at one time there were 14 praying towns. His book The Christian Commonwealth, published in England in 1659, called for an elected theocracy; after the accession of Charles II the General Court forced him in 1661 to retract it, banned the book and ordered every copy destroyed.

The praying towns were disrupted in King Philip's War of 1675 and over the following two centuries mostly lost their status as self-governing Indigenous communities. In 1689 Eliot gave 75 acres of land to support a school in Jamaica Plain, on condition that it accept Black and Native American students without prejudice. He died on 21 May 1690, his last words being "welcome joy!" Cotton Mather saw his missionary career as the epitome of New England Puritan ideals, and the seal of Newton shows him preaching to an Indigenous audience.
john-ernest-iv-duke-of-saxe-coburg-saalf: John Ernest was born on 22 August 1658, the tenth child but seventh surviving son of Ernest I, Duke of Saxe-Gotha, and Elisabeth Sophie of Saxe-Altenburg, both of the Ernestine line of the House of Wettin. When his father died in 1675, he at first governed Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg jointly with his six older brothers, as the will laid down.

By a treaty of 1680 the brothers divided their father's lands. As the youngest, John Ernest received the smallest share, the duchy of Saxe-Saalfeld with the towns of Gräfenthal, Probstzella and Pössneck. He and his brother Ernest soon found themselves overstretched, since the income of their eldest brother Frederick far exceeded theirs, and both protested.

The quarrel grew as the brothers Albert of Saxe-Coburg, Henry of Saxe-Römhild and Christian of Saxe-Eisenberg died without male heirs. John Ernest took possession of Coburg in 1699, and of Römhild and five-twelfths of Themar in 1714. The dispute over these inheritances, the Coburg-Eisenberg-Römhilder Erbstreit, was settled only in 1735 after repeated imperial arbitration, and his descendants kept Coburg; the descendants of his brother Bernhard, who also claimed it, accepted the decision.

He married Sophie Hedwig of Saxe-Merseburg, a daughter of Christian I, Duke of Saxe-Merseburg, at Merseburg on 18 February 1680, and secondly Charlotte Johanna of Waldeck-Wildungen at Maastricht on 2 December 1690. He died on 17 February 1729. Two of his sons, Christian Ernst and Francis Josias, each later became Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, while their brothers Wilhelm Frederick and Karl Ernst both died unmarried in 1720, the latter at Cremona. His daughter Charlotte Wilhelmine married Philip Reinhard, Count of Hanau-Münzenberg.
john-f-kennedy: John Fitzgerald Kennedy was born on 29 May 1917 in Brookline, Massachusetts, to Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., a businessman and politician, and Rose Kennedy. His maternal grandfather and namesake, John F. Fitzgerald, was a U.S. congressman and two-term mayor of Boston. He graduated from Harvard University in 1940. Medically disqualified from the Army's Officer Candidate School because of chronic back problems, he joined the United States Naval Reserve on 24 September 1941.

With his father's backing, Kennedy won the Democratic primary for Massachusetts's 11th congressional district in 1946 and sat in the House of Representatives from 1947 to 1953. In 1952 he narrowly defeated Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. for the Senate. After several spinal operations he published Profiles in Courage, which won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography in 1957.

He announced his candidacy for the presidency on 2 January 1960, took the nomination on the first ballot at the Democratic convention in Los Angeles, and chose Lyndon Johnson as his running mate. He was sworn in on 20 January 1961.

Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas at 12:30 p.m. on 22 November 1963, shot as his motorcade passed through Dealey Plaza, and was pronounced dead at Parkland Hospital at 1:00 p.m., aged 46. Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested and, on 24 November, shot dead by Jack Ruby before he could be prosecuted. The Warren Commission concluded that Oswald had acted alone, though conspiracy theories persist. Many of Kennedy's proposals passed after his death, including the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
john-forrest: Forrest was born on 22 August 1847 on his father's property outside Bunbury, Western Australia, the fourth of ten children of Margaret and William Forrest, Scottish immigrants who had come to the colony as domestic servants. His father later built a homestead and mill at Picton. In 1863, aged 16, Forrest was apprenticed to Thomas Campbell Carey, the government surveyor at Bunbury, and he became the colony's first locally born surveyor.

In 1869 he led a fruitless search for the explorer Ludwig Leichhardt, missing since 1848. The following year he surveyed Edward John Eyre's route along the Great Australian Bight from Perth to Adelaide, a route that might carry a telegraph line, and in 1874 he led a party from Geraldton east through the unknown centre of Western Australia to the overland telegraph line. His expeditions were noted for careful planning and record-keeping, and he published Explorations in Australia in 1875.

In January 1883 he became surveyor-general and commissioner of crown lands, with a seat on the Executive Council. On 22 December 1890 Governor William Robinson appointed him premier. With loans raised in London and the engineer C. Y. O'Connor, his government built railways, the Fremantle Harbour Works and the Goldfields Water Supply Scheme, which piped water from the Helena River over 550 kilometres to Kalgoorlie. He supported Federation on fair terms for Western Australia and represented the colony at the conventions of 1891 and 1897–8.

In federal politics he held office as Minister for Defence and Minister for Home Affairs, pressed for Dalgety as the national capital, served as Treasurer under Alfred Deakin and Joseph Cook, and was acting prime minister from 18 to 26 June 1907. In 1913 he lost the contest for the leadership of the Liberal Party to Cook by a single vote.

After a rodent ulcer was removed from his temple in 1915, the cancer returned, and he resigned from the ministry on 21 March 1918. He was nominated to the peerage by Billy Hughes but died on the way to England before it was confirmed. His biographer F. K. Crowley wrote of his snobbery, royalism and belief in racial superiority, and he took a paternalistic view of Indigenous Australians. John Forrest National Park and the Division of Forrest are named after him.
john-frederick-i-elector-of-saxony: John Frederick I was born on 30 June 1503, the eldest son of John, Elector of Saxony, by his first wife Sophie of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, who died fourteen days later. George Spalatin, a friend of Martin Luther, educated him, and he became devoted to Luther's teaching. His library was one of the largest in Germany. He urged the printing of the first complete Wittenberg edition of Luther's works and later promoted the Jena edition. In 1530 he signed the Augsburg Confession with his father, which won him the dislike of Emperor Charles V.

John Frederick succeeded his father as elector in 1532, ruling at first with his half-brother John Ernest and from 1542 alone. He set up an electoral consistory in 1542 and took a firmer stand than his father in favour of the Schmalkaldic League. He opposed a council called by the papacy, and asked Luther to summarise the articles he would uphold, which became the Schmalkald Articles. In 1541 he installed Nicolaus von Amsdorf as bishop of Naumburg in place of the elected Julius von Pflug, and in 1542 he expelled Duke Henry V of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel to protect Goslar and Brunswick.

In the Schmalkaldic War of 1546 his cousin Duke Maurice invaded his lands. At the Battle of Mühlberg on 24 April 1547 his army was dispersed, and a wound left a scar down his cheek. Charles V took him prisoner.

The emperor condemned him to death as a rebel but did not carry out the sentence. To save his life and protect his family, John Frederick accepted the Capitulation of Wittenberg, giving up the electoral titles and the Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg to Maurice, and his sentence became life imprisonment. Maurice's attack on the emperor ended his captivity, and he was released on 1 September 1552. He returned to Wolfersdorf Castle, which he renamed Schloss Froehliche Wiederkunft, and moved his government to Weimar. He planned the University of Jena in place of Wittenberg, and died in Weimar on 3 March 1554.
john-frum-movement: The movement drew on existing religious practice around Sulphur Bay on Tanna, above all the worship of Keraperamun, a god associated with Mount Tukosmera; a claim made in 1949 placed its beginnings as early as the 1910s. Accounts of the figure differ. In one he was first known as John Broom, who would return from a distant land to sweep away the White colonials. In another a local man named Manehivi took the alias John Frum and appeared in a Western-style coat, promising houses, clothes, food and transport.

Others hold that John Frum was a spirit vision induced by kava and a manifestation of Keraperamun. His followers were to reject money, Western education, Christianity and work on the copra plantations and return to kastom, the Bislama word for custom. In 1941 they spent their money, left the missionary churches, schools, villages and plantations and moved inland for traditional feasts, dances and rituals. Most had come from the Presbyterian church.

The colonial authorities tried to suppress the movement, arresting a Tannese man who called himself John Frum, humiliating him in public, imprisoning him and exiling him and other leaders to another island. During World War II 50,000 American troops were stationed in the islands with vast supplies, and about 10,000 Ni-Vanuatu men served in the Vanuatu Labor Corps of the United States Armed Forces during the Guadalcanal campaign. Their experience gave the faith the character of a cargo cult, and after the war followers built symbolic landing strips to draw American aeroplanes bringing cargo.

In 1957 the leaders formed the Tanna Army, a non-violent body that paraded with imitation American caps, singlets lettered T-A USA and bamboo guns. When the government moved against it, some members barricaded themselves in their headquarters with real guns, and the leaders were tried and jailed in Vila. In 1959 a follower told David Attenborough that if others could wait two thousand years for Jesus Christ, he could wait more than nineteen years for John.

In the late 1970s followers opposed the creation of a united, independent Vanuatu, fearing that a central government would favour Western modernity and Christianity over local custom. The movement reportedly had over 5,000 members in the 1990s and fewer than 500 by 2022. Europeans who claimed to be the leader of the prophecy, such as Claude-Philippe Berger, who styled himself traditional king of Tanna, gained status on the island by promising development and investment.
john-george-elector-of-brandenburg: John George of Brandenburg was born on 11 September 1525 into the House of Hohenzollern, the eldest son of Joachim II Hector, Elector of Brandenburg, and Princess Magdalena of Saxony. He was married three times. His first wife, whom he married in 1545, was Princess Sophie of Legnica, daughter of Frederick II of Legnica; their one child, Joachim Frederick, was born in 1546, and Sophie died that year. In 1548 he married Margravine Sabina of Brandenburg-Ansbach, who died in 1575. Of their children several died at birth or in early childhood, while daughters married into the ducal houses of Pomerania and the electoral house of Saxony.

John George was prince-elector of Brandenburg from 1571 to 1598. He faced large debts of 2.5 million guilder accumulated during his father's reign. To meet them he instituted a grain tax, which drove part of the peasantry into dependence on a nobility that was exempt from taxation. In 1573 he had the Jews expelled from Brandenburg, stripped of their assets and forbidden to return.

He was a staunch Lutheran opposed to the rise of Calvinism, yet he permitted the admission of Calvinist refugees from the wars in the Spanish Netherlands and France. On 13 July 1574 he founded the Berlinisches Gymnasium zum Grauen Kloster, the first humanistic educational institution in Berlin. After the death of Albert I, Duke of Prussia, in 1568 the duchy passed to his underage son Albert Frederick, and John George's father was a co-inheritor; in 1577 the Brandenburg electors became co-regent with Duke Albert Frederick.

In 1577 John George married his third wife, Princess Elisabeth of Anhalt-Zerbst, daughter of Joachim Ernest, Prince of Anhalt. They had many children, among them Christian, Joachim Ernest, Magdalena, who married Landgrave Louis V of Hesse-Darmstadt, and John, later Bishop of Havelberg. John George died on 8 January 1598 and was succeeded by his son Joachim Frederick.
john-george-i-duke-of-saxe-eisenach: Johann Georg was born at Weimar on 12 July 1634, the fifth but third surviving son of William, Duke of Saxe-Weimar, and Eleonore Dorothea of Anhalt-Dessau. When his father died in 1662, his eldest brother Johann Ernst II inherited Weimar and his second brother Adolf Wilhelm received Eisenach. Johann Georg was given an income from the new duchy of Saxe-Eisenach and lived in the small town of Marksuhl. On 29 May 1661 at Wallau he had married Countess Johannetta of Sayn-Wittgenstein, heiress of Sayn-Altenkirchen.

Adolf Wilhelm died in 1668, and his only surviving son, Wilhelm August, born eight days after his father's death, was duke from birth. Johann Georg became regent of the duchy and the boy's guardian. Wilhelm August died at two years of age, and the duchy passed to his uncle. In 1672 the death without heirs of Duke Frederick Wilhelm III of Saxe-Altenburg forced a new division of the family lands among Johann Georg, his surviving brothers and his cousin; Johann Georg was confirmed in Eisenach and gained some towns, while his younger brother Bernhard received Jena.

In the spring of 1672 he moved his residence from Marksuhl to Eisenach, an occasion marked by an Easter church service with music by Ambrosius Bach, and the town again became the capital of the principality. Johann Sebastian Bach was born in the duchy in 1685, during his rule.

Johann Georg died in a hunting accident at Eckhartshausen near Marksuhl on 19 September 1686. His eldest son, Frederick August, had been killed in battle at Pressburg in 1684, and two younger sons became dukes of Saxe-Eisenach in turn: Johann Georg II, who died of smallpox in 1698, and Johann Wilhelm, who lived until 1729. The line Johann Georg founded died out in 1741.

His daughter Eleonore Erdmuthe Luise married first Johann Friedrich, Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach, and then Johann Georg IV, Elector of Saxony; by her first marriage she was the mother of Caroline of Brandenburg-Ansbach, wife of King George II of Great Britain. Another daughter, Fredericka Elisabeth, married Johann Georg, Duke of Saxe-Weissenfels.
john-george-i-elector-of-saxony: John George was born in Dresden on 5 March 1585, the second son of Elector Christian I and Sophie of Brandenburg, and belonged to the Albertine line of the House of Wettin. To learn statecraft, law and history he and his brothers matriculated at Leipzig University, with which he kept close ties throughout his reign, often employing its medical and legal professors as advisors and physicians. He succeeded his elder brother Christian II as elector on 23 June 1611.

Saxony's geographical position gave its ruler weight in the Thirty Years' War more than its standing among German Protestants did. John George was a sound Lutheran, but he disliked the growing strength of Brandenburg-Prussia and the prestige of the Palatinate, and he favoured the Habsburgs. In August 1619 he voted for Archduke Ferdinand of Styria as emperor, and he occupied Silesia and Lusatia for him, so taking part in driving Frederick V, Elector Palatine, from Bohemia. Unease at imperial policy grew, and the Edict of Restitution of March 1629 deepened his fears, yet he only protested, calling a meeting of Protestant princes at Leipzig in February 1631.

Tilly's invasion of Saxony drove him into an alliance with Gustavus Adolphus in September 1631. The Saxons were routed at the Battle of Breitenfeld, and the elector fled. They later occupied Prague, but Wallenstein drove them back. In May 1635 he made the Treaty of Prague with Ferdinand II, receiving Lusatia and other territory. He then declared war on the Swedes but was beaten at Wittstock in October 1636. Saxony, ravaged by both sides, agreed a truce with the Swedes in September 1645, which ended the war there.

John George died on 8 October 1656, after the Peace of Westphalia, which for Saxony did little more than confirm the Treaty of Prague. John George II succeeded him, and three younger sons, Augustus, Christian and Maurice, inherited the duchies of Weissenfels, Merseburg and Zeitz. Swedish soldiers called him Öl Göran, Beer Göran, for his drinking and eating. An assessment holds that, though not without political skill, he was not a great ruler: his character was harsh, and Wallenstein spoke of him with contempt.
john-george-i-prince-of-anhalt-dessau: John George was born in Harzgerode on 9 May 1567, the eldest son of Joachim Ernest, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, and his first wife Agnes, daughter of Wolfgang I, Count of Barby-Mühlingen. In 1570 the death of his last surviving uncle, Bernhard VII, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, left his father sole ruler of all the Anhalt states, united for the first time since their first partition in 1252.

When his father died in 1586, John George inherited the united principality jointly with his younger brother Christian I and his five half-brothers, since the family law of the House of Ascania forbade any division of the lands among heirs. Because the half-brothers were still minors, he acted as regent. In 1603 the surviving brothers agreed to divide the principality. John George took Anhalt-Dessau together with the Seniorat, but he kept a regency over all the new principalities until 1606, when his brothers took over the government of their own lands.

In his own state he kept to the policies of the Reformation and worked hard to abolish the traditional customs and liturgy of the Roman Catholic Church. He was well regarded by his subjects and was thought learned abroad, especially in astrology and alchemy, and he owned a library of over 3000 volumes. On 24 August 1617, at Schloss Hornstein during the funeral of their sister Dorothea Maria, Duchess of Saxe-Weimar, he and his younger brother Louis of Anhalt-Köthen founded the Fruitbearing Society, with Louis as its first head.

He married twice. With his first wife, Dorothea, daughter of John Albert VI, Count of Mansfeld-Arnstein, whom he married at Hedersleben on 22 February 1588, he had five children before her death in 1594. On 21 February 1595 at Heidelberg he married another Dorothea, the only surviving child of John Casimir of Simmern, a son of Frederick III, Elector Palatine, and they had eleven children. John George died at Dessau on 24 May 1618, at the age of 51, and was succeeded as Prince of Anhalt-Dessau by his eldest surviving son, John Casimir.
john-george-iii-elector-of-saxony: John George III was born in Dresden, the only son of John George II and Magdalene Sybille of Brandenburg-Bayreuth, and belonged to the Albertine branch of the House of Wettin. He received a strictly Lutheran education, with language tuition and instruction in fortress building and warfare. Like his father he liked Italian music and theatre. Even as heir he led Saxon forces in the Rhine campaign of the Franco-Dutch War. On succeeding in 1680 he was also appointed Marshal of the Holy Roman Empire, and his enthusiasm for war earned him the nickname the Saxonian Mars.

As elector he reduced the size of the royal household and began to build a small standing army of 12,000 men on the model of Brandenburg, obtaining a commitment of funds from the estates. A Privy War Chancellery became its highest authority, and heavy pressure was used to find recruits. He broke off relations with the French crown and worked to win Brandenburg and other German princes for the imperial war against France. He hired out troops as well: 3,000 men to the Republic of Venice for its Morean War in 1685, and 5,000 to the emperor in 1686 for 300,000 thalers.

In 1683 he led an army of 10,400 against the Turks despite opposition from the Saxon estates, who disliked the cost and the support for a Catholic emperor. At the Battle of Vienna on 12 September 1683 he commanded the left wing, and at his request the battle cry was changed from Maria Help to Jesus and Maria Help. King John III Sobieski, who also fought there, called him an honest man with a straight heart. Three days later he marched home without taking leave of the emperor, probably because of the brusque treatment he had received as a Protestant.

In 1689, after a renewed French invasion, he led his troops to defend Franconia and took part in the siege of Mainz. Ill, he left the field, but in May 1690 he returned against his advisers' counsel and took overall command of the imperial army. Quarrels with Hans Adam von Schöning and the Austrian commander Aeneas de Caprara limited the results, and only the crossing of the Rhine at Sandhofen succeeded.

He died soon afterwards at Tübingen of an epidemic illness, probably cholera or plague, and was buried in Freiberg Cathedral. He had married Anne Sophie of Denmark in 1666; their sons John George IV and Frederick Augustus I, later king of Poland, both followed him as elector. Under him Dresden, rebuilt in the baroque style after the fire of 1685, became less provincial.
john-glenn: John Herschel Glenn Jr. was born on 18 July 1921 in Cambridge, Ohio, and grew up in New Concord, where his father ran a plumbing business. He first flew in an airplane with his father at the age of eight and built model airplanes. When the United States entered the Second World War he left college and became a Navy aviation cadet in March 1942, then transferred to the Marine Corps and was commissioned a second lieutenant in 1943. He married Anna Margaret (Annie) Castor on 6 April 1943. In the Korean War he flew 63 combat missions, and he later attended the Naval Test Pilot School. In 1957 he made the first supersonic transcontinental flight across the United States.

NASA was established on 1 October 1958 after the launch of Sputnik 1, and Project Mercury aimed to put a man into Earth orbit. Glenn was one of the Mercury Seven military test pilots selected in 1959 as the first American astronauts, and he was backup pilot for the first two crewed Mercury flights. For Mercury-Atlas 6 he named his spacecraft Friendship 7. On 20 February 1962 he became the first American to orbit the Earth, circling it three times, and the third American and fifth person in space. Buzz Aldrin wrote that the flight helped to galvanize the country's will to meet the technical challenges of human spaceflight.

Glenn resigned from NASA on 16 January 1964 and announced his candidacy for the Senate from Ohio, becoming the first astronaut-politician. He was elected to the Senate in 1974 and served until January 1999. He was chief author of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Act of 1978. In 1998, at the age of 77, he flew on the Space Shuttle Discovery on mission STS-95, as the oldest person then to enter Earth orbit.

Glenn received the Congressional Space Medal of Honor in 1978, entered the US Astronaut Hall of Fame in 1990 and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012. He and Annie were married for 73 years, and they had two children. He died on 8 December 2016, aged 95, the oldest and last surviving of the Mercury Seven.
john-glubb: John Bagot Glubb was born in Preston, Lancashire, and educated at Cheltenham College. His father, Major-General Sir Frederic Manley Glubb, had been chief engineer in the British Second Army during the First World War, and his mother, Letitia Bagot, came from County Roscommon. He gained a commission in the Royal Engineers in 1915 and suffered a shattered jaw on the Western Front, which later gave him the Arab nickname Abu Hunayk, "the father of the little jaw". In 1920 he was transferred to Iraq, then under a League of Nations Mandate, and in 1922 he was posted to Ramadi to maintain a floating bridge over the Euphrates.

Glubb became an officer of the Arab Legion in 1930. In 1931 he formed the Desert Patrol, made up only of Bedouin, to curb the raiding that plagued southern Jordan, and within a few years he had persuaded the Bedouin to give up raiding neighbouring tribes. He also took part in suppressing the Ikhwan revolt. In 1939 he succeeded Frederick G. Peake as commander of the Legion and transformed it into the best-trained force in the Arab world. During the Second World War he led attacks on Axis-aligned Arab forces in Iraq and on Vichy forces in Lebanon and Syria.

In May 1948 Glubb led the Arab Legion across the River Jordan to occupy the West Bank, and severe fighting took place at Kfar Etzion, Jerusalem and Latrun. He remained in charge of the West Bank's defence after the armistice of March 1949. After King Hussein I came to the throne, differences arose over defence arrangements, the promotion of Arab officers and the funding of the Legion, and Arab nationalists believed that Glubb's first loyalty was to the United Kingdom. Hussein dismissed him and several other British senior officers on 1 March 1956.

Glubb remained a close friend of the King and spent the rest of his life writing books and articles, mostly on the Middle East and his experiences among the Arabs. He was appointed OBE in 1925, CMG in 1946 and KCB in 1956. He died at his home in Mayfield, East Sussex, and King Hussein gave the eulogy at the service held for him in Westminster Abbey on 17 April 1986. A stained glass window in St Dunstan's Church, Mayfield, celebrates his life, and his papers were deposited with the Middle East Centre Archive at St Antony's College, Oxford.
john-graves-simcoe: Simcoe was born in Cotterstock on 25 February 1752, the only surviving son of John Simcoe, a Royal Navy captain who commanded HMS Pembroke at the siege of Louisbourg, with James Cook as his sailing master, and who died in 1759 before the siege of Quebec. The family then moved to Exeter. Simcoe was educated at Exeter Grammar School and Eton College and spent a year at Merton College, Oxford, before choosing the army. He joined the 35th Regiment of Foot as an ensign in 1770.

Sent to the Thirteen Colonies in 1775, he served at the siege of Boston and, as a captain of the 40th Regiment of Foot, was wounded at the Battle of Brandywine on 11 September 1777. That year he took command of the Queen's Rangers, which fought at Crooked Billet and Monmouth and defeated Daniel Nimham's Stockbridge Militia at Kingsbridge in 1778. Captured in 1779 and released at the end of the year, he joined Benedict Arnold's raid on Richmond and was taken again at Yorktown. In 1782 he married Elizabeth Posthuma Gwillim, and as Member of Parliament for St Mawes from 1790 he spoke against the Atlantic slave trade.

Appointed lieutenant governor on 12 September 1791, he reached Kingston on 24 June 1792. Prompted by the Chloe Cooley incident, and working with his Attorney-General John White, he secured the Act Against Slavery of 1793, the first legislation to limit slavery in the British Empire: it also freed children born to enslaved women when they reached 25. Soldiers of the Queen's Rangers began cutting Yonge Street in August 1793, and he also began Dundas Street between York and London, a place he had named. During the Northwest Indian War he hoped for an Indian barrier state and built Fort Miami, but after the Jay Treaty he evacuated the frontier forts.

Simcoe returned to England in July 1796, suffering from gout. He was governor of British-occupied Saint-Domingue from October 1796 until March 1797, when British forces faced Toussaint Louverture's troops. Appointed Commander-in-Chief, India, in 1806, he fell ill on the way and died in Exeter on 26 October, and was buried at Wolford Chapel near Honiton. Lake Simcoe, named after his father, and Simcoe Day in Toronto keep his name, and his regiment survives as the Queen's York Rangers.
john-gunther-i-of-schwarzburg-sondershau: John Günther, also called Hans Günther or Johann Günther, was born in Sondershausen on 20 December 1532, a son of Count Günther XL of Schwarzburg, known as Günther the Rich, and his wife Elisabeth, a daughter of Count Philip of Isenburg-Büdingen-Ronneburg. He was raised a Catholic and intended for a career in the church, but after his father's death in 1552 he became a Lutheran.

He spent time at the court of Elector Maurice of Saxony and fought on Maurice's side at the Battle of Sievershausen against Albert Alcibiades, Margrave of Brandenburg-Kulmbach. Maurice's successor, Augustus, confirmed his tariff privilege on the salt trade at Frankenhausen. He also fought in the Netherlands alongside his eldest brother, Günther XLI.

From 1552 he ruled Schwarzburg jointly with his three brothers, living at Sondershausen. In 1571 the brothers divided the county, and his share took the name Schwarzburg-Sondershausen after its capital. When Günther XLI of Schwarzburg-Arnstadt and William I of Schwarzburg-Frankenhausen died without male heirs, John Günther inherited Schwarzburg-Arnstadt, while the last brother, Albert VII, received Schwarzburg-Frankenhausen.

On 16 February 1566 he married Anna, daughter of Anthony I, Count of Oldenburg, who died in 1579. They had twelve children. Four of their sons, Günther XLII, Anton Henry, John Günther II and Christian Günther I, became counts of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen, a daughter, Catharina, was deaness of Herford Abbey, and the youngest, Dorothea, married Duke Alexander of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg in 1604. His mother Elisabeth had died on 14 May 1572, the year after the partition. John Günther died at Arnstadt on 28 October 1586 and is regarded as the progenitor of the Schwarzburg-Sondershausen line.
john-hanning-speke: John Hanning Speke was born on 4 May 1827 at Orleigh Court, near Bideford in North Devon. In 1844 he was commissioned into the Bengal Army and served in the Punjab campaign and the First Anglo-Sikh War. He became a lieutenant in 1850 and a captain in 1852, and spent his leave exploring the Himalayan Mountains. In 1854 he joined Richard Burton's expedition to Somalia, where a night attack by about 200 spearmen near Berbera left a fellow officer dead, Burton wounded through both cheeks and Speke captured and stabbed several times before he escaped.

In 1857 Speke and Burton set out from Zanzibar to find the Great Lakes of the interior and the source of the Nile. Both fell ill, and the daily work was done largely by porters, guides and soldiers. They reached Kazeh (Tabora) in November and Lake Tanganyika in February 1858. Burton was too weak to go further, so Speke went on alone with 34 men, led by Sidi Mubarak Bombay and Mabruki, and on 30 July 1858 became the first European to see Lake Victoria. He named it after the queen and judged from the boiling point of water that it stood about 4,000 feet above sea level.

The quarrel with Burton grew after their return to England in 1859, when Speke announced the discovery publicly. Speke then led a second expedition with James Augustus Grant, leaving Portsmouth on 27 April 1860. On 28 July 1862 he reached the lake again and found the Nile flowing out of it at the Ripon Falls. He spent time at the court of Muteesa I, the Kabaka of Buganda. At Gondokoro in January 1863 he met Samuel Baker and later sent a telegram from Khartoum: The Nile is settled. Burton objected that Speke had not followed the river all the way.

Speke and Grant reached England in June 1863 and were welcomed as heroes, but disputes with Burton and with John Petherick weakened his standing. The Royal Geographical Society arranged a public debate with Burton at Bath on 16 September 1864. On 15 September Speke died of a gunshot wound while shooting at Neston Park in Wiltshire. An inquest found the death accidental, while Burton spread the idea of suicide. He was buried at Dowlish Wake in Somerset.

In 1874 to 1877 Henry Stanley sailed round the shore of Lake Victoria and showed that Speke had been right about the lake and the Nile. Speke's account of East African peoples, in his Journal of the Discovery of the Source of the Nile (1863), described the physical features of African peoples and claimed to find among them a superior race.
john-hawkwood: John Hawkwood is believed to have been born at Sible Hedingham or Gosfield in Essex, the second son of Gilbert Hawkwood. Modern accounts often wrongly portray him as poor, but Gilbert was a tanner and minor landowner of considerable wealth. In Italy he was known as Giovanni Acuto, a form of his name that also meant "John Sharp" or "John the Astute", and his name appears in many spellings in the records. He began his career in the Hundred Years' War under King Edward III as a longbowman, and it has been argued that he fought at Crécy in 1346 and Poitiers in 1356.

After the Treaty of Brétigny of 8 May 1360 many free companies formed in France. Hawkwood joined the largest, later known as the White Company, and rose to command it. The company seized Pont-Saint-Esprit near Avignon at the end of December 1360 and was excommunicated, but in March 1361 it made peace with Pope Innocent VI, and Hawkwood crossed into Italy. He took command of the Pisan army in the winter of 1364–65 and lost the Battle of Cascina. At Rubiera on 2 June 1372 he outflanked a larger papal force and took most of its officers captive.

In 1375 he fought for Pope Gregory XI against Florence in the War of Eight Saints. Unpaid by the Pope, his men looted Faenza, and he later took part in the massacre at Cesena, after which he left papal service for Milan, Florence and their allies. Florence hired him, and the Paduan Chronicle credits his victory at Castagnaro with the capture of 4,620 fighting men. His last major campaign was the war against Milan of 1390–92. He was paid in gold florins, between 6,000 and 80,000 a year, when a skilled Florentine craftsman earned about 30.

Hawkwood died at his home in Florence on 17 March 1394 before he could retire to England. His funeral on 20 March was followed by a burial ceremony in the Duomo, where in 1436 the Medici hired Paolo Uccello to paint his portrait in terra verde, in imitation of a bronze statue. Its Latin inscription calls him the most prudent leader of his age. His second wife, married in 1377, was Donnina Visconti, a daughter of Bernabò Visconti of Milan. Arthur Conan Doyle's novel The White Company (1891) was loosely based on his exploits.
john-henry-margrave-of-moravia: John Henry was born at Mělník on 12 February 1322, the third surviving son of King John of Bohemia and the Přemyslid princess Elizabeth. His parents' marriage had already broken down, and his mother fled to the court of their son-in-law, Duke Henry XIV of Bavaria; John Henry was brought up in Cham in the Upper Palatinate. To reconcile himself with Henry, Duke of Carinthia and Count of Tyrol, whom he had deposed as king of Bohemia, King John betrothed John Henry in 1327 to Henry's daughter Margaret, hoping to gain Tyrol and its passes to Italy.

The couple married at Innsbruck on 16 September 1330. When Duke Henry died on 2 April 1335, Emperor Louis IV gave Carinthia and southern Tyrol to the Austrian dukes Albert II and Otto, and only after King John campaigned in Austria did a peace at Enns on 9 October 1336 leave Tyrol to Margaret and John Henry. His brother Charles governed as regent and came into conflict with the Tyrolean nobles, while husband and wife grew to dislike each other.

On 1 November 1341 Margaret, leading a revolt against him, refused him entry to Castle Tyrol. He fled to the Patriarchal State of Aquileia, and she claimed that their marriage had never been consummated. Louis IV, who wanted Tyrol for the House of Wittelsbach, had Marsilius of Padua and William of Ockham declare the marriage invalid, and in 1342 Margaret married his son, Margrave Louis I of Brandenburg. King John allied with Pope Clement VI, who banned Louis and Margaret, but Luxembourg rule over Tyrol was at an end.

Once the first marriage had been annulled under canon law in 1349, he married Margaret, daughter of Duke Nicholas II of Opava, and renounced all claims to the Bohemian throne. After her death in 1363 he married Margaret, daughter of Duke Albert II of Austria. He died on 12 November 1375 and is buried at St Thomas's Abbey in Brno.
john-hunyadi: The first reference to John Hunyadi is a royal charter of 18 October 1409, in which King Sigismund of Hungary granted Hunyad Castle and its lands to his father, Voyk, and four kinsmen including John. Voyk then served in the royal household as a court knight. Two 15th-century chroniclers, Johannes de Thurocz and Antonio Bonfini, say Voyk had moved from Wallachia at Sigismund's initiative, and several modern scholars accept this, while Ioan-Aurel Pop holds that he was a native of the region around Hunyad Castle. Hunyadi spent his youth serving at the courts of powerful magnates, but 15th-century authors give contradictory accounts of which ones. In 1432 he married Erzsébet Szilágyi; their sons were Ladislaus and Matthias Corvinus.

In 1439 King Albert appointed Hunyadi and his brother bans of Severin after Hunyadi had raided Ottoman besiegers during the siege of Smederevo. In 1441 he became voivode of Transylvania and captain of Belgrade, taking charge of the southern frontier. He favoured an offensive strategy, using well-equipped heavy cavalry and Hussite wagon forts and mobilising peasants alongside professional soldiers. In 1442 he defeated Mezid Bey at the Battle of the Iron Gate and a large army under Şehabeddin at the Battle of the Ialomița, the first time a European army had beaten so large an Ottoman force.

These successes led to the Long Campaign of 1443–1444, in which Hunyadi took Kruševac, Niš and Sofia before cold and lack of supplies stopped the army at Zlatitsa. His later crusades ended in defeat at Varna in 1444 and at the Second Battle of Kosovo in 1448. In politics he supported Vladislaus I in the civil war over the Hungarian throne. In 1446 the Diet elected him sole regent, with the title of governor, for the minor Ladislaus V. He held it until 1452, when the king gave him the title of perpetual count of Beszterce, the first hereditary title in Hungary. At his death he held land of about four million cadastral acres.

In 1456 Hunyadi defended Belgrade against an army led by Sultan Mehmed II, a victory that halted Ottoman expansion towards Europe beyond the Balkans for decades. Pope Callixtus III ordered church bells rung at noon to call the faithful to prayer for the defenders, and the custom of the noon bell is traditionally linked to this. Hunyadi died on 11 August 1456. His son Matthias Corvinus was elected king on 20 January 1458, the first time a nobleman without dynastic ancestry took the Hungarian throne. Hunyadi is regarded as a Hungarian national hero, and Romanian historiography also claims him.
john-hyrcanus: John Hyrcanus was born in 164 BCE, the son of Simon Thassi and nephew of Judas Maccabeus and Jonathan Apphus. He was not present at the banquet near Jericho at which his father and two of his brothers were murdered by his brother-in-law, Ptolemy son of Abubus. He took over his father's offices of high priest and ethnarch, but not that of king. Josephus explains that he was also known as Hyrcanus but gives no reason. Scholars have suggested a family origin in Hyrcania on the Caspian Sea, a Greek regnal name, or a name given by the Seleucids after he campaigned in the region alongside Antiochus VII Sidetes.

In his first year Antiochus VII marched into Judea and besieged Jerusalem for a year. Hyrcanus expelled those who could not help in the defence, then readmitted them at Sukkot and negotiated a truce. Its terms were 3,000 talents of silver, the dismantling of the walls and Judean service in the war against the Parthians, and he had to loot the tomb of David to pay. He accompanied Antiochus on the eastern campaign of 130 BCE. After Antiochus was killed in battle against Parthia in 128 BCE, Hyrcanus stopped paying tribute and raised a mercenary army.

Beginning in 113 BCE he besieged Samaria, with his sons Antigonus and Aristobulus in command. The siege lasted a year, the city was devastated and its inhabitants enslaved. He took Medeba after a six-month siege, reduced Shechem to a village and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim, an action dated archaeologically to about 111-110 BCE.

He conquered Adora and Maresha in Idumea and required the Idumeans to convert to Judaism, which some scholars dispute, believing they assimilated peacefully. He rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, built the Baris fortress north of the Temple, and issued coins inscribed "Yohanan the High Priest" and "The Assembly of the Jews". Two Roman Senate decrees established friendship with Judea.

Hyrcanus died in 104 BCE. By his will the high priesthood passed to his son Judas Aristobulus and civil authority to his widow, but Aristobulus imprisoned his mother and she starved. Josephus reports a quarrel with the Pharisees, after which Hyrcanus sided with the Sadducees. Rabbinic literature remembers him for enactments, among them an end to writing God's name in ordinary contracts and a limit on work during the intermediate days of festivals. His territorial gains laid the basis for the reigns of his sons Aristobulus I and Alexander Jannaeus, who took the title of king.
john-i-albert: John Albert was born on 27 December 1459 at Wawel Castle in Kraków, the third son among thirteen children of Casimir IV Jagiellon and Elizabeth of Austria. His second name honoured his maternal grandfather Albert II, in the hope of a future candidacy for the imperial throne. The chronicler Johannes Longinus (Jan Długosz) tutored him from 1467, and the Italian humanist Filippo Buonaccorsi, known as Callimachus, later became his mentor and friend, urging him to limit the power of the clergy and centralise government.

The throne came to him by chance. His eldest brother Vladislaus became king of Bohemia in 1471, and the next brother Casimir died of tuberculosis in 1484. John Albert twice invaded Hungary against Vladislaus and was defeated at Košice in 1491 and at Prešov in 1492, but received the Duchy of Głogów for life.

After Casimir IV died in 1492 the Lithuanian nobles elected Alexander Jagiellon grand duke, breaking the personal union, while John Albert claimed the title of Supreme Duke. An electoral assembly at Piotrków proclaimed him king on 27 August 1492, helped by the intervention of his brother Cardinal Frederick, and he was crowned at Wawel on 23 September. In January 1493 the first two-chamber parliament, the Senate and the Sejm, met at Piotrków. In 1495, after Duke Janusz II of Masovia died without heirs, he occupied Płock; a year later Konrad of Masovia paid homage and lost most of his holdings.

In 1497 he led an army of about 80,000 into Moldavia, aiming to put his brother Sigismund on the throne in place of Stephen III. The siege of Suceava failed between 24 September and 19 October, and the retreating Poles were routed at the Battle of the Cosmin Forest. He accepted a peace in 1499 that treated Stephen as an equal. Turkish raiders then reached Lwów, and he ordered new fortifications, among them the Kraków Barbican. In 1496 townspeople were forbidden to own land and the movement of peasants was restricted.

John Albert died suddenly on 17 June 1501 in Toruń, where he had gone to press the Teutonic Knights to render homage. The most likely cause was syphilis, though he suffered from other ailments and old wounds. He never married. He was buried at Wawel Cathedral on 28 July 1501, and his tomb, with an effigy by Stanisław Stwosz and a niche by Francesco Fiorentino, is regarded as the first Renaissance composition in Poland.

Historians have judged him a valiant soldier but no commander. His reign was short and ended in a military setback, and he was criticised in his lifetime for absolutist leanings, while he is credited with creating the bicameral parliament.
john-i-doukas: John was apparently the eldest son of Michael II Komnenos Doukas, Despot of Epirus, possibly by a mistress of the Gangrenos family. His full surname was Doukas Komnenos Angelos, and Latin writers, mistaking the name Doukas for a title, called him Duke of Neopatras. He first appears in 1259, married to a daughter of the Thessalian Vlach chieftain Taronas, leading Vlach troops before the Battle of Pelagonia. According to George Pachymeres and Marino Sanudo Torcello, Achaean knights coveted his wife and William II Villehardouin insulted him for his illegitimate birth, and he deserted to the Nicaeans, contributing to the allies' defeat.

He soon left the Nicaeans, was reconciled with his father and helped him recover Arta and relieve Ioannina. On Michael II's death his realm was divided: Nikephoros took Epirus proper and John the lands in Thessaly and Central Greece, from Mount Olympus to Mount Parnassus. Michael VIII Palaiologos married a daughter of John to his nephew Andronikos Tarchaneiotes, but John allied with Charles of Anjou, with whom he made a commercial treaty in April 1273, and with the Duchy of Athens.

He opposed the Union of the Churches concluded at the Council of Lyons in 1274. In 1275 a Byzantine army surprised him at Neopatras; he slipped through the lines disguised as a groom looking for a stray horse, obtained 300 horsemen from John I de la Roche, Duke of Athens, and scattered the besiegers. On 1 May 1277 a synod at Neopatras anathematized the emperor, the patriarch and the pope, and a synod at Hagia Sophia answered in kind. Another imperial army was later ambushed and crushed at Pharsalos.

After Andronikos II abandoned the Union, Nikephoros and his wife Anna lured John's son Michael to Epirus and had him sent to Constantinople, where he died in prison; John retaliated by raiding around Arta. He died in or shortly before March 1289, not in 1296 as historians long believed after Karl Hopf, and was buried in the monastery of Porta Panagia, which he had founded in 1283. His widow recognised the nominal suzerainty of Andronikos II to protect their young sons.
john-i-duke-of-brabant: John I, also called John the Victorious, was born in Leuven in 1252/53, the son of Henry III, Duke of Brabant, and Aleidis of Burgundy, daughter of Hugh IV, Duke of Burgundy.
