His sister Maria of Brabant became queen consort of Philip III of France. In 1267 his older brother Henry IV, Duke of Brabant, who was mentally deficient, was deposed in his favour. John ruled Brabant from 1267 to 1294 and held Lothier and Limburg from 1288.

His principal military victory was the Battle of Worringen in 1288, by which he came to rule the Duchy of Limburg. Although completely outnumbered, he led a successful invasion into the Rhineland and defeated the confederacy opposed to him, and in 1288 Limburg was formally attached to Brabant. He married twice. On 5 September 1270 he married Margaret, daughter of Louis IX of France, but she and their son died shortly after his birth. In 1273 he married Margaret, daughter of Guy, Count of Flanders, who died in 1285. Their children included John II of Brabant and Margaret, who married Henry VII, Holy Roman Emperor, in 1292.

On 3 May 1294, at marriage festivities at Bar-le-Duc, John was mortally wounded in the arm in an encounter with Pierre de Bausner. He was buried in the church of the Order of Friars Minor in Brussels, but since the Protestant iconoclasm of 1566 nothing remains of his tomb. In the 13th century he was venerated as a folk hero and painted as the model of a brave, adventurous and chivalrous feudal prince, and he was popular for poetry and literature. An ode to him was a candidate to be the anthem of North Brabant, the folk song Harbalorifa remains popular, and the beer Hertog Jan is named after him.
john-i-of-castile: John I was born on 24 August 1358, the son of Henry II of Castile and Juana Manuel of Castile, and came to the throne in 1379. In that year he formed the short-lived Order of the Pigeon, known for large feasts at which the order's namesake bird was eaten. Unlike his father, he seems to have been more tolerant towards Jews, and made legal exemptions for some, such as Abraham David Taroç. In the summer of 1380 a combined Spanish and French fleet under Fernando Sánchez de Tovar sacked and burned Gravesend.

On 17 May 1383 John married Beatrice, the ten-year-old daughter and only child of Ferdinand I of Portugal, at Badajoz. When Ferdinand died on 22 October 1383, John sought to enforce Beatrice's claim. A rebellion in Portugal, begun when the Master of Aviz killed Count Andeiro on 6 December 1383, led to the crisis of 1383 to 1385. John invaded at the end of December 1383 but failed to win Coimbra or Lisbon and withdrew to Castile in September 1384. The Portuguese Cortes at Coimbra proclaimed the Master of Aviz king as John I on 11 April 1385.

John of Castile returned in July 1385 with French cavalry and was utterly defeated at Aljubarrota on 14 August 1385, which ended any hope of reigning in Portugal, although he and Beatrice kept calling themselves king and queen of Portugal. He also faced the claim of John of Gaunt, husband of Constance, eldest daughter of Peter of Castile. It was bought off by the treaty ratified at Bayonne, which arranged in 1388 the marriage of his son Henry to Catherine, daughter of Constance and John of Gaunt.

John died at Alcalá on 9 October 1390 after falling from his horse during a fantasia, a display of horsemanship by light horsemen equipped in the Arab style. Archbishop Pedro Tenorio kept the death secret for days, saying the king was only wounded. His son Henry III succeeded him, and Castile was ruled by a minority government. The marriage with Catherine linked the Trastámara and Plantagenet dynasties. Beatrice had no children with John; a son named Miguel appears in later genealogies, but no contemporary document mentions him.
john-i-of-portugal: John was born in Lisbon on 11 April 1357, the natural son of King Peter I of Portugal and a woman named Teresa, whom the royal chronicler Fernão Lopes calls a noble Galician. He was raised by Nuno Freire de Andrade, Grand Master of the Order of Christ, who secured his appointment as Grand Master of the Order of Aviz in 1364. When Peter's son Ferdinand I died in October 1383 with no male heir, efforts were made to secure the succession for his daughter Beatrice, who was married to King John I of Castile. Popular feeling opposed this, and the interregnum of 1383 to 1385 followed, a period of anarchy in which no monarch ruled.

On 6 April 1385 the Council of the Kingdom met at Coimbra and declared John, then Master of Aviz, king. The king of Castile invaded again, with French cavalry, to take Lisbon, while English troops took John's side. John and his constable Nuno Álvares Pereira beat off the attack at the Battle of Aljubarrota on 14 August 1385, and the stability of the Portuguese throne was secured. On 2 February 1387 he married Philippa of Lancaster, daughter of John of Gaunt, which consolidated the Anglo-Portuguese alliance.

The Castilian king died in 1390 without issue by Beatrice, which ended a rival claim. Portugal conquered Ceuta in 1415 and defended it against a Moroccan counterattack in 1419, partly to control navigation off the African coast and trade routes from the interior. Pope Martin V's bull Sane charissimus of 4 April 1418 confirmed to John all the lands he might win from the Moors. Voyages organised under Prince Henry the Navigator found the uninhabited islands of Madeira in 1417 and the Azores in 1427.

John reigned for 48 years, the longest of all Portuguese monarchs, and died on 14 August 1433. Portuguese memory gave him the epithet Fond Memory. His education as master of a religious order made him unusually learned for a medieval king.

His sons are often called the illustrious generation: Edward, the future king, was a poet and writer, Peter, Duke of Coimbra, was among the most learned princes of his time, and Henry the Navigator invested in science and navigation. His daughter Isabella married Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, in 1430 and was the mother of Charles the Bold.
john-i-tzimiskes: John was born in 924 or 925, probably in what is now Çemişgezek in Tunceli Province, since Leo the Deacon says he died aged 51. His father came from the Kourkouas family, of Armenian origin, and his mother was the sister of the future emperor Nikephoros II Phokas, of the Phokas family of Cappadocia. The name Tzimiskes is thought to come from an Armenian word, either for red boot or for short stature. He joined the army young under his uncle Nikephoros, and held the command of the theme of Armenia before he was twenty-five. He married Maria Skleraina, sister of Bardas Skleros; she died before his rise to the throne.

Tzimiskes distinguished himself against the Hamdanid Emirate of Aleppo, including at the Battle of Raban in 958. After Romanos II died in 963 he urged his uncle to seize the throne. Later, deprived of his command by an intrigue, he conspired with Nikephoros's wife Theophano and the generals Michael Bourtzes and Leo Balantes to assassinate Nikephoros. He was crowned in December 969, sent Bardas Skleros against a rebellion by his cousin Bardas Phokas, and married Theodora, a daughter of Constantine VII.

In 970 Skleros defeated the Rus' at Arcadiopolis. In 971 Tzimiskes crossed Mount Haemus with the main army and besieged Dorostolon (Silistra) on the Danube for 65 days, defeating Grand Prince Sviatoslav I of Kiev, who withdrew under a truce. At Constantinople he held a triumph, stripped the captive Bulgarian ruler Boris II of his imperial symbols and proclaimed Bulgaria annexed. He moved Paulician colonies to Thrace, since he suspected them of sympathy with their Muslim neighbours in the east. In 972 he invaded upper Mesopotamia. In 975 his forces took Emesa, Damascus, Tiberias, Nazareth, Caesarea, Sidon, Beirut, Byblos and Tripoli in Syria and further south, but not Jerusalem.

He died suddenly in 976 returning from this campaign and was buried in the Church of Christ Chalkites, which he had rebuilt. Several sources say the chamberlain Basil Lekapenos poisoned him. He left his wealth to the poor and the sick, and was succeeded by his nephew Basil II, leaving an expanded empire. The Finnish researcher Paavo Hohti counts him among the most capable Byzantine generals.
john-ii-count-of-holland: John II was born in 1247, the eldest son of John I of Hainaut and Adelaide of Holland. He became Count of Hainaut on the death of his grandmother, Countess Margaret. In 1270 he married Philippa, daughter of Count Henry V of Luxembourg and Margaret of Bar. Their children included William I, who succeeded him in Hainaut, John of Beaumont, and Mary, who married Louis I, Duke of Bourbon. John also had illegitimate children, among them Willem de Cuser and Aleid van Zandenburg.

As Count of Hainaut, John continued the war between the House of Dampierre and the Avesnes family against Count Guy of Flanders for Imperial Flanders. He became Count of Holland in 1299 on the death of his cousin John I. The personal union he established between Hainaut and Holland and Zeeland lasted for another half-century. John I's father, Floris V, had been fighting against Flanders for Zeeland and had sought help from France. The French defeated the Flemish in 1300 and 1301, and the rebels in Zeeland were defeated as well. John's brother, Guy of Avesnes, became bishop of Utrecht, so that all his main enemies seemed gone.

The position changed after a Flemish uprising and the defeat of the French army at the Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302, where John's eldest son was killed fighting for the French. His sons-in-law Robert II of Artois and Raoul de Clermont, Lord of Nesle, also fell there. The Flemish attacked Hainaut, and Zeeland supported them with a dissatisfied population. Guy of Namur defeated John's son William in a battle on the island of Duiveland, and Bishop Guy of Utrecht was taken prisoner. Guy of Namur and Duke John II of Brabant conquered most of Utrecht, Holland and Zeeland.

Guy of Namur was finally defeated in 1304 by the fleet of Holland and France at the naval Battle of Zierikzee. John II regained most of his authority and died in the same year, on 22 August 1304. His son William I succeeded him in Hainaut.
john-ii-count-palatine-of-simmern: John II was born in Simmern on 21 March 1492 into the House of Wittelsbach, the eldest surviving son of John I, Count Palatine of Simmern, and Countess Joanna of Nassau-Saarbrücken, a daughter of Johann II of Nassau-Saarbrücken. In 1508 he married Beatrix of Baden, daughter of Margrave Christoph I.

John succeeded his father as Count Palatine of Simmern in 1509 and held the county until his death in 1557. He allowed printing to be established in Simmern and was a patron of sculpture. His introduction of the Reformation into Simmern raised tensions with his neighbours, the Archbishoprics of Trier and Mainz.

With Beatrix of Baden he had twelve children, born between 1510 and 1532. Their eldest son, Frederick III, was born on 14 February 1515 and lived until 1576; Georg died in 1569 and Reichard in 1598, while William died in infancy in 1527. Several daughters entered religious life: Katherine became abbess of the Kumbd monastery, Joanna abbess of Marienberg near Boppard, where her sister Ottilie was a nun, and Brigitte abbess of the Neuburg monastery. Sabina married Lamoral, Count of Egmont, and Elizabeth, Maria and Helena also lived to adulthood.

After nineteen years as a widower John married the thirty-one-year-old Countess Maria Jakobine of Oettingen, daughter of Louis XV, Count of Oettingen; this marriage remained childless, and after John's death she married Count Johann of Schwarzenberg-Hohenlandsberg. John died in Simmern on 18 May 1557, aged 65, and was buried with both his wives in the Wittelsbach family vault of Saint Stephen's Church at Simmern.
john-ii-doukas: John II Doukas, also called Angelos Doukas, was the son of Constantine Doukas of Thessaly and his wife Anna Euagionissa, and he succeeded to his father's lands in Great Vlachia, as Thessaly was also known, as a child in 1303. The Thessalian magnates chose his father's cousin, Duke Guy II de la Roche of Athens, as regent, and Guy set up an Athenian protectorate over Thessaly with Anthony le Flamenc as his deputy, or bailli.

The regency proved timely. Anna Palaiologina Kantakouzene, the regent of Epirus, had invaded Thessaly and was forced to retreat by Guy's forces. Guy was less successful against the Catalan Company, which burst into Thessaly in 1306 and ravaged the region for some three years.

Guy died in 1308, when John had just come of age. John resented the attempt of the new duke of Athens, Walter of Brienne, to keep the protectorate, and Walter hired the Catalan Company to assert his authority. The Catalans took many fortresses but insisted on garrisoning them themselves. Alarmed, Walter turned against them; the Catalans invaded his duchy in 1310 and defeated and killed him at the Battle of Halmyros, or Kephissos, in 1311.

As the Catalans moved into Boeotia, Attica and the coast of the Gulf of Corinth, John was able to exert more control over Thessaly, but he met the opposition of the local magnates, who had probably grown used to weak central authority. He sought to strengthen his position by drawing closer to the Byzantine Empire, and in 1315 he married Irene Palaiologina, the illegitimate daughter of Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos. He may have received the title of sebastokrator at this time, and he already relied on some Byzantine help against the Catalans within his lands.

John died in 1318 without heirs, and his realm did not survive him. Much of north-western Thessaly came under the control of the powerful magnate Stephen Gabrielopoulos, while the Catalans seized the southernmost areas around Neopatras and set up a principality of their own there, the Duchy of Neopatras.
john-ii-duke-of-bavaria: John was the third son of Duke Stephen II of Bavaria and Elizabeth of Sicily, a daughter of Frederick III of Sicily and Eleanor of Anjou. Through his mother he descended from the kings of Naples and of Hungary and, further back, from the Eastern Roman emperor Alexius III. In 1372 he married Catherine of Gorizia, daughter of Count Meinhard VI of Gorizia and Catharina of Pfannberg. Their children were Ernest, born in 1373, William III, born in Munich in 1375, and Sofia, born in 1376.

From 1375 to 1392 John ruled Bavaria-Landshut together with his brothers Stephen III and Frederick. In 1385 he and his wife inherited a third of the County of Gorizia with Lienz, which he sold to the Habsburgs in 1392. That year he pressed for a new partition of Bavaria, refusing to pay for the Italian ventures of his brothers, both married to daughters of Bernabò Visconti, or for Stephen's costly court. Bavaria-Landshut was reduced as Bavaria-Ingolstadt and Bavaria-Munich were created: Frederick kept Landshut, Stephen took Ingolstadt and John Munich.

Stephen soon came to regard his share as a disadvantage. After an armed conflict between the two brothers, John had to share power in Bavaria-Munich with Stephen again from 1395, so that he ruled the duchy alone for only three years.

John was buried in the Frauenkirche in Munich. His sons Ernest and William III succeeded him and in the end made good their sole rule over Bavaria-Munich against their uncle Stephen III. His daughter Sofia married King Wenceslaus in Prague on 2 May 1389, and an illegitimate son, Johann Grünwalder, became a cardinal and Bishop of Freising.
john-ii-komnenos: John was born on 13 September 1087, the eldest son of Alexios I Komnenos and Irene Doukaina, and so had the status of porphyrogennetos. He was crowned co-emperor as a child, in 1092. His accession was contested: Irene favoured Nikephoros Bryennios, husband of her eldest child Anna Komnene, and Anna herself is held by most historians to have aspired to the throne. As Alexios lay dying on 15 August 1118, John took the imperial signet ring from him with the help of his brother Isaac, rode to the Great Palace with armed followers, and was acclaimed emperor. Anna was later kept from society for thirty years.

Because of the family intrigues, John appointed men from outside the imperial family to high office, unlike his father. His brother Isaac, though given the title of sebastokrator, plotted against him and fled in 1130 to the Danishmend emir Ghazi; he was exiled in 1139 to Heraclea Pontica for the rest of John's life. In the west John kept an alliance with the German emperors against the Normans of southern Italy. His strategy relied on taking and holding fortified places, and he conducted about twenty-five sieges himself.

In 1119–1121 he defeated the Seljuq Turks in south-western Anatolia, and in 1122 he crushed a Pecheneg invasion at the Battle of Beroia, where the Varangian Guard broke the wagon laager. In 1124–1126 a quarrel with Venice, whose 1082 trading treaty he had refused to confirm, ended when he reconfirmed it. He also fought Hungary and Serbia in the late 1120s. In 1137 he took Tarsus, Adana and Mopsuestia from Armenian Cilicia, and Raymond of Poitiers of Antioch and Joscelin II of Edessa acknowledged him as overlord. He then led a joint campaign into Muslim Syria, which failed to take Aleppo. He also built the Monastery of Christ Pantokrator in Constantinople, with a hospital of five wards.

In 1142 John campaigned in Cilicia and Syria to bring Antioch under direct rule; his eldest son Alexios died of a fever during the campaign. While hunting wild boar on Mount Taurus he cut his hand on a poisoned arrow, and he died on 8 April 1143, probably of septicaemia. The suggestion of assassination has little support in the sources. His youngest son Manuel I succeeded him. Historians such as George Ostrogorsky and John Birkenmeier regard his reign as among the most successful of the Komnenian period.
john-ii-of-aragon: John II was born on 29 June 1398 at Medina del Campo, in the Crown of Castile, the son of King Ferdinand I of Aragon and Eleanor of Alburquerque. In his youth he was one of the infantes of Aragon who took part in the dissensions of Castile during the minority and reign of John II of Castile. Until middle life he was also lieutenant-general in Aragon for his brother and predecessor Alfonso V, whose reign was mainly spent in Italy. He was called the Great and also the Faithless.

John first married Blanche I of Navarre of the House of Évreux, and by her right was king of Navarre. On her death in 1441 he kept the kingdom for his lifetime. Their son Charles, Prince of Viana, was heir of Navarre, but John came to regard him with jealousy, which grew into hatred after his second marriage to Juana Enríquez, who encouraged it. He tried to deprive Charles of his right to act as lieutenant-general of Aragon in his absence, but the Aragonese took Charles's side and the attempt to name Juana instead was set aside.

A long Navarrese Civil War followed and ended only with the death of the prince of Viana in 1461, possibly by poison given by his father. The institutions of the Principality of Catalonia, which had adopted Charles's cause and had grievances of their own, called in a succession of foreign pretenders in the ten years' Catalan Civil War. John spent his last years contending with them. He pawned Roussillon to Louis XI of France, who refused to give it back. In old age he was blinded by cataracts and recovered his sight through an operation by his Jewish physician, Abiathar Crescas.

The Catalan revolt was pacified in 1472, but until his death on 20 January 1479 John carried on a generally unfortunate war with the French king. He was succeeded by Ferdinand, his son by his second marriage, who was already married to Isabella I of Castile. With that accession the unification of the realms of Spain under one royal house began in earnest. John's son by his first marriage, Charles, left no legitimate issue, and among John's illegitimate children were Alfonso de Aragón, Duke of Villahermosa, and Juan de Aragón, Archbishop of Zaragoza.
john-ii-of-castile: John was born on 6 March 1405, the son of King Henry III and Catherine of Lancaster, a granddaughter of King Peter. Peter had been ousted by Henry III's grandfather, King Henry II, so John united in his person the claims of both lines. He succeeded his older sister Maria, Queen of Aragon, as Prince of Asturias in 1405 and became king on his father's death on 25 December 1406. His mother and his uncle King Ferdinand I of Aragon acted as co-regents during his minority. After Ferdinand died in 1416 his mother governed alone until her death in 1418.

John's reign of 48 years was one of the longest in Castilian history, though he is described as not a particularly capable monarch, spending his time on verse-making, hunting and tournaments. His favourite, Álvaro de Luna, heavily influenced him until his second wife, Isabella of Portugal, gained control of his will. At her instigation he dismissed and executed Luna, a deed said to have caused him much remorse.

His regents issued the Valladolid laws in 1411, which restricted the social activity of Jews, requiring distinctive clothing and banning them from administrative posts. After John took the throne himself in 1418 he reversed these ordinances, probably under de Luna's political influence, and favoured a more tolerant attitude towards a Jewish population already battered by the mass conversions of 1391 to 1415. In 1431 he placed Yusuf IV on the throne of the Emirate of Granada in exchange for tribute and vassal status to Castile, an exchange depicted in the ballad Romance of Abenamar. He was the largest single contributor to the continuing construction of the Alcázar of Segovia and built the New Tower there, known today as the Tower of John II.

In 1418 John married Maria of Aragon, eldest daughter of his uncle Ferdinand I of Aragon. Of their children only the future Henry IV of Castile survived infancy. John was widowed in 1445 and married Isabella of Portugal, with whom he had two children, the future Queen Isabella I of Castile and Alfonso, Prince of Asturias. He died on 20 July 1454 in Valladolid.
john-ii-of-france: John was born on 26 April 1319 and was nine years old when his father, Philip VI, was crowned. Philip's accession was unexpected, since all three sons of Philip IV had died without sons and Edward III of England had been passed over. John became Duke of Normandy in 1332, where much of the nobility was already allied with the English. The defeat at Crécy on 26 August 1346 and the fall of Calais in 1347 damaged royal prestige. His first wife, Bonne of Bohemia, died of the Black Death on 11 September 1349, and on 9 February 1350 he married Joan I, Countess of Auvergne.

Philip VI died on 22 August 1350, and John was crowned at Reims on 26 September. In 1351 he issued military ordinances to address disorganisation, discipline and pay in the army, and on 16 November founded the Order of the Star, a chivalric order meant to unify the nobility under royal leadership and to counter Edward III's Order of the Garter. His favourite Charles de la Cerda, the Constable of France, was stabbed to death in 1354 by several barons. John signed the Treaty of Mantes with Charles II of Navarre on 22 February 1354, but the peace did not last.

In July 1356 Edward, the Black Prince, led a great chevauchée through France, and the two armies met southeast of Poitiers. John was captured and held in England, including at the Savoy Palace and the Tower of London, with royal privileges. The Treaty of Brétigny, drafted in May 1360, set his ransom at 3 million crowns, about two or three years of the Crown's revenue. John left the Tower on 30 June 1360. His son Charles, as regent, had overcome several rebellions, and John created the franc to stabilise the currency.

In 1363 John's son Louis, a hostage in exchange for him, broke his parole and escaped from Calais. John resolved to return to captivity, replying that if good faith were banned from the earth, it should find asylum in the hearts of kings. He landed in England in January 1364 and fell ill with an unknown malady. He died at the Savoy Palace in April 1364 and was buried at the Basilica of Saint Denis. He created seven duchies and counties, more than any other French monarch.
john-ii-of-portugal: John, called the Perfect Prince, was born in Lisbon on 3 May 1455, the second son of Afonso V of Portugal and Isabella of Coimbra. At one month old he was declared legitimate heir and received an oath of allegiance from the three estates. In 1471 he married his first cousin Eleanor of Viseu, and he was knighted that year after the conquest of Arzila in North Africa. At Toro in March 1476 he defeated the Castilian right wing. From 1477 to 1481 he and his father were practically co-rulers, and he helped negotiate the Treaty of Alcáçovas of 1479 with Spain, which gave Portugal hegemony in the Atlantic south of the Canary Islands.

John became king on his father's death on 28 August 1481. He set out to reduce the power the nobility had gained, requiring magnates at the Cortes of Évora to swear allegiance to him as their superior and taking from nobles the right to administer justice on their estates. Fernando, Duke of Braganza, was arrested, convicted of treason and beheaded in June 1483. In September 1484 John himself stabbed to death Diogo, Duke of Viseu, his cousin and the brother of the queen, after confronting him with evidence of treason.

African trade became a crown monopoly, and its profits paid for exploration. The fortress of São Jorge da Mina was founded in 1482, Diogo Cão found the Congo River in 1484, and in 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope. John received Christopher Columbus twice, in 1484 and 1488, and rejected his plan, as the king's advisers judged his estimate of the distance far too small. When Columbus returned in 1493, John claimed his discoveries under the Treaty of Alcáçovas, and the dispute led to the Treaty of Tordesillas.

After Spain expelled its Jews in 1492, John admitted tens of thousands of them at eight cruzados a head, for no more than eight months. About 20,000 families entered, and only 600 of the wealthiest won permanent residence. Those who could not leave in time were enslaved until Manuel's reign.

His only legitimate son, Afonso, died in a horse accident in July 1491. John named Queen Eleanor's brother Manuel as his heir in his will in September 1495, and he died of dropsy at Alvor on 25 October 1495. His remains were moved to the Monastery of Batalha in 1499. His epithet is taken to refer to Machiavelli's The Prince.
john-iii-doukas-vatatzes: John Doukas Vatatzes, born about 1192 at Didymoteicho, came from a military family and by about 1216 held the post of protovestiarites. Emperor Theodore I Komnenos Laskaris chose him as the second husband of his daughter Irene Laskarina. When John became emperor in December 1221 he had to suppress opposition from Theodore's brothers Alexios and Isaac, which ended at the Battle of Poimanenon in 1224, where his opponents were defeated despite support from the Latin Empire of Constantinople. The Latin Empire made territorial concessions in 1225, and John crossed into Europe and seized Adrianople.

Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus and Thessalonica drove the Nicaean garrison out of Adrianople in 1227. When Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria eliminated Theodore in 1230, John allied with Bulgaria against the Latin Empire. The alliance brought the restoration of the Bulgarian patriarchate in 1235 and the marriage of his son Theodore II to Elena of Bulgaria, and in 1236 the two allies attempted a joint siege of Constantinople.

Pope Gregory IX called for a crusade against Nicaea in 1237. John sought allies elsewhere and turned to Emperor Frederick II, who recognised him as Byzantine emperor under the title Emperor of the Greeks in exchange for mutual aid. In 1238 John sent troops to the Siege of Brescia. After his first wife died in 1240 he married Frederick's ten-year-old daughter Constance, who took the Greek name Anna, and the alliance lasted until Frederick's death in 1250. At the Council of Lyon in 1245 Pope Innocent IV, who called John that enemy of God and the church, deposed Frederick, and John sent troops and subsidies to Italy between 1247 and 1250.

John annexed Thessalonica and much of Bulgarian Thrace in 1246. By 1247 he had established a stranglehold on Constantinople, and his authority reached far to the west. He also extended Nicaean control over much of the Aegean and annexed Rhodes. Large Cuman communities he settled guarded western Anatolia against Oghuz-Turkmen invasions. He died at Nymphaion in 1254 and was buried in the monastery of Sosandra, which he had founded near Magnesia.

Later generations called him the Father of the Greeks. He was canonised about half a century after his death as John Vatatzes the Merciful, and his feast day is 4 November. He collected and copied manuscripts, and he ruled despite epilepsy.
john-iii-duke-of-bavaria: John was born at Le Quesnoy, the youngest son of Duke Albert I of Bavaria and Margaret of Brieg, of the House of Wittelsbach. His elder brother William II succeeded their father as count of Holland, Zeeland and Hainault in 1404, and his sister Margaret married Duke John the Fearless of Burgundy in 1385. As the youngest of three sons he was destined for the church, and at the age of 15, with the support of Pope Boniface IX, he was given the prince-bishopric of Liège.

His rule in Liège went badly. His authoritarian style clashed with the nobles and burghers, he was expelled several times, and a counter-bishop was elected. On 23 September 1408 a Burgundian army under John the Fearless came to his aid, and the men of Liège were decisively defeated near the village of Othee. The bishopric became a protectorate of Burgundy, and John had suspect burghers and nobles beheaded or drowned in the Meuse, which earned him his name.

When William's daughter Jacqueline succeeded as countess of Holland and Hainaut, John gave up holy orders and his bishopric, and in 1418 married Elisabeth, Duchess of Luxembourg, widow of Antoine, Duke of Brabant. With the aid of Emperor Sigismund, his wife's uncle, he made war on Jacqueline and her husband, Duke John IV of Brabant, with Dordrecht and Philip the Good on his side. After a failed siege of Dordrecht in 1419, John IV agreed to joint rule and finally left Holland and Hainaut to John. Jacqueline went to England in 1421 and married Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester.

John's court was known for its rich culture, and Jan van Eyck worked for him from at least 1422 until 1424. He died of poison at The Hague on 6 January 1425: his court marshal Jan van Vliet, already executed in 1424, had allegedly poisoned the pages of the ducal prayer-book. His marriage was childless, and Bavaria-Straubing was divided among the dukes of Bavaria, the greater part going to Bavaria-Munich.
john-iii-duke-of-cleves: John III of Cleves, known as John the Peaceful, was born on 10 November 1490, the son of John II, Duke of Cleves, and Mathilde of Hesse. In 1510, at the age of 19, he married Duchess Maria of Jülich-Berg, daughter of Duke William IV of Jülich-Berg and Sibylle of Brandenburg, who became heiress to her father's estates of Jülich, Berg and Ravensberg. He was also Count of Mark. In 1521 he became ruler of the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, which he is regarded as having founded, and in 1528 Lord of Ravensberg.

During the Protestant Reformation John took a compensatory attitude and sought a middle way between the two confessions. The real influence at his court was Erasmus, and many of his men were friends and followers of the Dutch scholar and theologian. In 1532 John drew up a list of church regulations, a Kirchenordnung, that expressed many of Erasmus's ideas. He had an instinct for balance, shown when he married his eldest daughter Sibylle to John Frederick, elector of Saxony, who later headed the Schmalkaldic League. His court was fundamentally liberal, serious-minded, theologically inclined and profoundly Erasmian, and it was there that his daughter Anne was raised.

John and Maria had four children: Sibylle (1512–1554), Anne (1515–1557), William (1516–1592) and Amalia (1517–1586). Anne became the fourth wife of Henry VIII of England; the marriage was annulled on 12 July 1540, after John's death, on the grounds of non-consummation and a pre-contract to Francis of Lorraine. William married Archduchess Maria, daughter of Emperor Ferdinand I, and Amalia became a princess of the House of La Marck. John also had a daughter, Elisabeth, with an unknown woman, and another daughter who became a nun. He died on 6 February 1539.
john-iii-of-portugal: John was born in Lisbon on 6 June 1502, the eldest son of King Manuel I and his second wife Maria of Aragon. He was educated by scholars including the humanist Luís Teixeira Lobo and studied Latin, Greek, mathematics and cosmography. At sixteen he was chosen to marry his first cousin Eleanor of Austria, but she married his widowed father instead. His chroniclers say he was deeply offended, and some historians see in this one reason for the piety that gave him his nickname. He was crowned on 19 December 1521 in the Church of São Domingos in Lisbon.

John continued the absolutist politics of his predecessors and called the Cortes only three times, in 1525, 1535 and 1544. He married Catherine of Austria, sister of Emperor Charles V, and his sister Isabella of Portugal married Charles, which secured peace with Spain. The empire was costly to run and burdened with debt, and pressure from the Ottoman Empire in the Indian Ocean and North Africa raised the cost of defence. To pay for it he gave up several North African strongholds, among them Safim and Azemmour in 1541 and Arzila in 1549. By the Treaty of Zaragoza of 22 April 1529 Portugal paid Charles 350,000 ducats and secured the Maluku Islands.

In Asia the Portuguese reached Japan in 1543 and gained a footing at Macau. In Brazil, French privateers and the attempted colony of France Antarctique prompted the twelve captaincies founded from 1534; the French were not expelled until 1565. John created the Governorate General in 1549 under Tomé de Sousa, who founded Salvador, and sugar began to compensate for falling revenue from Asia. The first enslaved Africans reached Brazil in 1539.

John's rule was marked by support for humanist writers and scholars, among them Gil Vicente and Luís de Camões. He moved the university to Coimbra in 1537 and appointed Francis Xavier to the East Indies in 1540. The Jesuits took over the Coimbra College of Arts in 1555. After ten years of negotiation with Rome he established the Portuguese Inquisition in 1536, with his brother Cardinal Henry as first Grand Inquisitor; it chiefly targeted New Christians, and at least 1,379 people were burned between 1543 and 1684.

Nine of his children died young. His heir, Prince John, died aged sixteen, eighteen days before the birth of his son Sebastian on 20 January 1554. John died of apoplexy in 1557, leaving his three-year-old grandson as heir. He is buried in the Monastery of Jerónimos in Lisbon.
john-iii-of-sweden: John was born at Stegeborg Castle on 20 December 1537, the son of Gustav I and his second wife Margareta Leijonhufvud. As Duke of Finland he quarrelled with his father by meddling in Livonian affairs, and he travelled to London for his brother Erik to woo Queen Elizabeth I; the mission failed, but John observed the new Book of Common Prayer. When Erik XIV became king and centralised power, the brothers fell out, and John signed the Articles of Arboga of 1561, which restricted his power, only with great reluctance. In 1562 he married Catherine Jagiellon in Vilnius against Erik's will.

The Estates found John guilty of treason in June 1563. He held out in Turku Castle for some weeks and surrendered on 12 August 1563. He was imprisoned at Gripsholm Castle with his wife for more than four years, in light conditions, and two of their children were born there. He was freed in October 1567, during Erik's insanity. In July 1568 John and his brother Charles rose against Erik; Stockholm opened its gates on 29 September 1568, Erik was captured, and John was recognised as king by the Riksdag in January 1569, after granting concessions to the nobility and to Charles.

John ended the Northern Seven Years' War, then fought Russia in the Livonian War, which the Treaty of Plussa in 1583 concluded with Narva confirmed as Swedish. His son Sigismund became king of Poland in 1587. John regretted this and demanded his return, but the high nobility opposed it, and he turned to Charles for support. Erik died in 1577 in captivity, probably as a result of John's order of 1571 to kill him if a rescue were attempted. John died in Stockholm on 17 November 1592 and is buried in Uppsala Cathedral.

John was a learned follower of the mediating theologian George Cassander and sought reconciliation between Rome and Wittenberg. He issued the Red Book liturgy, which reintroduced Catholic customs and caused the twenty-year Liturgical Struggle, and his talks with the Pope failed. He rewarded the nobility with privileges and estates, and was the most building-minded monarch Sweden ever had, restoring cathedrals and extending Kalmar, Vadstena and Tre Kronor and starting Borgholm Castle.
john-iv-duke-of-brittany: John IV, known as John the Conqueror, was the son of John of Montfort and Joanna of Flanders. His father claimed the title Duke of Brittany but could enforce the claim only briefly, and only the English king recognised it. For that reason French sources number the son John IV and call the father simply John of Montfort, while English sources have called him John V. After his father's death his mother Joanna continued the war against Charles of Blois in the name of her baby son and was known as Jeanne la Flamme. She was forced to retreat to England to ask Edward III for aid, and John and his sister were taken into the king's household.

John returned to Brittany with English help. In 1364 he won a decisive victory over the House of Blois at the Battle of Auray, with an English army led by John Chandos, and Charles of Blois was killed. His widow Joanna signed the Treaty of Guérande on 12 April 1365, giving up her rights and recognising John as sole master of the duchy. Having won with English support, he had to confirm English barons in strongholds around Brest, which the Breton aristocracy and the French monarchy resented. Although he declared himself a vassal of Charles V of France, he lost support and went into exile in England in 1373.

Charles V then tried to annex the duchy, sending Bertrand de Guesclin in 1378. The Breton barons revolted and invited John back, and he landed at Dinard in 1379. He reconciled with Charles VI of France, paid off an English army under Thomas of Woodstock and ruled in peace with both crowns for over a decade. He built the Château de l'Hermine at Vannes between 1380 and 1385.

In 1392 an attempt was made in Paris on the life of Olivier V de Clisson, Constable of France. The attacker, Pierre de Craon, fled to Brittany, and John was assumed to be behind the plot, but Charles VI was seized with madness before he reached the duchy. John was knighted by Edward III into the Order of the Garter between 1375 and 1376, and is believed to be the only Duke of Brittany to receive that honour. He married three times; his third wife, Joan of Navarre, was the mother of all his children and served as regent for their son John V. He died on 1 November 1399.
john-iv-laskaris: John IV Doukas Laskaris was born on 25 December 1250, a son of Theodore II Doukas Laskaris, the third emperor of Nicaea, and Elena of Bulgaria. His maternal grandparents were Emperor Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria and his second wife Anna Maria of Hungary, a daughter of Andrew II of Hungary. The Nicaean Empire was one of the Greek successor states formed after the sack of Constantinople by the Roman Catholics in the Fourth Crusade, and the Laskarid dynasty had done much to restore the Byzantine Empire.

John was only seven when he inherited the throne on his father's death, and he reigned from 16 August 1258. His first regent was the bureaucrat George Mouzalon, but the nobility murdered Mouzalon, and their leader Michael Palaiologos took over the post. On 1 January 1259 Palaiologos made himself co-emperor as Michael VIII; the two were second cousins once removed, both descended from Empress Euphrosyne Doukaina Kamatera.

Michael took Constantinople from the Latin Empire on 25 July 1261, and John was left behind at Nicaea. On his eleventh birthday, 25 December 1261, he was blinded on Michael's orders, which made him ineligible for the throne, and he was exiled and imprisoned in a fortress in Bithynia. The Patriarch Arsenius Autoreianus excommunicated Michael VIII for the act, and a revolt led by a Pseudo-John IV later broke out near Nicaea.

John spent the rest of his life as a monk at Dacibyza. A rescript of Charles of Anjou dated 9 May 1273 refers to a report that John had escaped and invites him to Charles's court, and further documents attest a pension. This contradicts the historians George Pachymeres and Nikephoros Gregoras, who record that John stayed at Dacibyza until long after Michael's death; Deno John Geanakoplos concluded that the documents were propaganda meant to attract Greek supporters of the Laskarid dynasty. In 1290 Andronikos II Palaiologos, Michael's son and successor, visited John to seek forgiveness for the blinding. John died about 1305 and was eventually recognised as a saint, whose memory was revered in Constantinople in the 14th century.
john-iv-of-portugal: John was born at Vila Viçosa on 19 March 1604. He succeeded his father Teodósio II as Duke of Braganza in 1630, when Teodósio died insane, and in 1633 he married Luisa de Guzmán, eldest daughter of Juan Manuel Pérez de Guzmán, 8th Duke of Medina Sidonia. His claim to the crown came through his grandmother Catherine, Duchess of Braganza, who had been a claimant during the Portuguese succession crisis of 1580. Since then Portugal had been joined to Spain in the Iberian Union.

Under Philip III of Portugal (IV of Spain) taxes on Portuguese merchants were raised, the Portuguese nobility lost influence and government posts were increasingly held by Spaniards. The king is also said to have tried to make Portugal a Spanish province. On 1 December 1640 a group known as the Forty Conspirators, drawn from the nobility and the bourgeoisie, killed the Secretary of State, Miguel de Vasconcelos, and imprisoned the Vicereine of Portugal, Margaret of Savoy, the king's cousin. Spanish troops were then occupied with the Thirty Years' War and a revolution in Catalonia.

Within hours, and with popular support, John was acclaimed king; according to legend his wife persuaded him to accept. Portugal allied with France on 1 June 1641 and with Sweden in August 1641, and the war with Spain lasted from 1641 to 1668. A Portuguese force defeated the Spanish at Montijo, near Badajoz, in 1644. Overseas the Dutch took Malacca in January 1641 and the Imam of Oman captured Muscat in 1650, but the Portuguese retook Luanda in 1648 and by 1654 had recovered northern Brazil. Colombo fell to the Dutch in 1656.

John died in 1656 and was succeeded by his son Afonso VI. His daughter Catherine of Braganza married King Charles II of England, and Bombay was given to the English as her dowry. John was also a composer and a writer on music, author of a Defence of Modern Music (Lisbon, 1649) and a defence of Palestrina, and he built up a very large library that was destroyed in the Lisbon earthquake of 1755. In 1646 he proclaimed the Immaculate Conception of Mary patroness of Portugal by royal decree.
john-j-pershing: John Joseph Pershing was born on a farm near Laclede, Missouri, on 13 September 1860, the son of the farmer and store owner John Fletcher Pershing and Ann Elizabeth Thompson. He became a West Point cadet in July 1882 and rose to First Captain, the highest cadet rank. He served with the 6th Cavalry in New Mexico, Arizona and South Dakota and was cited for bravery against the Apache. As a West Point instructor from 1897 he was unpopular for his strictness, and the nickname Black Jack that cadets gave him stayed with him for life.

In the Spanish–American War Pershing fought on Kettle and San Juan Hills in Cuba and was cited for gallantry; Theodore Roosevelt called him the coolest man under fire he had ever seen. In 1940 he was awarded the Distinguished Service Cross for leading an assault against Moro defenders at Mount Bagsak, on Jolo in the Philippines, on 15 June 1913. On 27 August 1915 a fire at the Presidio in San Francisco killed his wife, Frances Warren Pershing, and three of their daughters; only his son Warren survived. On 15 March 1916 he led an expedition of 10,000 men some 350 miles (560 km) into Mexico against Pancho Villa, which routed Villa's followers but failed to capture him.

President Woodrow Wilson chose Pershing to command the American Expeditionary Forces, and he was installed on 10 May 1917, with headquarters at Chaumont. He resisted British and French demands that American troops serve as replacements in their armies, although in March 1918, when General Philippe Pétain said he had few reserves left, he put all available American divisions at Pétain's disposal. American soldiers fought at Cantigny, Château-Thierry and Belleau Wood in June 1918, and at St. Mihiel in September the First Army, under his direct command, overwhelmed a German salient. In the Meuse-Argonne Offensive he kept about 600,000 soldiers in hard fighting for 47 days.

In September 1919 Congress authorized the promotion of Pershing to General of the Armies, a rank created for him. His memoirs, My Experiences in the World War, won the 1932 Pulitzer Prize for history. Historians have criticised his reliance on costly frontal assaults, and his failure to halt attacks in the last hours before the armistice of 11 November 1918; he said he followed the orders of Ferdinand Foch, and Congress found that no one was culpable. He mentored many later generals, among them George C. Marshall and Dwight D. Eisenhower. Pershing died on 15 July 1948 and was buried in Arlington National Cemetery.
john-king-of-england: John was the youngest son of King Henry II of England and Eleanor, Duchess of Aquitaine. He was born around Christmastide in 1166 or 1167, and historians debate the precise date. His father's lands, Anjou, Normandy and England, with Eleanor's Aquitaine, formed the Angevin Empire, a fragile union whose parts had their own traditions and governments. As a younger son John was not expected to inherit significant lands, and his father jokingly called him Lackland. In 1177 Henry appointed him Lord of Ireland. When Richard became king in 1189 he made John Count of Mortain and married him to the wealthy Isabella of Gloucester.

After Richard died on 6 April 1199, John's claim rivalled that of Arthur of Brittany, son of John's elder brother Geoffrey. John had the support of most English and Norman nobles and was crowned at Westminster Abbey, while Philip II of France backed Arthur. The peace treaty of Le Goulet in 1200 recognised John's continental lands. War returned after he married Isabella of Angoulême in August 1200, having set aside his first wife. Shortages of resources and his treatment of Norman, Breton and Anjou nobles led to the collapse of his empire in northern France in 1204. He spent the next decade trying to regain it, raising large revenues and reforming his forces. His judicial reforms had a lasting effect on English common law.

A dispute with Pope Innocent III over the election of Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury led Innocent to ban church services in England from 1208 until 1214 and to excommunicate John from 1209 until 1213. In 1209 John invaded Scotland and forced William the Lion to sign the Treaty of Norham, with a payment of £10,000.

In 1214 John's final campaign to retake Normandy failed when the French defeated his allies at the Battle of Bouvines. Barons who were unhappy with his fiscal policies and his treatment of nobles rebelled, many of them northerners who owed him large sums. John and the barons agreed to Magna Carta in 1215 as a peace treaty, but neither side complied with it, and civil war began. He died on 19 October 1216. Contemporary chroniclers mostly criticised him. Jim Bradbury describes the present view as that of a hard-working administrator, an able man and an able general, while historians also point to faults such as pettiness, spitefulness and cruelty.
john-knox: Knox was born in or near Haddington, East Lothian, sometime between 1505 and 1515, the son of a merchant. He studied at the University of St Andrews or possibly Glasgow, under John Major, and was ordained a Catholic priest in Edinburgh on Easter Eve 1536. He appears in the records as a priest and notary in 1540 and became tutor to the sons of two lairds who had embraced the new religious ideas. After the murder of Cardinal David Beaton in 1546 he became chaplain to the garrison of St Andrews castle. French galleys besieged it, and on 31 July 1547 the garrison surrendered; Knox was taken to France and forced to row in the galleys until 1549.

Knox took refuge in England and on 7 April 1549 was licensed to work in the Church of England. He became a royal chaplain to Edward VI and influenced the wording of the Book of Common Prayer. When Mary I restored Catholicism he left England for Frankfurt and then Geneva, where he met John Calvin. He was elected minister of the English congregation there and arrived on 13 September 1556.

Back in Scotland in 1559, Knox preached a sermon at Perth on 11 May after which a mob gutted the church and attacked two friaries. In August 1560 the Scottish Parliament asked him and five other ministers named John to draw up a confession of faith. The Scots Confession was presented within four days and approved, and Parliament abolished papal jurisdiction and forbade the Mass. The Book of Discipline of January 1561 was not approved, mainly for reasons of finance.

After Mary, Queen of Scots, arrived in August 1561 and heard Mass at Holyrood, Knox protested from the pulpit of St Giles' and refused to moderate his preaching when she summoned him. In 1564 he married Margaret Stewart, aged seventeen, when he was a widower of fifty. His influence waned as the nobility supported Mary. He died on 24 November 1572. His will declared that he had corrupted and defrauded none, and the small sum he left showed that he had not profited from the Kirk. He wrote his History of the Reformation in Scotland between 1559 and 1566.
john-kourkouas: John came from the Kourkouas family, a Hellenized form of the Armenian name Gurgen, which had become one of the great landholding military families of Anatolia in the 9th century. His grandfather of the same name commanded the Hikanatoi regiment under Basil I, and his brother Theophilos, his son Romanos and his great-nephew John Tzimiskes all became generals. He was born at Dokeia, now Tokat, and was educated by a relative, Christopher, metropolitan bishop of Gangra. In the regency of Empress Zoe Karbonopsina he commanded the Vigla palace guard and arrested officials who opposed the rise of Romanos Lekapenos.

In about 923 Romanos made him Domestic of the Schools, commander of the imperial armies in Anatolia, a post that Theophanes Continuatus says he held for 22 years and seven months. After suppressing the revolt of Bardas Boilas in Chaldia, he attacked Melitene in 926, forcing its emir to accept tributary status, and raided deep into Armenia, taking Khliat and Bitlis. Theodosiopolis fell after a seven-month siege in 931. On 19 May 934, at the head of 50,000 men, he took Melitene for good; only Christians or those who converted were allowed to stay, and the city was incorporated into the empire.

In 941, recalled to meet a Rus' fleet that raided around Constantinople, he fell on the Rus' plundering Bithynia. From 942 he campaigned in northern Mesopotamia with an army that Arab sources put at 80,000 men, storming Mayyafiriqin, Amida, Nisibis and Dara. Edessa's emir handed over the Mandylion in exchange for 200 prisoners, and it reached Constantinople on 15 August 944, the feast of the Dormition, and was placed in the palace church of the Theotokos of the Pharos.

Romanos's sons Stephen and Constantine, opposed to a planned marriage of his daughter Euphrosyne to the future Romanos II, had him dismissed in the autumn of 944. Constantine VII restored him to favour, and early in 946 he was sent with the magistros Kosmas to negotiate a prisoner exchange with Tarsus; nothing more is known of him. His successors as Domestic, Bardas Phokas the Elder, Nikephoros Phokas and John Tzimiskes, continued his eastward expansion, and the historian Steven Runciman judged that he reversed the age-old roles of Byzantium and the Arabs.
john-lambton-1st-earl-of-durham: Lambton was born on 12 April 1792 at 14 Berkeley Square, London, the son of William Henry Lambton and of Lady Anne Barbara Frances, daughter of George Bussy Villiers, 4th Earl of Jersey. After Eton College he served as a cornet in the 10th Hussars from 1809 to 1811. From his father, who died in 1797, he inherited a great fortune drawn largely from coal mining around Lambton Castle in County Durham. In 1812 he married Harriet Cholmondeley at Gretna Green; after her death in 1815 he married Lady Louisa Grey, daughter of Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey, in 1816.

Elected for County Durham in 1812, he held the seat until 1828, when he was made Baron Durham, and he supported liberal causes from the defence of Queen Caroline to the removal of disabilities on Dissenters and Roman Catholics. When his father-in-law Lord Grey became prime minister in 1830, he was made Lord Privy Seal and, with Lord Russell, helped draft the Reform Bill of 1832. He left the cabinet in 1833, was created Earl of Durham the same year and served as ambassador to Russia from 1835 to 1837. In 1825 he had become chairman of the New Zealand Company.

He arrived in Lower Canada with Edward Gibbon Wakefield on 29 May 1838. His handling of the prisoners of the rebellions led by Louis-Joseph Papineau and William Lyon Mackenzie met strong opposition at Westminster, and when he lost the support of Lord Melbourne he resigned on 9 October 1838. His report of January 1839 called French Canadians a people with no literature and no history and argued for their assimilation.

He died at Cowes on the Isle of Wight in July 1840, aged 48, and was buried at Chester-le-Street; his son George succeeded him. Some Canadian historians praise his recommendation of responsible government, which the British government did not accept and which came only in 1848; the union and the plan of assimilation are less well regarded, and the use of French in Parliament was restored in practice by 1844. Lambton County in Ontario and the Penshaw Monument in County Durham bear his memory.
john-lewis: John Robert Lewis was born near Troy, Alabama, on 21 February 1940, the third of ten children of Willie Mae and Eddie Lewis, sharecroppers in rural Pike County. His great-grandfather Frank Carter had been born enslaved in the same county in 1862 and lived until Lewis was seven. Troy University, then Troy State, denied him admission in 1957 because of racial segregation. As a student he became an activist, attending nonviolence workshops held by the Rev. James Lawson and the Rev. Kelly Miller Smith at Clark Memorial United Methodist Church in Nashville, and he practised the discipline of nonviolence for the rest of his life.

In the Nashville Student Movement Lewis organised sit-ins at segregated lunch counters, which brought the desegregation of the city's downtown lunch counters, and he was arrested and jailed many times. In 1961 he was one of the 13 original Freedom Riders, seven Black and six white riders who planned to travel on interstate buses from Washington, D.C. to New Orleans to challenge segregated seating, in support of the Supreme Court's decision in Boynton v. Virginia. After extreme violence broke out in South Carolina and Alabama, the Kennedy administration called for a cooling-off period.

In 1963 Lewis, a founding member, was elected chairman of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and he was the youngest of the Big Six leaders who organised the March on Washington. He was the fourth of twelve speakers that day, before Martin Luther King Jr.'s speech. In 1965 he led the first of three Selma to Montgomery marches across the Edmund Pettus Bridge, where state troopers and police attacked the marchers on what became known as Bloody Sunday. From 1970 to 1977 he directed the Voter Education Project, which added nearly four million minority voters to the rolls. He served on the Atlanta City Council from 1981 to 1986, then won Georgia's 5th district in 1986.

Lewis served 17 terms in the House and from 1991 was a chief deputy whip. His awards included the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2011. His memoir Walking with the Wind (1998) won several prizes, and in 2013 he became the first member of Congress to write a graphic novel, the March trilogy. He died in Atlanta on 17 July 2020, the last surviving Big Six leader. His casket crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge in a horse-drawn caisson on 26 July before he lay in state at the Alabama State Capitol.
john-locke: John Locke was born on 29 August 1632 in the village of Wrington, Somerset, to Puritan parents. His father, also John Locke, was an attorney who served as clerk to the Justices of the Peace in Chew Magna, one of whom was Alexander Popham, a Member of Parliament for Bath. Locke was 10 when the English Civil War began, and his father fought for the Parliamentarian side as a captain of cavalry under Popham.

In 1647, under Popham's sponsorship, he became a student at Westminster School in London. Locke wrote of those years, "I found myself in a storm." He then won a place at Christ Church, Oxford, where he spent 15 years, first as a student and then as a tutor, pursuing medical and other scientific interests.

In 1665 Locke travelled outside England for the first time, as secretary to Sir Walter Vane on a failed diplomatic mission to the Elector of Brandenburg. In 1666 he met Anthony Ashley Cooper, later Lord Shaftesbury, and in 1667 moved into Shaftesbury's London home as his personal physician. He studied medicine there under Thomas Sydenham, and was probably instrumental in persuading Shaftesbury to undergo the surgery that saved his life. Locke was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1668.

After Shaftesbury fell from royal favour and died, Locke spent five years in political exile in the Netherlands (1683–85), where he wrote some of his most important works. He returned to England in 1689, served as a Commissioner of Trade and Plantations and retired because of ill health. He is also listed as a shareholder in the Royal Company of Adventures Trading to Africa, which traded in slaves from 1663. He died on 28 October 1704.

In his Letters Concerning Toleration (1689–1692) Locke argued that earthly judges cannot dependably evaluate competing religious truth-claims, that belief cannot be compelled by violence, and that enforcing uniformity would cause more disorder than allowing diversity. In the Essay Concerning Human Understanding he held that the mind is at birth a blank slate, tabula rasa, and that knowledge comes only from experience. He is often credited with describing private property as a natural right, arising when a person mixes labour with nature. The phrase "long train of abuses" in the Declaration of Independence is taken from the Second Treatise.
john-lomax: Lomax was born in Goodman in Holmes County, Mississippi, to James Avery Lomax and Susan Frances Cooper. In December 1869 the family travelled by ox cart to Texas, where his father raised horses and cattle and grew cotton and corn near the Bosque River in Bosque County. The boy heard cowboy songs from childhood. At about nine he befriended Nat Blythe, a former slave working as a farmhand, who taught him songs and dance steps while Lomax taught him to read and write; the friendship, Lomax wrote later, perhaps gave his life its bent.

In 1895, at the age of 28, he entered the University of Texas at Austin to study English literature. When he showed the English professor Morgan Callaway the cowboy songs he had written down as a child, they were dismissed as cheap and unworthy, and he burned them. After graduating in 1897 he worked as the university's registrar until 1903.

At Kittredge's suggestion of a Texas branch of the American Folklore Society, Lomax and Professor Leonidas Payne founded the Texas Folklore Society, which had 92 charter members by April 1910. Lomax lectured on cowboy songs and ballads across the eastern United States, sometimes singing them himself, and in 1912 he was elected president of the American Folklore Society, serving a second term in 1913.

In 1931 his wife Bess Brown died and the Dallas bank where he worked failed, leaving him in debt and depressed. His son John Lomax Jr. urged him back onto the lecture circuit, and in June 1932 the Macmillan company accepted his proposal for an anthology of American ballads and folksongs. Finding the Library of Congress's recordings inadequate, he arranged to make field recordings for it with equipment paid for by private grants. In June 1933 he and his son Alan, then eighteen, began touring Texas prison farms, recording work songs, ballads and blues from prisoners such as James "Iron Head" Baker and Mose "Clear Rock" Platt.

The Archive of American Folk Song came to hold songs from 33 states and from parts of the West Indies, the Bahamas and Haiti, more than ten thousand discs gathered under the supervision of John and Alan Lomax. In 1936 Lomax became an adviser on folklore collecting to the Historical Records Survey and the Federal Writers' Project. For the narratives of former slaves he insisted that interviews be recorded verbatim, telling workers they "should not censor any materials collected". Benjamin A. Botkin, who succeeded him in 1938, edited the narratives as Lay My Burden Down in 1945.
john-louis-prince-of-nassau-hadamar: John Louis, known in German as Johann Ludwig, was born at Dillenburg on 6 August 1590, the son of John VI, Count of Nassau-Dillenburg, and his third wife, Johannetta of Sayn-Wittgenstein. After his father's death the Nassau lands were divided among five sons: William Louis received Nassau-Dillenburg, John received Nassau-Siegen, George received Nassau-Beilstein, Ernst Casimir received Nassau-Dietz and John Louis received Nassau-Hadamar.

In 1617 he married Countess Ursula of Lippe, daughter of Simon VI, Count of Lippe. The couple had 14 children, of whom six survived infancy. Their daughter Johanna Elisabeth married Frederick, Prince of Anhalt-Harzgerode, and Sofie Magdalene married Louis Henry, Prince of Nassau-Dillenburg. Their son Maurice Henry succeeded his father, while Hermann Otto, Johann Ernst and Franz Bernhard became canons in Trier, Mainz, Cologne and Münster.

John Louis was 28 years old when the Thirty Years' War broke out, and he tried in vain to keep Nassau-Hadamar out of it. Great numbers of Imperial and Protestant troops passed through his lands, plundering them and requisitioning supplies until the county was reduced to poverty. Heavily in debt, he was forced in 1643 to sell Esterau to Peter Melander Graf von Holzappel.

Raised a Calvinist, he was sent by his brothers to Vienna in 1629 as a diplomat to negotiate a truce with Emperor Ferdinand II. There he became a Catholic under the influence of Wilhelm Lamormaini. The emperor valued his diplomatic skill highly, and in 1638 John Louis successfully led peace negotiations in Cologne and Münster.

In 1645 he joined the imperial delegation under Count Maximilian von und zu Trauttmansdorff that was negotiating the Peace of Westphalia. By 1647 he had replaced Trauttmansdorff as head of the delegation, and it was he who finalised the treaty. For this King Philip IV of Spain awarded him the Order of the Golden Fleece, and Emperor Ferdinand III made him a prince (Fürst) and gave him a large sum of money. He died at Hadamar on 10 March 1653.
john-magufuli: John Pombe Joseph Magufuli was born on 29 October 1959 in north-western Tanzania, then Tanganyika, on the shores of Lake Victoria, into a poor family. As a boy he looked after cattle and sold milk and fish to help support them. He attended Chato Primary School from 1967 to 1974, then Katoke Seminary, Lake Secondary School and Mkwawa High School. He earned a Bachelor of Science in education from the University of Dar es Salaam in 1988, majoring in chemistry and mathematics, and a master's degree in chemistry in 1994 and a doctorate in 2009 at the same university.

He taught chemistry and mathematics at Sengerema Secondary School in 1982 and 1983, then worked as an industrial chemist for the Nyanza Cooperative Union Limited from 1989 to 1995. In 1995 he was elected a Member of Parliament for Chato and served as Deputy Minister of Works until 2000, when he became Minister of Works. From January 2006 he was Minister of Lands and Human Settlement, from 2008 to 2010 Minister of Livestock and Fisheries, and from 2010 to 2015 Minister of Works again.

The ruling party Chama Cha Mapinduzi nominated him as its presidential candidate on 12 July 2015. He won the election of October 2015 with 58 per cent of the vote, with Samia Suluhu as running mate, and was sworn in as president on 5 November 2015. He was re-elected in 2020. Magufuli died on 17 March 2021 and was succeeded by his vice-president, Samia Suluhu.
john-margrave-of-brandenburg-kustrin: John was born on 3 August 1513, the younger son of Joachim I Nestor of Brandenburg and Elizabeth of Denmark, and a member of the House of Hohenzollern. His father's will divided the country between him and his elder brother, Joachim II, who inherited the electoral title. When Joachim I died on 11 July 1535, John received the New March with Dramburg and Schivelbein, the Sternberg Land, Crossen an der Oder with Züllichau and Sommerfeld, and the lordship of Cottbus with Peitz, about 12,500 square kilometres in all. In 1537 he married Duchess Catherine of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel at Wolfenbüttel.

Unlike his extravagant brother, John was deeply religious and had a good grasp of economic and political affairs. He joined the Schmalkaldic League in 1538, yet in the Schmalkaldic War he fought on the side of Emperor Charles V, hoping to gain the Duchy of Pomerania; the emperor granted him only freedom of religion in the New March. At the Imperial Diet of Augsburg in 1548 he rejected the Augsburg Interim and refused to join the Corpus Christi procession. He escaped arrest through the intercession of King Ferdinand and because his brother was an Elector, and at home he never officially published the Interim.

He strengthened his defences and planned an anti-Habsburg alliance that never came about. After a dispute with Elector Maurice of Saxony at Annaburg in 1551 he stayed out of the princes' league against the Interim, refused the advances of Duke Albert of Prussia, and did not press his claim to Brandenburg-Kulmbach.

Joachim II died on 3 January 1571, and John died ten days later, on 13 January. He was buried in a crypt under the altar of St. Mary's church in Küstrin. His margraviate passed back to the March of Brandenburg under his nephew John George. John left a fortune of more than half a million guilders, while his brother left debts of 2.5 million. Of his two daughters, Elisabeth married to Margrave George Frederick I of Brandenburg-Ansbach and Catherine married Elector Joachim Frederick of Brandenburg.
john-marshall: John Marshall was born on 24 September 1755 in a log cabin in Germantown, in the Colony of Virginia. He was the oldest of 15 siblings. After the outbreak of the American Revolutionary War, John Marshall joined the Continental Army and served in numerous battles. Late in the war he was admitted to the state bar, and in early 1782 he won election to the Virginia House of Delegates.

He built a legal practice in Richmond. He favoured ratification of the United States Constitution and played a major role in Virginia's ratification. In 1797 President John Adams sent him to France with Charles Cotesworth Pinckney and Elbridge Gerry. Talleyrand's agents refused to negotiate unless the United States paid enormous bribes, an episode known as the XYZ Affair, and Marshall returned in 1798.

Marshall was appointed secretary of state in 1800, and Adams appointed him to the Supreme Court in 1801. He quickly became the key figure on the court, in large part through personal influence on the other justices, and it moved from seriatim opinions to a single majority opinion stating a clear rule. In Marbury v. Madison, decided in 1803, he upheld judicial review, the principle that courts may strike down laws conflicting with the Constitution, while avoiding a direct clash with the Jefferson administration.

Later decisions confirmed the supremacy of the federal government over the states. Fletcher v. Peck in 1810 was the first case in which the court ruled a state law unconstitutional, applying the Contract Clause. In McCulloch v. Maryland in 1819 Marshall upheld the Second Bank of the United States and laid down the theory of implied powers. In Worcester v. Georgia he held a Georgia statute on Native American lands unconstitutional.

Marshall wrote The Life of George Washington, a five-volume work published from 1804 to 1807, the first biography of a US president. He also owned slaves throughout his life and wrote seven of the court's fourteen decisions on slavery, siding against the enslaved in each. He died on 6 July 1835 in Philadelphia, after more than 34 years as chief justice, and was buried in Shockoe Hill Cemetery in Richmond beside his wife Polly.

Before him the court had been a minor organ of government. In his tenure it gained the weight of a co-equal branch, and the Marshall Court struck down an act of Congress in only one case, Marbury v. Madison, which established the court's power to overrule Congress, the president and the states. His Richmond home is preserved as a museum.
john-maynard-keynes: John Maynard Keynes was born in Cambridge on 5 June 1883 into an upper-middle-class family. His father, John Neville Keynes, was an economist and lecturer in moral sciences at the University of Cambridge, and his mother, Florence Ada Keynes, was a social reformer who became the town's second female mayor. He studied at King's College, Cambridge, graduating in 1904 in mathematics. In October 1906 he became a clerk in the India Office but resigned in 1908 to return to Cambridge and work on probability theory. He became a fellow of King's College in 1909.

In the First World War the British government sought his advice. A few days before hostilities began he went to London at its request and helped persuade the Chancellor, Lloyd George, not to suspend specie payments. At the Versailles peace conference he tried to stop German reparations being set so high that they would damage Germany's ability to pay and buy exports, and so harm the wider world economy; the experience shaped his outlook, though he was unsuccessful. In the 1920s he published A Treatise on Probability and criticised the return to the gold standard in 1925 at the pre-war valuation.

During the Great Depression he challenged the neoclassical view that free markets would automatically provide full employment. He argued that aggregate demand determined the level of economic activity and that inadequate demand could cause prolonged unemployment, and he advocated fiscal and monetary policy to counter recessions. He set out these ideas in The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, published in early 1936. In How to Pay for the War, published in 1940, he proposed financing the war through higher taxation and compulsory saving rather than deficit spending. He received a hereditary peerage in 1942 and helped to design the new international economic institutions, though the American delegation overruled him on several points.

Keynes suffered a series of heart attacks in 1946, beginning during the negotiations over the Anglo-American loan in Savannah, Georgia. He died at Tilton, his farmhouse near Firle in East Sussex, on 21 April 1946, aged 62. By the late 1930s leading Western economies had begun adopting his recommendations, and almost all capitalist governments had done so within two decades of his death. His influence waned in the 1970s, amid stagflation and criticism from Milton Friedman and other monetarists.
john-monash: Monash was born in West Melbourne to Jewish parents, Louis Monash and Bertha Manasse, both from Krotoschin in the Prussian province of Posen; the family spoke German at home. He spent part of his boyhood at Jerilderie in New South Wales, where his father ran a store, before the family returned to Melbourne in 1877. At Scotch College he passed the matriculation examination at 14 and was dux at 16, and he later took engineering, arts and law degrees at the University of Melbourne.

As a civil engineer he worked on bridge and railway construction and played a major role in introducing reinforced concrete to Australian practice, through partnerships with J. T. N. Anderson and later the Reinforced Concrete & Monier Pipe Construction Co. He also rose through the militia from 1884, commanding the 13th Infantry Brigade from 1912.

In the Gallipoli campaign his 4th Brigade held the line between Pope's Hill and Courtney's Post, where the valley behind became known as Monash Valley. In the August offensive its attack towards Hill 971 failed amid poor maps, heavy resistance and mountainous ground, and he was criticised for excessive delegation; by mid-August the brigade was down to 1,400 of its 3,350 men.

On the Western Front he trained the 3rd Division in England with attention to detail and led it at Messines, Broodseinde and the First Battle of Passchendaele. His appointment to the Australian Corps was opposed by Charles Bean and Keith Murdoch, who favoured Brudenell White; Bean later called his own intervention ill-judged. Monash stressed thorough planning, the combined use of infantry, artillery, tanks and aircraft, and the welfare of his troops, arranging hot meals for the front line at Hamel.

After the war Monash directed the repatriation of Australian troops from Europe, then headed the State Electricity Commission of Victoria from 1920 and was vice-chancellor of the University of Melbourne from 1923. He became president of the Zionist Federation of Australia and New Zealand in 1927 and helped plan the Shrine of Remembrance. He died of a heart attack on 8 October 1931; an estimated 300,000 mourners attended his state funeral. His face is on the Australian $100 note, and a proposal to promote him posthumously to field marshal was rejected in 2018.
john-morley-1st-viscount-morley-of-black: Morley was born on 24 December 1838 in Blackburn, Lancashire, the son of the surgeon Jonathan Morley. He was educated at Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School in Blackburn and Cheltenham College. At Oxford he quarrelled with his father, who wanted him to become a clergyman, over religion, and left without an honours degree; he alluded to the rift in On Compromise (1874). Called to the bar by Lincoln's Inn in 1873, he turned to journalism and later called leaving the law his long enduring regret.

He edited the Pall Mall Gazette from 1880 to 1883, with W. T. Stead as his assistant. After failing at Blackburn in 1869 and Westminster in 1880, he was elected Liberal MP for Newcastle upon Tyne at a by-election in February 1883.

A Gladstonian Liberal, Morley became Chief Secretary for Ireland in February 1886 and lost the post in July when Gladstone's government fell over Home Rule. He held it again from 1892, a tenure that was hardly a success, as the Irish gentry made things difficult for an avowed Home Ruler at Dublin Castle. He lost his Newcastle seat in 1895 and won Montrose Burghs at a by-election in February 1896.

From 1889 he resisted labour leaders' demands for a legal eight-hour day, which he said would be like thrusting an Act of Parliament like a ramrod into the machinery of British industry, and it brought him the hostility of John Burns, Keir Hardie and Robert Blatchford.

In December 1905 Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman made him Secretary of State for India, though he would have preferred the Exchequer. In May 1907 he sanctioned extreme measures against sedition, but he also appointed two Indians to the Council of India and took steps towards decentralisation. He became Viscount Morley of Blackburn in 1908, the first peer to decline a coat of arms. As a peer he helped secure the Parliament Act 1911, and he was Lord President of the Council until 1914. On 2 August 1914 he resigned with John Burns, hostile to fighting alongside Russia against Germany.

Morley's monographs on Voltaire (1872), Rousseau (1873), Diderot and the Encyclopaedists (1878), Burke (1879) and Walpole (1889) made his name as a writer, and he edited Macmillan's English Men of Letters series. His Life of William Ewart Gladstone (1903) sold more than 25,000 copies in its first year. He published Recollections in 1917. He died on 23 September 1923 at Flowermead, Wimbledon Park, and the viscountcy became extinct. He married Rose Mary Ayling in 1870 and they had no children. Mahomed Ali Jinnah was among those he inspired.
john-newton: John Newton was born at Wapping, London, on 4 August 1725, the son of a Mediterranean shipmaster. His mother died of tuberculosis in 1732. He first went to sea at 11 with his father and sailed six voyages. In 1743 he was pressed into the Royal Navy and became a midshipman aboard HMS Harwich. After he tried to desert he was flogged and reduced to common seaman.

He then moved to a slave ship, Pegasus, bound for West Africa. In 1745 he was traded to a slaver and taken as a servant to the coast of Sierra Leone, a time he later called being a servant of slaves in West Africa. Early in 1748 a sea captain sent by his father rescued him, and in a severe storm off County Donegal during the voyage home he began to pray for mercy. He dated his conversion to 21 March 1748, though he later said that he was not a believer in the full sense until considerably afterwards.

Newton returned to Liverpool in 1748 and became first mate of the slave ship Brownlow. He then made three voyages as captain, of the Duke of Argyle (1750) and the African (1752 to 1753 and 1753 to 1754). After a severe stroke in 1754 he gave up the sea but continued to invest in the slaving operations of Joseph Manesty. He married Mary Catlett on 12 February 1750. In 1755 he became tide surveyor at Liverpool and studied Greek, Hebrew and Syriac.

He applied to be ordained in 1757 and was accepted only after more than seven years. He became deacon on 29 April 1764 and priest on 17 June, as curate of Olney in Buckinghamshire, where John Thornton helped to pay his stipend. His preaching drew so many that a gallery was added to the church. In 1779 he became rector of St Mary Woolnoth in London. Visitors who sought his advice included the writer Hannah More and the young William Wilberforce, whom he encouraged to stay in Parliament.

The poet William Cowper moved to Olney in 1767 and worked with Newton on Olney Hymns, published in 1779. It included Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken, How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds and Faith's Review and Expectation, which came to be known by its opening phrase. Newton also published an anonymous autobiography, An Authentic Narrative, in 1764.
