In 1788 he broke a silence of 34 years with Thoughts Upon the Slave Trade, which described conditions on the slave ships in the Middle Passage. He called his part in the trade a subject of humiliating reflection and sent a copy to every Member of Parliament. He died on 21 December 1807, aged 82, after the Slave Trade Act had passed.
john-of-austria: John of Austria was born on 24 February 1547 in Regensburg. His mother was Barbara Blomberg, the daughter of a burgher, and his father was Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, who had been a widower since 1539. In 1554 the boy was taken to the castle of Luis de Quijada at Villagarcía de Campos, where Quijada's wife, Magdalena de Ulloa, took charge of his education. Charles recognised him in a codicil of 6 June 1554 and again in his last will of 1558.

Philip II returned from Brussels in 1559 and met his half-brother on 28 September at the Monastery of Santa María de La Santa Espina. Philip told him they shared a father and that he was a Habsburg, but that he was not to be addressed as Your Highness. John was styled Don Juan de Austria and Your Excellency, the form for a grandee. He studied at the University of Alcalá de Henares beside Prince Carlos and Alessandro Farnese.

In 1568 Philip gave John a naval command, and he spent three months fighting corsairs off North Africa. The Moriscos of the Kingdom of Granada had been ordered to give up their customs, language, clothing and religious practices, and almost 200 towns rose against the decree. Philip made John supreme commander of the royal forces. After the siege of Galera, which fell on 10 February 1570, the village was levelled and salt ploughed into its soil; between 400 and 4,500 inhabitants were killed and 2,000 to 4,500 more sold into slavery.

Philip joined the Holy League of Pope Pius V and Venice and named John commander-in-chief of its fleet. On 7 October 1571 John, with 207 galleys and six galleasses against nearly 300 Ottoman vessels, fought the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras at Lepanto. The Ottoman fleet was destroyed; the League suffered over 13,000 casualties and freed over 10,000 Christian slaves. Among the wounded was Miguel de Cervantes.

After Luis de Requesens died in March 1576, Philip appointed John governor-general of the Spanish Netherlands, and he entered Brussels on 1 May 1577. He took Namur on 24 July 1577 and defeated the rebels at the Battle of Gembloux in January 1578, which forced William of Orange to leave Brussels. John was beaten at Rijmenam, then fell ill with a fever and died on 1 October 1578, aged 31. His body was carried secretly overland to Madrid and buried at El Escorial.
A monument to him was raised at Messina in 1572, and a copy stood in Regensburg from 1978. G. K. Chesterton's poem Lepanto of 1911 called him the last knight of Europe.
john-of-biclaro: According to Isidore of Seville in his De viris illustribus, John was born of Gothic parents at Scallabis in Lusitania. How and when he became a Catholic is not known. While still young he was sent to Constantinople for his education; historians date his stay differently, Roger Collins placing it about 562 to 579 and Kenneth Baxter Wolf about 569 to 576.

On his return the Visigothic king exiled John to Barcelona for ten years. Isidore ascribed this to his refusal to join the Arian Church, but modern historians note that no contemporary Iberian source, John's own chronicle included, records a campaign against Catholics before the revolt of Hermenegild divided Visigothic loyalties. Another possible reason was his long stay in Constantinople, which may have made him suspect as a spy for the Byzantine governors in the far south of Iberia. John himself recorded that at the Arian council called by Leovigild in 580, conversion from Catholicism was made a simple rite without rebaptism.

After King Reccared I ordered his kingdom to embrace Catholicism, John was recalled in 589. He founded a monastery at Biclar and wrote a Rule for it that has since been lost. Between 589 and 592 he was ordained bishop of Girona, and he signed the acts of the synods of Saragossa in 592, Toledo in 597 and Barcelona in 599, and probably of Egara in 614.

Isidore says John wrote several works, but only the chronicle survives, probably finished soon after its last entry for 590. It was meant to continue the chronicle of Victor of Tunnuna, though the two have little in common beyond the starting point and the use of emperors rather than consuls to mark the years. Where Victor dwelt on church matters, John gave a balanced account of sacred and secular affairs, and he admired the Visigothic rulers, Arian and Catholic alike, giving them the symbolism long attached to the Christian Roman emperors.

The chronicle was first printed by H. Canisius at Ingolstadt in 1600 and edited by Mommsen for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in 1893. With the works of Hydatius, Isidore and the fragmentary Chronicle of Saragossa, it is one of the chronicles covering Visigothic Hispania.
john-of-bohemia: John was the eldest son of Emperor Henry VII and Margaret of Brabant. Born in Luxembourg and raised in Paris, he was French by education but deeply involved in the politics of Germany. In 1310 his father arranged his marriage, at the age of fourteen, to Elizabeth of Bohemia. The couple travelled to Prague under the protection of imperial regiments.

Czech forces took control of Prague and deposed the reigning king, Henry of Carinthia, on 3 December 1310. John and Elizabeth were crowned on 7 February 1311. His attempt to follow his father as King of the Romans failed when Louis IV of Bavaria was elected in 1314.

Much of the Czech nobility disliked John as an alien king. In 1311 he reached an agreement with the Bohemian and Moravian aristocracy, the so-called inaugural diplomas, which kept the right to elect the king and to decide extraordinary taxation with the nobles and abolished the king's right to appoint foreign officials. The settlement did not hold, and John, who preferred foreign politics, gave up the administration of Bohemia and travelled, leaving the country to be ruled by the barons. By 1318 he had reconciled with the nobility and recognised their rights.

Abroad he served his father as Imperial Vicar and pressed the Habsburgs and the House of Wettin for territory. After the House of Ascania died out in Brandenburg he regained Bautzen in 1319 and Görlitz in 1329. He supported Louis IV against Frederick the Fair at the Battle of Mühldorf in 1322 and received the region of Egerland as a reward, but allied with France and Austria against Louis in 1322 or 1323. In 1335, at the Congress of Visegrád, Casimir III of Poland paid a large sum for John to give up his claim to the Polish throne.

John lost his sight to ophthalmia while crusading in Lithuania. After the Hundred Years' War began in 1337 he allied with Philip VI of France and served as governor of Languedoc from 30 November 1338 to November 1340. On 26 August 1346 he commanded the French vanguard at the Battle of Crécy and was killed. Jean Froissart records that his companions tied their bridles together and led him into the fight.

His eldest son Charles succeeded him in Bohemia and his son Wenceslaus, by his second wife Beatrice of Bourbon, in Luxembourg. His remains were placed in the crypt of Notre-Dame Cathedral, Luxembourg, in 1945. He is regarded as a national hero in Luxembourg.
john-of-capistrano: John was born on 24 June 1386 and was named after the village of Capestrano in the Abruzzi; his father had come to Italy with the Angevin court of Louis I of Anjou. He studied law at the University of Perugia, and in 1412 King Ladislaus of Naples appointed him governor of Perugia. In 1416, sent as ambassador to broker peace in a war between Perugia and the House of Malatesta, he was thrown into prison, and began to study theology there. On his release he decided to become a Franciscan, citing a dream of Saint Francis; he had married before the war but asserted that the marriage was never consummated. He entered the Order at Perugia on 4 October 1416.

From 1420 John preached in many cities, and he was ordained in 1425. Unlike most Italian preachers of repentance, he was effective in northern and central Europe; at Brescia he preached to a crowd of 126,000. With Bernardine of Siena he worked to reform the Franciscan Order, and in 1429 both were acquitted by a commission of cardinals of charges of heresy raised over their devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus. In 1451 he went as apostolic nuncio to Austria, and as legate or inquisitor he persecuted the last Fraticelli of Ferrara, the Jesuati of Venice, Crypto-Jews, and above all the Hussites.

John preached extensively against Judaism in Germany, Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia and was called the scourge of the Hebrews. Between 1451 and 1453 his sermons persuaded many southern German regions to expel their entire Jewish populations. At Breslau, after an accusation that Jews had desecrated the communion bread, he supervised the torture of Jewish prisoners until they confessed; forty were burned alive, a rabbi hanged himself and the rest were expelled. Scholars of Catholicism and of Judaism have judged him differently: a 2005 encyclopedia of antisemitism said he was a forerunner of modern antisemitism in seeking the social isolation of Jews.

After the fall of Constantinople in 1453, Pope Callixtus III sent John, then aged 70, to preach a crusade against the Ottomans. Meeting little response in Bavaria and Austria, he concentrated on Hungary, and by July 1456 had raised a large but poorly trained force of peasants and landlords. With John Hunyadi he advanced to Belgrade, where together they had gathered about 40,000 to 50,000 troops. After a fierce battle the Ottomans withdrew and the siege was lifted, and John was called the Soldier Priest. He died of plague on 23 October 1456 at Ilok. His canonisation was marked in 1690 by Pope Alexander VIII. He is the patron saint of military chaplains and jurists.
john-of-gaunt: John was the son of Edward III and Philippa of Hainault, born in March 1340, most likely at Saint Bavo's Abbey in Ghent. The name Gaunt is an anglicised form of Ghent, though in his lifetime he was not called by it after the age of three, and its use was popularised by Shakespeare's Richard II. On 19 May 1359 he married his third cousin Blanche of Lancaster, younger daughter of Henry of Grosmont, Duke of Lancaster. The wealth she brought was the foundation of his fortune, and he was created Duke of Lancaster on 13 November 1362 after her father's death. Blanche died in 1368, and only three of their seven children survived to adulthood.

John was one of England's principal commanders in France in the 1370s and 1380s, though without the success of his elder brother, Edward the Black Prince. From 1374 to 1377, with his father and brother ill, he was effectively head of the English government. His vast estates made him the richest man in England, and his wealth and autocratic manner, and the failed peace talks at Bruges, made him a target of resentment. After Richard II's accession in 1377 there was rioting in London, and the rumour that he meant to seize the throne was believed by many, though he sought no regency. His expedition to St Malo in 1378 failed, and rebels destroyed his Savoy Palace in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

On marrying Constance of Castile in 1371 he took the title King of Castile and León, and insisted that nobles address him as my lord of Spain. In 1386 he landed at Corunna on 29 July with an Anglo-Portuguese fleet, but in 1387 England neared civil war and he returned in 1389, having given up his claim in 1388. His intervention persuaded the Lords Appellant and Richard to compromise, and Richard invested him with the Duchy of Aquitaine in March 1390. His daughter Philippa married John I of Portugal, which sealed the Anglo-Portuguese alliance of 1386. He was a friend and patron of Geoffrey Chaucer.

John died of natural causes on 3 February 1399 at Leicester Castle, with his third wife Katherine Swynford beside him, and was buried next to Blanche in St Paul's Cathedral. After his death Richard II seized the Lancastrian estates and exiled his son Henry Bolingbroke, who raised an army, deposed Richard and reigned as Henry IV from 1399 to 1413. The House of Lancaster ruled England until the Wars of the Roses. Katherine's children, surnamed Beaufort, were legitimised after their marriage, and through them he was an ancestor of Edward IV, Richard III and Henry VII. All English monarchs from Henry IV are descended from him.
john-of-gischala: John was the son of Levi and came from Gischala, known in Hebrew as Gush Halav. During the war with Rome he competed with Josephus for control of Galilee, gathering a large band of supporters from Gischala and Gabara and winning the backing of the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem.

When Titus marched on Gischala, which the Romans called Giscala and which was the last town in Galilee not yet conquered, he called on its people to surrender. John persuaded him not to enter the town that day because it was the Sabbath, a plea the ancient account says was made less out of regard for the seventh day than for his own preservation. John fled to Jerusalem that night, and Titus was greatly displeased that he had escaped punishment.

He found Jerusalem in an uproar. John urged the people to war, claiming that the Romans were weak and that men who had broken their engines of war against the walls of the villages of Galilee could never get over the wall of Jerusalem. His speeches won over many of the young men. Soon after his arrival he played an instrumental part in the outcome of the Zealot Temple Siege, which handed the city to the Zealots.

John then tried to make himself ruler of Jerusalem but was challenged in April 69 by Simon bar Giora, and both men were in turn opposed by a third faction under Eleazar ben Simon. John and the Zealots fought this civil war until Titus captured him during the Siege of Jerusalem. He was sentenced to life imprisonment, taken to Rome and paraded through the streets in chains.

John is the subject of the Italian drama Giovanni di Giscala (1754) by Alfonso Varano, which inspired the Italian opera Giovanni di Giscala (1855) by Giovanni Gaetano Rossi and Alfonso Cavagnar. He is a character in the Josephus Trilogy of Lion Feuchtwanger, which follows Josephus Flavius from the year 60 in Rome, and he was portrayed by the Israeli actor Igal Naor in the animated historical drama film Legend of Destruction, released in 2021.
john-of-ibelin-the-old-lord-of-beirut: John was the son of Balian of Ibelin, Lord of Nablus and Ibelin, and Maria Komnene, widow of King Amalric of Jerusalem. By 1198, before he was 20, he had become constable of Jerusalem. He later gave up the office in exchange for the lordship of Beirut, a city Saladin's conquest had left completely destroyed. Wilbrand of Oldenburg, a German ambassador, described his new palace in 1212: frescoes, mosaic floors resembling the sea, a painted ceiling of moving skies and a marble fountain with a dragon in the central hall. In 1207 his marriage to Melisende of Arsuf added Arsuf to his lands and made him one of the wealthiest nobles of the kingdom.

From 1205 to 1210 John was regent in Acre for his niece Maria of Montferrat. He helped arrange the marriage of Hugh I of Cyprus to Alice of Champagne and, in 1210, Maria's marriage to John of Brienne. His brother Philip of Ibelin was regent of Cyprus for the young Henry I of Cyprus from 1218, and on Philip's death in 1228 John took over the office. That year Emperor Frederick II arrived on the Sixth Crusade, claimed the overlordship of Cyprus and the lordship of Beirut, and forced John at a banquet ringed by armed guards to give up the regency.

After Frederick left, John's forces defeated the imperial bailiffs outside Nicosia on 14 July 1229, beginning the War of the Lombards. In 1231 he repelled the army of the imperial marshal Richard Filangieri at the Battle of Agridi, but the imperial fleet besieged Beirut, whose castle held out for months. In Acre his supporters formed a commune and elected him mayor in 1232; the commune relieved Beirut, and on 15 June the imperial forces were beaten on Cyprus, where Henry I, now of age, ruled undisputed.

Filangieri still held Jerusalem and Tyre, and neither side could prevail; in 1234 Pope Gregory IX excommunicated John and his supporters, a sentence partly revoked in 1235. In his last year John insisted, against his family's wishes, on joining the Knights Templar so that he could die as a Templar, and he was given a grand funeral in Acre in 1236. His son Balian succeeded him as Lord of Beirut.
john-of-leiden: John of Leiden, born Johan Beukelszoon on 2 February 1509, was the illegitimate son of a Dutch mayor and a tailor's apprentice by trade. He was born in the village of Zevenhoven, in what is now the province of South Holland, and was raised in poverty. He became an Anabaptist, secretly at first. By his own testimony he moved to Münster in 1533 because he had heard that inspired preachers were there, and he sent for Jan Matthys, who had baptised him, to join him.

Matthys became the principal leader of Münster, expelled the Catholics, outlawed money and forbade the owning of property. The city was then besieged by an army under Franz von Waldeck, Prince-Bishop of Münster, Osnabrück and Minden. Matthys led an assault on Easter Sunday 1534 and was killed. John took his place as prophet, and in September 1534 he proclaimed himself King of New Jerusalem. He set up a royal court and kingly costume, made from property taken from the citizens, and made promises of salvation to his starving subjects. His motto was "Gottes macht is myn cracht" ("God's might is my strength").

The city fell in June 1535. John was found in the cellar of a house and taken to a dungeon in Dülmen, then back to Münster. On 22 January 1536, convicted under the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina, he was tortured and executed with Bernhard Krechting and Bernhard Knipperdolling. The bodies were placed in three iron baskets and hung from the steeple of St Lambert's Church, and about fifty years later the bones were removed, though the baskets remain.

The conventional view is that John set up a polygamous theocracy, best known for a law that an unmarried woman must accept the first proposal of marriage made to her. Some sources say he took sixteen wives besides his queen, Divara van Haarlem, and had one of them, Elisabeth Wandscherer, beheaded. Karl Kautsky noted that this picture rests almost entirely on accounts by the Anabaptists' enemies, and he stressed their social equality, democracy and communal living. In Dutch, a saying about doing "a Jan van Leiden" of something means putting little effort into it. Giacomo Meyerbeer's opera Le prophète (1849) has John as its hero.
john-of-the-cross: John of the Cross was born Juan de Yepes y Álvarez at Fontiveros, a town of about 2,000 people near Ávila. His father, Gonzalo, a weaver who had been rejected by his family for marrying below him, died around 1545, and the family lived in poverty. His mother, Catalina, moved with her sons to Medina del Campo in 1551, where John entered a school for 160 poor children and later studied the humanities at a Jesuit school from 1559 to 1563. In 1563 he entered the Carmelite Order, and in 1564 he enrolled at Salamanca to study theology and philosophy. He was ordained a priest in 1567.

In Medina del Campo in 1567 John met Teresa of Ávila, who persuaded him to delay joining the Carthusian order and to follow her reform, which sought to restore the Primitive Rule of the Carmelite Order. On 28 November 1568 he founded a monastery for friars at Duruelo and took the name John of the Cross. After tensions among the Carmelites, a General Chapter at Piacenza in 1576 ordered the suppression of the Discalced houses.

On the night of 2 December 1577 Carmelites opposed to reform seized John in Ávila and took him to Toledo, where a court of friars sentenced him to imprisonment. He was lashed publicly at least weekly and held in a cell barely 10 by 6 feet. There he composed a great part of the Spiritual Canticle, and he escaped through a small window on 15 August 1578.

In 1580 Pope Gregory XIII authorised the separation of the Discalced Carmelites. John became a leader of the new order and in 1585 Vicar Provincial of Andalusia, founding seven monasteries there. After disagreeing with the order's leadership he was sent to La Peñuela in June 1591, fell ill and died of erysipelas at Úbeda on 14 December 1591. He was beatified in 1675, canonized in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926.

John's poems add up to fewer than 2,500 verses, and his theological works are largely commentaries on them. The Spiritual Canticle, in which the bride, representing the soul, searches for the bridegroom, Christ, is seen as a free Spanish version of the Song of Songs; its first 31 stanzas date from 1578, and it survives in versions of 39 and 40 stanzas. The Dark Night narrates the soul's journey to union with God through detachment, and the Ascent of Mount Carmel, composed between 1581 and 1585, is a systematic study of that ascetical path. His works were first published in 1618, and his writing influenced T. S. Eliot, Thérèse de Lisieux and Thomas Merton.
john-okello: John Gideon Okello was born on 26 October 1937 in Lango District in the Uganda Protectorate and baptised at the age of two. Orphaned at eleven, he left his relatives at fifteen and drifted through Uganda, Kenya and Tanganyika as a clerk, manservant, gardener and odd-job man before training as a bricklayer. Arrested in Nairobi on allegations of rape, he spent two years in prison, an experience that left him with an intense hatred of the British.

In 1959 Okello went to Pemba and joined the Afro-Shirazi Party of Sheikh Abeid Karume, which opposed the dominance of the Arab minority. His speeches against British rule, the South Asian merchants and the Arab ruling class won him a following, and the rigged victory of the Zanzibar Nationalist Party in 1961 convinced him that only violent revolution would bring the African majority to power. In 1963 he moved to Zanzibar, worked as a house painter and used his travels to build a small army bound by strict rules: no sex, no raw meat and no alcohol.

Okello said that God had ordered him in dreams to break the power of the Arabs. On the night before the rising he told his men to kill all Arabs between 18 and 25 years of age, sparing pregnant and elderly women. His poorly armed fighters surprised the police in Stone Town, and he announced over the radio that the Sultan must kill his family and himself, but Jamshid bin Abdullah had escaped and later reached Britain. Between 18 and 20 January between 2,000 and 4,000 Arabs, South Asians and Comorians were killed, thousands of rapes were committed, and within weeks a fifth of the population had died or fled.

Karume, made president, and Abdulrahman Muhammad Babu kept Okello at a distance. His Freedom Military Force was largely disarmed by March, and he was refused entry on returning from the mainland and formally removed as Field Marshal on 11 March. He lived in Kenya, Zaire and Uganda, was imprisoned several times, and was last seen with Idi Amin in 1971. The former diplomat Don Petterson wrote that most observers believed Amin had arranged his murder. Werner Herzog said he partly modelled Aguirre in Aguirre, the Wrath of God on Okello.
john-peter-zenger: Zenger was born in 1697 in the German Palatinate, the son of Nicolaus Eberhard Zenger, a schoolteacher, and his wife Johanna. The family emigrated to New York in 1710 with a large group of German Palatines; his father died before they settled. Under the governor's scheme for immigrants' children he was bound for eight years as an apprentice to William Bradford, the first printer in New York. He worked in Maryland by 1720, returned to New York by 1722, and in 1725 was responsible for producing Bradford's New York Gazette and briefly his partner.

He then set up as a commercial printer on Smith Street, where in 1730 he published Peter Venema's Arithmetica, considered the first arithmetic text printed in New York. In 1733 the politicians Rip Van Dam and Lewis Morris hired him to print The New-York Weekly Journal against the new governor, William Cosby, who had quarrelled with the council over his salary and removed Chief Justice Morris for ruling against him, replacing him with James DeLancey. The first issue reported Morris's victory over Cosby's candidate in an election at Eastchester.

Cosby condemned the paper's seditious reflections, and on 17 November 1734 the sheriff arrested Zenger. His first counsel, James Alexander, was disbarred for contempt. After more than eight months in prison Zenger was defended by Andrew Hamilton and William Smith, Sr. Rebuffed by DeLancey, Hamilton appealed directly to the jury, which returned after ten minutes on 5 August 1735 with a verdict of not guilty, an example of jury nullification. Their argument that truth is a defence had appeared in the paper in a Cato essay, the pen name of John Trenchard and Thomas Gordon.

Zenger died in New York on 28 July 1746, and his wife carried on the printing business. The case laid the groundwork for press freedom rather than a legal precedent: later governors restricted the press until the Revolution, and only after People v. Croswell in 1804 did New York allow truth as a defence against libel.
john-peters-humphrey: John Peters Humphrey was born on 30 April 1905 in Hampton, New Brunswick, the son of a shoe merchant. His father died of cancer when he was 13 months old; at six he was badly burned while playing with fire and lost his left arm the following year, and his mother died of cancer in 1916, leaving him an orphan. He entered Mount Allison University at 15, moved to McGill University and took degrees in commerce in 1925, arts in 1927 and law in 1929.

A fellowship took him to Paris, where he married Jeanne Godreau, whom he had met on the voyage. He practised law in Montreal for five years before becoming a professor at McGill, where he founded the McGill Debating Union. In the early 1940s he met Henri Laugier, a French refugee working for the Free French, who later became Assistant Secretary-General of the United Nations.

In 1946 Laugier appointed Humphrey director of the new Division of Human Rights. After consulting the executive group of the Commission on Human Rights, chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, he prepared the first preliminary draft of the Universal Declaration, which after later revisions was adopted unanimously by the General Assembly on 10 December 1948. In twenty years at the UN he oversaw the implementation of 67 international conventions and worked on the freedom of the press, the status of women and racial discrimination. In 1963 he proposed a United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, an office created more than thirty years later.

Back at McGill from 1966, Humphrey served on the Royal Commission on the Status of Women and with the International League for Human Rights, helped create the Canadian Human Rights Foundation, and took part in inquiries into abuses under Ferdinand Marcos in the Philippines and into the famine of 1932-33 in Ukraine. He died in Montreal on 14 March 1995. He was made an Officer of the Order of Canada in 1974 and received the UN Human Rights Prize in 1988, and Nelson Mandela unveiled a plaque to him in Ottawa in 1998.
john-pym: John Pym was born in London on 20 May 1584, the son of Alexander Pym, a lawyer from the minor gentry of Brymore in Somerset, who died seven months later. His mother then married Sir Anthony Rous, a wealthy Cornish landowner and friend of Sir Francis Drake, who gave his stepson a strong dislike of Spain, a zealous Puritanism and opposition to Catholicism and Arminianism. Pym studied at Pembroke College, Oxford, and the Middle Temple, and in 1604 married Anne Hooke, aunt of the scientist Robert Hooke.

Appointed a collector of taxes for the Exchequer in 1605, Pym entered Parliament for Calne in 1621 and from 1624 sat for Tavistock, a seat of the Earl of Bedford. He argued that in impeachments the Commons should decide guilt and the Lords only the penalty. In 1626 he led the attempt to impeach the Duke of Buckingham, and in 1628 he supported the Petition of Right. During the Personal Rule he was treasurer of the Providence Island Company from 1630, whose meetings later served as cover for co-ordinating the opposition.

In the Long Parliament Pym became the unofficial leader of the opposition. Archbishop William Laud was impeached and the Earl of Strafford attainted and executed in May 1641, and by one disputed account Pym's appearance at Strafford's trial gave rise to the word Roundhead. Unlike many colleagues, Pym believed Charles would not keep concessions forced from him and that only military defeat would bring meaningful reform. When the First English Civil War began in August 1642 he headed the Committee of Safety, holding a diverse coalition together.

In 1643, after Royalist victories and the death of John Hampden at Chalgrove Field, Pym's determination renewed Parliament's commitment to the war and secured its money and troops. He died, probably of cancer, at Derby House on 8 December 1643. Buried in Westminster Abbey, his remains were exhumed after the Restoration in 1660 and reburied in a common pit at St Margaret's, Westminster. His opponent the Earl of Clarendon praised his grave way of speaking. His reputation later suffered beside less complex figures such as Hampden and Viscount Falkland, but he is now generally viewed as an astute politician and effective speaker.
john-r-hodge: John Reed Hodge was born on 12 June 1893 in Golconda, Illinois, and attended Southern Illinois Teachers College and the University of Illinois. After an officer indoctrination programme at the Officer Candidate School at Fort Sheridan he was commissioned an infantry second lieutenant in 1917, and he served in World War I in France and Luxembourg.

He stayed in the army after the war, teaching military science at Mississippi State University from 1921 to 1925 and graduating from the Infantry School in 1926. After a posting to Hawaii he passed through the Command and General Staff School, from which he graduated in 1934, the Army War College and the Air Corps Tactical School.

At the start of the Second World War he was chief of staff of VII Corps in California under Major General Robert C. Richardson Jr. Promoted brigadier general in June 1942, he became assistant commander of the 25th Infantry Division under Major General J. Lawton Collins and went with it to Guadalcanal in November 1942. In April 1943, as a major general, he took over the 43rd Infantry Division from the exhausted Major General John H. Hester and led it in the Northern Solomons, then commanded the Americal Division on Fiji and in the Bougainville campaign.

Given the newly activated XXIV Corps, he led it at Leyte and Okinawa and was promoted lieutenant general in June 1945. Under orders from Douglas MacArthur he took the corps to Korea, landing at Incheon on 9 September 1945, and received the surrender of all Japanese forces south of the 38th parallel. As commanding general of United States Army Forces in Korea from 1945 to 1948 he refused to recognise the People's Republic of Korea and its People's Committees, and he outlawed it on 12 December 1945.

Back in the United States he commanded V Corps at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, from 1948 to 1950, and after the retirement of Lieutenant General Alvan C. Gillem he became commanding general of the Third Army. His last post was Chief of Army Field Forces from 8 May 1952; he was promoted to full general on 5 July 1952 and retired on 30 June 1953. He died in Washington, D.C., in 1963 at the age of 70. His service in the Solomons, at Leyte and at Okinawa had each earned him the Army Distinguished Service Medal.
john-redmond: Redmond was born on 1 September 1856 at Ballytrent House, Kilrane, County Wexford, the eldest son of William Archer Redmond, MP. The Redmonds had been a prominent Catholic gentry family in County Wexford for over seven hundred years, and both his grand-uncle and his father had sat for Wexford. Educated by the Jesuits at Clongowes Wood College, he studied law at Trinity College Dublin but left without a degree, and in 1876 went to assist his father at Westminster, where as a clerk in the House of Commons he attached himself to Charles Stewart Parnell.

Elected unopposed for New Ross on 31 January 1881, he was ejected from the Commons on the evening of his maiden speech, amid the uproar over the arrest of Michael Davitt. He later sat for North Wexford and, from 1891 until his death, for Waterford City. Called to the Irish bar in 1887, he took up agrarian cases and in 1888 served five weeks' imprisonment with hard labour after a speech. When the party split over Parnell's divorce case in 1890 he stayed loyal, and after Parnell's death in 1891 he led the Parnellite faction.

Chosen chairman of the reunited party on 6 February 1900 as a compromise between rival leaders, he never had his predecessor's control over colleagues such as John Dillon, William O'Brien, Timothy Healy and Joseph Devlin. He misjudged the threats of the Ulster unionists under Sir Edward Carson as bluffing. His appeal to the Irish Volunteers to enlist split them: a large majority of 140,000 followed him as the National Volunteers, while around 9,700 remained in the original body.

Redmond did not expect the Easter Rising, and he later acknowledged that it was a shattering blow to his lifelong policy of constitutional action. At the Irish Convention, which sat until March 1918, he backed Lord Midleton's plan for All-Ireland Home Rule, but on 15 January he withdrew his motion rather than split the nationalists. He died on 6 March 1918 and was succeeded by Dillon, and in the December general election the party kept only six seats.

Opinion of him has remained divided. The Taoiseach John Bruton hung a painting of Redmond in his office as his hero, while Gerry Adams called him a man of violence for encouraging Irish recruitment to the British army.
john-rolfe: Rolfe's birthplace is unproven, though family documents name Heacham Hall in Norfolk. Historians no longer accept the old belief that his parents were John Rolfe and Dorothy Mason; he had a brother, Henry, whom they are not known to have had. Spain then held a virtual monopoly of the tobacco trade, and Rolfe was one of several businessmen who hoped to undercut it from Virginia. He illegally obtained seed of a strain grown in Trinidad, although Spain had decreed death for selling such seed to a non-Spaniard.

In May 1609 he sailed with his wife Sarah on the Sea Venture, flagship of the Third Supply fleet. A storm drove the ship onto the reefs of Bermuda, where their daughter Bermuda was buried. In May 1610 the castaways reached Jamestown in two ships they had built, and found only 60 settlers alive after the Starving Time.

The native Virginia tobacco, Nicotiana rustica, did not please the English market. In 1611 Rolfe became the first to grow Nicotiana tabacum commercially in North America, naming his strain Orinoco, possibly in honour of Sir Walter Raleigh's expeditions up the Orinoco River. In 1612 he established Varina Farms on the James River, and the first four barrels of leaf were shipped to England in March 1614.

On 5 April 1614 he married Pocahontas, who had been baptised Rebecca by Alexander Whitaker; their son Thomas Rolfe was born in January 1615. In 1616 the Virginia Company brought the family to England to promote the colony, and Rolfe wrote A True Relation of the State of Virginia. Pocahontas fell gravely ill as they set out to return and was buried at St George's Church, Gravesend, on 21 March 1617.

Leaving the sick Thomas in England, Rolfe went back to Virginia, which shipped 20,000 pounds of Orinoco tobacco to England in 1617 and 40,000 more in 1618. His letters of 1620 contain the earliest mention of the arrival of enslaved Africans in Virginia, brought by a Dutch man-of-war in August 1619. About 1619 he married Jane Pierce, and their daughter Elizabeth was born in 1620. He may have died in the Indian massacre of 1622, but the evidence is uncertain. His tobacco remained the mainstay of Virginia's plantations for generations.
john-ross-cherokee-chief: Ross, known in Cherokee as Guwisguwi, was born on 3 October 1790 at Turkeytown on the Coosa River, in present-day Alabama, to Mollie McDonald and Daniel Ross, a Scots trader. Under the Cherokee matrilineal system he belonged to his mother's family and the Bird Clan. He grew up near Lookout Mountain, was taught in English and spoke Cherokee poorly. After schooling at home he studied with the Reverend Gideon Blackburn and finished at an academy at South West Point near Kingston, Tennessee.

At twenty Ross was appointed US Indian agent to the western Cherokee. In the War of 1812 he was adjutant of a Cherokee regiment and fought under Andrew Jackson at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend against the Red Sticks. He grew wealthy from a tobacco plantation in Tennessee worked by about 20 slaves, and in 1816 founded Ross's Landing, a ferry and trading post later renamed Chattanooga. Trained by Principal Chief Pathkiller and Charles R. Hicks, he became president of the National Committee in November 1818 and refused an offer of $200,000 for voluntary removal west of the Mississippi.

Elected principal chief on 17 October 1828, Ross found allies in Congress such as Henry Clay, Daniel Webster and Davy Crockett, but in 1829 President Jackson backed Georgia's claim to extend its laws over the Cherokee. On 7 November 1835 the Georgia guard arrested Ross at his home. After the Treaty Party signed the Treaty of New Echota, General Winfield Scott and 7,000 federal troops enforced removal in 1838, and Ross persuaded Scott to let him supervise much of it. In 1844 he married Mary Stapler in Philadelphia.

When the Civil War came Ross urged neutrality, but on 21 August 1861 he told a general assembly that, for the sake of tribal and inter-Indian unity, the nation should ally with the Confederacy. Stand Watie and many wealthy Cherokee backed the Confederacy, while the Keetoowah Society and other traditionalists stayed loyal to the Union.

Ross died on 1 August 1866 and was first buried beside Mary in Wilmington, Delaware; a few months later the Cherokee Nation moved his remains to the Ross Cemetery at Park Hill, Indian Territory. Several Cherokee Freedmen he had owned kept his surname, and one, Stick Ross, sat in the Cherokee Legislature from 1893 to 1894. His former home in Rossville, Georgia, is a National Historic Landmark, and his great-great-granddaughter Mary G. Ross became the first Native American woman engineer.
john-sevier: Sevier was born in 1745 in Augusta County in the Colony of Virginia, near the present-day town of New Market, the oldest of seven children of Valentine Sevier, of French Huguenot background, and Joanna Goad. Like his father he worked as a tavern keeper and trader, and New Market claims him as its founder. In 1761, at sixteen, he married Sarah Hawkins. In the 1770s he moved to the Watauga settlements on the Cherokee lands of what is now north-eastern Tennessee, where he sat on the five-man court of the Watauga Association and in July 1776 helped hold Fort Caswell against a Cherokee assault.

In September 1780 Sevier led 240 Washington County militia across the mountains with Isaac Shelby and William Campbell, paying for the march with a loan secured on his own property. At Kings Mountain on 7 October he and Campbell charged the high point of the Loyalist position, and Major Patrick Ferguson was killed trying to break through Sevier's line. Over the next two years Sevier routed the Cherokee at the Battle of Boyd's Creek and burned many of their towns, among them Chota, Chilhowee and Tallassee.

In August 1784 he presided over the convention at Jonesborough that set out to form the State of Franklin, and he negotiated the Treaties of Dumplin Creek and Coyatee with the Cherokee, which the United States Senate never ratified. His rivalry with John Tipton, who stayed loyal to North Carolina, led to the armed clash of February 1788 known as the Battle of Franklin. North Carolina issued a warrant for his arrest, and in October 1788 he was sent to Morganton to stand trial for treason, but Sheriff William Morrison released him before the trial began.

Sevier took the oath of allegiance to North Carolina in February 1789, was pardoned, and helped pass the act ceding Tennessee to the federal government. He commanded the militia of the Southwest Territory and, as governor of Tennessee, made the acquisition of Indian lands a priority. He served six two-year terms, from 1796 to 1801 and from 1803 to 1809. His feud with Andrew Jackson nearly ended in a duel in 1803. Elected to the House of Representatives in 1811, he died in 1815 in the Alabama Territory while surveying lands taken from the Creek.
john-sigismund-elector-of-brandenburg: John Sigismund was born in Halle an der Saale, the son of Joachim III Frederick, Elector of Brandenburg, and his first wife Catherine of Brandenburg-Küstrin. On 30 October 1594 he married Anna of Prussia, the eldest daughter of Albert Frederick, Duke of Prussia, who had no sons. She was the elder sister of his stepmother. The marriage made possible the union of Brandenburg and Prussia, and through his wife he became a major claimant in the War of the Jülich Succession.

He succeeded his father as margrave and elector in 1608. In 1611 he travelled from Königsberg to Warsaw, where on 16 November he did feudal homage to Sigismund III Vasa, King of Poland, whose fief the Duchy of Prussia then was. For several years before 1618 he acted as regent for the mentally disturbed Albert Frederick, and when the duke died he officially became Duke of Prussia. In the Treaty of Xanten of 1614 he received Cleves, Mark and Ravensberg. A stroke in 1616 left him without full recovery, and he died in 1619.

His most significant act was his move from Lutheranism to Calvinism. He had earlier equalised the rights of Catholics and Protestants in Prussia under pressure from the King of Poland. He probably became a Calvinist during a visit to Heidelberg in 1606, but he took communion publicly in the Calvinist rite only on 25 December 1613. Most of his subjects, and his wife Anna, stayed deeply Lutheran.

In February 1614 the elector and his Calvinist officials drew up plans for a mass conversion of the population, under the rule cuius regio, eius religio, and serious protests followed. In 1615 he gave up all attempts at forcible conversion and allowed his subjects to be Lutheran or Calvinist as conscience dictated, so that Brandenburg-Prussia became a bi-confessional state. His son George William succeeded him, and his daughter Maria Eleonora married Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden and was the mother of Christina of Sweden.
john-sigismund-zapolya: John Sigismund was born in Buda on 7 July 1540, the only son of John Zápolya and Isabella Jagiellon. His father had been elected king in 1526 after the Battle of Mohács, while a rival group of lords had proclaimed Ferdinand I of Habsburg. The Treaty of Várad of 1538 confirmed Ferdinand's right to reunite Hungary after John's death, but on his deathbed John Zápolya made those present swear to prevent the transfer of his realm to Ferdinand. The Diet elected the infant king on 13 September 1540, though he was never crowned with the Holy Crown of Hungary.

Sultan Suleiman invaded, saying he came to protect the child, and in 1541 his janissaries took Buda without opposition. Suleiman let John Sigismund keep the lands east of the river Tisza in exchange for a yearly tribute of 10,000 florins. The family settled in Gyulafehérvár in Transylvania, but in 1551 his father's treasurer, George Martinuzzi, forced Isabella to give up her son's realm to Ferdinand in return for two Silesian duchies and 140,000 florins, and they went to Poland. At Suleiman's urging the Transylvanian Diet called them back in 1556. Isabella ruled in her son's name until her death in 1559, and then he ruled for himself under the title king-elect.

A powerful lord, Melchior Balassa, deserted to Ferdinand in 1561, and most counties outside Transylvania followed. The Székely commoners also rose, and the king's army crushed them in 1562. John Sigismund paid homage to Suleiman at Zemun in 1566, and the Treaty of Adrianople of 1568 confirmed him in Transylvania and the Partium. Originally Catholic, he converted to Lutheranism in 1562 and to Calvinism in 1564. Influenced by his physician Giorgio Biandrata and his court preacher Ferenc Dávid, he later adopted Anti-Trinitarian views, becoming the only Unitarian monarch in history.

In 1568 the Diet at Torda passed the Edict of Torda, declaring that nobody should suffer for religious reasons and that faith is a gift of God. It expanded religious freedom beyond the standards of 16th-century Europe. By the Treaty of Speyer of 16 August 1570 John Sigismund acknowledged Maximilian II as the sole king of Hungary and took the title Prince of Transylvania and Lord of Parts of the Kingdom of Hungary. He died childless in Gyulafehérvár on 14 March 1571 and was buried in St Michael's Cathedral in Gyulafehérvár according to Unitarian rite. The Diet elected the Catholic Stephen Báthory to succeed him.
john-smith-explorer: John Smith was baptised on 6 January 1580 at Willoughby near Alford in Lincolnshire, where his parents rented a farm. After his father died he went to sea at sixteen and served as a mercenary in the army of Henry IV of France against the Spaniards, then traded and engaged in piracy in the Mediterranean and fought the Ottoman Turks in the Long Turkish War.

He became a cavalry captain fighting for the Austrian Habsburgs in Hungary in 1600 and 1601. He was knighted by the Prince of Transylvania after reputedly killing three Ottoman challengers in single combat. In 1602 he was wounded, captured by Crimean Tatars and sold as a slave, then sent to Rostov. He killed his master and escaped to Muscovy, reaching England in 1604.

In 1606 Smith joined the Virginia Company of London's plan to colonise Virginia, and the expedition sailed on 20 December 1606. He was charged with mutiny during the voyage and held under arrest, but when the ships landed at Cape Henry on 26 April 1607 the company's sealed orders named him one of the colony's leaders. Jamestown was founded on 14 May 1607 on a site chosen by Edward Maria Wingfield.

In December 1607 men led by Opechancanough captured Smith on the Chickahominy River and took him to Powhatan at Werowocomoco. In the summer of 1608 he explored the Chesapeake Bay region for food, and he was elected president of the council in September. He insisted that he who works not, eats not. Smith left in October 1609 after a gunpowder accident. In 1614 he explored the coast from Monhegan Island to Cape Cod and named the region New England.

Smith published eight volumes in his lifetime, including A True Relation of Virginia (1608), A Map of Virginia (1612) and The Generall Historie of Virginia, New-England, and the Summer Isles (1624). He wrote to encourage English colonisation, and the scholar Leo Lemay argues that he was straightforward about its dangers and offered industry rather than gold. The story of Pocahontas saving his life is missing from A True Relation but appears in the Generall Historie, and it is the episode critics scrutinise most. Lemay notes that no one in Smith's day doubted it.

Smith died in London on 21 June 1631 and was buried in 1633 in the south aisle of Saint Sepulchre-without-Newgate Church, the largest parish church in the City of London, where a stained glass window commemorates him. His books and maps encouraged English colonisation.
john-stuart-mill: Mill was born at 13 Rodney Street in Pentonville, then on the edge of London, the eldest son of Harriet Barrow and the Scottish philosopher James Mill. His father educated him, with the advice of Jeremy Bentham and Francis Place, and deliberately shielded him from children other than his siblings, aiming to create a genius intellect that would carry on the cause of utilitarianism. John Stuart was taught Greek at three, and by eight he had read Aesop's Fables, Xenophon's Anabasis and the whole of Herodotus, and had been taught arithmetic, physics and astronomy.

From 1823, at seventeen, until 1858 Mill worked for the East India Company. In 1836 he was promoted to its political department, handling correspondence with the princely states, and in 1856 he became Examiner of Indian Correspondence. When the Crown moved to take direct control of the Company's territories he defended Company rule and declined a seat on the Council of India, citing disapproval of the new system. He defended what he called a benevolent despotism over peoples he regarded as backward.

On 21 April 1851 Mill married Harriet Taylor after 21 years of friendship, declaring on marriage that he repudiated the rights the law gave him over her. He called himself, in the cause of women's rights, chiefly an amanuensis to his wife, who died in 1858. A member of the Liberal Party, he was the second Member of Parliament, after Henry Hunt in 1832, to call for women's suffrage. He died of erysipelas at Avignon on 7 May 1873, aged 66, and was buried beside his wife.

In A System of Logic (1843) Mill held, against William Whewell, that laws are found by observation and induction and need empirical verification. On Liberty (1859) addresses the limits of the power society may legitimately exercise over the individual: the only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over a member of a civilised community against his will is to prevent harm to others.

In Utilitarianism he defended the principle, drawn from Bentham and his father, that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness. In The Subjection of Women, published in 1869, he argued that the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong and should be replaced by perfect equality. In 1850 he answered Thomas Carlyle's defence of slavery in an anonymous letter, and he supported abolition in the United States.
john-talbot-1st-earl-of-shrewsbury: Talbot was the second son of Richard Talbot, 4th Baron Talbot of Goodrich Castle, and Ankaret, heiress of the Barons Strange of Blackmere, and was born at Black Mere Castle near Whitchurch in Shropshire. After his father's death in 1396 his stepfather, Thomas Nevill, 5th Baron Furnivall, shaped his early life, and before 1407 Talbot married Nevill's heiress Maud, styling himself Baron Furnivall. From 1404 to 1413 he fought with his elder brother Gilbert against the rebellion of Owain Glyndŵr, and in 1421 the death of his niece brought him the baronies of Talbot and Strange.

From February 1414 Talbot was for five years Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, where complaints were made of his harsh government. A dispute with James Butler, 4th Earl of Ormond, grew into a feud that divided the officials of Ireland until the Privy Council reprimanded both sides; it ended when Talbot's heir married Ormond's daughter. He fought at the Battle of Verneuil in 1424, which earned him the Order of the Garter, and from 1427 served in Maine and at the Siege of Orléans.

After his release from captivity in 1433 he became the main English general in the field, especially once the Duke of Bedford died in 1435 and the Burgundian government in Paris defected to the French. His method was speed and surprise: he routed La Hire and Xaintrailles at Ry in 1436, took Pontoise at dawn on 13 February 1437, scattered the army of Constable Richemont in December 1439 and retook Harfleur in 1440. His siege of Dieppe in 1442 and 1443 failed. Taken hostage at Rouen in 1449, he promised never again to wear armour against the French king, and kept to the letter of that promise while still commanding.

Sent to Bordeaux as the king's lieutenant in Aquitaine, he landed on 17 October 1452 and took Fronsac the next spring. At Castillon, misled by reports of a French retreat, he attacked the entrenched camp frontally against massed field artillery without waiting for his full force. Contemporaries reported that his horse, struck by a cannonball, pinned him down and a French soldier killed him with a battleaxe; his son John, Viscount Lisle, died with him. His heart was buried at St Alkmund's Church, Whitchurch, and the victors raised a monument on the field. Shakespeare portrayed him heroically in Henry VI, Part 1.
john-tengo-jabavu: Jabavu was born on 11 January 1859 near Healdtown in the Cape Colony. In 1875 he graduated from the Methodist mission school there and became a teacher at Somerset East, where he began writing articles for South African newspapers and apprenticed himself to a printer. In 1881 Reverend James Stewart of the Lovedale Mission School invited him to edit the institution's Xhosa-language journal, Isigidimi samaXhosa, The Xhosa Messenger.

By the early 1880s Jabavu had become an important political force. His writing warned of the threat of growing Afrikaner nationalism and demanded equal rights for the Xhosa population of the Cape Colony, and he also argued for the rights of women and for public education. In 1883 a group of prominent Cape politicians asked him to stand for the Cape Parliament in a constituency where Xhosa voters were numerous, such as Victoria East. He declined, fearing that his candidacy would unite and provoke the reactionary members of the parliament and so do more harm than good.

He later gave his support to the more liberal leaders of the Cape's South African Party against the repressive policies of Rhodes's Progressives. In 1884 he founded his own paper, Imvo Zabantsundu, Black Opinion. His movement, Imbumba, The Union, aspired to unity but was seen as a Xhosa party, and it met a growing rival in the South African Native National Congress led by Walter Rubusana, which was seen as drawing Xhosa and other Africans together. The rivalry largely ended when some degree of unity was reached under the African National Congress.

A year after founding Imvo, Jabavu married Elda Sakuba, who died in 1900, leaving four sons. The eldest, Davidson Don Tengo Jabavu, became an author and activist, and Jabavu died at his home at Fort Hare on 10 September 1921. The second son, Alexander, succeeded his father as editor of Imvo Zabantsundu. In 2006 the South African government awarded Jabavu the Order of Luthuli in recognition of his journalism and his support of democracy.
john-the-baptist: John is named in all four canonical Gospels. Only the Gospel of Luke tells of his infancy: he was the miraculous son of Zechariah, an old priest, and his wife Elizabeth, who was past menopause. The angel Gabriel is said to have announced his birth to Zechariah while he served in the temple at Jerusalem. Luke also states that John and Jesus were relatives, and on this account the Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran calendars place the feast of his nativity on 24 June, six months before Christmas. Some scholars think that John belonged to the Essenes, a semi-ascetic Jewish sect that expected a messiah and practised ritual baptism.

The Gospel of Mark introduces John as the fulfilment of a prophecy, a messenger sent ahead and a voice crying out in the wilderness. John wore clothes of camel's hair and lived on locusts and wild honey. He proclaimed a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sin and said that another would come who would baptise not with water but with the Holy Spirit.

Baptism was the central symbol of his movement. The majority of biblical scholars agree that John baptised Jesus, and several New Testament accounts report that some of Jesus's early followers had earlier followed John. The Gospel of Matthew has Jesus identify John as the Elijah who is to come, while the Gospel of John has John deny that he is the Christ or Elijah.

According to the New Testament, Herod Antipas had John executed around 30 CE, after John rebuked him for divorcing his wife and unlawfully marrying Herodias, the wife of his brother Herod Philip I. The Jewish historian Josephus also mentions John in his Antiquities of the Jews and states that Herod Antipas had him executed at the fortress of Machaerus.

Followers of John persisted into the second century, and some proclaimed him the Messiah. The Mandaeans, an ancient ethnoreligious group, regard him as their most important and final prophet. In Islam he is the prophet Yahya ibn Zakariya, and he is also honoured as a prophet in the Baháʼí Faith and the Druze faith. In Catholic martyrology he is the only saint whose birth and death are both commemorated.
john-the-exarch: Evidence about the life of John the Exarch is scarce. He was a writer and translator of the Preslav Literary School, active during the reign of Boris I (r. 852–889) and of his son Simeon I (r. 893–927). His writings show an excellent knowledge of Greek, and it is therefore assumed that he was educated in the Byzantine Empire.

Some historians take his sobriquet, the Exarch, to mean that he was Archbishop of Bulgaria, while others suggest that it did not denote a bishop's rank. There are also theories that identify him with Chernorizets Hrabar or with John of Rila. The Russian Orthodox Church canonised him, and his memory is honoured on 13 August (31 July in the old style); a manuscript of the Gospels held in the National Library of Serbia gives another date, 13 February (31 January in the old style).

John's literary work includes a number of translations of Byzantine authors. The most important is his translation, made around 895, of On Orthodox Christianity by the Byzantine theologian John of Damascus. Besides his translations he was the author of several original works and of compilations that combine translated and original material.

The chief of these is the Shestodnev, or Hexameron, which joins passages from several Byzantine authors, above all Basil the Great, to writing of John's own. Those original parts give valuable first-hand evidence about the Bulgarian Empire under Simeon I. John describes the royal palace and the ruler himself, including his attire, as well as the boyars and the social stratification of Bulgarian society and like matters.
john-the-fearless: John was born at the Palace of the Dukes of Burgundy in Dijon on 28 May 1371, the son of Philip the Bold and Margaret III, Countess of Flanders. His paternal grandfather was King John II of France, which made him a prince of the blood. In 1384 he received the County of Nevers, and in 1385 he married Margaret of Bavaria in a double wedding at Cambrai that consolidated his position in the Low Countries.

He led the French forces sent to aid Sigismund, King of Hungary, against Sultan Bayezid I, and at the Battle of Nicopolis on 25 September 1396 fought so bravely that he was given the name Fearless. His impetuous leadership ended in disaster; he was captured and freed only the next year after a very large ransom.

John inherited the Duchy of Burgundy on 27 April 1404 and the counties of Burgundy, Flanders and Artois on his mother's death in 1405. He at once clashed with Louis I, Duke of Orléans, the younger brother of the mentally ill King Charles VI, as both tried to fill the power vacuum. Though their uncle John, Duke of Berry, secured a vow of reconciliation on 20 November 1407, Louis was killed in the streets of Paris on 23 November. John admitted the deed and called it a justifiable act of tyrannicide, and in the treaty of Chartres of 9 March 1409 the king absolved him. Louis's son Charles allied with Bernard VII, Count of Armagnac, and the factions became known as Armagnacs and Burgundians.

When Henry V of England invaded France, John kept in contact with him but, wary of losing his popularity, allied himself with the Armagnacs; his troops took no part in the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. On 30 May 1418 his troops captured Paris, the new Dauphin, the future Charles VII, escaping to the Bastille, and John made himself protector of the king.

The Dauphin sought reconciliation, and the two swore peace on the bridge of Pouilly-le-Fort in July 1419. A second meeting was proposed for 10 September 1419 on the bridge at Montereau. John came with his escort, thinking it a diplomatic occasion, and was killed by the Dauphin's bodyguards, among them Tanneguy III du Châtel and Jean Louvet. He was buried at Dijon in 1420. His son and successor Philip the Good then allied with the English, which prolonged the Hundred Years' War. John and his father also played a part in the development of gunpowder artillery in European warfare.
john-troglita: Troglita's origins are unclear: he may have been born in Thrace, though his surname may point to Trogilos in Macedonia. Procopius of Caesarea and Corippus name his father as Evanthes. He fought in the Vandalic War under Belisarius, in which his brother Pappus was killed, and stayed in Africa as a regional dux, leading expeditions against the Leuathae and fighting the rebel Stotzas at Membresa in 536 and Scalas Veteres in 537. Sent east after 538, he became dux Mesopotamiae by 541. Corippus credits him with victories over the Persians near Nisibis, Theodosiopolis and Dara, but Procopius tells the first differently and omits the others.

Troglita reached Carthage as magister militum per Africam in late 546, with veterans who were mostly horse archers and cataphracts, and won the Moorish leaders Cutzinas and Ifisdaias to his side. In a long, bloody battle in late 546 or early 547, probably near Sufetula, he defeated Antalas and Ierna, chief priest of the god Gurzil, and recovered the standards Solomon had lost at Cillium in 544.

In summer 547 a coalition of Tripolitanian tribes under Carcasan, king of the Ifuraces, routed his army, weakened by three regiments sent to Italy, at Marta in the district of Gallica, and the Moors raided as far as the outskirts of Carthage. Troglita regrouped at Laribus, reconciled his allies and won over Iaudas. In 548, after surviving a mutiny that attacked his tent, he blockaded the Moors' fortified camp at the Fields of Cato. When they attacked, he killed Carcasan himself; seventeen principal Moorish leaders fell, and Antalas submitted.

Made patricius, Troglita stayed in command for at least four more years, restoring the civil administration with the prefect Athanasius, rebuilding Solomon's fortifications and returning the subdued tribes to the status of foederati. Peace lasted until 562. In late 551 he sent a fleet to retake Sardinia and Corsica from Totila, without success. He most likely died in 552 or soon after. John B. Bury called him, beside Belisarius and Solomon, the third hero of the imperial reoccupation of Africa.
john-v-duke-of-brittany: John V, known as John the Wise, was born on 24 December 1389 at the Château de l'Hermine, the eldest son of John IV, Duke of Brittany, and Princess Joan of Navarre. He became duke in 1399, when he was ten, and his mother served as regent in the first part of his reign. He began under the tutelage of Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy. Unlike his father he inherited the duchy in peace, though the Penthièvre family continued to plot against him. He made peace with Charles VI of France and married the king's daughter Joan of France.

The Counts of Penthièvre had lost the Breton War of Succession but had not renounced their claims. In 1420 they invited John to a festival at Châtonceaux and arrested him. Olivier, Count of Penthièvre, and his mother Margaret de Clisson spread rumours of his death and moved him to a new prison each day. His wife Joan called on the barons of Brittany, who besieged the Penthièvre castles one by one, and she ended the crisis by seizing the dowager countess and forcing her to free the duke. The citadel at Châtonceaux was destroyed and renamed Champtoceaux, Olivier lost his county and went into exile, and the Montforts declared the Treaty of Guérande broken.

During the Hundred Years' War John switched between the English and French sides. He missed the Battle of Agincourt, but took Saint-Malo in the confusion afterwards and signed the Treaty of Troyes, while letting his brother Arthur de Richemont fight for the French. He made a treaty with the Dauphin Charles at Sablé in May 1421, turned to England by the Treaty of Amiens in 1423, and allied with Charles again by the Treaty of Saumur in 1425. England declared war in 1426, and in 1427 John again recognised Henry VI of England as king of France.

John took part in the Praguerie revolt against Charles VII in 1440 and signed a neutrality agreement with the English in July of that year. With Bishop Jean de Malestroit he began a new cathedral at Nantes, laying the first stone in April 1434. He died on 29 August 1442 at the Manoir de la Touche and was succeeded by his eldest son Francis I. His reversals in the war served to strengthen the duchy and maintain its independence. He reinforced ducal authority, reformed the military and built a coherent system of taxation. His younger son Gilles, sent to grow up in Henry VI's household, was murdered on 24 April 1450.
john-v-of-portugal: John was born on 22 October 1689 at Ribeira Palace in Lisbon, the eldest surviving son of Peter II of Portugal and Maria Sophia of Neuburg. His education was first supervised by women, in the custom of the Portuguese nobility. In December 1696 he was invested as Prince of Brazil and Duke of Braganza. His mother died in 1699, and his aunt Catherine of Braganza, former queen consort of England, Scotland and Ireland, then directed his education until her death in 1705. Peter II died on 9 December 1706, and John was acclaimed king a month later. In 1708 he married Archduchess Maria Anna of Austria, his first cousin and the sister of Emperor Joseph I, a match meant to secure the Habsburg alliance.

John ruled as an absolute monarch. He never convened the Cortes and ignored meetings of the Council of State, preferring weekly private audiences with members of the three estates and a close circle of advisers. His main minister was Diogo de Mendonça Corte-Real, and the diplomat Luís da Cunha called him a despot. His foreign policy aimed at neutrality, except for Portugal's part in the War of the Spanish Succession, which he inherited through the Methuen Treaty of 1703. He cultivated Rome: a lavish entry for his ambassador in 1716 helped persuade Pope Clement XI to raise Lisbon to a Patriarchate, and he later received the title Most Faithful Majesty.

Under John the Americas became the base of Portuguese imperial power, as returns from Asia and Africa fell. Gold from Brazil and Maranhão, collected through the royal fifth, filled the treasury. It paid for embassies to Paris in 1715 and Rome in 1716 and for the Royal Palace-Convent of Mafra, begun in 1717 as a modest convent for a hundred friars and enlarged, with gold produced by slave labour in the colonies, into a convent-palace for three hundred friars with a basilica and library. A Swiss resident remarked in 1726 that the king meant to build a second Escorial.

John suffered three strokes in 1742, which left him paralysed on his left side. He remained active in government and would not let Crown Prince José take a role in it. He died on 31 July 1750, aged 60. Admirers called him the Magnanimous and the Portuguese Sun King. His reign marks the high point of Portugal's dependence on wealth from Brazil.
john-vi-count-of-nassau-dillenburg: John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg was born on 22 November 1536 in Dillenburg, the second son of Count William I of Nassau-Dillenburg, known as William the Rich, and his second wife, Juliane of Stolberg-Wernigerode. His elder brother was William I of Orange, William the Silent. He was also called Jan VI or Jan de Oude, John the Elder, a name that set him apart from his second son, known as John the Middle, and from his grandson, John the Younger.

John married three times and had 24 children in all. On 16 June 1559 he married Elisabeth of Leuchtenberg, who bore him 13 children before her death on 6 July 1579; among them were Count Willem Lodewijk, Count John VII, Count George and Count Ernst Casimir of Nassau-Dietz. On 13 September 1580 he married Kunigunde Jakobäa of Simmern, a daughter of Frederick III, Elector Palatine, who bore him four children before she died in 1586; only their daughter Maria Amalia lived to adulthood.

His third marriage, on 14 June 1586, was to Johannetta of Sayn-Wittgenstein, who bore him seven more children, among them Prince John Louis of Nassau-Hadamar. Several of his daughters married into other noble houses: Elisabeth to Count Philip IV of Nassau-Weilburg, Juliana to the Wild- and Rhinegrave Adolf Henry of Dhaun, Maria to Count John Louis I of Nassau-Wiesbaden-Idstein and Mathilde to Count Wilhelm V of Mansfeld-Arnstein.

John died in his native Dillenburg on 8 October 1606, aged 69. Besides his part as the principal author of the Union of Utrecht, he holds a special place in the history of the Netherlands as the male-line forefather of the House of Orange: the royal family of the Netherlands descends from him through his son Ernst Casimir of Nassau-Dietz.
john-vi-kantakouzenos: John Kantakouzenos was born in Constantinople, the son of Michael Kantakouzenos, governor of the Morea. Through his mother he was related to the reigning Palaiologos house, and through his wife Irene Asanina to Emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos. He supported Andronikos III against his grandfather Andronikos II Palaiologos and, after the accession in 1328, served as grand domestic. When Andronikos III died in June 1341, Kantakouzenos became regent for the nine-year-old John V Palaiologos. By his own account he had refused several times to be crowned co-emperor.

In September 1341, while Kantakouzenos was away raising an army, the Patriarch John XIV of Constantinople and Alexios Apokaukos overthrew his regency. His relatives were exiled or imprisoned and his mother died under house arrest. His army proclaimed him emperor at Didymoteichon in Thrace, and he accepted while still styling himself the junior ruler.

The civil war lasted six years and nearly ruined the empire. Kantakouzenos fled to Serbia, where Stefan Dušan sheltered him, but the Serbs later changed sides, and Umur of Aydin twice rescued him. He then allied with the Ottoman ruler Orhan Bey, giving him his daughter Theodora in marriage. Kantakouzenos entered Constantinople on 8 February 1347, agreeing that he would rule as senior emperor for ten years.

His reign was one of continuing decline. The Genoese fortified their colony at Galata and took as much as 87 per cent of the Bosphorus revenue. Kantakouzenos built a fleet to break their hold, but Genoa destroyed or captured it by early 1349. In 1351 he oversaw the Fifth Council of Constantinople, which declared the hesychastic theology of Gregory Palamas Orthodox. In 1354 the Ottomans annexed Gallipoli, their first foothold in Europe, as part payment of his debts.

John V removed him from power, and he became a monk on 10 December 1354 under the name Joasaph Christodoulos. In retirement he wrote a four-volume History of the years 1320–1356, an apologia for his actions and the only surviving account by a Byzantine emperor of his own reign.
john-vi-of-portugal: John was born in Lisbon on 13 May 1767, the second son of Maria, Princess of Brazil, later Queen Maria I, and Infante Peter, her paternal uncle, who became King Peter III. He grew up in the shadow of his elder brother José, and little is known of the substance of his education beyond instruction in religion, law, French and etiquette. In 1785 he married Carlota Joaquina of Spain, then ten years old, with a papal dispensation, since they were second cousins; the marriage was consummated five years later. After José died of smallpox in 1788, John became heir to the throne.

As his mother's mental illness grew, John took control of the country, though he rejected a formal regency, and from 1799 he was prince regent. He tried to gain time against Napoleon's pressure, refusing to obey the Continental System while a secret treaty with Britain promised help if the royal family had to flee. In October 1807 news came that a French army was approaching, and a British squadron arrived at Lisbon on 16 November. John chose British protection and sailed for Brazil, reaching Salvador on 22 January 1808.

In Brazil his first major act was the decree opening the ports to friendly nations, from which Britain gained most. He founded the Imprensa Régia, the Botanical Garden and the National Library of Brazil, along with schools, academies and a Royal Museum. He succeeded his mother on 20 March 1816 and was acclaimed on 6 February 1818. Carlota Joaquina repeatedly plotted for a monarchy of her own, and John's involvement in Spanish colonial politics led to the capture of Montevideo in 1817 and the annexation of Cisplatina Province in 1821.

The royal ships reached Lisbon on 3 July, and John swore loyalty to a new constitution on 1 October 1822, surrendering various prerogatives. Carlota Joaquina refused and lost her political rights. Meanwhile his son Pedro, who stayed in Brazil, proclaimed independence on 7 September 1822 and took the title of emperor. Tradition holds that John had told him to put the crown on his own head before an adventurer took it. His other son Miguel led a rebellion that sought to depose him. John was recognised as titular emperor of Brazil from 15 November 1825 and died on 10 March 1826.

Contemporaries thought him kind and benevolent, but later generations caricatured him, and historians have in recent decades restored his reputation as a king who balanced competing interests. Many consider him a mastermind of the modern Brazilian state.
john-vii-count-of-nassau-siegen: John was born at Siegen Castle on 7 June 1561, the second son of Count John VI the Elder and his first wife, Landgravine Elisabeth of Leuchtenberg. After the Counts' School in Siegen he went in 1576 to Heidelberg University with his brothers William Louis, George and Philip and his cousin Maurice of Nassau, but left the next year at his father's wish. On 9 December 1581 he married Countess Magdalene of Waldeck-Wildungen, a match of his own choosing that his father accepted. He was first called John the Younger and became John the Middle once his own son John came of age; historians numbered the counts only in the 19th century.

He saw his first campaign in 1583 under Count Palatine John Casimir and from 1584 strengthened the fortifications of Nassau Castle and Dillenburg Castle. When his father introduced general conscription, John made sure the men were trained: he ordered standard rifles of one calibre, so that one soldier could give another bullets, dressed them in a uniform, then something new, and invented the foot drill. His Kriegsbuch gathered the military knowledge of the time with many new ideas and contributed to the reform of the Dutch States Army by his cousin Maurice. He served in that army, was colonel general of the Palatinate and commander-in-chief of the Swedish army.

He worked for Protestant unity against the Counter-Reformation, in 1598 even promoting the election of Maurice as German king. After Duke John William of Jülich-Cleves-Berg died childless on 25 March 1609, John brought Count Palatine Wolfgang William of Neuburg and Elector John Sigismund of Brandenburg to agree on a common course at Dortmund on 10 June 1609.

His father died on 8 October 1606, and on 30 March 1607 the brothers divided their lands: John received Siegen, Freudenberg, Netphen, Hilchenbach, Ferndorf and the Haingericht, and their treaty forbade their heirs to leave the Reformed confession. He died at Siegen Castle on 27 September 1623, the father of 25 children by two marriages, and was buried in the St. Nicholas Church in Siegen.

A dispute followed at the reading of his will on 11 December 1623. John the Younger, holding an imperial decree, received the homage of Siegen on 12 January 1624 after slipping horsemen into the town in a snowstorm, but he then ceded the Hilchenbach district to his brother William, and until 1645 the county had two governments.
john-viii-count-of-nassau-siegen: John VIII was born at Dillenburg on 29 September 1583, the second son of John VII, Count of Nassau-Siegen, and Countess Magdalene of Waldeck-Wildungen. He was educated at Herborn, Kassel and Geneva, and in 1610 he served in the Dutch States Army at the conquest of Jülich. His open conversion to Catholicism horrified his family, and he entered the army of Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy.

When his elder brother John Ernest died in September 1617, John claimed his rights, but his father chose a Protestant successor. On 13 August 1618, in Brussels, he married the Catholic princess Ernestine Yolande de Ligne, daughter of Lamoral de Ligne, Prince d'Espinoy; they had six children. After his father's death in 1623 he occupied Nassau-Siegen at the head of a Habsburg army and began the Contra-Reformation there, and in 1624 he became a knight of the Order of the Golden Fleece.

In 1625 he took part in the Siege of Breda, which his second cousin Justinus van Nassau defended for eleven months before surrendering; Diego Velázquez painted him in The Surrender of Breda, third from the left in the Spanish camp, looking at the viewer. On 1 July 1629 he became an Imperial Field Marshal and acquired the barony of Ronse, where he built a castle modelled on the Luxembourg Palace in Paris. Captured by the Dutch in 1630, he was released the same year for a large sum. In 1631 he commanded the Spanish-Flemish fleet defeated at the Battle of the Slaak, fighting for the Spanish governor Francisco de Moncada, 3rd Marquis of Aitona.

In 1632 the Swedes conquered Nassau-Siegen, and his half-brother John Maurice of Nassau-Siegen restored Protestantism there. John VIII died at Ronse on 27 July 1638. His only son, John Francis Desideratus, succeeded him but had to cede part of Nassau-Siegen to the Protestant branch of the family. Of his daughters, Clara Maria married into the house of Ligne and Ernestine Charlotte married Maurice Henry, Prince of Nassau-Hadamar.
john-vorster: Balthazar Johannes Vorster was born on 13 December 1915 at Jamestown, Cape Province, the fifteenth child of a successful sheep farmer. At Stellenbosch University he became chairman of the debating society, deputy chairman of the student council and leader of the junior National Party. He graduated in 1938 and opened law practices at Port Elizabeth and Brakpan.

From 1939 he strongly opposed South Africa's entry into the Second World War on the side of the Allies, and joined the Ossewabrandwag, an anti-British, pro-Nazi organisation that carried out acts of sabotage during the war. He became a general in its paramilitary wing and was detained at Koffiefontein in 1942; he denied taking part in its violence and said he was interned for being anti-British. After his release in 1944 he became active in the National Party and entered the House of Assembly for Nigel in 1953.

Verwoerd appointed him Minister of Justice in 1961, adding Police and Prisons in 1966. The Rivonia Trial, in which Nelson Mandela was sentenced to life imprisonment for sabotage, came under him as Minister of Justice. After Verwoerd was assassinated in 1966 the National Party elected Vorster to succeed him.
