He continued apartheid legislation, including the abolition of the last four parliamentary seats for white representatives of Coloured voters, but dropped several proposed bills and repealed the ban on multiracial sports teams so that South Africa could attempt to compete at the 1968 Olympics; the IOC refused the team permission. The Terrorism Act and the Soweto Riots fell in his years as prime minister.

In foreign policy he was more pragmatic than his predecessors, allowing Black African diplomats to live in white areas. After Portuguese rule collapsed in Angola and Mozambique in 1975 he pressed Ian Smith of Rhodesia, in September 1976 under US pressure from Henry Kissinger, to accept in principle that white minority rule could not last. After the Soweto Uprising he let the Department of Information carry out secret activities financed from a secret defence account without telling his cabinet; the auditor general's critical report led to a scandal, and he resigned as prime minister in 1978.

Vorster then became State President, a largely honorary post, but a commission of inquiry concluded in mid-1979 that he had known everything about the Muldergate corruption, including a slush fund used to found The Citizen newspaper, and he resigned. He died in September 1983, aged 67, of a blood clot in the lung after a lung infection and emphysema. A building at Stellenbosch University, built on land taken from coloured residents under the Group Areas Act, was named for him and renamed in the 1990s.
john-william-duke-of-julich-cleves-berg: Johann Wilhelm was born on 28 May 1562, the son of William the Rich, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, and Maria of Austria, a daughter of Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor, and Anna of Bohemia and Hungary. He grew up and was educated in Xanten and was meant to become Bishop of Münster, but the unexpected death of his elder brother Karl Friedrich made him heir to the United Duchies, a combination of states within the Holy Roman Empire. He was also Count of Altena.

In 1585 he married Jakobea of Baden, daughter of Philibert, Margrave of Baden, who died in 1597; his second wife was Antonia of Lorraine, daughter of Charles III, Duke of Lorraine. Some have claimed an earlier morganatic marriage with Anna op den Graeff, said to have borne him a son, Herman op den Graeff, but no substantial evidence of any tie between them has been presented. The duke suffered from a serious mental illness, for which the physician Francesco Maria Guazzo treated him. The composer Konrad Hagius was among his court servants.

Johann Wilhelm died on 25 March 1609 without heirs. His lands were claimed through his two eldest sisters. Maria Eleonora of Cleves, wife of Albert Frederick, Duke of Prussia, had died in 1608, and her heir was the Protestant Anna of Prussia, Electress of Brandenburg. Anna of Cleves, wife of Philipp Ludwig, Count Palatine of Neuburg, was the mother of Wolfgang Wilhelm, Count Palatine of Neuburg, who became a Roman Catholic in 1613.

As disputes between Protestants and Catholics deepened toward the Thirty Years' War of 1618, the inheritance became a cause of conflict in its own right. In the end Brandenburg received Cleves-Mark and Neuburg received Jülich-Berg, after armies had crossed the lands several times and much of the wealth for which they had been known in his father's time was lost.
john-william-elector-palatine: John William, called Jan Wellem in Low German, was born on 19 April 1658 into the Wittelsbach dynasty. His father was Count Palatine Philip William of Neuburg and his mother Elisabeth Amalie of Hesse-Darmstadt. He was born in Düsseldorf, where he continued to reside, rather than in Heidelberg, which French troops largely destroyed in the Nine Years' War. The Jesuits educated him, and in 1674 he made a grand tour to Italy. His brother was Franz Ludwig, Count Palatine of Neuburg, and his sisters married Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I, Peter II of Portugal and Charles II of Spain.

On 25 October 1678 John William married Archduchess Maria Anna Josepha of Austria, a daughter of Emperor Ferdinand III. As a gift to the couple his father ceded to them the Duchies of Jülich and Berg in 1679. Their two sons died in infancy, and she died of tuberculosis in 1689. On 29 April 1691 he married by proxy Anna Maria Luisa de' Medici, daughter of Cosimo III de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, and they were officially married at Innsbruck. She miscarried in 1692, and they had no children. Historians long believed she had contracted syphilis from her adulterous husband, but an examination of her bones in 2012 found no traces of it.

He succeeded his father as Elector Palatine in 1690. In the Peace of Rijswijk of 1697 he regained many of the possessions the French had taken, on condition that the Electoral Palatinate not revert to Protestantism, a provision that made him unpopular in the Palatinate and among Protestants. During the War of the Spanish Succession he received the Bavarian Upper Palatinate, which was returned to Bavaria in 1714.

John William was more popular in Jülich-Berg, where he put up buildings such as Bensberg Castle and kept a lavish court that employed many artists, among them the painters Adriaen van der Werff, Godfried Schalcken, Rachel Ruysch and Jan Weenix. His large collection of paintings by Rubens can still be seen in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich. His widow Anna Maria Luisa, the last of the House of Medici, left the Medici collections to the Tuscan state on condition that they never leave Florence. He died in Düsseldorf on 8 June 1716 and was buried in the St. Andreas Church. Having no son, he was succeeded by his brother Charles III Philip. Düsseldorf's Jan-Wellem Square is named after him.
john-william-friso: John William Friso was born on 14 August 1687 in Dessau, Anhalt. His father was Henry Casimir II, Prince of Nassau-Dietz, and his mother Princess Henriëtte Amalia of Anhalt-Dessau; both were first cousins of William III. He belonged to the Nassau-Dietz branch of the House of Nassau and was educated under Jean Lemonon, a professor at the University of Franeker. Through the testamentary dispositions of William III he became the progenitor of a new line of the House of Orange-Nassau.

When William III died, the male line of William the Silent became extinct. Friso, a senior agnatic descendant of William the Silent's brother, claimed the stadtholdership in all the provinces William III had held, but the republican faction refused. Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht, Gelderland and Overijssel suspended the office, while Friesland and Groningen kept Friso as their stadtholder. His inheritance of the Principality of Orange was contested by Frederick I of Prussia, by a Catholic relative from Nassau-Siegen and by Louis XIV, who supported the Prince of Conti.

In the War of the Spanish Succession Friso joined the Dutch States Army in 1703 and was named General of Infantry in 1704, at first only nominally. He came of age in 1707. At the Battle of Oudenaarde he led a flank attack by 10,000 Dutch infantrymen that helped decide the battle. He commanded the Anglo-Dutch troops at the siege of Lille, where a cannonball killed his chamberlain, and at Malplaquet he led the Allied left. His assaults there failed with heavy losses, and he was criticised in the Republic for recklessness.

In 1709 Friso married Princess Maria Louise of Hesse-Kassel, and they had two children. On 14 July 1711, travelling from Flanders to meet the King of Prussia in The Hague about the succession dispute, he drowned when the ferry boat on the Moerdyk overturned in heavy weather. His son, born six weeks later, became William IV, Prince of Orange, and later stadtholder of all seven provinces. Monuments at Moerdijk and Strijensas mark the crossing, and two Dutch military units bear his name.
john-williams-missionary: John Williams was born on 29 June 1796 in Tottenham, near London, to Welsh parents. In 1810 his family moved to north London, where he worked as a clerk to an iron foundry and took an interest in smithing. His employer's wife first took him to church, and the pastor, Matthew Wilks, enrolled him in a class preparing for the ministry. He turned to missionary work, and the London Missionary Society commissioned him at Surrey Chapel in September 1816.

On 17 November 1816 Williams and his wife, Mary Chawner Williams, sailed for the Society Islands with William Ellis and his wife. After months on Eimeo helping to build a boat, they founded their first mission post on Raiatea. Landing on Aitutaki in 1821, they used Tahitian converts to carry Christianity to the Cook Islands. Of their ten children, only three survived to adulthood. In 1827 Williams built a ship from local materials, the Messenger of Peace, in fifteen weeks.

He reached Samoa in 1830 with a Samoan couple, Fauea and his wife Puaseisei, who proved important to the mission. After landing at Safune on Savaii, they met Malietoa Vaiinuupo at Sapapalii on 24 August 1830, and he accepted Christianity at once. Back in Britain from 1834, Williams oversaw the printing of his translation of the New Testament into Rarotongan and published his Narrative of Missionary Enterprises in the South Sea Islands. He returned to the Pacific in 1837 on the ship Camden.

In November 1839, on Erromango in the New Hebrides, where he was unknown, Williams and the missionary James Harris were killed and eaten. A memorial stone was raised on Rarotonga that year, his bones were buried in Apia, and the headquarters of the Congregational Church of Samoa bears his name.

The London Missionary Society named seven successive Pacific mission ships after him, paid for by children's donations, from the first, launched in 1844, to John Williams VII, decommissioned in 1968. In December 2009 descendants of John and Mary Williams went to Erromango to accept apologies from descendants of his killers, and Dillons Bay was renamed Williams Bay.
john-winthrop: John Winthrop was born in Edwardstone, Suffolk, to Adam and Anne Winthrop, and his birth was recorded in the parish register at Groton. His father's family had succeeded in the textile business, and his father was a lawyer and prosperous landowner. The family lived at Groton Manor, where John became lord of the manor, managing the estate, and later followed his father in practising law in London. He also sat on the county commission of the peace. In the late 1620s, with Charles I on the throne and married to a Roman Catholic, the outlook for Puritans grew bleak, and Puritan religious and business leaders began to consider emigration.

Winthrop took no part in founding the Massachusetts Bay Company in 1628, but joined it in 1629 and was elected governor in October. On 8 April 1630 four ships left the Isle of Wight with him and other leaders, Winthrop sailing on the Arbella with his sons Samuel and Stephen. First Church in Boston was founded on 30 July 1630. Between 1629 and 1649 he served 18 annual terms as governor or lieutenant-governor. He resisted widening the vote beyond a narrow class of religiously approved men and opposed codifying laws that would bind the magistrates. He clashed with Thomas Dudley, Roger Williams and Henry Vane.

In the Antinomian Controversy of 1636 and 1637 he opposed Anne Hutchinson and John Wheelwright, whose views he saw as dangerous heresy. After the Pequot War of 1636–1638 many captured Pequots were shipped to the West Indies as slaves, and Winthrop kept one male and two female Pequots as slaves. In 1643 he refused official aid to Charles de Saint-Étienne de la Tour in Acadia but let him recruit volunteers in the colony.

Winthrop rarely published, but he kept a journal from the voyage across the Atlantic through his years in Massachusetts, in three notebooks. It is acknowledged as the central source for the history of Massachusetts in the 1630s and 1640s. Noah Webster published the first two notebooks in 1790, the third, long thought lost, was found in 1816, and James Savage issued the complete journals in 1825 and 1826 as The History of New England. The second notebook was destroyed in a fire at Savage's office in 1825. Richard Dunn and Laetitia Yeandle produced a modern transcription in 1996.

The sermon A Modell of Christian Charitie, with its image of a city upon a hill, was long credited to him. The image became a lasting symbol in American political discourse. His reputation declined in the late 19th and early 20th century, when writers such as Nathaniel Hawthorne and H. L. Mencken pointed to the harsher sides of Puritan rule.
john-wycliffe: John Wycliffe was born in the village of Hipswell, near Richmond in the North Riding of Yorkshire, though the date is disputed: it is conventionally given as 1324, while records suggest the mid-1320s or, according to one scholar, a date after 1331. He is known to have been at Oxford around 1345. The book On the Cause of God Against the Pelagians by Thomas Bradwardine shaped his views, as did the Black Death, which reached England in the summer of 1348 and which he mentioned often in later life. He became a priest in September 1351 and completed his bachelor of arts at Merton College in 1356. In 1361 he was Master of Balliol College.

In 1374 Wycliffe was part of a group that negotiated at Bruges for the English government with the envoys of Pope Gregory XI, which may have begun his connection with John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster. He then began to write tracts and longer works. In De civili dominio he attacked the temporal rule of the clergy, the collection of annates, indulgences and simony. His theory of dominion held that the Church should not own property and that men in mortal sin could not exercise authority in Church or state, and he insisted on the poverty of all clergy.

In the summer of 1381 he set out his doctrine of the Lord's Supper in twelve short sentences, and the chancellor of the University of Oxford had some of them pronounced heretical. Wycliffe appealed to the king. Once he dismissed the doctrine of transubstantiation, he lost the support of John of Gaunt and many others. In his last years he argued that Scripture was the authoritative centre of Christianity, that the claims of the papacy were unhistorical, and that monasticism was corrupt.

Wycliffe withdrew to Lutterworth, where he sent out tracts against the monks and Pope Urban VI and left his last work, the Opus evangelicum, unfinished. He suffered a stroke while saying Mass on 28 December 1384 and died a few days later. Tradition credits him with a Middle English translation of the Vulgate Bible, now called Wycliffe's Bible, completed before 1384 and revised by John Purvey in 1388 and 1395, but more recent scholars suggest he had at most a minor part. His followers, called Lollards by their opponents, adopted many of his views, and his Latin writings greatly influenced the reformer Jan Hus.
john-zapolya: John was the oldest son of Count Stephen Zápolya and his second wife, Hedwig of Cieszyn. Stephen, descended from a Croatian noble family from Slavonia, became one of the wealthiest lords of Hungary and served as Palatine from 1492 until his death in 1499. John was born at Szepes Castle, now Spiš Castle in Slovakia, and he and his brother George inherited their father's domains in 1499, mostly in Upper Hungary. He wrote letters in Latin, which shows the education his mother gave him.

Zápolya began his public career at the Diet of Rákos in 1505, where a bill he prompted forbade the election of a foreigner as king. King Vladislaus II refused to ratify it. Zápolya became leader of a national party of the lesser nobility, who opposed the pro-Habsburg higher aristocracy. Vladislaus made him Voivode of Transylvania on 8 November 1510. In 1514 he defeated the peasant army of György Dózsa at Temesvár on 15 July, after a crusade proclaimed against the Turks had turned into a rebellion. The Diet hailed him as liberator of the realm.
His sister Barbara married King Sigismund I of Poland in 1512, but she died in 1515, and the same year his defeat by Sinan, Bey of Smederovo, weakened his position.

The Ottomans crushed the royal army at the Battle of Mohács in 1526 and killed King Louis II. Zápolya marched toward the battlefield with a large army but did not take part, for unknown reasons. On 10 November 1526 the lesser nobility proclaimed him king at Székesfehérvár, and he was crowned the next day. The magnates elected Archduke Ferdinand in Pozsony on 17 December. Ferdinand's German mercenaries captured Buda in 1527 and defeated John at Tarcal on 27 September, and in 1528 John fled to Poland.

In 1529 he agreed to make Hungary a vassal state of the Ottomans in return for support. Sultan Suleiman sent armies against Austria, including the Siege of Vienna, and John regained his position through the efforts of George Martinuzzi. In 1533 the Ottomans made peace and ceded western Hungary to Ferdinand. John married Isabella Jagiellon in early 1539, and their son John Sigismund was born on 15 July 1540. John died on 22 July 1540 in Szászsebes.
johor: Johor covers nearly 19,166 square kilometres in the south of the Malay Peninsula, with the South China Sea to the east, the Straits of Johor to the south and the Straits of Malacca to the west. Tanjung Piai is the southernmost point of mainland Eurasia. The landscape is flat, broken by inselbergs and massifs, with Mount Ledang the highest point, and its tropical rainforests include the Endau-Rompin National Park. The area was known to people in Siam as Gangganu or Ganggayu, meaning Treasury of Gems, and Arab traders called it jauhar, from which the name Johor came. The Old Javanese Nagarakretagama called it Ujong Medini, land's end.

A bronze bell estimated to date from about 150 CE was found near the Muar River, and the lost city of Kota Gelanggi, known from an old Malay manuscript, is placed by some in the forests of Kota Tinggi District. After the Portuguese took Malacca in 1511, Ala'udin Ri'ayat Shah II, a son of Sultan Mahmud Shah of Malacca, founded the Johor Sultanate in 1528 by moving the court to the Johor River. It spanned the southern peninsula, the Riau Archipelago including Singapore and parts of Borneo and Sumatra, and fought a three-way contest with the Portuguese and the Aceh Sultanate.

After Mahmud Shah III died, the Dutch recognised one son as heir in 1818 and the British recognised the other the following year. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 established Johor's modern borders. Sultan Abu Bakar wrote its state constitution in 1895, and in 1914 it became a British protected state within the Unfederated Malay States. Japanese forces invaded in January 1942 after the Battle of Muar. Johor joined the Malayan Union in 1946 and the Federation of Malaya in 1948, and became part of independent Malaya in 1957 and of Malaysia in 1963.

Johor is a state of Malaysia and a constitutional monarchy headed by a sultan, with Johor Bahru as the state capital and Muar as the royal capital. It is divided into ten districts. The 2023 census counted 4,100,900 people, making it the second most populous state. Malay is the official language, Islam the state religion, and the population includes Malay, Chinese and Indian communities. Johor keeps a private army, the Royal Johor Military Force, which has protected its rulers since 1886. In 2008 the International Court of Justice awarded Pedra Branca to Singapore.
johor-bahru: Johor Bahru lies along the Straits of Johor at the southern end of Peninsular Malaysia, on mostly flat land with some hills, bordering Singapore. Its climate is equatorial, with steady temperatures, high humidity and an average annual rainfall of around 2,350 mm, and two monsoon periods each year. The name means New Johor in Malay, distinguishing it from Johor Lama, Old Johor. The area was originally Tanjung Puteri, a Malay fishing village, and the city has also been spelt Johore Bahru, Johor Baru or Johor Baharu.

In 1819 a dispute between the Malays and the Bugis split the Johor-Riau Sultanate: the mainland portion came under Temenggong Daeng Ibrahim, and the Riau-Lingga Sultanate under the Bugis. The Temenggong already had a close relationship with the British, who wanted to control trade at Singapore. By a treaty signed in Singapore on 10 March 1855, Sultan Ali was to be crowned Sultan of Johor and receive 5,000 Spanish dollars and an allowance of 500 a month, and in return ceded the sovereignty of Johor, except Kesang in Muar, to the Temenggong. The Temenggong renamed the territory Iskandar Puteri and at first administered it from Telok Blangah in Singapore, then, after he arrived in 1858, from the new settlement.

Under Sultan Abu Bakar the town was modernised from a fishing village, with administrative centres, offices, schools and a railway to Woodlands. The State Mosque and Royal Palace were built with the aid of Wong Ah Fook, a patron of the sultan. Abu Bakar set up his administration under a British style and a state constitution, the Undang-undang Tubuh Negeri Johor. Although the British had long been advisers to the sultanate, it did not come under direct colonial rule until the adviser's status was raised to that of a Resident, as in the Federated Malay States, under Sultan Ibrahim in 1914.

General Tomoyuki Yamashita's Japanese forces invaded the town on 31 January 1942. The British retreated to Singapore and blew up the causeway the day before. The Japanese used the sultan's Bukit Serene Palace as their base, aware that the British would not attack it. After the war Johor Bahru became a cradle of Malay nationalism, and UMNO was formed at the Istana Besar in 1946. The town remained the state capital after Malaysia's formation in 1963 and was granted city status on 1 January 1994.

Johor Bahru is the capital of the Malaysian state of Johor and had a population of 858,118 in the 2020 census. Its people are mainly Malays, Chinese and Indians, and it is part of Iskandar Malaysia. Its cultural sites include the Royal Abu Bakar Museum in the Grand Palace building and the Johor Bahru Chinese Heritage Museum, and the main football club is Johor Darul Ta'zim.
joint-stock-company: A joint-stock company is a business entity whose shares can be bought and sold by shareholders. Each shareholder owns stock in proportion, evidenced by certificates, and may transfer shares to others without affecting the continued existence of the company. It is an artificial person with legal existence separate from its members: it can own property, enter into contracts, and sue and be sued in its own name. In modern corporate law the form is often synonymous with incorporation and limited liability, so that shareholders answer for debts only up to the money they invested. The company is managed on behalf of the shareholders by a board of directors elected at an annual general meeting.

Finding the earliest joint-stock company is a matter of definition. The earliest records appear in China under the Tang and Song dynasties. The Tang developed the heben, with an active partner and one or two passive investors. By the Song this had grown into the douniu, a large pool of shareholders whose funds were managed by merchants called jingshang, with compensation based on profit-sharing.

In Europe an early form was the medieval commenda, usually used for a single commercial expedition. Around 1350 at Toulouse, 96 shares of the Société des Moulins du Bazacle were traded at a value that depended on the profits of the mills it owned, making it probably the first company of its kind. The Swedish company Stora has documented a transfer of an eighth of the company as early as 1288. The Hudson's Bay Company, the oldest corporation in Canada, received its royal charter from Charles II in 1670.

A corporation requires a legal framework that grants it legal personality and shields its owners from corporate losses, which also encourages new investors by making stock marketable. Where shareholders have limited liability, many jurisdictions require the company to publish annual financial statements so that creditors can judge its standing. Most of the largest businesses in the world are publicly traded companies whose shares are sold on a stock exchange, but most corporations are privately held, with no ready market for their shares.
jokhang: The Jokhang stands in the centre of Lhasa, in Barkhor Square, about 1,000 metres east of the Potala Palace. It was built under Songtsen Gampo, the first king of a unified Tibet, who planned twelve temples across the country, with the Jokhang at its heart. After the king's death the city, once called Rasa, became Lhasa, place of the gods, and the temple took the name Jokhang, house of the Jowo, after its main image.

Tradition tells how the king tossed his hat and promised to build where it landed, in a lake where a white stupa then appeared. The lake was filled, leaving a small pond now seen as a well. In another version Queen Bhrikuti, the Nepalese wife of the king, founded the temple to hold the statue of Akshobhya Buddha she had brought. Craftsmen from Nepal and India are credited with its design and construction.

The temple covers 2.51 hectares and faces west, towards Nepal, in honour of Bhrikuti. It is built of wood and stone in the Tibetan style, with influences from China, Nepal and Indian vihara design, and its roof is covered with gilded bronze tiles and topped with golden deer flanking a Dharma wheel.

The four-storey Buddha Hall holds the Jowo Shakyamuni, a gilded bronze statue 1.5 metres tall showing the Buddha at the age of twelve. It was brought to Tibet by the Tang princess Wencheng, kept first at the temple of Ramoche and later moved to the Jokhang, and it has become the most revered statue in Tibet. Outside stands a pillar 5.5 metres high with an inscription dated 821 or 822 recording a treaty between the Tibetan king Ralpacan and the Chinese emperor Muzong that set the frontier between their lands.

Pilgrims walk around the temple on the Barkhor, spin prayer wheels and prostrate themselves before the Jowo. The temple's history includes hard times. During the reign of Tresang Detsan, from 755 to 797, Buddhists were persecuted, the images were hidden or moved and the monks were driven out. The Fifth Dalai Lama carried out the last major renovation in 1610. In 1966 Red Guards attacked the temple, and for a decade there was no worship. Renovation began in 1972, and the temple was mostly complete by 1980. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000, as an extension of the Potala Palace.
jokyu-war: In the early 13th century Go-Toba found his political moves blocked by the Kamakura shogunate. Seeking independence and the power he considered rightfully his as ruler of Japan, he gathered allies in 1221, chiefly members of the Taira clan and other enemies of the Minamoto, the victors of the Genpei War and the clan of the shōguns. The first accounts of an imperial banner date from this period: the earliest is said to be one Go-Toba gave to a general in this war, with sun and moon images in gold or silver on red brocade.

In the fifth lunar month of 1221 Go-Toba settled the line of succession without consulting the shogunate or the Hōjō clan. He then invited many eastern warriors in Kyoto to a great festival, so revealing the loyalties of those who refused; one important officer who showed his loyalty to the shogunate in this way was killed. Days later the court declared the regent Hōjō Yoshitoki an outlaw, and three days after that the whole of eastern Japan had officially risen in rebellion.

Yoshitoki sent three armies against Kyoto: one through the mountains, one from the north and the third, under his son Yasutoki, along the Tōkaidō road. They met little resistance. Go-Toba went to Mount Hiei to ask the warrior monks for help, but they declined, citing weakness. The remnants of the imperial army made a last stand at the bridge over the Uji River, where the opening battle of the Genpei War had been fought 41 years earlier, and Yasutoki's cavalry broke through and pressed on to the capital.

With Kyoto in the shogunate's hands, Go-Toba was banished to the Oki Islands, from which he never returned. His sons were exiled too, the retired emperor Tsuchimikado to Tosa and the retired emperor Juntoku to Sado. Emperor Chūkyō, Juntoku's first son, who had only recently been enthroned, was replaced by Emperor Go-Horikawa, a nephew of Go-Toba. The decisive battle at Uji was the third fought there in less than half a century.
jolo: Jolo is a volcanic island in the Sulu Archipelago, between Borneo and Mindanao, and the main island of the province of Sulu. Its population is approximately 500,000. The island holds the Jolo Group of Volcanoes, an active volcanic group with many cones and craters, among them the active Bud Dajo cinder cone. Mount Daho is its highest point, and the capital town of the same name stands on the island.

After a series of less successful attempts during the centuries of Spanish rule in the Philippines, Spanish forces captured the town of Jolo, the seat of the Sultan of Sulu, in 1876. The Spanish wanted to curb slave raiding once and for all and feared the presence of other Western powers: the British had established trading centres at Jolo and the French were offering to buy Basilan Island. On 21 February 1876 Admiral José Malcampo landed a force of 9,000 soldiers carried in 11 transports, 11 gunboats and 11 steamboats. Captain Pascual Cervera set up a garrison and served as military governor.

By 1878 the Spanish had fortified the town with a perimeter wall, tower gates, inner forts and two outer fortifications. The town was still attacked from time to time: on 22 July 1883 three juramentado attackers reached the plaza and killed three Spaniards, and Colonel Juan Arolas coined the word after he saw several such acts. A treaty of peace signed with the Sultan of Sulu on 22 July 1878 left Spanish sovereignty limited to military stations and pockets of settlement.

The Americans arrived in 1899. Brigadier General John C. Bates signed a treaty with Sultan Kiram to secure the sultanate's neutrality in the Philippine-American War. Its English text described complete dependency and its Tausug text a protectorate, and Bates later admitted it was a stop-gap. The Japanese occupied Jolo in World War II, and American troops landed in April 1945 and in three weeks of combat killed about 2,600 Japanese soldiers, with 37 Americans dead.

Jolo is the capital of Sulu province, and its Tausug name is Sūg. In February 2005 between 4,000 and 5,000 Philippine troops fought around 800 Islamist militants on the island, and up to 12,000 people fled. The Cathedral of Our Lady of Mount Carmel in Jolo was bombed on 27 January 2019.
jolof-empire: The region was first inhabited by the Soce and then the Serer, whom the Wolof had driven south by the 13th century, and it was ruled by Lamanes of the Mbengue, Diaw and Ngom families. Jolof was long a vassal of the Mali Empire. Wolof tradition names as founder the possibly mythical Ndiadiane Ndiaye, a stranger who appeared from a lake, settled a dispute among the Lamanes and was made king, after which the rulers between the Senegal and Gambia rivers submitted to him. Historians place the rise of the state in the 14th century, perhaps during a succession dispute within the Mali Empire around 1360.

The empire absorbed Cayor and Baol early, and Sine and an early Saloum in the late 14th century at the earliest, completing its core with Waalo. Portuguese ships reached the coast from the 1440s, and horses bought from them may have helped expansion. Around the 1450s Buurba Biram Njeme Eler conquered Namandirou, extended his authority over Takrur and moved the capital to Thieung. After his death five buurbas claimed the throne between roughly 1455 and 1489, sowing civil war.

In the 1480s Buumi Jelen, ruling for his brother, moved the seat of government to the coast for the Portuguese trade; opponents murdered the buurba in 1489, and Jelen fled to Lisbon, was baptised, and was killed by the commander of the force King John II sent to restore him. The coastal vassals then took most of the Atlantic trade's wealth. In 1513 Koli Tenguella seized Futa Toro, in 1520 Sine and Saloum broke away, and in 1549 Amari Ngoone Sobel Fall of Kayor defeated Jolof at the Battle of Danki, after which Waalo and Baol also left.

The Buurba was chosen by electors who included the rulers of the five main constituent kingdoms, Waalo, Kayor, Baol, Sine and Saloum, each of which chose its own ruler, kept practical autonomy and sent tribute. Society was divided into royal and other nobles, free men, occupational castes such as smiths and griots, and slaves. The Lingeer, head of all women, owned tribute-paying villages and was influential in politics. Trade ran through weekly markets in millet, salt, beans and cattle, with iron bars and cloth serving as money.
jomo-kenyatta: Kenyatta was born with the name Kamau in the rural village of Ngenda, to Kikuyu farmers named Mūigai and Wambūi. The Kikuyu kept no birth records, so his date of birth is not known; one biographer suggested 1890 or 1891, while a fuller analysis suggested about 1897 or 1898. During the First World War he lived among the Maasai, adopting a beaded belt called kĩnyata, from which he took his name.

He joined the Kikuyu Central Association. In February 1929 he sailed to Britain to press the Kikuyu land question. He returned to Britain in 1931 and did not go back to Kenya for fifteen years, studying phonetics at University College London and social anthropology under Bronisław Malinowski at the London School of Economics.

Influenced by his friend George Padmore, Kenyatta embraced Pan-African ideas and co-organised the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester. He returned to Kenya in September 1946, farmed an estate at Gatundu and became vice-principal of the Koinange Independent Teachers' College. In 1947 he was elected President of the Kenya African Union, which lobbied for independence and drew wide African support but the animosity of white settlers. In 1952 he was among the Kapenguria Six, arrested and charged with masterminding the Mau Mau Uprising. He protested his innocence, a view later historians share, but was convicted. He was held at Lokitaung until 1959, then exiled to Lodwar until 1961.

After his release Kenyatta joined the Kenya African National Union in October 1961 and accepted its presidency. KANU won 83 of 124 seats in the May 1963 general election, and on 1 June 1963 he was sworn in as prime minister of the autonomous Kenyan government. In December 1964 Kenya was proclaimed a republic with Kenyatta as executive president. KANU's only rival, Oginga Odinga's Kenya People's Union, was prohibited from competing in elections.

By 1975, in the historian Maloba's words, he had in effect ceased to actively govern. In March 1975 the backbencher Josiah Mwangi Kariuki was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, after which support for the government eroded. Kenyatta died on 22 August 1978 and was succeeded by Daniel arap Moi.

He was called Mzee, meaning grand old man, and Father of the Nation, and a cult of personality surrounded him. His government pursued capitalist policies, expanded education and health care. Critics called his rule dictatorial and neocolonial, accused him of favouring the Kikuyu and of enabling corruption, and noted that Kikuyu still held most important government positions.
jon-sigurdsson: Jón Sigurðsson was born on 17 June 1811 at Hrafnseyri, in Arnarfjörður in the Westfjords of Iceland, the son of Þórdís Jónsdóttir and the pastor Sigurður Jónsson. In 1833 he moved to Denmark to study grammar and history at the University of Copenhagen. There he developed syphilis and was bedridden for a long period; the historian Guðjón Friðriksson holds that he had shown little interest in politics before this illness. He worked at the Arnamagnæan Institute, home of the manuscripts of the Icelandic sagas, and became an expert on the sagas and on Icelandic history. He never graduated, as Icelandic politics came to take all his time.

Jón was elected to the restored Alþing in 1844 for Ísafjörður county and held the seat all his life, attending 13 of the 17 sessions held in his lifetime. He married his cousin Ingibjörg Einarsdóttir in 1845, when he first returned to Iceland since 1833. At the National Assembly of 1851 he led the Icelanders in resisting the adoption of Denmark's 1849 constitutional reform. Until 1874 the Alþing was only an advisory body to the Danish government and king; after years of struggle Denmark then granted a limited constitution giving autonomy in internal affairs. He was speaker of the Alþing from 1875 to 1877.

From Copenhagen he addressed the Icelandic public through the annual magazine Ný félagsrit, published almost every year from 1841 to 1873, to which he was the main contributor and financial backer. The historian Gunnar Karlsson describes him as a classical liberal and no extreme nationalist, a supporter of modernization, democracy and economic progress, who was never arrested. He asked for greater self-rule rather than full autonomy.

Jón died in Copenhagen in 1879. Icelanders often call him Jón forseti, President Jón, because he served as president of the Althing several times, first in 1849. His birthday, 17 June, was chosen as Iceland's national holiday. His Copenhagen apartment on Øster Voldgade, rented from 1852, has belonged to the Icelandic government since 1967 and serves as a cultural centre for Icelanders in Denmark.
jonah-metropolitan-of-moscow: From the late 1420s Jonah lived in the Simonov Monastery in Moscow and was close to Metropolitan Photius, who made him bishop of Ryazan and Murom. Russian rulers had sporadically pressed the patriarch of Constantinople to choose a metropolitan from the native population, but most appointees remained Greeks. After Photius died in 1431, Grand Prince Vasily II of Moscow and a council of Russian bishops chose Jonah at the end of 1432, but civil strife in Moscow delayed his journey to Constantinople until 1436. By then Patriarch Joseph II of Constantinople had already appointed the Greek bishop Isidore.

Isidore arrived in Moscow in 1437 and left five months later for the Council of Florence, which agreed the union of the churches of Rome and Constantinople. When he brought the news back in 1441, Vasily II and a council of bishops condemned the council, according to Russian sources, and Isidore escaped. The see then stood vacant for seven years, as Constantinople sent no replacement. On 15 December 1448 a majority of Russian bishops elected Jonah, though not all the Russian clergy supported him. It is possible that the failure to obtain Constantinople's blessing was not intentional, and in Russian eyes the fall of Constantinople in 1453, read as divine punishment, later justified the step.

As metropolitan Jonah tried to recover the lands lost to the Uniate church and added Lithuania and Kiev to his title, but not Galicia. From 1451 he purged them of Isidore's influence, yet in 1458 Lithuania was separated from his jurisdiction, and the Polish–Lithuanian rulers backed Gregory as metropolitan of a new see of Kiev. Envoys he sent to keep the Russian princes and nobles of Lithuania loyal to Orthodoxy failed, and he and Vasily II tacitly accepted two Orthodox hierarchies.

Jonah died on 31 March 1461 and was buried in the Dormition Cathedral in the Moscow Kremlin. He was the last metropolitan based in Moscow to keep the traditional title naming Kiev. Macarius canonised him at the Moscow Council of 1547, and the Orthodox Church keeps his main feast on 15 June.
jonang: The Jonang traces its origins in Tibet to the master Yumo Mikyö Dorjé (c. 11th-12th century), a pupil of the Kashmiri master Somanātha, whose treatises gathered sources on the approach to emptiness of the Kālacakra Tantra. The school takes its name from the Jomonang monastery, a kumbum or stupa-vihara in the Jomonang Valley about 160 kilometres northwest of Tashilhunpo Monastery, established by the monk Künpang Tukjé Tsöndrü (1243–1313). There he set up a practice tradition joining seventeen transmissions of the completion-stage yogas of the Kālacakra Tantra, which later teachers expanded.

The school's main practice is the Kālacakra tantra, the Wheel of Time Tantra, joined to the philosophy known as shentong, empty of other. Shentong holds that the non-dual nature of the mind, the buddha-nature, is real and not empty of inherent existence, while all other phenomena are empty in this way. Ultimate reality is empty of everything false and defiled, but not of the limitless Buddha qualities that are its own nature.

Dolpopa Sherab Gyaltsen, educated at Sakya monastery and later head of Jonang monastery, set out this view in works such as the Ocean of Definitive Meaning: A Teaching for the Mountain Hermit, known as Mountain Dharma. He took the tathagatagarbha sutras as his main sources for the ultimate truth.

Tāranātha, the school's best-known later scholar, stressed the Kālacakra Tantra, Sanskrit study and the history of Indian Buddhism. In the 17th century the Gelug school, now ruling Tibet under the Dalai Lamas, worked to suppress the Jonang. Modern historians point to political reasons: the Jonang were allies of the house of Tsangpa, the Gelug's rival for Central Tibet, and Tāranātha's tulku was found in Zanabazar, a son of Tüsheet Khan of the Borjigin lineage. Dolpopa's writings were sealed and banned, and the monasteries were gradually converted to the Gelug.

The tradition survived in Amdo, where Dzamtang Tsangwa dzong became its main seat, and spread from there to Golog and Ngawa. Modern Jonang scholars had close ties with masters of the Rime movement of the 19th century. The 14th Dalai Lama has supported the school in exile, giving buildings in Shimla for a Jonang monastery, and an estimated 5,000 monks and nuns practise in the tradition.
jonas-basanavicius: Jonas Basanavičius was born in the village of Ožkabaliai in the Augustów Governorate of Congress Poland, to a family of Lithuanian farmers. After birth complications his devout Catholic parents promised that their firstborn would be educated to be a priest. After the Uprising of 1863 Russification policies, meant to reduce Polish influence, allowed him to attend Marijampolė Gymnasium, where he came to value Lithuanian language, culture and history. After graduating in 1873 he persuaded his parents to let him go to Moscow University rather than a seminary, and after two semesters of history and philology he moved to the Moscow Medical Academy, supported by a fellowship for Lithuanian students.

In January 1880 Basanavičius took charge of a run-down hospital at Lom Palanka in the Principality of Bulgaria. He left in May 1882, afraid of persecution after the crackdown on liberal politicians that followed the assassination of Tsar Alexander II. In Prague he organised the publication of Aušra, the first Lithuanian-language newspaper, whose first issue appeared in March 1883 and is often cited as the beginning of the Lithuanian National Revival. It was smuggled into Lithuania, since Lithuanian publication was illegal in the Russian Empire. He soon lost editorial control to Jonas Šliūpas and could not return to Lithuania until 1905.

Back in Bulgaria he married Gabriela Eleonora Mohl in 1884, survived an assassination attempt in August 1887 that left a bullet lodged under his shoulder blade, and suffered illness that led him to resign his public post in 1893.

He returned to Vilnius in August 1905 and chaired the organising committee of the Great Seimas of Vilnius, held on 4 and 5 December 1905 with over 2,000 participants. It demanded autonomy for Lithuania and called for passive resistance to the Tsarist government. In 1907 he founded the Lithuanian Scientific Society and became its president. In 1917 the Vilnius Conference elected him to the Council of Lithuania. He chaired the session that adopted the Act of Independence on 16 February 1918 and was the first to sign it.

Basanavičius collected and published Lithuanian songs, fairy-tales, legends and riddles. As president of the Lithuanian Scientific Society he edited its journal Lietuvių tauta. In 1913 he and Martynas Yčas visited 84 Lithuanian communities in the United States in 120 days and raised $23,799 for a National House; the money was lost in a Russian bank during World War I. He held that Lithuanians descended from Thracians and Phrygians and were closely related to the Bulgarians, a thesis other scholars have not accepted.
jonesborough-tennessee: Jonesborough is the county seat of Washington County in the far north-eastern corner of Tennessee, and part of the Johnson City metropolitan area, within the Tri-Cities region. It lies where the watershed of the Watauga River meets that of the Nolichucky River, among the low hills and elongated ridges of the Appalachian Ridge-and-Valley Province. The main crest of the Appalachians rises a few miles to the south-east. It was named after the North Carolina legislator Willie Jones, who had supported the state's westward expansion across the Appalachian Mountains, and for a time it was spelled Jonesboro.

Settlers of European origin founded the town in 1779, seventeen years before Tennessee became a state, while the area was under North Carolina. It was first part of the Washington District. In 1784 it became the capital of the autonomous State of Franklin, named after Benjamin Franklin. Congress never recognised Franklin, and North Carolina reclaimed it in late 1788. In 1788 the future president Andrew Jackson spent several months practising law in Jonesborough, lodging in a cabin of Major Christopher Taylor.

The town was a centre of abolitionism. The Tennessee Manumission Society was founded in 1815, and in 1819 Elihu Embree of Jonesborough began the Manumission Intelligencier, renamed The Emancipator the next year, the first American periodical devoted only to the abolition of slavery. In the 1840s William G.

Brownlow published the Jonesborough Whig here, and in May 1840 he brawled in the street with the rival editor Landon Carter Haynes. In the summer of 1873 cholera reached the town. Of about 75 people who remained, 30 died by early August and 30 more fell ill but survived. The victims included the publisher George E. Gresham, who had cared for the sick.

Jonesborough styles itself Tennessee's oldest town, and its 2020 census population was 5,860. Its historic district was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1969. The Chester Inn, built in 1797, still stands downtown, and the Christopher Taylor House, built in 1777, was moved into the district and rebuilt there in 1974. The International Storytelling Center holds the National Storytelling Festival on the first full weekend in October, drawing on Appalachian traditions of storytelling.
jonestown: Jonestown, formally the Peoples Temple Agricultural Project, was a remote commune in Guyana established by the Peoples Temple, an American religious organisation led by Jim Jones. Jones formed the Temple in Indianapolis, Indiana, in 1955, and it moved to Redwood Valley, California, in 1965 after criticism of his integrationist views. In the early 1970s it opened branches in Los Angeles and San Francisco and made San Francisco its headquarters.

In the autumn of 1973, after critical newspaper articles and the defection of eight members, Jones and a Temple attorney prepared a plan for a crackdown. In October 1973 the Temple's directors resolved to establish an agricultural mission in Guyana. In the summer of 1977, under pressure from San Francisco media investigations, Jones and several hundred members moved to Jonestown. Its population was slightly under 900 at its peak in 1978. About 70 per cent of the residents were African American. Life there changed after Jones arrived, with lessons and lectures turned to his talk of revolution and enemies.

Leo Ryan, a US congressman from California, flew to Georgetown on 14 November 1978 with a delegation that included journalists, and reached Jonestown on 17 November. When the party left for the airstrip at Port Kaituma on 18 November with some defectors, Temple members murdered Ryan and four others, an act Jones had ordered.

At Jonestown itself 909 people died that day, all but two from apparent cyanide poisoning. Seventy or more were injected with poison, a third of the victims were minors, and armed guards had been ordered to shoot anyone who tried to flee. Jones and some members called the act revolutionary suicide, in a recording of the event and in earlier discussions. In Georgetown four Temple members died in a murder-suicide at the Temple's headquarters, making 918 deaths in all.

Terms for the deaths have changed. Many reports at the time called them a mass suicide, while later sources speak of a mass murder-suicide, a massacre or mass murder. After the deaths the Guyanese government tended the deserted compound and for a few years in the early 1980s let Hmong refugees from Laos live there. Local people looted the buildings, which were mostly destroyed by a fire in the mid-1980s, and the ruins were left to be reclaimed by the jungle.
jordanes: Jordanes, also written Jordanis or Jornandes, was an Eastern Roman bureaucrat of Gothic descent who became a historian later in life. His paternal grandfather Paria was secretary to Candac, a leader of the Alans who held Scythia Minor and Lower Moesia, a small client state on the Roman frontier. Jordanes himself served as notarius, or secretary, to Candac's nephew Gunthigis, also called Baza, a master of the soldiery of the Amali, the leading Gothic clan. He calls himself an unlearned man before his conversion. The nature of that conversion is obscure: it may have been from Arianism to the Nicene Creed, or it may mean that he became a monk or clergyman.

Jordanes wrote two works. The Romana is a history of Rome, written at the request of a certain Vigilius. The Getica, written in Constantinople about 551, interrupted the Romana at the request of a brother Castalius, who knew that Jordanes held the twelve volumes of the History of the Goths by Cassiodorus. Jordanes wrote an excerpt largely from memory, with his own knowledge and perhaps other material, and says he had only three days to review the work. He wrote in Late Latin rather than classical Latin.

The Getica opens with a geography of the north, especially Scandza, and begins the history of the Goths with the emigration of Berig in three ships from Scandza to Gothiscandza. The less fictional part begins when the Goths met Roman forces in the third century CE, and the work ends with their defeat by the Byzantine general Belisarius. With Isidore of Seville's Historia Gothorum, it is one of only two surviving ancient works on the early history of the Goths. Jordanes wrongly equated the Getae with the Goths, so that records concerning Dacians and Getae were attributed to Goths, and some scholars argue that he added fictional events, such as a Gothic war against Egypt.
jorge-amado: Jorge Leal Amado de Faria was born on 10 August 1912 on a farm in the village of Ferradas near Itabuna in the south of Bahia, the eldest of four sons. The village was then administered by the coastal city of Ilhéus, and he considered himself a citizen of Ilhéus. After a smallpox epidemic the family moved there when he was one year old. He attended high school in Salvador and by the age of 14 was writing for magazines and had helped found the modernist Rebels' Academy. His boyhood among the large cocoa plantations showed him the misery of workers living in almost enslaved conditions, a theme of several works, including The Violent Land.

Amado published his first novel, The Country of Carnival, in 1931, aged 18, and his second, Cacau, in 1933. His leftist activities made his life difficult under the regime of Getúlio Vargas: he was arrested for the first time in 1935, and two years later his books were publicly burned. Jubiabá won him a wide readership in France and was praised by Albert Camus. As a Communist militant he went into exile in Argentina and Uruguay in 1941 to 1942. He was later elected to the National Constituent Assembly for the Brazilian Communist Party with more votes than any other candidate in São Paulo.

After the party was declared illegal in 1947 he went into exile again, in France until he was expelled in 1950, and then lived in Czechoslovakia from 1950 to 1952. He won the Stalin Peace Prize in 1951. Back in Brazil in 1954 he left active politics and the party a year later, and gave himself wholly to literature. His second phase began in 1958 with Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon, which Jean-Paul Sartre called the best example of a folk novel. It turned in part from social realism to women characters and a smiling celebration of the traditions of Bahia. Its frank treatment of sexual customs scandalised Brazil, and for some years threats kept him out of Ilhéus.

Amado was elected to the Brazilian Academy of Letters on 6 April 1961 and held its 23rd chair until his death. He received the French Légion d'Honneur in 1984. His books have been translated into 49 languages, adapted for film, theatre and television, and he was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature at least seven times, from 1967 to 1973. He died in Salvador on 6 August 2001, four days before his 89th birthday.

The Fundação Casa de Jorge Amado, created in Salvador in 1987, protects his estate. The Casa do Rio Vermelho, the house where he lived with the writer Zélia Gattai, opened as a memorial in 2014, and the ashes of both are in its garden.
jorge-b-vargas: Jorge Bartolomé Vargas y Celis was born on 24 August 1890 in Bago, Negros Occidental. He graduated as valedictorian of Negros Occidental High School in 1909 and earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1911 and a Bachelor of Law degree with honours in 1914, both from the University of the Philippines. Admitted to the Philippine Bar in 1914, he became a law clerk for the Philippine Commission in 1915 and chief clerk of the Department of the Interior in 1917.

In 1918 Vargas was legislative secretary to Speaker Sergio Osmeña of the House of Representatives. In 1921 he succeeded Vicente Morente as director-general of the Philippine Carnival Association, which ran the Manila Carnival, and was followed by Arsenio Luz the next year. In 1936 President Manuel L. Quezon appointed him executive secretary, the first in the country to hold the post.

When Japan invaded in 1941, Vargas was first named secretary of the Department of National Defense and a few weeks later mayor of the City of Greater Manila, which he administered as an open city when the Imperial Japanese Army arrived on 2 January 1942. As chairman of the Japanese-sponsored Philippine Executive Commission he was once asked by the Japanese to take the presidency of the collaborationist Second Philippine Republic, but declined and served as its ambassador to Japan.

Shortly before Japanese troops were driven from Manila he was quoted as saying that Japan was destined for sure victory and prosperity for ages to come. After the war he chaired the National Planning Commission from 1946 to 1954 and sat on the Board of Regents of the University of the Philippines from 1961 to 1965.

A founding member in 1911 of the Philippine Amateur Athletic Federation, now the Philippine Olympic Committee, Vargas was its second chairman from 1935 to 1955 and the first Filipino member of the International Olympic Committee, where in 1960 he proposed the name Chinese Taipei for the Republic of China's committee.

He was a charter member of the Boy Scouts of the Philippines in 1936, its president from 1949 to 1961 and a member of the World Scout Committee from 1951 to 1957, and he received the Bronze Wolf in 1959. He died in Manila on 22 February 1980 at the age of 89.
jorge-eliecer-gaitan: Jorge Eliécer Gaitán Ayala was born in the Las Cruces neighbourhood of Bogotá to parents who were rank-and-file Liberals with a tenuous hold on the middle class. His father taught history, sold second-hand books and worked as a journalist, and his mother, Manuela Ayala de Gaitán, had liberal and feminist leanings. Against his father's wishes he entered the National University in Bogotá, where in May 1920 he and fellow students founded the University Center of Cultural Propaganda, which brought education to workers, rural people and prisoners.

Gaitán became widely known after a banana workers' strike in Magdalena in 1928, when the army fired on strikers on the orders of the United Fruit Company. As a lawyer he defended workers' rights and demanded accountability for the Santa Marta Massacre. In 1933 he founded the National Leftist Revolutionary Union after breaking with the Liberal Party, which he rejoined in 1935. He was mayor of Bogotá for eight months from June 1936, then Education Minister and Labor Minister. His oratory, often called populist, divided the country into an oligarchy and the people.

The Liberals lost the May 1946 election after splitting their vote between Gaitán, with 358,957 votes, and Gabriel Turbay, with 441,199, which let the Conservative Mariano Ospina Pérez win. In 1947 Gaitán became leader of the Liberal Party. His programme proposed protection of national industry, progressive taxes, land redistribution and reform of the Central Bank.

Gaitán was assassinated on 9 April 1948, during a presidential campaign he was widely expected to win. His alleged killer, Juan Roa Sierra, was killed by an enraged mob, and his motives were never established. Many people and groups have been accused of plotting the murder, among them the Ospina Pérez government, parts of the Liberal Party, the Soviet Union, the Colombian Communist Party and the CIA, but no firm evidence has appeared. The killing set off the riots of the Bogotazo and then La Violencia, the violence between Liberals and Conservatives from 1948 to 1958.
Because of the disorder Gaitán could not have a proper funeral, and his family buried him in his house, now the Jorge Eliécer Gaitán House Museum. His ideas became known as Gaitanismo.
jorge-icaza: Jorge Icaza Coronel was born in Quito on 10 July 1906. He began his literary career as a playwright, with El Intruso in 1928, La Comedia sin Nombre in 1929, Cuál es in 1931 and Sin Sentido in 1932; Flagelo was published in 1936. After his play El Dictador of 1933 was censured, he turned to novels about social conditions in Ecuador, above all the oppression of its indigenous people.

Huasipungo brought him international fame. Fragments of it first appeared in English translation in Russia, where it was received with enthusiasm, and Icaza was later appointed Ecuador's ambassador to Russia. His books brought him invitations to many colleges in the United States to lecture on the problems of Ecuador's indigenous people. He died of cancer in Quito on 26 May 1978.

Huasipungo became a well-known work of indigenismo, a movement in Latin American literature that aimed at realism in depicting the mistreatment of indigenous people. It has also been read as a proletarian novel, with the Indians taking the place that the European working class held in proletarian literature, and it is often compared with John Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath of 1939 as a work of social protest. Icaza rewrote it more than once, in 1953 and 1960; the first version was hard to read even for natives of other Hispanic countries, and the last is the definitive one.

The first complete English edition, translated by Mervyn Savill, appeared in England in 1962, and an authorised translation by Bernard H. Dulsey was published in 1964 as The Villagers. His other books include Sierra (1933), En las calles (1936), Cholos (1938), Media vida deslumbrados (1942), Huayrapamushcas (1948), El chulla Romero y Flores (1958) and Atrapados (1973). Critics such as Theodore Alan Sackett regard the last two as his finest achievements, but Huasipungo remains his most popular book and has been translated into over 40 languages.
jorge-luis-borges: Borges was born on 24 August 1899 into an educated middle-class family in Palermo, then a poor area of Buenos Aires. His mother, Leonor Acevedo Suárez, worked as a translator and came from a family of criollo origin that had been much involved in the Argentine War of Independence. In 1914 the family moved to Switzerland, where he studied at the Collège de Genève, and travelled widely in Europe, including Spain. When they returned to Buenos Aires in 1921 he had little formal education and few friends, and he brought with him the doctrine of Ultraism. He began publishing poems and essays in literary journals and worked as a librarian and public lecturer.

Borges's father died in 1938. On Christmas Eve that year Borges suffered a severe head injury and nearly died of sepsis. While recovering he began exploring the new style for which he became known. His first story after the accident, Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote, appeared in May 1939, and his first collection of stories, The Garden of Forking Paths, followed in 1941, composed mostly of works already published in Sur.

Under Juan Perón, he was told he was being promoted from his post at the Miguel Cané Library to inspector of poultry and rabbits at a municipal market; asked why, he was told that he had been on the side of the Allies. He resigned the next day, and the Argentine Society of Writers held a dinner in his honour. In 1955 he was appointed director of the National Public Library and professor of English literature at the University of Buenos Aires. He was completely blind by the age of 55. In 1961 he shared the first International Formentor Prize with Samuel Beckett, and by the 1960s his work was widely translated. He was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

His best-known collections, Ficciones and El Aleph, appeared in the 1940s and explore dreams, labyrinths, chance, infinity, archives, mirrors, fictional writers and mythology. He never wrote a novel; he preferred the short story, finding that a novel required padding. He was also a notable translator from English, French, German, Old English and Old Norse, beginning at ten with a Spanish version of Oscar Wilde's The Happy Prince. He held that a translation may improve upon the original, and that different, even contradictory, renderings can be equally valid. He also practised literary forgery and the review of an imaginary work, a form he drew from Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus.
jorge-rafael-videla: Jorge Rafael Videla was born on 2 August 1925 in Mercedes, the third of five sons of Colonel Rafael Eugenio Videla Bengolea. His family was prominent in San Luis Province, where his grandfather Jacinto had been governor from 1891 to 1893. He entered the National Military College on 3 March 1942 and graduated in December 1944 as a second lieutenant. He became a brigadier general in 1971. In August 1975 President Isabel Perón appointed him General Commander of the Army.

After Juan Perón's death his widow Isabel became president amid violence, unrest and economic problems. Videla headed the military coup that deposed her on 24 March 1976. A junta took power, with Admiral Emilio Massera for the Navy and Brigadier General Orlando Ramón Agosti for the Air Force, and two days later Videla assumed the presidency. The junta called its rule the National Reorganization Process. It came to power during attacks by left-wing groups such as the ERP and the Montoneros and by right-wing death squads, and 293 servicemen and police were killed in left-wing attacks in 1975 and 1976.

The repression targeted guerrillas but also the church, unions, artists, intellectuals and students. According to human rights groups, thousands of Argentines disappeared in custody, with estimates as high as 30,000, many held in clandestine detention camps, and between 1,500 and 4,000 were thrown alive from aircraft into the sea. Children born to women prisoners were taken and given to military families, with their identities hidden. On the economy Videla left policy to José Alfredo Martínez de Hoz, who freed prices, exports and imports. Pope John Paul II opened mediation in 1978 in the Beagle conflict over islands at the southern tip of South America. Videla handed power to Roberto Viola on 29 March 1981.

Democracy returned in 1983, and in the Trial of the Juntas Videla was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment in 1985. President Carlos Menem pardoned him in 1990. He was jailed again in 1998 for the kidnapping of children, and in 2007 a federal court struck down his pardon. In December 2010 he was sentenced to life in prison for the deaths of 31 prisoners and in July 2012 to 50 years for the theft of babies, which the court said involved an estimated 400 to 500 children. He described himself as a political prisoner. He died on 17 May 2013 in a prison at Marcos Paz, an autopsy finding that he had slipped in a shower five days earlier.

The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo began their demonstrations on 30 April 1977, asking where their disappeared children were. In 1980 Adolfo Pérez Esquivel received the Nobel Peace Prize for reporting the abuses to the world.
jorge-tadeo-lozano: Jorge Tadeo Lozano de Peralta was born in Santafé de Bogotá on 30 January 1771, a son of the Marquis of San Jorge, Jorge Miguel Lozano de Peralta, and María González Manrique, of one of the wealthiest families of the Viceroyalty of New Granada. He studied literature, philosophy and medicine at the Colegio Mayor del Rosario, then joined the Walloon Guards in Spain, fought against the French in the War of the Pyrenees and rose to captain. In Madrid he studied chemistry and mathematics at the Royal Laboratory of Chemistry in 1792 and 1793 before travelling in Europe.

Back in New Granada in 1797, he joined the tertulias of Bogotá, among them the Casino led by Antonio Nariño. That year, after paying for a church dispensation, he married his niece, María Tadea Lozano e Isasi; they had eight children.

In 1801 he and his relative José Luis Azuola y Lozano founded the weekly Correo curioso, erudito, económico y mercantil, the third newspaper of the viceroyalty, which ran to 46 issues; his own articles urged an economic alliance to promote the colony's economy. He was briefly mayor of Bogotá in 1799 and from 31 July 1807 Lieutenant Protector of the Indians for Bosa, Fusagasugá and Usaquén.

After the independence movement began he represented Soto in the constituent assembly and was elected president of its electoral college, which drafted Cundinamarca's first constitution. He took office as president on 1 April 1811 and used the style Jorge I of Cundinamarca. Criticised as weak, for his family's scandals, his ties to Spain and his noble title, and attacked by Nariño in the newspaper La Bagatela, he resigned on 19 September 1811.

In 1814 he founded the patriotic newspaper El anteojo de larga vista with José Ángel Manrique, which ran to 15 issues. During the reconquest, Pablo Morillo's purge of independence supporters made him a target as a former president, member of Congress and journalist. His property was seized, and after two months in custody he was shot on 6 July 1816 in the Orchard of Jaime, now the Plaza de los Mártires in Bogotá. He is regarded as a martyr and hero of Colombian independence, and the Jorge Tadeo Lozano University bears his name.
jorge-ubico: Jorge Ubico Castañeda was born on 10 November 1878, the son of Arturo Ubico Urruela, a lawyer and politician of the Liberal Party. He was tutored privately and educated in Guatemala, the United States and Europe, and in 1897 he was commissioned a second lieutenant, largely through political connections. He was a colonel at 28 and later governor of Alta Verapaz and Retalhuleu. In 1918 he fought a yellow fever epidemic by draining swamps, fumigating and distributing free medicine, and his punishment of banditry and smuggling was harsh but effective. In 1926 he ran unsuccessfully for president.

Ubico was elected in February 1931 with 305,841 votes, as the only candidate on the ballot, and soon assumed dictatorial powers. He allowed the United Fruit Company to become the most important company in Guatemala, with tax exemptions and control of the only railway and the port at Puerto Barrios. In 1934 the Reglamento de Jornaleros was replaced by a Vagrancy Law under which indigenous day labourers who could not show 100 to 150 days of work on estates were put to unpaid road building. His Probity Law required officials to declare their assets, and he was praised even by detractors for virtually eliminating corruption.

Opponents were repressed. In September 1934 five men were tortured and executed in the Guatemala National Penitenciary, accused of a plot against him, and the writer Efraín De los Ríos alleged that the plot was invented. After the death of the teacher María Chinchilla Recinos at a peaceful demonstration on 25 June 1944, a general strike and nationwide protests forced Ubico to resign on 1 July. A triumvirate and then General Federico Ponce Vaides followed, until the October Revolution of 1944 drove Ponce out.

Ubico went into exile in New Orleans, where he lived on the $200,000 he had transferred to a personal account. He died of lung cancer on 14 June 1946, aged 67, and was buried there. His remains were repatriated to Guatemala on 13 August 1963. Critics have described him as one of the most oppressive rulers Guatemala has had, while the middle class grew under his rule and later led the democratic revolution that removed him.
jorhat: Jorhat lies in Upper Assam, between the Brahmaputra River to the north and the state of Nagaland to the south, at an average elevation of about 116 metres above sea level. It stands on the banks of the Bhogdoi River and has a humid subtropical climate. The name comes from the Assamese words jor, meaning twin, and hat, meaning market. It refers to two historic markets, Macharhat and Chowkihat, which stood on opposite banks of the Bhogdoi.

In 1794 the Ahom king Gaurinath Singha made Jorhat the fifth and last capital of the Ahom Kingdom, after Moamaria rebels had occupied Rangpur. The city keeps monuments of the late Ahom period, among them the Rajamaidam, the maidams of Lachit Borphukan and Captain Gohain, the Rajmao Pukhuri tank and the Burhi Goshani Dewalaya temple. The Burmese Konbaung dynasty later occupied Assam. Its commander Mingimaha Tilwa installed Jogeswar Singha as a puppet king at Jorhat, and a Burmese army under Mingimaha Bandula defeated the deposed king Chandrakanta Singha at Mahgarh, near Jorhat.

Under British rule a narrow-gauge line, the Jorehaut Provincial Railway, opened in 1885 and helped the tea industry of the region to grow quickly. The Jorhat Municipal Board was founded in 1909. Jorhat Theatre was established in 1896 and the Chandrakanta Handique Bhawan, the headquarters of the Asam Sahitya Sabha, in 1926. In 1935 the first Assamese daily newspaper, Dainik Batori, was published in the city by Raibahadur Siva Prasad Barooah. The writer Birendra Kumar Bhattacharya, the first Assamese to win the Jnanpith Award, came from Jorhat.

Jorhat is the headquarters of Jorhat District and the fourth largest city in Assam. The 2011 census gave the municipality 71,398 people, and Assamese is the main language. Its economy rests chiefly on tea cultivation, processing and trade, alongside rice milling, handloom work and trade. The city holds research bodies such as the Tocklai Tea Research Institute and universities including Assam Agricultural University. The Jorhat Gymkhana Club has the oldest golf course in Asia and has held its annual horse races since 1877.
jos-plateau: The Jos Plateau, formerly known as the Bauchi Plateau, lies near the centre of Nigeria and gives its name to Plateau State, whose capital is Jos. It covers 8600 km2 and is largely bounded by escarpments of 300 to 600 metres. With an average altitude of 1,280 metres, it is the largest area over 1,000 metres in Nigeria, and its high point is 1,776 metres in the Shere Hills.

Several rivers rise on the plateau. The Kaduna River drains the western slopes and joins the Niger, the Gongola flows east to the Benue, and the Hadejia and Yobe rivers flow northeast into Lake Chad. The rocks are of three kinds: older granites from the late Cambrian and Ordovician, younger granites from the Jurassic that form part of a series including the Aïr Massif in the central Sahara, and basalt sheets and volcanoes extruded since the Pliocene. The younger granites contain tin.

The plateau lies in the Nigerian Middle Belt, a region known for cultural diversity, and it is unusually diverse even there. A survey of 1982 showed over 60 ethno-linguistic groups on the plateau, most speaking Chadic languages, part of the Afro-Asiatic family. Two of the largest groups are the Berom in the northern plateau and the Ngas in the southeast. The plateau is also home to the ancient Nok culture, known for its terracotta art.

At the start of the 20th century the British established Jos as a tin-mining centre. People from southern and northern Nigeria came for work and business because of the tin industry. Tin has been mined from the younger granites since the beginning of the 20th century, during and after the colonial period, and the mining disturbed some 320 km2 of agricultural land. Tourism, once important, was impeded in the early 21st century by conflict between Christians and Muslims, arising from tribal and political differences among the inhabitants.

The plateau's climate is tropical but cooler than the surrounding lowlands, with rain falling mostly between June and September. Its montane grasslands, savannas and forests make up the Jos Plateau forest-savanna mosaic ecoregion. Most of the plateau is now open grassland, since human activity has reduced the tree cover. It is home to West Africa's only population of klipspringer and to several endemic species, including the Nigerian mole-rat and the Jos Plateau indigobird.
joscelin-i-count-of-edessa: Joscelin came from the Gâtinais, the second son of Joscelin I of Courtenay and Elizabeth, daughter of Guy I of Montlhéry. Nothing is known of his early years; the historian Robert Nicholson suggests that he reached military age by 1101, which would place his birth around 1080. He went east with the Crusade of 1101 in the army of Stephen of Blois. The crusade ended in disaster at the Battle of Mersivan, where as many as four-fifths of the crusaders may have become casualties, and Joscelin reached the Levant with no patrimony and few resources.

In the Levant he entered the service of his cousin Baldwin of Bourcq, count of Edessa, who gave him the lordship of Turbessel, which included Cyrrhus, Duluk and Aintab. At the Battle of Harran on 7 May 1104 he and Baldwin were captured. Joscelin was ransomed for 20,000 dinars in 1107 and then worked to free Baldwin, offering himself as a hostage while Baldwin raised the rest of the ransom. By 1113 he had built a semi-autonomous state around Turbessel, but Baldwin, distrustful of him, imprisoned him and forced him to give it up.

Joscelin went to the Kingdom of Jerusalem, where King Baldwin I made him prince of Galilee. When Baldwin I died childless in 1118, Joscelin urged the nobles to elect Baldwin of Edessa, who became King Baldwin II, and was rewarded with the County of Edessa. On 18 September 1122 Belek Ghazi captured him at the Battle of Saruj, and Baldwin II, taken in April 1123, joined him at Kharput. Armenian soldiers hired by Queen Morphia freed them, and Joscelin then escaped from the besieged fortress, supposedly crossing the Euphrates on inflated wineskins, to seek help.

In 1131, during the siege of a small castle northeast of Aleppo, a sapper's mine collapsed and Joscelin was gravely injured. Hearing that the emir Gazi Gümüshtigin was besieging Kaysun, he had himself carried on a litter at the head of his army, and Gazi lifted the siege. He died soon after, in August 1131, and was succeeded by his son Joscelin II.

Matthew of Edessa called him a brave and mighty warrior, and William of Tyre credited him with temperance and prudence. Muslims seem to have seen him as an intermediary for the Franks. Nicholson calls his death a disaster for a state facing Imad al-Din Zengi. The County of Edessa was conquered by the Zengids in 1146.
joscelin-ii-of-edessa: Joscelin II was born around 1113 in the Principality of Galilee, where his father, Joscelin I, had gone after King Baldwin of Bourcq deprived him of his fief at Turbessel. His mother was Beatrice, daughter of the Armenian ruler Constantine. After the elder Joscelin helped Baldwin of Bourcq to the throne of Jerusalem, he received Edessa. Joscelin II was captured and exchanged in the wars that followed, and in 1131 his father was mortally wounded besieging a castle northeast of Aleppo, dying soon after the siege of Kaisun was lifted.

As count Joscelin first sided with Princess Alice of Antioch against King Fulk of Jerusalem. He and Fulk won the Battle of Qinnasrin in 1133 against Sawar, a lieutenant of Imad al-Din Zengi. When the Byzantine emperor John II Komnenos entered the northern Crusader states in 1137, Joscelin swore fealty, but he held back during the siege of Shaizar in 1138, and Raymond of Poitiers, prince of Antioch, became his overlord around 1140.

In 1143 Zengi renewed his war on Edessa. While Joscelin marched to aid his ally Kara Arslan, Zengi broke into Edessa on 24 December 1144 and into the citadel two days later, killing the Franks and sparing local Christians. Joscelin kept the half of the county west of the Euphrates. After Zengi was murdered on 14 September 1146, Joscelin entered the city on 27 October but could not take the citadel. Zengi's son Nur ad-Din routed him on 3 November, and the city was left desolate.

In 1150 Nur ad-Din's forces captured Joscelin as he travelled to take up a regency; he was blinded and imprisoned, and the county was divided among its neighbours. He died in captivity in May 1159, having refused conversion, and received his last sacraments from Ignace, the Jacobite Metropolitan of Aleppo. William of Tyre portrayed him as idle and dissolute, and many 20th-century historians followed that view. Malcolm Barber suggests William's dislike of Joscelin III coloured it, and Nicholas Morton holds that the county was not in decline before 1144.
jose-antonio-abreu: José Antonio Abreu Anselmi was born on 7 May 1939 in Valera, a small Andean city. He graduated summa cum laude as an economist from the Universidad Católica Andrés Bello in Caracas. For many years his official biography stated that he held a doctorate in petroleum economics from the University of Pennsylvania, but El Sistema withdrew that claim in December 2017. He was elected a deputy in the Chamber of Deputies of Venezuela in 1963 and served as director of planning at Cordiplan. He later taught economics and law at the Universidad Simón Bolívar and at his alma mater.

Abreu moved to Caracas in 1957 to study composition, and studied piano, organ, harpsichord and composition with several teachers there. In 1967 he received the Symphonic Music National Prize. In 1975 he founded El Sistema, formally the Foundation for the National Network of Youth and Children Orchestras of Venezuela, an educational method in which music was the main route to social and intellectual improvement. It brought him the National Music Prize in 1979. He founded the Simón Bolívar Symphony Orchestra and returned to politics in 1988 as Minister of Culture and president of the National Council of Culture, holding those posts until 1993 and 1994.
