Ordained in 1838, he was a vicar in Petrovaradin, studied in Vienna from 1840 and received a doctorate in philosophy and canon law in 1842. He was Habsburg palace chaplain from 1847 to 1859. On 18 November 1849 he was appointed Bishop of Đakovo, and he was consecrated on 8 September 1850. He supported repairing the schism between the Roman Catholic and Russian Orthodox churches and worked with the Russian ecumenist Vladimir Solovyov for reunion.

At the First Vatican Council of 1869 to 1870 he was one of the most notable opponents of papal infallibility, and Pius IX praised his Latin. A speech defending Protestantism caused a sensation, while another, allegedly delivered on 2 June 1870, was forged by José Agustín de Escudero. He later declared his submission to the pope.

In politics he supported the People's Party and advocated Pan-Slavism and Yugoslavism. He entered the Imperial Council in 1860, spoke against centralism and absolutism and supported federalising the Austrian Empire, and after his criticism the government made concessions on the official use of Croatian. In 1861 he joined the Croatian Sabor. In 1866 its majority, led by him, voted that Croatians should not join the Diet of Hungary, but the court ignored this and negotiated the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867. He opposed the Croatian–Hungarian Settlement of 1868, and left the Sabor in 1873.

He used his diocese's large revenues for educational and art institutions. He was instrumental in founding the Yugoslav Academy of Sciences and Arts in 1866 and re-establishing the University of Zagreb in 1874, initiated the Academy Palace, completed in 1880, and set up the Strossmayer Gallery of Old Masters in 1884. He built the cathedral at Đakovo. He aided the printing house at Cetinje and helped found the Matica slovenska, and supported Matica srpska.

Strossmayer died on 8 April 1905, having been bishop since 1849. His close friend Franjo Rački, the Academy's first president, died in 1894, and the two left four books of letters. Bishop Nikolaj Velimirović dedicated a booklet to him in 1915 as a great Croatian patriot. A genus of fungi, Strossmayeria, was named for him in 1881, and streets in Prague and Sarajevo bear his name.
josquin-des-prez: Little is known of Josquin's early years, and neither the year nor the place of his birth is known. He is now thought to have been born around 1450 and at the latest in 1455. Documents of 1483 found in Condé-sur-l'Escaut name him as Josquin Lebloitte dit des Prez. Nothing is known of his mother. Around 1466 his uncle and aunt named him their heir.

In 1484 he was in Milan and on 20 June entered the service of Cardinal Ascanio Sforza. He asked for a dispensation to be rector of the parish church of Saint Aubin without being ordained a priest. The motet Ave Maria... Virgo serena is dated to about 1485.

In August 1494 Josquin was in Cambrai, and he was ordained a priest at some point. In 1503 he arrived in Ferrara to serve Duke Ercole I d'Este. A courtier wrote that Josquin composed better than Heinrich Isaac but composed when he wished rather than when asked and demanded a salary of 200 ducats against Isaac's 120.

On 3 May 1504 he became provost of the collegiate church of Notre-Dame at Condé-sur-l'Escaut, where he directed a staff that included a dean, a treasurer, 25 canons, 18 chaplains, 16 vicars and 6 choirboys. In these years he composed some of his most admired works, among them the masses Missa de Beata Virgine and Missa Pange lingua, the motets Benedicta es and Inviolata and the chansons Mille regretz and Plus nulz regretz. Ottaviano Petrucci's publications spread his music across Europe, and his Misse Josquin of 1502 was the first anthology of masses by a single composer.

Josquin was a singer throughout his life, and his compositions are almost exclusively vocal: masses, motets and chansons in French. A line of musicologists credits him with moving away from long melismatic lines towards short motifs passed between voices and with an increasingly prominent imitative polyphony. His motets are his most admired works and were mostly for four voices, though he was also an innovator in five and six voices. Most of his masses are for four voices and fall into canonic, cantus firmus, paraphrase, parody and solmization types.

He died on 27 August 1521. Elders called him the first composer in the history of Western music not to have been forgotten after his death, and Martin Luther said that he was the master of the notes. After his death some publishers attributed works to him to meet demand, and a remark arose that he composed more when dead than alive.
jost-van-dyke: Jost Van Dyke is the smallest of the four main islands of the British Virgin Islands, measuring roughly 8 square kilometres. It lies about 8 kilometres north-west of Tortola and 8 kilometres north of Saint John in the US Virgin Islands, with Little Jost Van Dyke off its eastern end. Like many neighbouring islands it is volcanic in origin and mountainous, and its highest point is Majohnny Hill at 321 metres. The name may come from the seventeenth-century Dutch privateer Joost van Dyk, a former pirate said to have used its harbours as a hideout, though no factual evidence for this exists.

The English captured the British Virgin Islands in 1672, but Jost Van Dyke seems to have been mostly ignored until the mid-eighteenth century, and a map of 1717 does not show it. Sugar works above Great Harbour show that some cane was grown, and in 1815 140 acres were under cotton. The population then was 428, of whom 371 were enslaved, and by 1825 it had risen to 506. Emancipation came in 1838, and by 1853 there were 1,235 residents, 196 of whom died in a cholera outbreak that year. Afterwards people lived by small-scale fishing, farming and charcoal making, and many islanders worked at coaling wharves in St Thomas.

Hurricane Irma, a Category 5 storm, struck in September 2017, stripped the hillsides and destroyed most of the island's homes. The 298 residents set up a recovery and command centre at Foxy's Tamarind Bar and Restaurant, which held the island's only major surviving refrigerator and generators, and used a salvaged chainsaw to clear roads until the Royal Marines repaired others later that month.

Jost Van Dyke had a recorded population of 298 at the 2010 census, up from 140 in 1991. Tourism, especially yachting, is the mainstay of the economy. Great Harbour is one of the busiest ports in the territory, and in 2008 nearly 7,000 boats cleared through it. White Bay and the rock formation called the Bubbly Pool draw visitors, and ferries run from Tortola, Saint Thomas and Saint John. The architect William Thornton and the physician John C. Lettsome, founder of the Medical Society of London, are among the island's notable people.
jovan-nenad: Jovan Nenad, known in Hungarian as Fekete Iván, was born around 1492 in Lipova near the Mureș River in northern Banat. Little else about his origins is certain. He claimed descent from Serbian and Byzantine rulers, while some contemporaries thought him a descendant of the Serbian despots and others a man of low rank. He was called the Black Man because of a dark birthmark that ran in a stripe from his right temple down his body, which many took for a divine sign.

The death of King Louis at the Battle of Mohács on 29 August 1526 left Hungary contested between John Zápolya, Ferdinand of Habsburg and the Ottomans. Jovan Nenad appeared between the Tisza and the Danube at the head of a Serb regiment, drove the Ottomans from Bačka and parts of Banat and Syrmia, and ruled them himself. Hungarian nobles of Bačka who were refused the return of their estates turned against him, and his forces pillaged Hungarian estates and villages and terrorised their people, so that peasants as well as nobles became his enemies.

He made Radoslav Čelnik commander of his army and kept a guard of 600 soldiers at his court in Subotica. Drawing in Serbs from Ottoman lands, Vlachs from Banat and Transylvania and some Roman Catholics, his army numbered around 15,000 men by the beginning of 1527. He saw the struggle for the Hungarian throne as a passing matter, his main aim being to free the Serb lands from the Ottomans. In early April 1527 he defeated 300 knights sent by Zápolya under László Csáky, whom he executed, and later that month he beat an army under Péter Perényi, the Voivode of Transylvania, at the Battle of Szőlős.

A larger army led by Perényi and Bishop Czibak defeated him decisively at the Battle of Sződfalva, killing around 8,000 of his men. Trying to join Ferdinand's forces, he was badly wounded at Szeged and murdered at Tornjoš on his retreat towards Senta; his head was sent to Zápolya. Radoslav Čelnik led what remained of the army into Ottoman Syrmia. Jovan Nenad became a figure of legend among the Serbs, and many Serbian historians regard him as the founder of Vojvodina. Subotica raised a monument to him.
jovan-vladimir: Duklja was an early medieval Serbian principality whose borders coincided for the most part with those of present-day Montenegro. It rose in power after the early medieval Principality of Serbia disintegrated following the death of Prince Časlav around 943, and neighbouring Serbian principalities such as Travunia and Zachlumia came under its dominance. Around 1000 Vladimir, still a boy, succeeded his father Petrislav as ruler. A local tradition places his court at Kraljič, near Lake Skadar, close to the Prečista Krajinska Church.

His reign coincided with a protracted war between the Byzantine Emperor Basil II and Tsar Samuel of the First Bulgarian Empire. Both the Chronicle of the Priest of Duklja and the Byzantine historian John Skylitzes described Vladimir as a wise, pious, just and peaceful ruler.

Vladimir had a close relationship with Byzantium, but this did not save Duklja from Samuel, who conquered the principality around 1010 and took Vladimir prisoner. The chronicle asserts that Samuel's daughter, Theodora Kosara, fell in love with Vladimir and begged her father for his hand. The tsar allowed the marriage and returned Duklja to Vladimir, who ruled as his vassal and took no part in his father-in-law's wars.

Samuel was defeated by the Byzantines in 1014 and died soon after. In 1016 Vladimir fell victim to a plot by Ivan Vladislav, the last ruler of the First Bulgarian Empire. He was beheaded in front of a church in Prespa, the empire's capital, on 22 May, and was buried there.

Vladimir's relics were reported to heal the sick, and he was soon recognised as a martyr and saint, commemorated on 22 May. He was the first ruler of a Serbian state to be elevated to sainthood. Kosara later moved his remains to the Prečista Krajinska Church in Duklja, where she was also buried. In 1381 the Albanian lord Karlo Thopia rebuilt a church near Elbasan and dedicated it to him. Since 1995 his relics have been kept in the Orthodox cathedral of Tirana, and on his feast day they are taken to the church near Elbasan.

A cross he is said to have held at his death is kept by the Andrović family of Velji Mikulići and carried to the summit of Mount Rumija each Pentecost. His oldest hagiography is Chapter 36 of the Chronicle of the Priest of Duklja, which summarises a lost life written between 1075 and 1089. In the 18th century the friar Andrija Kačić Miošić composed the Poem of King Vladimir from it. Icons show him as a monarch holding a cross and his own head.
jovenel-moise: Jovenel Moïse was born on 26 June 1968 in Trou du Nord, in the Nord-Est department. His father, Étienne Moïse, was a farmer and mechanic and his mother, Lucia Bruno, a seamstress. The family moved to Port-au-Prince in July 1974, where he went to school and later studied political science at Quisqueya University, concentrating on local governance and rural development. In 1996 he married Martine Marie Étienne Joseph, a classmate, and they settled in Port-de-Paix; they had three children. Back in rural Nord-Est he argued that Haiti should address endemic poverty in part through an agrarian economy.

In the mid-1990s Moïse founded JoMar Auto Parts, which sold automobile components, and the next year began an organic banana plantation of more than 10 hectares in the Nord-Ouest department. In 2012 he founded Agritrans SA to run the Nourribo Project, a 1,000-hectare banana plantation in the Nord-Est presented as Haiti's first agricultural free-trade zone. It aimed to export bananas to Germany, but only two containers were shipped.

In 2015 President Michel Martelly named Moïse candidate of his centre-right Haitian Tèt Kale Party. In the first round on 25 October 2015 he officially received 32.8 percent of the votes, ahead of Jude Célestin, who called the results fraudulent. Protests forced the postponement of the runoff, and the ballot was annulled in June 2016. After a new election on 20 November 2016 Moïse was declared the winner in the first round with 55.67 percent of the vote on an estimated turnout of 21 percent, and he was sworn in on 7 February 2017.

Opponents held that his five-year term should have ended five years after Martelly's term ended, while Moïse maintained that it began with his inauguration in 2017. His policies concentrated on agricultural and water infrastructure. He also built roads, rebuilt the airport at Jérémie and had power plants and asphalt plants built in several provinces. Allegations of corruption, and a falling quality of life, led to mass demonstrations demanding his resignation.

On 7 July 2021, 11 days after his 53rd birthday, Moïse was shot dead when gunmen attacked his residence in Pèlerin 5, a district of Pétion-Ville. His wife Martine was wounded and flown to Miami for treatment.
joya-de-ceren: Joya de Cerén, Spanish for Jewel of Cerén, lies in the Zapotitán Valley. Its preservation beneath volcanic ash has earned it a comparison with Pompeii. The structures are grouped in northeastern, southeastern and northwestern areas. The houses had relatively earthquake-resistant wattle-and-daub walls and adobe columns, and the surrounding plots held milpas, a kitchen garden and fruit trees. Guava, agave, cacao and manioc were among the community's major crops.

The village produced agave fibres, manos, metates and pottery, and obtained obsidian and chert cutting tools, jade from the Sierra de las Minas to the north, and fine pottery from Copán. Households exchanged surplus goods with one another and with nearby places. Each household stored about 70 vessels for cooking and for serving food and drink.

Structures 10 and 12 are interpreted as ceremonial. Structure 10, a multi-roomed building, is thought to have served community festivals; a red-painted deer and twine headdress found there is connected by archaeologists with fertility and harvest rituals, and vessels of achiote seeds beside ceremonial objects suggest that the eruption interrupted a ceremony. Structure 12, whose niche held ceramic figurines, shell fragments, beans and antlers, may have been a diviner's place for divination. Household 1 appears to have supplied masa for ceremonies in the two buildings.

The Loma Caldera erupted around 600 CE and laid 10 metres of pyroclastic debris over the site, a layer 4 to 8 metres thick blanketing the village in a few hours. Cracks in the walls suggest an earthquake of about 4.0 before the eruption, giving people time to flee. Shovels and farm tools stood near the houses, fires were lit in hearths and sleeping mats were not yet unrolled, which suggests an evacuation in the early evening. Plaster casts of plants and stored beans and mature maize point to August or September. No human remains have been found.

A bulldozer driver levelling ground for a government agricultural project found the site in 1976. Payson Sheets of the University of Colorado at Boulder explored it in depth in 1978 and 1980, and excavation resumed in 1988 and has been continuous since. The buildings uncovered include storehouses, kitchens, living quarters, workshops, a religious structure and a communal sauna. UNESCO inscribed Joya de Cerén on the World Heritage List in 1993, and it is a major tourist attraction in El Salvador.
jozef-pilsudski: Józef Klemens Piłsudski was born on 5 December 1867 into a family of nobility at Zułow, near the village of Zułowo in present-day Lithuania, then under Russian rule. He knew Lithuanian as well as Polish. The family was impoverished but cherished Polish patriotic traditions. Held at Irkutsk while being taken to Siberia, he was beaten with other political prisoners after a protest, and the cold of his first night in prison nearly killed him. In 1893 he joined the Polish Socialist Party, and in 1894 he became chief editor of its underground newspaper Robotnik. He remained a Polish nationalist and held that socialism and nationalism should be combined to win independence.

In the early 1900s almost all parties in Russian Poland sought autonomy within the empire, while Piłsudski's party was prepared to fight for independence. In 1906, with the connivance of the Austrian authorities, he founded a military school in Kraków for paramilitary units. On 3 August 1914 he formed the First Cadre Company in Kraków, and his Legions fought alongside Austria-Hungary against Russia. In 1917 he withdrew support for the Central Powers, and the Germans imprisoned him at Magdeburg.

On 11 November 1918 the Regency Council appointed him Commander-in-Chief, and that day he proclaimed an independent Polish state. As Chief of State until 1922 he faced a country with nine legal systems, five currencies and 66 types of rail system. From 1919 to 1921 he commanded forces in six wars over the borders. In August 1920 his plan, a counteroffensive led by a Reserve Army of about 20,000 men, repelled the Soviet advance at the Battle of Warsaw. On 14 December 1922 he handed his powers to President Gabriel Narutowicz.

After retiring in 1923, Piłsudski returned to power in the May Coup of 1926. The Sejm elected him president, but he refused the office and became Minister of Military Affairs, which he held until his death. His Sanation government sought to reduce the influence of parties and strengthen the army, and constitutional amendments of 2 August 1926 curtailed the Sejm. Its methods were at times authoritarian, and the imprisonment of opponents at Bereza Kartuska remains controversial. He died of liver cancer on 12 May 1935 at the Belweder Palace in Warsaw. He is widely regarded as a founder of modern Poland and a father of the Second Polish Republic.
jozef-poniatowski: Prince Józef Antoni Poniatowski was born in Vienna, the son of Andrzej Poniatowski, an Austrian field marshal and brother of the last king of Poland, Stanislaus II Augustus, and Countess Maria Theresia Kinsky. His father died when he was ten, and the king became his guardian. He began his military career in 1780 in the Imperial Army and distinguished himself in the Austro-Turkish War at the storming of Šabac in 1788, where he was seriously wounded. In October 1789, at his uncle's request, he moved to the Polish army as a major general.

Poniatowski supported the 3 May Constitution of 1791. In the Polish–Russian War of 1792 he commanded the army in Ukraine, badly outnumbered, and won the Battle of Zieleńce on 18 June, after which the king created the Virtuti Militari order. When the king acceded to the Targowica Confederation he resigned. In 1794 he fought in the Kościuszko Uprising and helped defend Warsaw. His estates were confiscated, and he later lived in private life in Warsaw.

In 1807, after the Duchy of Warsaw was created, he became its minister of war, and he was commander in chief from March 1809. At the Battle of Raszyn on 19 April 1809 his force fought an Austrian army twice its size to a standstill. He then advanced into Galicia, taking Lublin, Zamość and Lwów, and reached Kraków on 15 July. In 1812 he commanded V Corps of the Grande Armée in the invasion of Russia, and he was badly injured at Vyazma.

Poniatowski stayed loyal to Napoleon even when Tsar Alexander I offered him amnesty. On 16 October 1813, during the Battle of Leipzig, he was made a Marshal of the Empire and entrusted with covering the French retreat. He fell back on a bridge over the White Elster, which the French blew up before he reached it. Badly injured, and probably shot by allies by mistake, he drowned in the river. His remains were buried in 1817 in the cathedral on Wawel Hill in Kraków, beside Kościuszko and John III Sobieski. He became an inspiration for Polish freedom fighters, especially in the November Uprising of 1830.
jozsef-antall: József Antall was born in Budapest on 8 April 1932 into an old family of the lower nobility. His father, József Antall Sr., was a jurist and civil servant and a founding member of the Independent Smallholders' Party; his mother, Irén Szűcs, had Jewish roots. Antall studied Hungarian language and literature, history and archival science at Eötvös Loránd University and took degrees in teaching, library science and museology. He began teaching in 1955 and led his school's Revolutionary Committee during the 1956 Hungarian Uprising. After the Soviet Union crushed the revolution he was arrested and released several times, and in 1959 he was banned from teaching.

He worked as a librarian for two years and in 1963 wrote biographies of 80 doctors for the Lexicon of Hungarian Biographies. This led him to the history of medicine, and at the Semmelweis Museum of Medical History he rose from research fellow to deputy director and in 1974 to director of the institute.

The Hungarian Democratic Forum sent Antall to the National Roundtable Talks on 22 March 1989, and on 21 October 1989 he was elected its president. The party won the 1990 elections with 164 seats, just short of a majority, and on 23 May 1990 he became the first prime minister since 1948 who was neither a Communist nor a fellow traveller. He headed a centre-right coalition with the Independent Smallholders and the Christian Democratic People's Party, the first in 44 years without Communists, and made a pact with the liberal Alliance of Free Democrats.

His government set up a legal system to promote a market economy and attract foreign investment, and carried out privatization. Unemployment rose from nonexistence to 14 percent and inflation ran at 23 to 35 percent a year. Antall took part in the dissolution of the Warsaw Pact and the end of Comecon, and in the withdrawal of Russian forces in 1991. He faced a taxi drivers' blockade in 1990, conflict over powers with President Árpád Göncz, and in February 1992 the withdrawal of the Smallholders from the coalition, which forced him to restructure his cabinet.

Antall was diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in the summer of 1990, and the cancer recurred half a year later. He died on 12 December 1993, before the end of his four-year term. Interior Minister Péter Boross, who had substituted for him in his last period, succeeded him and led the cabinet until the 1994 election, in which the Democratic Forum was defeated by the Socialist Party. Antall was buried on 18 December 1993, a day of national mourning, at Kerepesi Cemetery. In 2008 one of the buildings of the European Parliament in Brussels was named after him.
jozsef-mindszenty: József Mindszenty was born József Pehm on 29 March 1892 at Csehimindszent in Vas County, the son of a magistrate. He entered the diocesan seminary at Szombathely in 1911 and was ordained a priest on 12 June 1915. In 1919 he was arrested first by Mihály Károlyi's government and then by the communist government of Béla Kun. In 1939 he urged his followers to vote against the Arrow Cross Party, and in 1941 he adopted the Hungarian name Mindszenty. Consecrated Bishop of Veszprém on 25 March 1944, he protested to Miklós Horthy on behalf of converted Jews. The Arrow Cross government arrested him on 27 November 1944, and he was released in April 1945.

On 15 September 1945 he became primate of Hungary and archbishop of Esztergom, and on 21 February 1946 Pope Pius XII made him a cardinal. He fought the confiscation of church farmland and the state's seizure of parochial schools. Arrested on 26 December 1948 and charged with treason and conspiracy, he was beaten while in prison until he agreed to confess. His show trial began on 3 February 1949, and on 8 February he was sentenced to life imprisonment. Pius XII excommunicated all those involved in the trial.

Freed on 30 October 1956 during the Hungarian Revolution, he returned to Budapest and praised the insurgents. When the Soviet Union invaded on 4 November, he was granted asylum at the United States embassy, where he lived for fifteen years. After a compromise offered by Pope Paul VI he was allowed to leave on 28 September 1971 and lived in Vienna. In December 1973 the pope declared the see of Esztergom vacant.

Mindszenty died in exile in Vienna on 6 May 1975. His remains were brought to Esztergom in 1991 and buried in the basilica, where a museum is dedicated to him. His cause for sainthood opened in 1993, and Pope Francis declared him venerable on 12 February 2019. The Encyclopedia Britannica says that for five decades he personified uncompromising opposition to fascism and communism in Hungary. A single Western reporter, George Seldes, disputed that he had been tortured and accused him of collaboration, a charge the prosecution at his own trial did not make.
juan-bautista-alberdi: Juan Bautista Alberdi was born in San Miguel de Tucumán on 29 August 1810. His father, Salvador Alberdi, a Spanish Basque merchant, supported the patriots in the war of independence, and his mother died as a result of his birth. He was orphaned in 1822, studied in Buenos Aires and at the University of Córdoba, and wrote his first book, on music, in 1832. In Buenos Aires he joined Esteban Echeverría and Juan María Gutiérrez in the Generation of '37, liberal intellectuals who criticised both the federalists and the unitarians. After Juan Manuel de Rosas closed their literary hall, Alberdi emigrated to Uruguay in 1838.

Alberdi wrote against Rosas from Montevideo, settled in Valparaíso, Chile, in 1843 and worked as lawyer and journalist. After Rosas was defeated at Caseros in 1852, he wrote Bases and Starting Points for the Political Organization of the Argentine Republic, a draft for the new constitution heavily influenced by that of the United States. He blamed Argentina's problems on its low population density and proposed European immigration: "Gobernar es poblar", to govern is to populate. He also urged better ports and roads, the telegraph and railways, and economic freedom.

Justo José de Urquiza, president under the constitution of 1853, made him ambassador in Chile and then sent him to Europe to win recognition for the Confederation. He settled in Paris for 24 years. Napoleon III granted French recognition, and treaties with Spain were signed in 1857 and 1859 and ratified on 26 February 1860. The reunification of Buenos Aires with the Confederation in 1861 ended his post. He opposed the War of the Triple Alliance and began writing El crimen de la guerra.

Alberdi returned to Argentina in 1879 after more than forty years abroad. He later travelled to Europe, had a stroke on the journey and died near Paris on 19 June 1884. Argentina marks 29 August as Lawyer's Day in his honour, and his image appeared on banknotes, including the 5,000 peso note of 1983–1985. A town in Paraguay is named after him for his support of Paraguay in the War of the Triple Alliance, and in 2010 Paraguay granted him honorary nationality.
juan-bautista-de-anza: Anza was born in 1736 in Fronteras, New Navarre, most probably at Cuquiarachi but possibly at the Presidio of Fronteras. His father, Juan Baptista Anssa Sassoetta, and his maternal grandfather, Captain Antonio Bezerra Nieto, had both served Spain on the frontier. He enlisted at the Presidio of Fronteras in 1752 and was a captain by 1760. In 1761 he married Ana María Pérez Serrano, daughter of the mine owner Francisco Pérez Serrano; they had no children. His early service consisted mainly of forays against Native Americans such as the Apache, in which he explored much of what is now Arizona.

Spain had begun to colonise Alta California with the Portolá expedition of 1769–1770 and wanted a more direct land route. Anza proposed one in 1772, and on 8 January 1774 he left Tubac Presidio with 3 padres, 20 soldiers, 35 mules, 65 cattle and 140 horses, guided by Sebastian Tarabal, a California Native American who had fled Mission San Gabriel. Crossing the Colorado River at its meeting with the Gila, in Yuma country, he reached Mission San Gabriel Arcángel on 22 March 1774 and Monterey on 19 April.

Promoted lieutenant-colonel on 2 October 1774, he led colonists out on 23 October 1775 to strengthen Alta California against Russian advance from the north. They suffered greatly from the winter but reached San Gabriel in January 1776 and went on to Monterey. On 28 March 1776 Anza chose the sites of the Presidio of San Francisco and Mission San Francisco de Asis, which José Joaquín Moraga later founded. A revolt of the Yumas closed the overland route at the Yuma Crossing in 1781, and it was not reopened until the late 1820s.

As governor of New Mexico he led about 800 Spanish soldiers with Ute and Apache allies against the Comanche, who had raided Taos, and routed their main body on Greenhorn Creek, where Cuerno Verde and many other leaders were killed. After a further campaign in 1783 the Comanche sued for peace, and the treaty concluded at Pecos Pueblo on 28 February 1786 opened the way for the Comanchero trade. Appointed commander of the Presidio of Tucson in 1788, he died at Arizpe on 19 December 1788 before taking up the post. The route of his expeditions is the Juan Bautista de Anza National Historic Trail.
juan-bautista-sacasa: Sacasa was born in León on 21 December 1874, the eldest son of Roberto Sacasa and Ángela Sacasa Cuadra, his father's cousin twice removed. From 1889 to 1901 he studied in the United States and earned a medical degree from Columbia University. Back in León he taught at the National University, where he became dean of faculty, and he supported the Liberal regime of José Santos Zelaya. He married María Argüello Manning, a cousin of the later president Leonardo Argüello.

In 1924 Sacasa joined a political coalition headed by the moderate Conservative Carlos Solórzano, and soon afterwards the United States Marines, who had been in Nicaragua for thirteen years, withdrew. In October 1925 the former president General Emiliano Chamorro overthrew Solórzano's government, and Sacasa fled to Mexico. Chamorro failed to win recognition from the United States and resigned in favour of Adolfo Díaz.

After an uprising of Liberal soldiers at Puerto Cabezas, Sacasa returned in 1926, claimed to be the constitutional president and set up a government there. Armed by Mexico, the Liberal forces under General José María Moncada came close to taking Managua, but the United States forced both sides into talks. The resulting Pact of Espino Negro required both armies to disarm and let Díaz finish his term. Sacasa reluctantly gave up his claim but refused to sign and left the country, and Moncada signed for him. For the next six years Augusto Sandino led a guerrilla war against the Marines who stayed to enforce the pact.

Sacasa took office on 1 January 1933, the day before the Marines were due to leave. At the insistence of the United States ambassador he named Anastasio Somoza García director of the National Guard. The next month he met Sandino, who pledged loyalty in return for an amnesty and land for his followers, but Sandino kept demanding that the Guard be disbanded and in February 1934 was assassinated on Somoza's orders.

Sacasa disapproved but could not check Somoza. His standing fell as coffee prices collapsed in the Great Depression and fraud was alleged in the congressional elections of 1934, while Somoza built ties with Moncada and Chamorro. Early in 1936 the Guard purged local officials loyal to the president, and on 9 June Somoza forced him to resign. Sacasa went into exile in Los Angeles, where he died on 17 April 1946.
juan-bautista-topete: Juan Bautista Topete y Carballo was born on 24 May 1821 in San Andrés Tuxtla, Mexico; his father and grandfather had also been admirals of Spain. He entered the navy at the age of seventeen, cut out a Carlist vessel in 1839 and became a midshipman at twenty-two. He received the cross of naval merit for saving the life of a sailor in 1841 and became a lieutenant in 1845.

After three years on the West Indian station, where he was engaged in repressing the slave trade, Topete was promoted frigate captain in 1857. He was chief of staff to the fleet in the Moroccan War of 1859 and afterwards received the cross of Saint Hermenegild among other honours. Appointed chief of the arsenal at Cádiz, he was elected a deputy and joined the Union Liberal of O'Donnell and Serrano.

Sent to the Pacific in command of the frigate Reina Blanca, he was present at the bombardments of Valparaíso and Callao, where he was badly wounded, and in other engagements of the war with Chile and Peru. Made port captain at Cádiz on his return, he took the lead of the conspiracy in the fleet against the Bourbon monarchy. He sent the steamer Buenaventura to the Canary Islands for Serrano and the other exiles, and when Prim and Sagasta arrived from Gibraltar the stand of the fleet brought the people, garrison and authorities of Cádiz to its side.

Topete held posts in the revolutionary government, among them that of minister of marine, was elected to the Cortes in 1869 and supported the claim of Antoine, Duke of Montpensier, to the throne. He at first opposed the election of Amadeus, but later sat in several cabinets of that king's reign. Prosecuted under the federal republic of 1873, he again took charge of the navy under Serrano in 1874.

After the Restoration he was kept aloof for many years, until in 1877 he accepted the presidency of a naval board. He later sat in the Senate as a life peer until his death in Madrid on 29 October 1885.
juan-de-garay: Garay grew up in the household of his uncle Pedro Ortiz de Zárate, whose family had some standing: the uncle was appointed judge and alcalde mayor of Segovia, and a cousin attended the University of Salamanca. He was also related to Juan Ortiz de Zárate, third adelantado of the Río de la Plata. In 1543 he sailed to Peru with his uncle in the first expedition of Viceroy Blasco Núñez Vela.

In 1561 Garay took part in founding Santa Cruz de la Sierra, and in 1568 he moved to Asunción, where he rose to political prominence. In April 1573 the governor of Asunción sent him with eighty men on an expedition to the Paraná River, during which he founded Santa Fe de la Vera Cruz. Appointed governor of Asunción in 1576, he set out to establish Indian villages and systems of local government among the indigenous peoples.

Having reached the rank of captain general, he refounded Buenos Aires on 11 June 1580. Pedro de Mendoza's settlement of 1536, Nuestra Señora del Buen Ayre, had been destroyed by the natives. Garay landed at the place of the present Plaza de Mayo and named the city Ciudad de la Trinidad and its port Santa Maria de Buenos Ayres. In 1581–1582 he led an expedition in search of the City of the Caesars.

On 20 March 1583, travelling from Buenos Aires to Santa Fe with 40 men, a Franciscan priest and a few women, Garay camped on the banks of the Carcarañá River near the old Sancti Spíritus Fort. Querandíes warriors ambushed the group and killed Garay, the priest, a woman and twelve of the soldiers.

Buenos Aires became the main city of the Paraná basin and its most important port. Garay's daughter Jerónima de Contreras married Hernando Arias de Saavedra, governor of the Río de la Plata, and a house he built, the palace-baserri Garatikua, stands in the oldest part of the town of Garay in Biscay.
juan-de-grijalva: Juan de Grijalva was born around 1490 and was a relative of Diego Velázquez. He went to Hispaniola in 1508 and to Cuba in 1511. In 1518 he became one of the first to explore the shores of Mexico.

Hernán Cortés put the numbers of the 1518 expedition at 170 people, while Pedro Mártir gave 300. The main pilot was Antón de Alaminos, and the party included Francisco de Montejo, Pedro de Alvarado and Bernal Díaz del Castillo. Two natives of Yucatan, Julianillo and Melchorejo, who had been captured during the Hernández de Córdoba expedition, served as interpreters. The four ships left the port of Matanzas in Cuba on 8 April 1518.

After rounding the Guaniguanico in Cuba, Grijalva sailed along the Mexican coast, reached Cozumel on 3 May 1518 and arrived on 8 June at the Tabasco region in southern Mexico. The Río Grijalva was named after him. He was the first Spaniard to meet a delegation of Moctezuma II. One of the natives who joined the expedition was baptised Francisco and later served as a Nahuatl interpreter for Cortés. According to W. H. Prescott's Conquest of Mexico, Grijalva was the first Spaniard to bring back word of the gold of the Aztecs, which spurred the drive for conquest. Bernal Díaz del Castillo wrote about the voyage in his Historia.

In 1518 Cortés stayed at Grijalva's home in Trinidad, Cuba, at the start of his own Mexican expedition, and recruited men there, including the five Alvarado brothers. Grijalva was killed by natives in Honduras on 21 January 1527.
juan-de-onate: Oñate was born at Zacatecas, the son of the Spanish-Basque conquistador and silver baron Cristóbal de Oñate. His mother, Catalina Salazar y de la Cadena, was descended from conversos and was the daughter of Gonzalo de Salazar, who had helped govern New Spain while Hernán Cortés was in Honduras. Oñate married Isabel de Tolosa Cortés de Moctezuma, a granddaughter of Cortés and great-granddaughter of the Aztec emperor Moctezuma Xocoyotzin. On 21 September 1595 Viceroy Luís de Velasco chose him to colonise the northern lands, though his successor delayed the expedition to review its terms.

On 30 April 1598 Oñate claimed the lands beyond the Rio Grande for the Spanish Empire and then followed the river north, setting up his government at Ohkay Owingeh, which he renamed San Juan de los Caballeros. He granted land to colonists and let them demand tribute from the Native peoples. In October 1598 eleven Spaniards, among them his nephew Juan de Zaldívar, were killed at Acoma Pueblo in a fight over food. In January 1599 Vicente de Zaldívar destroyed the pueblo, and an estimated 800 to 1,000 Ácoma died. Oñate sentenced the survivors over 12 to twenty years of servitude and ordered a foot cut from each man over 25, though recent research suggests at most toes were cut.

In 1601 he led 130 soldiers and 12 Franciscan priests onto the Great Plains in search of Quivira, met the Escanjaques and the Rayados near the Arkansas River, and turned back after a battle with the Escanjaques, reaching San Juan on 24 November 1601. In 1604 and 1605 a party of about three dozen men went west and descended the Colorado River to the Gulf of California.

In 1606 Oñate was recalled to Mexico City. He resigned and was convicted of cruelty to natives and colonists, banished from New Mexico for life and exiled from Mexico City for five years. He later went to Spain, where the king made him head of all mining inspectors, and he died there in 1626.

He remains a disputed figure, honoured by some as an explorer and condemned by others for his cruelty at Acoma. On 29 December 1997 the right foot was cut from his statue in Alcalde, which was removed in 2020, and an equestrian statue unveiled in El Paso in 2007 drew protests from the Ácoma.
juan-de-salcedo: Salcedo was born in 1549 in the Kingdom of Mexico, in the viceroyalty of New Spain, the son of Pedro de Salcedo and Teresa López de Legazpi; his older brother Felipe de Salcedo was also a soldier. He joined the Spanish forces in 1564, at fifteen, for the voyage to the East Indies and the Pacific in search of gold and spices, following the routes of the earlier expeditions of Ferdinand Magellan in 1521 and Ruy López de Villalobos in 1543.

With Martín de Goiti, Salcedo led about 300 Spanish and Mexican soldiers and 600 Visayan allies against Manila, then held by the Sultanate of Brunei, fighting the chieftain Rajah Sulayman; the historian Carlos Quirino estimated that more than half of the expedition's members were Mexicans of mixed descent. In May 1572 he set out north with 45 Spaniards and many Filipino auxiliaries, founded settlements in Ilocos, defeated a flotilla of three Japanese pirate ships and occupied Vigan, where he left 30 men. He then sailed with 15 men in two open boats along the northern coast and explored Cagayan, returning to Manila three months later with 50 pounds of gold. King Philip II of Spain granted him estates and the city of Vigan.

In 1574, when the corsair Limahong laid siege to Manila with 6,500 men, Salcedo hurried back with 600 infantry, half of them Spaniards and Mexicans and half Filipino allies, and the attackers were driven off. In 1575 he pursued Limahong to Pangasinan, where the Spaniards besieged the pirates for four months before Limahong escaped.

After the war Salcedo returned to Ilocos to govern its settlements. He died suddenly in March 1576 after a short illness, probably dysentery or malaria, at the age of 27. His remains lie in a knight's tomb in San Agustin Church in Intramuros. The American historian William Scott called him the last of the conquistadors. A romance of his love for Kandarapa, a princess of Tondo, comes from the account of his aide Felipe Cepeda and was later published by the Jesuit Jose Ibañez.
juan-diego: According to major sources Juan Diego was born in 1474 in Cuauhtitlan, in the Aztec Empire under the Tlacopan, and lived there or in Tolpetlac at the time of the apparitions. He was a Nahua peasant, neither destitute nor rich or influential. He and his wife, María Lucía, were among the first to be baptised after the main group of twelve Franciscan missionaries arrived in Mexico in 1524. After the apparitions he was allowed to live beside the hermitage at the foot of Tepeyac and devoted the rest of his life to serving the Virgin at the shrine. His death is given as 1548.

The tradition, as told in the Nican mopohua, holds that at dawn on Wednesday 9 December 1531 the Virgin Mary appeared to him at Tepeyac and told him to ask Bishop Juan de Zumárraga to build a chapel in her honour. The bishop asked him to return later. Meeting her again, Juan Diego suggested she choose someone of greater standing, but she insisted on him. On 10 December the bishop asked for a sign.

When Juan Diego's uncle Juan Bernardino fell sick, he tried to avoid the hill, but the Virgin met him and asked, "Am I not here, I who am your mother?" She told him to gather flowers blooming out of season on the rocks. He carried them in his mantle to the bishop, and when he opened it the image of the Virgin was found imprinted on it. Juan Bernardino was found recovered. On 26 December 1531 the image was taken in procession to a small chapel at Tepeyac.

The Nican mopohua was first published in Nahuatl in 1649, after Miguel Sánchez's Spanish account of 1648, and Antonio Valeriano is traditionally considered its author. Historians dispute Juan Diego's historicity, chiefly because Zumárraga and the earliest ecclesiastical historians are silent about him, while others reply that silence does not prove he did not exist. Clear evidence of a Marian cult at Tepeyac appears by 1556.

The Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe at the foot of the hill houses the cloak traditionally said to be his. He was beatified on 6 May 1990. The miracle accepted for canonisation was the recovery of Juan José Barragán Silva, who fell from a balcony in Querétaro that month. John Paul II canonised him in 2002, the first indigenous American saint.
juan-esteban-montero: Montero was born in Santiago on 12 February 1879, the son of Benjamín Montero and Eugenia Rodríguez. He studied at the colegio de San Ignacio and the Universidad de Chile, qualified as a lawyer on 16 September 1901 and soon became professor of civil and Roman law there, while also working as a government lawyer and in private practice. He married Graciela Fehrman Martínez, with whom he had four children.

He entered politics only in 1931, when President Carlos Ibáñez del Campo made him Minister of the Interior and Social Welfare. After Ibáñez resigned on 26 July 1931, Montero reluctantly kept a similar post under Pedro Opazo, who resigned the next day, leaving Montero in charge as vice president. He at once called a presidential election and, to stand as the Radical Party's candidate, gave up the vice presidency on 20 August 1931 to Manuel Trucco. Trucco's caretaker government faced the Sailors' mutiny of 1 to 5 September 1931, put down only after the fleet was bombed from the air.

Backed by the Liberals and Conservatives as well as the Radicals, Montero won almost 64% of the vote, defeating José Santos Salas, a protégé of Ibáñez, and took office on 15 November. Facing the chaos that followed the crash of 1929, he cut public spending, salaries and the administration and increased the foreign debt. The currency kept falling, inflation soared and the Central Bank's reserves reached an all-time low, and the austerity caused widespread discontent.

On 4 June 1932 Colonel Marmaduke Grove seized the Air Force base of El Bosque in Santiago and demanded Montero's resignation. Montero refused to call on the army and resigned instead. That night the rebels formed a Government Junta of the retired General Arturo Puga, Eugenio Matte and Carlos Dávila, with Grove as minister of defence. Montero left politics for private practice and business, and died in Santiago on 25 February 1948, aged 69.
juan-facundo-quiroga: Juan Facundo Quiroga was born on 27 November 1788 in San Antonio, La Rioja, into a traditional but impoverished family of cattle breeders. Sent to school in San Juan, he ran away, and during his wanderings in the desert he is said to have killed a cougar, which earned him the nickname El Tigre de los Llanos. After the May Revolution he tried to join José de San Martín's Granaderos a Caballo Regiment in San Luis, but was imprisoned and expelled for his temper, and he returned to La Rioja as a businessman.

When the central government in Buenos Aires fell in 1820 and La Rioja became autonomous, Quiroga rose to command of the provincial army and took control of the government. Advised by the monarchist priest Pedro Ignacio de Castro Barros, he declared a religious war on Buenos Aires under the flag Religión o Muerte, against President Bernardino Rivadavia's anti-clerical laws, and overthrew the centralist governor of San Juan. A devout Catholic who could quote the Bible from memory, he called Rivadavia a persecutor of the Church.

After the Cisplatine War, returning Unitarian officers deposed the federalist governments. Beaten by José María Paz, Quiroga went into exile in Buenos Aires, then marched around Córdoba through lands still held by native peoples to take Mendoza, and finally defeated General Gregorio Aráoz de Lamadrid, who led the last Unitarian forces. He became, with Juan Manuel de Rosas and Estanislao López of Santa Fe, one of the leaders of federalism, though he told Rosas in his letters that his own ideas were Unitarian.

In 1834 Manuel Vicente Maza, governor of Buenos Aires, sent him to mediate between the governors of Tucumán and Salta. Warned of a plot, Quiroga returned by the same road, and at Barranca Yaco, between Córdoba and Santiago del Estero, gunmen led by Santos Pérez stopped his carriage and shot him through the left eye. The crisis forced Maza to resign and brought Rosas to power. The governor of Córdoba, José Vicente Reynafé, and his brother were hanged with Pérez in Buenos Aires in 1837. Quiroga is buried in La Recoleta Cemetery, and in La Rioja he is seen as a hero.
juan-gerardi: Juan José Gerardi Conedera, of partial Italian ancestry, was born in Guatemala City on 27 December 1922. He studied at the city's seminary and won a scholarship to study theology in New Orleans. Ordained a priest on 21 December 1946, he served in rural parishes such as Mataquescuintla, San Pedro Sacatepéquez and Palencia, as well as in the capital.

Elected Bishop of Verapaz on 9 May 1967, he stressed pastoral work among the Maya communities. During the civil war of the 1970s he pressed for the official recognition of Guatemala's indigenous languages and helped secure permission for two radio stations to broadcast in Mayan languages. In 1974 he became Bishop of Quiché. Between 1980 and 1983 the department saw rising violence between the army and guerrilla groups, and hundreds of Catholic catechists and community leaders, most of them Maya, were murdered; Gerardi repeatedly asked the military authorities to control their actions.

As president of the Guatemalan Conference of Bishops he spoke out about the Spanish embassy fire of 31 January 1980, in which 39 people died and which government forces were suspected of starting. Returning from a synod at the Vatican that year, he was refused entry to Guatemala, was denied asylum in El Salvador and lived in Costa Rica until the military president Romeo Lucas García was overthrown in 1982. In 1988 the bishops named him, with Rodolfo Quezada Toruño, to the government's National Reconciliation Commission, work that led to the human rights office of the archdiocese.

His attackers killed him with a concrete slab in the garage of the parish house of San Sebastian Church, and his body was identified by his episcopal ring. On 8 June 2001 Colonel Byron Disrael Lima Estrada, his son Captain Byron Miguel Lima Oliva and Sergeant José Obdulio Villanueva were sentenced to 30 years, and the priest Mario Leonel Orantes Nájera to 20 years as an accomplice, in the first trial of members of the military in a civilian court; an appeals court later cut the Limas' sentences to 20 years. Pope Francis declared Gerardi a martyr in 2020.
juan-gines-de-sepulveda: Sepúlveda was born at Pozoblanco in the province of Córdoba, of humble background; his parents were Ginés Sánchez Mellado, a craftsman, and María Ruiz. In 1510 he enrolled at the University of Alcalá de Henares, where he studied philosophy and Greek, and in 1513 he began theology at the College of San Antonio de Sigüenza. In February 1515 he obtained a letter of recommendation from Cardinal Cisneros to the Spanish College in Bologna, where he matriculated that September. There he studied under Pietro Pomponazzi and gained a lifelong expertise in the works of Aristotle, encouraged by his patron Alberto Pío, Prince of Carpi, and by Giulio de' Medici.

By 1523 Sepúlveda had earned doctorates in arts and theology and had taken religious vows as a Dominican priest. When Giulio de' Medici became Pope Clement VII in that year, he served at the papal curia in Rome, where he gained a reputation for scholarship and rhetorical skill. He translated several works of Aristotle from Greek into Latin, among them the Parva Naturalia in 1522 and De mundo in 1523.

He also wrote on the religious controversies of the day: De fato et libero arbitrio against Martin Luther in 1526, De ritu nuptiarum in 1531 against the divorce proceedings of Henry VIII, and the Antapologia against Erasmus in 1532. He despised Luther, but respected Erasmus and corresponded with him for many years. In 1529 he wrote Ad Carolum V, urging Emperor Charles V to unite Europe and fight the Turks.

In Democrates, of 1535, Sepúlveda defended the idea that a just war based on natural law was compatible with Christianity. His case for the conquest drew also on Saint Thomas Aquinas, on the Roman law of just war and the right of conquest, and on the Bible, which he used to justify forced conversion; his position differed from that of the School of Salamanca represented by Francisco de Vitoria. He had never been to America. He claimed that some, though not all, Amerindians were natural slaves as Aristotle defined them in Book I of the Politics, and compared them to children before parents.

Bartolomé de las Casas used the same sources in reply. He held that Christianity should be offered to the natives as an option, not imposed as an obligation, and that no Amerindians lacked the ability to rule themselves. Sepúlveda's later works include histories of the deeds of Charles V, of 1556, and of Philip II, of 1564, and De regno, of 1570. He died on 17 November 1573.
juan-jose-arevalo: Juan José Arévalo Bermejo was born in Taxisco, Santa Rosa, on 10 September 1904, into a lower-middle-class family. He trained as a teacher at the Central Normal School for Boys and, with his friend Luis Martínez Mont, founded a literary magazine, Alba. In 1927 he won a government scholarship to study pedagogy abroad and went to Argentina, where in 1934 he took a doctorate in philosophy and educational sciences at the National University of La Plata. In 1932 the government of Jorge Ubico cut the monthly pension for scholars like him from 175 to 116 quetzales.

Arévalo was elected in 1944 in what is generally reckoned Guatemala's first truly free election, with over 86 percent of the vote, and served from 15 March 1945 to 15 March 1951. His administration saw wide political freedom, a new constitution in 1945, a new minimum wage, new schools, hospitals and houses, and the formation of parties and trade unions. His philosophy, which he called spiritual socialism, aimed at the moral development of Guatemalans. He valued property rights but would subordinate them to the benefit of the country, and he rejected communism, exiling activists and refusing to legalise the Communist Party.

Even so he faced at least 25 coup attempts, as conservatives and foreign governments read his programme as communism. The benefits of his reforms did not reach the rural areas, which needed an agrarian reform that his party in Congress could not achieve. He handed power to Jacobo Árbenz in 1951.

After Árbenz's fall in 1954 Arévalo went into exile in Mexico, where in 1956 he wrote the allegory The Shark and the Sardines against the treatment of Latin America by the United States and American companies. He returned to Guatemala on 27 March 1963 to announce his candidacy, but a coup on 31 March put Enrique Peralta Azurdia in power and he fled again. He met President Vinicio Cerezo in January 1986 and died in Guatemala City in October 1990. His son Bernardo Arévalo became president of Guatemala in 2024.
juan-jose-flores: Juan José Flores was born on 19 July 1800 at Puerto Cabello, Venezuela, the illegitimate and only son of a Spanish merchant and a Venezuelan woman, Rita Flores Bohorques. His father returned to Europe and left mother and son in poverty. Flores had little formal education, and at fifteen he enlisted as a private in the royalist army of General Pablo Morillo.

Taken prisoner as a sergeant on 31 October 1817, he joined the patriot army of Simón Bolívar. Bolívar noted his courage at the Battle of Carabobo in 1821, and at twenty-three Flores became a colonel and then commandant general of the freed city of Pasto. He was self-taught and read Rousseau and Montesquieu, and the professors of the University of Quito gave him an honorary doctorate in 1842.

On 13 May 1830, the day Ecuador broke away from Gran Colombia, Flores was named supreme chief of the new country, and on 14 August provisional president. The assembly at Riobamba elected him constitutional president, and his term began on 22 September 1830 and lasted until 10 September 1834. It was marked by turmoil: he faced a rebellion led by Luis Urdaneta, who wanted to keep Ecuador in Gran Colombia, and a threat from Vicente Rocafuerte, with whom he agreed that Rocafuerte would be president next and Flores head of the army. He also fought an invading Colombian army in 1832 and again from 1834, defeating it at Miñarica, near Ambato, on 18 January 1835.

His second term ran from 1 February 1839 to 15 January 1843. After irregularities in the elections of 1842 he had the 1835 constitution annulled, and the new constitution, nicknamed the Carta de la esclavitud, let him begin a third term on 1 April 1843. A rebellion led by Rocafuerte and Vicente Ramón Roca overthrew him on 6 March 1845.

Flores remained active in Ecuadorian military and political life. He commanded Ecuadorian forces at the Battle of Cuaspud on 6 December 1863, where a defeat weakened the army and thwarted his and Gabriel García Moreno's efforts to strengthen state centralization. In 1864 he left Quito to fight an expedition led by the former president José María Urvina in the Gulf of Guayaquil. At the Battle of Santa Rosa he received a stray shot in the lower abdomen and died on 1 October aboard the steamer Smirck, near Puná Island. He is often called the Founder of the Republic, and Floreana Island in the Galápagos Archipelago is named for him.
juan-jose-linz: Linz graduated in law and political science from the Complutense University of Madrid in 1947 and moved to New York in 1950. At Columbia University he took classes with the sociologists Robert K. Merton, Paul Lazarsfeld, Robert Staughton Lynd and Kingsley Davis, worked closely with Seymour Martin Lipset, and wrote a dissertation of 900 pages on The Social Bases of West German Politics.

Between his years at Columbia and Yale he spent a short time in Spain helping to develop courses for the new Autonomous University of Madrid. He was a founding member of the International Sociological Association's Committee of Political Sociology, with Lipset, Raymond Aron, Shmuel Eisenstadt and Stein Rokkan, and its president from 1971 to 1979, and he was president of the Council for European Studies from 1973 to 1974 and of the World Association of Public Opinion Research from 1974 to 1976.

He supervised 65 dissertations, and his students included Alfred Stepan, Arturo Valenzuela and Jan T. Gross. He received the Prince of Asturias Award of Social Sciences in 1987, the Johan Skytte Prize in Political Science in 1996 and the Karl Deutsch Award in 2003. He died in New Haven, Connecticut, on 1 October 2013, aged 86.

Linz defined authoritarianism by four qualities: limited political pluralism; legitimacy based on appeals to emotion and on the regime's claim to be a necessary evil against easily recognisable problems; minimal political mobilisation, with suppression of anti-regime activities; and ill-defined executive powers. His work of 1975 set out a classification of regimes that also discussed sultanistic regimes, and offered a litmus test of conduct that puts democracy at risk, such as a refusal to disavow violence or a readiness to curtail civil liberties.

In The Breakdown of Democratic Regimes, four volumes edited with Alfred Stepan, he argued that the people in power in a democracy, not only its opponents, played a decisive role in its overthrow, and that breakdowns were contingent rather than inevitable. Problems of Democratic Transition and Consolidation compared thirteen countries and drew attention to stateness problems arising from nationalist conflicts.
juan-manuel-de-rosas: Juan Manuel José Domingo Ortiz de Rozas was born on 30 March 1793 in Buenos Aires, then the capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, the first child of León Ortiz de Rozas, an army officer, and Agustina López de Osornio, of a wealthy criollo family. His mother's father, a landowner, had died defending his estate from an attack in 1783. After the British invasions were repelled the family moved to their ranch, where Rosas worked among peons, most of them gauchos, who were drafted as a private defence force. He was suspicious of the May Revolution of 1810, which he saw as a movement of merchants and officials in the city, and he felt nostalgic for the stability of colonial times.

By 1826 Rosas had a power base of relatives, friends and clients and had joined the Federalist Party, though he cared chiefly for his native province. In 1827 he drove the Federalist takeover of Buenos Aires and became commander of the rural militias on 14 July. In December 1829 he became governor of Buenos Aires Province. The capture of the Unitarian leader José María Paz in March 1831 ended the Unitarian-Federalist civil war, and Rosas recognised provincial autonomy in the Federal Pact.

His term ended in 1832 and he left to wage the Desert Campaign. In October 1833 his supporters besieged Buenos Aires in the Revolution of the Restorers, and on 7 March 1835 the House of Representatives re-elected him governor with the sum of public power.

His rule used purges, banishments, censorship and terror; the armed Mazorca killed thousands, and he presented himself in a cult of personality. He declared war on the Peru-Bolivian Confederation on 19 March 1837, and France blockaded Buenos Aires from 28 March 1838. By about 1845 he held dominance over the region, and his army under Manuel Oribe besieged Montevideo from 1843. Britain and France blockaded Buenos Aires for most of the late 1840s but could not halt him.

When the Empire of Brazil began aiding Uruguay, Rosas declared war in August 1851, beginning the Platine War, and he was defeated. He arrived at Plymouth on 26 April 1852, where the British gave him asylum, and he lived his last years as a tenant farmer at Southampton until his death in 1877. His daughter Manuela followed him into exile. Efforts to reassess his reputation began in the 1880s with works by Adolfo Saldías and Ernesto Quesada, and a revisionist movement later idealised him. His remains were brought back to Argentina in 1989, and he remains a controversial figure.
juan-manuel-galvez: Juan Manuel Gálvez Durón, born on 10 June 1887, took office on 1 January 1949 for the National Party of Honduras, ending the 16-year rule of Tiburcio Carías Andino. He showed more independence than had been expected. Some of his predecessor's policies continued and grew: road building took nearly a quarter of the budget by 1953, coffee exports were developed, the external debt was reduced and the last of the British bonds was paid off. The fruit companies still received favourable treatment, and the United Fruit Company was given a twenty-five-year contract in 1949.

Education received a larger share of the budget, and Congress passed an income tax law, although it was enforced only sporadically. Press freedom was largely restored, the Liberal Party and other groups were allowed to organise, and some labour organisation was permitted. Laws established the eight-hour working day, paid holidays, limited employer responsibility for injuries at work and rules for the employment of women and children.

His hardest months came in 1954. Between 5 and 14 May workers struck in mining, brewing and textiles and at Coca Cola, the Standard Fruit Company and the United Fruit Company. Standard Fruit reached a collective agreement with more than 11,000 strikers on 21 May, the first such agreement by a private company in Honduras, while the strike against United Fruit grew from about 25,000 to about 100,000 workers. On 23 May Gálvez asked the Eisenhower administration to prepare the Marine Corps to land if the situation got out of control, and two US warships moved into the Gulf of Honduras. An agreement with the United Fruit strikers was reached on 9 July 1954.

In late September Tropical Storm Gilda killed 29 Hondurans and left about 3,000 homeless, and United Fruit dismissed 10,000 workers. Gálvez nonetheless held the scheduled elections on 10 October 1954.

The election left the government deadlocked by a split in his own party, and on 5 December 1954, while Gálvez was abroad for treatment of a heart condition, his vice president Julio Lozano Díaz deposed him. He lived another eighteen years and died in Honduras on 20 August 1972.
juan-montalvo: Montalvo was born in Ambato on 13 April 1832, the youngest of seven children of Marcos Montalvo Oviedo of Guano, a travelling seller of fabrics, and María Josefa Fiallos of Ambato. His grandfather, José Santos Montalvo, had come from Andalucía and gathered cinchona bark in Panamá, Venezuela and Colombia before settling in Ecuador. Juan studied philosophy and law in Quito, returned to Ambato in 1854 and held diplomatic posts in Italy and France from 1857 to 1859.

A liberal and anti-clerical writer, Montalvo founded a series of literary and political magazines, from La Razón in 1848 to El Cosmopolita in 1865 and El Regenerador in 1872. After an issue of El Cosmopolita attacked Gabriel García Moreno, he was exiled to Colombia, and García Moreno's assassination was later attributed to his writings. He was also an enemy of the writer Juan León Mera.

Under Ignacio de Veintemilla he was twice exiled to France, remaining there from 1879. Las Catilinarias, published in 1880, made him known in intellectual circles in the United States, Europe and Latin America. His essays of the Siete Tratados and the Geometría Moral were popular in Ecuador and were banned by Veintemilla. He married María Guzmán Suárez in Ambato on 17 October 1868 and had two children with her, and a third with Augustine Contoux, whom he met in 1882.

Montalvo died of tuberculosis in Paris on 17 January 1889. His body was embalmed and rests in a mausoleum in Ambato, where it is exhibited. Geometría Moral appeared after his death in 1902, and his sequel to Don Quixote, Capítulos que se le olvidaron a Cervantes, his only novel, was admired along with his other work by Jorge Luis Borges and Miguel de Unamuno. His likeness appears on the Ecuadorian five-centavo coin.
juan-negrin: Juan Negrín was born on 3 February 1892 in Las Palmas in the Canary Islands, into a deeply Catholic middle-class family; his father was a prosperous merchant. Having shown interest in medicine, he was sent at 15 to study in Germany, at Kiel and then at Leipzig. In 1912, aged twenty, he took a doctorate in medicine and became an assistant at the Institute of Physiology in Leipzig.

Returning to Spain at the end of 1915, he became a professor of physiology at the Complutense University of Madrid in 1922, and his laboratory became an internationally known research centre. Among his students was Severo Ochoa, later a Nobel laureate. Close to German social democracy, he joined the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) in 1929, sided with the moderate faction of Indalecio Prieto, and was elected deputy for Las Palmas in 1931, 1933 and 1936.

After the military uprising of 17 July 1936 he helped many people escape the revolutionary checas in Madrid and was nearly killed by anarchists. In September 1936 he became minister of finance under Francisco Largo Caballero. In October 1936, with the approval of President Manuel Azaña and other ministers, he sent Spain's gold reserves to the Soviet Union in return for arms; critics argued that this put the government under Stalin's control.

After the Barcelona May Days forced Largo Caballero to resign, Azaña named Negrín prime minister on 17 May 1937. His cabinet included Prieto at War, the communists Jesús Hernández Tomás and Vicente Uribe, and the republican José Giral. Under the slogan 'Resistir es vencer', 'To resist is to win', he sought to keep the Republic alive until a wider war brought it allies in Western Europe. He remained in Spain until the Republican front collapsed in March 1939.

Negrín lived in Paris until the fall of France in June 1940 and then in London, heading the Republican government in exile until August 1945, when he resigned and José Giral succeeded him. Franco's courts stripped him of his chair and fined him 100 million pesetas. The PSOE expelled him in April 1946 and rehabilitated him in 2008. He died of a heart attack in Paris on 12 November 1956, aged 64. Historians differ about him: later scholarship has portrayed him as a pragmatic social democrat who had no choice but to ally with the Soviets, because Britain and France would not support the Republic.
juan-nepomuceno-almonte: Almonte was born on 15 May 1803 at Nocupétaro in Michoacán, the son of the priest José María Morelos and Brígida Almonte, who was said to be of Amerindian ancestry. In 1815 Morelos sent him to New Orleans, where he was educated, learned fluent English and worked as a clerk; his stay ended when his father was executed on 22 December 1815. Between 1822 and 1824 he served on the staff of José Félix Trespalacios in Texas and then joined the Mexican delegation in London, helping José Mariano Michelena negotiate Mexico's first treaty.

In early life a partisan of Vicente Guerrero and an editor of the progressive newspaper Atleta, Almonte went into hiding when Anastasio Bustamante came to power. In 1836 he went to Texas as aide-de-camp to Antonio López de Santa Anna, kept a journal at the Alamo, and at the Battle of San Jacinto on 21 April 1836 surrendered to Thomas Jefferson Rusk after leading the last organised resistance. He shared Santa Anna's captivity as interpreter and went with him to meet President Andrew Jackson in Washington.

As minister of war under the centralist republic he led loyal troops to recover the National Palace during the Federalist Revolt of 1840, and he denounced Jose Maria Gutierrez Estrada's essay calling for a European prince as scandalous and treasonous. Sent as minister to the United States in 1841, he lobbied against intervention in Texas and asked for his passport when the Senate voted to annex it. His biographer Rivera Cambas wrote that this convinced him that American expansion must be opposed even at the cost of European intervention. He was minister of war again during the war with the United States and ran for president in 1845, 1848 and 1852.

As minister to Great Britain and then France, Almonte began to lobby for intervention, signed the Mon-Almonte Treaty with Spain on 27 September 1859 and, on 31 October 1861, with other monarchists signed the London Convention. After the French took the capital in 1863 he was one of the three-man executive chosen by the Junta Superior, which became the regency of the empire.

Almonte was serving as a diplomat in France when the French withdrew their troops, and he died in Paris on 21 March 1869, two years after the empire fell. The town of Almonte in Ontario was named after him in 1855, as was Almont in Michigan.
juan-odonoju: O'Donojú was born in Seville on 30 July 1762, the third of five children of the second marriage of Richard Dunphy O'Donnohue and Alicia O'Ryan. His surname is a Spanish spelling of the Irish O'Donoghue. Both his father's and his mother's families had come to Spain in the 1720s, fleeing the anti-Catholic Penal Laws imposed in the Kingdom of Ireland by the Protestant Ascendancy. He joined the army young.

In the Peninsular War he was chief of staff to General Gregorio García de la Cuesta at the Battle of Talavera, fought on 27 and 28 July 1809. On 11 July he had interpreted when Cuesta met the British commander, Lieutenant-General Sir Arthur Wellesley, to plan the campaign, tactfully explaining Cuesta's curt answers. Promoted to lieutenant general, he reached Cádiz, the only Spanish city free of French occupation, and in 1814 the Regency made him Minister of War. After Ferdinand VII returned he served as the king's aide-de-camp.

A friend of the liberal rebel Rafael del Riego and a high officer among the Spanish Freemasons, he was captain general of Andalusia when the Constitution of 1812 was restored in 1820. In 1821 the Cortes Generales made him captain general and jefe político superior of New Spain, with the authority of the former viceroys. His appointment has been credited to the Mexican deputies in the Cortes, Miguel Ramos Arizpe above all, and to Spanish liberals who hoped his principles would end the independence movement.

He landed at Veracruz from the ship Asia on 3 August 1821 to find only the garrisons of Mexico City, Veracruz and Acapulco still loyal. He issued a liberal manifesto, came to terms with Colonel Santa Anna, commander of the garrison at Veracruz, and met Agustín de Iturbide at Córdoba. The governor of Veracruz, José Dávila, withdrew to the fortress of San Juan de Ulúa rather than accept the treaty.

O'Donojú entered Mexico City on 26 September 1821. The next day he received Iturbide at the National Palace and watched the Army of the Three Guarantees march in from its balcony, and on 28 September he installed the provisional governing junta and signed the act of independence. He then fell ill with pleurisy and died on 8 October. The Spanish government disowned his recognition of independence and did not recognise the Mexican government until 1836.
juan-pablo-duarte: Juan Pablo Duarte y Díez was born on 26 January 1813 in Santo Domingo, into a middle-class family engaged in maritime trade and hardware. His father, Juan José Duarte Rodríguez, was a Spanish merchant from Vejer de la Frontera, and his mother, Manuela Díez Jiménez, came from El Seibo. Haiti's president Jean-Pierre Boyer sent an army that took over the eastern part of Hispaniola, and Duarte's father refused to sign the merchants' letter accepting the new order.

As a teenager Duarte left to study, spending time in the United States, England and France, where he learned English and perfected his French. According to a later account, a ship's captain told him that Dominicans had no name because they bowed to Haitian rule, and Duarte resolved to fight for independence.

On 16 July 1838 Duarte and others founded the secret society La Trinitaria, named after the Holy Trinity. His sister Rosa called it a youth movement, and conservatives mocked its members as filorios, romantics lacking realism. It was the first revolutionary group in the country with a political doctrine, a programme and an organisation, and its aim was to overthrow Haitian rule and found an independent state. Haiti's troubles in 1842 and 1843, among them an earthquake, favoured the conspirators, but Duarte was forced into exile.

He returned to the port of Santo Domingo on 15 March 1844 and was proclaimed General in Chief, though the government made him a brigadier general. He fought in the Battle of Azua and quarrelled with Pedro Santana over tactics. Offered the presidency, he declined unless a majority voted for him. On 15 July 1844 Santana moved against the governing junta, and Duarte was exiled again.

In Venezuela Duarte received news in February 1845 of the execution of María Trinidad Sánchez, took the guilt on himself and withdrew from public life into the Venezuelan interior. He lived for years at Achaguas and San Fernando de Apure, and the priest Juan Bautista Sangenis encouraged him to take holy orders, which he declined. He was the only Trinitario expelled in 1844 who did not return after the amnesty of 1848. He reached Monte Cristi on 25 March 1864, during the Restoration war, but was sent on a mission abroad that he had not sought.

Duarte died on 15 July 1876, suffering from tuberculosis and pneumonia. He is regarded as the foremost of the founding fathers of the Dominican Republic and bears the title Father of the Nation. His birthday, 26 January, is a national holiday, and Pico Duarte, the country's highest point, is named for him.
juan-peron: Juan Domingo Perón was born in Lobos, Buenos Aires Province, on 8 October 1895, the son of Juana Sosa Toledo and Mario Tomás Perón. His father's family was originally Spanish but had settled in Sardinia, and his great-grandfather emigrated to Argentina in the 1830s.

Perón entered military college in 1911 and rose through the ranks. He supported the 1930 coup against President Hipólito Yrigoyen, a decision he later regretted. Between 1939 and 1941 he served as a military attaché in Mussolini's Italy, where he developed many of his ideas.

Perón took part in the 1943 revolution and became Minister of Labor, then Minister of War and Vice President, gaining a name for labour reforms. Political disputes forced him to resign in October 1945, and he was arrested. On 17 October workers gathered in the Plaza de Mayo to demand his release. He won the presidential election of 24 February 1946 by about 11% against an alliance of the Radical Civic Union and other parties, after he turned the United States ambassador's accusation of fascist ties into a choice between Perón and Braden.

His first term brought industrialisation, expanded social rights, tuition-free universities and, in 1947, votes for women, a measure tied to the work of his wife Eva Duarte. The government nationalised the Central Bank. It also fired dissidents, controlled the press and dismissed over 2,000 university professors. Several Nazi war criminals found refuge in Argentina. Perón was re-elected in 1951, but his second term began amid drought and a trade deficit. After conflict with the Catholic Church, pro-Church elements of the armed forces bombed the Plaza de Mayo in June 1955, killing about 300 civilians, and a coup deposed him.

Perón lived in exile in Paraguay, Venezuela, Panama and Spain while the Peronist party was outlawed. When the Peronist Héctor Cámpora won the 1973 election, Perón returned on 20 June 1973 amid the Ezeiza massacre and was himself elected president in October. Violence between left- and right-wing Peronists continued, and he could not resolve it. He died on 1 July 1974 and his third wife, Isabel Perón, succeeded him as vice president.

Supporters praise the Peróns for efforts to reduce poverty and dignify labour; detractors consider them demagogues and dictators. The movement continues mainly as the Justicialist Party. Perón was buried in La Chacarita Cemetery; in 1987 his tomb was desecrated and his hands stolen, a crime that remains unresolved.
juan-ponce-de-leon: Juan Ponce de León was born in the village of Santervás de Campos, in what is now the Spanish province of Valladolid. Early historians placed his birth in 1460, but more recent evidence shows he was likely born in 1474. The identity of his parents is still conjecture, but the historian Aurelio Tió argued that he came from a distinguished noble family, with Rodrigo Ponce de León, Duke of Cádiz, as his first cousin. In September 1493, aged nineteen, he sailed as one of 200 gentleman volunteers on Christopher Columbus's second voyage, which anchored off the island the Taíno called Borikén, later Puerto Rico.

In 1502 Nicolás de Ovando arrived as governor of Hispaniola. When the Taíno overran a Spanish garrison at Higüey in 1504, Ovando sent Ponce de León to crush the rebellion. He took part in the Higüey massacre, about which the friar Bartolomé de las Casas tried to inform the Spanish authorities. Ovando rewarded him by making him frontier governor of the province, with a land grant and an encomienda of Indian labour, and in 1505 he founded the town of Salvaleón.

In 1508 Ferdinand II of Aragon gave him permission for the first official expedition to Puerto Rico, which left Hispaniola on 12 July 1508 with about 50 men and found placer gold in the west of the island. He founded settlements near the mines at San Germán and Caparra, where local people were compelled to work under the encomienda system. The Crown named him the island's first governor in 1509. A long legal dispute with Diego Colón, Columbus's son, ended in 1511 with Colón replacing him.

King Ferdinand then urged him to seek new lands outside Colón's authority. A royal contract of February 1512 gave him the right to search for the islands of Beniny, and in March 1513 he set out from Puerto Rico with three ships at his own expense and sixty-five people. He named La Florida, charted the Atlantic coast to the Keys and north along the Gulf coast.
