He later said he had evolved the whole of his political philosophy there. He returned in October 1952, married Maria Gabriel in January 1953 and taught history at St Francis' College.

In April 1953 Nyerere became president of the Tanganyika African Association, which under him turned to the pursuit of independence, and in 1954 he helped found TANU. Influenced by Gandhi, he preached non-violence and said that TANU was fighting colonialism, not the whites. Tanganyika gained independence on 9 December 1961, and six weeks later he resigned as prime minister to restructure TANU. It became a republic on 9 December 1962, with Nyerere as president.

After the Zanzibar Revolution Tanganyika united with Zanzibar as Tanzania in 1964. In January 1967 Nyerere presented the Arusha Declaration, committing the government to democratic socialism and self-reliance. Banks and major industries were nationalised and education and health care expanded. In the early 1970s villagisation moved about 13 million people into around 7,000 villages, and forced moves disrupted rural production; none of the villages had met productivity targets by 1978, and many depended on famine relief. His government also trained and aided movements fighting white-minority rule in southern Africa, and Tanzania's 1978–1979 war with Uganda overthrew Idi Amin.

Nyerere stepped down as president in 1985, succeeded by Ali Hassan Mwinyi, who reversed many of his policies. He remained chair of Chama Cha Mapinduzi until 1990. He died on 14 October 1999. Within Tanzania he is called the Father of the Nation.

Admirers praise him as an anti-colonialist and for keeping Tanzania stable and unified; critics point to his one-party state and detention without trial, and blame him for economic mismanagement. In the late 1990s he said he had made mistakes, particularly in pursuing nationalisation too early, but stood by the Arusha Declaration. In 2005 the Diocese of Musoma opened the cause for his canonisation, with the title Servant of God.
julius-sabinus: Julius Sabinus was a Roman officer, naturalised, as his name indicates. He claimed to be a great-grandson of Julius Caesar on the grounds that his great-grandmother had been Caesar's lover during the Gallic War. Taking advantage of the turmoil in Rome after the death of Nero and of the Batavian rebellion on the Rhine, he started a revolt in Belgian Gaul in 69, aiming to set up an independent Gaulish state.

His badly organised forces were easily defeated by the Sequani, who stayed faithful to Rome. Sabinus then told his servants that he intended to kill himself, burned down the villa in which he was staying and went into hiding in a nearby cellar known only to his wife Epponina and a few faithful servants. After the failure of the revolt the territory of the Lingones was detached from Belgian Gaul, placed under the direct supervision of the Roman army of the Rhine and made part of the province of Germania Superior.

Epponina lived for years as his supposed widow, once even visiting Rome with Sabinus disguised as a slave, and bore him two sons. According to Plutarch she concealed her pregnancies with an ointment that made her flesh swell, and gave birth alone and in secret. When the deception could no longer go unnoticed, the couple were arrested and taken to Rome to be questioned by Emperor Vespasian. He ignored her pleas, and when she berated him he ordered her execution along with her husband. Plutarch judged that no darker deed was committed in the whole of his reign.

Both sons survived; in Plutarch's time one lived in Delphi and the other had recently been killed in Egypt. The story, told for Epponina's loyalty, became popular in France, where the name Éponine stood for wifely virtue, patriotism and anti-imperialism. Michel-Paul-Gui de Chabanon's tragedy Éponine was performed in 1762 and was the basis of Sabinus, an opera by François-Joseph Gossec first staged at Versailles on 4 December 1773. De Lisle de Salles' novel Éponine led to his imprisonment during the Reign of Terror, and Victor Hugo gave the name to a character in Les Misérables.

Several paintings of the couple, among them works by Nicolas-André Monsiau and Etienne Barthélémy Garnier, usually show them hiding in a cave, a reference to a tradition that places Sabinus's refuge in a cave near Langres, still known locally as the Grotte de Sabinus.
july-crisis: At the Congress of Berlin in 1878 Austria-Hungary was given the right to occupy and administer Ottoman Bosnia and Herzegovina, and thirty years later it formally annexed the territory, upsetting the balance of power in the Balkans. On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir presumptive to the throne, toured Sarajevo with his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, after attending military exercises in Bosnia. Six armed irredentists, coordinated by Danilo Ilić, waited along the route, and Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist, shot them both.

Austria-Hungary's leaders wanted to inflict a military blow on Serbia, which they saw as a threat to the unity of their multi-national empire. Wary of Russia, Vienna sought a guarantee from Germany, and Count Hoyos travelled to Berlin on 5 July. Germany gave its support, later called the blank cheque, but urged a quick attack. On 7 July the Council of Joint Ministers agreed, with the Hungarian prime minister István Tisza alone opposing war, to present an ultimatum designed to be rejected. Meanwhile France and Russia met in St Petersburg between 20 and 23 July and reaffirmed their alliance.

The ultimatum was delivered on 23 July and gave Serbia only 48 hours. It demanded that Serbia condemn propaganda against Austria-Hungary, suppress hostile publications and dissolve the nationalist society Narodna Odbrana. Serbia mobilised on 24 July, Russia began a partial mobilisation, and Britain's foreign secretary Edward Grey offered mediation. After reading Serbia's reply, Emperor Wilhelm II remarked that every reason for war had disappeared, but Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia at 11:00 on 28 July. Russia ordered general mobilisation on 30 July.

Germany mobilised between 1 and 3 August, and most of the major European states were at war by early August. Britain, fearing that Germany might overrun France, declared war on 4 August and used the German invasion of Belgium to win popular support. By then the assassination had become a side-note to a larger European war. Historians debate the responsibility of each government. Samuel R. Williamson Jr. has emphasised the role of Austria-Hungary, which hoped for a limited war and expected German support to keep Russia out.
july-revolution: After the defeat of Napoleonic France in 1814, the Congress of Vienna restored the House of Bourbon in the person of Louis XVIII, and forced him to grant a constitution, the Charter of 1814. His brother Charles X, who succeeded him on 16 September 1824, was known for more reactionary politics. His popularity in Paris fell within months, over a law imposing the death penalty for profaning the Eucharist and over indemnities for property confiscated in the 1789 Revolution. On 17 March 1830 the Chamber of Deputies passed a motion of no confidence, the Address of the 221, against the ministry of Jules de Polignac. Elections held in July gave the liberal opposition a majority of 274 to 143.

The ordinances were published in Le Moniteur on 26 July. Members of the Paris Bourse refused to lend money, factory owners shut their workshops, and nearly 50 journalists met at the offices of Le National and signed a protest. On 27 July fighting began in the evening, when paving stones and roof tiles were thrown at soldiers; twenty-one civilians were killed before night.

On 28 July Charles X, remaining at Saint-Cloud, ordered Marshal Auguste Marmont to put down the unrest. Marmont's troops were too few and some line units were deserting. An opposition committee, including the banker Jacques Laffitte, petitioned for the withdrawal of the ordinances, but Polignac refused to see them. Marmont wrote to the King that it was no longer a riot but a revolution; Polignac advised resistance. By 29 July over 4,000 barricades had been built. The Louvre fell, the Tuileries Palace was sacked, and the Hôtel de Ville was taken by mid-afternoon. Looting was small, and the crowd protected the paintings of the Louvre.

Charles X and his son the Dauphin abdicated on 2 August. Charles had intended that his grandson, the Duke of Bordeaux, should reign as Henry V, but the provisional government placed Louis Philippe of the House of Orléans on the throne as a constitutional monarch. Supporters of the exiled senior Bourbon line became known as Legitimists. The July Column on the Place de la Bastille commemorates the revolution.

The example set off an uprising in Brussels in August that led to the Kingdom of Belgium. Revolutions in Italy and the November Uprising in Poland, inspired by it, failed. In 1832 Parisian republicans, disappointed with the outcome, rose in the June Rebellion, which was crushed within a week.
jumieges-abbey: In 654 Clovis II of Neustria, through the influence of his wife Balthild, gave forested land from royal holdings to Philibert, a former nobleman and courtier, who founded the abbey there; Balthild added gifts and pastures from the royal fisc. The house prospered under its second abbot, Aichardus, with around 900 monks. From 788 Charlemagne kept Tassilo III, the dethroned Agilolfing Duke of Bavaria, and his son Theodo under arrest there. In 841 the Vikings pillaged and burnt the abbey, and the community left first for the Abbey of Saint-Riquier and then for Haspres Abbey.

Under the dukes of Normandy the abbey gained greater security. William Longsword, the second duke, took a close interest in rebuilding it and asked for monks from Aquitaine: twelve came from the Abbey of Saint-Cyprien in Poitiers under their abbot Martin, and the community at Haspres was invited back. Longsword himself accompanied Martin from Rouen to Jumièges. On 5 April 942 the high altar of the restored church of Saint Peter was consecrated, and the abbey was rebuilt on a larger scale than before.

Jumièges became a centre of scholarship that educated the historian William of Jumièges. In 1015 William of Volpiano, abbot of Fecamp, introduced monastic reforms, and the abbey became a model for the monasteries of Normandy, known also for its relief of the poor. One of its abbots, Robert Champart, became Bishop of London in 1044 and later Archbishop of Canterbury under Edward the Confessor. The Romanesque church begun in 1040 was enlarged in 1256.

The abbey suffered in the English campaign in Normandy during the Hundred Years War and again in the French Wars of Religion; the church was restored in 1573, and the Maurists took the house over in 1649. When the monks were dispersed in the French Revolution, only the twin towers and western façade of the church and parts of the cloisters and library were left. Lord Stuart de Rothesay bought a gallery of the cloister to rebuild it at Highcliffe Castle near Bournemouth, and the library went to Rouen. The novelist Roger Martin du Gard wrote his dissertation on the ruins.
junagarh-fort: Rao Bika, a son of Rao Jodha of the Rathod clan, founded Bikaner in 1472 at a place then called Jungladesh, an oasis on the trade route between Central Asia and the Gujarat coast, and built a stone fort there in 1478. Raja Rai Singh, the sixth ruler, who reigned from 1571 to 1611, served the Mughal emperors Akbar and Jahangir as a general and used the revenue of his jagirs in Gujarat and Burhanpur to build a new stronghold about 1.5 kilometres from the city centre. Its foundation ceremony took place on 17 February 1589 and it was completed on 17 January 1594.

The fort was first called Chintamani. Rai Singh, who had won half of the kingdom of Mewar for the Mughals, was an expert in the arts and architecture, and the many monuments he built inside reflect what he had seen on his journeys. Remnants of Rao Bika's older fort survive near the Lakshmi Narayan temple.

The fort is a rectangle with a perimeter of 986 metres, walls 4.4 metres wide and 12 metres high, 37 bastions and seven gates, enclosing 5.28 hectares; its moat no longer exists. The entrance is Suraj Pol, of yellow sandstone, its doors studded with iron spikes against elephants. On the wall of Daulat Pol are forty-one red hand imprints of wives of Bikaner's rulers who committed sati.

Its palaces and Hindu and Jain temples are of red sandstone and marble. Each ruler built his own rooms: Karan Singh the Karan Mahal, Anup Singh the Anup Mahal and the zenana, Gaj Singh the refurbished Chandra Mahal, Dungar Singh the Badal Mahal with its painted rain clouds, and Ganga Singh the Ganga Mahal. The styles run from Rajput architecture with Gujarati and Mughal influence to semi-western and Rajput revival work.

The fort was the rulers' seat until 1902, when Ganga Singh moved to the new Lalgarh Palace and the old fort was renamed Junagarh. The Har Mandir served as the royal family's private temple, where the festivals of Dussera and Gangaur were held and weapons and horses were worshipped. In 1961 Maharaja Karni Singh founded the Junagarh Fort Museum, which shows Sanskrit and Persian manuscripts, miniature paintings, royal costumes, farmans, palanquins, arms and a First World War biplane.
junihitoe: Jūnihitoe is a common name applied later to women's layered court clothing of the Heian period rather than a formal name for the set, and the number of layers varied despite it. The formal set has been called itsutsuginu-karaginu-mo since the 19th century, after three of its parts: the itsutsuginu, a series of usually five differently coloured robes; the karaginu, a waist-length Chinese style jacket; and the mō, an apron-like train worn trailing down the back.

Beneath these lay the kosode, a short silk robe of red or white, and the nagabakama, a very long pleated red skirt sewn with split legs. Over the kosode came the hitoe, an unlined robe; the uchiginu, a scarlet beaten-silk robe that stiffened and supported the outer layers; and the uwagi, a patterned robe whose colour and fabric indicated the rank of the wearer. The obi was little more than a thin cord. On less formal occasions a shorter brocade robe, the kouchigi, took the place of the karaginu and mō.

The layers could be seen only at the sleeves, the hems and the neck. A Heian lady often sat hidden behind a sudare screen, with only the lower part of her body and her sleeve edges visible, so the arrangement of colours stood for the woman herself and showed an outsider her taste and rank. A combination called under the snow, for example, placed white over pink and green. It was fashionable to change one's robes just before the turn of each season.

Because of the weight, movement could be difficult, and ladies commonly slept in the innermost kosode and hakama. A painted fan of cypress slats, the hiōgi, served both to cool the wearer and to shield her from inquiring looks, since court women were not allowed to speak face to face with male outsiders. Suitors usually saw only the sleeves behind the blind, a practice described in the Tale of Genji. Sumptuary laws later reduced the number of robes worn.

Today the dress is mostly seen in museums, films, costume demonstrations and festivals such as the Saiō Matsuri in Meiwa, Mie, and the Aoi Matsuri in Kyoto. Empress Michiko wore it at the enthronement of Emperor Akihito in 1990, in a modified form from the Edo period rather than the Heian style, and the women of the imperial family wore it again at the enthronement of Emperor Naruhito in 2019, when the men wore the sokutai.
junipero-serra: Junípero Serra was born Miquel Josep Serra i Ferrer on 24 November 1713 in the village of Petra on Majorca. As a boy he worked the fields with his parents and attended the school of the Franciscan friary beside his home, where he learned Latin and Gregorian chant. On 14 September 1730 he entered the Franciscan Order at Palma and took the name Junípero. In 1749 he landed at Veracruz in New Spain and walked to Mexico City rather than ride, following the rule of Francis of Assisi. He then served in the Sierra Gorda missions among the Pame people. In 1752 the Inquisition in Mexico City appointed him its inquisitor for the region.

After the Spanish king expelled the Jesuits in 1767, Serra was made president of the missions of Baja California, heading fifteen friars. On 14 May 1769 he founded his first mission, at Velicatá, and on 1 July the Portolá and Serra party reached San Diego after trekking 900 miles from Loreto. On 16 July 1769 he founded Mission San Diego de Alcalá, where tensions with the Kumeyaay people made it hard to attract converts.

In 1770 he founded Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo, relocated in 1771 to Carmel, and he stayed there as president of the Alta California missions. Missions were also founded at San Antonio de Padua, San Gabriel Arcángel, San Luis Obispo, San Francisco de Asís, San Juan Capistrano and Santa Clara de Asís. He confirmed 5,309 people in his last years, and died of tuberculosis on 28 August 1784 at Mission San Carlos Borromeo.

Serra saw his purpose as saving the souls of Native Americans, and took a patriarchal attitude, writing that spiritual fathers punishing the Indians with blows was as old as the conquest of the Americas. Native American critics charged that he directed and approved of the torture and enslavement of Native people at missions that were religious and military installations. Others, among them members of the Juaneño Acjachemen and Ohlone peoples, supported his canonisation.

He was beatified by Pope John Paul II on 25 September 1988 and canonised by Pope Francis on 23 September 2015. In June 2020 activists toppled a replica of his statue in Golden Gate Park in San Francisco.
junkers: Junkers Flugzeug- und Motorenwerke AG, more commonly Junkers, was founded in Dessau in 1895 by Hugo Junkers, and at first made boilers and radiators. All Junkers diesel engines were two-stroke, opposed-piston designs, an arrangement Hugo Junkers invented in the early 1890s as an alternative to Nicholaus Otto's patented four-stroke engine, since it would run on low-grade fuels such as blast furnace waste gases. By 1896 his engines were generating electrical power in steelworks. During the First World War and after it the company became known for pioneering all-metal aircraft, beginning with the Junkers J 1 of 1915, the first full metal-structure aircraft.

The F 13, first flown on 25 June 1919, was the first all-metal airliner. The Treaty of Versailles initially forbade aircraft construction in Germany, and then allowed only civil designs. Junkers partly relocated to Fili, a western suburb of Moscow, and restarted aircraft manufacture in the Soviet Union in 1922. With the treaty restrictions ending in 1926, the W 33 and W 34 series sold widely and set records for duration, distance and altitude, and the four-engined G 38 was the largest landplane in the world when it entered service with Deutsche Luft Hansa. William Bushnell Stout in 1922 and Andrei Tupolev in 1924 adapted Junkers's corrugated duralumin airframe technology.

Around 1931 financial difficulties led to the collapse of the group of companies, and the shareholders pressed Hugo Junkers to leave. A plan to buy his engine patents into a new company, Junkers Motoren-Patentstelle GmbH, was formed in November 1932, but the collapse was solved instead by selling Junkers Thermo Technik GmbH to Robert Bosch GmbH. Hugo Junkers was removed by the Nazis in 1934, and during the Second World War the company produced planes for the German air force and piston and jet engines.

The company survived the Second World War, despite heavy bomb damage, and the founding of East Germany, and was reconstituted as Junkers GmbH. It merged into the MBB consortium through the Flugzeug-Union-Süd joint venture of Heinkel and Messerschmitt in 1958. Messerschmitt took control of the company in 1965 and absorbed it in 1967. In the 1950s and early 1960s Junkers GmbH did research on future aerospace transport, and in 1961 the Austrian engineer Eugen Sänger completed a design for an advanced orbital spacecraft there. The Junkers name disappeared in 1969.
junnar: Junnar stands at an average elevation of 689 metres, with the Kukadi River flowing to the north. On four hills around it are more than 220 individual rock-cut caves, which include the largest and longest cave excavations in India. The best known group is Lenyadri, about 30 mostly Buddhist caves 5 km north of the town. Cave 7 there is a Hindu temple of Ganesha, one of the Ashtavinayak, the eight prominent Ganesha shrines of Maharashtra.

The caves date from between the 1st and 3rd century CE, and the Ganesha shrine in Cave 7 is dated to the 1st century, though the date of its conversion to a Hindu shrine is unknown. In the numbered group Caves 6 and 14 are chaitya-grihas (chapels) and the rest are viharas, dwellings and cells for monks. All of them arise from Hinayana Buddhism.

Junnar has been an important trading and political centre for two thousand years, on the route that links the ports of the Konkan with the interior of the Deccan. Greco-Roman travellers of the first millennium mention it. Cave inscriptions at Manmodi show that the Indo-Scythian Western Satraps ruled here in the 2nd century CE, and Yavana donors left inscriptions of the same century at Lenyadri and Manmodi. One at Shivneri records a gift of two cisterns to the monks by a Yavana named Irila.

In the 1400s the Russian traveller Afanasy Nikitin spent two months at Junnar during the monsoon and described life in the area then ruled by the Bahamanis. After their state broke up, the breakaway Nizam Shahi state made Junnar its first capital in the 1490s, and the Nizam Shahi general Malik Ambar moved his capital there again in the early 1600s. Shahaji Raje Bhonsale, the father of Shivaji, worked for Malik Ambar early in his career.

Teak from the Junnar area was used extensively in building the Shaniwar Wada in Pune, completed in 1732 by Peshwa Bajirao I. The Saudagar Gumbaz, a 17th-century tomb with a double-storied facade, is on the list of Monuments of National Importance in Maharashtra. The census of 2001 recorded 24,740 inhabitants, and the government of Maharashtra declared Junnar the first tourism taluka in Pune district on 9 January 2018.
juno-beach: Juno was a 6-mile (9.7 km) stretch of shoreline between La Rivière and Saint-Aubin, taking in the villages of Courseulles and Bernières. It lay east of the British beach Gold and west of the British beach Sword. Taking it was the responsibility of the British Second Army, with the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division under Major-General Rod Keller landing as the assault force, carried and supported by a Royal Navy task force. The D-Day objectives were to cut the Caen-Bayeux road, seize Carpiquet airport west of Caen, and link the two British beaches on either flank.

The beach was defended by two battalions of the German 716th Infantry Division, with elements of the 21st Panzer Division held in reserve near Caen. Canadian training began in July 1943 and produced the amphibious Duplex Drive tanks among other techniques.

Heavy bombing by RAF Bomber Command through the night left the defences on Juno virtually intact. Rough seas delayed the first wave until 07:35, and the landings met heavy resistance. Assault companies of the Royal Winnipeg Rifles and the Queen's Own Rifles of Canada took heavy casualties in the opening minutes. The Queen's Own faced an 88 mm gun emplacement and machine-gun nests outside Bernières, where ten of the first eleven men from the first landing craft were killed or wounded. Infantry, artillery and armoured squadrons cleared most of the coastal defences within two hours.

Reserves began deploying at 08:30, but the 9th Brigade, landing from 11:40, found the beach so congested that most companies could not disembark at once. The push inland brought mixed results. The 7th Brigade made contact with the British 50th Division at Creully, while resistance at Saint-Aubin kept the Royal Marines from joining the British 3rd Division on Sword. When operations halted at 21:00, the Canadians had reached Objective Line Elm, about half way to their final objectives.

The 716th Division was scattered and practically wiped out, though the 21st Panzer Division had driven a temporary wedge between the British and Canadian 3rd Divisions. Of the 306 landing craft used on the run-in, 90 were lost or damaged. The Queen's Own Rifles lost 143 men, the most of any battalion, the Royal Winnipegs 128, the North Shore Regiment 125 and the Regina Rifles 108. Predictions had put casualties on Juno at about 2,000 men.

Although none of the final D-Day objectives was taken, some historians consider the assault on Juno, with Utah, the most strategically successful of the landings. The landing is commemorated at the Juno Beach Centre in Courseulles-sur-Mer.
jupiter-god: The name Iuppiter began as a vocative compound of an Old Latin form Iou and pater, father, and descends from a Proto-Italic phrase meaning sky father. Jupiter is thought to have originated as a sky god, and his Etruscan counterpart is usually taken to be Tinia. The Romans equated him with the Greek Zeus, and Latin literature and art adapted the myths of Zeus under his name. Georg Wissowa stressed that Jupiter is the one case among Indo-European religions in which the original sky god kept his name, identity and prerogatives.

His emblem was the thunderbolt and his main sacred animal the eagle, which became one of the commonest symbols of the Roman army; his sacred tree was the oak. As the sky god he was a divine witness to oaths, and the Romans saw in him the source of the auspices on which the relationship between the city and the gods rested. They believed that he granted them supremacy because they had honoured him more than any other people. The fetials, the college devoted to the religious side of foreign affairs, invoked Jupiter Lapis when a treaty was concluded.

He was served by the Flamen Dialis, the highest-ranking of fifteen flamines, and the augurs were considered the only official interpreters of his will. On the Ides of each month a white lamb was led along the Sacred Way to the Capitoline citadel and sacrificed to him, and more fixed holidays of the Republican calendar were devoted to Jupiter than to any other deity.

The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill was supposedly begun by Tarquinius Priscus, completed by the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, and inaugurated on 13 September 509 BCE, in the early days of the Republic. It was topped with a quadriga, a four-horse chariot, driven by Jupiter, and inside stood a large statue whose face was painted red on festival days. There Jupiter was worshipped with Juno and Minerva as the Capitoline Triad. The cult of Iuppiter Latiaris, practised on the Alban Mount, is the oldest known cult of the god.
juqu-mengxun: Juqu Mengxun was born in 368, when the region was ruled by Former Liang. His Lushuihu family was said to take its name from the office of left Juqu that its ancestors had held under the Xiongnu chanyus. He was known for his learning in history and military tactics, and to avoid the suspicion of the Former Qin governor Liang Xi and the Later Liang emperor Lü Guang he made a show of heavy drinking.

In 397 Lü Guang executed his uncles Juqu Luochou and Juqu Quzhou on false charges, and Juqu Mengxun raised the Lushuihu tribes in revolt. His cousin Juqu Nancheng persuaded Duan Ye, governor of Jiankang, to lead the rebels. Juqu Mengxun became a general and, from 399, one of Duan Ye's two prime ministers.

In 401, distrusted by Duan Ye, he tricked him into executing Juqu Nancheng, then used the killing to raise the people, took Zhangye, executed Duan Ye and took the title Duke of Zhangye. He was nominally a vassal of Later Qin while ruling independently, and fought Southern Liang and Western Liang for years. In 410 more than 10,000 households of Guzang surrendered to him, and in winter 412 he moved his capital there and took the title Prince of Hexi.

In 420 he lured the Western Liang ruler Li Xin into an attack on Zhangye and killed him in battle, then took Jiuquan, where he kept capable Western Liang officials such as Song Yao. When Li Xun held out at Dunhuang, he refused his surrender, took the city in 421 and slaughtered its people. He later submitted in turn to Jin, Liu Song and Northern Wei, and wore down Western Qin in repeated wars.

His heirs fared badly: Juqu Zhengde was killed fighting the Rouran in 423, and Juqu Xingguo was captured by Western Qin in 429. In 431 he sent his son Juqu Anzhou as a hostage to Northern Wei, whose emperor made him Prince of Liang. In old age he was described as cruel and arbitrary. When he fell ill in 433, his officials replaced his young heir Juqu Puti with the elder Juqu Mujian, who succeeded him on his death that year.
jura-mountains: The Jura range proper, the folded Jura, lies in France and Switzerland and mainly marks a long part of their border. To the northeast it continues as the Table Jura, which is not folded, through northern Switzerland and into the German states of Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria, and is crossed by the High Rhine. In France the range covers most of the Franche-Comté region and reaches its highest point at the Crêt de la Neige, at 1,720 metres, in the department of Ain. About 1,600 square kilometres of it are protected as the Jura Mountains Regional Natural Park.

The range is built of a sequence of geological folds, formed as the Alpine mountain building pushed northwards. Three bands date from the Lias, Dogger and Malm, the Early, Middle and Late Jurassic. The folds are young enough to show little erosion. The range separates the basins of the Rhine and the Rhône: the north and east drain to the Rhine through the Aare and the Ill, the west and south to the Rhône through the Doubs, the Saône and the Ain.

The name is first recorded as mons Iura in Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico, and the geographer Strabo gives a Greek form of it. Early Celtic scholars proposed that it was a Celtic word for mountains, but there are no clear cognates in the surviving Celtic languages, and its origin remains unclear. The range gave its name to the French department of Jura, the Swiss canton of Jura, the Jurassic period of the geological timescale and the Montes Jura on the Moon.

Much of the Swiss Jura had no historical association with early modern Switzerland and was incorporated into the Swiss Confederacy only in the 19th century. In the 20th century a separatist movement developed there, which led to the creation of the Canton of Jura in 1979. The Swiss Jura has been industrialised since the 18th century and became a major centre of watchmaking. High-lying towns such as La Chaux-de-Fonds, Le Locle and Sainte-Croix, known for its musical boxes, grew up there. In the French Jura the 11th-century Fort de Joux, near Pontarlier, was remodelled and strengthened by Vauban in 1690.

The range offers hiking, cycling and skiing, with signposted trails such as the 310-kilometre Jura ridgeway. Swiss attractions include the Creux du Van, the Chasseral, the Grottes de Vallorbe and the Taubenloch gorge. Le Locle and La Chaux-de-Fonds are together a UNESCO World Heritage Site for their watchmaking heritage.
jurchens: The Jurchens were a number of Tungusic-speaking peoples who lived in the part of north-eastern China known as Manchuria. They first entered Chinese records in 748, in the forests and river valleys of what is now divided between Heilongjiang Province and Russia's Primorsky Krai. Scholarship since the Qing period has traced their origin to the Mohe tribes, among them the Heishui or Blackwater Mohe, but this remains conjectural. They were culturally diverse, with groups living as hunter-gatherers, semi-nomadic pastoralists or settled farmers, and they generally lacked a central authority.

By the 11th century the Jurchens were vassals of the Khitan rulers of the Liao dynasty. Those near the Yalu River had been tributaries of Goryeo since the reign of Taejo of Goryeo, and they switched allegiance between Liao and Goryeo as it suited them, offering tribute to both courts for the material rewards it brought.

In 1115 Wanyan Aguda, chief of the Wanyan tribe, united the Jurchen tribes and declared himself emperor. The dynasty took the name Jin, meaning gold, after the Gold River of the Jurchen homeland. In 1120 he seized Shangjing, the northern capital of Liao. In the Jin–Song Wars the Jurchens overran most of northern China, captured the Northern Song capital Bianjing in 1127 and settled on a border with the Southern Song along the Huai River. Jurchens who settled in towns intermarried with other peoples, and the Jin rulers came to follow Confucian norms.

Under the Ming, Chinese officials sorted the Jurchens into three groups: the Jianzhou, the Haixi and the so-called Wild Jurchens. The Yongle Emperor found allies among them against the Mongols and set up 178 commanderies in Manchuria. From 1586 Nurhaci, a chieftain of the Jianzhou Jurchens, united the tribes over some 30 years. In 1635 his son Hong Taiji renamed his people the Manchus, a break from their past as Chinese vassals, and the dynasty founded the next year became the Qing.

Like the Khitans and Mongols, the Jurchens prized horsemanship, archery and hunting, and they used the title khan and the term beile for a powerful chief. Unlike the Mongols, most were sedentary farmers of grain and millet who also kept oxen, pigs, sheep and horses. They did not observe primogeniture, so any capable son or nephew could become leader. They practised shamanic rituals and revered a sky goddess, and under the Jin many turned to Buddhism. Wanyan Xiyin devised a Jurchen script in 1120, based on the Khitan script, but it died out soon after the Jin fell. Nurhaci's followers were organised into the Eight Banners and adopted a script based on Mongolian.
juri-vilms: Jüri Vilms was born on 13 March 1889 at Arkma in Kabala Parish, now part of Türi Parish, in the Governorate of Livonia. At Pärnu Gymnasium his high grades earned him free tuition, and from 1907 to 1911 he studied at the Faculty of Law of the University of Tartu, where he was elected chairman of the Estonian Students Association. In 1911 he began to practise as a lawyer, first as an associate and later in a firm of his own.

After the outbreak of the First World War Vilms joined the Estonian National Movement and published articles demanding autonomy for Estonia within the Russian Empire. He criticised Jaan Tõnisson, who sought only cultural autonomy, and Konstantin Päts, who saw political chances in working with the Baltic Germans. After the February Revolution he became a full-time politician, and Aleksander Looring called him the advocate of the Estonian people. With Heinrich Koppel, Otto Strandman and Jaan Raamot he prepared the legal texts for the reforms that created the Autonomous Governorate of Estonia, which became the basis of the Russian Provisional Government's decree of 30 March 1917. That year he founded the left-of-centre Estonian Labour Party, Eesti Tööerakond.

Empowered by the Maapäev, the Salvation Committee issued the Declaration of Independence amid the power vacuum left by the retreating Russian and advancing German armies. The Germans who occupied the country did not recognise Estonian independence, and the committee went underground. Vilms volunteered to go to Finland with funds and instructions for the Estonian missions working abroad to win diplomatic recognition, and on that journey he was captured and killed.

Estonia gained its independence after the German troops withdrew following the German Revolution, and the Estonian War of Independence ended with the Peace Treaty of Tartu. Vilms is remembered as the first Deputy Prime Minister of the Republic of Estonia. The writer Jaan Kross portrayed him in his historical novel Tabamatus, which has been translated into Swedish, Finnish and French.
jurji-zaydan: Jurji Zaydan was born in Beirut on 14 December 1861 to an Eastern Orthodox Christian family of limited means, which had probably come from the Hauran. His father owned a restaurant and, being illiterate, placed little value on schooling, so Zaydan left school after elementary education to help in the business.

He studied English at night classes and in 1881 was admitted to the Syrian Protestant College as a medical student. Samuel Smiles's Self-Help and the teaching of Cornelius Van Dyck shaped his belief that education was the key to a people's progress. In 1882 the dismissal of Professor E. Lewis for praising Charles Darwin brought student protests, and Zaydan was among those who left for Cairo.

In Egypt he spent a short time at the medical school and went with a British army expedition to the Sudan before turning to writing. He worked briefly as assistant editor of al-Muqtataf and travelled to London to research Arabic history in the British Museum. In 1890 he published a History of the World, cited as one of the first non-Islamic histories written in Arabic. He opened the publishing house Dar al-Hilal. In 1891 he married Maryam Matar and published his first historical novel, al-Mamluk al-Shariid, whose success let him give up teaching. In 1892 he began the magazine al-Hilal, which carried history, articles, news and serialised novels.

Zaydan wrote roughly a novel a year, usually in the summer, for serial publication in the autumn. Each began with a historical topic in Islamic history, which he read up thoroughly, and an outline built on fact, around which he placed a love story and a mystery between invented characters. His aim was to give ordinary Arabs an accurate sense of their own history in an accessible form, and he put accuracy before plot. He wrote 23 novels in all.

In 1910 the newly opened Egyptian University offered him a chair in Islamic history. He accepted reluctantly, aware of his unpopularity among conservative Muslims, and was dismissed before beginning after public outcry over his Christian origins and secular leanings. His secular History of the Islamic Civilization, published from 1901 to 1906, had been especially controversial. The episode embittered him, and he died unexpectedly on 21 July 1914.

Al-Hilal circulated in places as distant as Persia, India, Japan, Zanzibar and North and South America. His influence is traced in Taha Hussein, Naguib Mahfouz and Fadwa Tuqan, and he is considered one of the first thinkers to help formulate the theory of Arab nationalism. Several of his novels were translated into English in 2011 and 2012.
jury-trial: A jury trial is set apart from a bench trial, in which a judge or panel of judges makes all decisions. In ancient Athens the courts were made up of dikastai chosen by lot, up to 500 citizens in ordinary cases and 1,001 to 1,501 in capital cases, ruling by majority. Jurors voted in secret with ceramic disks whose axles were hollow or solid, held so as to hide which, and from Periclean times they were paid a day's wages for sitting.

In the Roman Republic and Empire judges were lay citizens rather than professionals. Roman law provided for the yearly selection of judices to resolve disputes, with a praetor performing many of the duties of a judge, and barred high officials, their relatives and those found guilty of serious crimes.

In the German lands, Hauenstein's charter of 1442 secured the right to be tried by 24 fellow equals, a Swabian ordinance of 1562 called for jurymen, and in Freiburg juries of 30 citizens and councillors sat. The modern jury trial came to the Rhenish provinces in 1798, usually with 12 citizens. In classical Islamic law, notaries certified the consistent testimony of three to twelve witnesses, a practice John Makdisi has compared with the jury trials of England under King Henry II.

In common law systems the jury finds the facts, the judge determines the law and usually sets the penalty. After the judicial reform of Alexander II, jurors in Russia had a third verdict besides guilty and not guilty: guilty, but not to be punished, since Alexander II believed that justice without morality was wrong. In France the jury sits with professional judges to decide guilt and then the penalty.

In 1665 a petit jury of twelve English and Portuguese jurors at Madras acquitted Ascentia Dawes of murdering her enslaved servant, and under Company rule in India the Crown Courts of the presidency towns used juries while the Company Courts outside them did not. In the Kuba Kingdom, in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, trial by jury arose independently before Europeans arrived in 1884. Other states gave juries up: Hungary used them from 1897 to 1919, Singapore and South Africa abolished them in 1969 and Malaysia in 1995, while Japan brought citizens into serious criminal trials as lay judges in 2009.
juscelino-kubitschek: Kubitschek was born on 12 September 1902 in Diamantina, Minas Gerais, into a poor family. His father, a travelling salesman, died when he was two, and his mother Júlia, a schoolteacher, raised him. He graduated in medicine in 1927 and later specialised in urology in Paris. He was elected a federal deputy in 1934 but lost the seat when the Estado Novo began in 1937. In 1940 he became mayor of Belo Horizonte, where he began his working relationship with the architect Oscar Niemeyer, and in 1950 he became governor of Minas Gerais.

Kubitschek campaigned in 1955 with the slogan of fifty years of progress in five and won the October election with 35.6 per cent of the vote, with João Goulart as his running mate. Opponents pressed to annul the result, and General Henrique Teixeira Lott led a military countercoup to secure his inauguration on 31 January 1956. His Goals Plan had 31 goals in six groups, with the construction of Brasília as the main one. Imported machinery was exempted from taxes where foreign capital was associated with national capital, and the motor industry grew. By the end of his term foreign debt had risen from 87 million to 297 million dollars, industrial production had grown by 80 per cent and inflation stood at 43 per cent.

Brasília had been envisaged in earlier constitutions, but planning began only in 1956. Lúcio Costa, Oscar Niemeyer and Roberto Burle Marx led the work, which started in February 1957 and brought some 30,000 workers to the savanna. The city was inaugurated by the target date of 21 April 1960. His government was often accused of corruption, particularly over the construction.

Kubitschek was elected senator for Goiás in 1961. After the military coup of 1964 he was accused of corruption and of communist support, his mandate was revoked and his political rights were suspended for ten years. He lived in voluntary exile in the United States and Europe, and returned to Brazil in March 1967. He died on 22 August 1976 in a car crash near Resende, and some 350,000 mourners attended his burial in Brasília, where he lies in the JK Memorial.
justicialist-party: Peronism took shape between November 1943 and October 1945, from an alliance of unions and two soldiers, Juan Domingo Perón and Domingo Mercante, who ran the National Labor Department, later raised to the level of Secretary of Labor and Social Security. Argentina was then governed by the military regime of the Revolution of 1943. In 1945 the American ambassador Spruille Braden helped organise an anti-Peronist movement against Perón and the labour laws. Perón resigned on 8 October 1945 after losing the support of officers at Campo de Mayo and was detained. Nine days later a large workers' mobilisation, Loyalty Day, forced the government to prepare his release and call elections, and that day is most often cited as the birth of Peronism.

The party was created in November 1946, ten months after Perón's election as president, under the name Single Revolutionary Party, later called the Peronist Party. It fused three parties formed in 1945 to support his candidacy: the Labor Party, the Radical Renovating Civic Union and the Independent Party. A Female Peronist Party led by Eva Perón followed the enactment of women's suffrage.

Perón nationalised public services, strategic industries and the farm export sector, enacted labour laws and social reforms, and increased public works. He raised taxes on the agrarian sector and promoted urbanisation, which won much of the working and lower classes but alienated the upper and middle classes. Censorship and repression grew, and after losing the support of the Catholic Church he was deposed by the Revolución Libertadora in 1955. All Peronist entities were then banned from elections, and civilian attempts to lift the ban from legislative and local elections in 1962 and 1965 ended in military coups.

In exile Perón chose the activist John William Cooke in 1956 to represent the movement, and Peronism moved gradually left under the influence of the Cuban Revolution and liberation theology. With Perón's encouragement Peronist youth formed revolutionary organisations such as the Montoneros and the People's Revolutionary Army. Perón governed again from 1973 to 1974, and his wife Isabel succeeded him. From the 1990s the party was divided, until 2020, between Kirchnerism, its left-wing populist main faction, and Federal Peronism, which lay on the centre and centre-right.

Until 1955 the party was, in the account of Lewinsky, created from above by agents of the State and extremely personalist. Its statutes of 1954 declared Perón the Supreme Leader, with authority to intervene in and replace local leaders, and banned party offices from displaying any photographs but his and Eva Perón's. Its main base has historically been the General Confederation of Labor. The historian Daniel James wrote that Perón was more a creature of the trade unions than they of him.
justin-ahomadegbe-tometin: Justin Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin was born on 16 January 1917 in Abomey, a direct descendant of the kings of Abomey. He attended the École William Ponty and the French West Africa School of Medicine in Dakar, served briefly in the French Army, reaching the rank of sergeant, and then took up dentistry, opening an office in Porto-Novo. Originally a member of the Dahomeyan Progressive Union, he founded the African People's Bloc in 1946 and was elected to the General Council soon afterwards. He criticised French rule and gained influence by allying with the trade unions, and in November 1956 he was elected mayor of Abomey.

In the territorial elections of 1959 his Dahomeyan Democratic Union won 162,179 votes but only 11 seats, against 37 for Sourou-Migan Apithy's party and 22 for Hubert Maga's. His supporters rioted so severely that French soldiers were called in, and Maga was chosen as a compromise prime minister on 22 May 1959.

After independence on 1 August 1960 Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin broke with the united front of the three parties and incited strikes and demonstrations. He was sentenced to five years for a plot to assassinate Maga, and the party was banned. Maga released the prisoners in November 1962. Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin served as president of the National Assembly from April 1959 to November 1960, and as prime minister and vice president from 1964 to 1965.

After a series of coups, the election of 28 March 1970 gave Maga 252,551 votes, Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin 200,091 and Apithy 186,332, with each winning his own region. The military leader Paul-Émile de Souza annulled the results from Atakora, and on 7 May 1970 the three leaders agreed on a Presidential Council whose chair rotated every two years. Maga chaired it first, and on 7 May 1972 handed power to Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin, the first non-military transfer of power in twelve years.

The council lost support over the expulsion of the Togolese opposition leader Noe Kutuklui in 1971 and the closing of a radical student union. On 26 October 1972 a coup led by Major Mathieu Kérékou overthrew it. The three men were held until 1981. Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin sat in parliament from 1991 to 1995, led his party until his death on 8 March 2002, and was given a state funeral.
justin-i: Justin was born to a peasant family in the hamlet of Bederiana near Naissus (modern Niš, Serbia), in the province of Dardania. He was of Thraco-Roman or Illyro-Roman descent and spoke Latin and only rudimentary Greek. According to legend he was a swineherd. As a young man he left Dardania with two companions to escape poverty and took refuge in Constantinople. Illiterate on arrival, he joined the newly formed palace guard, the excubitors, campaigned against the Isaurians and the Sassanian Persians, and rose to be comes excubitorum, commander of the palace guard, under Anastasius I Dicorus. He married Lupicina, whom Procopius described as a barbarian slave.

Anastasius died childless on the night of 8-9 July 518. Amantius, the chamberlain, backed Theocritus as successor and is said to have given Justin money to buy his support, but Justin used it for himself. He controlled a smaller but better group of soldiers and was proclaimed emperor in the Hippodrome. Amantius and Theocritus were executed nine days later. His wife took the name Euphemia, a sign of the couple's fervent Chalcedonian faith.

Justin was seen as an illiterate soldier with little knowledge of statecraft, and relied on advisers, above all his nephew Justinian, whom he adopted. Because Justin could not read or write, the palace made a wooden stencil spelling the Latin word LEGI, "I have read". On 28 March 519 Patriarch John II accepted the formula of Pope Hormisdas, ending the Acacian schism between Rome and Constantinople. Justin persecuted Miaphysites for his first three years, and in 523 issued a strict edict against Arianism.

He cultivated client states on the borders and avoided serious warfare until late in his reign. King Tzath of Lazica came to Constantinople in 521 or 522 to receive royal robes from him and to be baptised. In 526 an earthquake destroyed Antioch, with an estimated 250,000 deaths, and Justin sent money for relief and rebuilding.

Procopius wrote that Justin's mental faculties declined in old age. Justinian, consul in 521 and caesar in 525, took over more of policy, and Justin named him co-emperor and, on 1 April 527, his successor. Justin died on 1 August 527. His reign founded the Justinian dynasty, which included Justinian I and three later emperors. The Cilician city of Caesarea was renamed Justinopolis in his honour in 525.
justin-ii: Justin was a son of Vigilantia, the sister of Justinian I, and of Dulcidio. He married Sophia, the niece of Justinian's wife Theodora, possibly in the 540s. His early years are obscure, but under Justinian he served as curopalates at court. He is first attested in 552 and 553 as part of an embassy to Pope Vigilius, and in 562 and 563 he dealt with riots of the Blues and Greens in Constantinople. He built a network of supporters, and early on he was seen as an energetic and even well-liked man.

Justinian died childless on 14 November 565. Callinicus, the praepositus sacri cubiculi, claimed that Justinian had named Justin as heir on his deathbed, and modern historians suspect he may have invented it. The Excubitors blocked the palace entrances overnight, and the Patriarch John Scholasticus crowned Justin before the death of Justinian was announced. Justin repaid the treasury's debts, burned its bonds and remitted tax arrears back to 560, and he became consul on 1 January 566. In 569 he let provincial elites nominate their own governors. A rival, also named Justin, a son of Germanus, was assassinated in Alexandria soon after the accession.

Justin ended Justinian's practice of buying off potential enemies. Halting subsidies to the Avars upset the balance of power in the Pannonian Basin, and after the Avars and Lombards destroyed the Gepids, the Lombards moved west and invaded Italy in 568 under Alboin. They overran the Po Valley and in time much of the peninsula. Justin sought an alliance with the Turks, and a Turkic embassy arrived in Constantinople in 568. In 572 his refusal to pay tribute to the Persians, together with his overtures to the Turks, led to war. After two disastrous campaigns the Persians under Khosrow I overran Syria and captured Dara.

After 572 Justin suffered fits of insanity. John of Ephesus, whose Monophysite sect was persecuted under Justin, describes him behaving like a wild animal. Tiberius, commander of the Excubitors, directed the government with Sophia, who secured a one-year truce from Persia for 45,000 gold coins. In 574, at her suggestion, Justin made Tiberius Caesar and adopted him. As his condition worsened he became suicidal. Bladder stones led to a failed operation, and on 26 September 578 he made Tiberius Augustus. Justin died on 4 October 578.

Historians have judged his foreign policy unfavourably. Previte-Orton thought he lacked realism, and Warren Treadgold reports that contemporaries blamed his arrogance and parsimony for the disasters against the Persians. He was the last person to rule the entire Italian peninsula until Napoleon.
justinian-i: According to his contemporary Procopius, Justinian was born in the hamlet of Tauresium in the province of Dardania, near the city of Justiniana Prima that he later founded. Later scholarship places his birth around 482. Tauresium is most commonly identified with the archaeological site of Gradište, near the village of Taor southeast of Skopje in North Macedonia, though scholars debate the birthplace. From his uncle Justin he inherited ongoing hostilities with the Sasanian Empire.

Justinian reigned from 527 to 565 and pursued a restoration of the empire, partly realised. In 532 he concluded an Eternal Peace with Khosrau I at a cost of 11,000 pounds of gold. His generals Belisarius and Narses then conquered the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa and the Ostrogothic Kingdom, restoring Italy, Sicily and Dalmatia. The emperor himself never took part in campaigns.

The quaestor Tribonian oversaw the rewriting of Roman law. The first draft of the Codex Justinianeus appeared on 7 April 529, followed by the Digesta in 533, the Institutiones, a textbook, and the Novellae, new laws issued in Greek. In January 532 the Nika riots united the rival chariot-racing factions against him; he considered flight but stayed, apparently at the urging of his wife Theodora, and Belisarius and Mundus suppressed the revolt, in which Procopius says 30,000 unarmed civilians were killed. The destruction allowed him to rebuild the Hagia Sophia, completed on 26 December 537. In the early 550s two monks smuggled silkworm eggs from Central Asia.

Justinian grew isolated in his last years, and in the 560s he showed clemency to conspirators and pardoned Belisarius. He died in his sleep on the night of 14 November 565 and was succeeded by his nephew Justin II. Procopius, the main source, praised his buildings in one work and portrayed him as cruel and corrupt in the Secret History. The Corpus Juris Civilis is still the basis of civil law in many modern states, and many Eastern Christians regard him as a saint.
justinian-ii: Justinian II was the eldest son of Emperor Constantine IV and Anastasia. His father appointed him heir sometime after October 682, when his uncles Heraclius and Tiberius were deposed, and in 685, at sixteen, he became sole emperor. He was the last emperor of the Heraclian dynasty. His epithet Rhinotmetos, "the Slit-Nosed", recalls his mutilation after his first deposition.

The eastern provinces were stable when he ascended the throne. He raised the tribute paid by the Umayyad caliphs, regained control of part of Cyprus and in 688 signed a treaty with Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan that made Cyprus neutral ground with its tax revenue split. In 687 he removed 12,000 Christian Mardaites from Lebanon. In 688 and 689 he defeated the Slavs of Macedonia and entered Thessalonica, and he resettled the subdued Slavs in Anatolia as a force of 30,000 men. Most of them defected to the Arabs at the Battle of Sebastopolis, where Justinian was comprehensively defeated.

In 692 he convened the Quinisext Council at Constantinople. It highlighted differences between Eastern and Western practice, such as the marriage of priests, and he ordered Pope Sergius I arrested, but the militias of Rome and Ravenna sided with the pope. He created the theme of Hellas and tried to protect peasant freeholders against the aristocracy, but his taxes were unpopular. In 695 a rising led by Leontius, the strategos of Hellas, deposed him and cut off his nose, and he was exiled to Cherson in the Crimea.

In exile he gathered supporters, escaped and was received by Busir, khagan of the Khazars, who gave him his sister as a bride, whom he renamed Theodora. He then secured an army of 15,000 Bulgar and Slav horsemen from Tervel of Bulgaria, in return for a Caesar's crown and his daughter Anastasia's hand. In spring 705 he entered Constantinople through an unused water conduit and regained the throne on 21 August. His rivals Leontius and Tiberius III were executed, and his second reign was marked by war with Bulgaria and the Caliphate and by cruel suppression of opposition.

Cherson revolted under the exiled general Bardanes, who was proclaimed emperor as Philippicus, and Justinian was arrested and executed in November 711. His six-year-old son and co-emperor Tiberius was killed, ending the line of Heraclius. His coinage introduced the image of Christ and revived the loros, and he joined the office of consul to that of emperor.
justinus-kerner: Justinus Andreas Christian Kerner was born in Ludwigsburg, Württemberg, on 18 September 1786. After the classical schools of Ludwigsburg and Maulbronn he was apprenticed in a cloth factory, but in 1804 Professor Karl Philipp Conz helped him to enter the University of Tübingen. He studied medicine and kept company with Ludwig Uhland, Gustav Schwab and others, and he took his doctor's degree in 1808.

He settled as a physician in Wildbad, where he completed Reiseschatten von dem Schattenspieler Luchs (1811) and collaborated with Uhland and Schwab on the Poetischer Almanach for 1812 and the Deutscher Dichterwald of 1813. In 1815 he became district medical officer at Gaildorf, and in 1818 he moved to Weinsberg, where he lived for the rest of his life.

His house at the foot of Schloss Weibertreu, a gift of the townspeople, became a meeting place for writers, all of whom were made welcome. Gustav IV Adolf of Sweden came with a knapsack on his back, and the poets Christian Friedrich Alexander of Württemberg and Nikolaus Lenau were constant guests. In 1826 Friederike Hauffe, a forester's daughter from Prevorst and a somnambulist and clairvoyante, arrived; she is the subject of his Die Seherin von Prevorst (1829). His Gedichte appeared in 1826, followed by Der letzte Blütenstrauß (1852) and Winterblüten (1859).

His medical writings include Das Fettgift (1822), the first treatise on botulism, and a book on Wildbad and its healing waters. He also wrote on animal magnetism, a history of the siege of Weinsberg in 1525 (1820) and a memoir of his youth, Bilderbuch aus meiner Knabenzeit (1859).

Increasing blindness forced Kerner to retire from medical practice in 1851, and he lived at Weinsberg, tended by his daughters, until his death on 21 February 1862. He was buried beside his wife, who had died in 1854, under a stone with an inscription he had chosen: Friederike Kerner und ihr Justinus. The 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica judged him one of the most inspired poets of the Swabian school, with poems marked by deep melancholy and a leaning towards the supernatural balanced by a quaint humour. Robert Schumann set his poems in his Opus 35 of 1840, and the grape variety Kerner, bred in 1929, is named after him.
justo-jose-de-urquiza: Justo José de Urquiza y García was born in Entre Ríos on 18 October 1801, the son of José Narciso de Urquiza Álzaga, born in Castro Urdiales, Spain, and María Cándida García González, a Creole of Buenos Aires. Like many other nineteenth-century Argentine patriots he was a freemason.

He was governor of Entre Ríos while Juan Manuel de Rosas governed Buenos Aires with powers delegated by the other provinces. Rosas often offered his resignation as a political gesture, counting on its rejection. In 1851, resentful of the dominance of Buenos Aires, Urquiza accepted it and resumed for Entre Ríos the powers delegated to Rosas, and he demanded a national constitution.

Supported by Brazil and the Uruguayan liberals, Urquiza raised the Grand Army and forced Manuel Oribe to capitulate in October 1851, ending the siege of Montevideo. He defeated Rosas at the Battle of Caseros on 3 February 1852, and the provinces that had backed Rosas changed sides. In 1853 a constituent assembly adopted a constitution based chiefly on the ideas of Juan Bautista Alberdi, and Urquiza was elected president. He was inaugurated in March 1854, with Paraná as the provisional capital and the whole of Entre Ríos federalized.

His government encouraged public education and colonization, and agricultural colonies drew European immigrants; Urquiza founded Colonia San José in 1857. The Confederation lacked money, and a Law of Differential Duties in 1856 aimed to shift trade away from Buenos Aires, which had seceded. War broke out in 1859, and on 23 October Urquiza defeated Bartolomé Mitre at Cepeda, where the Buenos Aires army lost 2,000 prisoners. The Pact of San José de Flores, signed on 11 November, brought Buenos Aires back into the Confederation, though some federalists, among them Ricardo López Jordán, thought it too generous.

The settlement was short-lived, and in September 1861 Urquiza met Mitre's army again. The battle was indecisive, but Urquiza withdrew from the field and left the victory to Mitre. He retired to San José Palace in Entre Ríos, where he ruled until he was assassinated at the age of 69, together with his sons Justo and Waldino, by followers of his rival Ricardo López Jordán.

He supported a liberal constitution favouring economic liberalism, and some see him as a classical liberal. Streets and parks across Argentina bear his name, as does a commuter railway line in Buenos Aires, the Urquiza Line.
justo-rufino-barrios: Justo Rufino Barrios Auyón was born on 19 July 1835. He studied law in Guatemala City and became a lawyer in 1862. When revolt broke out in western Guatemala in 1867, where many wished to restore the former state of Los Altos, he joined the rebels in Quetzaltenango, proved a capable commander and rose to general. In July 1871 he and other generals issued the Plan for the Fatherland against the long-entrenched conservative government, which they soon overthrew; Miguel García Granados became president and Barrios commander of the armed forces, and he was elected president in 1873.

Barrios carried on García Granados's liberal reforms more aggressively. He expelled the regular clergy and confiscated their property, abolished compulsory tithes, made civil marriage the only official form, set up secular cemeteries and civil records, and closed the Pontifical University of San Carlos, putting a secular National University in its place. He brought the first telegraph lines and railways, rebuilt Guatemala City, created a new police force and set up free and compulsory elementary schools. A Congress pledged to his will enacted the constitution of 1879, under which he was re-elected for six years. He forced many opponents into exile and had numerous people imprisoned and tortured in the Central penitentiary he built.

Under Decree 170 communal Indian lands were sold off to army officers and German settlers in Verapaz. The Day Laborer regulations bound the native population to work on the coffee estates when owners required it, sent in batches by local authorities, and through forced advances kept labourers in debt and on the land.

On 28 February 1885 Barrios declared himself President of Central America. El Salvador's president, Rafael Zaldívar, withdrew from the union and sought Mexican help, and Porfirio Díaz sent troops to seize the disputed Soconusco. Barrios and his son, General Venancio Barrios, died at the Battle of Chalchuapa on 2 April 1885. The official account has him killed in action; other versions speak of a shot from his own side or a murder plot. His portrait is on the five quetzal note, and Puerto Barrios bears his name.
justus-moser: Justus Möser was born in Osnabrück on 14 December 1720. After studying law at the universities of Jena and Göttingen he settled in his native town as a lawyer and was soon appointed advocatus patriae, state attorney. From 1762 to 1768 he was justiciarius, chief justice, of the criminal court in Osnabrück, and in 1768 he became Geheimer Referendar, privy councillor of justice. For 20 years he was legal adviser to the lay Protestant bishop of Osnabrück, Prince Frederick, Duke of York and Albany, a son of George III of the United Kingdom and Queen Charlotte.

Möser's history of Osnabrück, published in 1768, with a second edition in 1780 and a third in 1819, stressed social and cultural themes and remains highly regarded. In his Patriotische Phantasien, which appeared from 1775 to 1786, he pleaded for a natural, organic development of the state in place of arbitrary laws imposed by the sovereign. He was also a poet, who published the tragedy Arminius in 1749, and wrote short stories, one of which, a witty letter from a lady to her chaplain on the terrors of idleness, was published in English.

He is generally seen as the founder of German conservatism. Jerry Muller has called him a precursor of modern conservatism whose views of capitalism would offend many later conservatives: for Möser the expansion of the market was mainly a threat, which with cameralism eroded the institutions he valued, and Muller contrasts him sharply with Adam Smith. He has also been seen as the German counterpart to Edmund Burke, and Knudsen sees him as a man of the Enlightenment.

Möser died in Osnabrück on 8 January 1794. His Vermischte Schriften appeared in 1797–1798, published by Christoph Friedrich Nicolai with a biography, and his collected works in ten volumes, the Sämtliche Werke, were edited by B.R. Abeken in 1842–1844; his daughter Jenny Voigts published his letters. Goethe wrote about him in his autobiography, and a statue of Möser by Drake was unveiled in Osnabrück in 1836.
justus-perthes: The founder, Johann Georg Justus Perthes, was born on 11 September 1749 in the Thuringian town of Rudolstadt, the son of a physician at the Schwarzburg court. From 1778 he worked as a bookseller in nearby Gotha, where in 1785 he founded the firm later known as Justus Perthes Geographische Anstalt Gotha. From that year it also issued the Almanach de Gotha, a statistical, historical and genealogical annual of the countries of the world in German and French, first published by Carl Wilhelm Ettinger in Gotha in 1763.

In 1814 his son Wilhelm Perthes, who had trained in the Hamburg publishing house of Justus's nephew Friedrich Christoph Perthes, joined the business. Justus Perthes died in Gotha on 2 May 1816, and Wilhelm took over the firm.

Wilhelm laid the foundation of the geographical branch for which the house became best known, publishing the Hand-Atlas of Adolf Stieler from 1817 to 1823. He engaged leading German geographers of the day, among them Heinrich Berghaus, Christian Gottlieb Reichard, who worked with Stieler on the atlas, Karl Spruner and Emil von Sydow.

The firm then passed to the founder's grandson Bernhardt Wilhelm Perthes, who worked with Bruno Hassenstein and with August Heinrich Petermann, under whose direction the periodical Petermanns Geographische Mitteilungen was first edited in 1855. In the next generation it was run by Bernhard Perthes, born after his father's death in 1857, who lived until 1919. In 1866 the house began the Geographisches Jahrbuch under the editorship of Ernst Behm, continued after his death in 1884 by Professor Hermann Wagner.
justus-von-liebig: Justus Liebig was born in Darmstadt in early May 1803, the son of a drysalter and hardware merchant who made paints and pigments. As a boy of 13 he lived through the year without a summer of 1816, a volcanic winter that destroyed crops and caused famine in Germany, an experience said to have shaped his later work. He studied at Bonn under Karl Wilhelm Gottlob Kastner and followed him to Erlangen. On 26 May 1824, aged 21 and recommended by Humboldt, he became professor extraordinarius at Giessen, and he received the full chair in chemistry on 7 December 1825.

The university Senate refused to host an institute for training pharmacists and manufacturers, so Liebig ran it privately from 1826. From 1825 to 1835 the laboratory occupied a guardroom of a disused barracks, about 38 square metres, where he could work with eight or nine students at a time. Students came from many German states, Britain and the United States, and the laboratory became a model for teaching practical chemistry.

In 1830 Liebig developed an apparatus, the Kaliapparat, for determining the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen content of organic substances, which made quantitative organic analysis routine. With Friedrich Wöhler he showed that the explosive silver fulminate and the harmless silver cyanate had the same composition, which led Berzelius to propose the idea of isomers, and in 1832 their work on the oil of bitter almonds supported the doctrine of compound radicals. He founded the Annalen der Chemie, which he edited from 1832.

His book Organic Chemistry in its Application to Agriculture and Physiology (1840) argued that chemistry could raise yields and lower costs, and attacked the humus theory of plant nutrition. He emphasised nitrogen and minerals as plant nutrients and popularised the law of the minimum. A formula for beef extract, published in 1847, led to Liebig's Extract of Meat Company at Fray Bentos in Uruguay, of which he became scientific director in 1865.

In 1852 Liebig accepted an appointment from King Maximilian II of Bavaria to the University of Munich and became the king's scientific adviser, and in 1858 perpetual president of the Royal Bavarian Academy of Sciences. He had received the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1840 and was made a Freiherr in 1845. He died in Munich in 1873 and is buried in the Alter Südfriedhof. The University of Giessen was renamed Justus-Liebig-Universität in 1946, and he is called the father of the fertilizer industry.
jutes: According to Bede, the Jutes were one of the three most powerful Germanic nations that came to Britain, along with the Angles and the Saxons. From them, he wrote, descended the people of Kent, of the Isle of Wight and those in the West Saxon province opposite the island. Historians have no consensus on their origins. Bede inferred a homeland on the Jutland peninsula, and one hypothesis holds that they left Jutland after a Danish invasion and moved to the Frisian coast. Analysis of grave goods, however, links east Kent, southern Hampshire and the Isle of Wight to northern Francia or Frisia more than to Jutland, and some sources seem to use the names Frisians and Jutes interchangeably.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, which historians regard as giving foundation legends, says that Hengist and Horsa came in 449 at Vortigern's invitation to help against the Picts and landed at Ebbsfleet; later settlers came from the Old Saxons, the Angles and the Jutes, who took Kent, the Isle of Wight and Hampshire. It names Wihtgar and Stuf as founders of the Isle of Wight and Port with his sons as founders of the Meonwara in southern Hampshire. Contemporary writing is scarce before the 7th century, and some archaeological findings challenge the Chronicle's early dates. The Jutes probably settled Kent first and spread from there.

In 676 King Æthelred of Mercia ravaged Kent and destroyed Rochester. In 681 Wulfhere of Mercia advanced into southern Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, which he gave to Æthelwealh of Sussex. In the 680s Cædwalla of Wessex conquered Sussex and the Jutish lands in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. Bede says he killed the island's king, Arwald, and tried to destroy its inhabitants and replace them with people from his own province, but that Jutes remained the majority there. The island was then permanently under West Saxon control and the Meonwara joined Wessex. Kent kept its independence.

Brooches and bracteates found in east Kent, the Isle of Wight and southern Hampshire show strong Frankish and North Sea influence from the mid-fifth to the late sixth century. Kent was culturally distinct east from west until the late 6th century, when west Kent adopted east Kent's material culture. The Frankish princess Bertha came to Kent around 580 to marry King Æthelberht, bringing a bishop, and Pope Gregory I sent Augustine in 597. The Isle of Wight was the last area of Anglo-Saxon England to be converted, in 686. The Jutes practised partible inheritance known as gavelkind, which was kept in Kent until its abolition in 1925.
jutland: The Jutland peninsula stretches from the Grenen spit in the north to the confluence of the Elbe and the Sude in the south-east, and it is bounded by the North Sea, the Skagerrak, the Kattegat and the Baltic Sea. Its land is flat, with comparatively steep hills in the east. West Jutland has open land, heaths, plains and peat bogs, while East Jutland is more fertile, with lakes and forests. As a cultural region, Jutland usually means only the Danish part, though the Eider, which was the southern border of Denmark and the cultural and linguistic boundary between the Nordic countries and Germany from about 850 to the 18th century, is sometimes taken as its limit. The peninsula is also called the Cimbric peninsula.

According to Ptolemy, Jutland or the Cimbric Chersonese was the home of Teutons, Cimbri and Charudes. Angles, Saxons and Jutes migrated to Britain from around 450. The Angles gave their name to England, and the kingdom of Kent is associated with Jutish origins, as Bede says and the archaeology of Kent supports. From the 5th century the pagan Danes began the Danevirke, a defensive wall inland from near present-day Schleswig, to protect themselves from invasion by the Frankish emperors.

The pagan Saxons inhabited the southernmost part of the peninsula until the Saxon Wars of 772 to 804, when Charlemagne subdued them and forced them to convert. The Abodrites, Wendish Slavs who had pledged allegiance to Charlemagne, were moved in to settle the area, which was later called Holstein. In medieval times the Law Code of Jutland, the Jyske Lov, governed the part north of the Eider, as well as Funen and Fehmarn.

The peninsula is divided among three Danish regions and the German states of Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg north of the Elbe and a small part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. The Kiel Canal crosses the south of the peninsula so that ships need not sail around it. Until industrialisation in the 19th century most people lived as farmers and fishers; the farmers of West Jutland were mostly free owners of their land, which was never feudalised. Jutlandic dialects differ substantially from standard Danish. The Battle of Jutland of 1916 was fought in the North Sea to the west of the peninsula.
juvenal-habyarimana: Juvénal Habyarimana was born on 8 March 1937 at Gisenyi, in Ruanda-Urundi, into a wealthy Hutu family. He studied at the College of Saint Paul in Bukavu in the Belgian Congo and in 1958 began medical studies at Lovanium University in Léopoldville. After the Rwandan Revolution began he left and entered the officer training school in Kigali, graduating with distinction in 1961. He married Agathe Kanziga in 1962. In June 1963 he became head of the Garde Nationale Rwandaise, and two years later he was made Minister of the National Guard and Police. He served in several security posts under President Grégoire Kayibanda, including minister of defence.

On 5 July 1973 Habyarimana, then army chief of staff and minister of defence, seized power in a coup against Kayibanda. In 1975 he created the Mouvement Révolutionnaire National pour le Développement as the only legal party. Government remained almost wholly in military hands until a new constitution was approved in 1978, when he was elected president as the only candidate. He was reelected in 1983 and 1988, again unopposed, with 98.99, 99.97 and 99.98 percent of the vote. Every citizen became a party member at birth, and the people took part in compulsory weekly labour called umuganda.

At first he won favour among Hutu and Tutsi alike, but he came to follow the policies of Kayibanda, and quotas again disadvantaged Tutsi in jobs and universities. His support shrank to the akazu, a circle of Hutu from the north-western provinces of Gisenyi and Ruhengeri. Under pressure from France, the IMF and the World Bank and from his own citizens, he allowed other parties in 1990. In October 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front, a force of Tutsi refugees who had served in the Ugandan army, invaded from Uganda. France sent troops to help him, and the war went on for three years until the Arusha Accords of 4 August 1993.

On 6 April 1994 his private jet was shot down near Kigali International Airport. President Cyprien Ntaryamira of Burundi, the Rwandan army's chief of staff and others died with him, and the plane crashed in the grounds of the presidential residence. The circumstances remain unclear. Hutu Power media blamed the Rwandan Patriotic Front, while the Front and others accused extremists in his own party of planning it to provoke anti-Tutsi anger and take power.

His death set off a genocide against the Tutsi and against Hutu who had opposed the government or backed the peace accords. Within 100 days between 491,000 and 800,000 Rwandans were killed. His family fled to France. His remains were kept by President Mobutu Sese Seko of Zaire in a private mausoleum at Gbadolite, and on 16 May 1997 they were burned at Kinshasa.
jyotirao-phule: Jyotirao Phule was born in Satara District in 1827 into the Mali caste, traditionally fruit and vegetable growers, placed in the Shudra category of the four-fold hierarchy. His family took the name Phule, "flower-man", after training as florists in Poona, and the Peshwa Baji Rao II granted them 35 acres of tax-free land. His mother died before he was one. After primary school his father withdrew him, but a man of the same caste persuaded the father to let him attend the Scottish Mission High School, and he finished his English schooling in 1847. In 1848 he was insulted at a Brahmin friend's wedding, which shaped his view of caste.

In 1848 Phule read Thomas Paine's Rights of Man, taught his wife Savitribai to read and write, and with her started the first indigenously run school for girls in Pune. The family and community ostracised the couple, and Usman Sheikh and his sister Fatima Sheikh gave them shelter. By 1852 three Phule schools taught 273 girls, but all had closed by 1858. In 1863 he started a home for pregnant widows and a centre to prevent infanticide. On 24 September 1873 he formed the Satyashodhak Samaj, which opposed idolatry and the caste system, and he published Gulamgiri (Slavery) that year.

In Gulamgiri Phule argued that Aryan conquerors had built the caste system to subjugate the indigenous people, and he took the mythical King Bali as a hero. He is credited with bringing the word Dalit into use for people outside the varna system. In 1882 he asked an education commission for compulsory primary education in villages. He was also a businessman and contractor, and served on the Poona municipal council from 1876 to 1883.

Phule received the title Mahatma in 1888, the year he suffered a stroke that left him paralysed, and he died in Pune in 1890, aged 63. B. R. Ambedkar acknowledged him as one of his three gurus. A postage stamp was issued in his honour in 1977, and the Mahatma Phule Museum in Pune, the Mahatma Phule Mandai market and a statue at the Maharashtra Vidhan Bhavan commemorate him.
